pdf_index.anonymized_output_policy: Store separately verified anonymized outputs under data_extra/anonymized/pdf; preserve every original file.
pdf_index.is_anonymized_semantics: True only when a verified anonymized PDF and completed receipt are linked by this index; false means no verified copy is linked.

C1.justification: v1 principally claims a sufficient upper bound and diffeomorphism approximation capability. v2's abstract and introduction additionally claim an exact geometric characterization of Leaky-ReLU minimum width and a sharp width of 4 for two-dimensional inputs and outputs.

C2.justification: Remark 21 newly explains sharpness when dy=2dx for Leaky-ReLU. Section 3.4 also qualifies the recovered n+m+alpha bounds as weaker than existing results for ReLU and other activations. The conclusion's broader interpretation and future-work discussion remain substantially unchanged.

D1.justification: Neither version supplies computational implementation settings, hardware information, or code/data access instructions. The added definitions and constructions concern mathematical proofs rather than an implemented experimental procedure.

E1.justification: Neither version uses datasets or training/evaluation tasks. The new two-dimensional function-space result is a theorem, not added empirical coverage.

E2.justification: Neither version evaluates baseline algorithms. The additional prior bounds in Table 1 are theoretical comparisons, not newly evaluated comparison methods.

E3.justification: Neither version reports an experimental protocol, data splits, training budgets, or empirical evaluation settings.

E4.justification: Neither version contains empirical ablations, robustness tests, or supplementary experimental analyses. v2's level-set robustness and winding-number arguments are mathematical proof components.

E5.justification: Repeated runs, seeds, uncertainty estimates, confidence intervals, and statistical tests are absent from both versions.

E6.justification: Table 1 retains the original upper-bound formulas but adds exact minimum width 4 for ReLU and Leaky-ReLU on C([0,1]^2, R^2), plus a lower bound of 4 for its stated broader activation class. Remark 21 additionally derives exact Leaky-ReLU width 2dx+1 when dy=2dx. These are substantial new analytical results, not measured performance gains.

M1.justification: Equation (4) changes the allowed layerwise Leaky-ReLU slopes from arbitrary real numbers in v1 to positive real numbers in v2, narrowing the defined model family to increasing activations. The underlying MLP architecture and approximation construction are retained.

P1.justification: The abstract and substantial portions of the introduction are rewritten around the geometric characterization. v2 adds an organization subsection and restructures Section 3 into characterization, upper-bound, and lower-bound arguments. It also converts notation prose into a list and moves references after the appendices.

P2.justification: The document changes throughout from a compact JMLR-style layout with running headers to an Elsevier preprint format, altering typography, spacing, headings, and equation layout. Table 1 is structurally expanded with a Kim et al. row and three additional author-result rows. Neither version contains figures.

R1.justification: v2 adds Li et al. (2023) and Kim et al. (2023), explicitly contrasting their reported bounds to motivate its research position. It also adds Bendich et al., Hatcher, and Munkres as foundations for the new topological analysis. This materially expands both positioning and theoretical connections.

T1.justification: v2 introduces the geometric quantity w(n,m), proves upper and lower relations to network width in Theorem 16 and Proposition 17, and obtains the Leaky-ReLU equality in Corollary 18. Section 3.5 and new Appendix A.4 supply the homology and winding-number proof of w(2,2)=4. v1's main upper bound survives as Theorem 20, while existing appendix arguments receive smaller revisions.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the theoretical contribution beyond v1's sufficient-width construction: Corollary 18 adds a necessity characterization, and Theorem 26 with Appendix A.4 supplies a detailed argument for a sharp two-dimensional result. These address optimality directly and clarify when bounds are tight. Projection-index inconsistencies in Theorem 16 and other editorial errors weaken precision, but the added theoretical support represents a substantial overall gain.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same author's minimum-width research. Their complete text, equations, Table 1, and appendices are readable, allowing retained material to be matched despite substantial expansion and reformatting.

after.justification: v2 remains theoretical, including the new topological argument in Appendix A.4. It reports no experimental, simulation, user-study, or data-analysis outcomes.

before.justification: v1 reports mathematical approximation theorems and proofs, including Appendix A.1–A.3. Table 1 summarizes theoretical bounds; no original empirical outcomes are reported.

results.title: Minimum Width for Deep, Narrow MLP: A Diffeomorphism Approach

C1.justification: v1 emphasizes density-guided OT recommendations, a market interpretation of modification cost, and CE desiderata. v2 makes population-dynamics modeling, explicit competition penalties, guarantees for an unbalanced relaxation, and comparative empirical effectiveness central contributions. The collective-recourse goal persists, but the claimed scientific contribution is substantially redefined.

C2.justification: The loan-intermediation and utility interpretations in v1 give way to resource scarcity and deviations from population equilibrium in v2. New qualifications address fixed resources, partial compliance, unmodeled strategic deviations, and application-specific competition weights. Causality changes from deferred work to a proposed connection through causal metrics, although full integration remains deferred.

D1.justification: Beyond v1's synthetic-data parameters and OT pseudocode, v2 documents CARLA usage, selected dataset features, baseline hyperparameters and VAE configurations in Table 1, and the new solvers' update rules. It also supplies a back-and-forth implementation link and promises experimental code after review; it does not establish that this code is already available.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates a two-dimensional Gaussian mixture with three prescribed classifier boundaries. Those simulations are replaced by Adult, COMPAS, HELOC, and Moons in v2, substantially expanding represented domains to real datasets. Recourse evaluation remains restricted to two selected features per dataset.

E2.justification: v1 compares classical nearest-point CE with balanced and unbalanced OT variants. v2 Figure 4 evaluates a substantially broader recourse comparator set: Wachter, Growing Spheres, CLUE, FOCUS, C-CHVAE, and ROAR. ROAR appears for Adult, COMPAS, and Moons, but is absent from the HELOC comparison.

E3.justification: v1 uses 100 synthetic samples, prescribed classifiers, and δ=0.2. v2 introduces 80/20 training/test splits, MLP or random-forest predictors, and 1,000 instances per class for the new benchmarks. Evaluation adds grid-based, weighted χ² competition cost and combined cost, replacing the earlier KL target-mismatch analysis. These are new experimental protocols, not comparable reruns of v1.

E4.justification: The central sensitivity question remains the tradeoff between modification cost and distribution matching. v1's KL-based λ2 sweeps over [0,1] and boundary-specific Gaussian examples are replaced by a χ²-based sweep over [0.01,0.3] in v2 Figure 5, alongside revised trajectory and recourse illustrations. This updates existing analysis questions without adding a distinct systematic robustness or component-ablation investigation.

E5.justification: v1 reports no repeated-run counts or uncertainty estimates. v2 reports 100 experiments with different random seeds, means and standard-deviation bars in Figure 4, and confidence intervals in Figure 5. This introduces uncertainty reporting across the empirical study; the confidence-interval level and construction are unspecified.

E6.justification: The Gaussian-mixture cost curves and transport results are replaced by new benchmark and visualization results. v2 Figure 4 reports the lowest competition and combined costs for CCE across the four datasets, while its modification cost is not lowest. These findings concern changed datasets, objectives, and protocols and therefore do not establish a same-setting performance improvement over v1.

M1.justification: v1 centers CCE on transport to a fixed δ-confidence distribution, with a KL-penalized unbalanced variant. v2 replaces this with a population-equilibrium objective penalizing χ² divergence from the positive-class distribution, incorporates partial compliance, and adds projected-gradient and entropy-based solvers. The path-guided and ordered-classifier formulations also change; the utility-based extension is removed.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, contribution list, and substantial portions of the methodological narrative are rewritten. The OT overview moves from main-text Section 2 to Appendix B, related work moves from Section 1.2 to Section 6, and computational exposition becomes a dedicated numerical-study section. The appendices are reorganized around definitions, background, population dynamics, proofs, algorithms, and experiments.

P2.justification: The Gaussian-density illustrations and simulation panels are replaced by redrawn Moons illustrations, a multi-dataset bar-chart comparison with error bars, a combined sensitivity/Adult figure, and HELOC/COMPAS recourse panels. v2 adds a baseline-hyperparameter table and removes the earlier notation table. These substantially redesign the visual presentation beyond numerical updates.

R1.justification: v2 retains the earlier distribution-aware and collective-CE comparisons but substantially expands positioning around group counterfactuals, strategic classification, externalities, and mean-field population dynamics. Section 6 adds several group-CE approaches and explicitly distinguishes social-welfare optimization from modeling strategic deviations. Novelty is repositioned around population dynamics.

T1.justification: v2 introduces a population-dynamics PDE, equilibrium and compliance assumptions, a measurable-selection lemma, the χ² mixture identity, and propositions on relaxed-plan existence, consistency, and computational complexity, with derivations and proofs in Appendices C–D. Several earlier CCE map guarantees and the utility-based derivation disappear. Much of the generic OT background is retained in Appendix B rather than newly introduced.

improvement.justification: v1 explicitly deferred real-data evaluation and formal externality modeling. v2 addresses both with an explicit population model and broader baseline comparisons, supported by 100-seed uncertainty reporting and implementation details. This substantially strengthens the paper's empirical support and transparency. Two-feature evaluation and deferred code release limit practical conclusions, and Appendix D.5 describes a normalization step absent from Algorithm 1, so the added technical material still needs reconciliation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same collective counterfactual explanation research, despite the changed title and substantial reformulation. Their main texts, equations, figures, algorithms, and appendices are available and readable, supporting reliable comparison.

after.justification: Section 5 and Appendix F report original experiments on Adult, COMPAS, HELOC, and Moons, including baseline comparisons, sensitivity results, and recourse visualizations.

before.justification: Section 5 and Appendix B.4 report original Gaussian-mixture simulations comparing classical CE with optimal-transport approaches, including regularization tradeoffs and transport trajectories.

results.title: Collective Counterfactual Explanations: Balancing Individual Goals and Collective Dynamics

C1.justification: The central claim that diffusion priors enable efficient contextual Thompson sampling, supported by exact linear-case inference and regret analysis, remains. v2 adds broader contribution claims for diffusion-prior posterior inference beyond bandits and presents dTS as online diffusion fine-tuning from implicit feedback (Introduction and Conclusion).

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive applicability limits concerning scarce or biased offline data, unstructured or purely online regimes, and unquantified approximation errors. It explicitly acknowledges that the linear-Gaussian theoretical setting does not require diffusion models. New interpretations explain the pretraining-depth tradeoff and the approximate posterior's retained diffusion structure (Sections 3.2–5.2 and Appendices D and H).

D1.justification: v2 adds a code-repository link and a pretraining recipe specifying JAX, a two-layer ReLU network, noise-prediction loss, Adam with learning rate 0.001, 20,000 epochs and batch size min(2048, sample size). It also describes MovieLens embedding construction and reports 30-CPU hardware (Appendices G.2 and J). These disclosures go substantially beyond v1's synthetic-generator settings.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates only diffusion-generated synthetic bandits. v2 adds Swiss-roll action distributions, semi-synthetic MovieLens recommendations, CIFAR-10 classification-derived bandits and mismatched-prior scenarios. Appendix G.4 also states that similar MNIST results were obtained, without displaying them.

E2.justification: The synthetic comparisons retain LinUCB, LinTS, HierTS, UCB-GLM and GLM-TS in their corresponding settings. v2 adds targeted comparisons against MCMC-Fast and MCMC-Slow on MovieLens (Table 2), plus an exact Gaussian posterior reference for approximation validation (Figure 5).

E3.justification: The main synthetic comparison adds the configuration d=5, K=100, L=2, and nonlinear-diffusion plots extend from 1,000 to 5,000 rounds. New protocols vary prior perturbations, pretraining sample sizes from 10 to 50,000, diffusion depth from 2 to 100 and CIFAR-10 offline-data fractions. v2 also introduces regret ratios, percentage improvements and timing comparisons.

E4.justification: Existing action-count, dimension, depth and reward-misspecification analyses are retained. v2 adds prior-perturbation robustness, pretraining-data and depth sensitivity, CIFAR-10 offline-data ablations, learned-distribution visualizations, posterior-quality checks against exact inference and MCMC, and numerical comparisons of regret bounds (Figures 2c–6 and Appendix G).

E5.justification: Both experimental sections specify 50 random simulations and average regret with standard errors. No changed run count, seed policy, confidence-interval procedure or significance-testing practice is reported.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial results for new configurations, datasets and analyses. Table 2 reports dTS regret improvements of 50.6% against MCMC-Fast and 12.7% against MCMC-Slow. Table 3 reports CIFAR-10 improvements with 1% offline data of 69.11% against HierTS and 87.74% against LinTS. These are newly reported comparisons, not same-setting gains over v1.

M1.justification: Remark 3.1 explicitly formulates a shared-parameter variant using action-dependent features, which Appendix G.4 applies to CIFAR-10; v1 only discusses this alternative setting when explaining dependence on K. The main hierarchical sampler, Gaussian likelihood approximation and nonlinear-link approximation remain substantively unchanged.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, method exposition and experimental narrative are extensively rewritten. The four linear/nonlinear method cases become a consolidated posterior-approximation presentation; formal theory moves to appendices while informal insights remain in the main text. Terminology and notation are revised, and the appendices are substantially reorganized.

P2.justification: The document changes from a two-column main text to a single-column layout. The graphical-model diagram is removed; v1 Figures 2 and 4 become an expanded comparison grid, while Figures 3 and 5 reappear as v2 Figures 2a and 2b. New empirical plots, distribution visualizations, a notation table and two result tables substantially change the presentation.

R1.justification: v2 adds relevant references including Kveton et al.'s diffusion-prior posterior sampling, diffusion inference, lower bounds and offline learning. It more explicitly attributes the fully linear precursor to Aouali (2023), previously mentioned as a preliminary workshop version. Most of Appendix A's positioning relative to hierarchical and structured bandits remains.

T1.justification: The main regret theorem, sparsity proposition and regret proofs survive as Theorem E.1, Proposition E.2 and Appendix F. However, v1 Appendix B's detailed action- and latent-posterior proofs, including Lemma B.3, are omitted. v2 retains the update formulas and refers their derivation to earlier work, removing a substantial self-contained mathematical component.

improvement.justification: Section 5.2 and Appendix G substantially address v1's main evidential gap: practical effectiveness was supported only on diffusion-generated synthetic problems. Learned-prior evaluations, robustness checks and approximation comparisons provide broader support, while implementation details and explicit applicability limits improve transparency. These gains outweigh reduced self-containment from omitted posterior proofs, although some new benchmark and MCMC settings remain sparsely documented.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same diffusion Thompson sampling work. Their text, equations, figures, tables and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison despite extensive reorganization.

after.justification: v2 reports original synthetic, Swiss-roll, MovieLens and CIFAR-10 experiments, including robustness and posterior-approximation evaluations in Section 5 and Appendix G.

before.justification: v1 reports original synthetic-bandit simulations, algorithm comparisons and parameter-scaling experiments in Section 5 and Appendix D.

results.title: Diffusion Models Meet Contextual Bandits

C1.justification: Question 1 is narrowed from approximating optimal utility for unit-demand buyers to approximating optimal welfare in the explicitly i.i.d. setting. The introduction now identifies generalization of Hartline and Roughgarden's identical-item results as the main contribution. The central constant-factor and tight logarithmic guarantees remain the same.

C2.justification: New Remarks 3–5 discuss how utility should improve with the number of items, why bidder heterogeneity can break favorites alignment, and why item copies need not provide a useful upper bound. The duality discussion changes its explanation from single-item versus multi-item problems to single-bidder versus multi-bidder problems. The main limitations concerning symmetry and welfare remain.

D1.justification: Neither version supplies implementation, hardware, runtime, code, or data-access information. v2 Definition 2 relocates and explains the single-item subroutine already specified in v1 Section 3.4; it does not disclose a new implementation procedure.

E1.justification: Neither version uses datasets or conducts training or empirical evaluation. The additional probability distributions in v2 are mathematical constructions for proofs, not added evaluation coverage.

E2.justification: Neither version empirically evaluates comparison methods. The replacement of Vickrey-Favorites by VCG in the copies-setting counterexample is a proof revision, assessed under T1.

E3.justification: Neither version contains experimental protocols, data splits, evaluation budgets, or testing procedures. The distributions and parameter regimes describe theoretical models.

E4.justification: Neither version reports ablations, empirical robustness tests, sensitivity experiments, or case studies. Changes to mathematical counterexamples and applicability arguments are covered under T1 and C2.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated experiments, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The new concentration-bound reasoning in v2 is theoretical analysis, not statistical uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: The explicit analytical guarantee for Prior-Free-Favorites changes from E[Welfare]/[2e(1+log(n/m+1))] in v1 Section 4.2 to OptWelfare/[17.8(1+log(n/m))] in v2 Section 3.3. The logarithmic asymptotic guarantee remains unchanged. This is a revised theoretical bound, not an empirical performance change.

M1.justification: Random-Favorites and Prior-Free-Favorites retain their procedures. However, v2 removes Iterative Random-Favorites, the explicitly defined multi-round variant proposed for future analysis in v1 Section 4.1.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, and contribution narrative are substantially rewritten. Main results move ahead of the general-complexity discussion, while mechanism motivation and definitions are regrouped with their analysis. This substantially changes the reading order and exposition beyond simply inserting new proofs.

P2.justification: Both PDFs retain the same single-column text-and-equation presentation and contain no figures or tables. Pagination changes follow the expanded and reorganized text rather than a substantive visual-layout redesign.

R1.justification: v2 emphasizes its relationship to Hartline and Roughgarden (2008), adds discussion of subsequent results by Ezra et al. (2024), and cites Lundy et al. (2024). The Ganesh and Hartline (2023) discussion and reference are removed. Most related-work coverage is retained.

T1.justification: v2 Sections 3.3–3.4 substantially revise the central proofs: Lemma 2 replaces the favorites-alignment argument, Lemma 3 addresses dependence between participation counts and maximum values, and Definition 3 with Lemmas 4–5 supplies an explicit tightness reduction for both n and m. v1 instead used a short Jensen argument and directly invoked an existing lower bound. The copies-setting proof also replaces Vickrey-Favorites with VCG and explicitly relaxes the constraint on allocating bidder copies.

improvement.justification: v1 invokes a lower bound without establishing its transfer from identical items to i.i.d. heterogeneous items and leaves dependence unaddressed in its short Jensen argument. v2 Sections 3.3.1 and 3.4 supply a dedicated dependence analysis and an explicit tightness construction with utility and welfare comparison lemmas. These substantially improve the completeness and checkability of the central argument, supported by clearer organization. The explicit approximation constant becomes more conservative, but the asymptotic guarantees are retained.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same utility-maximization research despite the changed title and organization. All 16 pages of v1 and 22 pages of v2 are readable, including equations, proofs, and references. Neither contains appendices, figures, or tables.

after.justification: v2 remains entirely theoretical. Its additional lemmas and tightness construction are mathematical results, not empirical outcomes.

before.justification: v1 reports theoretical guarantees and constructed mathematical counterexamples, but no original experimental, simulation, user-study, or data-analysis outcomes.

results.title:
Multidimensional Bayesian Utility Maximization: Tight Approximations to
  Welfare

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction replace the dimensionality-led motivation with central claims that gradient-estimation noise transfers poorly across batches and harms large weights more than small weights. Investigating this mechanism becomes an explicit contribution. The proposed method, inference-level memory claim, nine-point RTE improvement and 3.5-fold speedup claims remain.

C2.justification: v1 speculates that large weights are already well trained while smaller weights have more room for improvement. v2 instead interprets the new diagnostics through gradient noise, poor transfer between batches and greater noise resilience of small weights, linking selection to larger usable learning rates. The limitation concerning the gap to first-order fine-tuning remains.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code repository link, explicit percentile-based threshold instructions and Mistral hyperparameter and sparsity settings. However, it omits v1's explicit 20,000-step budget, evaluation every 100 steps and random 1,000-training/1,000-test sampling description. These are documentation changes, not evidence that the retained experiments used different procedures.

E1.justification: The original SST-2, RTE, BoolQ, WIC, MultiRC and COPA coverage remains. v2 Section 4.3 adds PIQA, SIQA and AQuA evaluations, substantially extending coverage into additional commonsense reasoning and mathematical reasoning.

E2.justification: v2 Table 1 adds LoRA and MeZO-LoRA to the LLaMA-7b comparison, and Table 4 adds LoRA memory measurements. The new LLaMA2 comparison in Table 2 evaluates ZO-SGD-Cons, ZO-SGD-Sign, ZO-SGD-Adam, ZO-AdaMU and AdaZeta alongside retained comparators.

E3.justification: v2 adds Mistral-7B-v0.1 and LLaMA2-7b evaluation configurations and a Mistral-specific hyperparameter grid. New diagnostic protocols split 32 examples into 16 gradient-estimation and 16 held-out examples, and resume training using the smallest or largest 20% of weights. These are additional experiments; the original LLaMA-7b search grid remains unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 adds learning-rate sensitivity, cross-batch loss-change measurements, small/large-weight recovery experiments and a MeZO-versus-SGD diagnostic (Figures 2 and 4). The four-task median-split comparison in v1 Figure 3 disappears. The retained sparsity analysis is narrowed, omitting the 0.75 and 0.85 settings shown in v1 Figure 6.

E5.justification: Both versions report three seeds. All original LLaMA-7b means and uncertainty values reappear unchanged in v2 Table 12, and the convergence plots retain their shaded bands. The nearby reference to LLaMA2 conflicts with Table 12's labels and retained values; it does not establish new uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: v2 adds extensive results, including LLaMA2 RTE accuracy of 77.6 for S-MeZO versus 70.2 for MeZO, and Mistral AQuA accuracy of 26.6 versus 24.0. Original core accuracy tables remain unchanged. Some shared sparsity scores change: WIC at 0.8 is approximately 64.1 in v1 Figure 6 versus 64.3 in v2 Table 10. Removed ablation settings also remove result entries.

M1.justification: Algorithms 1–3 retain the same sparse perturbation, small-weight selection, dynamic mask and parameter-update procedures. The forward-pass memory implementation is unchanged. Explicit percentile-threshold instructions and correction of the displayed gradient formula clarify the existing method rather than establish a changed algorithm.

P1.justification: The abstract, motivation and contribution narrative are substantially rewritten around gradient noise. Preliminaries are condensed, the method exposition is reorganized, and convergence theory, helper algorithms and OPT results move to expanded back matter. This constitutes substantial restructuring beyond inserting new experiments.

P2.justification: The main text changes from two columns to a single-column layout. v1's two implementation diagrams and median-split bar chart disappear; v2 introduces diagnostic plots and several new or expanded tables. The sparsity plot becomes a reduced table, while the original uncertainty table and OPT table move to the appendices.

R1.justification: v2 expands positioning around contemporary MeZO variants, Wanda/SparseGPT pruning and dynamic sparse training, while dropping several classic pruning references. It removes the earlier distinction that related sparse zeroth-order methods primarily train from scratch. Sections 13 and 15 newly attribute the convergence analysis and a proof bound specifically to Ohta et al. (2020).

T1.justification: The assumptions, lemmas, convergence theorem and proofs are largely retained in v2 Sections 13–16. v2 restores the missing z_hat multiplier in the main gradient definition. It also changes the bound factor from 4(d_hat+4) to 4(d_hat+4)^2 (v1 Equation 24; v2 Equation 23), but leaves the following step-size substitution unchanged, so the proof remains inconsistent.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens practical validation: LoRA accuracy and memory comparisons and newer zeroth-order baselines address important omissions in v1, while additional model families and reasoning tasks test applicability beyond the original evaluations. New diagnostics also investigate the weight-selection rationale. Missing training details, reduced sparsity coverage and the unresolved proof inconsistency limit reproducibility and rigor, but the stronger comparative evidence provides a clear substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Sparse-MeZO with the same authors, algorithm and substantial shared results. All 17 pages of v1 and 24 pages of v2, including figures, equations and appendices, support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds LLaMA2 and Mistral evaluations, reasoning tasks, additional baselines and gradient-noise diagnostics.

before.justification: v1 reports original fine-tuning accuracy, convergence, memory measurements and sparsity experiments on LLaMA and OPT.

results.title: Sparse MeZO: Less Parameters for Better Performance in Zeroth-Order LLM Fine-Tuning

C1.justification: V2's main chordal theorem explicitly claims polynomial dependence on alphabet size k for fixed indegree, extending v1's fixed-k technical guarantees. Its headline tree theorem changes from an agnostic (ε,3)-approximation to realizable learning. Semi-agnostic learning remains in the detailed results with factor 4, although the new conclusion inconsistently retains factor 3.

C2.justification: V2 adds substantive qualifications about obtaining the required known skeleton, explains the dependence on indegree, and distinguishes MLE's proper-learning guarantees from EWA's realizable improper-learning advantage. It also explicitly limits the contamination comparison to cases with small KL contamination. These refine applicability and interpretation within the existing framework.

D1.justification: V2 specifies the preliminary sample batch and passes it explicitly through revised chordal-learning pseudocode. Remark 2.3 and Section 9.3 add operation counts and sample-pass details for computing conditional distributions and edge weights. Neither version supplies an executable implementation or empirical resource information.

E1.justification: Neither version uses datasets or executes evaluation tasks. Trees, chordal graphs, and bounded-vertex-cover graphs are theoretical learning classes, not experimentally evaluated coverage.

E2.justification: Neither version experimentally evaluates comparison methods. V2's new Table 2 compares guarantees and assumptions of prior work; it is not a baseline experiment.

E3.justification: Neither version reports an experimental evaluation protocol. Revised sample allocations and algorithm parameters concern the proposed learning procedures and theoretical guarantees.

E4.justification: Neither version contains empirical ablations, sensitivity tests, robustness experiments, or case studies. The contamination discussion and supplementary proofs are theoretical.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated experimental runs, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. PAC success probabilities and concentration arguments are theoretical guarantees, not experimental uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Neither PDF reports measured performance, experimental runtimes, or empirical qualitative findings. Changes to sample-complexity bounds and approximation factors are formal results assessed under T1.

M1.justification: V1 constructs experts through clipping and bucketing conditional probabilities, then samples both structures and conditional distributions. V2 instead estimates one add-one distribution per DAG using a separate sample batch, substantially changing expert construction and subsequent sampling. Section 12 also introduces a maximum-likelihood adaptation of the dynamic programs.

P1.justification: V2 rewrites the abstract and introductory narrative, promotes results, techniques, related work, and open problems into separate sections, and presents chordal learning before tree learning. It integrates the former appendices into the numbered body and adds a concluding Discussion section. This is substantial reorganization beyond renumbering.

P2.justification: New Tables 1 and 2 consolidate sample-complexity regimes and comparisons with prior work. V2 redisplays learning pseudocode in the techniques overview and reformats technical algorithm blocks. V1's vertically stacked chordal illustrations become a horizontal Figure 2 with a combined caption; Figure 1 retains its content but changes caption placement.

R1.justification: V1 claims that learning high-dimensional distributions through online learning had not been reported previously. V2 Section 4 acknowledges earlier approaches by Catoni, Yang, and van der Hoeven et al., positioning its contribution around computational efficiency for structured distributions. Additional KL-learning, density-estimation, and MLE literature substantially expands and corrects the research positioning.

T1.justification: V1's clipping/bucketing cover analysis is replaced by a uniform add-one estimation guarantee in Theorem 7.8. For fixed d, proper agnostic complexity changes from ~O(n^3 k^(d+1)/(ε^2 δ^2)) in v1 Theorem 3.13 to ~O(n^3/(ε^2 δ^2) + nk^(d+1)/ε) in v2 Theorem 7.12. Improper, tree, and vertex-cover bounds also change. The semi-agnostic approximation factor becomes 4 instead of 3. Section 12 adds MLE reasoning; the former lower-bound appendix is retained.

improvement.justification: The add-one construction and its analysis address an important restriction: v1's detailed sampler is efficient only for constant alphabet size, whereas v2 supports polynomial dependence on k and substantially tighter agnostic bounds. V2 also corrects its broad novelty claim. These gains outweigh the weaker approximation factor, although summary inconsistencies remain: Section 2 overstates the near-optimal agnostic guarantee, and Section 13 still claims factor 3 instead of the theorems' factor 4.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work and provide readable text, mathematics, diagrams, and algorithms. V1's Appendices A, B, and C correspond to v2's Sections 10, 11, and 9.3, respectively; their relocation does not represent missing material.

after.justification: V2 remains theoretical. Its new maximum-likelihood section describes an algorithmic approach and guarantees, without reporting an executed experiment or empirical outcomes.

before.justification: V1 presents algorithms, sample-complexity guarantees, and proofs, including its appendices, but no original experimental, simulation, or data-analysis outcomes.

results.title: Distribution Learning Meets Graph Structure Sampling

C1.justification: The introduction adds non-uniform differential privacy and guarantees depending on average rather than maximum delta as a central contribution. This substantially expands the claimed theoretical contribution, while retaining the original claims about growing-data generalization, adaptive scheduling and square-root query dependence.

C2.justification: Appendix C.2 newly explains that the fully adaptive privacy filter cannot exploit non-uniform accounting and therefore retains looser uniform guarantees. Section 4.2 also explains the substantial initial dataset and clarifies that optimized privacy parameters can vary across plotted points. The existing i.i.d. and worst-case limitations remain.

D1.justification: v2 explicitly describes per-point numerical optimization and reports typical values of sigma approximately 0.008, beta approximately 10^-5 and epsilon approximately 0.04. Appendix C.3 makes baseline construction explicit, and Appendix D describes binary search for the conversion parameter. These improve documentation without establishing that the existing optimization procedure changed.

E1.justification: Both versions numerically evaluate statistical-query guarantees for growing i.i.d. data, retaining fixed-growth-ratio, fixed-initial-size and batching scenarios. No dataset, application domain or distinct task is added; the new fixed-query evaluation changes settings and reported metrics.

E2.justification: Split, JLNRSS and JLNRSS+ remain evaluated. The later comparisons distinguish Ours-N from Ours-U, the uniform counterpart of v1's Ours, providing an additional comparison variant. JLNRSS+ also uses the revised privacy-conversion expression.

E3.justification: New Figure 5 fixes k = 10,000 and evaluates error tolerance across dataset sizes at 95% coverage, whereas earlier plots primarily fix error tolerance and evaluate query capacity. Section 4.2 also corrects n0 = 3n to n0 = n/3; both versions' captions already specify growth ratio three, so this does not establish an actual change of experimental data.

E4.justification: Comparing Ours-N with Ours-U adds an analysis of the benefit of non-uniform privacy accounting, including within the retained growth and batch-count sweeps. Those sensitivity studies already existed in v1; they are extended rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: Both versions use theoretical coverage guarantees, including 95% coverage in the numerical comparisons, without repeated-run statistics, empirical error bars or significance tests. The new confidence-width plot evaluates the existing uncertainty guarantee rather than introducing a new uncertainty-estimation practice.

E6.justification: v2 adds non-uniform-bound curves and fixed-query confidence-width results, and materially revises existing baseline curves. At n = 1,500,000, growth ratio three and five batches, JLNRSS+ lies below Split in v1 Figure 2 but above it in v2 Figure 3 under the same stated error and coverage targets. These are revised numerical guarantees, not measured query-answering accuracy gains.

M1.justification: Algorithms 1 and 2, the Gaussian response rule and clipping procedure are unchanged. Non-uniform privacy revises the accounting analysis and guarantees; it does not introduce a different query-answering or privacy-filter algorithm.

P1.justification: The introduction and stability definitions receive explanatory rewrites, and minimization-query definitions, theorem and proof are consolidated in Appendix A. Results gain section-based numbering, while the six main sections and much of the existing narrative remain intact.

P2.justification: v2 expands the visual exposition with a new interaction schematic and a new four-panel confidence-width figure. It also redraws the theorem-dependency diagram and revises the numerical displays with separate uniform/non-uniform curves, changed legends and scales, and a reorganized appendix figure layout.

R1.justification: v2 adds connections to personalized privacy and concurrent work on concentrated queries with correlated data, together with supporting privacy references. The central positioning against static-data adaptive analysis remains. Publication updates to retained references are not new cited works.

T1.justification: Uniform privacy is generalized to per-record delta(t), with transfer bounds depending on its sum and corresponding proof revisions. New Appendix D develops non-uniform DP and zCDP definitions, composition, post-processing and conversion results; Appendix C.3 derives the batched JLNRSS bound. Conversely, the Gaussian corollaries now assume constant noise rather than the earlier round-dependent scaling.

improvement.justification: The non-uniform extension addresses the conservatism of v1's uniform privacy aggregation and strengthens the paper's central guarantees, with supporting derivations in Appendix D and explicit uniform/non-uniform comparisons. The baseline derivation and optimization disclosures also make the numerical evidence more assessable. Constant-noise specialization narrows the Gaussian corollaries, and fully adaptive filtering remains uniform, but these limitations do not outweigh the substantial theoretical and explanatory gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same growing-data adaptive analysis framework. Their main text, equations, figures and appendices are readable, and corresponding results can be matched across renumbering and relocation.

after.justification: Section 4.2 and Appendix E report original numerical comparisons of uniform and non-uniform guarantees, including query capacities and confidence widths (Figures 3–6). The paper explicitly states that simulation is unnecessary.

before.justification: Section 4.2 and Appendix D report original numerical evaluations comparing query-capacity guarantees across dataset sizes and batching settings (Figures 2–4). These evaluate theoretical bounds rather than simulated datasets.

results.title: Adaptive Data Analysis for Growing Data

C1.justification: The central contributions—localizing safety neurons, explaining alignment tax and constructing a safeguard—remain. v2 adds a headline claim that ablation-selected neurons are ineffective in its verification setting and broadens capability-preservation language from general language modeling to general ability. These refine the contribution claims without replacing the central research thesis.

C2.justification: v2 extends the alignment-tax interpretation to competition during joint training, attributes some safeguard predictiveness to neuron layer distribution, and introduces Hydra-effect compensation as a possible weakness of ablation approaches. Appendix D.1 revises its explanation of the preferred model comparison. The principal limitations are retained and moved to Appendix F.

D1.justification: v2 adds patching pseudocode, explicit (IA)3 implementation, Qwen2.5 dimensions, baseline-selection details and benchmark-specific evaluation instructions. Its abstract supplies a repository address described as available, replacing v1's promise of future release; availability was not externally verified. Existing core training hyperparameters, hardware and reported runtime remain.

E1.justification: v2 adds direct capability evaluation on MMLU, GSM8K, BBH and TruthfulQA, substantially extending v1's Wikitext-2 perplexity assessment to knowledge, mathematics, reasoning and truthfulness. The original red-teaming and preference-learning datasets remain. Appendix B.3 also documents circuit-breakers training data used for the SN-Tune baseline.

E2.justification: v2 adds evaluated Pruning and SN-Tune localization baselines, called Param and Neuron in Table 8, beyond v1's random-neuron controls. Safeguard comparisons add unrestricted RN-All and remove the Majority classifier. Matched-layer and last-layer random controls remain under revised names.

E3.justification: v2 introduces normalized causal-effect evaluation, changes principal patching budgets from 20,000 neurons to 5%, and adds Qwen2.5-3B. Alignment-tax interventions select shared neurons using Safety/SHP rather than Harmless/Helpful. Safeguard evaluation changes from Beavertails-trained testing to averaging training-on-one/testing-on-pooled-others combinations. Appendix B.2 specifies new prompting, sampling and scoring protocols for the added capability benchmarks.

E4.justification: v2 adds causal comparisons across preference-neuron sets (Figure 3b) and a joint helpfulness/harmlessness training intervention (Appendix E.4, Table 10). Expanded safeguard sensitivity analysis tests whether layer distribution explains predictiveness. Existing model, prompt and token-position ablations remain, but their detailed cross-benchmark tables from v1 Tables 9–10 are omitted.

E5.justification: v2 Figure 2 reports confidence bands for random-neuron curves as well as safety-neuron curves. v1 Figure 2 lacked these bands, while Figure 3 reported intervals for safety neurons. Five training trials, 95% confidence intervals, five random draws for classifier comparisons and the t-test remain; no increased repetition count is documented.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial baseline, Qwen2.5, capability and joint-training results and revises patched-model scores. For example, patched Llama2 Base's Beavertails cost changes from -7.2 in v1 Table 1 to -5.7 in v2 Table 8 under the revised neuron budget. Safeguard accuracy changes from 79.4% to 76.2% under different validation protocols, so this is not a same-setting decline.

M1.justification: The activation-difference scoring, dynamic patching and logistic-regression detector remain unchanged; generation-time is renamed inference-time. A limited proposed inference extension appears in v2 Section 6: flagged prompts may continue with a refusal prefix, whereas v1 describes rejecting output. The reported safeguard evaluation still scores accepted responses.

P1.justification: Beyond the new title and terminology, v2 substantially rewrites the introduction into a framework explanation and contribution bullets, separates Preliminaries from the introduction, integrates the former workflow discussion elsewhere, and rewrites related work. Limitations move to an appendix, and ethical considerations become a shorter Broader Impacts section.

P2.justification: v2 switches to a single-column layout, redraws Figure 1, combines sparsity/stability and safeguard displays, and changes plot axes to neuron percentages and causal effects. Results are reorganized into a colored comparison table and expanded appendix table. Token projections are split between main text and appendix, and new alignment-tax displays are added.

R1.justification: v2 substantially recasts related work around neuron-level interpretability and safety mechanisms, distinguishing representation engineering from mechanistic interpretability. It positions activation enhancement against pruning, ablation, attention-head and safety-layer approaches, adding substantive discussion of Wei, Zhao, Zhou, Li, Arditi and McGrath, among others. The earlier general preference-learning discussion is removed.

T1.justification: v2 Equation 4 introduces an explicit normalized causal-effect definition and explains its zero and unit reference values. The original activation-difference formula and component-preservation assumption remain. No theorem or proof is added; Equation 5 mainly formalizes the already-described (IA)3 implementation.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens tests of the central claims through evaluated localization alternatives, capability assessments beyond perplexity, and additional causal alignment-tax controls. Expanded implementation and code-access information also improves reproducibility. These gains outweigh the loss of detailed safeguard and ablation tables. A material weakness remains: the abstract overstates capability preservation, since v2 Table 8 shows effects such as Mistral Base's GSM8K accuracy falling from 0.285 to 0.125 after patching.

A1.justification: Both complete PDFs, including their appendices, are readable and describe the same safety-neuron study. Methods, experiments and displays can be matched despite the changed title, structure and layout.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds Qwen2.5 experiments, evaluated localization baselines, general-capability benchmarks and joint-alignment analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original experiments on three LLMs, including neuron patching, training-seed stability, alignment-tax interventions and safeguard classification.

results.title: Towards Understanding Safety Alignment: A Mechanistic Perspective from Safety Neurons

C1.justification: The abstract, introductory contribution list, and conclusion retain the central claim: SVDD optimizes rewards in continuous and discrete pretrained diffusion models without differentiable proxy models or generative-model fine-tuning. Naming docking objectives in v4 makes the empirical support more specific without replacing this central contribution.

C2.justification: v4 adds substantial explanations of SMC diversity loss, batch-size dependence, parallelization, and approximation-error propagation. It replaces v1's categorical naturalness assurance with more qualified discussion and empirical validity evidence. Appendix F also acknowledges that learned rewards can still require over-optimization controls, which are not implemented.

D1.justification: Appendix F substantially expands v1's sparse implementation information with network architectures, hyperparameter search ranges, dataset sizes and sequence lengths, image prompts, docking settings, software, and hardware. These mostly document settings rather than establish changed implementations. Hardware reporting is internally inconsistent: F.1.2 specifies A100 GPUs, while F.2 specifies RTX 2080Ti or A6000. The code-access link is retained.

E1.justification: v4 adds molecular docking optimization against Parp1, 5ht1b, Jak2, and Braf using QuickVina 2. It removes the RNA-stability evaluation associated with Agarwal and Kelley, retaining RNA MRL, enhancer activity, image rewards, and molecular QED/SA. These change the evaluated task requirements, not merely dataset labels.

E2.justification: SMC becomes an evaluated comparator across the retained tasks in Table 2 and in a dedicated diversity comparison. In v1, its algorithm appeared only as an appendix extension without comparative results. Pretrained sampling, Best-of-N, and DPS remain; v4 also describes discrete DPS as combined with Nisonoff et al.'s guidance. DiGress is discussed but explicitly not empirically compared.

E3.justification: Table 2 replaces the 20% quantile with the 50% quantile while retaining the 10% quantile. New evaluation designs include validity and distributional metrics on 512 molecules per method, runtime/memory measurements, and expanded M sweeps. The principal pretrained models, denoising-step counts, and default SVDD settings remain unchanged; newly disclosed tuning details do not establish changes to earlier experiments.

E4.justification: v4 expands the original aesthetic-score M ablation to include molecular QED, image compressibility, runtime, and memory. It adds an SMC-versus-SVDD diversity case study and quantitative molecular validity, novelty, and stability analyses. The existing MRL and enhancer training curves are retained with corrected captions; the RNA-stability curve is replaced by a docking-value-model curve.

E5.justification: v1 Table 2 reports point estimates, whereas v4 Table 2 adds stated 95% confidence intervals. Neither version explains interval construction or provides seed or repeated-run counts. This establishes added uncertainty reporting, without establishing additional experimental repetitions.

E6.justification: v4 adds docking, SMC, image SVDD-MC, validity, and computational results, while removing RNA-stability and 20% quantile entries. Retained numerical entries also change: enhancer top-10 values for SVDD-MC and SVDD-PM change from 5.75 and 7.02 to 5.639 and 6.980. Several image and molecular values are retained or merely rounded; the revision does not establish a uniform same-setting performance improvement.

M1.justification: The core SVDD sampling procedure and MC/PM value estimators remain intact. Appendix D and Algorithm 5 add an optional arbitrary-proposal extension: candidates can come from q rather than the pretrained policy, with importance weights corrected by the pretrained-policy-to-q density ratio.

P1.justification: The abstract and introductory exposition receive wording edits, conditional notation is simplified, and extensions and limitations are reordered. Autoregressive related work moves to Appendix A, and experimental details gain clearer subdivisions. These are localized editorial and organizational changes within the retained problem-method-experiments narrative.

P2.justification: The expanded quantitative table moves from the appendix into the main results, while reward-distribution plots move to the appendix and gain panels. v4 adds SMC-diversity displays, molecular-validity Table 3, resource plots, and docking visualizations, and expands image examples across M values. It also corrects mislabeled training-curve captions and reorganizes the ablation into multiple panels.

R1.justification: v4 substantially revises the relationship to prior sampling research. It identifies SVDD as an instantiation of nested-IS SMC, adds Naesseth and diffusion-SMC references, and recasts v1's particle-filter extension as a comparison with existing methods. Section 6 and Appendices B/C also develop distinctions from standard SMC, discrete guidance, and DiGress.

T1.justification: Appendix C introduces a discrete-guidance rate-matrix formulation and an informal asymptotic-equivalence derivation connecting Nisonoff et al.'s formulation to Theorem 1. The original target distribution, central theorem, SMC weight derivation, and soft-Q-learning identities are retained. Suppressing conditional notation while explicitly retaining conditional applicability is not a substantive theoretical change.

improvement.justification: v4 addresses important weaknesses in v1: missing evaluation against closely related SMC methods, incomplete attribution to that literature, and little quantitative evidence about naturalness or computational cost. The added comparisons, validity measurements, docking experiments, and implementation details substantially strengthen assessment of the central contribution. Removing RNA stability narrows coverage, and unexplained confidence intervals plus contradictory hardware and Figure 3 resource descriptions remain weaknesses, but they do not outweigh these gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SVDD research, with matching authors, core algorithms, and retained experiments. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices support comparison; no material reading gaps remain.

after.justification: v4 Section 7 and Appendices B and F report original reward comparisons, molecular docking experiments, diversity and validity evaluations, and computational measurements.

before.justification: v1 Section 6 and Appendix C report original generation experiments for images, molecules, enhancers, and RNA, including reward comparisons, training curves, and an ablation.

results.title:
Derivative-Free Guidance in Continuous and Discrete Diffusion Models
  with Soft Value-Based Decoding

C1.justification: v2 makes eliminating biased minibatch optimization deviations and achieving unbiased learning without additional training cost central scientific claims. v1 briefly discussed bias as a theoretical obstacle in Section 5, but did not make these explicit optimization and cost claims in its abstract or contributions. The representation-learning and end-to-end guarantee claims remain.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive explanations of accumulated optimization bias, when correlation regularization fails to ensure alignment, and how dimensionality, domain shift, and augmentation-set growth affect sample complexity. Appendix E expands the interpretation of assumptions through concrete examples. Conversely, v1's concluding discussion of unresolved minimax rates and lower bounds is removed.

D1.justification: v2 documents tested regularization values, implementation information for new baselines, revised hyperparameters, and training time/memory. However, v1's PyTorch-style pseudocode documenting normalization and standardization is omitted, and its explicit four-positive-views setting is no longer stated. These are localized additions and losses in reproducibility information.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate classification on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Tiny ImageNet. v2 Appendix D.4 adds a distinct transfer scenario: pretraining on CIFAR-100 and evaluating the representation on CIFAR-10, beyond v1's within-dataset evaluations.

E2.justification: v2 Table 3 retains SimCLR, BYOL, and both W-MSE variants while adding VICReg and LogDet. Table 1 introduces evaluated comparisons against Barlow Twins and Beyond Separability. These substantially broaden the comparisons and directly address the biased-loss methods central to v2's argument.

E3.justification: Compared with v1 Section 3, v2 Appendix C changes embedding dimensions from 64 for CIFAR and 128 for Tiny ImageNet to 512 throughout. Pretraining weight decay changes from 1e-6 to 1e-3, and linear-probe weight decay from 1e-6 to 1e-4. New experiments also introduce parameter sweeps, augmentation/component controls, and per-epoch resource measurements. These are substantive reported setting changes.

E4.justification: v1 contains no corresponding empirical ablations. v2 Appendix D adds a nine-value regularization-parameter sweep, progressive removal of augmentation operations, and comparisons with versus without the explicit alignment term. Tables 5–7 provide substantial new evidence about sensitivity and component contributions.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed counts, repeated-run counts, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. The added experiments continue reporting point estimates; probability bounds in the theoretical analysis are not empirical uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: The proposed method's benchmark values change throughout: CIFAR-10 linear/5-NN accuracy changes from 92.11/90.01 in v1 Table 1 to 93.01/90.97 in v2 Table 3. Revised training settings prevent treating these as controlled version-to-version gains. v2 additionally reports baseline, resource, ablation, and transfer results, including 80.57/73.41 for CIFAR-100-to-CIFAR-10 transfer. BYOL retains the Tiny ImageNet linear lead: 51.00 versus Adv-SSL's 50.21.

M1.justification: The formal minimax objective and downstream classifier are retained. However, the reported minibatch procedure changes: v1 Algorithm 3 computes detached G from the current batch before backpropagation, whereas v2 Algorithm 1 carries G between iterations and refreshes it after the encoder update. Detachment itself was already present in v1.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, and introduction are extensively rewritten, and ACT is renamed Adv-SSL. Theory now precedes the main benchmark comparison; related work and experimental details move into appendices. The appendices are reorganized into A–G with a contents list, notation guide, and substantially expanded explanatory prose.

P2.justification: A compact conference layout replaces v1's spacious manuscript format. The benchmark table is redesigned and expanded, and new tables display targeted comparisons, resource costs, notation, ablations, and transfer results. The existing Lipschitz-constant table is retained as Table 9. Algorithm displays are also reorganized, with the separate downstream and PyTorch-style displays omitted.

R1.justification: The positioning shifts from a broad transfer-learning survey to a taxonomy of self-supervised methods and a focused critique of biased regularization and incomplete error analyses. v2 adds works including Chuang's debiased/robust contrastive learning, Caron's clustering/transformer approaches, and Zhang's LogDet work, while removing much of v1's regression and minimax transfer-learning literature.

T1.justification: v1 Theorem 4.2's probability-qualified bound is replaced by v2 Theorem 1's expectation over source and target samples, with an explicit inverse-square-root labeled-sample term and revised unlabeled-sample rates. Appendix F.4.7 revises the supporting derivation. v2 also adds a growing-augmentation-count bound and formal arguments about alignment and augmentation continuity, while retaining many earlier lemmas under new numbering.

improvement.justification: v1 supports its transfer-learning method mainly through within-dataset accuracy comparisons. v2 substantially strengthens that evidence with direct cross-dataset transfer testing, targeted baselines, and ablations examining alignment, augmentation, and regularization (Tables 1–2 and Appendix D). The reorganized presentation also makes the analysis easier to assess. These gains outweigh the loss of detailed pseudocode, although absent uncertainty reporting and changed benchmark settings still limit conclusions about performance improvements.

A1.justification: The PDFs describe the same research despite renaming ACT to Adv-SSL. Their shared minimax objective, classification framework, experiments, and overlapping proofs establish continuity. Both versions' main text and complete appendices support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 reports original Adv-SSL classification results, computational costs, ablations, and CIFAR-100-to-CIFAR-10 transfer results in Tables 1–3 and 5–8.

before.justification: v1 Section 3 and Table 1 report original ACT classification results on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Tiny ImageNet.

results.title: Adv-SSL: Adversarial Self-Supervised Representation Learning with Theoretical Guarantees

C1.justification: V1 emphasizes zero-gap convergence for non-convex objectives and linear zero-gap convergence under strong convexity. V2 drops the strongly convex claim and distinguishes general convergence to a neighborhood from exact stationarity under additional directional conditions. The central normalized-aggregation mechanism, linear aggregation complexity, and Byzantine/non-IID robustness claims remain.

C2.justification: V1 presents directional heterogeneity as a relaxed assumption. V2 Appendix A and Remark 3.10 discuss how its restrictiveness depends on gradient norms and why exact convergence requires suitable bounds throughout training. V2 also adds architecture-based interpretations of TinyImageNet failures and explicitly identifies broader zero-gap guarantees as a limitation. Some robustness interpretations remain overstated relative to the tables.

D1.justification: Appendix B substantially expands reproducibility information, including dataset-specific architectures and learning-rate schedules, GM/MCA tolerance of 10^-5, LIE and FoE coefficients, and TensorFlow versus NumPy implementations for timing. Hardware and PyTorch version remain unchanged. These disclosures accompany the experimental revisions without establishing changes to previously unspecified implementations.

E1.justification: V2 adds CIFAR10 and TinyImageNet image classification to the original MNIST coverage. MNIST experiments with both LeNet and MLP remain in Appendix C. Evaluation also adds LIE and FoE adversarial scenarios alongside the retained Gaussian, Same-value, and Sign-flip attacks.

E2.justification: V1 evaluates FedAvg, Median, Krum, and Geometric Median against Fed-NGA. V2 retains these and adds Maximum Correntropy Aggregation (MCA) and Centered Clipping (CClip), including in the retained MNIST comparisons in Table 4. These are evaluated comparators, not merely new citations.

E3.justification: Appendix B changes the client count from 100 to 50, batch size from 512 to 32, and MNIST training budget from 10,000 to 500 iterations. The common constant learning rate of 0.02 becomes separate decaying schedules for Fed-NGA and baselines. MNIST MLP dimensions and the Gaussian attack distribution also change; new datasets receive explicit model configurations and budgets.

E4.justification: The existing attack-intensity and heterogeneity sweeps are substantially extended to LIE/FoE robustness and interactions across three datasets. Appendix C also expands a single aggregation-timing comparison into systematic analysis across attack types, intensities, and heterogeneity. The new stress tests expose severe TinyImageNet failures under high attack ratios, extending the questions addressed by v1's MNIST analyses.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed counts, repeated-run counts, error bars, confidence intervals, or specified significance tests. V2 introduces statements about statistically significant gains, but supplies no corresponding statistical procedure or uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: V2 replaces the MNIST results under revised protocols and adds extensive accuracy and timing results. For MNIST/LeNet at beta = 0.6 without attacks, Fed-NGA changes from 98.38% in v1 to 98.50% in v2 Table 4, with FedAvg changing from leading to trailing; this is not a same-setting improvement. New TinyImageNet results include 0.50% for Fed-NGA versus 31.63% for Krum under Sign-flip at attack ratio 0.4 and beta = 0.6.

M1.justification: The operative Fed-NGA mechanism remains client-gradient upload, individual normalization, weighted aggregation, and model broadcast. V2 explicitly writes sampled subdatasets and stochastic gradients into Algorithm 1, but v1 already documents minibatch training in Appendix B. This clarifies the stochastic formulation without establishing a new aggregation component or newly introduced empirical sampling procedure.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, method exposition, results discussion, and conclusion undergo extensive rewriting. The theory is reorganized around two assumption families, Appendix C is reorganized by attack performance, timing, and heterogeneity, and Appendix A is repurposed. The old notation definition moves into the main text, and the contents page is removed.

P2.justification: V2 restructures Table 1, reorganizes accuracy tables around methods and attack ratios, and adds extensive timing tables. The repeated learning-curve grids are replaced by a different mixture of attack-ratio plots, convergence plots, and grouped timing charts. A new geometric illustration appears as Figure 5. These are substantial display changes beyond numerical replacement or renumbering.

R1.justification: V2 adds substantive positioning against normalization research in optimization and federated learning, including work by Cutkosky and Mehta, Dai, Jakovetic, Li, and Wang. Table 1 and Appendix D add MCA/CClip and revise median-based aggregation complexity from O(pM) to O(pM log M), strengthening the claimed computational distinction from prior methods.

T1.justification: V2 removes the strongly convex theorem, bounded-gradient assumption, and associated lemma/proofs. It introduces unbiased stochastic gradients and Type I/II noise and heterogeneity assumptions. New Theorem 3.7 gives a residual bound depending on noise and heterogeneity; Theorem 3.9 extends v1's directional non-convex result with stochastic directional error. Appendices E and F are substantially revised, and the old Appendix G is removed.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially improves applicability assessment through broader adversarial evaluation that reveals failure regimes beyond v1's MNIST experiments. It also removes the problematic linear-to-zero claim—v1 Remark 3.8 gives a nonzero constant-step residual—and separates general neighborhood convergence from conditional exact stationarity. Expanded implementation details improve reproducibility. These gains outweigh remaining weaknesses, including absent uncertainty reporting, overbroad robustness prose, and new reporting inconsistencies: Table 6 gives 2.20% for TinyImageNet Same-value at beta = 0.6 and attack ratio 0.4, while Figure 11(b) plots roughly 24%.

A1.justification: Despite the changed title, both PDFs describe the same Fed-NGA work. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support comparison. The substantial theoretical and experimental revisions do not prevent matching retained content.

after.justification: V2 reports original accuracy and aggregation-time experiments on MNIST, CIFAR10, and TinyImageNet under multiple attacks and heterogeneity settings, including extensive results in Appendix C.

before.justification: V1 reports original MNIST experiments with LeNet and MLP, including accuracy under Byzantine attacks, heterogeneity sensitivity, and aggregation timing in Section 4 and Appendix C.

results.title: Efficient Federated Learning against Byzantine Attacks and Data Heterogeneity via Aggregating Normalized Gradients

C1.justification: The central application claim broadens from station-based weather forecasting to atmospheric time series forecasting, including air quality. V2 newly claims the first lightweight model designed for ATSF and distinguishes competitive STELLA-10k performance from optimized-model superiority. The underlying claim that spatial-temporal knowledge can substitute for complex architectures remains.

C2.justification: V2 adds substantive limitations concerning neglected multivariate coupling, overly smooth extreme-event forecasts, and limited MLP capacity (Section 5 and Appendix G). Appendix E explains limited gains for linear models and distinguishes input-based physical priors from PINN constraints. These substantially extend v1's brief discussion of future physical integration.

D1.justification: V2 adds a code-repository pointer and Table 6's dataset-specific dimensions, layer counts, epochs, dropout, weight decay, and learning-rate schedules. It newly documents coordinate normalization and baseline loss/search practices, and updates software and hardware disclosures. Conversely, v1's explicit 7:1:2 training/validation/test split statement disappears.

E1.justification: GlobalWind and GlobalTemp remain, while Wind_CN and Temp_CN become ChinaWind and ChinaTemp. The 27-station Wind_US benchmark is removed and replaced by the reported ChinaPM2.5 air-quality task covering 1,316 Chinese stations, substantially changing the represented population and target domain.

E2.justification: Table 1 adds AGCRN, MTGNN, GTS, iTransformer, DUET, N-BEATS, and FITS, while removing TimesNet, GPT4TS, and Time-LLM. The embedding-transfer comparison in Table 4 also replaces MRIformer with iTransformer, although MRIformer remains in the main comparison.

E3.justification: V1 specifies 48 input and 24 forecast steps throughout; v2 changes the retained Chinese weather tasks to 60/30 and introduces 72/72 for air quality, retaining 48/24 globally. Main evaluation changes from MSE/MAE to RMSE/MAE. V2 also evaluates separate STELLA-10k and optimized configurations and adds a CPU training/inference protocol.

E4.justification: V2 newly tests whether STPE benefits DLinear (Appendix E.3), adds comparative station-level cases (Figures 9–11), and examines the geographic distribution of embedding clusters (Figure 5). Existing embedding-removal and relative-position ablations expand from two global datasets to all five datasets.

E5.justification: Both versions report five-run means and standard deviations for the proposed model's main results. However, v2 removes v1 Table 2's explicit statement that efficiency measurements were averaged over three runs. This is reduced repetition disclosure, without evidence that the actual run count decreased.

E6.justification: Table 1 adds separate STELLA-10k/STELLAopt results and new comparator and ChinaPM2.5 scores, while removing Wind_US results. GlobalWind MAE changes from 1.295 for LightWeather to 1.294/1.284 for the two STELLA configurations; their differing models and settings prevent treating these as controlled performance gains. Tables 8–10 add CPU, lightweight-efficiency, and linear-transfer outcomes.

M1.justification: The spatial encoder changes from a single fully connected layer in v1 Eq. (3) to a two-layer ReLU feed-forward network in v2 Eq. (3). This is a limited architectural revision: additive calendar embeddings, the residual MLP backbone, and the forecasting head remain.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, terminology, and contribution narrative are substantially rewritten around ATSF and STELLA/STPE. The methodology is reorganized, visualization and case-study material are reordered, and existing appendix content is redistributed alongside new discussion and limitations sections.

P2.justification: The document changes from two-column to single-column formatting. Architecture and mechanism diagrams are redrawn, comparison tables are restructured, and the embedding visualization gains a geographic panel. New proof diagrams, configuration/efficiency tables, and station-level plots are added; the existing global forecast maps are retained and renumbered.

R1.justification: V2 expands positioning and citations around graph models, lightweight forecasters, attention alternatives such as SOFTS, and physics-informed approaches. Appendix E.2 introduces an explicit novelty distinction from PINNs. V1's discussion of gridded radar/reanalysis methods and references associated with removed TimesNet and language-model baselines are dropped.

T1.justification: Theorem 1 gains explicit dependence on the atmospheric state. V1's scalar corollary is replaced by a multi-step formulation with a history-dependent residual and a matrix-norm condition. Appendix A adds a full atmospheric-equation derivation, rewrites the corollary proof, and revises the parameter-count theorem and proof.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens the accuracy-efficiency argument by testing relevant graph and lightweight alternatives and directly measuring CPU operation, addressing important gaps in v1's validation. Detailed configurations and explicit failure limitations also make the work easier to assess and reproduce. These gains outweigh reporting regressions: the split ratio and efficiency repetition count disappear, and Table 7 retains MSE labels although its numerical-method values are square roots of v1's MSE values. The improvement rests on stronger validation and transparency, not simply broader claims or lower reported errors.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same embedding-plus-MLP forecasting work, renamed from LightWeather to STELLA. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices support reliable comparison despite substantial revision.

after.justification: V2 reports original forecasting experiments, ablations, CPU measurements, embedding-transfer experiments, and comparative prediction cases, including results in its appendices.

before.justification: V1 reports original forecasting experiments on five datasets, embedding ablations, hyperparameter studies, and efficiency measurements.

results.title: On the Integration of Spatial-Temporal Knowledge: A Lightweight Approach to Atmospheric Time Series Forecasting

C1.justification: The full-trajectory scaling law, unseen-scheduler prediction, model-size extension and computational-saving claims remain. v2 adds explicit contribution claims about validity across model architectures and fitting publicly released model curves in the abstract and introduction, modestly extending the stated contribution set.

C2.justification: Section 3.3 adds a loss-surface interpretation in which annealing reduces oscillation along a slide's walls. Section 6.1 additionally qualifies the connection between momentum-window size and optimal annealing duration by requiring smoothly changing learning rates. Existing limitations concerning near-zero learning rates, unexplained delay mechanisms and post-training applicability remain.

D1.justification: Table 3 documents new MoE and long-run configurations, including expert selection, auxiliary-loss weight and sequence lengths, and newly discloses sequence length for retained settings. v2 also supplies implementation-code access information and identifies the public-log sources and exact evaluation fields used in Figure 27. These substantially expand reproducibility information without establishing changes to the retained experiments.

E1.justification: Appendix C.4 adds externally generated BLOOM and OLMo training trajectories, including OLMo's Pile evaluation losses. The existing Fineweb, RedPajama-CC and multilingual-mixture coverage remains. New model architectures and longer training budgets primarily change experimental settings, not the underlying language-modeling task.

E2.justification: Chinchilla remains the explicit alternative scaling-law comparator, and the alternative annealing-term formulations in Section 6.3 are retained. BLOOM and OLMo supply additional curves to fit; they are not competing prediction methods.

E3.justification: The main model-size experiment changes from fitting all five sizes to fitting four and predicting the held-out 1214.4M model (v1 Figure 6b; v2 Figure 7b). Added protocols include 60K-step MoE fitting with WSD curves and fitting 30K-step curves to predict a 350K-step, 1.7B-model run (Appendices C.2–C.3). These substantially extend the evaluation design.

E4.justification: v2 adds substantial generalization checks addressing transfer to MoE architectures, extrapolation beyond ten times the fitting horizon, and prediction at a held-out model size. Existing warmup, optimizer-momentum, decay-factor, annealing-function and alternative-formulation analyses are retained rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: Both versions report the same means and standard deviations of R-squared over 1,000 sampled parameter tuples in Table 1. v2 introduces no new seed counts, repeated-training-run uncertainty, confidence intervals or significance-testing procedure.

E6.justification: New results include MoE prediction errors of 0.191%, 0.134% and 0.273% (Figure 24), a 350K-step prediction error of 0.359% (Figure 26), and BLOOM/OLMo fitting R-squared values of 0.99640/0.99869 (Figure 27). The main model-size fit changes from R-squared 0.99889 to 0.99880 under the revised holdout protocol, so these values are not a same-setting performance comparison.

M1.justification: The proposed forward-area and annealing-momentum formulation, model-size extension, and Huber-loss fitting procedure remain unchanged. MoE is an additional experimental architecture, not a new component of the proposed scaling-law method.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, preliminaries, derivation and takeaway sections undergo extensive rewriting and streamlining. WSD background moves into Appendix D, supplementary experiments are organized into Appendix C subsections, and a future-applications subsection is added. This is a broad narrative and structural revision beyond the added experiments.

P2.justification: v2 adds the loss-surface illustration in Figure 6 and experimental displays in Figures 23–27, expands Table 3 into two configuration blocks, and revises numerous axes, legends and captions. Retained appendix fitting and prediction figures are consolidated and rearranged; the older model-size and annealing-function plots remain under new numbering.

R1.justification: v2 broadens citations covering scaling-law variants, MoE and public models, and attributes the existing cyclic scheduler to Smith (2017). Its central positioning relative to Chinchilla and its disagreement with Hägele et al. remain. The renamed Llama references correspond to works already cited in v1.

T1.justification: v2 explicitly supplies the initial condition m1 = 0 in Section 3.2 and corrects the undefined k index in the alternative momentum recurrence to i (v1 Equation 10; v2 Equation 9).
