after.justification: v2 retains original segmentation experiments and adds original results on challenging domains, longer learning sequences, alternative training settings, component choices, and computational resources.

before.justification: v1 reports original segmentation experiments with fc-clip and X-Decoder, baseline comparisons, component ablations, timing measurements, and qualitative results, including supplementary results.

results.title: OVS Meets Continual Learning: Towards Sustainable Open-Vocabulary Segmentation

C1.justification: The central contribution remains scalable, training-free constrained generation through posterior-mean projection. The abstract's headline changes from approximately 10% TSTR and 42% DTW improvements to 70% DS and 22% DTW improvements with expanded comparisons. The introduction also narrows its description of convergence analysis from convex constraints to linear constraints with Gaussian data.

C2.justification: V2 adds substantive explanations of how projecting noisy latents can harm denoising and diversity, why noise correction may hurt CPS, and why performance can remain useful with non-convex constraints. It replaces the evaluation's emphasis on a unique matching test sample with distributional and per-sample comparisons, and explicitly discusses the Gaussian and unique-solution restrictions of its convergence results.

D1.justification: V2 substantially expands reproducibility information: GPU hardware, training-epoch limits, checkpoint selection, conditional metadata fields, four-process projection parallelism, the DS classifier, and new baseline settings are documented. These are principally additional disclosures, not demonstrated changes to existing training. V1 promises future code release; v2's checklist states that supplementary code and data are supplied, although their availability cannot be verified from the PDFs.

E1.justification: The original datasets and six evaluation settings remain. V2 substantially extends task requirements through non-convex autocorrelation constraints combined with OHLC constraints on stocks and direct time-series imputation using observed-value constraints. The latter differs from v1's downstream imputation evaluation of synthetic training data.

E2.justification: V2 adds evaluated comparisons with Diffusion-TS, PDM, PRODIGY, and Loss-DiffTime (Tables 1–3); v1 explicitly excluded Loss-DiffTime. Figure 5 also changes comparator membership: PDM and PRODIGY replace Guided DiffTime alongside the retained COP-FT comparison.

E3.justification: V2 adds Discriminative Score and removes SSIM and constraint-violation-rate reporting. The new direct-imputation protocol uses 50% masking and MAE, while the existing TSTR protocol retains 75% masking. Guided DiffTime's stated weight-selection criterion changes from violation rate to violation magnitude; this documents a protocol revision without establishing that earlier experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained increasing-constraint analysis, v2 adds penalty-schedule comparisons, individual-constraint analyses, guidance-weight sensitivity results, and the noise-correction ablation (Appendix B). It also adds latency scaling and multiple generated samples for identical constraints (Appendices D and E), substantially expanding evidence about design choices, efficiency, and diversity.

E5.justification: Three-seed TSTR reporting is retained. V2 adds five-seed Discriminative Score results, timing summaries averaged over ten runs, and generated-sample mean and standard-deviation bands. Its checklist also explicitly identifies DTW dispersion as variation across test samples. These additions do not establish an increase in runs for the retained experiments.

E6.justification: V2 adds extensive results in Tables 2–9 and Figures 7–11, adds DS entries, and removes SSIM and violation-rate entries. Retained CPS results in Table 1 are unchanged, but some comparator values change: COP's Air Quality FD changes from 0.2165 to 0.2206 and TSTR from 0.22 to 0.25. Table 8's Traffic CPS DTW conflicts with Table 1 and cannot establish a performance improvement.

M1.justification: The standard CPS algorithm, denoiser, projection objective, and exponential penalty schedule are retained. V2 adds an experimental noise-correction variant that recomputes the noise estimate from the projected posterior mean before the DDIM update (Section 3 and Appendix B.7). This is a limited procedural variant tested as an ablation, rather than a replacement for CPS.

P1.justification: The introduction, background, method explanation, and experimental narrative are extensively rewritten. Related work gains separate training-based and training-free subsections, theory becomes a standalone section, and results move from question-led discussion to organized findings. Appendices are reorganized, with new checklist, acknowledgements, and societal-impact material.

P2.justification: Table 1 is redesigned, Figure 2 changes its headline metric, and Figure 5 is redrawn with different comparator curves. The qualitative grid is transposed and compressed, while v1 Figure 3 moves to the appendix as v2 Figure 6. Eight additional tables and five additional figures substantially expand the visual presentation, alongside the conference-format layout.

R1.justification: V2 substantially broadens positioning around training-based versus training-free constrained generation, adding discussion of PDM, PRODIGY, Mirror Diffusion Models, and constrained-domain diffusion. It develops the distinction between projecting clean estimates and noisy latents and expands time-series diffusion coverage in Appendix A. The earlier GLACIER/COMET counterfactual discussion is removed.

T1.justification: The Gaussian/linear-constraint framework and most proofs are retained. V2 extends the existing convergence argument with an explicit O(1/T) rate statement and a tolerance-dependent choice of k (Theorem 4.4 and Appendix C.2), and adds projection-convergence discussion in Appendix D. It also replaces v1's formal maximum-likelihood objective with a typical constrained-sample formulation.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens the evidence for CPS's central projection choice through comparisons with closely related projection methods, targeted ablations, non-convex constraints, and direct imputation tests. Runtime measurements and expanded implementation details address important gaps in v1's assessment of practicality and reproducibility. The Traffic DTW inconsistency between Tables 8 and 1 limits confidence in that ablation entry, but the broader gains in empirical support and transparency clearly outweigh this localized reporting problem.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Constrained Posterior Sampling work. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support comparison, including material relocated between versions.

after.justification: V2 retains original empirical results and adds baseline comparisons, non-convex constraint experiments, imputation results, ablations, and inference-time measurements in Section 5 and the appendices.

before.justification: V1 reports original experiments on stocks, traffic, air quality, and synthetic waveforms, including conditional settings, quantitative comparisons, and increasing-constraint analyses in Section 4.

results.title: Constrained Posterior Sampling: Time Series Generation with Hard Constraints

C1.justification: V3 elevates low memory requirements into the abstract and introduction and explicitly claims the first combination of recurrent forecasting with mixing architectures. Its conclusion expands demonstrated applicability to probabilistic forecasting and classification, previously outside the established contributions. The reported long-term dominance changes from 41/56 to 27/56 cases against the revised comparisons.

C2.justification: V3 develops a state-tracking explanation for choosing sLSTM, interprets cross-variate attribution and ordering experiments, and explains why excessive lookback can hurt short-horizon forecasts. It adds conclusions about probabilistic transfer and extra views. Limitations now explicitly address irregular or missing timestamps, channel-dependent resource scaling, and attribution difficulties, extending v1's brief channel-count limitation.

D1.justification: V3 newly documents 32-bit training, GluonTS integration, Captum and scikit-posthocs usage, baseline-result provenance, and the zero-baseline/horizon-aggregation procedure for Shapley attribution. The original hardware, optimizer, training budget, search ranges, and code-access information remain substantially unchanged. These additions mainly improve documentation rather than establish changes to retained experiments.

E1.justification: V3 adds GIFT-Eval's heterogeneous univariate and multivariate probabilistic forecasting coverage and ten classification datasets, including Heartbeat, Handwriting, and SpokenArabicDigits. The seven original long-term forecasting datasets remain. V1's dedicated PEMS03/PEMS08 short-term point-forecasting comparison is removed.

E2.justification: The long-term comparison adds TimeMixer++, CycleNet, S-Mamba, Chimera, ModernTCN, Timer-XL, and MoiraiBase, while removing FEDFormer, Autoformer, and MICN from that experiment. iTransformer and TimesNet remain in v3's full Table 6. NLinear joins the lookback analysis. New comparisons also include GIFT-Eval forecasters such as TiRex and classification baselines such as DTW, XGBoost, and ROCKET.

E3.justification: V3 introduces probabilistic evaluation using MASE and quantile-based CRPS, classification evaluation using accuracy, and training-step time/memory measurements across lookback lengths. The plotted lookback sensitivity sweep extends from 1024 to 2048 steps. The original long-term horizons, MAE training objective, and hyperparameter search ranges remain unchanged; additional descriptions of baseline tuning do not establish rerunning the retained comparisons.

E4.justification: Table 3 expands from ten to fourteen configurations, testing mLSTM, LSTM, GRU, and DLinear substitutions. New analyses examine computational efficiency, Shapley-based cross-variate dependencies, random variate orderings, additional views, and dataset Hurst exponents. These directly investigate architectural and robustness questions left untested or deferred in v1. Existing token visualizations and hidden-dimension analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions specify the same three seeds, 2021–2023. V3 extends uncertainty reporting with forecasting means and standard deviations in Table 7 and introduces Friedman tests, Conover post-hoc comparisons with Holm correction, and critical-difference diagrams. It restricts the long-term significance analysis to MSE at horizon 96 to avoid correlated horizons inflating significance.

E6.justification: Matched long-term entries and retained ablation configurations have unchanged numerical scores. Against the revised comparator set, xLSTM-Mixer's tabled wins change from 18 MSE/23 MAE to 11/16. New results include GIFT-Eval CRPS 0.510 and second place in Tables 2/8, classification accuracy of 74.1% versus ModernTCN's 74.2% in Table 14, and efficiency, permutation, view-count, and recurrent-cell results. The dedicated PEMS results disappear.

M1.justification: The three-stage forecasting backbone in Section 3 is retained. V3 adds a quantile-prediction head for probabilistic forecasting, a softmax classification head trained with cross-entropy, and an experimental extension of view mixing beyond two views. These are limited adaptations of the existing architecture.

P1.justification: The experimental narrative is reorganized into separate forecasting, GIFT-Eval, classification, model-analysis, and ablation sections. Appendices are restructured into A–J; societal-impact discussion and token visualizations move there, and a NeurIPS checklist is added. The introduction, conclusion, headings, and explanatory passages receive substantial revision, although much of the core method exposition remains recognizable.

P2.justification: V3 adds an introductory efficiency figure, critical-difference diagrams, attribution heatmaps, and tables for uncertainty, GIFT-Eval, permutations, extra views, and classification. The ablation table gains columns and separates recurrent type from recurrence order. Earlier sensitivity plots are combined into Figure 4, with a revised logarithmic lookback axis; token plots move to the appendix. Title, author, header, and page styling also change.

R1.justification: Section 5 substantially expands positioning to distinguish state-space, mixing, and pretrained forecasting approaches, discussing works such as Mamba, Chimera, Chronos, Moirai, and Timer-XL. Concurrent xLSTM research and newer mixing architectures are incorporated. The explicit first recurrent–mixing combination claim also sharpens the stated relationship to prior work.

T1.justification: The forecasting formalization and core sLSTM equations are retained. Appendix B adds standard recurrence formulas and an intuitive state-tracking explanation; Appendix C documents standard evaluation metrics. These additions do not introduce substantive formal assumptions, derivations, theorems, or proofs.

improvement.justification: V3 substantially strengthens the empirical justification: controlled recurrent-cell substitutions test the central sLSTM choice, and ordering/view experiments address questions deferred in v1. Updated comparators, measured efficiency, significance analyses, and broader task evaluation make the claims more assessable. There are localized reporting defects: Table 7's TimeMixer averages conflict with Tables 1/6, and GIFT-Eval prose disagrees with its tables on some CRPS values. These defects and removal of the dedicated PEMS comparison do not outweigh the stronger validation and clearer limitations.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe xLSTM-Mixer with the same authors and core architecture. The main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison despite substantial expansion and reorganization.

after.justification: The retained original experiments are supplemented by probabilistic forecasting, classification, efficiency measurements, and additional model analyses.

before.justification: Section 4 and Appendix A report original forecasting experiments, component ablations, and sensitivity analyses, including short-term PEMS results.

results.title: xLSTM-Mixer: Multivariate Time Series Forecasting by Mixing via Scalar Memories

C1.justification: The central contribution remains rectified optimization of per-pair safety constraints. V2 narrows the conclusion from best performance in both helpfulness and harmlessness to strongest safety improvement without sacrificing initial-model helpfulness. Renaming safety interference as safety compensation largely preserves the original substantive claim.

C2.justification: V2 interprets the multiplier as a cumulative penalty, revises the explanation for capping it, and connects objective scaling to preventing meaningless high-scoring outputs. It distinguishes low average cost from proximity to critical safety and interprets the SafeRLHF comparison as an ablation. V1's explanation linking SACPO's GPT-4 performance to reduced reward-model overfitting is removed.

D1.justification: Appendix C adds detailed Llama SFT, preference-model and alignment recipes, model access information, and the new safety-evaluation template. It newly specifies Alpaca cost scaling and the PTX coefficient. Reported inference hardware changes from RTX 3080 Ti to RTX 2080 Ti. Conversely, v1's RePO code-access link is absent from v2.

E1.justification: V2 adds directly conducted instruction tuning on Alpaca data and preference/safety prediction evaluations for newly trained critic-initialization models (Appendix C.3). V1 used already-trained initial and preference models. Downstream evaluation retains PKU-SafeRLHF, PhysicalSafety, CoNa, Controversial and MaliciousInstructions.

E2.justification: The main quantitative comparator algorithms remain SACPO and PPO-Lagrangian/Beaver, renamed SafeRLHF. V2's Appendix D adds GPT-4o reference responses alongside RePO and the baseline outputs. V1's GPT-4o response appeared only in a separate comparison with Beaver in Appendix A.

E3.justification: V2 adds Llama3.2-3B experiments with SFT, critic fitting and model-specific training settings, plus a separate GPT-4o safety assessment using a score above five. Existing Alpaca comparisons switch from locally trained SACPO to its released checkpoint. Table 1 also changes the stated harmlessness metric from relative cost change to average cost.

E4.justification: The training analysis expands from one initial regime to expected-unsafe, nearly-expected-safe and expected-safe data regimes (v2 Figures 1 and 3), directly testing the proposed safety-compensation mechanism. Appendix D replaces the extensive example gallery with two cross-model cases, removing earlier examples including RePO's unsafe bleach/ammonia response in v1 Table 15.

E5.justification: V1 Figures 1 and 4 and v2 Figure 3 report five independent runs with different seeds and show means and standard deviations. Additional training conditions use the same reporting practice. Neither version supplies confidence intervals or significance tests for the main benchmark tables.

E6.justification: V2 adds Llama3.2-3B results, including RePO safety rates of 91.46% under model evaluation and 68.60% under GPT-4 evaluation, plus safety-rate breakdowns. Alpaca SACPO's model-based safety entry changes from 75.85% to 80.72% with the checkpoint replacement; RePO's 96.08% is retained. Reported PKU-SafeRLHF GPT-4 win/loss rates against initial Alpaca change from 88%/5% to 82%/10%.

M1.justification: Both versions retain the safe/unsafe batch split, clipped surrogate objectives, normalized unsafe objective, capped cumulative penalty and two-critic updates. V2 expands the pseudocode and explicitly includes scaling factors; v1 already documents reward scaling in Appendix C.3. The additional backbone experiments do not establish a new RePO procedure.

P1.justification: V2 extensively rewrites the related work, motivation, method explanation and experimental narrative. The former preliminary pitfalls subsection becomes a standalone section; implementation becomes numbered subsections; experiments are reorganized into setups and results; and the appendix showcase is substantially condensed. Terminology changes throughout.

P2.justification: V2 replaces the opening example graphic with a policy-set diagram and multipanel diagnostics, replaces circular GPT-4 charts with stacked bars, expands Table 1 across models and evaluators, and expands the scatter plot into six appendix panels. Evaluation templates become tables, and the qualitative tables are replaced and consolidated.

R1.justification: Related work is substantially refocused from a defense-layer taxonomy toward RLHF versus DPO and constrained safety alignment. V2 adds discussion of Huang et al., alignment comparisons by Xu et al. and Li et al., and strong-duality work by Paternain et al., while removing much of the filtering and inference-guidance positioning.

T1.justification: Theorem 1 and its Appendix B proof retain the same rectified min-max equivalence. V2 adds a two-prompt counterexample distinguishing expected from critical safety, formalizes the corresponding policy sets, and discusses Slater's condition and strong duality in Remark 1. No new convergence theorem or algorithmic safety guarantee is established.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens evidence for the central safety-compensation argument: it tests different initial safety regimes, extends evaluation beyond one backbone, and measures absolute GPT-4 safety rates alongside joint preference judgments. Expanded training recipes and clearer mathematical framing improve assessability. Removing the code link and useful failure examples weakens reproducibility and qualitative transparency, but these losses are outweighed by the more direct and broader empirical testing.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same RePO research, with matching authors, central problem, algorithm and theorem. The complete main texts, figures, tables, equations and Appendices A-D are readable and support reliable comparison.

after.justification: V2 reports original experiments on Alpaca-7B and Llama3.2-3B, additional safety-condition analyses, GPT-4 safety assessments and preference-model accuracy results.

before.justification: V1 reports original RePO fine-tuning experiments on Alpaca-7B, reward/cost evaluation, GPT-4 comparisons and repeated-seed training curves.

results.title:
Enhancing Safety in Reinforcement Learning with Human Feedback via
  Rectified Policy Optimization

C1.justification: The central claims about transferring architectural priors and rescuing unsuitable networks remain. v2 strengthens the initialization claim from evidence that better initializations likely exist to an explicit guidance-only initialization scheme, and its conclusion adds evidence of scaling within models of 150M parameters or fewer. These refine rather than replace the main contribution.

C2.justification: v2 substantially expands mechanism explanations: locality and weight sharing reflected in alignment statistics, connections to kernel/generalization theory, delayed intrinsic-dimensionality collapse, and layer-dependent credit assignment. It uses linear decoding to argue against readily accessible class information explaining random-guide benefits. Appendix I.1 explicitly leaves a guidance-specific proof unresolved. These extend well beyond the retained explanations about architectural priors and trained features.

D1.justification: v2 provides additional reproducibility details, including distillation temperature 2 and weight 0.5, ridge penalties 10 and 100, projection and representation-splitting procedures, and linear-probe sample counts of 4000 training and 1000 validation images. Architecture descriptions and learning-rate tables are updated. The abstract replaces the direct code-repository link with a project website; actual online availability is not established by the PDFs.

E1.justification: Both versions use ImageNet-1K and CIFAR-10 classification, WikiText-103 language modeling, copy-paste and parity. CIFAR-10 moves from the MSE experiment to layer ablations; it is not newly introduced. Larger models, probing and alternative training procedures operate within retained data and task coverage.

E2.justification: v1 discusses distillation without experimentally comparing it against guidance. v2 evaluates basic logit/KL knowledge distillation with trained and untrained teachers across image and sequence settings (Figure 5), and adds Deep FCN loss and error-consistency comparisons in Appendix H. This supplies a substantive new comparator for the paper's central distinction.

E3.justification: The documented language-model target changes from a five-layer, 512-unit tanh RNN to a four-layer ReLU model, with an additional six-layer, 1024-unit model using context length 128. Table 4 changes guided copy-paste learning rates from 1e-5 to 1e-4 and guided language-model rates from 5e-5 to 1e-4. Initialization changes from disconnecting guidance after 150 task-training steps to 300 alignment-only steps. These are reported setting changes, not evidence that retained results were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds tests of layer selection and mapping, early versus late alignment dynamics, guide-to-guide similarity, intrinsic-dimensionality trajectories and intervention, linear decodability, and ridge alignment. These investigate design choices and possible mechanisms absent from v1. The initialization analysis is revised, while v1's CIFAR-10 MSE-loss ablation is removed. Noise-fed guidance and RSA analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions specify five random seeds, standard-error reporting and selection using the lowest seed-averaged validation loss. The v2 checklist reiterates this practice without adding a statistical procedure or increasing the stated run count. Changed standard-error values belong to E6.

E6.justification: v2 adds large-RNN perplexities of 89.13 unguided, 36.91 with a trained guide and 47.17 with an untrained guide, plus distillation, layer-ablation, ridge and intrinsic-dimensionality results. Most earlier headline means remain, but untrained-Transformer perplexity changes from 51948.8 to 5.19e5, and Deep/Wide FCN standard errors change from 0.51/1.21 to 1.21/0.91. Initialization findings are replaced and MSE results removed. Results under added or revised settings do not establish same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: The core frozen-guide objective remains, but v2 adds an intrinsic-dimensionality regularization loss (Appendix I.2) and projected ridge-regression alignment (J.2). It also replaces guidance disconnected during task training with alignment-only initialization on noise before unguided task training. Algorithm 1 changes the layer-index clipping bound from the guide-layer count to the target-layer count. These are substantive procedural additions and revisions.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, results and conclusion undergo substantial rewriting and compression. Sequence modeling precedes vision, numbered experimental subsections become shorter thematic paragraphs, and CKA details, alignment-loss analysis and error-consistency mathematics move into reorganized appendices. A NeurIPS checklist is added. These are extensive narrative and structural changes.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is redrawn, and Figure 2 combines previously separate training/validation panels while adding the larger language model. The main result tables are reordered and expanded. The original alignment-loss figure is split into appendix displays; initialization plots are replaced, the MSE plot disappears, and new distillation, geometry, probing and ablation displays are added. The document also adopts conference formatting.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands positioning through FitNets, teacher-guided architecture search, random-feature learning, intrinsic dimensionality and theoretical representation alignment. Appendix I.1 newly connects guidance to work by Insulla and colleagues, Baratin and colleagues, and Shan and Bordelon. Several earlier distillation and canonical-correlation references are removed. This changes the scientific framing beyond citation-format updates.

T1.justification: Appendix I.2 introduces a substantive mathematical construction of an intrinsic-dimensionality penalty using singular values, cumulative explained variance and sigmoid penalties, particularly Equations 10–14. Appendix J.2 also formalizes projected ridge alignment. Existing CKA, RSA and error-consistency mathematics largely remains. The discussion of prior generalization theory does not provide a new guidance-specific theorem or proof.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses important evidential gaps: the distinction from logit distillation is directly tested, and previously untested layer-mapping choices receive informative ablations (Figure 5; Appendices H and K). Initialization-only training and the geometric intervention further strengthen the paper's explanatory value. These gains outweigh removal of the MSE generality test. Reporting weaknesses remain: the language-model prose overstates some Table 2 gains, and setting inconsistencies limit interpretation of scaling. The improvement rests on stronger controls and targeted analyses, not higher headline scores.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same guidance framework and research work. Their main text, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices are readable and support comparison, including matching material moved between sections.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds larger language models, distillation comparisons, geometric analyses, intrinsic-dimensionality regularization and layer-selection ablations.

before.justification: v1 reports original image-classification, copy-paste, parity and language-modeling experiments, plus appendix experiments using noise, MSE loss and RSA alignment.

results.title: Training the Untrainable: Introducing Inductive Bias via Representational Alignment

C1.justification: The central contribution is recast from stochasticity control and singularity mitigation to unifying stochastic interpolants with endpoint conditioning and preconditioning. The abstract and introduction drop the explicit fivefold acceleration and training-stability emphasis, while the headline empirical scope expands to deblurring. The conclusion also strengthens the diversity claim: modifying the starting distribution is described as required, rather than simply beneficial.

C2.justification: v2 introduces a lossy-compression and data-processing interpretation of base-distribution perturbation, explains AFD's complementarity to FID using controlled examples, and develops noise-dependent failure explanations and tuning guidance in Appendix D. v1's explicit singularity and truncation-error rationale is removed. Task dependence and the quality-versus-diversity tradeoff were already acknowledged in v1.

D1.justification: Appendix F/Table 9 substantially expands the training documentation beyond v1's two handbag configurations, adding a gamma_max = 0.25 handbag configuration and two DIODE configurations with hardware, batch sizes, learning rates and training times. Budgets are now expressed in epochs rather than iterations, without establishing that existing training runs changed. The architecture and preconditioning details are largely retained, while sampling settings and new evaluation procedures receive additional documentation.

E1.justification: v2 retains Edges-to-Handbags and DIODE depth-to-RGB translation and adds ImageNet uniform and Gaussian deblurring in Table 5. ImageNet also supplies the class-conditioned resampling and color-augmentation experiments validating AFD in Appendix A. The expanded DIODE results concern an existing dataset, rather than newly introduced coverage.

E2.justification: The new deblurring comparison introduces DDRM, DDNM, CDSB and the method labeled 'Pallette' in Table 5, alongside I2SB. The conditional-diversity comparison in Table 4 also replaces the DDBM-checkpoint-plus-DDBM-sampler baseline with DDBM-checkpoint-plus-DBIM-sampler. The former baseline remains illustrated elsewhere in v2, but its membership in this table changes.

E3.justification: The reported sampling minimum time changes from 0.01 to 0.001, and DIODE receives rho = 0.8 instead of the previously general rho = 0.6. Table 4 changes the diversity comparison to common budgets of 5, 10 and 20 NFEs. New protocols include deblurring on 10,000 ImageNet validation images, controlled resampling and 16 augmentations per image for AFD validation, and a 446-image test comparison. These reported changes do not establish that retained results were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds component ablations for discretization and final-step noise control, quantitative sensitivity to noise magnitude and schedule shape, and qualitative failure analyses for excessive or insufficient noise (Figure 4 and Appendix D). Appendix A adds two controlled validations of AFD. Conversely, v1's complete numerical eta sweep using pretrained DDBM-VP is reduced to the eta = 0.3 row in v2 Table 2, with additional qualitative comparisons elsewhere.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed counts, repeated-run performance summaries, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. Multiple generated outputs for AFD and the newly specified augmentation counts are evaluation samples, not uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: The shared pretrained-sampler scores and original handbag FIDs of 0.89, 0.67 and 0.56 are retained. v2 adds gamma_max = 0.25 results, trained-model DIODE results including FID 3.27 at 20 NFEs, deblurring FIDs of 1.11 for uniform blur and 0.41 for Gaussian blur, and extensive AFD results. v1's DDBM-200-NFE and DBIM-100-NFE rows and most numerical eta-sweep entries disappear. These are added or removed results, rather than demonstrated gains under identical settings.

M1.justification: The denoiser, preconditioning, controllable sampling SDE, base-distribution perturbation and mixed discretization are retained under the ECSI name. Algorithm 1 changes its branch condition from N >= 2 to i >= 2, a limited correction to the written sampling procedure. The prose in both versions already prescribes deterministic final steps, so this does not establish a newly implemented sampler.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction and conclusion are extensively rewritten, and SDB is renamed ECSI. The stochasticity-control and score-reparameterization sections become a question-driven narrative about bridge paths, samplers and starting distributions. Background and related work are revised, core lemmas move into the appendices, and the appendix organization is substantially expanded.

P2.justification: v2 adds design-space diagrams, a characteristics table, ablation plots and new sample comparisons; redraws the base-distribution illustration; and restructures the main results into broader dataset and fixed-NFE tables. Retained material is also relocated: v1 Figure 1 becomes v2 Figure 9, and v1 Table 1 becomes the revised Table 8. Several appendix image grids are reused unchanged, while the document's typography and layout are reformatted.

R1.justification: v2 explicitly positions ECSI as an extension of stochastic interpolants combining their flexibility with practical diffusion-bridge components, supported by a new characteristics table and fuller DBIM discussion. It adds connections and citations to data-dependent stochastic interpolants, augmented and inverse bridge matching, TrigFlow, and the VAE compression analogy. This substantially changes the research positioning beyond citation-format edits.

T1.justification: The principal sampling and denoising results and their proofs are retained through Proposition 4.1 and Appendix B; their reorganization does not constitute new theory. Limited additions include Appendix D's time-reparameterization argument for linear interpolation and Appendix F's derivation of TrigFlow as a special case. The mathematical definition of AFD is unchanged.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens support for central contributions that v1 introduced with limited direct validation. Appendix A tests AFD under controlled diversity changes, while Figure 4 and Appendix D test the sampler ingredients and noise-design choices. Matched-NFE diversity comparisons and additional restoration evidence make the main tradeoffs easier to assess. Some useful earlier comparison rows are lost, and parameter inconsistencies remain, including the different b values attached to the same reported result in Figures 5 and 20. These limitations constrain reproducibility but do not outweigh the substantial gain in empirical support.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research, with shared methods, proofs, experiments and sample images despite substantial rewriting and the SDB-to-ECSI renaming. All 23 pages of v1 and 36 pages of v2, including appendices, are readable and support comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains original translation results and adds ImageNet deblurring, controlled AFD validation and additional ablations in the main text and appendices.

before.justification: v1 reports original image-to-image translation experiments, including sampler comparisons, trained-model results and conditional-diversity measurements in Tables 2–4 and Appendix D.

results.title: Exploring the Design Space of Diffusion Bridge Models

C1.justification: Beyond v1's population-level recovery and adaptability claims, v2's contributions assert finite-sample O(kd/n) adaptation rates and a task-dependent disadvantage for standard retraining. The abstract, introduction and conclusion also expand the empirical success claim from LoRA language adaptation to vision tasks and last-layer fine-tuning.

C2.justification: V2 attributes Reptile's poorer performance to mismatch between gradient-based adaptation and PEFT at test time, discusses shallow-network variability and outliers, and analyzes when zero-mean asymmetric adapters could allow standard retraining to recover shared parameters. It replaces v1's interpretation favoring larger fine-tuning than retraining rank with an interpretation of robustness across matched ranks.

D1.justification: V2 adds synthetic inner/outer optimization schedules, expanded hyperparameter tables, MLP-Mixer architecture and preprocessing details, language-head/tokenizer/loss descriptions, asset information and training pseudocode. Real-data hardware changes from an A40 to an H200. These substantially expand reproducibility documentation, although v1's average per-persona sample counts are no longer stated.

E1.justification: V1 evaluates synthetic linear regression and ConvAI2 conversation-continuation selection. V2 retains these and adds CIFAR-10 binary image-classification tasks and nonlinear scalar-regression data generated by shallow sigmoid networks, substantially broadening the evaluated domains and task relationships.

E2.justification: V1 primarily compares Meta-LoRA against standard retraining followed by LoRA. V2 adds Reptile+LoRA to the ConvAI2 comparisons and evaluates SR+Last-Layer and Reptile+Last-Layer against Last-Layer-ML. The expanded comparator family also appears in the new CIFAR-10 evaluation.

E3.justification: ConvAI2 changes from RoBERTa-Large to RoBERTa-base, from 30 to 10 training epochs, and from best-heldout-epoch to last-epoch fine-tuning results. Batch sizes and learning rates also change (v1 Appendix C; v2 Appendix E.2). Synthetic evaluation changes from population loss to a stated sample prediction error, while the new vision experiments introduce paired-class tasks and image augmentation.

E4.justification: V2 adds synthetic adaptation-rank sensitivity and shallow-network sweeps over task count, sample counts, rank and dimension. ConvAI2's rank-8 retraining/rank-16 fine-tuning investigation is replaced by a matched-rank sweep over 1, 4, 8 and 16. The earlier spurious-local-minima analysis is retained in Appendix F rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: V1 reports language-result medians across five trials without uncertainty estimates. V2 retains five language trials but reports means and standard errors, explicitly reports five-trial linear averages with full-range shading, and introduces ten-trial shallow-network medians with ranges covering the central six outcomes. This substantially changes statistical reporting, without establishing an increased ConvAI2 run count.

E6.justification: ConvAI2 results are replaced: v1 Table 1a reports 45.76 for Meta-LoRA-8 and 41.52 for SR+LoRA; v2 Table 2 reports 47.4 ± 1.9 and 35.0 ± 4.1 under revised settings. New CIFAR-10 results include 86.09 for LoRA-ML, 85.29 for SR+LoRA and 81.30 for Reptile+LoRA. Shallow-network and additional rank-sweep results are also added. These are not controlled cross-version performance gains.

M1.justification: V2 adds a Last-Layer-ML instantiation that adapts only the final layer, alongside LoRA. The generic base-weight/adapter objective remains unchanged under the Meta-Adapters/Meta-LoRA to PEFT-ML/LoRA-ML renaming. Algorithm 1 primarily documents optimization of the existing framework.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction and contribution narrative are extensively rewritten, and method terminology changes throughout. Main-text proof sketches are removed while full proofs remain in Appendix B. Experiments become a compact overview supported by reorganized and expanded appendices. This substantially changes the exposition and organization of retained material.

P2.justification: V1's four-panel Figure 1 becomes a two-panel main figure with expanded appendix plots. V2 adds shallow-network figures, vision tables, redesigned language comparisons and a pseudocode display, while repeating some main results in the appendices. The original spurious-minimum plot is retained as Figure 12. Figures 8 and 9 incorrectly reuse an identical plot under different sample-count captions.

R1.justification: V2 adds Reptile, Saunshi et al., reduced-rank-regression and minimax references, and CIFAR-10/MLP-Mixer references; Mirsky is removed. It sharpens the distinction from shared-subspace meta-learning and connects LoRA fitting to reduced-rank regression. These are targeted extensions of largely retained PEFT research positioning; publication-year updates alone are not substantive additions.

T1.justification: V2 adds finite-test-sample prediction bounds and corollaries, quantitative standard-retraining loss results, and asymmetric-adapter analysis in Appendix C. Retraining theory still assumes infinite samples. It also relaxes the requirement that all task-adapter columns be jointly independent and states explicit dimension conditions for the retained recovery and stationarity theorems. The core landscape proofs remain.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens evaluation of the general PEFT framework through another adaptation method, Reptile comparisons, vision and nonlinear tasks, and explicit uncertainty reporting. Finite-test-sample analysis and considerably fuller implementation documentation address important theoretical and reproducibility gaps in v1. Revised ConvAI2 settings prevent direct accuracy comparisons, and the duplicated Figures 8–9 weaken one supplementary analysis, but these limitations do not outweigh the substantial gains in evidence and assessability.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same PEFT meta-learning framework and core linear-model landscape results. Renamed methods and relocated material can be matched, and both versions' text, equations, figures, tables and appendices support reliable comparison.

after.justification: Section 4 and Appendices D–F report original linear and shallow-network experiments, CIFAR-10 and ConvAI2 evaluations, and numerical optimization-landscape results.

before.justification: Sections 4.1–4.2 report original synthetic linear-regression and RoBERTa-Large/ConvAI2 experiments. Appendix D.2 also reports numerical evidence of spurious local minima.

results.title: Provable Meta-Learning with Low-Rank Adaptations

C1.justification: The central claims about DNC suboptimality, low-rank bias and width-dependent persistence remain. The contribution statement strengthens one retained claim from a positive-semidefinite leading-order Hessian to a positive-semidefinite full Hessian at sufficiently small regularization. The new experiments primarily support the existing scientific thesis.

C2.justification: V2 adds the interpretation that asymptotically comparable Hessian flatness cannot alone explain preferential convergence to DNC, and emphasizes initialization and implicit bias as unresolved mechanisms. It removes v1's extended criticism of the single-layer UFM regularization assumption and adds explicit limitations concerning generalization, robustness and underparameterized regimes. The imbalance discussion also identifies STEP imbalance and unspecified depth bounds as applicability limits.

D1.justification: V2 supplies substantial previously absent experimental documentation: ResNet-20 architecture, head depths and widths, learning rates and regularization coefficients in figure captions, plus sampling, input standardization and batch size in Appendix D. These disclosures make the numerical evidence substantially more reproducible, although code access, hardware and initialization specifics remain unreported.

E1.justification: V2 adds actual image-classification experiments on MNIST and CIFAR-10 to the deep-UFM numerical observations reported in v1. The new class-imbalance material is theoretical and does not establish additional empirical population coverage.

E2.justification: The comparison remains between DNC and lower-rank solutions, using the same constructed solution families and DNC loss bounds. V2 quantifies these comparisons and extends them to full networks, but adds no distinct competing learning method.

E3.justification: The newly reported full-network experiments introduce ResNet-20 backbones, specified linear/ReLU heads, UFM-style versus all-parameter regularization, loss and spectral diagnostics, balanced MNIST subsampling and batch-size-10,000 training. These are protocols for added experiments; newly supplied UFM hyperparameters do not establish that v1's unspecified experiments were changed or rerun.

E4.justification: Figures 2 and 5 add quantitative sensitivity analyses of DNC frequency and converged rank versus width and regularization, beyond v1's qualitative observations. The full-network experiments also examine whether low-rank behavior persists with ReLU activations and standard weight decay, providing substantial additional evidence about applicability.

E5.justification: V2 reports averages over 10 runs for Figures 2 and 5 and explicitly identifies most other experiments as single indicative runs. V1 provides no corresponding run counts. This adds reporting transparency without establishing an increase in runs; confidence intervals, error bars and seed specifications remain absent.

E6.justification: V2 adds extensive concrete outcomes: loss trajectories, DNC probabilities, average ranks, logit heatmaps and singular-value spectra. Section 4 reports four singular values above 10^-6 for MNIST and three for CIFAR-10 in the linear-head experiments. These are newly reported results, not demonstrated same-setting performance improvements over v1.

M1.justification: The analyzed model family changes substantially: v1's minimally nonlinear MSE model, including Hadamard-power activation variants in Appendices A/C, is removed. V2 instead develops the unequal-class-size CE formulation. The principal linear/ReLU CE architecture and regularized objective remain unchanged; this is a change in model scope rather than a redesigned optimization algorithm.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, background, conclusion and proof exposition are extensively rewritten and condensed. Contributions become a bullet list, terminology shifts from DUFM to deep UFM, and the background is consolidated. A numerical-experiments section and Appendix D are added, while Appendices A/C are repurposed.

P2.justification: V1 has no figures or tables. V2 introduces eight multi-panel figures across the main text and Appendix D, displaying loss curves, parameter sweeps, logit heatmaps and singular-value spectra. This substantially changes the visual presentation of evidence, while retaining the single-column document format.

R1.justification: V2 removes the entire loss-surface related-work strand covering spin-glass models, Hessian spectra and shallow/linear-network landscapes. It adds work on imbalance, next-token prediction, multivariate regression and initialization/implicit bias. Appendix A newly develops the relationship to Thrampoulidis et al. and Hong and Ling, substantially reshaping the literature coverage.

T1.justification: Theorem 4 strengthens leading-order Hessian positivity to positivity of the full Hessian, with a new proof. V2 adds Theorem 6 on asymptotic Hessian-norm ratios and a rank-two diagonally superior construction, improving v1's class-dependent bound. Appendices A/C replace the MSE/Hadamard-power results with imbalance theorems and proofs. Definitions and proofs explicitly handle general n, and DNC3 broadens collinearity to linear combinations. V1's ReLU Theorem 6 survives as Theorem 7 with unchanged class/depth thresholds.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens support for the central thesis: the full-Hessian analysis addresses the limitation of v1's leading-order argument, the rank-two construction sharpens the theory, and specified simulations and real-network experiments replace largely undocumented empirical assertions. Removing the MSE/Hadamard-power appendix reduces theoretical breadth, and convergence explanations remain heuristic with mostly single-run network evidence. Nevertheless, the gains in theoretical support, empirical substantiation and reproducibility constitute a substantial overall improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work, with matching authors, central models and principal theorems despite the shortened title. The complete main texts and appendices, including equations and v2's figures, support reliable comparison.

after.justification: Section 4 and Appendix D report original deep-UFM simulations and MNIST/CIFAR-10 network experiments, including losses, convergence frequencies, ranks, singular values and logit matrices.

before.justification: V1 reports original qualitative experimental outcomes. Section 3.4 describes structures recovered in the authors' CE-DUFM experiments and states that Assumption 1 held in every observed DNC case, although no experimental figures or detailed protocols are supplied.

results.title: The Persistence of Neural Collapse Despite Low-Rank Bias

C1.justification: The central claim that constrained end-to-end learning can discover meaningful data structures remains. v2 adds introduction-level claims of competitiveness on FashionMNIST/SIFT and transfer of a learned CountMinSketch insight to a practical dataset (Section 1.2), modestly extending the claimed demonstrated scope.

C2.justification: Beyond v1's scale discussion, v2 explicitly examines neural inference and preprocessing overhead, explains why optimized quadratic attention can outperform linear attention, and discusses a high-skew frequency-estimation failure requiring suitable initialization (Section 5; Appendices C.7 and D). These materially qualify efficiency and the conditions under which learning succeeds.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code-repository link, the full CNN layer specification, input/output projection details, and fuller training-data and benchmarking documentation. However, v1's synthetic frequency-estimation universe size and Zipfian exponent are no longer specified for that experiment. The repository's actual availability cannot be verified from the PDFs.

E1.justification: v2 adds FashionMNIST and SIFT nearest-neighbor evaluation and tests modified CountMinSketch on CAIDA network traffic. These substantially broaden the represented data beyond v1's synthetic distributions and constructed MNIST tasks. Earlier Zipfian, extra-space, and MNIST frequency-estimation experiments remain in the appendices.

E2.justification: Table 1 adds ITQ, KMeans, and NeuralLSH to the existing hypersphere comparison, which previously used LSH and model ablations. The retained three-digit MNIST experiment gains a label-space oracle hashing comparator, labeled LSH, alongside binary search (Figure 19). These are substantive additions to evaluated comparator sets.

E3.justification: The reported maximum NN training budget changes from four million to two million steps; this does not establish that retained results were rerun. New protocols include FashionMNIST PCA preprocessing, 16-partition learned-hashing comparisons, CAIDA memory/delta sweeps, and throughput testing across dataset sizes, lookup budgets, and depths. SIFT dimensionality remains inconsistent between the 100D prose and Figure 17's 128D label.

E4.justification: v2 adds controlled linear-versus-quadratic attention comparisons (Figure 26), a FashionMNIST clustering example (Figure 18), and extensive computational-overhead sensitivity analysis (Appendix D.3). The CAIDA delta/memory sweep expands the investigation of reduced CountMinSketch updates, while v1's synthetic delta-validation plot, Figure 22, is removed.

E5.justification: Appendix B.2 adds three-seed plots for the 1D, 2D, and hypersphere experiments, and Appendix D.3 specifies averaging timings over ten trials. The checklist newly identifies bootstrapped confidence intervals. v1 already contains shaded uncertainty bands but does not give corresponding seed counts or a bootstrap explanation.

E6.justification: Substantial new results include E2E accuracies of 67.2% on FashionMNIST and 46.9% on SIFT (Table 1), CAIDA update-delta results (Figure 23), and throughput tables (Appendix D.3). These extend the evidence rather than establish same-setting performance gains over v1. The earlier synthetic CountMinSketch delta-validation curves are absent.

M1.justification: v2 adds a linear-attention Performer alternative to the data-processing transformer, evaluated in Appendix D.1. The core permutation-learning and query mechanisms remain intact. Shared query weights and reduced-delta CountMinSketch already appeared in v1; the newly specified CNN layers are additional documentation.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, results summary, and conclusion are extensively rewritten, with a broader Discussion section. Zipfian NN results, extra-space experiments, and frequency-estimation implementation details move into reorganized topical appendices. A contents list and conference checklist are also added.

P2.justification: v2 substantially reorganizes the displays: it combines LSH/MNIST visualizations in Figure 4, rearranges the k-d-tree heatmaps, converts v1's extra-space Figure 8 into Table 2, and adds comparison tables, seed plots, CAIDA figures, attention comparisons, and throughput tables. Numerous retained plots are resized or relocated.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands positioning against neural algorithmic reasoning and neural sketching, including Meta-sketch, Learning to Sketch, and Lego Sketch (Section 4; Appendix C.6). It distinguishes discovery with limited inductive biases from scalable sketching and relates the reduced-update insight to Aamand et al. These are substantive contextual additions.

T1.justification: The substantive mathematical formulations for nearest-neighbor search, lookups, hashing, and sketch updates are retained. Neither version provides formal theoretical results or proofs. Appendix C.7's new two-element failure explanation is presented as an informal mechanism hypothesis.

improvement.justification: The real-data comparisons against learned hashing methods and the CAIDA transfer experiment substantially strengthen v1's limited evidence beyond controlled examples. Runtime measurements, seed checks, fuller research positioning, and explicit failure conditions also make the framework's scope more assessable. These gains outweigh the removed synthetic delta-validation plot and settings, although inconsistencies such as SIFT dimensionality and the reversed CAIDA ratio-axis label reduce reporting precision.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same data-structure discovery framework. Their main text, figures, tables, equations, and complete appendices are readable and support comparison, including matching material moved or renumbered in v2.

after.justification: v2 retains original experimental results and adds real-data benchmarks, hashing comparisons, seed-variability plots, attention ablations, and throughput measurements.

before.justification: v1 reports original nearest-neighbor and streaming frequency-estimation experiments, including architectural ablations and analyses of learned structures.

results.title: Discovering Data Structures: Nearest Neighbor Search and Beyond

C1.justification: The central claims about complete PySC2 actions, multimodal observations, multi-agent support, and unreliable LLM decisions remain. v2 additionally claims query latency is independent of agent population and expands its stated empirical contribution to complete games, while retaining the platform's original purpose and novelty claims.

C2.justification: v1 recommends SMAC-based comparisons with reinforcement learning; v2 explicitly discourages direct comparisons because control frequencies differ. v2 also develops explanations involving detailed-control failures and uncritical trust in teammates, and newly interprets the retained Llama results as showing limited benefits from scaling beyond 70B parameters.

D1.justification: Appendices A-D add rollout/query pseudocode, retry handling, detailed action-to-function mappings, system prompts, observation and communication examples, system requirements, agent assignments, victory conditions, and difficulty specifications. These substantially extend v1's high-level implementation description. The code-access link remains unchanged, and newly documented settings do not automatically imply changed experiments.

E1.justification: v2 adds complete Simple64 games against seven opponent difficulty levels, requiring economic development, construction, and sustained military planning beyond v1's mini-scenarios. The original SMAC and eight custom task families remain documented, including 2s_vs_1sc in Appendix D despite its omitted numerical results.

E2.justification: The corresponding mini-scenario comparisons retain the same six LLMs for SMAC and nine for custom tasks. The new full-game table compares configurations using GPT-4o-mini. TextStarCraft II is discussed through a cited performance comparison, without a separately reported baseline evaluation.

E3.justification: v2 adds a full-game protocol using GPT-4o-mini, role-specific textual and image inputs, and three control/build configurations across seven difficulty levels. Table D1 also reports StarCraft II 9.0.14 (93333), whereas v1 reports 5.0.13 (92440). These descriptions do not establish that the retained mini-scenario results were rerun.

E4.justification: The new full-game mode comparisons investigate performance when detailed combat or building control is enabled. Appendix E substantially expands error analysis with combat, construction, skill-use, and collaboration cases supported by observations and responses. v1's coordinate-confusion example is retained within Figure E7 rather than being an entirely new analysis.

E5.justification: v2 reports 12 repetitions for the new full-game experiments. The original mini-scenario counts remain 20, or 50 for GPT-3.5-turbo. Neither version reports seeds, confidence intervals, or formal significance tests; no increase in repetitions for existing results is established.

E6.justification: v2 adds full-game winning rates: at difficulty level 3, Table 1 reports 92% for ECEB and 0% for both SCEB and ECSB. It also adds qualitative failure observations. Shared entries from v1's three result tables remain numerically unchanged, while the six 2s_vs_1sc result entries are omitted.

M1.justification: v2 introduces optional Easy Build and Easy Control variants that automate building placement or replace CombatGroup control with coarse Commander actions (Section 2.4 and Appendix B). The underlying observation wrappers, text-action interface, communication system, and concurrent LLM queries already existed in v1; their expanded documentation does not establish a wholesale architectural change.

P1.justification: The abstract and introduction are extensively rewritten, related-work discussion is integrated into the introduction, explicit contributions are listed, and the method sections are reordered with a dedicated multi-agent section. Experiments are reorganized around macro-decisions and micro-operations, with supporting material organized into five new appendices.

P2.justification: v2 redraws the framework and action diagrams, combines observation explanations, and adds contribution, multi-agent, and full-game illustrations. It also introduces extensive appendix tables and annotated examples. Existing benchmark tables are reordered and regrouped, and the original hallucination illustration is incorporated into a larger display.

R1.justification: v2 substantially broadens positioning to robotics, finance, workflow systems, and social simulation, and adds comparisons with SwarmBrain, VLMs Play StarCraft II, and SMAC-Hard. It also removes some earlier citations, including Weighted QMIX and Agent-Pro. This changes the research context beyond bibliographic updates to retained works.

T1.justification: v2's equations express the existing agent-environment interaction and existing KD/WR metrics. They add explanatory notation rather than substantive mathematical reasoning. Neither version presents theoretical results, proofs, or a formal latency analysis.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses substantial validation and documentation gaps: complete-game experiments test capabilities not evaluated in v1, while Appendices A-D make the interface, prompts, and task conditions much more inspectable. Appendix E strengthens failure diagnoses with concrete traces. The unmeasured constant-latency claim, inconsistent task-4 enemy specifications in Tables D5-D6, and omitted 2s_vs_1sc scores limit the gains, but do not outweigh the substantial improvement in empirical support and reproducibility information.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe LLM-PySC2 and retain identifiable methods, scenarios, and result tables. The complete documents are readable, including v2's Appendices A-E; v1 ends with references and has no appendices.

after.justification: v2 retains original benchmark results in Tables 2-4 and adds full-game experiments in Table 1 and observed failure cases in Appendix E.

before.justification: v1 reports original repeated StarCraft II evaluations of LLMs, including kill/death ratios and winning rates in Tables 1-3.

results.title: LLM-PySC2: Starcraft II learning environment for Large Language Models

C1.justification: V1 foregrounds the randomized minimax guarantee; v2 foregrounds the round-robin, instance-dependent guarantee while retaining the randomized result. V2 adds a principal claim of O(log(T)) communication rounds with regret O(R log(A)/m + A log(A) log(T)), where R is the single-agent gap-dependent bound. It also explicitly reframes the core contribution as a new analysis of an existing cooperative SE variant.

C2.justification: V2 adds qualifications about when randomized selection improves the bound, why the main lower bound concerns the existence of a hard agent, and how diameter terms behave on grids and cycles. Section 8 identifies simultaneously achieving small messages and few communication rounds as unresolved. The central interpretation of diameter independence and the open additive dependence on A remain.

D1.justification: V2 makes the empirical-mean input explicit in detailed Coop-SE pseudocode, revises message fields to omit certain timestamps, and adds field-by-field message-size accounting in Lemma 25. Algorithms 4 and 12–13 document clustering, counters, and forwarding for the new protocol. Neither version supplies executable code, hardware details, or runtime measurements.

E1.justification: Neither version uses datasets or executes training or evaluation scenarios. V2's additional communication constraints and graph examples are theoretical settings, not empirical coverage.

E2.justification: Neither version empirically evaluates comparison methods. V2 Table 1 compares theoretical guarantees for Coop-UCB2, DDUCB, UCB-TCOM, and the proposed variants; this changes research positioning rather than evaluated baseline membership.

E3.justification: Neither version reports experimental splits, evaluation metrics, training budgets, or testing procedures. Changes to mathematical communication models and assumptions are covered under M1 and T1.

E4.justification: Neither version contains empirical ablations, robustness tests, sensitivity studies, or error analyses. The additional graph arguments and algorithm analyses in v2 are formal theoretical developments.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated experimental runs, seeds, error bars, or significance tests. Algorithmic confidence bounds and probabilistic proof events do not constitute experimental uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Neither version reports empirical scores, rankings, or qualitative experimental outcomes. Added and revised analytical regret and communication bounds are assessed under T1.

M1.justification: V2 introduces Coop-SE-Comm-Cost, using growing tree clusters and phased information gathering, synchronization, and sampling (Algorithms 4 and 13). Main Coop-SE and the CONGEST variant now select actions round-robin rather than uniformly. Round-robin was already mentioned in v1 Remark 1, and the randomized variant remains in v2 Appendix F. Coop-SE-CONGEST develops the existing Coop-SE-Low-Comm rather than being entirely new.

P1.justification: The introduction, contribution narrative, proof sketch, communication discussion, and concluding section are extensively rewritten. The warm-up proof moves to Appendix D, additional related work to Appendix A, and the retained randomized analysis to Appendix F. Appendices are reorganized around separate algorithm variants, and a NeurIPS checklist is added.

P2.justification: V2 adds the multi-column theoretical comparison Table 1 and removes v1 Figure 1 illustrating implicit synchronization. Main-text algorithm displays are substantially simplified, detailed algorithms are regrouped in Appendix J, and new algorithm boxes are added. NeurIPS typesetting changes typography, title treatment, spacing, and display placement throughout.

R1.justification: New Section 1.3 explicitly connects Coop-SE to prior cooperative SE algorithms by Yang and Zhang and limits the novelty claim to its analysis. The earlier claim of resolving Kolla's question becomes a complementary contribution. Section 1.4 and Table 1 substantially expand comparisons of graph dependence, communication, and required graph knowledge, with added references including Zhang et al. and distributed averaging work.

T1.justification: V2 Appendix E supplies the round-robin analysis omitted in v1 Remark 1 and adds a diameter-sensitive refinement in Theorem 7. Appendix H.2 introduces clustering lemmas and amortized regret and communication-count proofs for the new phased algorithm. The CONGEST guarantees are revised, including the claimed message bound from O(log(mTA)) to O(log(mA)). Section 2 adds the assumption m, A <= poly(T). V1's randomized analysis is retained in Appendix F.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially improves theoretical completeness by developing the round-robin result that v1 left without proof and providing a constructive protocol and detailed analysis for limited communication rounds. Its explicit acknowledgment of prior cooperative SE algorithms also makes the contribution more precise. A drawback is the new abstract's omission of the log(A) factor present in Theorem 5 and the contribution list. This reporting inconsistency does not outweigh the substantial gains in analytical support and research positioning.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same cooperative stochastic bandit research, with shared authors, model, algorithms, and regret analysis. The main text, mathematical material, displays, and complete appendices support comparison despite substantial reorganization and extensions.

after.justification: V2 remains theoretical throughout its main text and appendices. Table 1 compares analytical guarantees, and the NeurIPS checklist explicitly confirms that the paper contains no experiments.

before.justification: V1 reports algorithms, theoretical regret bounds, and proofs. Neither the main text nor appendices contain original experiments, simulations, or data analyses.

results.title: Individual Regret in Cooperative Stochastic Multi-Armed Bandits

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same framework, dataset, and data-engine contributions and claims about generalization, robustness, and explainability. The headline 24.7% localization and 35.8% explanation-score improvements are unchanged; new experiments support the existing claims.

C2.justification: Beyond v1's computational-cost and evaluator limitations, Appendix E explains semantic errors despite correct localization and failures on small manipulations in complex scenes, and qualifies STS as measuring similarity rather than correctness. Appendix C attributes FakeShield's weak full-set results to missed detections and distinguishes these from conditional localization performance.

D1.justification: v2 adds dataset counts, sources, and manipulation types in Table 8, FakeShield implementation provenance, and statements that code, data, and weights have been released, with application-controlled data access. Conversely, v1 Appendix B.2 and Figure 17's authentic-image training-text construction details are removed. Existing hardware and optimization details move to Appendix D.1 unchanged.

E1.justification: The training sources, six public test datasets, ForgeryAnalysis subsets, and manipulation types remain unchanged. The added similarity scoring, human evaluation, and classification results examine existing data and capabilities; they do not establish new dataset or task coverage.

E2.justification: v2 adds FakeShield, a direct multimodal forgery-detection competitor absent from v1, across localization and explanation evaluations in Appendix C, Tables 9–12. This fills a substantive comparator gap beyond the retained traditional detectors and general multimodal models.

E3.justification: v2 adds STS evaluation using three sentence-embedding models, human scoring by 14 volunteers with 30 random samples each, and image-level classification accuracy. FakeShield evaluation introduces zero masks for images classified as real and a separate true-positive-only protocol. Existing training settings and dataset splits are retained.

E4.justification: The existing component/data ablations and NIST16 distortion tests are unchanged. v2 adds focused analyses of FakeShield's missed detections versus conditional localization, qualitative comparisons, and semantic-description and small-manipulation failures. v1's short successful-example panel in Figure 6 is removed, while its detailed appendix comparisons are retained.

E5.justification: v2 Section 5.1 and the checklist newly state that stochastic evaluations are conducted twice and averaged. v1 does not specify this run count. This is additional reporting, not evidence of increased repetitions; no error bars, confidence intervals, or significance-test results are added.

E6.justification: The original localization, robustness, and ablation numbers are unchanged. New results include MiniLM-L6 STS scores of 0.926 for ForgerySleuth and 0.725 for GPT-4o, FakeShield's GPT-graded overall score of 5.55, human overall ratings of 9.44 for ForgerySleuth and 7.18 for GPT-4o, and classification accuracies of 0.989 on Columbia and 0.910 on CASIA1. These are additional evaluations, not improvements to the earlier same-setting scores.

M1.justification: Both versions retain the same multimodal LLM, frozen SAM backbone, constrained-convolution trace encoder, three-layer fusion mechanism, training stages, and text/mask losses. The redrawn architecture and expanded explanations do not establish an algorithmic revision. Removal of authentic-image training documentation does not establish that the procedure changed.

P1.justification: v2 makes localized wording and affiliation edits, clarifies the data-engine description, moves implementation details and limitations into dedicated appendix sections, reorganizes the appendices, and adds a NeurIPS checklist. The main section sequence and much of the prose remain unchanged.

P2.justification: v2 switches the paper from two-column to single-column layout, redraws the dataset and architecture diagrams, and incorporates the former separate fusion diagram into Figure 3. It adds evaluation and dataset tables and new comparison/failure figures, removes two example panels, and substantially relocates and resizes retained displays.

R1.justification: v2 adds FakeShield and Sentence-BERT references. Section 2.2 and Appendix C acknowledge concurrent FakeShield and explain differences in structured reasoning, expert verification, and trace-feature fusion. This is a focused positioning addition; the broader related-work account remains intact.

T1.justification: Equations 1–9 retain the same model formulation, losses, and convolution-kernel constraints. Neither version presents theoretical guarantees or proofs, and the added STS evaluation introduces no new formal derivation.

improvement.justification: v1's explanation-quality evaluation relied on GPT-4 grading and lacked a direct multimodal forgery competitor. v2 substantially strengthens this central evidence through human evaluation, complementary STS scoring, and FakeShield comparisons, while documenting concrete failure modes. These gains improve validation and qualification of the claims, outweighing the loss of authentic-image training documentation, although statistical uncertainty remains inadequately reported.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe ForgerySleuth and ForgeryAnalysis. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support reliable matching despite substantial reformatting and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds semantic textual similarity scores, FakeShield comparisons, human evaluations, classification accuracies, and failure cases.

before.justification: v1 reports original manipulation localization, explanation evaluation, robustness tests, ablations, and qualitative results in Section 5 and Appendix C.

results.title: ForgerySleuth: Empowering Multimodal Large Language Models for Image Manipulation Detection

C1.justification: The model-agnostic detection claim remains, but v2 adds a central contribution concerning sandbagging without explicit underperformance instructions. Its abstract and introduction specifically claim detection and full performance recovery in the Mistral Large no-goal setting, extending v1's emphasis on prompted and fine-tuned concealment.

C2.justification: v2 develops an interpretation based on reduced incentive-related deliberation in reasoning traces and emphasizes recovering concrete examples of capability alongside detection. It adds substantive limitations concerning absent competing baselines, reliance on one no-goal case, and prompt brittleness, and recommends complementary defenses. v1's proposed extensions to backdoors and sycophancy are removed.

D1.justification: v2 adds an explicit implementation-repository link, reports Inspect integration, and documents vLLM use, LoRA rank, GSM8k prompts, prefilled tool interactions, control notes, and additional model identifiers. Appendix G extends hardware and cost reporting to the new experiments, including an eight-A100 configuration for Mistral Large. These materially expand reproduction information; repository contents were not externally verified.

E1.justification: GSM8k, proposed only as future work in v1, becomes an evaluated open-ended mathematical reasoning task in v2. The new no-goal scenario also changes the input environment through deployment incentives without explicit instructions to underperform. MMLU, AI2, WMDP, and BoolQ coverage is retained.

E2.justification: Appendix F.1 adds an evaluated linear classifier comparator to XGBoost. The existing password-locked Mistral experiment gains a password-present standard comparator, where v1 Table 1 reported 'Not applicable.' These are limited additions; v2 still lacks comparisons against competing sandbagging-detection techniques.

E3.justification: v2 replaces the classifier's fixed held-out evaluation with leave-one-model-out cross-validation and reports accuracy and weighted F1. It adds DeepSeek Math and Mistral Large configurations, a controlled 30-question no-goal protocol, and fixed-noise experiments sampling up to 100 vectors. The password-locked plot's reported noise sweep also changes from 0–0.00075 in steps of 0.000075 to 0–0.001 in steps of 0.00005.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained prompt-length control, v2 adds performance recovery versus seed count, classifier sensitivity to one through five trials, individual-trial success probabilities, model-specific error analysis, and a direct-versus-LoRA comparison (Figure 4, Appendix E, Appendix F). The no-goal case adds reasoning-trace analysis and a reported prompt-brittleness check.

E5.justification: The main Welch-test, Benjamini-Hochberg, and standard-error framework is retained. v2 newly reports uncertainty for the previously single-measurement BoolQ results, reports five rather than two seeds for the password-locked plot, and defines standard-deviation bands across five 100-seed experiments in Figure 4.

E6.justification: The original 15 main multiple-choice improvement-ratio pairs are retained, but substantial new results appear. These include Mistral Large improving from 66.6% to 100% on 30 GSM8k questions and reported classifier accuracy of 96.2% under the new cross-validation protocol. Table 1 replaces BoolQ ratios of 1.000/1.259 with 1.05/1.21 and the password-locked sandbagging ratio of 2.737 with 3.12; changed repetitions and procedures prevent interpreting these as same-setting performance changes.

M1.justification: v2 introduces LoRA-based noise injection alongside v1's direct weight perturbation. This new procedure modifies linear-layer parameters through rank-8 adapters and is used for password-locked and no-goal experiments (Section 3.1). The improvement-ratio feature and XGBoost classifier remain.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, and discussion undergo substantial rewriting. Methods becomes four numbered subsections, discussion and conclusion are separated, the standalone social-impact section disappears, and the appendices are reorganized and expanded. These are extensive narrative and structural changes.

P2.justification: v2 changes the main text from two columns to one and substantially expands the visual presentation. v1 Figures 1–3 survive as v2 Figures 2, 3, and 5. New displays include the conceptual illustration, seed-sampling curves, no-goal setup and results, LoRA comparison, and supplementary Tables 2–4; the password-locked plot is replaced with a multi-seed comparison including standard performance.

R1.justification: v2 substantially revises positioning around demonstrated sandbagging and alignment faking, adding Meinke et al., alignment-faking work, Poser, The Elicitation Game, and linear-probe research. It frames noise injection as a complementary defense and removes portions of v1's situational-awareness and backdoor literature discussion. These changes go beyond bibliography updates.

T1.justification: Appendix E adds a mathematical treatment absent from v1: LoRA perturbation expansion, independence assumptions, variance calculations, and a rank-dependent scaling postulate yielding sigma_LoRA = r^(1/4) sqrt(sigma_direct). This substantially expands the mathematical content, although the asserted equivalence in Section 3.1 depends on a postulate rather than being established by the variance calculation alone.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens v1's narrow empirical validation through open-ended reasoning, a controlled no-goal case, broader classifier validation, and analyses of noise-sampling reliability.
