Fuller protocols and implementation information also improve reproducibility. These gains address important gaps in generalization and robustness evidence. Qualifications remain: the no-goal case is small and prompt-sensitive, Appendix E does not establish the claimed mathematical equivalence, and some reporting is inconsistent, such as Table 2 claiming consistent XGBoost superiority despite its lower one-trial accuracy.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same noise-injection study. Their complete text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support comparison, including matching retained material across extensive reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds GSM8k evaluations, a Mistral Large no-goal experiment, classifier comparisons, and noise-sampling analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original noise-injection experiments on prompted and password-locked models, classifier evaluations, and prompt-length controls in Table 1 and Appendices A and C.

results.title: Noise Injection Reveals Hidden Capabilities of Sandbagging Language Models

C1.justification: The central claim that temporal forecasting improves unsupervised LiDAR representation learning remains. v2 emphasizes a LiDAR-specific decoder, changes the advertised relative improvement from up to 90% to up to 400%, and removes v1's explicit first-work claim. Segmentation becomes prominent in the abstract, although its effectiveness was already claimed in v1's appendix.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations concerning nuisance suppression, training stability, forecasting-horizon predictability, decoder choice, and complementarity with image priors. Appendix I newly identifies the absence of explicit semantic modeling as a limitation. The pedestrian-shape explanation was already present in v1 and is largely restated.

D1.justification: v2 newly discloses GPU counts, batch size, ego-motion sources, the four-frame horizon, and pretraining timing, and supplies a project link while still promising release. Curriculum epochs and the 0.9 masking rate are relocated disclosures. Conversely, v1's Cylinder3D encoder adaptation, MMDetection3D implementation, and best-mIoU checkpoint-selection details are omitted.

E1.justification: The four benchmark datasets and both downstream tasks are retained: SemanticKITTI segmentation already appeared in v1 Appendix B. v2 modestly expands the evaluated input regime through NuScenes comparisons explicitly using 2D image priors to pretrain LiDAR encoders (Appendix G).

E2.justification: v2 adds ALSO and Occupancy-MAE, introduces five pretrained comparators into the previously scratch-versus-TREND Once comparison, and adds UniPAD on Waymo and Occupancy-MAE/UniPAD on SemanticKITTI. Appendix G additionally evaluates first-stage LiMoE and Sonata, spelled Sonota in the text. SLiDR is cited there but has no reported comparison result.

E3.justification: The principal datasets, label fractions, and convergence-matched fine-tuning approach remain. Added protocols test 3/4/5-frame horizons, 80/90/95% masking, alternative ray-sampling controls, curriculum removal, and decoder substitutions; forecasting range error is also evaluated (Appendices D–F). The default-budget NuScenes and 20%/100% Once comparisons reported in v1 are omitted.

E4.justification: The original component ablation is retained, while v2 adds substantial tests of decoder choice, forecasting horizon, curriculum learning, masking, and ground filtering/sampling. Moving-versus-static feature visualizations and forecast-versus-observation examples add diagnostic evidence absent from v1 (Figure 3 and Appendices D–F).

E5.justification: v1 provides no repeated-run or seed information. v2 states that main experiments use a fixed seed and reports five repetitions with means and standard deviations for random initialization, UniPAD, and TREND on Once with 20% labels (Appendix B, Table 7). This introduces uncertainty estimation, although the caption inconsistently calls the dispersion variance and coverage remains limited to one setting.

E6.justification: v2 adds extensive comparator, repeated-evaluation, sensitivity, and forecasting results. The Once 100%-label TREND entry changes from 65.66 to 66.09 mAP alongside the revised method description, rather than establishing a same-method performance gain. NuScenes 33.17 mAP and SemanticKITTI 31.12 mIoU are retained. Several default-budget and per-class entries disappear, and Waymo results are replaced by aggregate reporting.

M1.justification: v1 uses a range-only reconstruction loss. v2 adds an intensity prediction head using ray-direction and point features, plus intensity-error and zero-surface-SDF penalties (Sections 3.3–3.4, Equations 10–11). These substantively change the model outputs and pretraining objective; recurrent embedding and curriculum learning remain.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and related-work discussion are substantially rewritten. Once precedes NuScenes, experimental discussions are consolidated, and segmentation moves from the appendix into the main text. The appendix structure is extensively reorganized, with new discussion, limitations, acknowledgments, and checklist material.

P2.justification: The document changes from two-column to single-column presentation. Figure 1 is redrawn and relocated, Figure 2 incorporates the revised decoder, and new feature/forecast visualizations appear. Tables gain comparator rows, lose or aggregate class-level detail, and are reorganized into different layouts; repeated-evaluation and image-prior comparison tables are added.

R1.justification: v2 removes the CAD-model pretraining survey and substantially expands positioning against image-prior methods, ViDAR, occupancy approaches, newer scene-flow work, and Gaussian-splatting decoders. It also introduces information-bottleneck literature and reframes the decoder contribution around LiDAR-specific geometry and intensity modeling.

T1.justification: New Section 3.6 introduces sufficient/minimal representations, an information-bottleneck objective, a nuisance-variable causal chain, and a mutual-information inequality. This adds mathematical reasoning beyond v1's method equations, but supplies no accompanying proof or established TREND-specific guarantee.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens empirical support through direct competitors across the retained benchmarks, repeated-evaluation evidence, and controlled decoder and sensitivity studies (Tables 1–7; Appendices B, D, F, G). These address important gaps in v1's comparisons and robustness evidence. Added resource disclosures also improve assessability. The gains outweigh omitted segmentation implementation details and class-level results, although uncertainty labeling is inconsistent and the new information-theoretic discussion remains unproved.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe TREND and contain readable main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices. Their shared methods and experiments can be matched despite substantial reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains original detection and segmentation experiments and adds baseline comparisons, repeated evaluations, sensitivity studies, and forecasting analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original detection experiments on NuScenes, Once, and Waymo, component ablations, and SemanticKITTI segmentation results in Appendix B.

results.title: TREND: Unsupervised 3D Representation Learning via Temporal Forecasting for LiDAR Perception

C1.justification: The central claims about higher-order convolution, optimal third/fourth-order expansions, and distinctive representations remain. The novelty claim is qualified: v1 emphasizes fundamentally differing through embedding higher-order operations inside convolution, whereas v2 acknowledges extending and complementing earlier Volterra approaches and emphasizes higher-order analysis and mechanistic insights.

C2.justification: v1 already acknowledges computational overhead and sensitivity to targeted perturbations. v2 develops quantitative computation and memory limitations, distinguishes targeted statistical sensitivity from common-corruption robustness, interprets depth scaling and fine-grained results, and discusses possible complementarity with attention. Sections 5.1–5.2 substantially expand applicability boundaries and future directions.

D1.justification: v1 promises code release upon publication; v2 Appendix A.1 supplies a code-repository link. v2 also documents GPU types, training-time estimates, concrete symmetry savings, and detailed CUB optimization, augmentation, and training-budget information. These materially improve the documented reproduction path, although the repository itself was not inspected.

E1.justification: v2 adds full ImageNet, CUB-200-2011 fine-grained bird classification, and common-corruption scenarios on CIFAR-10-C and CIFAR-100-C. The original synthetic textures, MNIST, FashionMNIST, CIFAR datasets, and Imagenette remain. Imagenette moves to Appendix A.6 rather than being removed.

E2.justification: v2 Table 4 adds ResNet-18/34/50 comparisons on the four smaller benchmarks, substantially expanding experiments previously centered on shallow CNNs and a deeper plain CNN. The existing Imagenette comparisons with ResNet-18 and VOneNet are retained. The expanded discussion of prior Volterra methods does not introduce empirical comparisons against those methods.

E3.justification: New evaluation designs include a FLOP-controlled CIFAR-10 comparison, ResNet depth scaling, and normalized corruption accuracy, with severity-1 results tabulated. ImageNet and CUB introduce additional training protocols; CUB specifies 224-pixel inputs, augmented training, momentum SGD, cosine scheduling, and 100 epochs. These supplement the retained small-benchmark and Imagenette settings.

E4.justification: Appendices A.2, A.4, A.5, and A.8 add computational profiling and FLOP controls, depth-scaling analysis, common-corruption robustness tests, and qualitative bird-classification error analysis. Earlier placement, kernel-size, nonlinearity, targeted-perturbation, and representation analyses are retained.

E5.justification: v2 specifies five independent ImageNet runs with mean and standard deviation and explicitly identifies CUB results as single-run. Table 2 now distinguishes benchmark-specific run counts. The original 50-run small-benchmark protocol and single-run Imagenette status remain; the latter was already disclosed in v1 Appendix A.3. No specified significance test or confidence-interval procedure is added.

E6.justification: Original benchmark and perturbation scores are retained. New results include ImageNet accuracy of 69.47 ± 0.09% for HoResNet-18 versus 68.62 ± 0.08% for ResNet-18, and CUB accuracy of 72.31% versus 68.24%. Tables 3–6 additionally report FLOP-controlled performance, ResNet scaling, and corruption outcomes. These are added experimental results, not same-setting improvements over v1.

M1.justification: The Volterra-style convolution, independent weights across orders, normalization, and early-layer higher-order blocks are retained. The additional ResNet evaluations apply the existing approach to different model configurations; no new higher-order operator, objective, or inference procedure is documented.

P1.justification: The abstract is substantially compressed, biological motivation and related work are rewritten, and the discussion is reorganized into limitations and future directions. Imagenette moves from the main experiments to the appendix, supplementary sections are reorganized, and a NeurIPS checklist is added. These changes substantially revise the narrative and document structure.

P2.justification: Figure 1 gains a texture inset, Figure 3 simplifies the full-network diagrams into block comparisons, and Figure 4 removes its distance-distribution panel while that analysis remains in Figure 11. New tables display computational, scaling, corruption, and CUB results; Imagenette receives a separate appendix table. The document also adopts a different conference layout.

R1.justification: Section 1.1 substantially revises positioning relative to Zoumpourlis and Roheda, adds Li et al.'s Volterra-convolution work, and distinguishes contributions through expansion order and analysis. Section 5.2 adds substantive comparison with Vision Transformers. Dataset and corruption references are added, while several biological and adversarial-analysis citations are removed.

T1.justification: The polynomial formulations, tied-weight expansion, symmetry-based parameter formula, normalization, and asymptotic complexity expressions are retained. Neither version supplies formal theorems or proofs. v2's numerical symmetry savings and FLOP measurements add implementation and computational evidence rather than new mathematical reasoning.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses v1's limited evidence for large-scale applicability and computational fairness through five-run ImageNet evaluation, deeper-network comparisons, and FLOP controls. Corruption tests, more precise novelty positioning, explicit limitations, and documented code access further strengthen assessment and reproducibility. Single-run CUB results and unexplained uncertainty terms in Tables 5–6 limit some additions, but the expanded validation and transparency provide a substantial overall quality gain.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same higher-order convolution study. The main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable matching of retained, relocated, and added content.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds ImageNet, fine-grained bird classification, corruption robustness, computational benchmarking, and ResNet scaling results.

before.justification: v1 reports original texture-classification and image-benchmark experiments, architectural ablations, perturbation tests, and representation analyses.

results.title: Convolution goes higher-order: a biologically inspired mechanism empowers image classification

C1.justification: V2 explicitly frames the contribution as improving spatial/depth perception without harming general reasoning, including in the introduction and conclusion. The central probing and distillation contributions, single-encoder inference claim, and headline gains of 2.5% overall and 8.7% on depth are retained.

C2.justification: V2 adds interpretations of encoder-free models' layerwise behavior, projector information loss, and task-dependent correlations, including negative correlations for distance estimation. It explicitly acknowledges stronger multi-encoder depth performance and untested scaling to large LLMs. However, it removes v1's explicit caveats about inferior background-depth reconstruction and both models' background-segmentation failures.

D1.justification: V2 supplies reproducibility details for the added experiments, including timing hardware, batch size, Cambrian-1 training controls, and Chameleon answer extraction. It adds a reference to LLaVA-1.5 for remaining hyperparameters and changes the front-page repository link from OLA-VLM to VisPer-LM. The original method's principal implementation settings remain documented and unchanged.

E1.justification: V2 adds evaluations on POPE, GQA, MMMU, and VizWiz in Table 2, plus BLINK spatial-relation, relative-depth, and counting tasks in Table X. These expand the evaluated data and task coverage, including object hallucination, multidisciplinary reasoning, and questions from blind users. The original training datasets and evaluation benchmarks remain.

E2.justification: V2 adds RADIO-ViT-L-based LLaVA-1.5 and a data-matched Cambrian-1 to Table 1, beyond v1's single-encoder and feature/token-concatenation baselines. Table XII additionally compares Chameleon-7B and EVE-7B. These methods were discussed or cited in v1 but were not participants in its reported comparisons.

E3.justification: New experiments introduce SigLIP-SO400M configurations, Cambrian-1 training with the matched LLaVA datasets and batch size 512, and Qwen-2.5-72B-Instruct extraction of Chameleon's multiple-choice answers. V2 also introduces batch-one forward-pass timing on an A100 GPU and direct projector-output probing. The original method's PT/IFT budgets and probing protocol remain unchanged.

E4.justification: V2 adds throughput analysis, direct testing of the improved-projector hypothesis, encoder-free model probing, and correlations between probe quality and benchmark performance across six models. Conversely, v1's full layer-position sweep in Figure 5 is removed, as are two layer-set configurations and the special-token ablations at 4 and 12 tokens. Most other ablations are retained, sometimes relocated.

E5.justification: V2 first reports means and standard deviations across ten runs for the new throughput experiment in Table VIII. V1 contains no corresponding repeated-run uncertainty reporting. This addition is limited to timing; the retained accuracy tables do not acquire seed-based uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: The original Table 1 scores and downstream probe scores remain unchanged, but v2 adds substantial results. For example, Table X reports BLINK averages of 58.8 for VisPer-LM and 55.6 for LLaVA-1.5, while Table VIII reports throughput of 9.86 versus 5.32 samples/second for VisPer-LM and the multi-encoder baseline. Additional benchmark, projector, and correlation results are new; several ablation entries are removed.

M1.justification: The renamed method retains the same teacher encoders, Perceiver embedding predictors, special task tokens, Smooth-L1 and contrastive losses, training stages, and single-encoder inference. The revised explanation and notation do not establish a change to the proposed procedure.

P1.justification: The title and method name change, and the abstract, introduction, and substantial portions of the explanatory prose are rewritten. Downstream probe evaluation and several analyses move into the appendix, which gains dedicated projector, encoder-free probing, and correlation sections. Future work is integrated into a limitations-and-future-work discussion within the conclusion.

P2.justification: V2 replaces the two-column presentation with a single-column conference layout and extensively resizes and relocates tables and figures. It adds benchmark, timing, projector, and correlation displays, removes the layer-sweep figure, and reduces the generation-probe montage. Retained results such as v1 Table 8 become appendix displays rather than new evidence.

R1.justification: V2 adds connections to pause-token and implicit-chain-of-thought research, newer representation analyses, and the additional benchmarks, while removing some earlier references such as PaliGemma and MAE. It sharpens the limited-data comparison with encoder distillation, but retains the original related-work organization and fundamental novelty positioning.

T1.justification: V1's grouped loss formulation is equivalently reorganized into Equations 1–4 in v2. Neither version supplies theoretical propositions or proofs, and v2's explanations of representation quality and layer selection do not introduce substantive formal mathematics.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens evidence for the central claims through additional perception/general-reasoning benchmarks, controlled RADIO and Cambrian comparisons, measured inference throughput, and direct projector probing. This reduces v1's reliance on one primary perception benchmark and indirect efficiency/mechanism evidence. The gains outweigh trimmed ablations and removed failure caveats, although the new correlation reporting needs correction: Appendix D states 0.80 for depth-probe versus Relation performance, while Table XIII and Figure V show 0.70.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research, renamed from OLA-VLM to VisPer-LM. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable matching despite extensive reformatting and reorganization.

after.justification: V2 retains original experimental results and adds benchmark comparisons, throughput measurements, projector probing, encoder-free model evaluations, and correlation analyses.

before.justification: V1 reports original benchmark evaluations, layerwise probing, training and architecture ablations, and downstream probe results, including Tables 1–8 and appendix analyses.

results.title: Elevating Visual Perception in Multimodal LLMs with Visual Embedding Distillation

C1.justification: V1 centers its contribution on more precise and stable certification against poisoning. V2's abstract, introduction and conclusion broaden this to natural data errors, categorical data and structured perturbations, explicitly claiming support for threat models unavailable to prior methods. Precision and stability remain contributions, but the claimed scientific scope expands substantially.

C2.justification: V2 adds interpretations connecting missingness and reporting bias to prediction robustness, and explains computational cost through activation switches and solver branching. Its discussion emphasizes practical applications and additional scalability strategies. Although computational expense remains acknowledged, v1's explicit warning that costs may be prohibitive for large models and its emphasis on smaller models are softened.

D1.justification: V2 adds an implementation repository address, Gurobi 10.0.1 and licensing information, dataset generation and split details, and baseline-preprocessing clarification concerning class separation and polynomial features. V1 already supplied architecture, learning-rate, batch-size and hardware defaults. The additional Two-Moons details are disclosures, not sufficient evidence that its underlying settings changed.

E1.justification: V1 evaluates only synthetic Two-Moons classification. V2 retains it and adds binary and three-class Iris, Breast Cancer Wisconsin, and NPHA medical survey classification. NPHA introduces categorical inputs and distinct scenarios involving missing mental-health values, missing values across features, and optimistic self-reporting.

E2.justification: The Two-Moons accuracy comparators remain FullCert and Sosnin et al. V2 additionally compares runtime against FullCert and Sosnin's IBP/CROWN variants in Appendix E.2, whereas v1 reports only its own method's runtime. BagFlip's inclusion in the new capability table is qualitative positioning, not an added empirical baseline.

E3.justification: V2 adds dataset-specific evaluation splits and perturbation settings, batch-size controls, and one-epoch width/depth sweeps. NPHA introduces certification rate and describes certified accuracy conditional on certification, unlike the all-test-sample definition retained for Two-Moons. Runtime reporting changes from a ten-epoch trajectory to first-five-epoch averages; this does not establish that the retained timing experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's perturbation-radius and epoch-runtime analysis, v2 adds solver-branch sensitivity to batch size and radius (Table 5), network-width and depth runtime ablations (Tables 6–7), and controlled missingness/reporting-bias case studies (Section 5.2). The detailed ten-epoch timing trajectory is removed rather than simply relocated.

E5.justification: Both versions report Two-Moons means and standard deviations. However, v2 removes v1's explicit 5–10-run statement and Appendix B's ten-run, matched-seed description, referring instead to unspecified iid seeds. This reduces reporting specificity without establishing a change in the number of runs actually performed.

E6.justification: V1 Table 1 and v2 Table 2 report Sosnin et al.'s accuracies as 85.6%, 84.0%, 44.9% versus 83.8%, 82.3%, 69.0%, respectively; the proposed method and FullCert values remain unchanged. The PDFs do not explain the numerical revision. V2 adds UCI, NPHA, branching and architecture results, while replacing per-epoch timing entries with five-epoch summaries and baseline timings.

M1.justification: The per-step optimization and parameter-bound relaxation remain, but v2 substantially expands the constraint formulation. Section 5.2 introduces integer constraints for categorical missing values and conditional adjacent-category perturbations, beyond v1's norm-bounded continuous inputs. Appendix C also introduces convolution and sigmoid/tanh relaxation encodings. These extend the supported method beyond its renaming.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, formal setup, complexity discussion and conclusion are substantially rewritten. BiCert/BMIP becomes MIBP-Cert/MIBP, definitions precede the worked example, an explicit contribution list is introduced, and algorithm explanations move to Appendix B. Implementation material is reorganized into Section 3.4 and Appendix D.

P2.justification: V2 adds a capability matrix, a three-part UCI table, NPHA results, branching counts and architecture/runtime tables. The original timing table is replaced by differently structured summaries and comparisons. Figure 1 is retained but resized and placed beside text; the algorithms move to the appendix and are reformatted within the new conference layout.

R1.justification: V2 expands positioning from tighter bounds than existing certifiers to uniquely combining deterministic certification, continuous/categorical features and complex constraints. New Table 1 explicitly contrasts these capabilities with FullCert, Sosnin et al. and BagFlip. Optimization, health-bias and dataset references are added, while foundation-model poisoning references are removed; the basic ensemble-versus-bound taxonomy remains.

T1.justification: V1 Definition 1 restricts dataset perturbations to input norm balls with unchanged labels. V2 Definition 3.1 replaces this with a general constraint over datasets, permitting coupled inputs, labels, integer variables and global restrictions. Appendix C adds explicit activation bounds, and Section 5.3 adds reasoning about binary-decision counts and search complexity. The underlying iterative soundness argument is retained.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially addresses v1's narrow empirical support: real tabular and multiclass evaluations, together with explicit categorical-corruption case studies, test applicability beyond synthetic Two-Moons. Comparative runtime and architecture analyses make computational tradeoffs more assessable, while dataset details and a code location strengthen reproducibility information. These gains outweigh the loss of explicit run counts and late-epoch timing detail, although large-model scalability remains unestablished.

A1.justification: Both PDFs are readable in full, including their appendices, equations, figures and tables. Shared authors, certification framework, worked example and Two-Moons experiments establish continuity despite the rename from BiCert to MIBP-Cert.

after.justification: Section 5 and Appendix E report original results on Two-Moons, Iris, Breast Cancer and NPHA, together with solver-complexity and architecture experiments.

before.justification: Section 5 reports original Two-Moons certified-accuracy and training-runtime experiments in Tables 1–2.

results.title: MIBP-Cert: Certified Training against Data Perturbations with Mixed-Integer Bilinear Programs

C1.justification: V2 explicitly frames DPA as a single metric for classification and model selection, claiming it removes the need for multiple metrics to check directionality, sign, and balanced-data behavior. The underlying contribution claims about these capabilities, normalization, and attacker robustness are retained.

C2.justification: New Section 5.2 explains that aggregation can hide opposing effects for individual attribute–task pairs. The hiring example is revised to equal acceptance rates with unequal counts and adds an explicit warning about under-reporting amplification. V2 also develops model-selection applications and interpretations involving unlabeled background cues and shortcuts.

D1.justification: Appendix I newly documents the inverse-cross-entropy quality function and attacker optimizers, learning rates, epochs, batch sizes, and depths. Appendices D.2 and F add robustness-network and shortcut construction/training details. These substantially expand reproducibility information. V1's forthcoming-code statement disappears; neither PDF supplies a code link.

E1.justification: ImSitu changes from a motivating example to an evaluated gender/activity dataset covering 205 activities in balanced and unbalanced subsets. Appendix F also introduces a COCO sink/not-sink task with controlled one-pixel shortcuts and tests with and without those shortcuts. Existing COMPAS and COCO masking coverage is retained.

E2.justification: V1's benchmark comparisons evaluate BA→ and Multi→ against DPA. V2 adds leakage amplification to the retained VGG COCO comparison (Table 9), and evaluates BAMALS alongside these metrics in the ViT COCO comparison (Table 2). These substantially expand the competing metric families tested. COMPAS comparator membership remains unchanged.

E3.justification: COCO adds ViT_b_16 alongside VGG16, and the reported unbalanced sampling constraint changes from 1/2–2 to 1/3–3; unchanged sample counts do not establish whether sampling was rerun. New protocols rank nine ImSitu models against concept sensitivity scores and evaluate shortcut-controlled COCO training and test conditions.

E4.justification: V2 adds attacker-width sensitivity experiments on ImSitu (Appendix D.2), a controlled hidden-bias intervention using shortcuts (Appendix F), and additional attribution case studies (Figure 5). The earlier synthetic robustness experiment and simulated heatmaps are retained in Appendices D.1 and J, rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: V1 displays uncertainty using unlabeled ± entries in its result tables. V2 explicitly identifies corresponding uncertainties as confidence intervals and links DPA uncertainty estimation to repeated label-flipping iterations. Neither version specifies iteration counts, seeds, or confidence levels, so an increase in repeated runs is not established.

E6.justification: V2 adds ImSitu rankings, ViT masking scores, shortcut results, and real-data robustness findings. Retained VGG COCO DPA values also change: unbalanced/original increases from 0.0006 in v1 Table 4 to 0.0034 in v2 Table 9, alongside revised protocol reporting. COMPAS counts and scores remain unchanged in Tables 6–7.

M1.justification: The direction-specific attackers and normalized predictability difference remain equivalent: v1 Equations 9–14 correspond to v2 Equations 1–6. Label-flipping quality equalization was already used in v1's COMPAS analysis. V2 expands its explanation and discloses experimental choices without establishing a changed DPA procedure.

P1.justification: V2 retitles the paper and extensively rewrites the abstract, introduction, and method explanation. It folds the standalone leakage discussion into the motivation, combines experimental setup and results, moves COMPAS and several analyses into appendices, and introduces a dedicated limitations section. This substantially reorganizes the narrative.

P2.justification: The document changes from two columns to one. V2 adds a directional-method diagram, model-ranking tables with colored discrepancies, a real-data robustness plot, and an attribution grid. COCO tables gain comparator rows, existing displays move to appendices, and uncertainty values are reformatted as subscripts.

R1.justification: The related-work taxonomy and central positioning against BA→, Multi→, and leakage amplification remain largely unchanged. V2 adds references on bias-amplification theory, language models, attacker sensitivity, shortcuts, concept sensitivity, model architectures, and the Rashomon effect to support its expanded experiments and applications.

T1.justification: The stated DPA range changes from (-1,1) in v1 Section 4.2 to [-1,1] in v2 Section 3.2. Appendix B recasts the conditional-probability directionality argument explicitly around DPA. The core metric definitions and the Multi→ absolute-difference derivation are retained.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially closes v1's validation gap by directly comparing against leakage amplification, checking model rankings against ImSitu concept sensitivity, and testing attacker robustness on real data. Explicit aggregation limitations and implementation details improve assessability and reproducibility. These gains outweigh new reporting errors: Appendix F claims only DPA increases although Multi→ also increases in Table 8, and Table 11's exact-ranking caption contradicts its entries.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DPA research despite the changed title. Their complete main texts, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison.

after.justification: V2 retains original experiments and adds ImSitu evaluations, ViT masking results, controlled shortcut experiments, and real-data attacker robustness results.

before.justification: V1 reports original COMPAS and COCO experiments, simulated metric heatmaps, and attacker robustness results in Appendix B.

results.title: DPA: A one-stop metric to measure bias amplification in classification datasets

C1.justification: The central contribution of unified, modular VFM-feature forecasting remains unchanged. V2 narrows the abstract's blanket claim of outperforming existing methods to strong performance and emphasizes one model handling four tasks. The intermediate-feature benefit remains claimed in the introduction and appendix despite losing its separate headline contribution.

C2.justification: V2 adds substantive interpretations favoring continuous semantic representations, full future masking, cross-dataset transfer and scaling. Appendix B specifies diffusion/Gaussian-mixture extensions and newer encoders while dropping earlier PCA-replacement and action-conditioning directions. Some new interpretations overreach: Tables 11–12 contain small regressions despite claims of consistently improved performance.

D1.justification: The detailed DPT/Mask2Former recipes and hardware information are largely retained. V2 adds tokenizer specifications, model widths and attention-head counts, VISTA fine-tuning sequence lengths, nuScenes frame-selection details and an inference-runtime comparison. The abstract replaces the direct repository link with a project-page/code link. These extend the existing reproducibility documentation.

E1.justification: V1 evaluates Cityscapes. V2 adds nuScenes training and evaluation for depth and surface normals at 0.75-second and 1.5-second horizons, Cityscapes-to-nuScenes zero-shot transfer, and joint-dataset training. This substantially broadens represented driving environments and transfer scenarios while retaining the original task types.

E2.justification: V2 Table 1 adds evaluated comparators including Futurist, FeatReproj3D, Bayesian S2S, IndRNN-Stack and DiffAttn-Fuse. Tables 2–3 add VAE-latent and 4M-tokenized comparisons. V1's Mask H2F and separate Segmenter Oracle/Copy-Last comparisons disappear. The original 3Dconv-F2F row is retained as 3Dconv-F2F-RGB, rather than being a new comparator.

E3.justification: VISTA changes from the original 22-future-frame setup with separate task models to dataset-specific fine-tuning, shorter sequences and shared DINOv2/DPT evaluation. The reported predictor learning rate changes from 1.6e-4 to 6.4e-4, without establishing that retained experiments were rerun. New protocols include nuScenes rollouts, matched single-layer/no-register quantization controls, fixed-duration model scaling and equal-probability dataset mixing.

E4.justification: V2 adds analyses of VAE versus VFM representations, discrete versus continuous features, cross-dataset transfer, single versus multiple encoder layers, masking strategies, loss functions, model capacity and training-data scale. These test substantially more design and robustness questions. The original PCA and intermediate-transformer-feature analyses are retained; the latter moves from Section 4.4 to Appendix A.2.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed counts, repeated-run uncertainty, confidence intervals or formal significance tests. The expanded discussion of stochastic future prediction concerns possible model extensions, not uncertainty reporting for the experiments.

E6.justification: Instance forecasting scores change: short-term AP50/AP rises from 44.8/23.0 to 50.5/26.6, while the corresponding oracle changes from 56.1/32.1 to 66.2/40.4; the cause is not specified. Original semantic, depth and normal scores largely remain unchanged. V2 adds extensive nuScenes and ablation results and replaces VISTA scores and qualitative outputs under changed settings, so these are not same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: The default PCA-based continuous feature predictor, factorized transformer and SmoothL1 objective remain intact. V2 Section 4.2 adds a quantized DINO-Foresight variant that predicts 8192 discrete codes with cross-entropy and decodes them into DINO features. This introduces a limited procedural variant.

P1.justification: The introduction, contribution list, related-work discussion and conclusion are extensively rewritten around the distinction between VFM features and generative latents. Existing material is substantially reorganized: intermediate-feature learning moves to Appendix A.2, metric definitions and evaluation scenarios move to Appendices E–F, and the appendix structure expands.

P2.justification: V2 replaces the two-column layout with a single-column conference format, consolidates separate comparisons into a broad multi-task table, and adds several comparison and ablation tables. It relocates the intermediate-feature plot, rearranges the main qualitative panels and updates VISTA images and captions. The original long-horizon rollout images are retained.

R1.justification: V2 introduces substantial positioning against VAE-based latent generative models and distinguishes its dense forecasting task from concurrent DINO-WM planning. Related work also expands its discussion of individual semantic forecasting methods, including Futurist, and connects the new representation comparisons to 4M and continuous generative modeling.

T1.justification: Equation 1 replaces summation over all positions with a binary future-frame mask by direct summation over future positions, an equivalent formulation. The feature definitions and SmoothL1 mathematics remain unchanged. Metric formulas move to Appendix E, and no new theoretical results or proofs appear.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens validation of claims that v1 supported mainly through Cityscapes results. NuScenes transfer and controlled representation, masking and scaling studies directly test generalization and design choices. Fine-tuning VISTA and using common prediction heads also improves the fairness of the central comparison. Unexplained instance-score revisions and overstated uniform scaling gains remain weaknesses, but they do not outweigh the substantial gains in experimental support and comparison quality.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe DINO-Foresight. Their complete main texts, equations, tables, figures and appendices are readable, supporting reliable comparison despite substantial reorganization.

after.justification: V2 retains original forecasting results and adds nuScenes experiments, transfer evaluations, representation comparisons and scaling studies.

before.justification: V1 reports original Cityscapes forecasting experiments for segmentation, depth and surface normals, with ablations and qualitative results.

results.title: DINO-Foresight: Looking into the Future with DINO

C1.justification: The central claims of efficient artifact removal, optimization of unseen regions and no additional inference memory remain. v3 adds explicit generalization across NeRF architectures and datasets as a headline contribution in the abstract, introduction and conclusion, extending v1's emphasis on efficient cleanup.

C2.justification: v3 explains density-output versus weight regularization, interprets lambda robustness, and qualifies the free-space assumption for underwater imaging. Its new limitations section specifies failures involving inconsistent images, moving objects, poor bundle adjustment and input noise; Appendix A.8 demonstrates persistent color bias. These substantially expand v1's more general discussion of static-scene epistemic uncertainty.

D1.justification: v3 newly specifies the predicted-mask accumulation threshold of 0.98, visualization lambda settings and reconstruction sampling of 4,096 rays with 352 samples each. It retains the main hardware and training-budget disclosures, but omits v1's explicit 32/512 samples-per-ray ablation settings and 2^18-point histogram sampling count.

E1.justification: v3 Figure 1 and Section 5.4 add LeRF language-based scene understanding, Seathru underwater scenes and KITTI-360 semantic segmentation. Appendix A.8 also evaluates Gaussian-corrupted input images. The original Nerfbusters coverage and supplementary Garden, Basket, Playground and Trevi examples are retained.

E2.justification: The central Nerfbusters comparison retains Nerfacto, Nerfbusters, BayesRays and Gaussian Splatting, while adding an L2 weight-regularization baseline and a training-time FSP variant in Figures 3 and 11 and Table 4. These are limited additions to the existing comparison set.

E3.justification: v3 adds geometric protocols using 35,000-point clouds and depth references from a NeRF trained on training and test images, sparse/dense training-view configurations, additional NeRF backbones, and varying cleanup sample counts. Appendix A.4 additionally evaluates GT-mask PSNR. The original predicted-mask benchmark and its stated pretraining and cleanup budgets remain unchanged.

E4.justification: New analyses test geometry preservation, cleanup sample-count sensitivity, sparse/dense-view robustness, training-time FSP, noisy-input failure and underwater density behavior. The original ray-only sampling ablation and terrestrial density analyses remain. Appendix A.5 interprets the existing lambda sweep rather than introducing a new sweep.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed counts, repeated-run variability, confidence intervals or significance tests. Reporting point estimates and averages across benchmark scenes remains the practice in v3.

E6.justification: All shared benchmark rows in v1 Table 1 and v3 Table 4 are identical, as are the reported cleanup runtimes and ray-sampling ablation scores. v3 adds L2 results, including PSNR 17.10 and coverage 87.09%, six training-time FSP rows, geometric and sparse/dense results in Tables 2–3, GT-mask results, and new qualitative and robustness outcomes.

M1.justification: The main post-hoc procedure, global sampling and combined reconstruction/free-space loss remain unchanged. However, v3 Section 5.2 and Table 4 add an application of the loss during NeRF training from scratch, eliminating the separate cleanup stage. This is a limited procedural extension.

P1.justification: v3 substantially rewrites and condenses the introduction, background and results narrative, separates density analysis from ablations, and reorganizes the experimental sections. Implementation details move to the appendix, supplementary material moves after the references, and dedicated robustness and limitations sections are introduced.

P2.justification: The document changes from two columns to a predominantly single-column layout. v3 replaces the point-cloud teaser with a multi-architecture comparison, redraws the method diagram, rearranges density plots, converts the runtime graph into a table, expands qualitative grids and the results table, and adds several experimental displays.

R1.justification: v3 adds citations to Zip-NeRF, OpenNeRF, LeRF, Seathru-NeRF and KITTI-360. Related work expands the discussion of distortion/interlevel regularization and its remaining floater problem. The principal positioning against Nerfbusters, BayesRays and existing priors is retained.

T1.justification: The rendering, reconstruction and free-space loss equations remain mathematically equivalent despite renumbering and notation cleanup. v3's L2/ridge analogy and underwater discussion add conceptual explanations, without new formal assumptions, derivations, theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens evidence for scene preservation and practical applicability through geometric consistency tests, sparse/dense-view evaluations, an L2 comparison and broader architecture demonstrations. The explicit limitations and noisy-input failure example also better qualify the cleanup claims. Cross-architecture evidence remains largely qualitative, and some original ablation details are lost, but the added validation addresses important gaps in v1 while preserving its original benchmark evidence.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Free Space Prior research. All 12 pages of v1 and 18 pages of v3, including their supplementary sections, are readable. Equations, experiments, figures and tables can be reliably matched across the reorganization.

after.justification: v3 retains those empirical results and adds geometric evaluations, sampling and view-density studies, additional architecture and task demonstrations, and a noisy-input experiment.

before.justification: v1 reports original cleanup-quality and runtime experiments on Nerfbusters, density analyses, a ray-sampling ablation and qualitative evaluations on additional datasets.

results.title: Optimize the Unseen -- Fast NeRF Cleanup with Free Space Prior

C1.justification: The central contribution remains an expressive continuous-time MTPP combining LLH layers with efficient parallel computation. v2 revises the headline likelihood advantage from 38% to 33% and adds an explicit claim of best-or-second-best average performance across six metrics, supported by a new composite ranking.

C2.justification: Sections 7–8 substantially expand applicability and mechanism discussion. Beyond v1's implementation-complexity and interpretability caveats, v2 discusses numerical integration for expected times, inability to represent temporal point masses, unsuitability when interpretation is crucial, and untested censored/adversarial conditions. It also expands the continuous-state explanation and changes the multivariate Hawkes interpretation to emphasize comparable performance across methods.

D1.justification: v1 promises a release and mentions supplementary code; v2 reports completed EasyTPP integration, provides integration and reproduction-repository links, and offers checkpoints on request. It documents EHRSHOT preparation code and credentialed-access restrictions, dates baseline implementations to May 2025, and supplies MHP search settings and architectures for the new synthetic studies.

E1.justification: The eight real-world datasets and existing Poisson and multivariate Hawkes coverage remain. v2 substantially broadens synthetic coverage with self-correcting dynamics and a controlled trigger–target process containing long delays and distractor events, testing conditions absent from v1 (Section 5, Appendices D.4–D.5).

E2.justification: Mamba Hawkes Process (MHP), discussed but not evaluated in v1, becomes an evaluated comparator across the real-world benchmarks, calibration analyses, and retained synthetic experiments. Adding this closely related SSM-based competitor materially strengthens the comparison; the original six baselines remain.

E3.justification: Appendix D.1 replaces thinning-based next-time estimation with trapezoidal integration. The reported MIMIC-II architecture changes from h=256, p=64, L=2 to h=64, p=16, L=2. v2 also introduces composite ranking and new synthetic protocols while retaining real-world splits. The new self-correcting coefficient is inconsistent between Section 5 and Appendix D.4.

E4.justification: v2 adds controlled intensity-recovery analyses for self-correcting and univariate Hawkes processes, plus qualitative and quantitative tests of long-range dependency recovery (Appendices D.4–D.5). These directly probe expressivity and memory. The original forward/backward ZOH and input-dependence ablation is retained unchanged, and the speed study moves to Appendix B.5.

E5.justification: v2 extends mean-and-standard-deviation reporting to next-event RMSE, mark accuracy, and calibration results (Tables 2 and 15), whereas their v1 counterparts reported point values. Five-seed likelihood reporting and 20-seed runtime summaries already existed. This broadens uncertainty disclosure without establishing an increase in training runs or introducing significance tests.

E6.justification: v2 adds MHP results and new synthetic findings, including long-range likelihood ratios of 97.8% for S2P2, 99.7% for AttNHP, and 87.9% for NHP (Table 13). Accuracy, RMSE, and calibration entries are extensively revised. MIMIC-II likelihood changes from 1.243 to 0.919 under a smaller architecture, and the aggregate likelihood advantage changes from 38% to 33%. Revised RMSE values use a different estimator, precluding simple same-setting performance comparisons.

M1.justification: The LLH recurrence, input-dependent dynamics, discretization, stacked architecture, likelihood objective, and parallel-scan algorithms remain unchanged despite renaming. A limited removal is v1's optional trained linear-probe head for next-event-time prediction (Appendix D.1, Table 9); v2 reports intensity-based expected-time prediction without that auxiliary variant.

P1.justification: v2 extensively rewrites the abstract, introduction, preliminaries, and method exposition, changes the title and model terminology, and reorders the method subsections. Synthetic and real-world experiments become separate sections, a dedicated discussion is added, and runtime material moves to the appendix. These changes go well beyond accommodating additional experiments.

P2.justification: The original three-part architecture figure is split and redrawn into v2 Figures 1a and 2, with a new ranking summary in Figure 1b. Appendix accuracy and RMSE tables are incorporated into the main three-part Table 2. New synthetic plots are added, multivariate Hawkes panels are consolidated, and the runtime figure moves to the appendix.

R1.justification: v2 adds references on mixed-type events, SSM approximation and interpretability, and censored/adversarial point processes, while removing some earlier references such as the CNN-based discussion. MHP was already cited, but its relationship is sharpened around discrete encoder–decoder states versus continuously evolving states. The underlying Hawkes/SSM research positioning remains.

T1.justification: Section 2.1 changes the stated LHP positivity restriction from nonnegative beta to nonnegative exp(-beta), alongside nonnegative alpha. Appendix B.5 extends the theoretical complexity analysis to MHP. The principal LLH and ZOH derivations remain, and no new theorem or proof is supplied.

improvement.justification: v2 resolves important evidential gaps by evaluating the closely related MHP baseline and directly testing long-range dependency recovery, rather than relying mainly on scaling evidence. Expanded uncertainty reporting, clearer exposition, and concrete reproduction/access information further improve assessability. These gains outweigh localized inconsistencies: the self-correcting formula differs between Section 5 and Appendix D.4, and some IFTPP/MHP ranks in Figure 1b disagree with Table 2. The improvement rests on stronger validation and transparency, not higher reported performance.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research, with DLHP renamed S2P2 and the title changed. The main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices A–D support reliable comparison despite substantial reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical evaluations and adds synthetic self-correcting, univariate Hawkes, and long-range dependency experiments, alongside expanded baseline comparisons.

before.justification: v1 reports original experiments on eight real-world datasets, synthetic Poisson and multivariate Hawkes processes, runtime measurements, ablations, and calibration analyses.

results.title: Deep Continuous-Time State-Space Models for Marked Event Sequences

C1.justification: The abstract and central claims about spatial/adversarial alignment and cross-architecture transferability remain essentially unchanged. v2 adds empirical guidance for selecting surrogate and witness models as an explicit contribution in the introduction.

C2.justification: v2 adds model-selection guidance, interpretations supporting the loss and supervision choices, and explicit limitations concerning residual architectural gaps and alignment cost. Appendix F develops a face-forgery misuse scenario and proposed mitigations. These substantially expand v1's interpretation and applicability discussion; the lack-of-theory caveat was already present.

D1.justification: v2 adds detailed loss pseudocode, identifies timm as the model-weight source, and discloses the 1:1 adversarial-to-training-sample ratio. Appendix C reports batch sizes, RTX 3090 hardware, 2,794 MB memory use, and approximately ten hours for SAA versus two for MA. It also points to supplementary code, whose actual availability cannot be verified from the PDFs.

E1.justification: Both retain the 1,000-image ImageNet-compatible dataset and untargeted image-classification attacks. v2 extends testing to defended-input scenarios, including randomization, compression, denoising and purification in Table 6. It adds no dataset, application domain or prediction task.

E2.justification: The original alignment and transfer-attack comparators remain. v2 adds FDA and FDA-MI comparisons with and without SAA in Table 11, plus direct unaligned logit ensembles as comparators in Table 5. The defenses in Table 6 are evaluated targets, rather than additional attack baselines.

E3.justification: Sections 3.3–3.4 introduce two- and four-model logit-ensemble protocols and evaluation against 12 defenses using an ensemble of separately aligned surrogates. These substantially expand the evaluation design. The original MI perturbation budget, ten iterations, momentum and one-epoch alignment settings remain unchanged; no changed protocol is stated for the revised Table 3 scores.

E4.justification: v2 adds comparisons of KL/TV/JS/NCE global losses, witness versus surrogate supervision, and hard versus soft local labels, alongside defense testing, computational-cost analysis and target-model Grad-CAM examples. The original component ablation is retained as Table 7, and the unchanged epoch analysis moves to Appendix C.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, uncertainty intervals or significance tests for its results. v2's checklist cites computational cost to explain the absence of statistical reporting, but introduces no uncertainty estimates or statistical procedures.

E6.justification: Table 3 revises ViT-B and Swin-B scores throughout and changes most averages. For example, SSA-DI-TI-MI-SAA average ASR changes from 92.0% to 88.2%, reducing its reported advantage from 5.1 to 2.0 percentage points under the same stated setup. v2 also adds substantial results in Tables 5–6 and 8–11 and Figure 4. Tables 1, 2 and 4 remain numerically unchanged.

M1.justification: The core spatial and adversarial losses and example-generation procedure remain intact. However, v1's explicit multi-witness averaging extension in Equation 7 is removed; v2 presents single-witness updates. Algorithm 1 primarily clarifies existing classifier-head and pseudo-label computations.

P1.justification: The abstract and much of the original prose are closely preserved. Related Work moves to Appendix A, the epoch discussion moves to Appendix C, and localized methodological explanations and affiliations are revised. New experimental subsections, appendices and a limitations paragraph organize the additions, without extensive rewriting of the retained narrative.

P2.justification: The two-column presentation becomes a single-column NeurIPS layout, substantially changing table sizing, figure placement and text wrapping. v2 adds six tables, Algorithm 1 and Figure 4. Existing displays are retained or relocated, including the unchanged training-epoch Figure 3 in Appendix C.

R1.justification: The existing related-work discussion and positioning against MA are retained in Appendix A. Additional citations support the defense evaluations, FDA comparison, contrastive-loss ablation and architectural discussion. This extends the literature coverage without substantially redefining the research position.

T1.justification: Equation 7 narrows the formal update from averaging over a witness-model set to using one witness. Equation 2's pseudo-label rewrite is equivalent once local logits are clarified. Neither version supplies theoretical guarantees, theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation and transparency: defended-target evaluations and controlled loss/supervision comparisons address previously untested aspects, while pseudocode and measured resource costs clarify implementation and practical tradeoffs. Table 3 also resolves its MI-result disagreement with Table 2. Missing uncertainty estimates and new FDA prose/table discrepancies remain, but the added diagnostic evidence and reproducibility information provide a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SAA research, with readable text, equations, tables and figures. All supplied pages were inspected: v1 ends with references, while v2 includes Appendices A–F and a checklist. The retained material can be reliably matched.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds ensemble and defense evaluations, loss and supervision ablations, resource measurements, and feature-based attack comparisons.

before.justification: v1 reports original ImageNet attack-success measurements, feature-similarity analyses, Grad-CAM visualizations, and component and training-epoch ablations.

results.title: Boosting Adversarial Transferability with Spatial Adversarial Alignment

C1.justification: The zero-shot planning contribution remains, but v2 adds formal STL-satisfaction guarantees as a central abstract, introduction, and conclusion claim. Its conclusion also expands the empirical contribution to more complex robotic dynamics and higher robustness values. The formal theorem conditions satisfaction on successful allocation and constraint-compliant generation.

C2.justification: New Appendix B substantially develops incompleteness, lack of optimality, low-dimensional planning and navigation-task restrictions, and Time Predictor coverage limitations. v2 explicitly separates logical soundness from dynamic feasibility and adds interpretations of controller compensation and failures under complex dynamics, beyond v1's shorter failure discussion.

D1.justification: v2 adds exact OGBench dataset identifiers, controller input/output dimensions, control-frequency settings, additional parameter rows, and a project-page link. It clarifies control timing versus robustness subsampling and the recursive implementation of allocation. Conversely, v1's explicit SafeDiffuser CBF/QP equations and Algorithm 3 are replaced by a prose summary.

E1.justification: v2 adds OGBench AntMaze quadruped locomotion and Cube robotic-arm end-effector motion to the retained Maze2D and custom environments. These substantially broaden the evaluated dynamics and spatial coverage. Cube evaluates Cartesian waypoint motion, rather than object manipulation (Sections 5.2 and F.4).

E2.justification: The comparator membership remains RGD for Maze2D and the optimization-based method attributed to Gilpin et al. for the custom environment. The new Cube, AntMaze, and pipeline tables report only the proposed framework; newly cited methods are not added experimental baselines.

E3.justification: v2 introduces average robustness evaluation, 100 tasks per template in each new domain, and a separate 1,000-start–goal-pair protocol per environment. AntMaze uses two control updates per planning step. The retained Maze2D and custom experiments keep their 150 and 200 tasks per template, respectively, and their previously listed parameters.

E4.justification: New Appendix F.6 tests whether predicted travel times, generated segments, and execution control work together on sampled start–goal pairs. This is a targeted additional pipeline analysis, rather than a component ablation. The earlier custom allocator evaluation and qualitative failure analysis remain.

E5.justification: v2 explicitly identifies runtime dispersion as standard deviation and specifies discarding the top and bottom 5% when estimating average robustness (Appendix F.3). v1 already reported runtime values with ± dispersion. Neither version reports experimental seed counts or repeated-run uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: All shared numerical entries in the Maze2D and custom-environment tables are unchanged. v2 adds robustness scores, Cube success rates of 84–100% and AntMaze rates of 60–94% (Table F.3), and pipeline success rates of 93.9/89.0/83.7/84.8% across U-Maze/Medium/Large/AntMaze (Table F.5). These are additional results, not same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: The three-stage planner, TimePredict model, and SafeDiffuser generator remain. However, the specified until decomposition changes invariance intervals from I(a, lambda, mu) to I(0, lambda, mu), with a corresponding correction for nested until (v1 Section 3.2; v2 Appendix D). These are localized procedural corrections; trajectory stitching already existed in v1.

P1.justification: v2 rewrites the abstract, contribution framing, framework discussion, and conclusion; reorganizes experiments into separate subsections; and moves semantics, decomposition details, task templates, and full Maze2D results into reorganized appendices. This substantially changes the narrative structure beyond simply appending new scientific content.

P2.justification: The document changes from two-column to single-column layout with wrapped figures and algorithms. Figure 1 is revised; Maze2D results become a partial main-text table and an expanded appendix table with robustness columns. v2 also adds an environment montage and new results tables while relocating and resizing existing illustrations.

R1.justification: New Appendix A.3 positions the framework against four trajectory-stitching works, distinguishing global STL satisfaction from data augmentation and goal-reaching applications. The introduction adopts this positioning, and additional references cover constrained diffusion and time prediction. These substantive additions extend the retained STL-decomposition and diffusion-planning discussion.

T1.justification: v1 has no formal soundness lemmas or proofs. v2 introduces feasible-assignment definitions, decomposition and allocation lemmas, an overall conditional soundness theorem, and proofs in Appendix G. Appendix D also corrects until intervals and formalizes independent variable copies for nested always decomposition.

improvement.justification: Corrected decomposition rules and explicit conditional soundness arguments address an important gap in v1's correctness justification. Cube, AntMaze, and pipeline evaluations substantially broaden empirical support, while the expanded limitations clarify what logical guarantees and execution results establish. Removing detailed SafeDiffuser pseudocode and equations reduces self-contained reproducibility, and dynamic feasibility remains empirical, but the stronger justification and clearer applicability boundaries provide a substantial overall improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work, with matching authors, planning framework, and retained experiments. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds Cube, AntMaze, and predictor–generator–controller evaluations.

before.justification: v1 reports original Maze2D experiments, a custom-environment comparison, and successful and failed trajectory examples.

C1.justification: The central claims about sample complexity for a single hyperparameter and the two neural-network applications remain. v4 drops v1's explicit introductory assertion that the setting naturally captures cross-validation and focuses the framing on learning model hyperparameters across tasks.

C2.justification: v4 explains the geometric roles of the revised regularity conditions and conjectures that Assumption 1 can be removed (Remarks 2–3). Its conclusion develops the obstacle to extending bounded oscillations to multiple hyperparameters, while dropping the earlier conclusion's Pfaffian-function and computational-efficiency research directions. The ERM-oracle and flatness limitations in the appendices remain.

D1.justification: Neither version supplies an experimental implementation, hardware specifications, training times, or code/data access resources. The application architectures and symbolic parameter specifications are retained; the expanded technical material concerns mathematical proofs.

E1.justification: Neither version trains or evaluates on concrete datasets. The activation-function and graph-kernel applications, including their classification and regression cases in Section 6 and Appendix D, remain theoretical.

E2.justification: Neither version evaluates competing methods against the proposed framework. Discussions of Bayesian optimization, NAS, and Hyperband remain literature comparisons rather than experimental baseline comparisons.

E3.justification: No empirical evaluation protocols, data splits, training budgets, or testing procedures are introduced or revised. The retained applications specify theoretical model and loss settings.

E4.justification: Neither version reports ablations, robustness tests, error analyses, or empirical case studies. Appendix E's conceptual discussion of flat optima is retained; the new mathematical analyses are covered under T1.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated experimental runs, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The probability statements in the learning guarantees are theoretical bounds, not empirical uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: There are no empirical scores, rankings, or measured findings to compare in either version. Changes to analytical bounds and mathematical conclusions are assessed under T1.

M1.justification: The ERM-oracle formulation, activation interpolation, two-layer polynomial-kernel GCN, losses, and Appendix E curvature surrogate are retained. The revised perturbation constructions are proof devices, not changes to a training or inference procedure.

P1.justification: The introduction and problem formulation are substantially rewritten, with clearer explanations of tasks, datasets, and model hyperparameters. Section 5's proof exposition is reorganized, Appendix C regroups and expands its mathematical background, and the conclusion is rewritten. These are extensive narrative and structural revisions beyond renumbering.

P2.justification: The same four figures and single-column format are retained. Figures 1 and 3 move from pages 10 and 14 in v1 to pages 9 and 13 in v4; captions receive small corrections, and revised equation displays change local layout. No new figures or tables are introduced.

R1.justification: v4 adds mathematical sources, including Bochnak et al. (2013), Nocedal and Wright (1999), Still (2018), and algebraic-curve references. It removes some earlier citations, including Khovanski (1991) and Rockafellar and Wets (2009). The broader positioning relative to data-driven algorithm design, NAS, and Hyperband remains substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: v4 replaces Assumption 1's regular-value condition with ELICQ and nondegeneracy conditions, and revises Assumption 2 to allow finitely many exceptional hyperparameter values. It introduces B-monotonicity, revises Lemma 5.1 accordingly, adds Proposition C.22, and changes Theorem 5.4's intermediate bounds. The scalar perturbation argument in v1's Lemma 5.7 is substantially rebuilt through Propositions 5.6–5.8 and Lemma 5.9. Appendix C also revises foundational definitions and proofs and removes v1's Proposition C.14. The leading generalization-rate expression in Theorem 5.3 is retained.

improvement.justification: v4 addresses important weaknesses in the theoretical foundation: Lemma 5.1's problematic finite-local-maxima treatment of constant branches is replaced by B-monotonicity, supported by Proposition C.22. The short perturbation argument in v1 is substantially rebuilt with explicit conditions and supporting proofs in Sections 5.2.1–5.2.2. Together with the clearer problem formulation, these changes make the central reasoning substantially more defensible and checkable. The leading rates and applications remain unchanged, and the reformulated assumptions should not be interpreted as establishing uniformly broader applicability.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work, with matching authors, framework, and neural-network applications. Their text, equations, four figures, and Appendices A–E are available and support a reliable comparison.

after.justification: v4 also contains theoretical results and illustrative figures without original empirical evaluations. The expanded Section 5 and Appendix C supply mathematical definitions and proofs.

before.justification: v1 presents mathematical analyses and sample-complexity bounds, including theoretical applications in Section 6 and Appendix D. Its figures illustrate proofs; no original experimental, simulation, user-study, or data-analysis outcomes are reported.

C1.justification: V1 presents O(n ln T) as improving the best-known O(n^4 ln T) bound by n^3. V6 acknowledges Gollapudi et al.'s existing O(n ln T) bound and instead claims the first logarithmic-regret method with T-independent per-round complexity. The two-dimensional finite-regret result also ceases to be a headline contribution.

C2.justification: V6 explains that previously known finite regret with exponential dimension dependence makes its two-dimensional result an illustrative analysis. The new conclusion discusses possible gradient-norm tradeoffs and finite polynomial regret when line-segment feasible sets are revealed before prediction. Existing explanations of suboptimal feedback and higher-dimensional geometric obstacles remain.

D1.justification: V6's MetaGrad pseudocode explicitly sends both the aggregate prediction w_t and gradient g_t to each expert, whereas v1 sends only g_t. This clarifies implementation of the surrogate loss, which already depended on both quantities in v1.

E1.justification: Neither version trains on or evaluates datasets. The inverse optimization settings and constructed instances are studied theoretically.

E2.justification: Neither version experimentally evaluates comparison methods. The newly included Gollapudi comparison in Table 1 and Appendix A concerns theoretical guarantees and complexity.

E3.justification: Neither version reports empirical evaluation protocols, training budgets or testing procedures. The revised feasible-set normalization in Appendix C is a theorem assumption, not an experimental setting.

E4.justification: Robustness to suboptimal feedback remains a theoretical guarantee in Section 4. Neither version contains ablations, empirical robustness tests or experimental case studies; the geometric discussion is retained in Appendix C.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run statistics, seeds, confidence intervals or statistical tests. Expectations in the regret bounds concern theoretical randomness.

E6.justification: Neither version reports empirical performance values, measured runtimes or experimental findings. The new Table 1 summarizes theoretical bounds rather than experimental results.

M1.justification: The ONS and MetaGrad designs are retained, but Appendix B.3 changes MetaGrad's dyadic learning-rate grid endpoint from ceil((ln T)/2) to ceil((log_2 T)/2). This changes the number and range of experts and is a limited algorithmic correction. The two-dimensional algorithm is retained in Appendix C.

P1.justification: The title, abstract and introduction are substantially rewritten around computational efficiency. Related work expands, a conclusion is added, and the former Section 6 becomes Appendix C. Together these changes substantially reorganize the paper's narrative.

P2.justification: V6 adds Table 1 comparing theoretical regret and computational complexity. Figures 1–2 and the two-dimensional pseudocode move to Appendix C, preserving the diagrams. Typography, captions and algorithm numbering are also revised.

R1.justification: Adding Gollapudi et al. (2021) substantially changes the nearest-prior-work account and novelty positioning. V6 also expands contextual-search, corruption-robustness and online-portfolio literature, and Appendix A develops a detailed comparison of centroid-based computation. These changes go substantially beyond citation or publication-metadata updates.

T1.justification: The principal regret bounds are retained. However, v6 tightens the two-dimensional result's feasible-set radius from 1 to 1/2, supporting the proof's unit-diameter bound; Theorem 6.2 becomes Theorem C.2. It also corrects the lower-bound proof's quantifier order and strengthens the MetaGrad grid argument. Appendix A adds a computational-cost derivation for the prior centroid method. These are local corrections and extensions rather than new main theorems.

improvement.justification: V6 resolves a central novelty overstatement by acknowledging Gollapudi et al.'s existing O(n ln T) bound and identifying computational efficiency as its contribution, supported by Table 1 and Appendix A. The corrected MetaGrad grid and feasible-set assumption also strengthen mathematical reliability. These changes substantially improve the paper's accuracy and positioning while retaining its principal guarantees.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same online inverse linear optimization work. Their complete text, equations, algorithms, figures and appendices support comparison despite retitling and reorganization.

after.justification: V6 remains theoretical throughout its main text and appendices. Its new Table 1 compares asymptotic guarantees and computational complexity, not empirical measurements.

before.justification: V1 contains theoretical algorithms, regret bounds, proofs and geometric illustrations, but no original experimental, simulation or data-analysis outcomes, including in its appendices.

C1.justification: The abstract/introduction revise the headline harmful-score reduction from 21.5% to 21.2%, and the introduction changes the accuracy improvement from 0.3% to 0.4%, reflecting revised aggregation. The three principal contributions and the conclusion's substantive claims remain unchanged.

C2.justification: New Appendices B, C, and F explain the alternative objective's failures, discuss layer-safety interpretations, identify difficult topics and high-contamination weaknesses, and explicitly acknowledge LoRA-only evaluation, limited model scale, and model-dependent hyperparameter tuning. v2 also removes v1's discussion of the high-noise harmful-score rebound.

Table 1 drops the 0.25 harmful ratio, while Appendix B adds ratios 0.3–0.5 and additional evaluation controls. Shared training defaults remain unchanged.

These test questions beyond v1's retained perturbation on/off ablations, training curves, hyperparameter sweeps, and case studies.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run or seed counts, error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests. v2's checklist asserts that experiments across varied settings establish statistical significance, but supplies no additional statistical estimation procedure.

E6.justification: v2 adds extensive results; for example, Table 6 reports HS 41.73 for Panacea versus 84.81 for SFT under the 0.1 cross-source attack setting. Shared scores in Tables 1–3 largely remain unchanged; Table 1's revised averages reflect omission of the 0.25 setting. Figure 4 also removes v1's high-noise HS rebound and its report of HS exceeding 80 at noise 0.1.

M1.justification: The max-max objective, gradient-based perturbation, parameter updates, and final perturbation application remain unchanged in Equations 1–3 and Algorithm 1. The alternative objective evaluated in v2 is an ablation, not a revision to Panacea.

P1.justification: v2 retitles Section 3, rewrites the exploration discussion with descriptive subheadings, condenses the contribution list, and moves system evaluation and the impact statement into appendices. It adds acknowledgments and a checklist, while much of the existing introduction, methodology, conclusion, and experimental-detail prose remains intact.

P2.justification: v2 replaces the two-column main-text layout with a single-column format, adds eleven tables, expands existing comparison tables, and removes the 0.25 columns from Table 1. Figures and tables are extensively resized or relocated; Figure 2's labels are corrected and Figure 4's curve and caption change.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands the cited attack and defense literature. Section 4 newly acknowledges Security Vectors as a related prior idea and distinguishes its perturbation construction from Panacea. Appendix C adds detailed comparisons with six prior approaches to identifying safety-critical layers.

T1.justification: The equations and Taylor/Hölder derivation are retained. Appendix A adds a short scaling argument that the linearized inner objective becomes unbounded without the perturbation norm constraint, providing an additional mathematical justification for that constraint.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the empirical case by addressing v1's concentration on alignment-stage comparators and BeaverTails safety evaluation through additional defenses, external benchmarks, and cross-source testing. New objective ablations and explicit limitations improve understanding of effectiveness and scope. Reporting weaknesses remain: uncertainty is unquantified, some accuracy-ranking claims are stale after adding Antidote, and Figure 4's high-noise revision is unexplained. These issues temper but do not outweigh the substantial gains in comparative and robustness evidence.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Panacea. Their main texts, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable matching despite the expanded evaluation and changed layout.

after.justification: v2 retains these empirical results and adds baseline comparisons, safety benchmarks, cross-source evaluations, and supplementary analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original safety and downstream-task evaluations, perturbation ablations, training trajectories, resource measurements, and qualitative examples.
