C1.justification: Both versions claim a unified framework for jointly recovering a low-rank connection matrix and graphon through subgraph moments and interpolation, with consistency and computational advantages. The rewritten abstract, contributions and conclusion retain this scientific scope; additional empirical support does not redefine the central contribution.

C2.justification: v2 substantially expands interpretation of graphon estimation's generative utility, behavior outside smoothness assumptions, and consequences of rank misspecification. It also acknowledges that rank-1 spectral estimation can achieve quadratic complexity. Some new interpretations overreach: Appendix H describes overestimation effects as minimal despite substantial deterioration for setting 2 in Table 9.

D1.justification: Section 4 adds a code-repository link, and Appendix H explicitly discloses that main simulations assume known rank and that the simulation threshold 0.2 is heuristic. The previously reported hardware, R version, baseline defaults and power-iteration stopping settings remain unchanged.

New sparsity-sensitivity and political-blog motif comparisons reuse four existing baselines, omitting power iteration only from those additional comparisons; no existing matched comparison loses a baseline.

The school-data rank-selection threshold also changes from 0.2 to 0.25, although retained rank and eigenvalue results do not establish that this experiment was rerun.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's limited rank-selection analysis, v2 tests scalability, varying sparsity, violation of Lipschitz assumptions, rank overestimation and underestimation, and estimation after selecting rank. Appendix A additionally examines structural preservation under node subsampling, substantially expanding robustness and diagnostic evidence.

E5.justification: v1 reports means for its main accuracy comparisons, with standard deviations confined to power-iteration counts. v2 adds standard deviations for MSE and maximum error throughout the main comparisons and uncertainty for additional analyses. Both versions already specify 100 independent trials for the main simulations; an increased run count is not established.

E6.justification: Retained benchmark means are mostly preserved at greater precision, while substantial new results appear. Examples include graphon sup-norm errors of 0.12053 and 0.15539 for settings 3 and 4 (Table 3), correct rank selection in 89/100 trials for setting 7 (Table 8), and political-blog motif errors and runtimes (Table 13).

M1.justification: The core moment estimation, normalization, interpolation, computational corrections and rank-selection algorithms remain unchanged. Remark 3.8 adds an optional procedure that tries different reference components and selects the estimated graphon whose motif densities best match observed densities.

P1.justification: The title changes, much of the introduction and methodological exposition is rewritten, and the rank-r explanation is reorganized around cycle and path expectations. References move before the appendices, the school example moves into a dedicated applications appendix, and the original appendix subsections become a broader A–L structure.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a substantially different page design, restructures the main comparison tables into paired blocks with uncertainty columns and highlighted best values, and adds multiple result tables and scalability, robustness and political-blog figures. Existing graphon-definition and school displays are relocated; the school heatmap gains a color scale.

R1.justification: New Appendix B broadens positioning to cut-distance estimation, sparse oracle inequalities, matrix completion, transfer learning and machine-learning applications. Additional discussion connects moment estimation and eigenratio selection to relevant literature. This substantially extends v1's focused estimator review; the Wu et al. publication-year update represents the same existing work.

T1.justification: The principal assumptions, convergence theorems and appendix proofs are retained after renumbering. Appendix H newly asserts asymptotic correctness of rank selection when the threshold tends to zero at an appropriate rate, but supplies neither that rate nor a proof. Expanded moment explanations largely restate mathematics already present in v1.

improvement.justification: v1's validation concentrates on connection-matrix errors and illustrative graphon plots. v2 substantially strengthens evidence for its central graphon-recovery claims through direct sup-norm measurements, uncertainty reporting, structural-preservation experiments and tests of rank choice and assumption violations. Some interpretations remain overstated: within v2, overestimating setting 2's rank raises MSE from 2.452 to 6.11 times 10^-4 despite the 'minimal differences' claim. This weakens that robustness conclusion but does not outweigh the substantial gains in empirical validation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same low-rank graphon research. Their main text, equations, algorithms, figures, tables and appendices are readable, and retained material can be matched across substantial reorganization and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds graphon-error measurements, sensitivity studies, network-regeneration experiments and political-blog data analysis.

before.justification: v1 reports original graphon simulations, baseline comparisons, rank-selection experiments and analysis of primary-school contact data.

Its I2I interpretation changes from lowest ASR across all scenarios to lowest average ASR. The earlier limitations concerning image-based attacks and closed-source models remain.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DES framework by the same authors, despite the changed title. Their complete main texts, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable, allowing retained, relocated, and newly added content to be matched.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds experiments on newer diffusion models, additional concepts, adaptive attacks, and benign-prompt semantic preservation.

before.justification: v1 reports original diffusion-model defense experiments, image-quality measurements, inpainting evaluations, ablations, and embedding analyses in the main text and appendices.

The abstract broadens empirical applicability to GSM8K reasoning and claims gains across models ranging from 200M to 8B parameters, extending the practical contribution without redefining the main algorithmic contribution.

It also interprets blockwise gains through LLaDA's preference for left-to-right generation and qualifies the reasoning advantage as primarily occurring at low NFE (Section 6.4 and Appendix D.4).

D1.justification: V2 adds a project code-repository link, identifies GPT-2 Large and LLaMA 3 evaluator checkpoints, and documents the LLaDA checkpoint, noise schedule, early stopping, temperature, block lengths, hardware, and evaluation harness. V1 already supplied RADD/MaskGIT checkpoint information and implementation settings; v2 substantially expands this reproducibility information.

E1.justification: V2 adds GSM8K mathematical reasoning with LLaDA-Instruct, substantially extending task coverage beyond text and image generation. The RADD/OpenWebText, MaskGIT/ImageNet, and toy experiments remain. Renaming the toy experiment from 15-dimensional to 15-state does not introduce different data; v1 Appendix D.2 already specifies 15 states.

E2.justification: V2 adds FHS to the reported text and image comparisons and Semi-AR to RADD text generation. Its new GSM8K comparison evaluates confidence-based and random-remasking Semi-AR variants. FHS was discussed in v1 but was absent from these benchmark comparisons; existing comparators are retained.

E3.justification: V2 adds LLaMA 3 perplexity and unigram-entropy evaluation. The new GSM8K protocol uses an 8B model, zero-shot 256-token responses, 64–256 NFEs, temperature 0.5, and full-sequence versus blocksize-8 conditions. Existing toy, RADD, and MaskGIT sampling budgets are retained; these additions do not establish reruns of the original experiments.

E4.justification: V2 adds positivity measurements across NFE budgets, directly probing a convergence-theory assumption (Table 6), and a blockwise versus full-sequence reasoning comparison probing generation order (Table 7). Existing convergence and theta-sensitivity studies remain; their relocation and renumbering do not constitute new analyses.

E5.justification: V2 Table 6 newly reports plus/minus quantities alongside positivity percentages, but does not define their statistical meaning or associated repetition counts. The toy experiment retains 1,000 bootstrap resamples and 95% confidence intervals. An increase in repeated runs is not established.

E6.justification: V2 adds baseline, LLaMA 3, entropy, positivity, and GSM8K results. On GSM8K, Trapezoidal scores 38.4% versus random Semi-AR's 34.3% at NFE 128, but 39.7% versus 40.3% at NFE 256. Shared GPT-2 perplexities remain unchanged in v2 Table 3; however, v2 Table 1 inconsistently reports RK-2 as 36.330 instead of 33.971 at NFE 1024.

M1.justification: The two principal solvers remain. V2 adds a current-state jump-validity indicator to RK-2 Algorithm 1, absent from both v1 Algorithm 1 and its practical Algorithm 4, and introduces a blockwise Trapezoidal variant in Appendix D.4. Positive-part clipping and the wider theta range already existed in v1 Appendix D.1.

P1.justification: V2 edits and condenses prose while retaining the basic narrative. It merges v1 Section 3.3 into Section 4, moves stochastic formulations into Appendix C.1, integrates the practical RK-2 presentation into Algorithm 1, and converts the hyperparameter section into a remark. Most existing exposition and proof text remain.

P2.justification: The main text changes from two columns to a single-column format with wrapped algorithms and tables. Figure 1 gains a solver schematic, comparison plots gain FHS curves and legends, and tables are added or expanded. Existing sensitivity plots and the identical Figure 7 image samples are retained and relocated.

R1.justification: V2 substantially expands references and positioning toward diffusion-LLM reasoning, discrete neural sampling, and inference-time scaling, including LLaDA, Dream, and d1. Section 1.1 and Appendix A also add numerical CTMC and diffusion-solver literature. These are substantive literature additions beyond the switch to numbered citations.

T1.justification: V2 introduces periodic boundary conditions in Section 5.1 and an O(kappa) rejection argument in Remark C.4. Remark C.6 adds an expected-positivity derivation. Proposition C.20 revises v1 Proposition C.16's local error bound from O(Delta_n^3 epsilon_II + Delta_n^4) to O(Delta_n^3), with altered reasoning. The final second-order KL convergence rate is retained.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens practical validation through previously missing sampler comparisons, additional text-quality and diversity measurements, and an 8B reasoning evaluation. Positivity diagnostics, more explicit theoretical conditions, and expanded code and implementation information improve assessability and reproducibility. These gains outweigh the localized RK-2 table inconsistency and undefined plus/minus reporting. The empirical positivity checks nevertheless do not remove the theorem's positivity assumption.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work and contain readable main text, equations, figures, tables, and Appendices A–D. Algorithms, proofs, and experiments can be matched across relocations and renumbering.

after.justification: V2 retains these original experiments and adds GSM8K reasoning results, additional sampler comparisons and text-quality measurements, and empirical intensity-positivity diagnostics.

before.justification: V1 reports original toy-model convergence experiments, RADD text-generation perplexities, MaskGIT image-generation FIDs, and parameter sensitivity studies in Section 6 and Appendix D.

results.title: Fast Solvers for Discrete Diffusion Models: Theory and Applications of High-Order Algorithms

C1.justification: V2 withdraws the introductory contribution claiming provably greater information retention with a linearly growing advantage, replacing it with an empirical memory-enhancement contribution. It extends the headline experimental claims to Crafter and explicitly restricts the introductory Atari superiority claim to methods without look-ahead search.

C2.justification: V2 explains the offsetting world-model and actor-critic timing costs, explicitly acknowledges diffusion's computational overhead, and distinguishes acceptable Crafter prediction discrepancies from memory failures (Appendices A, D.8 and D.11). These add qualifications and mechanism explanations while retaining the central memory-based interpretation.

D1.justification: V2 explicitly documents parallel-scan execution and the probe inputs, prediction heads and feature source. Core hyperparameters and RTX 4090 profiling information remain. Conversely, v1's explicit 4:1 ViZDoom frame-skipping disclosure disappears; this omission does not establish an actual setting change.

Atari, MiniGrid and the five ViZDoom scenarios remain. The new probing and MSE analyses reuse existing environments.

E3.justification: New protocols include Crafter evaluation with a 1M-step budget, probes using 50 training and 10 validation trajectories with 50/100 training epochs, and pixel-MSE evaluation over specified imagination horizons (Appendices D.6-D.7). The existing Atari budget and default hyperparameters remain unchanged.

E4.justification: V2 adds representation probing, quantitative generation-quality analysis, a Transformer-versus-Mamba ablation and Crafter memory/error case studies. Existing GRU/LSTM, cross-attention and harmonizer analyses are largely relocated, not newly introduced. V1's PredictPosition qualitative case figure is omitted.

E5.justification: Appendix D.6 specifies five independent seeds for the new probing experiments. Existing benchmark and ablation reporting retains three-run averages, standard-deviation curves and bootstrap intervals. This does not establish increased run counts for retained experiments; probe uncertainty intervals are not supplied.

E6.justification: Retained Atari tables are numerically unchanged, including EDELINE's 1.866 mean HNS. New Crafter results report 11.5 ± 0.9 versus DIAMOND's 2.8 ± 0.5 (Table 2). Tables 3, 4 and 8 add probing, normalized pixel-MSE of 0.918, and Transformer comparison results. Figure 4 adds ViZDoom learning curves.

M1.justification: The proposed Mamba REM, diffusion predictor, shared prediction heads, harmonized losses and actor-critic procedure remain. V2 clarifies parallel execution and timestep sampling; v1's Algorithm 1 already includes burn-in and random target selection. The Transformer variant is an ablation comparator.

P1.justification: The title and abstract are revised, the training explanation is substantially rewritten, and related work is divided into four subsections. Main-text ablations move into Appendix D, which consolidates many previously separate appendices. Background, algorithm and objective sections are also reorganized.

P2.justification: The main text changes from two columns to one, with extensive figure resizing, repositioning and pseudocode reformatting. V2 adds four result tables, ViZDoom learning curves and a Crafter image sequence; it removes the PredictPosition image sequence and harmonizer summary bar chart while relocating other displays.

R1.justification: V2 adds references to Crafter, Transformers, GAIA-1, GAIA-2 and Pandora, with limited expansion of generative-game-engine discussion. The principal positioning around combining diffusion models and SSMs remains. The changed citation style and expanded author names are presentation edits.

T1.justification: V1's Appendix F information-retention theory is removed, including the superiority and information-growth theorems, supporting proofs, critical threshold and optimality conditions. V2 retains the background diffusion/SSM mathematics and actor-critic objectives, largely through relocation and renumbering.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens validation of the central contributions: Crafter and the Transformer ablation broaden the memory tests, while probing and pixel-MSE analyses quantify representation content and prediction fidelity previously supported mainly through architectural arguments and selected images. Withdrawing the broad theoretical guarantee and acknowledging computational costs better calibrate the claims. Some new comparison details remain underspecified, and the frame-skipping disclosure is lost, but these drawbacks are smaller than the gains in direct empirical support.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same EDELINE research, with matching architecture and retained experiments. All pages, including appendices, are readable and support comparison despite substantial reorganization.

after.justification: V2 retains original empirical results and adds Crafter evaluations, representation probes, generation-error measurements and a Transformer-based architectural comparison.

before.justification: V1 reports original Atari, MiniGrid and ViZDoom evaluations, architectural ablations, qualitative predictions and training-time measurements.

results.title: EDELINE: Enhancing Memory in Diffusion-based World Models via Linear-Time Sequence Modeling

C1.justification: v1 foregrounds low-rank parameter structure, compression benefits, and the claimed necessity of catch-tag-release for averaging. v2 instead foregrounds semantic information in tags, stronger manifestations in reasoning-distilled models, and persistence with QK normalization. Its theoretical claim is narrowed to a constructive solution and empirical emergence through training.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations involving semantic denoising, reasoning-related segmentation, tag orthogonality, activation steering, and MLP reinforcement of shared tags. Appendix K explicitly acknowledges that the mechanism is not proved necessary, optimization can fail, reasoning correlations are not causal evidence, and threshold-based detection is incomplete. These substantially qualify v1's stronger explanations.

D1.justification: v2 adds synthetic-data generation and optimization details, initialization and scheduling information, probe extraction layers/heads, a model inventory, and GPU/runtime estimates (Appendices G, J, L–M). It removes v1's pruning calibration/hyperparameter recipe and project-page link. These substantially revise the available reproducibility information.

E1.justification: v2 removes MMLU evaluation and C4 pruning calibration. It adds city/country truth classification, SST-2 sentiment classification, QuALITY text analysis, and empirical synthetic averaging tasks, including a two-separator task. Several original qualitative prompting scenarios remain in the reorganized visualization appendix.

E2.justification: The evaluated OATS, Wanda, and SparseGPT comparisons in v1 disappear, along with their dense and low-rank-removal controls. v2 introduces comparisons between tag-only, non-tag, and full-activation mass-mean probes in Tables 1, 5, and 7. OATS remains cited but is no longer experimentally compared.

E3.justification: The removed pruning evaluation used 50% sparsity and 0–5-shot MMLU testing. New protocols include aggregation over 170 prompts truncated to 150 tokens, a sink threshold of 0.2, a tag-subspace projection metric, balanced 400/200 probe construction/validation splits, and synthetic-model training for 50 epochs. Model configurations also expand substantially.

E4.justification: v2 removes the low-rank deletion and pruning interventions. It adds sink-token taxonomies, tag-separability measurements, twelve-threshold sensitivity analysis, initialization sensitivity, and a multihead synthetic experiment (Appendices B–D, F, K). Comparisons across reasoning and QK-normalized models add further analyses; these are comparisons between checkpoints, not controlled architectural ablations.

E5.justification: v1 reports no repeated-run analysis. v2 Table 8 reports success frequencies across ten runs for each initialization. Figure 3 also explicitly defines distribution quartiles and percentile whiskers across heads; these describe heterogeneity rather than confidence intervals. Repeated-run uncertainty reporting remains localized.

E6.justification: v1's MMLU curves and pruning findings are removed. New results include 92.5–99.5% cities tag-probe accuracy (Table 1), average sink counts of 1.125 versus 2.196 for pretrained versus distilled Qwen 14B (Figure 5), sentiment accuracies, and initialization success rates of 4/10, 3/10, and 0/10 (Table 8). These are newly reported experiments, not matched-setting performance gains over v1.

M1.justification: The original mechanism and two-layer construction remain, but v2 adds activation decomposition into tag/non-tag components and corresponding mass-mean probing procedures (Section 4). Appendix C introduces a two-separator model with three-dimensional embeddings, two heads per layer, and learned output projections, substantially extending the methodological content.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, research questions, contribution list, and conclusion are extensively rewritten around semantic and quantitative analysis. The pruning-centered narrative is replaced, the main proof moves into Appendix E, and the appendix structure is extensively reorganized. This is substantial narrative revision beyond added experiments.

P2.justification: v2 changes the main text from two columns to one, redesigns the retained mechanism/PCA displays, and removes pruning plots and activation-outlier panels. Numerous new violin plots, box plots, heatmaps, histograms, prompt diagrams, and result tables substantially change the visual presentation. Several original appendix examples are retained in compact, rearranged panels.

R1.justification: The compression-focused literature discussion is substantially reduced. v2 adds or expands positioning around over-mixing, positional encodings, QK normalization, semantic probing, and activation steering (Sections 1.3 and 8; Appendix I). These changes go beyond publication updates to retained references such as OATS.

T1.justification: The averaging theorem's parameter assumptions, convergence result, and most proof steps are retained, moving from v1 Section 4/Appendix A to v2 Section 7/Appendix E. Limited changes include corrected causal summation bounds and removal of explicit low-rank/outlier assertions from the theorem statement. v2 also formalizes sink/tag projections and decompositions, but supplies no new theorem for the multihead extension.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens evidence for the mechanism's generality and semantic role through quantitative measurements, controlled probe comparisons, and sensitivity analyses. It also resolves v1's central overstatement of theoretical necessity by explicitly distinguishing a constructive solution from necessity and acknowledging optimization failures. Removing the pruning/MMLU evidence and project-page link sacrifices practical evidence and access information, but the broader empirical support and better-calibrated conclusions provide a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same catch-tag-release research, with matching authors, Phi-3 examples, and sequence-averaging construction. Their text, figures, equations, and appendices support reliable comparison despite substantial restructuring.

after.justification: v2 reports original sink measurements, semantic-probe accuracies, model comparisons, synthetic training results, and supplementary analyses throughout the main text and appendices.

before.justification: v1 reports original activation visualizations, pruning interventions, and MMLU few-shot measurements in Sections 2–3 and Appendix B.

results.title: Attention Sinks: A 'Catch, Tag, Release' Mechanism for Embeddings

C1.justification: The central ALIGN contribution remains. v2 adds explicit claims of data efficiency, faster convergence and larger gains under low-resource training. Its conclusion narrows the claim about open-source instructed models from outperforming them to achieving competitive performance.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantial interpretations concerning efficient learning from linguistic priors, suitability for resource-constrained settings, compact vocabulary coverage and potential pruning. Appendix A.2 explains why the extra LM head allegedly adds little computational overhead. The detailed punctuation/whitespace mechanism discussion is removed, while the VCR proper-name failure interpretation is preserved.

D1.justification: v2 documents the additional training recipe through learning rates, batch sizes, epochs, frozen components, GPU count, resolution and token counts. It explicitly clarifies shared settings for the existing connector comparison. The future code-release promise becomes a stated code/artifact release with a project address. Original three-stage hyperparameters are retained.

E1.justification: v2 adds training on LLaVA-558K and LLaVA-NeXT-779K and evaluates general vision-language capabilities on MMMU-dev, SeedBench, MMVet, POPE and GQA. This substantially extends coverage beyond document-focused evaluation. The original document benchmarks and VCR remain; the small, manually curated word-crop probe from v1 Appendix A.2 is removed.

E2.justification: Table 1 adds Qwen2.5-VL-3B/7B, InternVL-3-2B/8B and Fuyu-8B while retaining the original comparators. The new low-resource comparison additionally evaluates H-Reducer (1×4) and HoneyBee (C-Abstractor) alongside MLP, Perceiver and Ovis, substantially broadening the evaluated alternatives.

E3.justification: Section 5.2.2 introduces a separate two-stage low-resource protocol with connector-only pretraining, subsequent component-specific learning rates, new image-resolution settings and smaller training budgets. Additional protocols include restricted-vocabulary evaluation, 2,500-sample runtime measurements and cosine-distance measurement under noise. The original three-stage hyperparameters and retained benchmark splits are unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 adds low-resource connector analysis, PCA and vocabulary-restriction experiments, runtime/memory comparisons, and embedding-distance evidence for noise robustness. It removes v1's word-crop token-decoding analysis and Figure 6. The VCR experiment, its failure examples and the other document case studies are retained, with VCR relocated to Appendix A.3.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, run-to-run variability or formal significance tests. The additional results remain point estimates; average runtime reporting does not establish uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: Matched values in Tables 1–2, VCR results and noise-related accuracy drops are unchanged. v2 adds substantial results: ALIGN averages 59.32 on document tasks and 56.88 on general tasks in the new low-resource regime; restricted-vocabulary evaluation yields 58.69 versus 58.81 with full embeddings. It also adds baseline scores, runtime measurements and noise cosine distances of 0.0036 for ALIGN versus 0.3938 for MLP. These are additional experimental results, not same-setting improvements over v1.

M1.justification: The main architecture, LM-head initialization and probability-weighted text embedding connector remain unchanged. Section 5.3 adds a limited, evaluation-only inference variant retaining approximately 3.4K embeddings instead of the full 128K vocabulary; this does not replace the main connector.

P1.justification: v2 makes targeted revisions to the title, abstract, introduction and result interpretations while retaining much of the original prose and section sequence. Section 5.2 is divided into high- and low-resource regimes, VCR moves to the appendix, and the Impact Statement is removed.

P2.justification: The document changes from a two-column format to a predominantly single-column layout. v2 adds low-resource, vocabulary-restriction and runtime tables plus a PCA figure, expands Table 1, removes the visual-to-token grid figure, and resizes or relocates existing displays, including the VCR figures.

R1.justification: Related work adds convolution-based connectors as an explicit category, discussing HoneyBee, H-Reducer and ResNet. References expand to newer Qwen2.5-VL and InternVL3 models and the added general-vision benchmarks. The overall deep/shallow-fusion framing and positioning against MLP and Ovis remain.

T1.justification: The connector equations, convex-hull argument and mathematical comparisons with MLP and visual embedding tables are retained. The new PCA, pruning and distance analyses provide empirical evidence rather than new definitions, derivations or proofs.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens evidence for applicability and practical efficiency through controlled low-resource comparisons, general-vision evaluations, broader baselines, vocabulary ablation and runtime measurements—important gaps in v1's empirical support. These benefits outweigh removal of the word-crop diagnostic and a localized new reporting error: Fuyu-8B's nine Table 1 scores average approximately 27.98, not the reported 22.97. The faster-convergence claim still lacks direct convergence evidence.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ALIGNVLM research. Their complete main texts and appendices, including equations, tables and figures, are readable and support matching retained, relocated and revised content.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds low-resource evaluations, vocabulary-restriction results, embedding analysis and runtime measurements.

before.justification: v1 reports original model evaluations, connector comparisons, noise experiments, VCR results and qualitative analyses in the main text and appendix.

results.title: AlignVLM: Bridging Vision and Language Latent Spaces for Multimodal Document Understanding

C1.justification: The central claims about selective unlearning, utility preservation and recovery resistance remain. The introduction changes the claimed contribution from theoretical insights to empirical insights and frames MI as an auxiliary signal. The conclusion now explicitly extends the effectiveness claim across diverse tasks.

C2.justification: New discussion explains why MI-selected layers can remain fixed under modest updates, explicitly identifies white-box access requirements, and proposes an untested surrogate/prompt route to black-box use (F.2 and F.4). It also adds interpretations of sampling stability and comparative recovery, plus an extended discussion of ECO's detector vulnerabilities. The original text-only and small-model limitations remain.

D1.justification: v2 adds Algorithm 1, fixed-selection and typical 1-3-layer guidance, OpenUnlearning framework/access information, and documentation for the new benchmark metrics. The abstract supplies an implementation URL where v1 only promised a future release. v2 nevertheless retains that future-release wording in Appendix D, so the PDFs establish added access information rather than verified repository availability.

E1.justification: v2 adds copyrighted news-content unlearning through MUSE News and fictitious-author entity unlearning through TOFU (Section 5.2). Appendix E.7 adds a direct RMU-versus-FALCON recovery analysis. Original component-ablation scores, logit-lens probing and QA/chat recovery tests are retained, with the ablation moved to Appendix E.5.

Existing MMLU uncertainty reporting is retained. Table 12 adds recovery values with undefined ± terms, without establishing additional runs or supplying seed counts.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial results: MUSE FALCON scores of 0.02/0.03/0.54, TOFU Forget05 FQ/MU of 0.92/0.59, efficiency and MI-sampling measurements, and comparative recovery scores (Tables 2-3, 7-9 and 12). These are newly reported evaluations, not same-setting improvements over v1. Most original scores remain unchanged, but RMU's Mistral WMDP-Bio score changes from 31.1 in v1 Table 4 to 34.1 in v2 Table 5.

M1.justification: The MI-guided selection, SVD-derived principal offset vectors, contrastive forget loss, retention loss and gradient-projection procedure remain substantively unchanged. Algorithm 1 and the fixed-layer discussion expand documentation. Different optimizer configurations and numerical gradient weights are reported experimental settings.

P1.justification: The introduction, related-work discussion and experimental narrative are substantially rewritten. Experiments are reorganized around harmful-knowledge unlearning, cross-domain generalization, efficiency and recovery; component ablations move into the appendix. New practical-implications and discussion sections substantially expand the narrative structure.

P2.justification: The main text changes from two columns to one, with extensive resizing and placement changes for figures and tables. Figure 1 is revised and moved into the introduction. Six new tables present benchmark, efficiency, MI and recovery results, while existing displays are reformatted or relocated, including the ablation table.

R1.justification: Related work expands to NPO/SimNPO, representation noising, circuit breakers, additional logit-based approaches and contrastive unlearning, alongside TOFU, MUSE and OpenUnlearning. Section 2 and Appendix F.3 introduce a substantive positioning argument distinguishing ECO's filtering from parameter-level unlearning. These changes extend beyond bibliographic and citation-style updates.

T1.justification: Equations 1-16 retain the same substantive definitions and mathematical formulations, including MI selection, KDE, principal offset vectors, losses, gradient projection and entropy. No theorem, proof or substantive derivation is added. New pseudocode and conceptual explanations document the existing formulation.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially reduces gaps in v1's support for generalizability and efficiency: MUSE and TOFU test distinct forgetting objectives, Appendices E.3-E.4 quantify computational costs and selection stability, and E.7 supplies a recovery comparator. Pseudocode and implementation/framework links improve reproducibility information. These gains outweigh reporting weaknesses, including undefined recovery uncertainty and the MUSE prose claiming lowest forgetting scores despite smaller baseline values in Table 2.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe FALCON, with matching core methodology and original experiments. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison despite substantial reformatting and additions.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds MUSE and TOFU evaluations, computational-efficiency measurements, MI sampling analysis and comparative recovery results.

before.justification: v1 reports original WMDP, MMLU and perplexity evaluations, gradient-conflict analysis, component ablations, logit-lens probing and adversarial knowledge-recovery experiments.

results.title: FALCON: Fine-grained Activation Manipulation by Contrastive Orthogonal Unalignment for Large Language Model

C1.justification: The central claim remains training-free acceleration through adaptive temporal token reuse with little loss of task success. V2 adds an explicit abstract claim of a 15% control-frequency increase and emphasizes compatibility with optimized, high-frequency VLA architectures. These extend the claimed benefits without replacing the core contribution.

C2.justification: V2 adds substantive applicability qualifications: extensive motion reduces reuse, other decoder backbones remain untested, and standalone diffusion policies are outside the method's direct scope. It also interprets the object-mask comparison through contextual relevance and discusses robustness under camera motion. The main interpretations of the retained benchmarks remain stable.

D1.justification: V2 adds a project-page pointer for code and videos and clarifies real-world success criteria, randomization, fixed-horizon single-attempt evaluation, and absence of intervention. Most hardware, preprocessing, precision, sampling, and fine-tuning details already appear in v1 and are relocated or condensed.

E1.justification: LIBERO, both SIMPLER settings, and the four real-world tasks remain. V2 adds PickPot evaluations with moving background objects and people, plus fixed-camera and moving wrist-camera inputs through OpenVLA-OFT. These extend input conditions within the retained manipulation tasks.

E2.justification: FastV and SparseVLM remain the OpenVLA acceleration comparators. V2 adds unaccelerated OpenVLA-OFT comparisons, an object-mask relevance variant using Efficient Track Anything in Table 8, and an explicit OpenVLA baseline row in the component ablation. Newly cited ToMe, PuMer, and MADTP are not evaluated.

E3.justification: V2 adds policy control frequency as an evaluation metric across the principal comparisons and evaluates the action-chunking OpenVLA-OFT configuration. New controlled experiments vary background motion, relevance proxies, token budgets, and relevance thresholds. The original default thresholds, fine-tuning budget, and hardware remain; newly disclosed real-world trial procedures do not establish reruns.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained component and token-budget ablations, v2 tests robustness to moving backgrounds, compares attention against object-mask relevance selection, and studies OpenVLA-OFT sensitivity to token budgets and relevance thresholds (Tables 7–10). These substantially expand evidence about robustness and the selection mechanism.

E5.justification: Appendix E.4 newly specifies 20 randomized trials for PickPot and PutSausage and 30 for PlaceCube and WipeTable, with success/failure counts. This discloses evaluation repetitions rather than establishing an increase in runs. Neither version reports confidence intervals, seed-level variability, or significance tests.

E6.justification: Most original LIBERO and SIMPLER scores are retained. V2 adds control-frequency results and substantial OpenVLA-OFT, robustness, and sensitivity results; its Table 2 reports 96.8% versus 97.4% success and 65.10 versus 78.98 Hz for OpenVLA-OFT without versus with caching. Real-world WipeTable success changes from 73.0% to 73.3%, and the average from 84.5% to 84.6%. Component-ablation FLOP entries are omitted.

M1.justification: Both versions use patch similarity to select static tokens, attention to exclude task-relevant tokens, entropy-based layer adaptation, and selective KV-cache reuse. Splitting the algorithm and testing additional architectures do not establish a changed proposed procedure; the object-mask alternative is an ablation.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, acceleration discussion, and experimental narrative undergo extensive rewriting. Preliminary material is incorporated into Methodology, implementation receives a separate section, the algorithm is split, and the appendices are reorganized into limitations, impact, complexity, inference, and experimental sections.

P2.justification: The main text changes from two columns to one. Figures 1 and 2 are redrawn, simulation and real-world task illustrations are merged, and the main visualization gains dynamic-background and wrist-camera panels. Tables gain frequency columns and model rows, new analysis tables appear, and retained appendix visualizations are relocated and renumbered.

R1.justification: V2 adds discussion and citations for ToMe, PuMer, MADTP, π0-FAST, HiRT, OpenVLA-OFT, Gemma2, and Efficient Track Anything, while dropping several preliminary-background references. It more explicitly positions caching as complementary to high-frequency architectures. The original distinction from pruning and retraining-based acceleration remains.

T1.justification: The entropy-based reuse definition, KV-update equations, FLOP savings model, and selection-overhead analysis are mathematically retained. V1's complexity appendix becomes Appendix C in v2. Renotation and condensation of repeated inference equations introduce no substantive assumptions, proofs, or derivations.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens the central practical-efficiency argument through control-frequency measurements, an already optimized OpenVLA-OFT baseline, and targeted robustness and relevance-selection tests. These address important gaps in v1's evidence, while clearer limitations and trial protocols improve interpretability. Local reporting errors temper the gain: Table 7 implies approximately 29% FLOP and 26% latency reductions, not the stated 42% and 35%; Table 11's pooled counts imply 81% and 84%, whereas its displayed percentages are task averages. These problems do not outweigh the substantial evidential improvements.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same VLA-Cache research. Their main texts, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support reliable matching despite substantial reorganization.

after.justification: V2 retains these empirical results and adds OpenVLA-OFT evaluations, control-frequency measurements, dynamic-background tests, and further ablations.

before.justification: V1 reports original LIBERO and SIMPLER evaluations, token-selection and token-budget ablations, and Kinova Jaco2 experiments, including success rates and computational measurements.

results.title: VLA-Cache: Efficient Vision-Language-Action Manipulation via Adaptive Token Caching

C1.justification: The central claims about physically structured, globally stable learning from sparse data and surrogate modeling remain. v2's introduction and conclusion add the claim that providing the equilibrium as prior knowledge improves accuracy and reduces data requirements. Its novelty claim is also refined through more specific comparisons with existing stable models.

C2.justification: v2 substantially expands interpretation of the equilibrium prior, explaining its advantage under scarce data and distinguishing bounded trajectories from convergence to the appropriate equilibrium. It adds a low-pass-filter explanation for noise robustness and discusses sNODE trajectory-training failures. It also clarifies that convexity is sufficient rather than necessary, discusses input warping, and reframes applicability around globally stable behavior within the region of interest.

D1.justification: v2 newly provides a stated code/model-weight access link, Glorot initialization, hardware and operating-system details, computational timings, additional training-trajectory identifiers and explicit latent encoder/decoder formulas. These materially improve reproducibility documentation. Some detail is lost when matrix parameterization is condensed, including explicit output dimensions and the softplus/absolute-value rules for Cholesky diagonals.

E1.justification: All four application domains remain. v2 adds a food-processing scenario with Gaussian-corrupted input and temperature observations during training, followed by evaluation on clean data (Section 4.3, Table 1). Additional food-processing trajectories otherwise remain within the existing dataset and task coverage.

E2.justification: v1 primarily compares sPHNN with NODE and PHNN, adding sPHNN-LM for tanks. v2 evaluates bounded PHNNs across the applications, adds Kolter–Manek sNODEs to the rigid-body comparison, and extends sPHNN-LM to the other applications. The bPHNN comparator is an OnsagerNet-inspired adaptation supporting time-dependent inputs, not an evaluation of unchanged OnsagerNet.

E3.justification: v2 introduces controlled food-processing experiments varying training-set size from one to fifteen trajectories, plus 5%, 15% and 25% Gaussian-noise conditions with evaluation on clean training and test data. These substantially expand the evaluation design. Existing training budgets, learning rates, network widths and core benchmark settings remain; v1 already specifies the fifteen-trajectory food test set despite its erroneous Figure 6 caption.

E4.justification: v2 adds substantial analyses of data requirements and noise robustness, expands fixed-versus-learned equilibrium comparisons, and tests the weaker boundedness constraint through bPHNN. Existing augmented-dimension and tank extrapolation studies remain, with saturation moved to Appendix D. Conversely, the direct comparison between learned Hamiltonians and physical energy in v1 Figure 3 is removed.

E5.justification: Both versions report ten rigid-body model instances and twenty instances per configuration for the other benchmarks, using boxplots and interquartile means/ranges to summarize variability. Added comparisons retain these practices. No increased repeat counts, seed specifications, confidence intervals or significance tests are introduced.

E6.justification: v2 adds extensive comparator, data-size, noise and timing results. For example, Table 1 reports sPHNN test RMSEs of 1.170, 2.595 and 3.177 at increasing noise levels, versus bPHNN's 1.572, 2.828 and 5.231. Section 4.1 newly reports an equilibrium-estimation distance of 0.010 for sPHNN-LM. The learned-Hamiltonian curves and energy-recovery finding from v1 Figure 3 are dropped.

M1.justification: The proposed sPHNN retains its normalized convex Hamiltonian, constrained matrices and derivative/trajectory fitting procedures. Learning the equilibrium location was already supported and tested in v1. The POD description in v2 expands the existing truncated-SVD procedure. bPHNN is introduced as a comparison model.

P1.justification: The narrative is substantially reorganized: port-Hamiltonian motivation and rigid-body equations move into the background, the random-model experiment becomes part of the architecture explanation, matrix descriptions are consolidated, and tank setup/saturation material moves to a new appendix. The introduction, experimental discussion and conclusion are extensively revised.

P2.justification: The main text changes from two columns to one, with substantial figure redesign. Architecture and random dynamics are combined; comparison plots are split into panels; food-processing plots are expanded; manufacturing figures gain heat-source and comparator displays. New noise/timing tables and a latent-model diagram appear. The manufacturing error plot and tank saturation plots are relocated and expanded.

R1.justification: v2 replaces v1's broad statement that the intersection of physical structure and stability is largely unexplored with substantive comparisons to latent linear port-Hamiltonian identification, OnsagerNet and projection-based stable learning. Discussions of Rettberg, Yu and Schlaginhaufen distinguish nonlinear global stability, time-dependent inputs and trajectory-training compatibility. This changes the research positioning beyond routine citation updates.

T1.justification: The central stability theorem and proof remain. Appendix A adds a Hessian condition to Lemma A.1 and an alternative coercivity argument; the main text removes v1's asserted finite-time zero-dissipation condition for nonconverging solutions. These are limited mathematical revisions. The new assertion that strict convexity requires an everywhere positive-definite Hessian is incorrect.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the evidence for the central contribution. v1's comparisons largely establish advantages over models without stability guarantees; v2 adds bounded and stable comparators and controlled studies separating equilibrium knowledge, data availability and noise robustness. These address important weaknesses in attributing the reported benefits. Better research positioning and new reproducibility information further improve assessability. The gains outweigh the removed energy-recovery diagnostic and localized problems, including Table 1's median/average wording inconsistency and Appendix A's incorrect strict-convexity remark; the central architecture and stability proof are retained.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same sPHNN research, with matching architecture, stability theorem and four application domains. The main text, equations, figures, tables and complete appendices are readable, allowing additions to be distinguished from relocations and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical evaluations and adds baseline comparisons, training-data and noise studies, equilibrium-estimation results and computational timings.

before.justification: v1 reports original model-training and prediction results for a spinning rigid body, cascaded tanks, thermal food processing and additive manufacturing, including extrapolation and augmented-state experiments.

results.title: Stable Port-Hamiltonian Neural Networks

C1.justification: The central adaptive-pruning and near-lossless-accuracy claims remain. v3 foregrounds 1.4× acceleration over existing sparse attention, whereas v1 emphasizes larger gains over dense implementations. The conclusion revises the generic additional speedup from 2× to 1.4×, a limited refinement of the claimed benefit.

C2.justification: v3 adds substantive discussion of the extra 1/8 KV-cache memory cost, why p is easier to tune, and the efficiency tradeoff of sharing selected tokens within GQA groups. Appendix F explicitly limits the favorable operating regime to cases where token loading dominates, acknowledges estimation overhead and architecture-integration difficulties, and identifies MLA support as future work.

D1.justification: v3 adds a project-code URL and extensive implementation documentation: asynchronous loading, two-stage pipelining, FP16 dequantization, per-head scales and zeros, PTX conversion, bit packing, and flattened KV-cache scheduling. It also discloses DS configuration provenance and MagicPIG settings. Conversely, the accuracy setup no longer explicitly states v1's 8192-token initial selector budget for Longbench.

E1.justification: v3 adds RULER, including specialized non-retrieval CWE/FWE tests, alongside the retained Longbench, GSM8K, COQA, and PG-19 coverage. Appendix E also evaluates CPU-resident KV-cache offloading, introducing a distinct execution environment beyond v1's GPU-resident evaluation.

E2.justification: MagicPIG becomes an evaluated comparator on LLaMA-3.1 Longbench and RULER results. Appendix D adds StreamingLLM and SnapKV comparisons against DS-Twilight on Longchat Longbench; these methods were only discussed in v1. Quest, DS, and the existing dense-attention comparators remain.

E3.justification: The stated medium-context baseline budget changes from 64 to 128 tokens; this documents a protocol revision without independently establishing reruns. Added protocols include RULER at 16k–96k with 4%/8% baseline budgets, 4096-token token-dropping comparisons, threshold and kernel sweeps, and CPU-offloading latency tests.

E4.justification: v3 adds threshold-p sensitivity measurements (Figure 9), quantization-dependent SpGEMV latency (Figure 12), and padded versus head/group-variable-length attention comparisons (Figure 13). It also adds cumulative-weight and multilevel budget-dynamism examples. v1's quantization-accuracy and timing-breakdown analyses are retained and relocated, not removed.

E5.justification: Neither version reports independent-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or formal significance tests. Added averages and relative score changes remain point summaries rather than new uncertainty-reporting practices.

E6.justification: v3 adds substantial benchmark and diagnostic results, including offloading latencies of 8490.95 versus 527.77 microseconds for Quest versus Quest-Twi at 30k (Table 7). Medium-context comparator scores change under the revised budget, such as LLaMA-3.1 DS GSM8K flexible accuracy from 0.3806 to 0.6194; this is not a same-setting gain. Figure 7's maximum Quest-Twi/FA2 speedup changes from 15.4× to 15.8×. Longbench averages persist, but the final three task headers are reassigned without moving their values, preventing straightforward task-level performance comparisons.

M1.justification: Both versions retain the conservative token selector, INT4 attention-weight estimation, binary-search top-p pruning, and final sparse attention. v3 elaborates head/group scheduling and quantization implementation, but does not establish that these replace a different v1 procedure; v1 already evaluates MHA and GQA models.

P1.justification: v3 extensively rewrites explanatory prose throughout the introduction, method, and evaluation. It simplifies nested evaluation subsections, moves quantization-accuracy discussion into the implementation narrative, and reorganizes the appendix into six topical sections. The retained short-context experiments are consistently reframed as medium-context experiments.

P2.justification: The document changes from two-column to predominantly single-column layout. The architecture diagram is redrawn, attention-distribution plots change presentation and normalization, and several existing plots are restyled or relocated. v3 adds a main-text Longbench summary, RULER and supplementary comparison tables, and new sensitivity, budget-dynamism, and kernel figures. The detailed Longbench table also changes task headers.

R1.justification: Section 2 substantially expands positioning beyond top-k methods, distinguishing MagicPIG's sampling, SampleAttention's prefill focus, and concurrent top-p work Tactic's distribution fitting. HShare, NSA, and MoBA are also added, alongside implementation-related references. This broadens the substantive comparison with prior and concurrent research, beyond bibliographic updates.

T1.justification: The sparse-attention, oracle top-k, and oracle top-p definitions, attention-error bound, and hierarchical runtime model are retained. v3 specifies the Frobenius norm and makes selected-weight summations explicit, clarifying the existing argument without adding a substantively different theorem, proof, or formal result.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens validation of the central adaptive-budget claim: v1 lacked threshold sensitivity and evaluated primarily against Quest and DS, while v3 adds those checks, non-top-k and token-dropping comparisons, and RULER coverage. Detailed implementation documentation and explicit memory, overhead, and GQA limitations also improve assessability. These gains outweigh reporting weaknesses, including the 15.8× Figure 7 maximum versus 15.4× in the conclusion and the unexplained Longbench column relabeling.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Twilight and provide readable text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices. Corresponding material can be matched across renumbering and relocation, including v1 Appendix A and v3 Appendices A–F.

after.justification: v3 retains original empirical results and adds RULER evaluations, further baseline comparisons, sensitivity and kernel experiments, and CPU-offloading measurements.

before.justification: v1 reports original benchmark accuracy, A100 latency measurements, quantization analysis, and timing breakdowns in Section 5 and Appendix A.

results.title: Twilight: Adaptive Attention Sparsity with Hierarchical Top-$p$ Pruning

C1.justification: The abstract's principal NUQLS, GP-connection, and efficiency claims remain. v2 makes VMSP, already proposed in v1 Section 5.3, an explicit fourth introductory contribution. Remark 1.1 additionally argues that Bayesian methods should prioritize uncertainty estimation over predictive gains, refining the paper's stated contribution and focus.

C2.justification: New Appendix C substantially develops the distinction between epistemic uncertainty and prediction quality, including critiques of NLL, calibration, and OOD-detection metrics. Appendix H.1 interprets NUQLS and PNC as complementary across training/width regimes, and the conclusion adds dependence on adequate training and local linearization as a limitation. The cross-entropy theoretical caveat already existed in v1.

D1.justification: v2 adds a separate NUQLS package link, pretrained ImageNet-weight provenance, implementation settings for convergence and coverage experiments, and detailed BDE, BatchEnsemble, SNGP, and SGLD configurations. Appendix E adds computational and memory guidance. Existing experimental-code access and much original implementation documentation are retained, while classification tuning guidance is shortened.

E1.justification: v2 adds SVHN classification with CIFAR-10 as OOD data, ImageNet classification with ImageNet-O evaluation, Gaussian synthetic regression for convergence testing, and sinusoidal regression for confidence-interval evaluation. The original UCI, toy-regression, and image-classification coverage is retained.

E2.justification: v2 adds PNC to confidence-interval comparisons and evaluates BatchEnsemble, SNGP, and SGLD in classification comparisons. BDE, already evaluated on toy regression in v1, is additionally compared on UCI datasets and FashionMNIST. These are actual comparator additions in Tables 3–4, 8, and 11 and Figure 6.

E3.justification: v2 introduces explicit NTK-variance convergence and confidence-interval coverage/width protocols. Existing settings also change: ResNet9/FashionMNIST NUQLS uses 2 instead of 5 epochs and gamma 0.1 instead of 0.6; ResNet20 uses 100 instead of 50 ensemble members. Table 7 adds a ResNet32 configuration. UCI runtime reporting now includes base-network training while separately retaining post-hoc costs. These are protocol and accounting changes, not same-setting performance comparisons.

E4.justification: New Section 4.1/Figure 2 tests convergence toward NTK-GP variance across training duration, ensemble size, and network configurations. Appendix H.1 compares confidence-interval behavior under extremely wide, partially trained versus finite-width, fully trained networks. Conversely, v1 Appendix C.2/Figure 3's classification sensitivity analysis over gamma, learning rate, and epochs is removed.

E5.justification: v2 Figure 2 reports 95% sample confidence intervals over 10 random realizations, and Appendix I.5 specifies 100 or 50 repetitions for coverage experiments. Conversely, NUQLS's ResNet20 standard deviations disappear between v1 Table 5 and v2 Table 7. The established repeated-run reporting for UCI and LeNet experiments is retained.

E6.justification: v2 adds convergence curves, coverage/width results, BDE regression scores, and additional classification results. ResNet9/FashionMNIST incorrect/OOD VMSP medians change from 0.041/0.119 to 0.182/0.217 alongside changed training settings. ResNet20 NLL changes from 0.236±0.001 to 0.228 with a larger ensemble. Original UCI predictive metrics remain unchanged; larger reported runtimes reflect added base-training costs, such as Energy NUQLS changing from 0.151 seconds to 8.374 seconds total, retaining 0.151 in parentheses.

M1.justification: The core linearized sampler, training objective, Gaussian initialization, and eNUQLS extension are retained. For the new confidence-interval experiments, however, v2 Appendix I.5 adds a 1.5 multiplier to NUQLS variances alongside the existing gamma-tuning procedure, a limited adaptation of uncertainty postprocessing.

P1.justification: v2 substantially reorganizes the narrative: main-text related work is consolidated into Appendix B, predictive classification evaluation moves to Appendix G, and experiments begin with convergence validation. The introduction is reframed around uncertainty evaluation, classification tuning discussion is shortened, and the appendices are reorganized into dedicated interpretation, cost, and experimental sections.

P2.justification: The main paper changes from two-column to single-column layout. v2 adds convergence Figure 2, four-panel Figure 6, confidence-interval and BDE tables, and expanded comparison/settings tables; removes v1's sensitivity Figure 3; and relocates predictive Table 2 to the appendix. Table 7 also introduces grouped model columns and colored rankings. Several original plots are retained or relocated.

R1.justification: Appendix B substantially expands positioning against PNC, SNGP, efficient ensemble methods, and Miani et al. (2024b)'s null-space posterior approach. Additional literature supports the new discussion of epistemic uncertainty and limitations of calibration metrics. BDE's positioning changes from largely explaining its exclusion to discussing broader direct comparisons.

T1.justification: The main assumptions, convergence theorem, GP derivation, and Appendix A proofs are substantively retained. New Appendix D presents an almost-sure noncollapse argument for parameter samples, while Appendix E derives approximate per-epoch computational costs and ensemble-memory scaling. These supplement rather than replace the central theoretical analysis.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation through direct NTK-convergence testing, broader comparator evaluations, and an explicit failure-regime study. Including base-network training costs makes the central efficiency comparison more complete, while expanded implementation details improve reproducibility. Removing the hyperparameter sensitivity study and ResNet20 error bars weakens some reporting, and ImageNet is compared only with a random baseline. Nevertheless, the gains in empirical support, applicability assessment, and cost transparency provide a substantial overall improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same NUQLS research, with matching authors, core algorithm, theory, and retained experiments. The complete 24-page v1 and 39-page v2, including appendices and v2's checklist, provide readable material for a reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds NTK-convergence experiments, confidence-interval evaluations, further comparator results, and SVHN/ImageNet evaluations.

before.justification: v1 reports original NUQLS results on toy regression, UCI datasets, image classification, uncertainty evaluation, and hyperparameter sensitivity.

results.title: Uncertainty Quantification with the Empirical Neural Tangent Kernel

C1.justification: The three principal contributions—point augmentation, 3D regularization, and PointVid—are retained. v2 drops the introduction's explicit claim of accurately resolving dynamic contacts and emphasizes visual plausibility and integration across video models. This modestly recalibrates the claimed outcome rather than replacing the central contribution.

C2.justification: Section 5 adds an explicit motion-magnitude versus smoothness trade-off. Appendix A.2 explains that excessive regularization suppresses motion, whereas excessive diffusion-loss dominance permits artifacts, and discusses balancing these effects. The limitations also shift from future transformer adoption to larger backbones and improved tracking. These are substantive but focused qualifications of the retained interpretation.

D1.justification: New Appendix A.2 documents the equal Panda70M/internal-data mixture, 640×360 two-second source clips, backbone-specific configurations, A100 80GB hardware, loss scheduling, and computational overhead: approximately 9 versus 4.75 seconds per iteration and less than 2GB additional memory. Section 3.2 clarifies bidirectional cross-attention and inference inputs. Conversely, v2 omits v1's project-page link and explicit ZoeDepth dependency disclosure.

E1.justification: Appendix A.4 adds evaluation using the official VBench test batch; v1 used VBench metrics on a Panda70M test batch. Otherwise, the Panda70M/internal training sources, Kubric examples, and task-oriented/general-video domains remain. Increased sample counts and additional backbone configurations do not themselves expand task coverage.

E2.justification: v1's quantitative Table 1 compares only against I2VGen-XL. v2 adds SVD, LTX Video, and CogVideoX 1.5 to that comparison and evaluates the proposed DiT model against its corresponding backbone. Figure 1 also adds CogVideoX 1.5 and LTX Video; DynamiCrafter remains a qualitative comparator.

E3.justification: The reported training collection increases from approximately 70K to 100K videos. The main test batch changes from 387 clips to 372 images, with random initial-frame selection now specified; the user study is also tied to this revised batch. v2 adds a 1360×768, 48-frame DiT configuration alongside the retained 448×256, 16-frame UNet configuration, plus point-MSE evaluation, quantitative ablations, and an official VBench-batch evaluation.

E4.justification: v1 already tests point augmentation, regularization, cross-attention, and diffusion loss qualitatively, including Appendix C. v2 adds numerical subject/background-consistency measurements for these ablations in Table 3 and directly evaluates point-trajectory reconstruction before training, without regularization, and with regularization in Table 2. These substantially strengthen component and mechanism analysis beyond relocating existing illustrations.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, generation seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or statistical significance tests. Both retain 10 human labelers and report aggregate preference fractions without uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: Table 1 replaces the I2VGen-XL/UNet physical-commonsense scores of 0.32665/0.37434 with 0.32876/0.37805 under revised settings, so this is not a same-setting performance gain. New results include DiT physical commonsense of 0.41384 versus CogVideoX's 0.36549, point MSEs of 0.2125/0.0031/0.0020, quantitative ablations, and official-batch scores. Qualitative examples are also added or replaced. The user-study percentages remain identical between v1 Table 2 and v2 Table 5.

M1.justification: v1 implements the framework with a UNet, whereas v2 adds a CogVideoX 1.5 DiT implementation, substantially extending the implemented model architectures. Appendix A.2 also specifies regularization every five iterations, qualifying v1's per-step description. The point-processing pipeline and core loss components remain unchanged; the explicit two-pass cross-attention description is additional implementation detail.

P1.justification: The main section sequence and substantial portions of the introduction and method are retained. v2 revises the abstract and experimental narrative, clarifies training versus inference, incorporates former appendix ablation discussion into Section 4.3, and reorganizes the supplement into A.1–A.5. These are localized narrative and organizational revisions rather than a wholesale rewrite.

P2.justification: The document changes from a two-column presentation with an opening comparison page to a single-column conference layout. Comparison figures are substantially rearranged, the dataset workflow becomes horizontal, and a dual-backbone comparison is introduced. Existing ablation panels are redistributed across Figures 6–7. Table 1 expands, three new numerical tables appear, and the existing user-study table moves to Table 5.

R1.justification: v2 adds a focused concurrent-work discussion distinguishing its 3D representation from VideoJam's optical flow and Track4Gen's 2D correspondence. It also adds references to LTX Video, DDIM, DELTA, and SpatialTrackerV2, while removing ZoeDepth. Most related-work discussion and the overall research positioning remain intact.

T1.justification: The reconstruction, rigidity, and combined-loss equations retain their mathematical content. Renaming the diffusion-loss term from Lddim to Ldiff does not introduce a new derivation. Neither version provides formal theorems or proofs, and the added standard MSE evaluation does not introduce new theory.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses v1's narrow quantitative comparison and reliance on qualitative component evidence through additional comparators, a second architecture, point-reconstruction measurements, and numerical ablations. Implementation and computational disclosures, together with the motion-suppression discussion, improve reproducibility and interpretation. Reporting ambiguities remain: full-UNet scores differ between Tables 1 and 3, and user-study percentages are unchanged despite the revised test batch. These limitations temper, but do not outweigh, the substantial gains in empirical support and transparency.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same PointVid augmentation and regularization framework. Their complete main texts, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching relocated material.

after.justification: v2 reports original evaluations of UNet and DiT implementations, numerical point-reconstruction and component-ablation results, additional benchmark results, and the retained user-study outcomes.

before.justification: v1 reports original video-generation evaluations, qualitative component ablations, synthetic point-cloud examples, and a 10-labeler user study, including results in its appendices.

results.title: Towards Physical Understanding in Video Generation: A 3D Point Regularization Approach

C1.justification: The novelty claim narrows from the first learning-based critical-token identification approach to the first learning-based approach directly predicting attention patterns. v3 foregrounds a unified predictor shared across layers and its size relative to SeerAttention. The headline compression claim changes from 16x to 13x, and the claimed offloading speedup changes from 1.4x to 5.6x based on the revised evaluation.

C2.justification: v3 adds interpretations linking attention structure to RoPE, query/key continuity and evolving patterns, and uses these to explain predictor sharing and transfer. New discussions explain advantages over previous-token/layer heuristics and argue for prediction quality over selection-policy complexity. Appendix E explicitly limits generalization across substantially different architectures and leaves necessary conditions for particular patterns unresolved.

D1.justification: v3 adds a code-availability link, architecture details specifying channels, padding, ReLU and adaptive pooling, fuller offloading-baseline implementation descriptions, and resource-license links. These materially improve implementation documentation. However, v1's exact disclosure of five training examples per LongBench task is replaced by an approximate 3% description.

E1.justification: v3 retains LongBench and GSM8K and adds AIME2024 long-output reasoning, InfiniteBench Math Find and Choice, RULER QA, MMLU and GPQA with CoT, and Needle In A Haystack retrieval. These substantially expand task requirements and input/output conditions. The 512-token LongBench evaluations remain in the appendix.

E2.justification: v3 adds Cascade to LongBench comparisons and SeerAttention to the LLaMA LongBench results. Further comparisons include InfLLM, previous-layer/token attention, two MInference variants, and MagicPIG using published MagicPIG scores. The timing comparison adds H2O but no longer reports v1's cross-layer-prefetching-plus-AttentionPredictor control.

E3.justification: The main attention diagnostic changes from attention recovery in v1 Table 1 to normalized prediction accuracy, Rrec(pred)/Rrec(target), in v3 Table 3. Timing evaluation expands from a 32K-context, 1K-budget setting to multiple context lengths and budget ratios. Added protocols include QwQ-32B reasoning, single-task training followed by transfer evaluation, and a training-data sweep with a held-out 20% test split.

E4.justification: The original architecture and hyperparameter ablations are retained. v3 adds query/key similarity across lags, cross-task transfer, training-data sensitivity, comparisons testing whether learned prediction is necessary, MInference and selection-strategy analyses, and latency/memory breakdowns. These investigate mechanisms and resource costs beyond v1's analyses, although the matched cross-layer-plus-predictor timing control is lost.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. The added averages and similarity measurements do not introduce uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Many benchmark and resource-cost results are added. Existing LLaMA LongBench means change, including 47.73 to 47.06 at budget 512 and 47.80 to 48.58 at 1024; GSM8K per-length scores also change while their reported mean remains 54.33. v3 Tables 1 and 8 disagree at budget 2048, reporting 48.04 and 48.33. Renormalized attention scores and redesigned timing results do not establish same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: v3 Section 3.4 adds an inference shortcut that predicts and updates critical-token indices every several steps, whereas v1 describes prediction for successive decoding steps. The interval is unspecified. The CNN, MSE training objective, block compression, periodic calibration and cross-token prefetching remain; the fuller architecture specification does not establish an architectural change.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction and related-work narrative are substantially revised. The separate Observation section is integrated into Method, experimental sections are reordered, and GSM8K and several ablation discussions move to expanded appendices. The appendices are reorganized into implementation, accuracy, efficiency, limitations, impacts and licensing sections.

P2.justification: Figure 1 gains a training-based comparison panel, and Figure 3 is redrawn around the unified predictor. New displays cover AIME, latency scaling, needle retrieval and cross-task transfer, alongside numerous new tables. The prefetch timeline moves to the appendix, and the original three-panel hyperparameter figure is reduced to block size while the other results remain tabulated.

R1.justification: v3 substantially revises positioning around existing learning-based approaches, adding SeerAttention, Attention-Gate, MoBA and NSA and distinguishing direct temporal attention prediction from their representations. It also adds discussion of FlexPrefill, InfLLM, RoPE research and MagicPIG. This changes the novelty argument and comparison landscape beyond bibliographic updates.

T1.justification: v1's adjacent-query attention argument is substantially extended in v3 Section 3.3. New mathematical content includes approximate invariance under joint temporal/spatial shifts, a perturbation norm bound, and a RoPE trigonometric derivation connecting relative positions to sequential and periodic attention structure. These extend the reasoning beyond notation changes.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens v1's evidence for applicability and the value of learned prediction through long-output reasoning tests, broader context and retrieval evaluations, relevant learned baselines, and direct necessity, transfer and resource-cost analyses. Architecture details and code-access information also improve reproducibility. Unreconciled LongBench values and the loss of the matched timing control weaken parts of the evidence, but the additions address important validation gaps and provide a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs are readable, materially complete versions of the same AttentionPredictor study. The method, experiments, figures and appendices can be matched despite extensive reorganization and additions.

after.justification: v3 retains original empirical results and adds benchmark evaluations, predictor-necessity and generalization experiments, and detailed latency and memory measurements.

before.justification: v1 reports original LongBench and GSM8K evaluations, attention-recovery measurements, predictor and hyperparameter ablations, query-similarity analysis and decoding-latency experiments.

results.title: AttentionPredictor: Temporal Patterns Matter for KV Cache Compression

C1.justification: The central claim remains that matching supervision to the target model's distribution improves SFT performance and efficiency over stronger-teacher responses, larger datasets and existing selection approaches. The headline gains in the abstracts are retained; the additional experiments support this existing claim.

C2.justification: v3 Section 7 explicitly qualifies GRAPE's applicability by candidate-pool quality and the base model's inherent capabilities. It also explains that response selection can complement instruction-level selection. These are useful qualifications beyond v1's existing warning about self-generation and reduced diversity.

D1.justification: v3 newly specifies the Question/Answer scoring template and length-normalized log probabilities in Section 3.2. Appendix C adds LESS and NV-Embed implementation details, and the checklist discloses greedy pass@1 evaluation. These improve documentation without establishing changes to the retained experiments; the GPU and batch-size disclosures remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Appendices B.3–B.4 add long-chain-of-thought training using an OpenR1-Math/LUFFY subset and OpenThoughts-114k. Evaluation expands to AIME24/25, AMC, Minerva, OlympiadBench, ARC-C, GPQA-Diamond and MMLU-Pro. OpenHermes coverage is retained through relocation to Appendix B.2.

E2.justification: v3 Table 2 adds evaluated LESS and Emb-NV baselines for all three target models. Appendix B.1/Table 7 adds response selection using Skywork-Reward-Llama3.1-8B-v0.2. LESS was discussed in v1's related-work appendix but was not an evaluated comparator there; the original comparison methods remain.

E3.justification: The original main experiments retain their reported one-epoch training and learning rate. Added experiments introduce Qwen2.5-1.5B/3B configurations, a second selection-and-training round, and a study sampling 1,000 Tulu instructions. The new LESS comparison specifies four warmup epochs on 5% of the data and 8192-dimensional gradient projection.

E4.justification: Figure 4 and Appendix H newly examine how response-source preferences differ across base models. Appendix G tests whether selection remains useful after initial fine-tuning, while Appendix B.4 tests extending likelihood-based supervision to token losses. The earlier single-generator, self-distillation, parameter-distance and UltraInteract subset analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run or seed counts, error bars, confidence intervals or significance tests for its experimental results. v3's checklist invokes greedy pass@1 evaluation, but this adds no uncertainty estimates or statistical testing procedure.

E6.justification: The original benchmark results are retained, but v3 adds substantial results for new comparators and experiments. Table 9 reports Qwen2.5-1.5B MATH accuracy of 0.396 with GRAPE versus 0.330 with highest-perplexity selection. Table 10 reports token-level GRAPE versus baseline scores of 60.20 versus 55.60 on MATH, but 3.23 versus 4.38 on AIME-25. These are newly reported comparisons, not improvements over v1 scores.
