M1.justification: The main response-selection procedure is retained, but Appendix B.4 introduces a distinct training objective that weights token losses by token likelihood. Appendix G also adds iterative selection using the fine-tuned checkpoint before another training round. These extend the procedure beyond selecting responses followed by standard SFT.

P1.justification: v3 substantially rewrites the abstract, experimental introductions, baseline descriptions and conclusion. Related work is integrated into the background, OpenHermes moves to the appendix, and the single-generator and self-distillation discussions become an ablations section. Dedicated discussion/limitations, acknowledgments and a conference checklist further reorganize the document.

P2.justification: The main paper changes from two-column to single-column formatting with extensive figure and table repositioning. The original three figures are retained and rearranged; a response-selection heatmap is added. Table 2 gains comparator rows, four new result tables appear, and the OpenHermes table moves to the appendix.

R1.justification: v3 adds references and discussion concerning SPIN, newer data-selection work by Dai and Ivison, NV-Embed, and long-chain-of-thought resources. It clarifies complementarity with instruction selection. The underlying positioning of GRAPE as model-dependent response selection remains stable, as does most of the detailed selection-method survey.

T1.justification: The computational-cost definitions, assumptions and derivations in v1 Appendix E are retained in v3 Appendix F. No new theorem or proof is introduced. The standard perplexity formula added in Section 3.2 explains score computation without adding a theoretical result.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens the central empirical argument by supplementing v1's S2L and data/response controls with gradient-based, embedding-based and reward-based selection comparisons. The model-specific selection analysis, clearer scoring instructions and explicit applicability limits also improve assessment of the method. Uncertainty remains unquantified, and some new reporting overstates the evidence: Appendix B.1 claims superiority on every benchmark despite Table 7's Mistral length-controlled win rates of 13.6 for GRAPE versus 13.9 for reward selection. These localized weaknesses do not outweigh the stronger comparative evidence.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same GRAPE study. Their text, figures, tables, equations and appendices are readable and support comparison, including matching material moved between the main text and appendices.

after.justification: v3 retains those empirical results and adds evaluated selection baselines, long-chain-of-thought experiments, token-weighted training and iterative GRAPE results.

before.justification: v1 reports original fine-tuning experiments on UltraInteract, Tulu–Olmo, OpenHermes and Magpie-Zoo, together with self-distillation and other analyses.

results.title: The Best Instruction-Tuning Data are Those That Fit

C1.justification: The central claims of adaptive regularization, optimal global complexity and quadratic local convergence remain. The abstract and introduction extend the practical contribution to competitive training of medium-scale PINNs, without replacing the original theoretical contribution.

C2.justification: v3 interprets the PINN advantages through globalization and adaptive regularization. Appendix A.2 newly identifies multiple CG iterations as a computational limitation and notes that nonsmooth activations such as ReLU may violate the Hessian assumption. The earlier CUTEst tradeoffs and failure-mode discussion remain.

D1.justification: Appendix H adds substantial implementation information: Python version, P100 GPUs, network architecture, double precision, tanh activation, Xavier initialization, sampling mesh, preconditioning and optimizer schedules. Appendix G adds the ARCqK implementation source. The checklist promises a code release, but the PDFs do not establish that release occurred.

E1.justification: v3 retains the 124 CUTEst problems and adds PINN training for convection, reaction and wave PDEs. This substantially extends evaluation from conventional optimization benchmarks to neural approximation of physical equations.

E2.justification: v3 adds adaptive cubic regularization method ARCqK to the CUTEst comparisons and NNCG with regularization coefficients 0.1 and 0.01 to the new PINN comparisons. CAT and AN2CER remain. Adam and L-BFGS serve as shared preliminary training stages.

E3.justification: The added PINN experiments introduce an 81,201-parameter network, 10,000 residual training points, a 101×257 evaluation mesh, Adam/L-BFGS warm starts and final-stage time budgets of 7.5, 2 and 18 hours. Training loss and test relative error are new evaluation metrics. The existing CUTEst tolerance, iteration limit and time limit remain unchanged.

E4.justification: The fallback, regularization-exponent and linesearch sweeps, together with the HIMMELBG and ROSENBR local-convergence cases, are retained from Appendix F as Appendix G. Their tested questions and reported outcomes remain unchanged; the added PINN material supplies optimizer comparisons rather than a new targeted ablation or robustness study.

E5.justification: v1 reports benchmark aggregates without repeated-seed uncertainty. v3 introduces eight random-seed runs per PINN experiment, mean and individual trajectories, and mean-plus-standard-deviation results in Table 7. Checklist item 7 identifies the uncertainty as standard deviation and explicitly describes CUTEst experiments as deterministic.

E6.justification: Existing CUTEst table entries are unchanged, while Tables 3–6 add ARCqK results, including 16.16 s shifted geometric mean runtime and 87.10% success. Tables 2 and 7 and Figures 3 and 7 add substantial PINN results. For example, Table 7 reports reaction mean training loss of 2.04×10^-9 for ARNCGg versus 5.20×10^-8 for NNCG0.01.

M1.justification: The central regularizers, fallback logic, capped CG and linesearch procedures remain unchanged; LipEstimation separates previously inline update rules. Appendix H.1 adds randomized Nyström preconditioning to CG for the PINN implementation, a limited procedural adaptation.

P1.justification: The abstract and introductory framing are rewritten, Section 2.1 substantially expands the method's intuition, and Section 3 reorganizes the technical narrative. Related work and the summarized descent lemma move into appendices. These changes substantially restructure existing exposition beyond simply adding experiments.

P2.justification: v3 adds PINN Figures 3 and 7 and Tables 2 and 7, expands CUTEst displays with ARCqK, and revises the theoretical comparison table. Conference formatting substantially resizes and repositions displays, while algorithm formatting adds line numbers and a separate LipEstimation block.

R1.justification: The earlier related-work discussion is substantially expanded in Appendix A.1, distinguishing regularization, linesearch, adaptivity and proof techniques from Royer, He, Gratton and trust-region methods. v3 also adds positioning against adaptive cubic regularization and PINN optimization literature, including Dussault, Rathore and Nyström-preconditioning work.

T1.justification: The principal assumptions, complexity guarantees and appendix proofs are retained or relocated. Section 3 adds an argument about a theta-independent neighborhood with order-3/2 convergence and a K1+K2 bound on additional iterations before quadratic convergence. This is a limited theoretical refinement.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens the practical evidence beyond v1's CUTEst evaluation through three PINN tasks, a specialist comparator, matched time budgets and eight-seed uncertainty reporting. ARCqK also makes the existing benchmark comparison more informative. Expanded method explanations and explicit applicability limits improve assessment of the largely unchanged theoretical contribution. The PINN evidence remains limited to three PDE settings, but the combined gains in empirical support and clarity are substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ARNCG research and contain readable text, algorithms, equations, figures, tables and appendices. Material can be reliably matched across the extensive reformatting and renumbering.

after.justification: Section 4 and Appendices G–H retain the CUTEst experiments and add original physics-informed neural network training results.

before.justification: Section 4 and Appendix F report original CUTEst comparisons, parameter ablations and local-convergence experiments.

results.title: A Regularized Newton Method for Nonconvex Optimization with Global and Local Complexity Guarantees

C1.justification: v3 adds theoretical regret guarantees as a headline contribution and makes structured linear scaling and compact PDT representations central to its claimed advantages over earlier prompt tuners. v1 primarily foregrounds empirical improvement of frozen PDTs and the custom environment, without a theoretical contribution. The core claim of adaptation without backbone weight updates remains.

C2.justification: v1 emphasizes high variance from ignoring segment correlations. v3 instead develops a weak-interaction explanation based on independent prompt sampling during pretraining, supported by attention analyses, while acknowledging possible prompt overfitting. It also reframes encoded features primarily as an efficiency benefit rather than a prerequisite for strong returns and adds an explicit limitation concerning offline-RL extrapolation.

D1.justification: v3 adds optimizer names, approximate pretraining/adaptation times, hyperparameter-selection information, and MuJoCo implementation provenance. Its checklist describes a supplementary code archive with reproduction instructions, replacing v1's placeholder access statement; the archive itself is not available in the supplied PDFs. Shared hyperparameters are largely unchanged, and v1's explicit Half Cheetah held-out task IDs are no longer listed.

E1.justification: Beyond the retained Sparse 2D Point and Half Cheetah tasks, v3 evaluates Ant directional locomotion and Meta-world Pick-place manipulation, including held-out tasks. Section 5.3 also introduces an evaluated synthetic vector-selection task with combinatorial choices and aggregate reward, substantially broadening task and domain coverage.

E2.justification: v3 evaluates ZORankSGD explicitly rather than only citing its source paper. Its Half Cheetah comparisons additionally include CQL oracle and hill-climbing results absent from the corresponding v1 tables. The synthetic experiment adds standard flat epsilon-greedy, UCB, and Thompson-sampling comparators. v1's Gaussian-perturbation baseline is retained under the hill-climbing name.

E3.justification: v3 adds 2,000-round synthetic size sweeps, controlled prompt permutations and attention masking, and runtime evaluations. MuJoCo aggregation is now described as covering all training tasks rather than v1's selected set, while retaining 250 rollouts and final-10 averaging. An extended ZORankSGD evaluation adds a larger budget, although Figure 6 inconsistently labels it as 1,500 episodes versus 1,250 rollouts in the caption.

E4.justification: New analyses test segment independence through permutations and attention interventions, scaling through synthetic problem-size sweeps, and feature-encoding efficiency through runtime comparisons. Extended-budget ZORankSGD curves are also added. The expert/novice mixture analysis is retained in Appendix D.2, whereas v1's Appendix C.3 diagnostic comparing offline loss with OOD online performance is removed.

E5.justification: The three-seed design and standard-deviation bands are retained. v3 explicitly identifies main-table entries as mean ± standard deviation and states the uncertainty convention globally in the checklist; v1 leaves its main-table ± notation undefined while defining standard deviation for appendix plots. This clarifies reporting without establishing additional runs or new significance tests.

E6.justification: Many shared 2D and in-distribution Half Cheetah entries remain unchanged, but Half Cheetah OOD results are replaced: for example, untuned PDT at J=1,H=5 is −36.83±2.58 in v1 Table 5 and −64.78±36.91 in v3 Table 2. These are revised reported outcomes, not established matched-setting gains. v3 adds extensive benchmark, comparator, regret, attention, and timing results, while removing the dedicated 2D OOD table and fine-tuning diagnostic.

M1.justification: v3 adds Thompson sampling as an evaluated exploration option alongside epsilon-greedy and UCB. The underlying procedure remains unchanged: independent reward models select prompt segments, receive rollout-return feedback, and optionally use frozen PDT features. Factorization and PDT-based feature extraction already appear in v1; Algorithms 1–3 are relocated to Appendix A.

P1.justification: The paper is retitled, its abstract and introduction are substantially rewritten, and the experimental narrative shifts from the custom 2D environment to MuJoCo benchmarks first. Algorithms and existing demonstration-quality discussion move to appendices, which are reorganized substantially; a conference checklist is also inserted.

P2.justification: The main text changes from two columns to one. Benchmark tables expand into multi-environment comparisons, and Figure 3 replaces the bandit's temporal sequence with a cross-method visualization paired with a results table. New regret plots, attention heatmaps, learning curves, and timing tables accompany extensive relocation and resizing of retained displays.

R1.justification: v3 substantially sharpens positioning against earlier PDT prompt tuners through claims about goal-conditioning expressiveness, causal consistency, and unstructured search scaling. It adds distinctions from MGPO, Meta-DT, and future-conditioned DT, while removing v1's discussion of LLM demonstration selection and ordering. This changes the novelty argument beyond merely expanding the bibliography.

T1.justification: v1 has no corresponding original regret theorem. v3 Section 4.3 adds a reward decomposition with bounded segment interactions, Theorem 4.1 bounding total regret by average slot regret plus 2Kε, and Corollary 4.2. Appendix G supplies the proof. These are substantive theoretical additions conditional on the stated interaction and slot-regret assumptions.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens validation: Ant and pick-place evaluations and a dedicated ZORankSGD comparison address v1's narrow coverage and reliance on an approximate comparator. Attention interventions and runtime measurements directly examine important mechanism and scalability claims, while conditional theory makes assumptions explicit. The removed 2D OOD diagnostic and inconsistent extended-budget labeling are drawbacks, but the broader and more targeted evidence provides a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same bandit-based PDT prompt-tuning work despite the changed title and substantial expansion. The main text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support matching retained, relocated, revised, and added content.

after.justification: v3 retains original experiments and adds Ant, Meta-world Pick-place, synthetic bandit, attention-intervention, and runtime results.

before.justification: v1 reports original Sparse 2D Point and Half Cheetah experiments, including prompt-tuning comparisons, demonstration-quality tests, and OOD evaluations.

results.title: Prompt Tuning Decision Transformers with Structured and Scalable Bandits

C1.justification: The central claim of near-optimal Õ(ε^-1) nested-expectation estimation and quadratic advantage over classical MLMC remains. The introduction changes its claim about directly applying QA-MLMC: v1 reports a partial speedup, whereas v2 reports no improvement over classical MLMC, strengthening the stated comparative advantage.

C2.justification: Section 3.1 corrects the mechanism explanation: the new hierarchy improves bias and variance exponents while retaining a similar cost exponent, rather than preserving statistical exponents and improving cost. V2 also explicitly identifies fault-tolerance requirements and current NISQ limitations, and clarifies that vector-valued applications require an extension.

D1.justification: V1 largely refers readers elsewhere for its computational access model. V2 Section 3 explains the requirement for sampling-procedure access and describes reversible circuit implementation using Toffoli/NOT gates and work registers. These are additional implementation disclosures, not evidence of a newly implemented or tested system.

E1.justification: Neither version uses datasets or executes training or evaluation tasks. Conditional stochastic optimization already appears in v1; v2 develops a theoretical application rather than adding an evaluated domain.

E2.justification: Table 1 retains the nested estimator of Rainforth et al., classical MLMC of Giles, and QA-MLMC of An et al. V2 Section 3.1 additionally analyzes directly nested quantum mean estimation as an alternative costing Õ(ε^-2). This is an analytical comparison, not an empirical baseline experiment.

E3.justification: Neither version specifies an empirical evaluation protocol. Revised accuracy allocations, oracle assumptions, and success guarantees concern the algorithm and its mathematical analysis, not experimental settings.

E4.justification: Neither version reports ablations, sensitivity experiments, robustness tests, error analyses, or instantiated case studies. The additional application bounds and lower-bound construction are theoretical analyses.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental repetitions, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. V2's explicit median-trick proof and failure-probability corrections concern theoretical algorithm guarantees rather than empirical uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Table 1 changes An et al.'s analytical cost from Õ(ε^-1.5) to Õ(ε^-2), now matching classical MLMC rather than improving its exponent. The proposed method remains Õ(ε^-1). Section 4 adds parameter-dependent application costs and a finite-optimization bound; these are theoretical results, not measured performance gains.

M1.justification: The quantum-inside-quantum construction is retained. Algorithm 4 corrects the returned sum to include level zero, changes per-level accuracy from ε/(2L) to ε/(2L+2), and changes failure probability from 0.1^l to 0.1^(l+1). Section 4 also adds a finite-decision-set optimization procedure combining the estimator with quantum minimum finding.

P1.justification: V2 substantially condenses and rewrites the introduction, removes the standalone preliminary examples section while retaining overlapping applications, and standardizes quantum-accelerated terminology. It adds a proof agenda and reorganizes Appendix A into four named subsections. These changes substantially revise the narrative and organization beyond adding mathematical content.

P2.justification: The document is comprehensively retypeset into a compact conference format with a redesigned title/author block and substantially different spacing and equation placement. Table 1 and Algorithm 1 become wrapped displays, and median amplification receives boxed instructions. The single comparison table is retained; neither version contains figures.

R1.justification: V2 adds literature supporting reversible computation, quantum minimum finding, the lower-bound reduction, and hardware limitations, and explicitly distinguishes its approach from classical many-body Quantum Monte Carlo. It also positions An et al.'s general QA-MLMC framework as worst-case optimal while retaining the principal nested-expectation literature.

T1.justification: V2 adds Proposition 2.3 and Appendix C's COUNT–PARITY lower-bound construction, plus the median-trick proof in Appendix A.4. It changes the formal treatment from vector-valued to scalar inner functions, revises the main parameter dependence from S+KV to K√(SV), and corrects telescoping, variance, and cost calculations. The high-confidence theorem also replaces v1's corollary that still stated 80% success.

improvement.justification: V2 repairs important correctness defects in Algorithm 4 and Appendix A, including the missing level-zero contribution and inconsistent error/failure budgets, and corrects the central QA-MLMC comparison. The new lower-bound proof and clearer applicability conditions substantially strengthen the paper. A qualification remains necessary: v2 drops S ≥ 1 while Appendix A.3 simplifies its cost as though S were bounded away from zero. This limits the revised parameter guarantee but does not outweigh the substantial corrections.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same nested-expectation algorithm despite retitling and substantial revision. The main text, equations, algorithms, table, and complete appendices—A–B in v1 and A–C in v2—support reliable comparison.

after.justification: V2 remains theoretical. Its additional lower bound and application analyses do not report executed experiments, simulation studies, or data analyses.

before.justification: V1 reports algorithms, complexity bounds, proofs, and illustrative applications. Table 1 contains theoretical costs; neither the main text nor the appendices report original empirical outcomes.

results.title: Quantum speedup of non-linear Monte Carlo problems

C1.justification: The core adaptive-mixing, convergence, fairness, and empirical-performance contributions remain. v2 adds explicit claims of a near-tight bound and near-optimal per-iteration decrease, and broadens the stated comparison beyond static and heuristic mixing. This refines and strengthens the contribution statement without changing the central research objective.

C2.justification: v2 explains that the variance term prevents excessive emphasis on noisy tasks and interprets the estimation ablation as supporting single-batch statistics. It expands the rationale for balanced task learning and suggests downstream-feedback integration. The existing data-abundance limitation and perplexity-versus-accuracy interpretation remain.

D1.justification: Table 7 revises hyperparameters and newly specifies an estimation batch size of 256. Appendix G.7 documents task-specific batch portions and averaging across sample subsets, while Table 8 supplies detailed runtime and overhead measurements. The underlying hardware, training infrastructure, tokenization, and general implementation disclosures remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same mC4 language coverage, including the six-language gradient study, the same six GLaM domains, and the same HellaSwag, ARC-Easy, CommonsenseQA, and PIQA tasks. Added shot settings and ablations reuse these datasets and tasks.

E2.justification: v2 newly evaluates FAMO and ADO across multilingual and GLaM configurations in Tables 1–2 and 13–14; v1 only cites these methods. This substantially extends comparisons to scalable multitask optimization and adaptive mixing. Existing baselines, including the PCGrad/AdaTask comparison in Figure 7, remain.

E3.justification: Table 7 replaces the reported tuning grid: for example, zeta2 changes from {5, 10, 15} to values between 0.001 and 0.01 in specified parameter pairs. Tables 9–12 add complementary zero-/seven-shot evaluations and controlled variance-coefficient and estimation-budget sweeps. The small three-language model header changes from 300M to 270M. These reported changes do not establish reruns of retained results.

E4.justification: New Appendices G.6–G.7 test whether the variance term matters and whether averaging additional gradient-statistic estimates improves performance. Appendix G.4 adds training-overhead profiling. These substantially extend v1's analyses, while retaining its gradient-interaction, sampling-trajectory, and fairness investigations.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed counts, repeated-training-run uncertainty, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Table 12's additional gradient-statistic estimates concern an algorithmic estimation budget, not replicated performance measurements or uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Original numerical benchmark rows are retained, but v2 adds extensive results for FAMO, ADO, Balanced-PiKE on GLaM, complementary shot settings, overhead, and ablations. For example, Table 2 adds 48.2% average accuracy for Balanced-PiKE with tau=5; Table 11 reports 47.0% with zeta2=0.005 versus 45.3% when the variance term is omitted.

M1.justification: Algorithms 1–3 retain the same conceptual optimization, practical sampling update, and tilted-risk extension. Fair-PiKE becomes Balanced-PiKE, and removing the common exponential factor from its normalized weights is algebraically equivalent. Newly documented gradient-estimation details do not establish a changed method.

P1.justification: The abstract and introduction are extensively rewritten, and the former preliminaries/motivation sequence becomes three 'building blocks.' Gradient-study discussion moves into Appendix C, method and proof sections are reorganized, and Fair-PiKE is renamed Balanced-PiKE throughout. This is substantial narrative restructuring beyond the scientific additions.

P2.justification: v2 expands the main benchmark tables and the former appendix Tables 8–9, now Tables 13–14, and adds five tables for profiling, shot comparisons, and ablations. It introduces a boxed feature summary and colored equation annotations, and resizes or relocates retained figures, including a text-wrapped Figure 3.

R1.justification: v2 expands the existing scalability critique in Appendix B and explicitly positions its gradient observations as extending GradVaccine from multilingual BERT to larger autoregressive models. It adds references on fair resource allocation and metadata conditioning and removes the Gemma reference. The fundamental positioning around scalable optimization under low conflict remains.

T1.justification: v2 adds a tightness construction for the descent bound at zero conflict/alignment in Theorem H.4 and a static-uniform-SGD complexity comparison in Appendix H.3. It also revises stochastic conditioning and convergence reasoning and changes the main theorem's step-size and iteration expressions. These extend the formal content beyond v1's existing proofs.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens evidence for PiKE's advantage and practicality: FAMO/ADO comparisons address missing adaptive competitors, component and estimation ablations test design choices, and measured 1.2–2.4% overhead substantiates the efficiency claim. These resolve important evidentiary gaps in v1. Formal analysis and implementation reporting also expand. Uncertainty reporting remains absent, and Theorems 3.5 and H.5 disagree on the iteration bound, but these limitations do not outweigh the substantial empirical improvements.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same PiKE research, with matching algorithms and experiments. Text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable, allowing additions to be distinguished from renaming and relocation.

after.justification: v2 retains the original empirical results and adds baseline comparisons, runtime measurements, complementary evaluation settings, and ablations in Tables 1–2 and 8–14.

before.justification: v1 reports original language-model pretraining experiments, downstream evaluations, gradient-interaction measurements, and an adaptive-mixing simulation, including Tables 1–2 and 8–9.

results.title: PiKE: Adaptive Data Mixing for Large-Scale Multi-Task Learning Under Low Gradient Conflicts

C1.justification: v1 foregrounds optimal architectural prescriptions and the efficiency of overtraining. v2 replaces these headline contributions with evidence that deeper models improve loss and benchmark performance per FLOP while wider models train faster under its parallelism setup. The abstract also drops the claim that Gemstones is the most comprehensive open-source scaling-law dataset.

C2.justification: v2 interprets cross-dataset rank stability as supporting alternative validation distributions, attributes benchmark-fit variability to architectural diversity, and links leave-one-out robustness to convex-hull fitting. It identifies poor accuracy extrapolation and develops the distinction between compute-efficient depth and time-efficient width. The existing limitation concerning parallelism-dependent timing results is retained.

D1.justification: v2 specifies Dolma 1.7, documents task-loss construction and benchmark checkpoint selection, and explains recalibrating GPU-hour analyses using measured step times on other hardware. Most architecture, optimizer, initialization, and FLOP-counting details are retained. v1's promise of a later training-code release is dropped, without establishing an actual availability change.

E1.justification: Beyond the retained Dolma evaluation, v2 evaluates FineWeb, FineWeb-Edu, and DCLM-baseline. It also adds MMLU, WinoGrande, OpenBookQA, ARC-Easy/Challenge, CommonsenseQA, PIQA, SIQA, and HellaSwag evaluations. These substantially expand task and validation-distribution coverage.

E2.justification: Kaplan and Chinchilla remain the central scaling-law comparators. v2 drops the configuration-level comparisons against Gemma, Llama, and Qwen2 models accompanying v1's shape prescriptions in Figure 5 and Appendix D. Selected Qwen2.5 and Llama validation-loss references remain in the retained overtraining analysis.

E3.justification: v2 introduces benchmark evaluation at 10B-token intervals, length-normalized accuracy comparisons, held-out 2B-model extrapolation using a 1.8B cutoff, and validation-loss relative error measured over 250B–350B tokens. Leave-one-model-out fitting adds another evaluation design. The reported learning-rate validation budget also changes from 2B tokens to 1,000 steps totaling 4.2B tokens; this does not establish that those experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds tests of validation-distribution stability, larger-model extrapolation, and sensitivity to omitting individual model shapes (Section 4.3 and Appendices D–E). Conversely, v1's dedicated width/depth-law ablations, including alternative functional forms and relaxed integer constraints, disappear. Existing learning-rate, cooldown, and grid-size analyses are partly retained.

E5.justification: v2 adds minimum/maximum prescription ranges across leave-one-model-out refits in Figure 13 and error bars in benchmark Figures 8 and 15. The benchmark bars' construction is not explained. Neither version reports training-seed replication or confidence intervals, so additional repeated training runs cannot be inferred.

E6.justification: v2 adds benchmark scores, stable model rankings across validation corpora, and contrasting error-versus-accuracy extrapolation findings. Appendix D reports validation-loss relative errors of 0.68% when fitting all checkpoints and 0.63% when withholding the largest models; these use different fitting conditions. v1's detailed optimal-width/depth prescription results are removed, while its overspending and overtraining results remain.

M1.justification: v2 removes the explicit width/depth-aware loss models and exhaustive architecture-search procedure developed in v1 Section 4.1 and Appendix D. It adds loss-to-benchmark-error and task-loss-to-accuracy predictors in Section 4.3. The transformer architecture, learning-rate scaling rule, and convex-hull fitting procedure remain unchanged.

P1.justification: The introduction, contribution statements, related-work narrative, and experimental organization are substantially rewritten. Architecture and learning-rate explanations move into Appendix A, while overspending and overtraining move into Appendices H–I. The appendices are extensively reorganized around the revised narrative.

P2.justification: v2 changes the main text from two columns to one, adds numerical sensitivity tables and benchmark, extrapolation, and uncertainty displays, and removes the extensive shape-prescription figure series. Several existing figures are resized or relocated, including the retained overspending and overtraining plots.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands positioning around downstream scaling through Gadre and Bhagia, depth benefits and pruning through Gemma 2, Zuo, and Gromov, and newer depth-transfer work. It also positions Gemstones against a gap associated with Pile-trained model suites. Earlier literature is largely retained, sometimes relocated.

T1.justification: The mathematical modeling scope changes: v1's four-term width/depth/parameter/token loss definition and alternative three-term law are absent from v2, which instead defines exponential benchmark-error and sigmoidal accuracy mappings in Equations (2)–(3). Appendix B.1 restates previously used Chinchilla mathematics rather than supplying a new derivation. Neither version contains theoretical proofs.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens empirical validation: v1 lacked direct downstream evaluation and held-out extrapolation tests, whereas Section 4.3 and Appendices D–E test practical performance, distribution stability, extrapolation, and model-selection sensitivity. Reporting poor accuracy extrapolation also exposes an important boundary. Removing the width/depth-law specification makes the retained overtraining analysis less self-contained, and benchmark error bars remain unexplained, but these shortcomings do not outweigh the stronger support for the paper's central empirical contributions.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the Gemstones study and retain the same underlying model suite. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable, supporting comparison despite substantial restructuring.

after.justification: v2 retains original training and scaling results and adds downstream benchmarking, validation across text datasets, extrapolation tests, and leave-one-model-out analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original training results for 22 transformer configurations, learning-rate experiments, fitted scaling laws, and resource-efficiency analyses.

results.title: Gemstones: A Model Suite for Multi-Faceted Scaling Laws

C1.justification: v2 expands the central contribution from diagnosing edge-dropping failures to proposing a sensitivity-preserving remedy and claiming superiority over graph-rewiring methods. The abstract and introduction also foreground feature/message dropout and synthetic and graph-level tasks. These materially broaden the paper's claims beyond v1's diagnostic focus.

C2.justification: v2 introduces the interpretation that graph-level pooling may reduce over-squashing's impact, explicitly questions homophily as a task-range proxy, and discusses potentially loose sensitivity bounds. It adds architecture-specific limitations of DropSens supported by poor GIN results, while removing v1's GraphSAGE/ResGCN extrapolation. The local-overfitting explanation is retained.

D1.justification: Appendix E adds hardware specifications, dataset splits, synthetic-data construction, readout details, learning-rate scheduling, DropSens parameter searches and a Python implementation. Table 9 records selected configurations. These substantially expand reproducibility information, although v1's explicit failed-GAT-run exclusion thresholds are no longer documented.

E1.justification: v2 adds SyntheticZINC regression, PubMed and Actor node classification, and graph classification on Mutag, Proteins, Enzymes, Reddit-Binary, IMDb-Binary and Collab. Proteins appeared in v1 only in sensitivity simulations. The additional datasets surveyed in Appendix A.2 are not all experimentally evaluated.

E2.justification: SkipNode, evaluated in v1 Table 2, disappears from v2's comparisons. v2 adds DropSens comparisons against fully adjacent layers, DIGL, SDRF, FoSR, GTR and undirected variants (Tables 2 and 8). Table 2 explicitly imports comparator scores from prior papers rather than reporting new baseline runs.

E3.justification: The primary evaluation shifts from correlations across dropping probabilities to comparisons of selected dropout configurations against NoDrop. Reported real-world training changes from learning rate 0.003 and weight decay 0.0005 to 0.001 and no weight decay. New protocols include 11-layer SyntheticZINC regression with MAE and a two-parameter DropSens search.

E4.justification: v2 adds controlled information-mixing experiments, direct Monte Carlo influence comparisons in nonlinear GCNs, and an exact-versus-approximate DropSens probability analysis. Existing propagation-matrix analyses switch from Proteins to Cora. The underfitting investigation survives in Appendix F.3, but v1's ResGCN influence study and homophilic probability-sweep panels are removed.

E5.justification: v1 reports five runs per configuration and probability–accuracy correlations. v2 reports 20 runs for configuration selection and 30 additional runs for final 50-sample comparisons, adding one-sided t-tests, normality checks, power calculations and Hedges' g. Appendix F also adds error bars, although their meaning is not specified in the captions.

E6.justification: v1's correlation table is replaced by accuracy differences, synthetic MAEs, effect sizes and rewiring-comparison results. For example, v2 Table 2 reports DropSens at 53.01% versus SDRF plus Undirected at 44.46% on Chameleon, but 22.38% versus SDRF at 28.42% on Actor. These are newly reported comparisons, not same-setting improvements over v1.

M1.justification: v1 analyzes existing dropping methods without proposing a replacement. v2 introduces DropSens: incoming-edge dropping probabilities depend on the receiving node's degree and a prescribed fraction of preserved expected message weight, with probability clipping and an approximate solution (Section 4; Appendix E.3).

P1.justification: The title, abstract, contributions and conclusion are substantially rewritten. Nonlinear theory and several experimental discussions move into reorganized appendices, while DropSens and the expanded evaluation become central sections. An appendix contents page and separate experimental-analysis sections considerably change navigation and narrative structure.

P2.justification: v2 redesigns Figure 1, adds synthetic-performance and DropSens plots, introduces several comparison and configuration tables, and replaces the correlation display with significance-colored accuracy tables. Probability-sweep figures are revised with error bars and fewer panels; the ResGCN figure disappears. The document also adopts a different title, heading and table layout.

R1.justification: v2 adds a substantial review of homophily bias in previous evaluations, including a dataset inventory and exceptions (Appendix A.2). New citations support expanded benchmarking, architectures, implementation and statistics. DropSens also changes the research positioning from critique of existing methods to an alternative compared with established rewiring techniques.

T1.justification: The central sensitivity lemmas, theorem, proofs and nonlinear extensions are retained, with substantial relocation. v2 adds the DropSens retained-information equation and its approximate solution, corrects the linear Monte Carlo propagation expression, and changes Appendix D.2's erroneous equality to an upper-bound inequality.

improvement.justification: v1 relies chiefly on homophily proxies and correlations across dropping probabilities. v2 substantially strengthens the central evidence through controlled SyntheticZINC mixing experiments, selected-configuration comparisons against NoDrop, statistical analysis and a documented constructive method. The gain is tempered by overstated DropSens superiority: Table 2 contains clear losses and Table 8 shows poor GIN performance, contradicting the abstract's consistency claim. Nevertheless, the stronger experimental design and reproducibility address important weaknesses of v1.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research on random dropping and over-squashing, with matching core sensitivity results. All 24 pages of v1 and 34 pages of v2, including appendices, support comparison despite substantial additions and reorganization.

after.justification: v2 reports original sensitivity simulations, synthetic regression and real-world classification experiments, and evaluations of the newly proposed DropSens method.

before.justification: v1 reports original node-classification experiments, sensitivity simulations, and a ResGCN influence analysis in the main text and appendices.

results.title: Effects of Dropout on Performance in Long-range Graph Learning Tasks

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution statement, and conclusion retain the central claim that WN stabilizes CrossQ and enables sample-efficient scaling without resets across 25 tasks. Introductory Figures 1–2 add explicit matched-UTD comparisons and a throughput-advantage claim against SIMBA and BRO, extending the efficiency positioning without redefining the contribution.

C2.justification: The central weight-growth/ELR/plasticity explanation remains. v2 removes the specific conclusion that Q-bias is not responsible, adds the interpretation that soft L2 regularization may require task-specific tuning or scheduling, and discusses limited benefits from resets. Section 7 newly acknowledges that the theory does not establish RL convergence rates or sample-efficiency guarantees.

D1.justification: v2 discloses RTX 3090/A5000 training hardware, parallel execution of 10 seeds through jax.vmap, and RTX 4090 timing hardware, and supplies SIMBA hyperparameters. Its checklist explicitly states that code is unavailable and a release is planned. Reproducibility remains imperfect: Table 1 lists only UTD 1 and 5 for CrossQ + WN despite Figure 4 evaluating additional ratios.

E1.justification: The same 15 DeepMind Control and 10 MyoSuite tasks appear in v1 Figure 3 and v2 Figure 7. Separating these into difficulty groups changes aggregation, not task coverage. Newly discussed robotics, Atari, and vision work is cited research rather than additional experiments by this work.

E2.justification: v2 adds evaluated SIMBA and TD-MPC2 comparisons in Figures 1, 4, and 6, and SAC + LN + WN and regularization/reset variants in Figure 5. Standalone SAC disappears from the replacement training-diagnostic comparison. BRO, CrossQ, and SR-SAC remain represented; SR-SAC moves to the appendix aggregate comparison.

E3.justification: Table 1 changes CrossQ and CrossQ + WN actor/critic learning rates from 0.0001 to 0.0003 and target entropy from |A| to |A|/2. Figure 4 extends WN evaluation from UTD 1, 2, and 5 to include 10 and 20. v2 introduces difficulty-specific 200k/1M-step summaries and an RTX 4090 throughput comparison, while retaining the stated 1M-step training budget. These are reported protocol changes; they do not establish which experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 replaces the three-task Q-bias diagnostic with grouped measurements of parameter norms, gradient norms, effective learning rates, and dead neurons. It adds L2-penalty sweeps, parameter-reset and SAC + LN + WN comparisons, and substantially extends UTD sensitivity testing. Conversely, v1's Q-bias analysis and Appendix D's individual ablation learning curves are removed.

E5.justification: Both versions report 10 seeds, IQM, and stratified bootstrap uncertainty, but v2 changes the default confidence level from 95% to 90%. Its replacement diagnostics also use 90% bootstrap intervals, whereas v1 described 95% interpercentile ranges for weight norms. No increase in repeated-run counts is stated.

E6.justification: v2 adds comparator, throughput, UTD 10/20, and regularization/reset results. Existing curves also change: CrossQ + WN's myo-pose-hard success is essentially zero in v1 Figure 3 but approaches one in v2 Figure 7. Section 5.4 changes the reported MyoSuite target-network effect from insignificant to small but significant. Changed hyperparameters, aggregation, and confidence levels prevent treating these as controlled same-setting improvements.

M1.justification: Both versions normalize the first two linear layers after gradient updates, apply weight decay to unbounded parameters, and use target critics with joint-batch statistics and Polyak averaging. v2's explicit normalization formula and additional experimental variants do not establish a change to the proposed algorithm.

P1.justification: Much of the abstract, method exposition, contribution statement, and conclusion is retained. v2 makes localized narrative revisions, changes section headings, combines conclusion and limitations, reorganizes appendices, updates authorship and funding, and appends a conference checklist. The main argumentative sequence remains recognizable.

P2.justification: The document switches from two-column to single-column presentation and extensively redesigns its visual evidence. Aggregate learning curves become introductory bar charts, a throughput scatterplot is added, diagnostics and ablation panels are rebuilt, and UTD scaling is plotted against UTD rather than training steps. The per-task benchmark grid moves to Appendix E, while the separate per-task ablation grid is removed.

R1.justification: Section 6 substantially broadens positioning around spectral normalization, SIMBA, Dreamer, plasticity-preserving Atari methods, and model-augmented high-UTD learning. Added citations also include foundational weight normalization and TD-MPC2. The Double Q-learning citation associated with the removed Q-bias discussion disappears; these changes extend substantive research context beyond bibliographic updates.

T1.justification: The scale-invariance and inverse-gradient theorems and their Appendix A–B proofs retain the same mathematical substance. v2's normalization equation makes the existing norm constraint explicit; background notation, equation numbering, and presentation change without a new theoretical result or substantive proof correction.

improvement.justification: v1 supported its scaling rationale mainly through weight-growth observations and tests up to UTD 5. v2 substantially strengthens that support with direct ELR/plasticity diagnostics, tests through UTD 20, alternative-regularization controls, stronger comparator coverage, and measured throughput. These additions address important gaps in validating the central mechanism and practical efficiency. The loss of per-task ablation traces and inconsistencies between Table 1 and figures reduce reproducibility, but the expanded evidence and clearer theoretical limitations provide a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same CrossQ + WN research. Their text, figures, tables, equations, and complete appendices are readable and support comparison despite substantial changes to experimental reporting and presentation.

after.justification: v2 reports original CrossQ + WN experiments, expanded training diagnostics, computational-throughput measurements, and additional ablations. Some comparator results are explicitly borrowed from their authors, but original empirical results are clearly present.

before.justification: v1 reports original continuous-control experiments on 15 DeepMind Control and 10 MyoSuite tasks, including training diagnostics and normalization, target-network, and UTD ablations.

results.title: Scaling Off-Policy Reinforcement Learning with Batch and Weight Normalization

C1.justification: v2 makes both corruption-supervised and label-free QoI-aware controller training central contributions, expanding v1's contribution scope. It also sharpens the emphasis on strictly bounded compute budgets and evaluations with realistic sensor corruptions. The core joint-adaptation claim and up-to-75% FLOP reduction claim remain.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations connecting autoencoder reconstruction to QoI clustering, noisy allocation gradients to task-loss-only training failures, and frozen encoder weights to seed stability. It qualifies the earlier batching-support language as future work and explicitly states that the evaluations exclude QoI variation across distributed nodes or within a sample's frames.

D1.justification: v2 substantially expands corruption-construction instructions, newly documents a corruption-only initial training epoch, and adds task hyperparameters, pretraining hardware/time, and a named GitHub code location. Some earlier specifics, including 100×100 controller input downsampling, are omitted. Table 13 also reverses image/depth corruption assignments relative to Appendix A.3, creating a reproducibility inconsistency.

E1.justification: v2 adds AVE audiovisual classification and AudioSet pretraining/evaluation, plus lowlight, depth saturation, blur, rain, and background-audio corruption scenarios. GDTM, MM-Fi, and ImageNet remain. The two-modality binary and continuous Gaussian evaluation suites disappear, although the three-modality binary-noise experiment is retained.

E2.justification: v2 adds one evaluated comparator, Modality Network Selection (MNS), across its main comparisons. This budget-matched expert-selection adaptation draws on AdaMML, DynMM, and DynaFuse; those cited methods are not separately evaluated. The earlier upper-bound, naive allocation, scratch-training, and unimodal comparator families remain.

E3.justification: Added protocols include an unequal-cost AVE evaluation using 12/16/24/32 audio-layer budgets, with each image layer costing three units (Table 4). AudioSet evaluation introduces balanced-subset finetuning and test-split assessment. New training settings include AVE LayerDrop of 0.4 and separate 100/200-epoch lowlight/blur finetuning schedules. These are added experimental designs, not established reruns of v1 experiments.

E4.justification: v2 adds a task-loss-only controller ablation, autoencoder latent-space visualization, universal-controller comparison, unequal-computation analysis, AudioSet layer-removal ablation, and qualitative allocation/failure examples. Existing ImageNet and GDTM LayerDrop analyses remain. The straight-through comparison retains the earlier discrete/Gaussian results but omits its binary and continuous cases.

E5.justification: v1 provides three-seed localization results without standard-deviation summaries. v2 Appendix A.5 reports six seeds for both ADMN and ADMN_AE across GDTM, MM-Fi, and AVE, with means and standard deviations. This substantially expands reported replication and uncertainty coverage; it does not establish that retained seed results were rerun.

E6.justification: v2 adds extensive results for ADMN_AE, MNS, new corruptions, AVE, AudioSet, and controller analyses. The corresponding eight-layer GDTM discrete/Gaussian ADMN summary changes from 37.5 to 39.0 cm alongside expanded seed averaging. Binary/continuous two-modality summaries are removed. Conversely, v1's ImageNet Table 7 is retained as v2 Table 8 with unchanged values.

M1.justification: v2 adds ADMN_AE, which pretrains an autoencoder, freezes its perceptual encoder, and learns allocation using task loss without corruption labels. It also extends corruption supervision to categorical labels and introduces a preliminary universal controller using budget-specific context tokens (Appendix A.1). The original LayerDrop and differentiable top-L selection remain.

P1.justification: The introduction, controller explanation, and results narrative are extensively rewritten. v1's standalone implementation section is redistributed or condensed, evaluations are regrouped, and discussion becomes Limitations and Discussions. The appendices are reorganized and expanded, and v2 adds an author and the NeurIPS checklist.

P2.justification: v2 replaces the two-column main layout with a single-column format, restructures the combined results table into task-specific tables, and redraws the controller diagram to include autoencoder training. Existing latency plots are merged, while new analysis tables, a t-SNE plot, and corruption/allocation illustrations substantially expand the visual presentation.

R1.justification: v2 adds Once-for-All and DynaFuse discussions and references supporting audio pretraining, autoencoders, and corruption generation; several earlier robustness/action-recognition references disappear. It elaborates unimodal subnetworks and the existing distinction between strict budgets and average-case efficiency. The basic positioning around LayerDrop-based, QoI-aware multimodal allocation remains.

T1.justification: Neither version presents new theoretical results or proofs. The substantive Gumbel-Softmax/straight-through justification in Appendix A.2 remains unchanged. v2 shortens the standard sampling equations and exposition without introducing a new derivation or formal guarantee.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses important limitations of v1's predominantly Gaussian-corrupted visual evaluations and dependence on corruption labels. The tested label-free controller, audiovisual coverage, varied sensor corruptions, diagnostic ablations, and six-seed uncertainty reporting substantially strengthen practical applicability and empirical support. Table 13's conflicting corruption assignments and some lost implementation specifics weaken reproducibility locally, but these drawbacks do not outweigh the substantive gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe ADMN and retain identifiable methods, experiments, and results. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison despite substantial expansion and reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds AVE classification, AudioSet evaluations, controller variants, corruption studies, and repeated-seed results.

before.justification: v1 reports original GDTM localization, MM-Fi classification, computational-efficiency measurements, and LayerDrop/controller ablations, including appendix results.

results.title: ADMN: A Layer-Wise Adaptive Multimodal Network for Dynamic Input Noise and Compute Resources

C1.justification: The central metric-dependent efficiency claim remains. V2's abstract and introduction explicitly qualify the linear sampling-step requirement as a worst-case result, narrowing v1's broader wording. They also foreground the empirical claim that current large MDMs have unfavorable reasoning accuracy/cost trade-offs.

C2.justification: V1 cautions that its GSM8K baseline uses different experimental settings. V2 identifies differing private pretraining datasets as a specific confound and motivates within-checkpoint controls. Appendix A.1 additionally explains that LLaDA's sequential configuration does not stop at EOS and can increase runtime. The limitations concerning HMMs and other diffusion families remain.

D1.justification: New Appendix A and Tables 3–4 document model-specific sampling implementations, block lengths, temperatures, top-p, prompting and generation limits, evaluation libraries, and timing on eight RTX 4090 GPUs. Appendix F records revised synthetic-model and timing configurations. The added checklist explicitly defers code/data release until publication; v1 provides no corresponding release statement.

E1.justification: V2 removes the free-text generation experiment using OpenWebText-trained MDLM-OWT and adds MBPP program synthesis. GSM8K mathematical reasoning and 2-, 3-, 4-gram and HMM generation remain. This substantially changes the natural-language task coverage.

E2.justification: The GPT2-medium text-generation baseline disappears, and the GSM8K comparator changes from Qwen2-Math-1.5B to Qwen2.5-7B. V2 additionally evaluates left-to-right decoding of Dream-v0-Base-7B and LLaDA-8B-Base as within-model baselines on GSM8K and MBPP. Matched autoregressive baselines remain in the synthetic experiments.

E3.justification: Formal-language settings change from length 512, hidden size 512, eight heads and eight layers (ten for 4-grams) to lengths 512/1024/2048, hidden size 768, twelve heads and ten layers. Timing batch size changes from 16 to 1, and reported sampling steps from 8–2048 to 128–2048. New large-model protocols specify eight-shot GSM8K, three-shot MBPP, and relative accuracy and measured runtime.

E4.justification: V1 primarily sweeps sampling steps at one formal-language sequence length. V2 Table 1 adds joint length/step sensitivity analysis, directly examining TER stability and SER deterioration with length. Figures 1–2 also compare recommended sampling against each checkpoint's left-to-right decoder, testing decoder effects while controlling for model and training differences.

E5.justification: V1 reports averages over 2000 generated sequences without repeated-run uncertainty or significance testing. V2 Appendix F.2 first discloses five runs and mean/standard-deviation reporting; Table 1 adds these uncertainties and t-test-based highlighting against AR baselines. This establishes new reporting, not an increase over a documented v1 run count.

E6.justification: Results are substantially replaced and expanded. V1 Section 5.2 reports AR-like perplexity at roughly 64 steps; v2 reports roughly 512 under its revised model and length settings, so this is not a matched-setting deterioration. V2 Table 2 adds timings, including 4.7 seconds for MDM versus 7.0 for AR at length 2048. New GSM8K/MBPP plots show Dream/LLaDA below Qwen2.5-7B in both accuracy and efficiency, and no joint improvement over their own sequential decoders; v1's natural-language curves are removed.

M1.justification: The analyzed MDM framework, factorized denoising, ELBO training, and synthetic-language generation algorithms remain unchanged. Larger Transformer configurations are experimental settings. The additional decoding strategies are existing methods evaluated or analyzed, rather than newly proposed method components.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and experimental narrative are substantially rewritten. Large-model observations now motivate the theory in Section 3 instead of following it in v1 Section 6. Metric and caching discussions are consolidated in Appendix B, experimental appendices are reorganized, and a conference checklist is added.

P2.justification: The main text changes from two columns to one. Formal-language bar charts are replaced by length-by-step result tables with uncertainty and significance highlighting, plus a timing table. Large-model curves are replaced by relative accuracy/efficiency scatterplots, and protocol tables are added. The dependency illustration is retained and relocated.

R1.justification: Section 2 adds recent large diffusion models and remasking/token-ordering work, and explicitly distinguishes this paper's inference trade-off analysis from Li et al. (2024)'s learning/statistical-complexity focus. References associated with the removed GPT2/OpenWebText/SlimPajama experiments disappear. The overall research positioning remains.

T1.justification: The original assumptions, TER/SER definitions, Theorems 4.2–4.4, and their proofs are retained. V2 Appendix E.3 substantially broadens the analysis to remasking: it introduces the ReMDM transition law, proves a last-sampling probability lemma (E.10), and argues that the SER lower bound extends to this setting. V1 has no corresponding remasking analysis.

improvement.justification: V2 addresses important weaknesses in v1's validation: Table 1 directly tests sequence-length scaling instead of using one length, adds repeated-run uncertainty, and Figures 1–2 introduce within-checkpoint decoding controls that reduce cross-model confounding. The worst-case qualification improves claim precision, and Appendix E.3 extends the theoretical scope. Removing the OpenWebText fluency experiment weakens natural-text support for the positive claim, but the stronger testing of the central efficiency trade-off provides a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same study of masked diffusion models and retain the central TER/SER theory. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison despite substantial reorganization.

after.justification: Sections 3 and 5 and Appendix A report original formal-language experiments and Dream/LLaDA evaluations on GSM8K and MBPP, including accuracy and execution-time measurements.

before.justification: Sections 5–6 report original formal-language training experiments, MDLM-OWT text-generation evaluations, and GSM8K evaluations, including quality and efficiency results.

results.title: Theoretical Benefit and Limitation of Diffusion Language Model

C1.justification: v1 emphasizes superior extraction performance and an approximately 18% benchmark advantage. v2's abstract distinguishes comparable downstream retrieval from better information retention, while its contribution list introduces two benchmark tasks and improved scaling as central contributions. This materially changes the scope and emphasis of the headline claims.

C2.justification: v2 distinguishes downstream answer quality from conformity to traditional KG structure and attributes scaling benefits to de-duplication and relation reuse. It newly acknowledges possible LLM-judge bias and domain-specific limitations in medicine and finance. The corpus-size limitation changes from short texts to evaluation up to 5M tokens, still below the proposed web-scale application.

D1.justification: v2 supplies resolution parameters such as 128-item groups and 16 retrieved candidates, revised extraction/resolution prompts, and new RAG answering and judging prompts. Table 3 adds per-stage token usage, runtime, throughput, and cost, while the checklist adds laptop/API resource guidance. Both versions retain the same project repository reference.

E1.justification: The original synthetic-article MINE task remains as MINE-1. v2 adds WikiQA-based retrieval over an aggregated Wikipedia corpus, entity extraction on human-annotated SemEval-2010 Task 8 sentences, and extraction/scaling experiments using The Name of the Wind. These expand both represented text sources and task requirements.

E2.justification: OpenIE and GraphRAG remain the competing extractors in the matched MINE/MINE-1 comparison. The added retrieval and scaling experiments use the existing GraphRAG comparator; OpenIE remains in MINE-1 but is excluded from the new MINE-2 task because it lacks source-chunk links. Cross-model tests evaluate KGGen variants.

E3.justification: v2 introduces hybrid retrieval of 10 triples plus 10 two-hop triples, source-text-assisted answering, and answer judging for MINE-2. It adds manual-validation sampling and a 100-sentence SemEval protocol with markup removal and flexible entity matching. The described extraction backend changes from GPT-4o to Gemini 2.0 Flash. MINE article length is revised from approximately 1,000 words to a mean of 592; this does not establish that the corpus was regenerated.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained qualitative graph examples, v2 adds sensitivity to the underlying LLM, a human audit of 60 fact–graph judgments, manual validity assessment of 100 triples per extractor, and analyses of relation reuse, de-duplication, and computational scaling. These test reliability and practical behavior that v1 did not investigate.

E5.justification: v2 adds error bars to the MINE-2 comparison in Figure 5, whereas v1 reports across-article score distributions without such bars. Their meaning and calculation are not specified, and neither version provides experimental seed or repeated-run counts. The checklist's assertion of error-bar reporting supplies no further statistical definition.

E6.justification: The original MINE scores remain 66.07% for KGGen, 47.80% for GraphRAG, and 29.84% for OpenIE. Added results include MINE-2 scores of 80.63% versus 81.20%, SemEval extraction success of 96/100, and Table 1's model scores of 73%, 66%, and 44%. Triple-validity rates are reported as 98%, 0%, and 55% for KGGen, GraphRAG, and OpenIE. Tables 2–4 add de-duplication, runtime, and cost outcomes; these are additional evaluations, not demonstrated same-setting gains over v1.

M1.justification: v1 Section 3.3 uses repeated full-list LLM clustering, cluster validation, and subsequent batch reassignment. v2 Section 4.3 replaces this with S-BERT/k-means grouping, BM25/embedding candidate retrieval, and LLM duplicate identification with canonical aliases. Appendix A also revises extraction constraints and replaces the clustering/validation prompts with a duplicate-resolution prompt.

P1.justification: The introduction is substantially rewritten, Related Work moves from Section 7 to Section 2, and method and benchmark explanations are reorganized. Appendix prompts are consolidated, the redundant validation appendix is removed, and the retained MINE prompts and example article are renumbered. A broader-impact section and NeurIPS checklist are added.

P2.justification: v2 adds the MINE-2 bar chart, four numbered tables, and Appendix D's scaling plot, substantially expanding the presentation of evidence. Existing figure images are retained and resized or relocated; v1 Figure 5 becomes v2 Figure 6. Typography, headings, prompt-box layout, and the title page are reformatted for the NeurIPS template.

R1.justification: Most extraction and KG-evaluation literature is retained. v2 adds the WikiQA citation and removes several references accompanying the shortened introduction, including Edge et al., Luo et al., and Pujara et al. It also revises the GraphRAG description to distinguish graph nodes and relationships from community summaries. The broader literature positioning remains recognizable.

T1.justification: Neither version presents formal theoretical results, proofs, or derivations. v2's new procedures and descriptive evaluation ratios do not introduce a substantive mathematical theory.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses v1's reliance on short synthetic texts and unvalidated LLM judging through downstream Wikipedia retrieval, human-annotated entity evaluation, and manual checks of judgments and triples. Resource measurements and more specific limitations also improve practical assessment. These gains are tempered by reporting inconsistencies: Figure 1 still depicts the old procedure, Figure 5 leaves error bars undefined, and GraphRAG's 1M-character runtime is 2,079.17 seconds in Table 4 but 2,319 seconds in Section 6.6. These weaknesses limit particular claims without outweighing the broader validation gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe KGGen and the MINE benchmark. All 16 pages of v1 and 24 pages of v2, including figures, tables, appendices, and the added checklist, are readable. Retained experiments and illustrations can be matched reliably.

after.justification: v2 retains the original results and adds retrieval, human-annotated entity extraction, model comparisons, manual validation, and scaling/cost experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original MINE evaluations of KGGen, GraphRAG, and OpenIE, including quantitative scores and extracted-graph examples in Figures 3–5.

results.title: KGGen: Extracting Knowledge Graphs from Plain Text with Language Models

C1.justification: V3's abstract moderates 'outperforming' the self-constructed ARM baselines to performing comparably. The introduction also frames its question around specific core capabilities rather than LLM intelligence broadly. The principal contributions concerning scaling, in-context learning, instruction-following, and reversal reasoning remain intact.

C2.justification: V3 adds substantive explanations linking multidirectional conditioning to generalization, autoregressive Instruct failures to complete-sentence SFT data, and KV-cache speedups to prompt length (Section 3.1 and Appendices B.4/B.7). It also interprets low-confidence remasking through reduced diversity, identifies fixed generation length as an efficiency limitation, and explicitly limits claims of general speed superiority.

D1.justification: V3 newly documents corpus sources, the 11% Chinese/61% English/28% code mixture, cleaning and BERT-based quality filtering, and the SFT split of one million human and 3.5 million synthetic samples. It adds baseline learning rates, batch sizes and tuning information, detailed scaling checkpoints, and A100-80GB/bfloat16/batch-size-one efficiency settings. These are substantial documentation additions, without evidence of changed training corpora or retraining.

E1.justification: The training corpora and benchmark/task coverage are retained, including the standard language benchmarks, iGSM, and 496 Chinese poem pairs. Added guidance, sampling, and efficiency experiments reuse existing tasks. V3's additional corpus-composition information documents existing training data rather than establishing a coverage change.

E2.justification: The main benchmark and poem-completion comparator rosters remain unchanged. However, v3 adds autoregressive and variable-length block-diffusion samplers to the sampling comparisons, alongside the retained fixed-length strategy. Its efficiency analysis also compares against LLaMA3 with and without KV caching, whereas v1's sampling-step analysis evaluated only LLaDA. These additions substantially expand the evaluated comparisons.

E3.justification: V1 uses tuned classifier-free guidance on six likelihood benchmarks and block sampling for several Instruct benchmarks; v3's main results omit guidance and use pure diffusion. Instruct generation lengths also change, including GSM8K from 256 to 512 and GPQA from 128 to 64. Base-model generation evaluation switches to lm-evaluation-harness except HumanEval-FIM. Ablation settings are revised, and throughput and memory protocols are added.

E4.justification: V3 replaces the GSM8K-only remasking comparison with broader sampling-strategy and remasking analyses, adds a six-benchmark guidance ablation, and expands sampling-step analysis into speed-quality and memory studies. The length ablation expands to five Base-model tasks but drops the Instruct-model sweep. The iGSM analysis and dialogue case studies are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions state that the 8B pre-training and SFT experiments were executed once and retain the same one-sample or 128-sample Monte Carlo likelihood-estimation practice. V3 adds no seed reporting, repeated-run uncertainty estimates, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests.

E6.justification: Many benchmark values and rankings change. In Table 2, LLaDA Instruct GSM8K changes from 78.6 to 69.4, Math from 26.6 to 31.9, and MBPP from 34.2 to 41.0. Its poem forward/reversal scores change from 48.8/42.4 to 51.8/45.6. Given revised evaluation and decoding settings, these are revised results rather than established same-setting gains or losses. V3 also adds substantial ablation and efficiency results; iGSM scores remain unchanged.

M1.justification: The architecture, masking objective, pre-training, and SFT procedures remain unchanged. V3 introduces an inference adjustment that sets EOS-token confidence to zero during pure-diffusion Instruct sampling on five benchmarks (Appendices B.4 and B.6). The renamed fixed-length 'block diffusion LLaDA' strategy corresponds to v1's semi-autoregressive remasking.

P1.justification: The main section sequence and much of the method, theory, and case-study prose are retained. V3 edits the framing and explanations, renames semi-autoregressive remasking, reorganizes Appendix B, and moves the Impact Statement to Appendix C. These refine the existing narrative rather than replace its overall structure.

P2.justification: The main text changes from two-column to single-column layout. Figure 1 gains an Instruct panel, Figure 4 becomes a three-strategy diagram, and Figure 5 replaces sampling-step plots with four throughput-quality plots. Ablation and memory tables are added or substantially restructured. Tables 18-19 newly tabulate the existing scaling figure, while several case-study displays are retained and relocated.

R1.justification: V3 substantially expands positioning through discussion of concurrent Mercury, protein diffusion, and sampling-acceleration and distillation research. It explicitly contrasts its objective with MaskGIT and broadens foundational attribution to Shi and Sahoo alongside Ou. Magpie and Magicoder are added for synthetic-data methodology. These changes go beyond citation-style and bibliographic updates.

T1.justification: The mathematical formulation, likelihood bound, equivalent masking objectives, any-order autoregressive connection, and guidance formula are retained in Equations (1)-(16). V3 adds explanatory comparisons and expands attribution, but introduces no substantive new theorem, proof, assumption, or derivation.

improvement.justification: V3 substantially improves the interpretability and reproducibility of the empirical claims. It separates unguided pure-diffusion main results from guidance and block-decoding alternatives, tests sampling choices across multiple tasks, measures speed and memory, and supplies important data-preparation and baseline-training details. This addresses v1's limited characterization of dependence on inference choices and practical resource costs. These gains outweigh the removal of the Instruct length sweep, although statistical uncertainty reporting remains unchanged.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same LLaDA research. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison despite substantial reformatting and renumbering.

after.justification: V3 retains original empirical results and reports additional sampling, classifier-free guidance, throughput, and memory analyses.

before.justification: V1 reports original model training, scaling experiments, benchmark evaluations, sampling ablations, iGSM results, and poem-completion experiments.

results.title: Large Language Diffusion Models

C1.justification: V2 refocuses the abstract and conclusion on robust cross-task length generalization, adds a first-framework novelty claim, and prominently claims superiority over leading long-CoT models. Its abstract highlights 95% accuracy on 30-digit addition versus 72% for DeepSeek-R1-671B and 32% for QwQ-32B. V1 primarily claims transferable rule-following improvements over its original baselines.

C2.justification: V2 adds interpretations about outcome-reward RL encouraging direct-answer shortcuts, the necessity of diverse pretraining tasks, and amortized computational efficiency. Appendix A explicitly limits applicability to controlled tasks and identifies unresolved legal/workflow applications and length definitions. V1's discussion of cheaper direct-answer or scratchpad approaches sometimes outperforming vanilla RFFT is removed.

D1.justification: V2 adds annotator training, qualification, and validation procedures; a catalogue of all 86 tasks with splits and length definitions; H800 hardware and training-time breakdowns; and PPO hyperparameters (Appendices C.1, D.2-D.3, and H). The original core training hyperparameters remain in Table 5, previously Table 3.

E1.justification: Table 1 revises reported BBH coverage from eight tasks to six, reducing total/pretraining task counts from 88/76 to 86/74. The four domains and twelve downstream tasks remain. V1 does not identify the two formerly counted tasks; v2's full task catalogue primarily adds documentation.

E2.justification: Beyond the retained direct-answer, scratchpad, and vanilla-RFFT baselines, v2 evaluates DeepSeek-R1-671B, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-7B, QwQ-32B, PPO-trained Qwen-7B, and Tulu3. It also introduces a single-task RF-pretraining control. These are reported comparisons in Tables 2-3 and Figures 7, 10-11, and 17.

E3.justification: V2 adds ACC_Len30 and Max_Len_90% aggregate metrics, long-CoT testing with temperature zero and a 24,000-token cap, PPO training, and a Llama-3.1-8B comparison. That comparison uses target fine-tuning for Meta-RFFT versus one-shot Tulu3 prompting. The original lengths 1-5 training, lengths 6-30 testing, and 100 examples per test length remain.

E4.justification: V2 adds a one-versus-74 pretraining-task ablation, an outcome-reward PPO comparison, and worked DeepSeek-R1 and PPO failure cases (Figure 17, Figure 7, and Tables 8-9). These examine task diversity and failures of rule adherence. Existing loop-count, natural-language-rule, training-curve, and data-size analyses are retained, including material moved into Appendix E.

E5.justification: V1 Figure 3 explicitly identifies error bars as 95% confidence intervals; v2 Figure 4 drops that explanation while retaining error bars. The same three-seed training curves remain in v1 Figure 10 and v2 Figure 14. No increase in repeated runs or new statistical procedure is established.

E6.justification: V2 adds long-CoT, PPO, Tulu3, task-diversity, and four-task NUPA one-shot results, together with aggregate scores in Tables 2-3. Existing results also change: 7B vanilla RFFT on LC Move Zeroes at length six rises from approximately 51% to 97% in v1 Figure 2 versus v2 Figure 3. The original 32B fine-tuning curves are retained.

M1.justification: Meta-RFFT retains supervised multi-task rule-following pretraining followed by target-task fine-tuning or one-shot adaptation. Rule recitation, variable-state traces, and synthetic augmentation from 22 snippets are retained. PPO is introduced as a comparison method, not a component of Meta-RFFT.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, related work, and results narrative are extensively rewritten. V2 creates a standalone Analysis section, consolidates data-size discussion in the appendix, relocates the impact statement, and reorganizes the appendices with a contents page. These are substantial language and structural revisions.

P2.justification: The main text changes from two columns to one. V2 separates and redraws the overview diagrams, rearranges error-analysis panels, changes plot colors and legends, and expands one-shot grids from eight to twelve tasks. It adds comparison plots, aggregate and compute tables, error-case tables, and a multipage task catalogue.

R1.justification: V2 adds substantial positioning against instruction-following approaches, citing Tulu3, Alpaca, WizardLM, and Super-NaturalInstructions, and develops comparisons with long-CoT reasoning and outcome-supervised RL. It removes the expert-versus-novice cognitive analogy and associated references. This changes the research framing beyond bibliographic updates.

T1.justification: V2 Appendix D.3 adds explicit mathematical definitions of the PPO policy objective and value loss in Equations 1-2, absent from v1. This is a limited formal addition for the new comparator; no theorem, proof, or theoretical guarantee for Meta-RFFT is introduced.

improvement.justification: V2 resolves important documentation gaps through the complete task catalogue, annotation procedures, and compute disclosures. New long-CoT comparisons and the task-diversity control test important alternatives left unexamined in v1, while explicit limitations better bound applicability. These substantially improve assessability and reproducibility.
