The unequal Tulu adaptation settings and broad interpretation of the limited PPO experiment weaken some new conclusions, and the confidence-interval explanation is lost, but these drawbacks do not outweigh the gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Meta-RFFT research despite the changed title and organization. The complete main texts, figures, tables, equations, and appendices support comparison.

after.justification: V2 retains original experiments and adds evaluations of long-CoT models, PPO training, Tulu3, and pretraining task diversity in Sections 4-5 and Appendix E.

before.justification: V1 reports original Qwen-7B and Qwen-32B fine-tuning and one-shot experiments, error analyses, and training ablations in Section 4 and Appendix C.

results.title: Beyond Single-Task: Robust Multi-Task Length Generalization for LLMs

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction now present a new fine-grained causal intervention method as a central contribution, whereas v1 applies existing path patching. The abstract and conclusion explicitly emphasize generalization from word-identified components to sentence translation. The sparse-head, specialized-role, English-intermediary, and 64-head fine-tuning claims are retained.

C2.justification: v3 adds a training-distribution explanation for pivot-language emergence, including Chinese rather than English in Qwen2.5, and discusses language-dependent head roles. It also interprets specialized-domain performance gaps, gender-related failures, literal translations, noise sensitivity, and hallucinations. These substantially expand applicability boundaries beyond v1's brief limitations discussion.

D1.justification: v1 promises code and data after acceptance; v3 supplies a GitHub code-access link and states that detection and validation datasets are separate. It also supplies additional task-specific counterfactual examples. The disclosed learning rate, batch size, epochs, gradient rescaling, and eight-A100 hardware configuration are retained.

E1.justification: v3 adds Swahili, Bengali, and Arabic analysis; MGSM mathematical reasoning; medical and legal translation using ELRC-Medical-V2 and M3T; CAMT cultural translation; and French/Spanish gender and formality evaluations. Original WMT sentence-translation coverage, including Russian, Japanese, and Czech directions, remains present.

E2.justification: Standard full-vector path patching becomes an explicitly evaluated comparator to the new subspace method across four translation directions, covering component importance, knockout effects, and targeted SFT (v3 Table 9). Appendix F also adds a randomly initialized model comparison. The original Base, Full SFT, and Random SFT comparators are retained.

E3.justification: New protocols include top-five knockout/top-32 fine-tuning comparisons, shared versus sentence-specific head ablations, validation on 132 randomly selected samples including errors, and Qwen2.5 pivot analysis. Added evaluations use sentence perplexity, BLEU-1, chrF, TER, and CSI-Match. The original fine-tuning hyperparameters remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained head-count and MLP-count tuning ablations, v3 adds MLP knockout validation, error-inclusive sample robustness, word/sentence shared-head interventions, cross-language head-role analysis, pivot-language investigations, gender/formality and cultural-bias analyses, and qualitative translation-error cases (Appendices E–N). These test substantially broader mechanistic and failure-mode questions.

E5.justification: v3 adds standard-deviation bars for attention distributions, Kolmogorov–Smirnov tests for training-stage comparisons, a Wilson confidence interval and binomial test for head behavior, and a paired t-test for cultural preservation. v1 lacks these statistical reporting practices. Repeated training-run counts and seeds remain unspecified.

E6.justification: Most original fine-tuning scores persist. The appendix En→Zh Targeted SFT entry changes from 27.6/80.0/62.5 (v1 Table 8) to 30.7/81.4/64.3 (v3 Table 14), matching the already-reported main result. Substantial new findings include 46.9% word/sentence head overlap, subspace-versus-standard patching results, and Targeted SFT trailing Full SFT on medical/legal translation (Tables 9, 12, 20).

M1.justification: v1 uses standard whole-activation path patching. v3 introduces subspace-intervened patching: contrastive activation differences and an SVD-based decomposition identify a translation-steering subspace, and interventions replace only its projection while preserving the orthogonal component (Section 4.1, Algorithms 1–2). The targeted fine-tuning strategy remains broadly unchanged.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, behavioral analysis, and fine-tuning narrative are extensively rewritten. The standalone overview section is removed, detection is reorganized around the new method, and fine-tuning setup/results are consolidated. Appendices are substantially reorganized, with expanded explanations, relocated limitations, and a conference checklist.

P2.justification: The document changes from two-column to predominantly single-column layout. v1's overview figure is removed; main translation tables are merged; attention panels and representation plots are reformatted; knockout plots gain MLP series; and attention distributions gain error bars. Numerous new analysis tables and heatmaps accompany retained and relocated figures.

R1.justification: v3 adds a related-work discussion of encoder–decoder NMT interpretation and head pruning, positioning the work as the first investigation of decoder-only LLM translation mechanisms. It also grounds the new method in linear-representation, subspace-intervention, and common/specific decomposition research, including Geiger, Makelov, Park, Piratla, and Xie.

T1.justification: v3 adds an orthogonal common/specific subspace assumption, a low-rank optimization objective, projection-based intervention equations, and Theorem 1 asserting optimality of the SVD procedure. v1 has no corresponding subspace theory. Appendix C refers the theorem's proof to cited work rather than providing a complete proof locally.

improvement.justification: v1's mechanistic validation largely relies on curated correct word translations and descriptive analyses. v3 substantially strengthens that evidence through direct method comparisons, error-inclusive validation, sentence-level interventions, statistical support, and explicit domain and gender failure analyses. These additions address important weaknesses in validation and applicability. Technical reporting remains imperfect: Algorithm 1 contains dimensional inconsistencies, and sentence-level PPL-change signs conflict between Section 4.2 and Appendix E.2. These problems limit confidence in parts of the revision, but the broader validation and clearer failure boundaries provide a substantial overall gain.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research, with matching research questions, models, and retained experiments. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support comparison despite substantial expansion and reorganization.

after.justification: v3 retains original empirical results and adds method comparisons, sentence-level interventions, multilingual reasoning, statistical analyses, and domain and bias evaluations.

before.justification: v1 reports original component-patching, knockout, representation-analysis, and fine-tuning experiments, including Tables 1–5 and appendix results.

results.title: Exploring the Translation Mechanism of Large Language Models

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the same central contributions: diffusion regularization enables efficient policy inference, and gradient manipulation balances reward with soft safety constraints. The new title and expanded experimental support do not materially change these claims.

C2.justification: New discussion explains asymmetric reward/cost critic conservatism, gradient-conflict handling, the relevance of the idealized KL-free analysis and failure modes of overly fast or slow temperature growth. Pretraining overhead is elaborated, while dataset-quality and safety limitations were already acknowledged. v2 also newly describes temperature schedules as similarly effective despite retaining a caption favoring square-root growth.

D1.justification: v2 adds details about separate critics and obtaining gradients through saved policy parameters and independent critic-driven updates. It specifies linear slack decay, describes temperature growth from 0.04 to 1.0, supplies CAPS/CCAC hyperparameters and discloses 20 evaluation episodes. Most existing architecture and training-budget information remains unchanged.

E1.justification: Reported evaluation expands from four velocity-control tasks to thirteen tasks. Table 1 and Appendix C add CarGoal1/2, PointGoal1/2, PointButton1, PointCircle1, CarRun, BallCircle and CarCircle, substantially broadening coverage to navigation and additional Bullet-Gym control tasks.

E2.justification: Table 1 adds CAPS and CCAC and changes the BC comparison to explicitly safe-trajectory BC-Safe. The inference comparison adds FISOR. BEARL matches the earlier BEAR-Lag, and TREBI matches the previously labelled Diffuser from Lin et al. (2023); these are renamings rather than additional comparators.

E3.justification: v1 Section 5.3 specifies cost limit l=10 for Table 1, whereas v2's table averages over three cost-limit scales, substantially changing the main comparison protocol. New CarRun experiments introduce slack-initialization and cost-limit sweeps. These are reported evaluation-design changes; the PDFs do not establish that every retained experiment was rerun.

E4.justification: Appendix C.1 adds CarRun sensitivity tests for initial slack values 0.1, 0.3, 0.5 and 0.7, plus training curves under cost limits 10, 20 and 30. These extend hyperparameter robustness analysis. The earlier HalfCheetah cost-limit and temperature-schedule analyses remain as Figures 2(b) and 3.

E5.justification: v1 contains shaded training traces without specifying seed counts or defining their statistical meaning. v2 Table 1 specifies five random seeds, and Appendix C.3 explicitly describes means and standard deviations across five independent seeds. This adds statistical reporting without establishing an increase from a previously stated run count.

E6.justification: Substantial new results include DRCORL return/cost pairs of 0.91/0.00 on CarGoal1 and 0.79/0.60 on CarGoal2. The four original DRCORL table entries remain unchanged, while other entries change: CDT HalfCheetah becomes 0.96/0.61 from 0.48/3.65. The revised cost-limit aggregation prevents interpreting this as a same-setting gain. Appendix training traces are also replaced and expanded.

M1.justification: The core diffusion regularization, Gaussian policy and gradient manipulation remain. Algorithm 1 removes continued diffusion updates and the explicit actor-pretraining step; Appendix B.1 explicitly freezes diffusion after pretraining. v2 removes the separate CRPO procedure and optional PID objective, and corrects cost equations, including r(s,a) to c(s,a) in the cost-critic target. The cost-only objective already appeared in v1's practical algorithm.

P1.justification: The practical-method explanation, experimental discussion, related work and conclusion are substantially rewritten or condensed. Computational efficiency becomes part of Section 5.1; the former Appendix C is incorporated into Appendix B, and experimental Appendix D is reorganized as Appendix C. A clarification subsection is added and the paper is retitled.

P2.justification: Table 1 is redesigned with separate reward/cost columns and best-safe-policy highlighting, and both tables expand. Earlier Figures 2 and 3 become a combined figure; the temperature plot moves to the appendix. New ablation plots and numerous redrawn or added training curves substantially change the visual presentation. Figure 1 and Algorithm 1 also adopt compact text-wrapped layouts.

R1.justification: The introduction and related-work discussion substantially broaden coverage of recent safe RL methods, adding works on CAPS, CCAC, VOCE, FAWAC, SafeDiffuser, OASIS, Saformer and additional trust-region/gradient approaches. These expand positioning around safe diffusion, conditional modeling and constraint adaptation. The Tessler et al. (2018) reference is removed.

T1.justification: The principal propositions, theorem, assumptions and derivations are retained. However, v1 Appendix A.2 explicitly assigns weight 1/2 to aligned-gradient iterations; v2 omits this case from the weight definition following Equation 41, leaving that definition incomplete. The added discussion of omitting KL regularization supplies interpretation rather than a new proof.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the empirical basis for the claimed reward-safety balance beyond v1's four locomotion tasks, adding navigation tasks and stronger safe baselines. Explicit multi-seed variability and implementation details improve assessability and reproducibility. These gains outweigh localized regressions, particularly the omitted aligned-gradient weight in Appendix A.2 and the inconsistent temperature discussion. Changed aggregation means revised scores should not be read as same-setting performance improvements.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe DRCORL despite the changed title. Their text, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices are readable and support a reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 reports original benchmark comparisons, inference timings, additional ablations and training curves with stated multi-seed aggregation in Section 5 and Appendix C.

before.justification: v1 reports original reward and cost measurements, inference timings, hyperparameter ablations and training curves in Section 5 and Appendix D.

results.title: Don't Trade Off Safety: Diffusion Regularization for Constrained Offline RL

C1.justification: The central claims of accurate, interpretable, robust out-of-sample supervised visualization remain. The introduction updates the scalability contribution from landmarks to prototypes, and the discussion now explicitly claims a better balance between informative-structure preservation and class separability, refining v1's emphasis on local/global structure preservation.

C2.justification: v3 replaces the KL-asymmetry explanation with a JSD-based rationale and attributes prototype benefits to implicit regularization and class-level denoising. It develops the structure-versus-separability interpretation and revises practical hyperparameter guidance. Organ-anatomy interpretations replace immune-lineage analyses, and the broader-impact discussion adds a specific proposed use for assessing diagnostic prediction reliability.

D1.justification: Beyond v1's existing architecture and optimizer details, v3 documents the importance-classifier implementations, model-specific baseline settings, GPU/CPU memory requirements, 1–6-hour experiment runtimes, and Hydra configuration management. It also announces code/configuration release and describes an anonymized supplementary zip. The PDFs alone do not establish actual access to those resources.

E1.justification: v3 adds HAR, USPS, Blood MNIST, and OrganC MNIST, while removing Crowdsourced Mapping, White Wine Quality, and the reported Zilionis single-cell experiments. The artificial tree remains in the appendix with expanded noise conditions, although it leaves the benchmark dataset table. Coverage shifts materially toward activity recognition and biomedical images.

E2.justification: P-UMAP and PaCMAP enter the benchmark and visualization comparisons, while LOL is removed. Most comparators remain, including RF-PHATE (Ker.), renamed RF-PHATE. Encoder-only and unregularized RF-AE leave Table 1 but remain as the λ = 0 and λ = 1 ablations in v3 Tables 2 and S3.

E3.justification: Evaluation changes from k-NN-derived importances and ranks based on QNX/Spearman to ensemble-derived importances, four SIA metrics, and embedding classification accuracy. Neighborhood sizes change from 10–200 to 5–sqrt(Ntrain). Reported RF-AE batch size changes from 64 to 512, default λ from 0.001 to 0.01, and 2,000 landmarks to 10% prototypes. The noise experiment also changes its split and training budget.

E4.justification: The single-noise artificial-tree comparison becomes a multi-level SNR study with learning curves. Separate loss-weight and landmark studies become joint λ-by-prototype ablations. v3 adds pixel-importance analysis, alternative classification-importance strategies, and prototype timing experiments. OrganC case studies replace Zilionis analyses, and the additional MNIST qualitative case study is removed.

E5.justification: Ten repetitions were already reported in v1. v3 explicitly identifies different seeds and extends mean ± standard-deviation reporting to the central benchmark and ablations, beyond v1's rank-only main table and limited appendix uncertainty entries. New noise-learning curves show medians and 25th–75th percentiles across ten repetitions. The earlier Mann–Whitney landmark tests are removed.

E6.justification: v1 Table 1 reports an average RF-AE rank of 4.38; v3 replaces that summary with new results, including 0.831 ± 0.011 classification accuracy and 0.776 ± 0.051 Spearman-based SIA. Classifier, OrganC, sensitivity, and runtime results are added, while Zilionis results disappear. Changed methods, datasets, and protocols prevent interpreting these as same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: v1 uses KL reconstruction loss and PCA/k-means landmarks with probabilities summed over clusters. v3 Sections 3.2–3.3 replace these with Jensen–Shannon divergence and class-wise FasterPAM k-medoids prototypes, renormalizing probabilities over selected samples. These changes alter the objective, network inputs, and out-of-sample proximity computation, while retaining the overall RF-PHATE-regularized autoencoder framework.

P1.justification: The methods exposition consolidates separate architecture, loss, and inference discussions. Evaluation and results are substantially rewritten around SIA and class separability. The appendices are reorganized into dedicated theory, evaluation, implementation, and analysis sections; the impact statement moves to an appendix, and a conference checklist is added.

P2.justification: The document changes from two columns to one. Figure 1 is redrawn horizontally, Table 1 changes from ranks to five score columns, and Figure 2 replaces Zilionis with OrganC. New displays include importance heatmaps, noise-learning curves, joint ablation grids, and timing charts. Comparison grids and dataset tables are also redesigned.

R1.justification: v3 adds references supporting JSD, f-divergences, prototype selection, FasterPAM, PaCMAP, and expanded evaluation metrics, while removing references associated with discarded comparisons and single-cell analyses. The main positioning relative to RF-PHATE, GRAE, and linear kernel extensions remains substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: v3 adds Appendix A's assumptions, Proposition A.1, proof, and finite-forest remarks, replacing v1's unconditional self-similarity assertion with a qualified asymptotic claim. Structural importance is also redefined as the drop from the unperturbed preservation score, whereas v1 Section 3.6 specifies the perturbed score itself. These are substantive formal changes.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens empirical assessability: explicit SIA definitions, classifier-performance checks and alternative importance strategies address previously unexamined dependence on one evaluation proxy. Scores with dispersion, joint ablations, and timing measurements better substantiate quality, robustness, and efficiency claims; implementation and hardware details improve reproducibility. Single-cell evidence is lost, and Appendix A's cross-similarity rewrite omits the required out-of-bag indicator, so the added proof is not an unqualified gain. Nevertheless, the improved empirical validation and transparency provide a substantial net benefit.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same RF-AE research work. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison despite substantial revisions and reorganization.

after.justification: v3 reports original benchmark results and visualizations, noise experiments, joint hyperparameter ablations, feature-importance sensitivity analyses, and runtime measurements.

before.justification: v1 reports original benchmark results, out-of-sample visualizations, a noisy artificial-tree experiment, and loss-weight and landmark-count ablations.

results.title: Random Forest Autoencoders for Guided Representation Learning

C1.justification: V2 makes preventing safety-alignment failures a central contribution and adds the headline claim of reducing jailbreaking by 91%, beyond v1's emphasis on predicting behavior and accelerating CoT. The introduction also strengthens the data-efficiency claim from fewer than 1,000 to fewer than 500 training instances. The central predictive-capability and CoT acceleration claims remain.

C2.justification: V2 adds a substantive argument that probe-based acceleration can complement speculative decoding and architectural optimizations (Section 5), and interprets the revised safety task as an intervention against disproportionately costly errors. It drops the early-token miscalibration interpretation while retaining the limitations concerning longer outputs and knowledge unavailable to the LM.

D1.justification: V2 newly documents balanced formatting train/test samples, deterministic greedy decoding, approximately two hours to generate hidden states for 10,000 instances, and probe training under 30 seconds. Appendix C clarifies GPU memory, while the checklist adds code-access and hidden-state-data availability information. These disclosures do not establish changes to previously unspecified settings.

E1.justification: The dataset roster is retained, but the task on SelfAware, KnownUnknown, and WildJailbreak changes substantially. V1 predicts the LM's refusal decision; v2 evaluates inappropriate answering/compliance using answerability or maliciousness labels and tests a forced-abstention intervention. This changes the prediction requirements of the safety evaluation.

E2.justification: V2 adds a fine-tuned bert-large-uncased input-text classifier to formatting, confidence-estimation, and safety comparisons (Figures 2–3 and Table 1). V1 has no corresponding trained text-only comparator. Vanilla CoT remains the acceleration comparator; speculative decoding is discussed but not evaluated as a baseline.

E3.justification: The revised safety evaluation conditions on answered/complied-with instances and adds precision, recall, and residual jailbreak-success measurements, replacing the earlier refusal-prediction evaluation. V2 also reports alpha=0.8 alongside alpha=0.9 for formatting and confidence estimation. These changes prevent treating the safety scores as directly comparable performance gains.

E4.justification: Most training-size, layer, threshold, model-size, and cross-model analyses are retained or relocated to Appendices A–B. V2 removes the confidence-versus-token-position curve, the input-length correlation result, and the HealthVER layer-ablation panel. It adds threshold comparisons for formatting and confidence-estimation tasks.

E5.justification: V1 shows whiskers and shaded bands without specifying seeds or their statistical meaning. V2 Figure 2 and checklist item 7 explicitly report five seeds, variation from training/validation splits, mean aggregation, and 2σ intervals/significance claims. This substantially expands uncertainty documentation; it does not establish an increase in runs.

E6.justification: V2 adds BERT and alpha=0.8 results and replaces the main abstention-prediction results with safety-failure results, including a reported WildJailbreak success reduction from 30% to 2.7%. Confidence-estimation values also change: MSMarco verbalized-confidence coverage is 31.13% in v1 Figure 4e versus 42% in v2 Figure 3 at alpha=0.9. The headline 65% CoT cost reduction, 1.34% worst accuracy loss, and Appendix A Mistral/DeepSeek scores are retained.

M1.justification: The linear input-state probe and calibration rule remain unchanged. The safety application changes procedurally: v1 predicts whether the LM will abstain, while v2 trains on responding instances to predict whether it should have abstained and forces abstention for predicted failures (Section 4.1 and Appendix C.2.2).

P1.justification: The abstract and introduction are extensively rewritten around early warning and safety. Section 3 replaces the MCQA running example with formatting failures, safety applications precede CoT acceleration, and Section 6 consolidates the ablation narrative. Appendix B gains subsections, and acknowledgments and a conference checklist are added.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is redrawn around safety intervention. V1's stacked early-warning plots are replaced by grouped comparison bars and a safety table; separate IID/OOD acceleration panels are merged. Ablation panels are reorganized between the main text and Appendix B, while the standalone MCQA consistency figure and selected diagnostic panels disappear.

R1.justification: V2 substantially expands positioning around guardrails, alignment, introspection, response planning, and conformal prediction applications. Section 7 discusses works such as Looking Inward, Emergent Response Planning, and Future Lens, refining v1's broad priority claim toward the combination of hidden-state probes and conformal early-warning systems.

T1.justification: Sections 2 and 3.1 retain the same score function, quantile construction, exchangeability assumption, probability bound, and calibration inequality in Equations 1–3. No original theorem or proof is added; v2's checklist explicitly identifies the theoretical results as borrowed.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens empirical assessability by adding trained input-text controls where v1 lacked them, explaining five-seed uncertainty reporting, and evaluating a concrete safety intervention. Clearer research positioning and implementation disclosures further improve the paper. These gains outweigh the removal of several diagnostics. Some overstatement remains: Table 1 gives KnownUnknown recall of 72.8% for the probe versus 93.1% for BERT, contrary to the blanket outperformance claim, and the revised safety results concern a filtered task.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work on predicting LM behavior using input-state probes and conformal calibration. The main texts, equations, figures, tables, and Appendices A–C are readable, as is v2's additional checklist.

after.justification: V2 retains original empirical evaluations and reports additional BERT comparisons and a revised safety intervention experiment.

before.justification: V1 reports original behavior-prediction and CoT acceleration experiments, parameter ablations, and evaluations on multiple model families.

results.title: Language Models Can Predict Their Own Behavior

C1.justification: The central contribution of relational group-level selection improving pretraining and achieving a DCLM state of the art remains. v2 replaces the headline 10%/5% improvement statements with 3.5%-9.4% gains across three scales and adds explicit claims of up to 1.75 times fewer tokens and reduced total FLOPs.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations involving longer-trajectory modeling difficulty, diversity loss under aggressive selection, and efficiency under equal compute. Appendix D explicitly limits validation to 412M-2.8B models and identifies unresolved production-scale stability challenges. Conversely, it drops v1's specific difficulty with strong amplification effects and its educational-filter overfitting interpretation, while retaining the case-study explanations.

D1.justification: v2 replaces the pair-collection recipe with 20,000 trajectories and explicit rollout length and width. It newly specifies two pretraining stages, a 50% selection ratio, Z-score normalization, regression-weight initialization, and H100 80GB training hours, alongside 3B hyperparameters. It also adds a code-release link; repository availability was not externally checked.

E1.justification: Both versions use DCLM pretraining data, FLAN reference examples, the same downstream task coverage, and the C4 experiment with nine evaluation tasks. The added 3B model and compute-budget experiments expand configurations within existing coverage.

E2.justification: v2 adds WebOrganizer to the DCLM 1B-1x comparison in Table 1, explicitly using its published results under the matching setup. The existing Random, Edu Classifier, MATES, and Quad comparisons and the C4 comparator set are retained.

E3.justification: v2 adds a 2.8B-parameter, 55.9B-token setting and equal-total-FLOP controls that train random-selection models on additional tokens. It introduces rollout-length, selection-ratio, and inference-scaling protocols. HellaSwag's 0-shot and 10-shot labels also reverse in the detailed tables while baseline numerical rows remain unchanged; those label changes do not establish rerunning.

E4.justification: v2 adds equal-compute controls, rollout-length and selection-ratio sensitivity studies, clustering runtime measurements, and an influence-prediction ablation without relationship weights. It removes v1's oracle/model relationship-overlap analysis, repeated-bootstrap-iteration comparison, individual-influence approximation comparison, and clustering variance/correlation diagnostics. The education and mathematical case studies remain, relocated to Appendix C.8.

E5.justification: v2 removes v1 Section 5.3's statement that analyses use five data splits with means and standard deviations, although shaded loss curves remain. It also removes all per-task standard errors from the retained C4 Table 8. These are reporting losses; a reduction in actual run counts cannot be inferred.

E6.justification: Under the revised method, main Group-MATES Core scores change from 0.23514 to 0.23362 at 400M-4x and from 0.30685 to 0.30747 at 1B-1x. The earlier 1B result survives as the length-2 ablation. v2 adds the 3B result of 0.36846, equal-compute results, and sensitivity and timing findings, while revising several diagnostic results. C4 accuracies remain unchanged.

M1.justification: v1 trains on total influences of data pairs and bootstraps pairs using individual influence and similarity. v2 predicts conditional marginal influence along training trajectories, averages relationships to previously selected points, and bootstraps through conditional predictions. Its default length-10 rollout replaces the pair-based procedure; v2 Table 6 retains the earlier 1B result as the length-2 variant.

P1.justification: The paper is retitled and extensively rewritten across the abstract, introduction, related work, methods, and results. v2 separates preliminaries from methods, organizes results around the speed-quality frontier, and reorganizes theory, case studies, experimental details, and broader impacts across expanded appendices.

P2.justification: v2 changes the main text from two columns to one, redraws Figure 2 around trajectory rollouts, expands Table 1, and substantially reworks the bootstrapping and clustering figures. It adds token/FLOP efficiency panels and sensitivity tables, removes several diagnostic panels, and relocates the case-study and FLOPs tables.

R1.justification: v2 adds references including WebOrganizer, Data Shapley, Datamodels, and second-order group influence functions, while removing references including DOGE, DoReMi, and Gumbel-Top-k. Positioning emphasizes retraining-based oracles and approximating costly group selection, while retaining the principal distinction between individual and interacting group influences.

T1.justification: v2 adds formal leave-n-out and leave-one-out oracle definitions and a Hessian-based influence-function derivation. Appendix A develops the trajectory-specific influence expression from SGD perturbations, replacing v1's brief presentation and independent-plus-interaction decomposition. Clustering complexity is also reformulated explicitly as O(Nn/d).

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the central efficiency argument: Figure 3 and Table 5 evaluate benefits after accounting for selection overhead, addressing a gap left by v1's cost breakdown and principally equal-token comparisons. Larger-model validation and rollout/selection-ratio studies strengthen the method's empirical justification, while implementation and code-release information improve reproducibility. Removing standard errors, the five-split explanation, and the amplification-error analysis reduces transparency, but these losses do not outweigh the stronger controlled evidence for the paper's main contribution.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Group-MATES research despite the changed title and substantial revision. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support a reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and reports additional larger-model experiments, equal-compute comparisons, rollout and selection-ratio studies, and inference timing.

before.justification: v1 reports original Group-MATES pretraining results on DCLM and C4, component ablations, influence-model evaluations, and clustering analyses.

results.title: Group-Level Data Selection for Efficient Pretraining

C1.justification: The central pointwise-undetectability claim and two primary attack contributions remain. The conclusion now claims a demonstrated extension using attacked stronger models to improve weaker-model free-response answers, while the abstract explicitly directs mitigation research toward multi-point defences.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive qualifications about easy or flawed synthetic questions, hallucinated answer details, and capability tests using questions already answered without an attack. It interprets successful distribution-level detection and proposes entropy-based monitoring. The impact discussion changes from asserting no short-term risk increase to acknowledging misuse risks and describing mitigations.

D1.justification: v2 newly documents distractor generation, supplies additional dataset examples, and provides the distribution-level monitor prompt in H.2.5. Existing attack templates and training details persist. Data-access plans change from a planned public Copyright-MCQ release and no IED-MCQ release to request-based Copyright sharing, case-by-case IED sharing, and reconstruction guidance.

E1.justification: v2 adds GPQA graduate-level questions, BSD-Cyber malicious cybersecurity questions, and SimpleQA free-response factual questions. These substantially broaden evaluated domains and task requirements beyond the retained synthetic harmful MCQs and existing benign-training and monitor datasets.

E2.justification: The existing CMT-Walnut, CMT-EndSpeak, no-attack, and pointwise-monitor comparisons remain. Appendix E adds a substantive new defence comparison using distribution-level monitors based on o3 and o4-mini. Appendix B.2 additionally compares GPT-4.1 Nano alone with the stronger-model selection pipeline.

E3.justification: The original dataset splits and attack-training settings are retained. New protocols include direct versus encoded prompting before and after fine-tuning, chain-of-thought controls, four-candidate SimpleQA selection, and monitoring groups of 5 to 30 examples with labeled attack and benign demonstrations. These expand evaluation design rather than establish reruns of the original experiments.

E4.justification: v2 adds controlled analyses of capability degradation and cross-domain generalization (C.1), two human dataset-quality audits (D.1), and sensitivity of distribution-level detection to group size and monitor model (E). The original plausibility checks, output-variation analysis, and monitor-error examples are retained.

E5.justification: v1 already reports standard errors for monitor calibration. v2 adds binomial standard errors to the existing attack results in Figures 8–9 and sample-based standard errors to Figure 6. Section C.4 newly states that each question is evaluated once per setup; it does not establish additional runs or seeds.

E6.justification: The original main attack scores and three tables retain their values. Substantial new findings include SimpleQA accuracy of 7.2% for Nano alone versus 12.6% with selection, capability results on GPQA/BSD-Cyber, and o3 detection with 76% true-positive and 92% true-negative rates for classify at N=15. v2 also reports audit findings and Gemini accepting harmful training data without the attack.

M1.justification: The core classify and flower procedures remain unchanged. Appendix B.2 adds a two-model inference extension: a weaker model generates four free-form candidates and an attacked stronger model selects among them. The letter-by-letter generation proposal in B.1 already appeared in v1.

P1.justification: The appendices are extensively regrouped into free-form generation, core attack details, dataset details, continued discussion, and monitoring material, with a new contents list. Much of the main discussion moves to Appendix F. The title, author order, explanatory passages, and cross-references are also revised.

P2.justification: v2 replaces the two-column main-text format with a single-column conference layout and substantially relocates appendix figures and tables. New Figures 6 and 12 display capability and distribution-level detection results; Figures 8–9 redisplay existing results with error bars. The original diagrams, plots, and tables remain.

R1.justification: v2 adds references supporting the theorem, new benchmarks, and harmful-fine-tuning terminology, including Blahut, Rein, Brown, Wei, Huang, Rosati's Immunization work, and Vassilev. The central positioning against Halawi's attacks remains, and much existing related-work discussion simply moves to Appendix F.

T1.justification: v1 gives a conceptual construction without a formal theorem. v2 Section 3.2 adds Theorem 1 and a proof defining a base-model likelihood threshold, an accepted-output set, and a cardinality condition for communication. The argument explicitly models detection through likelihood thresholding.

improvement.justification: v1 relied heavily on small synthetic harmful benchmarks and left harder-task capability preservation and actual multi-sample defences weakly tested. v2 addresses these gaps through controlled GPQA/BSD-Cyber evaluations and distribution-level monitoring, while audits and uncertainty estimates make the evidence more assessable. These additions substantially strengthen validation and clarify limitations. The free-response demonstration remains limited to benign SimpleQA, and the new proof's argument covers its specified likelihood-threshold detector.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same classify and flower fine-tuning attacks and retain matching core experiments. The text, figures, tables, and complete appendices support comparison despite substantial reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains those results and adds capability evaluations, a SimpleQA selection experiment, human dataset audits, and distribution-level detection experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original fine-tuning experiments, attack success rates, benign-training transfer, output-variation experiments, and monitor evaluations in the main text and appendices.

results.title: Fundamental Limitations in Pointwise Defences of LLM Finetuning APIs

C1.justification: The central claims about feature resonance, RSL and OOD separability remain. v2 explicitly broadens the applicability claim to settings without a defined classification pretext task, whereas v1 primarily motivates the work through unavailable multi-category node labels.

C2.justification: v2 adds an information-bottleneck interpretation of mid-training resonance and explains supervision and homophily effects through representation quality. Appendix G.4 newly discusses dependence on validation data, uncertain cross-domain applicability and limited direct use of available labels. These substantially extend v1's discussion, which focused mainly on distinctions from gradient-based methods.

D1.justification: v2 adds a repository link, explicitly identifies the GCN backbone, and documents hyperparameters and processing details for additional evaluations. The original hardware, software, hyperparameters and timing results are retained. Code-access statements are inconsistent: the abstract and checklist promise code, while checklist item 13 says no new code is released.

E1.justification: v2 adds Cora, Citeseer, Pubmed and Chameleon to the original five node datasets. It also introduces graph-level detection using ENZYMES/PROTEINS and ClinTox/LIPO, plus CIFAR-10-based image detection against standard and harder OOD datasets, substantially expanding domains and task granularity.

E2.justification: Table 2 adds NodeSafe and GRASP under both true-label and pseudo-label settings while retaining the earlier comparators. New comparisons also evaluate methods absent from v1's benchmark tables, including GPN, graph-kernel and contrastive-learning detectors, GOOD-D variants, and image methods such as CSI, SSD+ and KNN+.

E3.justification: New protocols vary supervised-pretraining label proportions, rewire Citeseer edges to alter homophily, and compare GCN/GAT/GIN encoders. Graph-level evaluation introduces 90% ID training with balanced ID/OOD testing; image evaluation uses ResNet-18 features trained with cross-entropy or supervised contrastive loss. The original five-dataset splits and metrics remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Tables 4, 5 and 12 newly test sensitivity to available labels, graph homophily and encoder choice. These directly investigate representation initialization and structural dependence. The earlier classifier/synthesis ablations, target-vector comparisons, sliding-window analyses and visualizations are retained, sometimes relocated.

E5.justification: Both versions report averages over five runs; no increase in runs is established. v2 newly reports ± quantities for graph-level results in Table 13, but does not define their statistical meaning. Its checklist's affirmative statistical-significance answer supplies no additional test or uncertainty procedure.

E6.justification: Matched original scores and plot contents remain unchanged, but v2 adds substantial results in Tables 3–5 and 12–15, including RSL's 94.14 AUROC on Cora and 72.03±2.87 on ClinTox/LIPO. The reported headline FPR95 reduction changes from 18.51% to 15.20% alongside expanded comparisons; this is not a same-setting improvement.

M1.justification: The core node-level RSL algorithm, losses, resonance scoring and synthetic-node procedure remain unchanged. The new image application in Appendix F.7 introduces a limited adaptation: it aligns pretrained image features to their known-ID mean, whereas v1 specifies randomly generated alignment targets.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introductory motivation and related-work narrative are revised. v2 removes the standalone preliminaries, consolidates the main experimental discussion, moves several analyses into the appendix, and reorganizes discussion material into expanded subsections. It also adds acknowledgements and a conference checklist.

P2.justification: The document switches from a two-column ICML layout to a predominantly single-column NeurIPS layout. v1 Figures 1–2 are combined into v2 Figure 1; several plots and the timing table move to the appendix. Existing plot images are retained, while multiple new result tables and expanded dataset/comparator tables substantially change presentation.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands positioning around independence from classification pretext tasks. It discusses newer node detectors including NodeSafe, GRASP, GOLD, EDBD and DeGEM, adds graph-level comparator families, and connects resonance to information-bottleneck and feature-learning literature. This exceeds bibliographic updating or isolated citation additions.

T1.justification: v2 removes v1's explicit task and wild-data definitions, including the Huber-mixture equation in Section 2. The resonance definitions, error bounds, assumptions, proofs, ETF mathematics and feature-change derivation are retained after relocation or renumbering. The added information-bottleneck discussion provides explanatory motivation rather than a new proven guarantee.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation by adding newer competitors, controlled tests of supervision, homophily and encoder dependence, and evaluations beyond node detection. These address important uncertainties about the method's comparative strength and applicability; explicit validation-set limitations also improve transparency. Undefined uncertainty quantities, removal of formal preliminaries and inaccurate checklist statements weaken reporting, but do not outweigh the substantial gains in empirical scrutiny.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same feature-resonance/RSL work despite changed titles and formatting. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables and appendices support reliable comparison and matching of relocated content.

after.justification: v2 retains the original empirical results and adds node-level, graph-level and image evaluations, together with new controlled analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original toy experiments, five-dataset node-detection results, ablations, timing measurements and representation analyses.

results.title: Harnessing Feature Resonance under Arbitrary Target Alignment for Out-of-Distribution Node Detection

C1.justification: v3 adds a qualified priority claim for a fully shared multitask model achieving specialist-comparable performance with much less data. Its central contributions now emphasize preserving pretrained priors, guidance benefits, pixel-aligned training and matting-level detail preservation. The conclusion also removes v1's qualification that performance may be acceptably below specialist models. The original data-efficiency and few-shot-adaptation claims remain.

C2.justification: v3 adds mechanisms linking guidance sensitivity to pixel precision, few-step inference to flow-matching trajectories, and detail preservation to pixel-aligned training. It distinguishes unsuccessful one-step training from successful reduced-step inference after multistep training. Small-object entity-segmentation weaknesses are reattributed from limited-data overfitting in v1 to post-processing in v3. New task-composition discussion explicitly acknowledges a very low success rate.

D1.justification: v3 newly documents aligned RoPE positions for input/noisy tokens, empty negative prompts, the guidance default, ControlNet placement in the first half of SD3 blocks, and the 600M PixArt backbone. It also specifies random selection of the five evaluation points and replaces project/demo pointers with a code-and-model repository link. Existing optimizer, hardware, training-duration and LoRA details are largely retained.

E1.justification: The principal training datasets and benchmark suite in Table S1 are retained. v3 adds BAID/generated-image examples for detail preservation and exploratory referring-segmentation and point-conditioned depth-composition examples (Figures S7, S12 and S13). Renaming semantic segmentation to text-based instance segmentation, and point-prompted segmentation to interactive segmentation, does not itself add coverage.

E2.justification: v3 substantially expands targeted comparisons: ControlNet is evaluated for pose prediction, directly adapted SD3 for few-shot highlighting, and IC-Light for detail preservation (Figures S4, S6 and S7). The original quantitative benchmark comparator sets are retained. Removing the entirely blank Painter and One Diffusion rows from the normal-estimation table does not remove evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: v3 adds controlled token/channel-concatenation experiments, a 600M-parameter PixArt configuration, CFG sweeps from 1 to 5, inference-step sweeps for DICEPTION and comparison models, and matched SD3 few-shot comparisons. Main depth/normal results now correspond to CFG=2; v1 values are reproduced as CFG=1 in Tables S6–S7. The retained benchmark metrics and main training budget remain unchanged.

E4.justification: New Appendix B substantially expands analysis of input injection, backbone choice, ControlNet conditioning, guidance sensitivity, reduced-step inference, adaptation speed and detail preservation. Appendix E adds exploratory task-composition cases. The original U-Net failures, one-step-training failures, point-count comparison and post-processing error examples remain, sometimes relocated; those are not new analyses.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests or comparable uncertainty estimates. The new sweeps continue reporting point estimates. Surface-normal mean and median values are prediction-error metrics, not estimates of run-to-run uncertainty.

E6.justification: Tables 1–2 contain revised model results under the newly reported guidance setting: depth AbsRel changes from 0.072 to 0.061 on NYUv2 and from 0.243 to 0.289 on DIODE. These are not same-setting gains; the original rows survive as CFG=1 results. Unified-IO's DIODE delta1 changes from 0.906 to 0.708. Tables S2–S12 add extensive backbone, guidance and inference-step results, including segmentation mIoU of 47.10 at 28 steps versus 42.53 at one step. Main pose, entity and instance-segmentation scores are retained.

M1.justification: The RGB representation, point embeddings, flow-matching objective, LoRA adaptation and post-processing remain. v3 adds guided inference combining task-conditioned and empty-prompt predictions, with CFG=2 as the default, and presents a PixArt-alpha backbone variant. These extend the existing framework; expanded descriptions of token concatenation and RoPE alone do not establish changes to the original architecture.

P1.justification: The abstract, contribution list and conclusion are substantially rewritten. A method overview replaces the preliminary subsection, experimental analysis is reorganized, U-Net discussion moves into the expanded appendix, and one-step failures move into the main text. Post-processing discussion gains separate subsections, limitations become a broader discussion section, and task terminology is revised throughout.

P2.justification: v3 changes the document to a predominantly single-column layout, redraws the pipeline as a multi-panel diagram, and replaces the opening visualization arrangement. The original point-count bar chart becomes Table 5, while existing failure figures are relocated. Numerous new ablation tables, plots and comparison panels are added; most earlier appendix visualization grids are retained.

R1.justification: The Related Work sections and central positioning around pretrained diffusion priors are largely retained. v3 adds references to PixArt-alpha, classifier-free guidance, BAID/BacklitNet, RoFormer and IC-Light, strengthens its qualified novelty claim, and adds targeted positioning concerning few-step inference and detail preservation.

T1.justification: Appendix B.4 adds an explicit mathematical definition of the guided prediction as a combination of conditional and unconditional outputs (Equation S1). The original flow-matching objective and point-embedding definitions remain equivalent. No new theorem or proof is provided; the explanations involving denoising trajectories are qualitative.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens evidence for design choices that v1 supported only sparsely. Controlled conditioning comparisons, alternative-backbone tests, guidance sweeps and inference-step experiments clarify how the framework works and distinguish one-step-training failure from useful few-step inference. Added SD3 comparisons also strengthen the adaptation argument. Some expanded claims remain insufficiently qualified, especially specialist parity and attributing low scores entirely to post-processing, and uncertainty reporting remains absent. Nevertheless, the new experimental evidence substantially improves support for the paper's central design and efficiency arguments.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe DICEPTION. Their main text, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching renamed tasks and relocated results.

after.justification: v3 retains original model evaluations and adds experiments on input conditioning, alternative architectures, guidance, inference steps and few-shot adaptation.

before.justification: v1 reports original quantitative evaluations of depth, normals, segmentation and human keypoints, together with architectural experiments and qualitative few-shot adaptation results.

results.title: DICEPTION: A Generalist Diffusion Model for Visual Perceptual Tasks

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the central claims that excessive CoT scaling can harm accuracy, optimal effort depends on task difficulty, and TOPS improves efficiency and effectiveness. Calling QwQ-32B-Preview the teacher in the revised abstract clarifies an already documented relationship.

C2.justification: v2 adds an answer-consistency interpretation and explains why removing erroneous solutions helps easier tasks but can sacrifice useful correction behavior on harder tasks, motivating step masking. Section 7 newly discusses the predominantly mathematical and SFT scope and proposes an explicitly untested extension to RL. These substantially expand the interpretation and applicability discussion.

D1.justification: v2 newly states that code, data and models are available and supplies a project repository reference, materially extending reproducibility information. Appendix E also discloses training hardware, including four or eight H100 80GB GPUs depending on stage, and four A100 80GB GPUs for evaluation. Existing hyperparameters and prompts are largely retained or relocated.

E1.justification: v1's empirical coverage is mathematical reasoning. v2 adds WebInstruct-verified data for general-reasoning training and self-improvement, with evaluation on MMLU-Pro and GPQA-Diamond in Appendix J. This substantially extends task coverage while retaining the mathematical datasets.

E2.justification: Figure 1 adds DeepSeek-R1 and DeepSeek-V3-0324 to the preliminary model comparison, and Appendix H evaluates QwQ-32B alongside QwQ-32B-Preview. The main TOPS comparator set remains unchanged: QwQ-32B-Preview, STILL-2-32B, Sky-T1-32B-Preview, Random and the base model.

E3.justification: v2 introduces controlled masked-loss and filtered-data experiments, an answer-diversity metric, full TOPS evaluation on LLaMA3.1-8B, and a Qwen2.5-7B general-reasoning setup. Appendix H specifies a 32K limit for the newly evaluated QwQ-32B. These are substantial added protocols; the retained main experiments' hyperparameters and decoding settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 adds interventions testing the effect of erroneous training steps through loss masking and solution filtering. It also adds answer-consistency analysis, MATH500 difficulty breakdowns, prompt-following and direct-prompting analyses, and an o1-mini token-estimation check. These substantially extend v1's reasoning-effort and erroneous-round analyses.

E5.justification: v1 reports five-seed averages without dispersion. v2 adds accuracy standard deviations across the main LLaMA and Qwen comparisons in Appendix K, including retained results, substantially expanding uncertainty reporting. The five-seed count is unchanged; Appendix J separately specifies one sample per prompt for the new general-reasoning evaluations.

E6.justification: Every numerical row in v1 Table 2 is retained in v2 Table 3, but substantial new results appear elsewhere. For example, LLaMA TOPS-SFT obtains 61.28% on MATH500 versus Random-SFT's 60.52% (Table 4), while TOPS-General obtains 56.50% on MMLU-Pro and 38.38% on GPQA-Diamond (Table 10). These are newly reported experiments, not improvements over revised v1 scores.

M1.justification: TOPS retains format imitation, reasoning-effort-conditioned generation, shortest-correct-response selection and supervised self-improvement. The iterative SFT and DPO procedures also remain unchanged. New loss-masking and filtering experiments are diagnostic variants, not revisions to the proposed TOPS procedure.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main section sequence are preserved. v2 makes localized wording and terminology corrections, relocates prompts, training details and the impact statement, and adds a LLaMA results subsection, limitations and appendix sections. The retained narrative is not extensively rewritten.

P2.justification: v2 adds numerous diagnostic, model-comparison, general-reasoning and uncertainty tables plus a loss-masking plot. Figure 1 gains model points and revised axis ranges; the erroneous-round plot gains a ratio curve and secondary axis. The original prompt panel moves to Figure 7, while the main results table is preserved as Table 3.

R1.justification: v2 adds seven references, including DeepSeek-V3, QwQ-32B, General-Reasoner, MMLU-Pro, Star-R1, DeepCritic and TinyR1. These update experimental context and related research, while the related-work taxonomy and positioning against efficiency-focused overthinking studies remain substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: The thinking-optimal-response definition, optimization objectives and token-estimation formula are retained. Equation 2 clarifies conditional-distribution notation without changing the described sampling procedure. No substantive mathematical assumptions, derivations or proofs are added.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens v1's largely correlational explanation of harmful training errors with masking and filtering interventions, and tests TOPS beyond its original backbone and mathematical tasks. Standard deviations, explicit limitations and artifact-access information further improve evidential transparency and reproducibility. General-reasoning evaluations remain single-sample and RL applicability remains speculative, but these limits do not outweigh the substantial gains in validation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same TOPS research, with matching methods and retained main results. The complete text, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains these experiments and adds original masking, filtering, LLaMA self-improvement and general-reasoning results, including Figure 5 and Tables 4, 9 and 10.

before.justification: v1 reports original reasoning-effort experiments, erroneous-round analysis, and TOPS self-improvement results on GSM8K, MATH500 and AIME2024, including Figures 3–5 and Table 2.

results.title: Towards Thinking-Optimal Scaling of Test-Time Compute for LLM Reasoning

C1.justification: The central gradient-free LSVI and Gaussian-complexity contributions remain. However, v3's abstract claims competitiveness rather than v1's outperformance, and the variable-selection novelty claim is narrowed to use of the Bernoulli product family. These qualify the scope of retained contributions rather than replace the paper's central thesis.

C2.justification: v3 replaces v1's concluding algorithm-selection discussion with substantive applicability limitations and possible extensions to mixtures, non-Gaussian directions, and dependent discrete approximations. Remark 2.6 discusses the practical limits of convexity assumptions. The checklist additionally acknowledges that convergence guarantees for LSVI-MF, LSVI-FC, and subsampling remain open, materially clarifying the boundaries of the theory.

D1.justification: v3 newly supplies access information for an LSVI JAX package and describes implementations, experiment pipelines, usage documentation, and licensing; v1 has no corresponding LSVI code-access disclosure. Appendix C adds baseline and Census preprocessing details and updates Python/JAX versions and hardware specifications. These substantially expand reproducibility information, although the package itself cannot be verified from the PDFs.

E1.justification: v3 adds Census-Income to logistic-regression evaluation. Pima, Sonar, binary MNIST, Concrete variable selection, and the toad-displacement simulation remain. Removing the Sonar mean-field configuration changes experimental settings, rather than removing the Sonar dataset or task.

E2.justification: v1's logistic-regression comparisons primarily use ADVI implementations. v3 substantially broadens the comparator set with NGD on Pima and MNIST, and GMMVI on Pima; NGD also participates in the new Census experiment. These are evaluated comparisons in Figures 1, 2, 5, and 7, while SMC and MCMC remain the respective variable-selection and BSL references.

E3.justification: v3 removes the Sonar mean-field configuration, revises the reported Pima LSVI-FC schedule from an unrestricted variance threshold to a bound of 10, and adds MNIST misclassification and elapsed-time evaluation. It also introduces sample-count timing sweeps and a Census protocol with replacement sampling and estimated KL loss. The Census batch size is unresolved: Tables 1–2 specify 1,000, whereas Appendix C.2 states 10,000.

E4.justification: v1 already compares step-size schedules and two Sonar sample counts. v3 extends computational sensitivity analysis with iteration-cost measurements across multiple Monte Carlo sample counts for Sonar and MNIST in Figures 4–5. The variable-selection score-distribution analysis and BSL posterior case study are retained rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: v3 newly reports means and standard-deviation intervals over 100 repetitions for logistic-regression curves. Variable-selection LSVI explicitly changes from three runs in v1 to 100 repetitions with min-max intervals in v3; SMC retains three repetitions. Five-repetition runtime means and standard deviations already existed in v1, so the substantial change is broader uncertainty reporting beyond that table.

E6.justification: v3 adds NGD/GMMVI comparisons, Census outcomes, MNIST classification results, and sample-count timing results, while removing Sonar mean-field results and revising existing curves and runtimes. For example, fixed-step MNIST LSVI-MF runtime changes from 50.0 seconds in v1 Table 2 to 10.4 seconds in v3 Table 1. Changed hardware and software prevent interpreting this as a same-setting speedup. BSL results are substantially retained.

M1.justification: The core generic, mean-field, and full-covariance LSVI procedures are retained. v3 adds a subsampling adaptation for Census-Income: Appendix C.2, Equation 21 replaces full-data log-target evaluations with estimates from a fresh batch sampled with replacement at each iteration. This is a limited procedural extension.

P1.justification: v3 extensively rewrites the introduction and explanations, adds an outline of contributions, and places practical algorithms before Gaussian specialization. The mean-field derivation and adaptive-schedule algorithm move to appendices; experimental details precede proofs, with a contents page, expanded notation section, and checklist. This is substantial narrative and structural reorganization.

P2.justification: The main text changes from two columns to one, and the principal comparison plots are substantially redesigned with combined panels, error bars, broken axes, and zooms. v3 combines MNIST and variable-selection plots, rearranges the retained BSL panels, adds timing, classification, and Census displays, and restructures the runtime and schedule tables. These exceed numerical updates or renumbering.

R1.justification: v3 explicitly credits Salimans and Knowles with the regression interpretation of the fixed-point mapping, absent from v1. It substantially expands positioning against natural-gradient VI, earlier Gaussian approximation methods, gradient-free mixture inference, and stochastic subsampling literature. The earlier Dehaene attribution is removed. These changes affect substantive research positioning, beyond bibliography formatting.

T1.justification: v3 replaces uniform boundedness of sufficient statistics with fourth-moment assumptions, adds a second-moment assumption on the log target, and develops new concentration and gradient-variance arguments in Lemmas D.5 and D.10. Theorem 3.4 revises v1's Theorem 4.5 and Corollary 4.6 with explicit sample-dependent variance terms and revised rates. The bounded-statistic result survives as Lemma D.4. Equation 1 also corrects the reversed KL logarithm.

improvement.justification: v3 addresses important weaknesses in v1's evidence and positioning through NGD/GMMVI comparisons, repeated-run uncertainty for convergence results, additional classification and computational checks, and explicit attribution of the regression connection to prior work. More qualified performance claims and clearer limits on theoretical guarantees improve credibility. The Census batch-size conflict and reversed min/max entries in some runtime rows impair reproducibility, but these localized defects do not outweigh the substantial gains in evidential support and scientific transparency.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same LSVI research, with matching authors, core algorithms, and principal applications. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support comparison despite substantial reorganization.

after.justification: v3 retains original results for these three applications and reports additional comparisons, Census-Income experiments, classification results, and computational measurements in Section 5 and Appendix C.

before.justification: v1 reports original logistic-regression, discrete variable-selection, and Bayesian synthetic-likelihood experiments, including convergence plots, posterior approximations, and runtime measurements in Section 5 and Appendix B.

results.title: Least squares variational inference

C1.justification: v2 withdraws the introduction's claimed first algorithm-independent deterministic lower bound. Its conclusion changes from contributing new upper and lower bounds to contributing an upper bound. The central nearly-optimal GP-UCB and constant cumulative-regret claims are retained.

C2.justification: New discussion addresses unresolved SE simple-regret optimality, Bayesian versus frequentist cumulative regret, and GP-UCB's empirical disadvantage against EI despite its worst-case guarantees. Footnote 4 newly qualifies the information-gain analysis's eigenfunction assumption and discusses an alternative route. Conversely, Table 1 drops v1's REDS level-set qualification.

D1.justification: New Appendix B describes the 50-term random kernel-expansion objective, distributions of coefficients and centers, exact RKHS-norm calculation, kernel matching, and initialization and hyperparameter choices. This supplies substantial reproduction information for experiments absent from v1.

E1.justification: v2 introduces empirical evaluation on synthetic RKHS functions over a two-dimensional domain. Cumulative-regret experiments use squared exponential and Matérn kernels with smoothness 3/2 and 5/2; simple-regret experiments use both Matérn settings. v1 contains no empirical task instances.

E2.justification: v2 newly evaluates PE and REDS against GP-UCB for cumulative regret, and EI against GP-UCB for simple regret. These methods appeared in v1's theoretical comparison tables, but were not experimentally evaluated there.

E3.justification: v2 introduces controlled experimental protocols using a 50-by-50 grid on [0,1]^2, matching generating and model kernels, lengthscale 0.25, exact RKHS-norm confidence widths, a shared random initial point, and initial batch size 5 for PE and REDS. v1 specifies no experimental protocol.

E4.justification: Neither version reports ablations, robustness tests, sensitivity analyses, or error analyses. The new kernel-specific plots and Appendix B.2 provide direct performance comparisons rather than separate diagnostic analyses.

E5.justification: v2 introduces basic repeated-run reporting: Figure 1 averages 3,000 independent runs, while Figure 2 specifies 100 seeds. No confidence intervals or significance tests are reported. v1 has no empirical statistical reporting.

E6.justification: New Figure 1 shows lower cumulative regret for GP-UCB than PE and REDS across all three kernel settings. New Figure 2 shows EI achieving lower simple regret than GP-UCB in both Matérn settings. These are newly reported findings; v1 provides no corresponding empirical results.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 retains the noiseless GP posterior, confidence multiplier B, and query rule maximizing posterior mean plus B times posterior standard deviation. Explicitly listing the kernel input and rewording posterior updates clarify the existing procedure.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, and preliminaries receive substantial rewriting and expanded explanations. Preliminaries are reordered, the detailed posterior-deviation lemma moves to Appendix A.2, and a discussion section replaces the lower-bound section. These changes substantially revise the narrative and organization.

P2.justification: v2 adds a three-panel cumulative-regret figure and a two-panel simple-regret figure. Both comparison tables are redesigned with their Remark columns removed and captions revised. The document also adopts a conference template with different title formatting, typography, and text layout.

R1.justification: v2 attributes the cumulative-regret lower bound to Li and Scarlett (2024), replacing v1's original-contribution positioning. It also expands discussion of the posterior-variance open problem, information-gain assumption concerns, and neural tangent kernel extensions, with corresponding references. Cai and Scarlett (2021), used for the removed proof, disappears.

T1.justification: v2 removes v1's deterministic cumulative-regret lower-bound Theorem 7 and its Appendix B proof. It also corrects the SE kernel's missing negative sign, the Matérn kernel's missing power, and the exponent in v1 Equation (37), now v2 Equation (40). The principal upper bounds remain; v1's detailed Lemma 3 is retained as Lemma 8 in v2 Appendix A.2.

improvement.justification: v2 materially strengthens the paper's support and transparency. Figures 1–2 and Appendix B substantiate its empirical motivation while exposing GP-UCB's disadvantage against EI. It withdraws the original-lower-bound novelty claim, corrects mathematical expressions, and acknowledges an important assumption behind the theory. The lost REDS qualification and limited uncertainty reporting remain drawbacks, but the gains in attribution, mathematical clarity, and evidence substantially improve overall quality.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same noise-free GP-UCB research. Their complete main texts, tables, equations, and appendices are readable, allowing retained, relocated, added, and removed material to be matched reliably.

after.justification: v2 reports original synthetic experiments comparing cumulative regret against PE and REDS in Figure 1, and simple regret against EI in Figure 2. Appendix B documents the experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports theoretical bounds and proofs, including literature comparisons in Tables 1–2. Neither the main text nor the appendices contain original empirical results.

C1.justification: The main rectangular guarantee changes from O-tilde(m n^(1-1/d) + n) under v1's corruption definition to O-tilde(n m^(1-1/d) + m) under v3's revised definition. The non-Boolean guarantee is now parameterized by distinct values per column instead of the earlier threshold count. The headline square-matrix exponent and principal dynamic graph applications remain.

Remark B.10 adds applicability to ternary neural-network inference. The concern about linear threshold-count dependence already existed in v1; its Natarajan-dimension and parsing/clique conjectures are removed.

V1 provides theoretical pseudocode but no comparable implementation or experimental resource information.

E1.justification: V3 introduces actual empirical coverage through synthetic Boolean matrices generated from points and halfspaces, with ambient dimensions 2 through 12 and random real query vectors. V1 contains no corresponding original evaluation; its graph and learning applications are theoretical or supported by cited work.

The additional discussion of ternary-matrix inference methods is theoretical positioning, not another experimentally evaluated baseline.

It computes exact MSTs for implementation convenience and excludes preprocessing performance from the study. These are new experimental settings, not revisions to existing v1 experiments.

E4.justification: V3 adds a focused sensitivity analysis of how ambient dimension affects spanning-tree weight and multiplication time while matrix size stays fixed. Figures 1 and 2 investigate the proposed structural explanation; no corresponding analysis exists in v1. The study does not test the corruption guarantee.

E5.justification: V3 reports 1000 random-vector products per dimension, runtime means and standard deviations, and one-sigma error bars in Figure 2. V1 has no empirical uncertainty reporting. These are timing measurements across queries; independent matrix-generation repetitions or random seeds are not specified.

E6.justification: Figures 1 and 2 add the first original measured results: MST weights and MST-based query times generally increase with ambient dimension, while NumPy times remain comparatively stable and the runtime advantage narrows. V1 has no matching empirical results, so these are newly reported findings rather than improvements over earlier measurements.

M1.justification: The non-Boolean procedure is substantially revised. V1 Appendix A.3 expands rows into an Am-by-n threshold matrix and reconstructs the output afterward. V3 Appendix B.4 instead constructs an m-by-nT column-threshold matrix and transforms the query vector using successive threshold differences. The underlying Boolean MST algorithms and dynamic bucketing framework are largely retained.

P1.justification: The introduction, related work and technical exposition are extensively condensed and rewritten. V3 adds supplementary preliminaries, reorganizes the proof appendices, moves the tree-linearization proof out of the main text, and replaces the future-work conclusion with limitations and societal-impact paragraphs. These changes extend beyond renumbering or newly added scientific content.

P2.justification: The document is globally reformatted from the preprint layout to a conference layout, changing the title/author arrangement, text block, running headers and contents placement. V3 adds two experimental plots with axes, captions and timing error bars, and replaces the displayed threshold-encoding example. Algorithm 1 is retained and relocated.

R1.justification: V3 consistently attributes the foundational MST algorithm to Björklund and Lingas (2001), replacing several attributions to Gasieniec and Lingas (2003); both works were already cited in v1. The overall research positioning remains.

T1.justification: Definition 2's O(n^(1-1/d)) corruptions per row become O(m^(1-1/d)) per column in Definition 1.2. improvement.justification: V3 substantially strengthens the central argument by correcting v1's primal/dual VC-dimension and maximum-versus-total-crossing mismatches, adding an explicit dimension-dependent proof, and revising the non-Boolean reduction. Original timing evidence, uncertainty reporting and reproducibility information also improve assessability. The gains remain qualified: Appendix B.4 contains indexing/example inconsistencies, and the experiments cover one synthetic matrix size without measuring preprocessing.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same matrix-vector multiplication work. All 36 pages of v1 and 32 pages of v3, including appendices, equations, algorithms and v3's figures, support reliable comparison.

after.justification: Appendix E reports original simulations on synthetic 4096-by-4096 Boolean matrices. Figures 1 and 2 present measured spanning-tree weights and matrix-vector multiplication runtimes.

before.justification: V1 reports theoretical algorithms, bounds and proofs. Empirical observations about practical efficiency and graph VC-dimensions are attributed to earlier works; no original experiments appear in its appendices.

Conversely, v1's discussion of star-convex action domains and associated dosage/GLM applicability is removed.

MATLAB, linprog, coneprog, and the underlying matrix-source link are retained. v1's explicit description of alternating algorithm iterations for timing control is omitted; this is a documentation loss, not evidence that the procedure changed.

The added scalability experiment reuses the latter family, with parameter-range changes assessed under E3. The application examples in v2 Appendix B are illustrative, not new empirical evaluations.

The new scalability study extends the existing s-colts versus safe-LTS comparison. DOSS is discussed theoretically but explicitly not implemented in either version.

Figure 6 reports timing averaged over 50,000 iterations. These are settings for an added experiment; the retained nine-dimensional experiment still uses T=50,000 and delta=0.1.

Existing noise-scale, resampling, and noise-coupling analyses remain, including the relocated constraint-count study of optimism and unsaturation.
