Appendix I.2.1 also distinguishes the 50-run regret display from mean per-run regret ratios over 100 runs and discusses their uncertainty. This substantially changes uncertainty reporting, without establishing increased repetitions for existing experiments.

E6.justification: The added constraint-count study reports s-colts speedups growing from about 1.3 to over 18 times, and safe-LTS regret 2.7–3.4 times larger for m>=10. Table 2 adds exact terminal summaries, and the resampling curves change between v1 Figure 2 and v2 Figure 4. Because aggregation is not fully specified in v2, these revised curves do not establish same-setting performance improvements between versions.

M1.justification: v2 Algorithm 1 explicitly falls back to the known safe action when the sampled optimization problem is infeasible; v1 Algorithm 1 lacks this guard. The central coupled perturbations, action scaling, forced exploration, and resampling procedures remain. Moving e-colts to Appendix H.2 does not remove that method.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, setup, and analysis narrative are extensively rewritten and condensed. Section 5 prioritizes r-colts, with detailed e-colts treatment moved to Appendix H.2; simulations are largely consolidated in Appendix I. New appendices provide a glossary and application examples, while related-work and optimism discussions are reorganized.

P2.justification: v2 adds a geometric analysis schematic, a terminal-results table, an application table, and a glossary table. Algorithms become compact wrapped displays; Table 1 omits the e-colts row while retaining its treatment elsewhere. Empirical figures are relocated and redesigned with uncertainty curves, a four-panel resampling display, and new scalability plots.

R1.justification: v2 adds application-oriented references, convex-method comparisons, and feasibility-testing literature, including a new discussion of discovering a safe point in Appendix C. References to Carlsson et al., Filippi et al., and the Russo et al. survey disappear. The principal positioning relative to safe-LTS, DOSS, and earlier Thompson-sampling analyses remains.

T1.justification: v1 Theorem 10 gives e-colts risk as O-tilde(sqrt(d^3 T)); v2 Theorem 12 adds an instance-dependent term involving d^3||a||^4/(kappa^2 Gamma(a)^4). Appendix H.2 revises the proof to account for exploration caused by infeasible sampled programs. Appendices G.2 and G.5 also repair scaling calculations and an omitted reward-estimation term. The exploration condition and kappa definition change, so the changed kappa exponent alone is not a rate improvement.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses substantive mathematical and reporting weaknesses: it accounts for previously omitted e-colts infeasibility costs, repairs proof steps, tests the previously anticipated growth in computational advantage, and reports uncertainty across central comparisons. The reorganized analysis and new schematic also substantially improve accessibility. Some aggregation details remain unclear and timing-control documentation is lost, but these limitations do not outweigh the gains in mathematical accuracy and assessability.

These substantially extend the tests of mechanism and robustness.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, training seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests, or run-based error bars. The attention-output variance plots investigate the proposed mechanism and are not uncertainty estimates for benchmark performance.

E6.justification: v3 adds substantial COCO, RIFLEx, and sensitivity results; for example, Table 4 reports COCO FID 29.89 for LEMMDiT versus 34.58 for MMDiT-RIFLEx. Appendix A.1 also tests AlphaFold2-predicted, noise-perturbed, and randomly selected MD conformations as input structures.

E2.justification: V2 adds evaluated comparisons with BioEmu on ATLAS and de novo proteins, and MDGen, Str2Str, and ESMDiff on ATLAS (Tables 1–2 and A.3). It also tests a modified AlphaFlow parser on a multi-chain complex. The original comparator set is retained; NMA and MSA subsampling remain literature-based comparisons rather than newly evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: V2 adds DCCM and Ramachandran-distribution evaluation, input-structure perturbation protocols, training/inference sweeps of the prior parameter, and dataset-averaged speed–accuracy comparisons. Reported inference hardware changes from A100-40GB to A100-80GB. The ATLAS split, 250 generated conformations per protein, training budget, and default 20 timesteps remain unchanged.

E4.justification: V2 revises the feature-ablation comparison and adds initial-structure sensitivity, prior-parameter sensitivity, backbone-dihedral analysis, ensemble case studies, and backbone-versus-sidechain runtime analysis. Conversely, v1's timestep sweep (Table A.2) and per-protein PCA plots (Figure A.3) are absent from v2, rather than merely relocated.

E5.justification: Both versions estimate finite-sampling errors using 100 bootstraps of MD conformations and display errors above the reported precision. V2 adds no distinct seed-reporting, repeated-training-run, confidence-interval, or significance-testing procedure; its checklist reiterates the existing practice.

E6.justification: Results expand substantially through new baselines, multi-chain tests, robustness studies, and BBFlow-light. For revised BBFlow, ATLAS RMSF MAE changes from 0.47 to 0.42 Å, while de novo RMSF MAE changes from 0.23 to 0.26 Å (Tables 1–2). ATLAS transient-contact J changes from 0.35 to 0.29 (v1 Table A.1; v2 Table A.9). These are mixed results for revised configurations, not a uniform same-setting gain.

M1.justification: V1 uses absolute/relative residue-position encodings and excludes directional features from default BBFlow. V2 removes index encodings and incorporates directional features for residues within 5 Å. Appendix A.6 also introduces BBFlow-light with three rather than six CFA blocks and smaller feature dimensions. The conditional-prior construction and training loss remain.

P1.justification: Related work is reorganized into distinct ensemble-generation categories, the AlphaFlow/FAPE background is condensed, and detailed metric exposition moves from the main text to Appendix A.3. The discussion and conclusion are rewritten around MD emulation and limitations, while the appendix is extensively reorganized and a conference checklist is added.

P2.justification: The main text changes from two-column to single-column layout. V1 Figures 3–4 are combined into v2 Figure 2, and the prior illustration moves to Appendix Figure A.4. Tables gain different metric columns, and new ensemble, DCCM, dihedral, and speed–accuracy displays accompany removal of the PCA montage and timestep table.

R1.justification: V2 substantially reorganizes positioning around standardized MD emulation versus broader ensemble generation. It adds discussion and citations for MDGen, Str2Str, ESMDiff, accelerated AlphaFlow, dynamics-aware design, and applications of short-timescale MD. It also introduces multimer novelty positioning and explicitly qualifies comparisons with models trained on different ensemble distributions.

T1.justification: The flow equations, geodesic conditional prior, and loss retain their mathematical substance; the prior parameter is renamed from δt to ξ. Added training pseudocode and the standard DCCM formula explain procedures and metrics. Removing the FAPE background exposition does not change the underlying theory, and neither version introduces proofs or theoretical results.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens validation through input-structure robustness tests, local-geometry checks, broader comparisons, and demonstrated multimer transfer. Its explicit restriction to short MD-derived distributions and discussion of transient-contact weaknesses address important gaps in v1's applicability claims. Some scores worsen and the timestep/PCA diagnostics disappear, but the stronger supporting evidence and clearer limitations provide a substantial net improvement in paper quality.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe BBFlow and retain matching methodological and experimental content. Text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support comparison, including identification of moved and removed material.

after.justification: V2 reports original evaluations on ATLAS, de novo proteins, and multi-chain systems, alongside robustness experiments, ablations, and BBFlow-light results.

before.justification: V1 reports original BBFlow training and evaluation, simulations of de novo proteins, feature ablations, and a timestep study.

results.title: Learning conformational ensembles of proteins based on backbone geometry

C1.justification: Both versions claim a unified ECG time-series/image/text model, a 30,000-pair heartbeat-grounded dataset, and the Grounded ECG Understanding task, with improved prediction, explainability and grounding. Additional validation and the updated headline grounding margin do not redefine these central contributions.

C2.justification: Section 4.5 newly hypothesizes links between missed abnormalities and representation/data-coverage limitations, and between exaggerated severity and missing patient context. v2 also interprets its new results as supporting out-of-domain reasoning and open-source generation. Appendix A.6 explicitly restricts intended use to research and assistance, extending v1's discussion of GPT-4o disagreements and future improvements.

D1.justification: Section 4.1 changes ECG-Grounding availability from a promised release to a reported completed release, and the abstract explicitly advertises code, model and data access. Appendix A.3 expands evaluation-response examples, while the checklist states that instructions and settings accompany the code. These are documentation and access claims in the PDFs; external availability was not verified.

E1.justification: The Grounded ECG Understanding task expands from MIMIC-IV-ECG alone to an additional out-of-domain PTB-XL evaluation with 2,041 samples. Although PTB-XL already appeared in ECG-Bench, evaluating detailed grounded interpretations introduces distinct task coverage and external generalization evidence. Existing training datasets and ECG-Bench coverage remain.

E2.justification: Deepseek-R1 enters the clinician-rated comparison of generated training data and GEM outputs in v2 Tables 4–5. PULSE remains the grounded-task comparator, and Random, GPT-4o and PULSE remain the ECG-Bench comparators. The comparator expansion is confined to the new generation-quality evaluation.

E3.justification: Section 4.4 supplements qualitative expert highlighting with a structured assessment of 200 outputs each from GPT-4o, Deepseek-R1 and GEM by eight cardiologists, using seven criteria scored from 1 to 5. Appendix A.2 also changes the stated lead-coverage measure from a count to a percentage and explicitly describes lead accuracy as a percentage. These are reported evaluation changes, not evidence that existing experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds the PTB-XL distribution-shift evaluation, tests an open-source substitute for instruction generation, and introduces expert-feedback-based failure analysis in Section 4.5. The latter identifies missed waveform abnormalities and overstated severity. The original TS-only/TS+IMG ablations and six case studies in Figures 4–9 are retained.

E5.justification: Tables 4–5 newly report means and standard deviations for cardiologist ratings; v1 has no analogous dispersion reporting. This addition is limited to human assessments. Training-seed variability, confidence intervals and formal significance tests are not introduced; v2's checklist explicitly states that formal significance testing was omitted.

E6.justification: v2 adds PTB-XL grounded results and quantitative clinician ratings, while revising existing MIMIC-IV-ECG results. PULSE and GEM-LLaVA diagnosis accuracy change from 75.94 and 86.34 to 81.14 and 87.24. GEM-LLaVA grounding changes from 74.48 to 75.48, reversing the GEM-backbone ranking on that metric. Lead scores also change, and the former Average entries disappear. ECG-Bench results are unchanged. The revised scores should not be treated as established same-setting gains because their provenance is unexplained and scoring documentation changes.

M1.justification: Sections 3.2–3.5 retain the ECG-CoCa and CLIP encoders, projection and concatenation procedure, physiological features, diagnosis guider, training objective and frozen-encoder training. Grounding Feature Extractor renames the existing FeatureDB component. Testing Deepseek-R1 as an alternative data generator does not establish a revised GEM procedure.

P1.justification: Targeted rewrites clarify the introduction's modeling and data challenges, rename methodological headings and revise the conclusion. Metric descriptions move from the main text to Appendix A.2, and the appendices gain a contents page and reorganized subsections. The main section sequence and most methodological prose remain stable.

P2.justification: The document changes from a two-column layout to a predominantly single-column NeurIPS layout. v1 Tables 1–2 are consolidated into an expanded v2 Table 1, and four new tables present clinician results and scoring rubrics. Figures are resized and architecture labels revised; the six original case-study figures retain their content.

R1.justification: Section 2.2 adds discussion of JoLT. References are refreshed with Deepseek-R1, newer vision-language surveys and medical models including MedGemma, UniECG and ECG-LM, while older citations such as MiniGPT-4, Shikra and CardioGPT disappear. The principal positioning around combined ECG modalities and grounded interpretation remains unchanged.

T1.justification: Equations 1–10 retain the same mathematical formulations for encoding, alignment, data generation and training. Neither version supplies theoretical results or proofs, and v2 introduces no substantive derivation or formal assumption.

improvement.justification: v1 supported its grounded-understanding task primarily through single-dataset GPT-4o scoring and illustrative expert cases. v2 adds a 2,041-sample external evaluation and a defined eight-cardiologist assessment of 600 outputs, with scoring rubrics and dispersion reporting. These additions substantially strengthen evidence about generalization and interpretation quality, while specific failure analysis clarifies limitations. Unexplained revisions to existing scores and absent formal significance tests remain weaknesses, but do not outweigh the added validation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe GEM, with matching core methods, datasets and experiments. The main text, equations, tables, figures and appendices support reliable comparison, including matching the relocated case studies.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds PTB-XL grounded understanding results and quantitative cardiologist assessments of GPT-4o, Deepseek-R1 and GEM outputs.

before.justification: v1 reports original grounded ECG understanding and ECG-Bench results, modality ablations and qualitative cardiologist assessments.

results.title: GEM: Empowering MLLM for Grounded ECG Understanding with Time Series and Images

C1.justification: The headline contributions remain characterizing SoIR, introducing suitable benchmarks, and proposing a two-stage MaO framework producing a single descriptor. The abstract and contribution list retain the same principal superiority and scalability claims; additional experiments mainly supply supporting evidence.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations concerning generalization to larger objects and another backbone, MLLM retrieval limitations, and the tradeoff between faster online search and more expensive offline encoding. Appendix F substantially expands detector-dependence discussion and newly identifies shortcomings on faces, individuals, and landmarks, while retaining the earlier occlusion and heavy-clutter limitations.

D1.justification: v2 adds a project-page link stating code/data availability, specifies comparator configurations and reranking participation, and reports additional encoding and OVD preprocessing costs. The optimizer, LoRA rank, batch size, hardware, and refinement settings remain unchanged. Actual availability of the linked resources cannot be verified from the supplied PDFs.

E1.justification: Appendix C adds ILIAS, covering small, medium, and large objects, and PODS, whose average object area is approximately 20% of the image. This substantially extends evaluation beyond the retained small-object and clutter benchmarks. VoxDet-SoIR is a clarified name for the existing VoxDet retrieval benchmark.

E2.justification: Table 2 adds AMES across the original benchmarks while retaining the previous comparators. Appendix D adds Qwen2.5-VL as a pairwise-matching comparator, and Appendix C incorporates SIGLIP and linearly adapted backbone comparisons. These expand the comparison methods beyond simply extending existing baselines to another dataset.

E3.justification: New evaluations introduce distractor-free ILIAS testing with mAP@1K, additional backbone configurations, a Qwen comparison using 100 queries and 200 gallery images with accuracy reporting, and separate encoding/search timing over 2,000 queries. The original training settings are retained. Newly explicit reranking descriptions do not establish that the retained Table 2 experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Table 4 adds a Stage A-only control, separating multi-object fine-tuning from subsequent optimization. Section 4.4 adds runtime analysis, and Tables F2–F3 examine detector recall by object size and clutter. The existing clutter experiment moves from Figure 3c to Figure F1; the regularization and iteration sweeps are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed counts, repeated-run uncertainty, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The added experiments continue reporting point estimates; the existing descriptive dataset statistics are retained.

E6.justification: The original Table 2 scores remain unchanged, but many results are added. Examples include AMES at 48.68 mAP on VoxDet, Stage A at 75.04/63.14 on VoxDet/VoxDetW, and PODS MaO-CLIP/MaO-DINOv2 scores of 0.368/0.393. New ILIAS, Qwen, runtime, and detector-recall results further expand the evidence. These are additional results, not improved versions of the original scores.

M1.justification: The object-cropping pipeline, contrastive multi-object fine-tuning, and LeGrad-based descriptor optimization remain unchanged, including Equation (1). Applying MaO to SIGLIP and explaining single-vector backpropagation more explicitly do not establish a changed method.

P1.justification: The main narrative is largely retained, with localized rewrites and clearer explanations of object proposals and unified-vector optimization. VoxDet gains the VoxDet-SoIR name, a runtime subsection is inserted, and the appendix reorganizes detector evaluation and limitations. This is a limited narrative revision rather than a wholesale rewrite.

P2.justification: The document changes from two-column to single-column presentation, with extensive resizing and relocation of displays. Figure 1 is redesigned, Figure 3's clutter panel becomes Appendix Figure F1, and the resolution axis changes from resize scale to image size. New tables, expanded ablation/comparison tables, revised captions, and corrected plot legends substantially alter presentation.

R1.justification: Related work gains a focused local-feature subsection and discussion of AMES and reranking transformers. New benchmark and modular-pipeline references include ILIAS, PODS, Grounded SAM, Open3DIS, and TROY-VIS. These extend the existing positioning around compact retrieval and detector-based representations without replacing its central novelty argument.

T1.justification: The optimization objective and Appendix A's LeGrad formulation, Equations (1)–(5), are unchanged. No new theorem, proof, or substantive mathematical assumption is introduced; the explicit object-size ratio wording clarifies an existing measure.

improvement.justification: The Stage A-only control resolves an important attribution gap, while detector breakdowns substantially strengthen failure analysis beyond v1's aggregate recall. AMES and the additional datasets broaden validation, and runtime reporting exposes the practical online/offline cost tradeoff. These materially strengthen the empirical case. Some additions remain weaker: ILIAS excludes distractors, the Qwen protocol is sparsely specified, and Appendix C overstates DINOv2-based superiority relative to Table C1, where adapted SIGLIP scores 58.70 against MaO-DINOv2's 48.85.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MaO research work. Their full text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison despite substantial reformatting and expanded evaluation.

after.justification: v2 retains those experiments and adds original benchmark evaluations, runtime measurements, a Stage A ablation, and detector-recall analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original retrieval experiments, component ablations, sensitivity analyses, and detector evaluations in the main text and supplementary material.

results.title: Find your Needle: Small Object Image Retrieval via Multi-Object Attention Optimization

C1.justification: The substantive central claims remain the ECC task, interactive ECCD benchmark, and zero-shot ATE/NLBN approach balancing counting accuracy against exploration cost. v2 describes ZECC as a baseline and consolidates the contribution bullets, but retains these claims and the best-trade-off assertion. The additional experiments primarily supply supporting evidence.

C2.justification: v2 identifies a concrete failure condition: building occlusion can cause the MLLM to skip low-altitude exploration over crowds (Appendix E). The conclusion explicitly defers dynamic targets and further real-world application. It also corrects the cluster-size explanation to associate smaller clusters with more navigation points and interprets the new MVC and real-world findings.

D1.justification: Beyond v1's brief implementation paragraph, v2 supplies ATE/NLBN pseudocode, the actual MLLM prompt and panoramic input arrangement, Open3D normal estimation, and 0.25 m voxel deduplication. It also adds CPU/GPU/RAM specifications, real-drone reconstruction and control details, manual annotation information, and a code repository link. These substantially expand reproducibility documentation.

E1.justification: Both versions retain the 60-environment ECCD benchmark. v2 Appendix F extends evaluation beyond simulation to two real outdoor crowd scenes with drone observations and reconstructed geometry, introducing materially different input conditions. These tests evaluate NLBN viewpoint adjustment, rather than the complete autonomous ZECC pipeline.

E2.justification: v1 evaluates FBE, CoW, and OpenFMNav with GL or Grounding DINO. v2 retains these comparators and adds an entire multi-view counting comparison using MVF and CountFormer at three camera-grid spacings in Table 3. The changed CoW citation does not establish a different comparator.

E3.justification: v2 introduces multi-view camera grids at 10, 20, and 30 m with camera-count evaluation, travel-distance-limited exploration, an occlusion test with a 0.5 m threshold, and a manually annotated real-drone evaluation protocol. Existing sensitivity sweeps also change: navigation angles span 10–80 degrees in v1 Figure 6 versus 10–40 degrees in v2 Figure 5(b).

E4.justification: v2 retains the original component ablations but adds controlled travel-budget comparisons, trajectory case studies, quantitative obstruction analysis, an MLLM planning failure case, and real-world comparisons with and without NLBN. These directly examine efficiency, occlusion reduction, and failure conditions. The sensitivity analyses are also revised.

E5.justification: v1 reports point estimates without uncertainty bars. v2 adds ± values to Tables 2–3 and error bars to Figure 4, but does not specify run counts, seeds, or whether the uncertainty represents standard deviations, standard errors, or confidence intervals. Additional runs therefore cannot be inferred.

E6.justification: Overall results are revised: ZECC changes from 18.91% MAPE and 3804.63 m in v1 Table 1 to 18.71 ± 1.41% and 3722.45 ± 73.78 m in v2 Table 2. New results include MVC comparisons, real-world NLBN counting, and obstruction ratios of 4.52% for ZECC, 42.81% for OpenFMNav, and 21.77% for MVC-30. Sensitivity curves and reported cluster-size travel costs also change.

M1.justification: The core ATE, NLBN, and FDC procedures remain intact. Appendix F adds a real-drone adaptation using VGGT to reconstruct relative geometry and poses, followed by GPS-based conversion of NLBN waypoints into absolute navigation commands. Appendix C mainly documents previously unspecified implementation details.

P1.justification: Substantial introduction, NLBN, and experimental discussion passages are rewritten or condensed. Experimental settings and results become separate top-level sections, while a case-study subsection, acknowledgments, checklist, and organized appendices substantially restructure the document.

P2.justification: The document changes from two-column to single-column layout, with extensive resizing and relocation of displays. v1 Figures 3–4 become panels of v2 Figure 2; sensitivity plots are regrouped beside a new budget plot. New dataset, MVC, occlusion, and real-world tables accompany trajectory, prompt, failure-case, and dataset visualizations.

R1.justification: v2 adds references including OpenFly, AerialVG, CountFormer, and VGGT, plus a structured dataset comparison in Table 1. It emphasizes ZECC's role as a baseline for the new task. The central positioning between passive crowd counting and embodied navigation remains unchanged.

T1.justification: Appendix D adds a mathematical obstruction criterion using nearest-navigation-point vectors, projections, and a distance threshold in Equations 8–12. The crowd-generation and navigation equations remain unchanged. Neither version supplies theoretical guarantees or proofs.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses v1's limited comparison scope and sparse reproducibility information. Multi-view baselines and controlled budget analyses better test the accuracy–cost claim, while occlusion measurements, a failure case, and limited real-world NLBN tests make applicability more assessable. Exact prompts, pseudocode, and deduplication details materially improve reproducibility. Undefined uncertainty bars and the narrow real-world validation remain weaknesses, but do not outweigh these gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Embodied Crowd Counting, ECCD, and ZECC. Their text, equations, tables, and figures support reliable comparison. v1 ends with references; v2 additionally includes a checklist and Appendices A–F, all inspected.

after.justification: v2 retains original simulation experiments and adds multi-view comparisons, occlusion analysis, and two real-world NLBN evaluations in Section 5 and Appendices D–F.

before.justification: v1 reports original ECCD experiments, including navigation comparisons, component ablations, and parameter studies in Section 4.

results.title: Embodied Crowd Counting

C1.justification: The headline framework and O(1/epsilon^2), O(1/epsilon), and strongly convex-set complexity claims remain. The abstract broadens the empirical comparison from standard FW to other projection-free algorithms, and the introduction/conclusion replace neural-network training with partially observed alignment in their highlighted experimental contribution.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive explanations of decomposition-dependent gap geometry and curvature retention, qualifies criticality versus stationarity for nonsmooth problems, and explains alignment runtime differences through oracle costs. It also warns that FW-M backtracking can fail with inaccurate objective evaluations. The existing limitation concerning unproved stochastic extensions remains.

D1.justification: v2 supplies gradients and exact line-search derivations for two additional QAP decompositions and documents the added CGS implementation. It specifies full-SVD implementations of the alignment subgradient and linear oracle, together with data dimensions, masking, regularization, and initialization. Existing hardware, software, neural-network architecture, and adaptive-tolerance details are retained.

E1.justification: v2 adds English-French word-embedding alignment with partially observed target embeddings, introducing a distinct language domain and nonsmooth optimization task. QAPLIB and both CIFAR classification datasets remain; the neural-network experiments move to Appendix C rather than being removed.

E2.justification: The added QAP comparison evaluates nonconvex CGS from Qu et al. alongside FW and three DC-FW variants. The new alignment experiment evaluates FW-K from Khamaru and Wainwright and FW-M from Millán et al.; fully observed Procrustes supplies an additional quality reference. v1's experiments compared against standard or stochastic FW.

E3.justification: The new alignment protocol uses 300-dimensional embeddings, 10,000 words, observation probability 0.1, regularization 10^-4, and initialization at zero, evaluating FW gap against iterations, SVD computations, and runtime. Appendix B adds a 10-hour stopping cap and an adapted CGS tolerance strategy for its additional QAP comparison. The retained main QAP and neural-network settings are substantially unchanged.

E4.justification: Appendix B newly compares three DC decompositions on QAP, directly testing whether decomposition choice affects solution quality. Section 4 and Figure 1 add a numerical case study comparing projected-gradient and proximal-point measures around different stationary points. The earlier neural-network constraint-radius sensitivity analysis is retained.

E5.justification: v2's additional QAP comparison reports ten Monte Carlo instances per method and dataset, with means and 90% confidence intervals in Figure 4. v1 provides no corresponding repeated-run counts or uncertainty intervals. This is new statistical reporting, without establishing that the original main-text experiment used fewer runs.

E6.justification: New results include DC-FW variant 1 beating CGS on 68.7 QAP instances on average, versus 46.4 in the reverse comparison. Alignment results report 88 DC-FW subgradient calls versus 10,000 for FW-K/FW-M, and 93.11% of fully observed Procrustes alignment quality. These are added experiments; the original QAP summary remains 73 wins, 43 losses, 18 ties, and mean errors 0.0085 versus 0.0112.

M1.justification: The two-loop DC-FW solver, smooth decompositions, and adaptive tolerance strategy remain. Equation (2) now explicitly uses an arbitrary subgradient for nonsmooth g, and Section 5 develops conditional and proximal subgradient specializations. These are limited adaptations of the existing framework; the additional QAP variants instantiate decompositions already present in v1.

P1.justification: The exposition is substantially reorganized: proofs are collected in Appendix A, strongly convex-set analysis moves into the general framework, a nonsmooth section is introduced, and neural-network experiments and implementation details are consolidated in Appendix C. The motivation, contributions, and related-work narrative are also revised.

P2.justification: v2 adds the stationarity contour illustration, alignment convergence/cost plots, and QAP comparison heatmap with confidence intervals. Existing neural-network plots move to the appendix and are resized with revised axes and legends. The title block, typography, and page layout also change substantially.

R1.justification: v2 adds Khamaru and Wainwright as a close predecessor, substantially expands the comparison with Millán et al., and distinguishes their oracle costs from DC-FW. It also expands the CGS positioning around momentum and stationarity measures, and discusses Pokutta's 2025 work as a subsequent extension. These changes go beyond bibliographic updates.

T1.justification: Definition 1 now minimizes over the subdifferential, and Lemma 1 adds a formal critical-point characterization with a proof in Appendix A. Corollary 6 extends the strongly convex-set result beyond the earlier smooth CGS specialization, while Section 5 states nonsmooth oracle guarantees. The proximal-point lemma also changes from claiming equality with the DC gap to an upper-bound relationship.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens evidence for the central decomposition and oracle-efficiency claims through direct decomposition comparisons, repeated QAP evaluations with confidence intervals, and cost comparisons against closely related methods. It preserves the earlier experiments and clarifies nonsmooth criticality, addressing important weaknesses in v1's support and scope specification. Some inconsistencies remain, including gradient notation in Algorithm 1 despite the subgradient formulation, but the net gains are substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DC-FW research, with matching authors, problem formulation, core algorithm, and retained experiments. All 16 pages of v1 and 20 pages of v2, including appendices, are readable and support comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains those experiments and adds partially observed embedding alignment, repeated QAP comparisons, and a numerical illustration of stationarity measures.

before.justification: v1 reports original QAPLIB experiments and CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100 neural-network training results, including an appendix analysis of constraint-radius sensitivity.

results.title: Revisiting Frank-Wolfe for Structured Nonconvex Optimization

C1.justification: v2 adds an explicit claim that SIS is the first quantification method to tackle covariate shift systematically, whereas v1 principally emphasizes first classifier-based graph quantification. The two headline contributions—SIS for covariate shift and NACC for class identifiability—and their general effectiveness claims remain.

C2.justification: v1 attributes CiteSeer's poor PPR performance broadly to kernel mismatch. Appendix B supplies a more specific explanation involving disconnected components, small effective samples, and interpolation. It also relates PPR weighting to GNN prediction similarity. Section 4.3 adds qualifications about weaker real-world benefits and classifier dependence, while Appendix D discusses feature-kernel applicability and efficiency.

D1.justification: Appendix A adds a code-repository link, a pointer to versioned dependencies, software libraries and licenses, and CPU/GPU/RAM specifications absent from v1. Appendix C documents dense PPR computation, sparse pruning for Twitch, and GPU shortest-path computation. These materially expand reproducibility information without establishing that previously undocumented implementation choices changed.

E1.justification: v2 retains the five citation/co-purchase datasets and adds Twitch Gamers, estimating explicit-content-streamer prevalence within five language communities under natural distribution shift. It also adds random-walk-induced structural shifts. The unshifted evaluation shown in v1 Figure 2 is no longer reported.

E2.justification: v2 Table 1 adds the previously published Ego-network Quantification method, represented by EgoNet with PACC, and evaluates its SIS/NACC extensions. Appendix D additionally compares structural SIS against feature-only importance sampling. MLPE and the standard count baselines remain; the existing shortest-path comparison moves to Appendix B.

E3.justification: v2 adds Twitch's training and language-partition evaluation design and random-walk sampling with length 10 and teleportation parameter 0.1. It drops KLD, retaining AE and RAE. SIS now uses interpolation weight 0.9, while the shortest-path decay parameter changes from 0.5 to 3. The original five-dataset split proportions and neural-network sizes remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Appendix B substantially extends the existing kernel comparison with PPR-interpolation and shortest-path-decay sensitivity sweeps. Appendix D adds a structural-versus-feature-kernel ablation. These examine kernel choice and sensitivity beyond v1's fixed-setting comparisons. Conversely, v1's classifier-accuracy-versus-quantification-error plot is removed.

E5.justification: The retained benchmark protocol still uses ten splits, ten classifier trainings per split, and the same 95th-percentile one-sided t-test. Both versions omit numerical standard errors from tables and leave plotted shaded bands statistically undefined. v2 explains the omission of standard errors but introduces no new uncertainty-estimation procedure.

E6.justification: v2 adds Twitch, random-walk, EgoNet, sensitivity, and feature-kernel results while removing KLD and the old unshifted/hard-classifier plot results. Retained entries also change: PubMed MLP-PACC under PPS changes from AE/RAE 0.0311/0.1071 to 0.0181/0.0649 in Table 1, without an explanation. SIS results additionally reflect revised kernel settings and therefore do not establish same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: SIS changes from approximating importance weights using only test-density KDE in v1 Equation 13 to separately estimating training and test densities for their ratio in v2 Equation 12. v2 also introduces interpolation between PPR and a constant kernel. These change the central weighting procedure, although the reported experiments use a constant training kernel. NACC's one-hop construction remains unchanged.

P1.justification: The main section order and much of the introduction, ACC explanation, and NACC discussion are retained. v2 makes targeted language and notation revisions, separates synthetic and real-world result discussions, and moves shortest-path discussion into the new appendix structure. Citation style and author/header presentation also change.

P2.justification: v2 removes the large classifier-accuracy comparison figure, adds a Twitch visualization and two kernel-sensitivity figures, and substantially restructures Table 1. Tables 2–4 provide new displays, including the relocated and revised shortest-path comparison. The conference template also changes text width, headers, typography, and page layout.

R1.justification: v2 adds Milli et al.'s social-network quantification work and explicitly relates ENQ to neighborhood classification plus ACC. It also adds sources for Twitch, PyTorch Geometric, and sparse graph computation. The broader literature framing remains largely intact, and the first-classifier-based-work wording is not reconciled with the newly acknowledged ENQ predecessor.

T1.justification: New Appendix C develops computational-complexity analyses for SIS, dense/sparse PPR computation, shortest-path kernels, and NACC. It includes an optimizer-iteration assumption and contrasts the stated ACC and NACC complexity bounds. v1 contains no corresponding runtime analysis. Most probability-notation changes in Sections 2–3 restate existing mathematics.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses important weaknesses in v1's support for its methods: it adds a natural-shift study, evaluates an existing graph-quantification method, investigates kernel failures and sensitivity, and supplies substantial implementation information. These additions improve empirical credibility, applicability assessment, and reproducibility. Unexplained PubMed revisions and novelty wording inconsistent with the ENQ discussion remain weaknesses, but they do not outweigh the substantial gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SIS/NACC graph-quantification work. Their text, equations, figures, and tables are readable and support comparison. v1 has no appendix; v2's Appendices A–D were included in the comparison.

after.justification: Sections 4.2–4.3 and Appendices B and D report original benchmark, Twitch, kernel-sensitivity, and feature-kernel comparison results.

before.justification: Section 4, Figure 2, and Table 1 report original quantification experiments on five graph datasets under unshifted and synthetically shifted conditions.

results.title: Adjusted Count Quantification Learning on Graphs

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion expand the contribution from the evaluated single-turn hierarchy to a multi-turn framework using parameter sharing and turn-level optimization for efficiency and stability. The original claims about separating meta-thinking from execution and improving reasoning generalization remain.

C2.justification: v3 adds explanations concerning long-turn weighting, clipping stability, credit assignment, state drift, and multi-turn collapse. Its rewritten limitations emphasize interaction dynamics and rollout efficiency, while removing explicit caveats about small models, inconsistent superiority, and unassessed overthinking. The restriction to mathematics and judging tasks remains acknowledged.

D1.justification: v3 adds a project-code link and a detailed multi-turn reproduction recipe: VeRL, LlamaFactory, math_verify, conversation construction, loss masks, stopping rules, SFT and RL hyperparameters, A800 hardware, training times, and new prompts (Appendices D.2 and G.2). Existing single-turn implementation details are mostly retained.

E1.justification: The original mathematics and judging coverage remains. v3 additionally uses LIMO-derived reasoning conversations for multi-turn initialization and evaluates AIME25 in Figure 8. These extend training material and mathematical test coverage within the existing domains.

E2.justification: Tables 1–2 retain VRP, VRP-RL, and MRP-RL. New multi-turn comparisons evaluate Token-Ratio GRPO and Turn-Ratio Separate Params against shared-parameter Turn-Ratio training (Figure 6). Conversely, v1 Appendix C's comparisons against untuned MRP and MAMRP disappear with its before/after-RL analysis.

E3.justification: New multi-turn protocols include SFT initialization, GRPO without KL regularization, 500-step training, varied turn/token limits, and 300-step ablations on 133 problems (Appendix D.2). Figure 3's stated setup also changes: v1 specifies an Instruct planner guiding a base reasoner, whereas v3 describes SFT/RL on the base model. The unchanged curves do not establish that this experiment was rerun.

E4.justification: v3 adds sensitivity tests for interaction length, comparisons of turn-level versus token-level optimization and shared versus separate parameters, and observations of repetition and empty-response collapse (Section 4.3). It removes v1 Appendix C's direct before/after-RL analysis. Existing generalization, reward-induced role reversal, model-scale, and qualitative analyses are largely retained.

E5.justification: Neither version supplies experimental seed counts, repeated-run estimates, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Figure 3's shaded curves remain without additional explanation of their statistical meaning. The new rollout sample counts describe training procedures, not repeated experimental runs.

E6.justification: The benchmark scores in Tables 1–2 remain unchanged. v3 adds multi-turn convergence, benchmark, and sample-efficiency results, including reported training accuracy rising approximately 55% to 70% and about 5% average test improvement within the new experiment. v1's Figure 5 RL-gain results disappear. The redrawn Figure 4 also changes or omits some early 1B action data points.

M1.justification: v1 implements single-turn ReMA and discusses multi-turn interaction as an extension. v3 adds an operational multi-turn method with shared parameters, simultaneous updates, a turn-level GRPO ratio and trajectory-averaged objective, supervised initialization, and termination-dependent rewards (Section 3.2.2; Appendix D.2). The original single-turn method remains.

P1.justification: v3 substantially condenses and rewrites the preliminaries and single-turn exposition, organizes experiments around five questions, and separates single-turn from multi-turn development. Related work, limitations, and reward-behavior analysis move into regrouped appendices with a new contents list. These are extensive structural changes beyond the added scientific material.

P2.justification: Figures 1–2 are redesigned, Figure 4 is replotted, and new multi-turn Figures 5–6 and 8 replace or supplement earlier displays. v1's RL-gain Figure 5 is removed. Table 1b loses a duplicated loose-split average row whose values remain in Table 2. The document template and figure placements also change substantially.

R1.justification: New Appendix A.4 substantially expands discussion of RL optimization and multi-turn agents, including Dr. GRPO, DAPO, Search-R1, ArCHer, and RAGEN. v3 also adds Satori/COAT and RAISE discussions while preserving the MAPoRL/COPRY distinction. Some earlier references, including Williams's REINFORCE paper and Tree of Thoughts, disappear.

T1.justification: v3 adds a formal multi-turn trajectory factorization and mathematical definitions of the turn-level ratio and training objective (Equations 6 and 12–13). The existing convergence and leader-follower arguments mostly remain. The convergence discussion drops v1's assertion of convergence to optimal policies and changes its stated endpoint from a stationary point to a fixed point.

improvement.justification: v1 leaves multi-turn interaction largely prospective. v3 supports it with an explicit optimization procedure, controlled component comparisons, documented failure conditions, and detailed implementation instructions, substantially strengthening the evidence and reproducibility of interactive meta-thinking. Removing the before/after-RL analysis and several useful caveats weakens completeness, and Figure 3's setup becomes less precise, but these losses are outweighed by the new experimental substantiation and technical clarity.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe ReMA and provide readable text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices. Corresponding material can be matched despite substantial reorganization and the addition of multi-turn methods and experiments.

after.justification: v3 retains original single-turn experiments and adds multi-turn training results, component comparisons, and benchmark curves in Figures 5–6 and 8.

before.justification: v1 reports original mathematical reasoning and LLM-as-a-Judge results in Tables 1–2, alongside training comparisons, reward analyses, and qualitative case studies.

results.title: ReMA: Learning to Meta-think for LLMs with Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list and conclusion expand the methodological contribution from learning a conjugate potential using samples to learning it using either samples or an unnormalized target density. The central factorization claim and claimed first ICNN generation of MNIST remain substantively unchanged.

C2.justification: The interpretation that conjugate Gibbs factors better match target distributions remains. v2 adds explanations of ELU/Hessian difficulties, the LMC efficiency–quality tradeoff, and why ordinary moment-potential regression is harder. It removes v1's concluding qualification that ICNN training difficulties currently hinder performance.

D1.justification: v2 adds code listings for the previously described 1D algorithms (Appendix B.3), explicit benchmark energy formulas, quadratic-input architecture details, and CMFMA hyperparameter tables, including Softplus with beta 10. It documents Cartoon preprocessing with Gaussian noise of standard deviation 0.2. Reported hardware changes from V100 or A100-40GB to V100-32GB.

E1.justification: The original Gaussian mixtures, five synthetic 2D distributions and MNIST remain. v2 adds the Cartoon dataset, three energy-defined 2D target distributions, learning with energy-function access, and reconstruction of half-masked MNIST and Cartoon images. These substantially extend the represented data and task requirements.

E2.justification: v2 adds evaluated Gaussian-to-data generative ICNN baselines for the retained 2D datasets and MNIST, as well as Cartoon (Figures 13, 5 and 15). Amos (2023) supplied a solver in v1 but was not evaluated there as this generative comparator. The original standard moment-measure comparisons remain.

E3.justification: Tables 1–2 revise reported training budgets: 2D gradient steps increase from 700,000 to 1,000,000, MNIST steps decrease from 100,000 to 50,000, and generation-time LMC steps increase from 6,000 to 10,000. Diag-Checkerboard batches change from 4,096 to 1,024. v2 also introduces architecture-matched baseline comparisons, Sinkhorn evaluation with 2,048-sample batches, and half-image masking protocols.

E4.justification: Appendix E adds brief qualitative sensitivity and failure analyses: reducing training LMC steps to 50 degrades performance, and ELU activations cause discontinuities in learned 1D CMFMA potentials, motivating Softplus. These are limited supplementary observations rather than a substantial ablation or robustness study.

E5.justification: v1 provides no seed-based variability assessment. v2 introduces evaluations across 100 random seeds and boxplots of Sinkhorn divergences for all five 2D datasets (Appendix D.1, Figure 13). This establishes a new variability-reporting practice. The seeds vary generated and reference samples; 100 independent training runs are not established.

E6.justification: v2 adds quantitative Sinkhorn comparisons, CMFMA energy-fitting and pushforward results, Cartoon generation, and MNIST/Cartoon reconstruction outcomes. Figure 13 shows broadly overlapping ICNN and CMFGen distributions with modest differences. The original 1D findings remain, including v1 Figure 5 as v2 Figure 8. Revised settings prevent interpreting refreshed generation examples as controlled before-and-after performance gains.

M1.justification: The original fixed-point learner is retained as CMFGen. v2 adds CMFMA, which learns from an unnormalized density through a Monge–Ampère regression objective involving the Hessian determinant (Section 4.3). It also replaces fixed LMC step sizes with a Hessian-adaptive rule and introduces learned-density optimization for inpainting.

P1.justification: Existing material is substantially reorganized: Background is condensed, the main proof sketch moves to Appendix A, the univariate transport recipe moves from experiments into methods, and the fixed-point method is named CMFGen. The methods and experimental narratives are rewritten, and the appendix is reorganized into separate theory, sample-based, energy-based, evaluation and implementation sections.

P2.justification: The 2D display changes from two rows with overlaid targets and potentials to three separate rows. MNIST receives a baseline-comparison panel, while Cartoon uses the earlier schematic format. New energy plots, Sinkhorn boxplots and reconstruction grids substantially expand the visual evidence. Hyperparameter tables separate shared solver settings and add CMFMA configurations; the original 1D convergence display is retained.

R1.justification: The main moment-measure and optimal-transport positioning remains. v2 adds Dalalyan (2016), Ramdas et al. (2017), Rezende and Mohamed (2015), and Royer et al. (2018), supporting sampling, evaluation, the normalizing-flow analogy and Cartoon data. It also explicitly positions its ordinary moment-measure solver as addressing a previously unavailable method.

T1.justification: v2 adds the Monge–Ampère density and energy characterizations in equations (8)–(9), providing the mathematical basis for energy-based learning, and an additional variational proof of Proposition 1. It corrects the 1D transport formula from B to its gradient and removes the earlier entropy–OT variational formulation. The central existence theorem and Schauder proof are retained; v1 Theorem 2 becomes Appendix A's Lemma 1.

improvement.justification: v1's practical generative claims relied mainly on qualitative demonstrations. v2 materially strengthens their assessment through architecture-matched ICNN comparisons and repeated sample-level quantitative evaluations (Appendix D.1), while adding a tested energy-based method and substantial reproducibility details. Image evaluation remains qualitative, the earlier general training caveat is removed, and Section 4.3 contains a log-determinant sign inconsistency with equation (9). These drawbacks do not outweigh the substantial gains in empirical support, methodological utility and reproducibility.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same conjugate moment measure framework. All 16 pages of v1 and 25 pages of v2, including proofs, experimental appendices, figures and tables, support comparison. Retained material can be matched across relocation and renumbering.

after.justification: Section 5 and Appendices B–E report original sample-based and energy-based experiments, quantitative ICNN comparisons, Cartoon generation and image reconstruction.

before.justification: Section 5 and Appendix A report original experiments on univariate Gaussian mixtures, five synthetic 2D distributions and MNIST generation.

results.title: Sample and Map from a Single Convex Potential: Generation using Conjugate Moment Measures

C1.justification: The central contribution remains joint distributional learning of sparse affine interventions. V3 expands the headline image claim to concept mitigation and induction, narrows the advertised support reduction from 100–1000 times to 100 times, and deemphasizes compositionality as a headline contribution while retaining its results.

C2.justification: V3 adds substantive qualifications about evaluating paired-data methods on unpaired toxicity data and applying interventions indiscriminately to all tokens. It contextualizes composition success against prompting at 19% versus 17%, and distinguishes the contribution of end-to-end training from sparsity. New interpretations address UNet sparsity sensitivity and inverse-map behavior; Appendix A replaces the generic impact statement with discussion of harmful conditioning and safeguards.

D1.justification: V3 adds GPU specifications, memory requirements, timing tables across language models and DMD2, and implementation settings for the added baselines. It supplies exact prompting baselines and expanded image-prompt examples. The first page provides a code-repository link where v1 only promised release; the PDFs do not verify repository availability. Existing PPO hyperparameters and TruthfulQA procedures are retained.

E1.justification: The image evaluation changes from COCO-based style induction and a smaller generated concept set to removal and induction across 15 concepts spanning styles, objects and perspectives. Appendix L adds 50 MEN concepts and 20 human-rated similarity pairs. Toxicity, language concept composition and TruthfulQA coverage remain; DeepSeek results are retained in the appendix.

E2.justification: V3 adds prompting, CAA with all-layer and middle-layer variants, ReFT and LoFIT-RL to toxicity comparisons, retaining LRTC-RL in Appendix E. It also adds ITI-c to image comparisons and prompting to language concept composition. These are evaluated comparators, rather than citation additions or baseline renamings.

E3.justification: Image IMGScore switches from CLIP to DINOv2-small embeddings. The revised image setup reports learning rate 1e-4 and gamma 0, versus 5e-4 and 1e-4 in v1. New protocols include a fixed-hyperparameter data sweep from 1 to 1024 examples, a language preference study with 20 volunteers and 20 prompts each, and an image study with 10 participants and 100 comparisons each. These changes preclude direct comparison of image scores across versions.

E4.justification: V3 adds a detailed data-size sensitivity sweep, DMD2 intervention-layer and sparsity sweeps, and analysis relating intervention similarity to human semantic judgments. Appendix K expands layer-support analysis into separate bias and weight panels. Earlier toxicity sparsity, composition and TruthfulQA analyses remain, often relocated.

E5.justification: Appendix L adds statistical correlation estimation between intervention similarities and human judgments over 20 MEN pairs. Existing repeat counts remain four generation seeds for toxicity, three sparsity sweeps and five seeds for TruthfulQA. The PDFs do not establish increased repetitions for retained experiments or new significance-testing procedures.

E6.justification: V3 adds substantial baseline, ablation and human-evaluation results, including LinEAS preference shares of 57.70% for language and 63.3% for images. Table 1 changes the reported Qwen-7B LinEAS RTP/TET toxicity values from 1.88/15.39 to 1.95/14.95, although v3 Table 9 retains the earlier values. TruthfulQA results remain numerically unchanged; the replacement image results use different tasks and metrics.

M1.justification: V3 Section 4.4 introduces inverse-map inference, applying the inverse learned affine transformations to induce concepts after training for removal. The core coordinate-wise affine maps, jointly optimized Wasserstein loss, sparsity penalties and optimization framework remain unchanged.

P1.justification: V3 retitles the paper and substantially rewrites the abstract, introduction, related work and image-evaluation narrative. Optimization details, refitting, composition and group-sparsity discussion move into appendices, while data sensitivity and a dedicated limitations section enter the main text. This is extensive narrative restructuring beyond adding experiments.

P2.justification: V3 replaces the two-column main layout with a single-column report and redesigns the opening illustration. It expands comparison tables, adds preference and timing tables, data-sensitivity plots and correlation heatmaps, and replaces the image galleries with induction/removal displays. The formerly combined composition/support figure is separated, with support distributions expanded into four panels.

R1.justification: Related work is reorganized from single-property versus multi-property steering into strong versus weak supervision, substantially changing LinEAS's positioning around unpaired data and oracle access. V3 adds discussion of BitFit, LoRA and diffusion-guidance approaches, while removing the dedicated multi-property discussion and its associated works, including van der Weij, Liu, Scalena and Zhang.

T1.justification: V3 Equation D.1 corrects the L2 proximal threshold from lambda1 in v1 Equation 7 to tau. Algorithm 1 removes an extra affine transformation of activations already transformed in their definition. Appendix B.1 adds computational and memory complexity expressions. The central loss and regularization mathematics remain, without a new theorem or proof framework.

improvement.justification: V3 substantially strengthens v1's reliance on a narrow comparator set and automated quality measures through additional evaluated baselines, human preference studies in both modalities, and targeted data-size and image-steering robustness analyses. Clearer supervision caveats, limitations, mathematical corrections and implementation disclosures make the claims easier to assess. These benefits outweigh remaining reporting problems, notably inconsistent Qwen values between Tables 1 and 9 and reversed CLIPScore direction arrows in Table 15. The improvement concerns evidential quality, not a demonstrated same-setting performance increase.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe LinEAS, despite the changed title and presentation. Their complete main texts, equations, tables, figures and appendices are readable and support reliable matching across the substantial reorganization.

after.justification: V3 retains original experiments and adds human preference studies, expanded comparisons, image-steering analyses and analysis of intervention similarity against human judgments.

before.justification: V1 reports original toxicity-mitigation, sparsity, concept-composition, TruthfulQA and text-to-image experiments, including appendix results.

results.title: LinEAS: End-to-end Learning of Activation Steering with a Distributional Loss

C1.justification: The introduction narrows the convergence claim from a neighborhood of a minimum to a neighborhood of a stationary point. The central recycling contribution, accuracy-preservation claim, and headline AG News communication cost of 17% remain unchanged.

C2.justification: v2 replaces v1's increased-server-memory limitation with an argument and measurements for lower memory under its aggregation implementation. It changes heterogeneity advice from larger batches to smaller learning rates, explains deterministic recycling failures through excessive staleness, and adds interpretations concerning robustness, scalability, and environmental benefits.

D1.justification: v2 supplies a code-repository link and states that code is public. It adds FedBAT hyperparameters, including coefficient 6 and warm-up ratio 0.5, and describes the memory-measurement implementation using 16 local models per process and MPI_Allreduce. Existing software, hardware, optimizer, and training hyperparameter disclosures are largely retained.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same classification tasks on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, FEMNIST, and AG News. The added heterogeneity and client-count sweeps vary partitions and population sizes within this retained coverage.

E2.justification: v2 adds FedBAT to the four main benchmark comparisons and PruneFL to the LUAR compatibility comparisons. Tables 4–5 introduce random, positional, gradient-norm, deterministic-selection, and update-dropping comparators. The compatibility table omits its former FedAvg rows. FDA in Table 2 corresponds to the existing FedDropoutAvg baseline.

E3.justification: v2 adds fixed-recycling-depth controls, per-process memory measurement, Dirichlet concentration sweeps over 0.1, 0.5, and 1.0, and total-client counts of 64, 128, and 256 with 32 active clients. Existing training settings are retained; AG News using concentration 0.5 was already documented in v1's appendix. These are additional protocols rather than evidence that the original experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained recycling-depth sensitivity analysis, v2 directly tests alternative layer-selection policies, stochastic versus deterministic selection, and recycling versus dropping. Section 3.4 and Appendix A.4 add memory analysis and robustness studies across data heterogeneity and client counts, substantially expanding examination of the method's design choices and operating conditions.

E5.justification: Both versions retain the at-least-three-run statement and tables containing ± values. v2 adds several tables without uncertainty and a checklist statement that only means are reported after three runs, conflicting with its retained ± entries. This changes uncertainty documentation without establishing additional runs, new seeds, or statistical tests.

E6.justification: The original main benchmark scores and recycling-depth sweeps retain their values. v2 adds substantial results for FedBAT, PruneFL with LUAR, selection controls, dropping, memory, and robustness. For example, Table 5 reports FEMNIST accuracy of 73.17% with recycling versus 64.69% with dropping at the same normalized communication cost of 0.18 and recycling depth of two layers.

M1.justification: Algorithm 2 changes the initial recycling set R0 from all layers to an empty set, allowing fresh updates to be aggregated before recycling begins. The layer-priority metric, stochastic selection rule, and subsequent recycling procedure remain unchanged.

P1.justification: Much of the introduction, method exposition, conclusion, and proof narrative is retained. v2 polishes language, condenses baseline descriptions, moves the recycling-depth discussion into Appendix A.4, and reframes Section 4.4 as an ablation study. It also adds an appendix roadmap, acknowledgments, broader impacts, and a conference checklist.

P2.justification: v2 substantially reformats the paper into the conference layout, wraps text around Figures 1–2, and recolors existing charts. It merges the two compatibility tables, combines the existing AG News and CIFAR-10 curves into Figure 4, and adds memory, ablation, and robustness tables. The former main-text recycling-depth table is removed while its results remain in the appendix.

R1.justification: v2 expands discussion and citations for FedBAT, SpaFL, GossipFL, BCRS, decentralized averaging, and YOGA, explicitly distinguishing YOGA's decentralized setting. It also replaces the cited You et al. CNN training work with the BERT optimization work. The overall positioning around compression and update recycling remains intact.

T1.justification: The main-text masked-gradient definition is corrected to refer to recycled layers, matching v1's appendix, rather than zeroing those layers. Section 3.4 also adds the memory-footprint derivation a(d-k)+k versus ad. The existing convergence assumptions, bounds, and appendix proofs retain their mathematical content.

improvement.justification: v1 asserted advantages for its selection metric and recycling over dropping without direct controlled comparisons. v2 Tables 4–5 supply those tests, substantially strengthening support for the central design choices. Corrected initialization and a narrower convergence claim also improve precision. Inconsistent recycling-depth labels in Tables 13 and 15 and contradictory uncertainty documentation limit reproducibility, but the stronger evidence for the core method supports a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same FedLUAR research by the same authors. Their complete main texts, figures, tables, equations, and appendices support comparison, including material relocated in v2.

after.justification: v2 retains these empirical results and adds baseline comparisons, controlled ablations, memory measurements, and heterogeneity and client-count experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original federated classification experiments on four datasets, including accuracy, communication costs, learning curves, and recycling-depth sensitivity results.

results.title: Layer-wise Update Aggregation with Recycling for Communication-Efficient Federated Learning

C1.justification: V1 presents a history-aware streaming reconstruction framework as its primary contribution. V2 redefines the central contribution as a reusable Fuse-and-Refine module for existing feed-forward Gaussian models, emphasizing redundancy reduction and flexible primitive placement, with streaming as an application. Static-only training, interactive speed, and strong static/dynamic reconstruction claims are retained.

C2.justification: V2 adds substantive explanations concerning pixel-aligned redundancy, constrained primitive placement, and why learned refinement improves upon heuristic fusion. It interprets the new temporal controls and explicitly limits gains when initial primitives are poor or camera baselines are large. The conclusion replaces v1's emphasis on repeated per-frame reconstruction and high-resolution scalability with these input-quality limits and persistent dynamic-region warping artifacts.

D1.justification: V2 adds a project-page link, component runtime details, an A100 timing comparison, and concrete retraining details for the DepthSplat extension. Most architecture, optimizer, training-budget, voxel-grid, and tracking parameters were already supplied in v1's appendix. The PDFs alone do not establish whether the new project link provides downloadable code.

E1.justification: Both versions use RealEstate10K, DL3DV, Neural3DVideo, and LongVolumetricVideo for the same reconstruction tasks. V2 adds input-availability scenarios involving train/test camera-count mismatches: four-view training with two-, eight-, and sixteen-view inference, and two-view training with four-view inference. No new dataset or domain is introduced.

E2.justification: V2 adds TranSplat, HiSplat, OmniScene, and DepthSplat to the RealEstate10K comparison, plus Gaussian Graph Network and a retrained DepthSplat comparison in Tables 13–14. Table 5 adds GS-LRM with warping and with warping plus concatenation/dropout. The DL3DV 'Non-learning Fusion' baseline matches v1's 'Naive Baseline (Mean GS)' rather than introducing another comparator.

E3.justification: V2 adds evaluation designs for varying inference-view counts, joint versus staged training, and simple temporal-fusion controls. The DepthSplat experiment uses 128×192 images, 1,000 training scenes, ten test scenes, and two-view training/four-view testing. Joint DL3DV training uses the existing 200K total budget instead of the 100K-plus-100K staged schedule; the original benchmark protocols and metrics otherwise remain.

E4.justification: New analyses test camera-count robustness, whether warping or simple fusion suffices, joint versus staged training, component runtime costs, and portability to DepthSplat (Tables 3, 5, 6, 8, and 14). These substantially extend the original spatial and temporal component ablations. The earlier convergence plot is retained, not newly generated evidence.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. The retained training curves contain no uncertainty bands.

E6.justification: V2 adds substantial numerical evidence for new comparators, view-count robustness, fusion controls, training schemes, and runtime. Its DL3DV headline PSNR changes from 30.34 to 30.61 through the newly reported joint-training variant; the original two-stage result remains in Table 8. The new DepthSplat comparison reports 16.57 versus 17.66 PSNR. Most retained streaming results are unchanged, but 3DGS's LongVolumetricVideo PSNR changes from 18.588 to 18.56.

M1.justification: V2 adds joint training from scratch as an alternative to staged training and integrates the refinement module with DepthSplat. The core voxel hierarchy, transformer, warping, and error-aware fusion remain unchanged. Explicitly concatenating Gaussian attributes in the fusion equation clarifies information already documented in v1 Appendix A.2.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, contribution statements, related work, and conclusion are extensively rewritten around fusion and refinement. V2 introduces reconstruction preliminaries, separates the general module from its streaming application, moves detailed streaming mathematics into the appendix, and adds a societal-impact section.

P2.justification: V2 changes the document from two-column to single-column formatting, adds a dedicated Fuse-and-Refine diagram and several experimental tables, and restructures existing tables. The original streaming overview, teaser, and close-ups move to the appendix; earlier qualitative grids and the convergence plot remain. These are substantial display and layout changes beyond renumbering.

R1.justification: V2 substantially expands positioning against learned Gaussian graph, voxel, and point-based methods, including Gaussian Graph Network, SCube, EvolSplat, and Splatformer. It also discusses point-voxel processing networks and heuristic Gaussian merging, while shortening earlier dynamic-scene and animation coverage. This changes the research context beyond citation updates.

T1.justification: The interpolation kernel, triangulation derivation, residual decoding, linear-blend skinning, losses, and flicker definition are retained, sometimes relocated. V2's standard 3DGS rendering preliminaries explain the existing component rather than changing its mathematics. No new theorem, proof, or substantive formal assumption is introduced.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens the empirical justification for learned refinement. The new temporal-fusion controls, camera-count tests, Gaussian Graph Network comparison, and DepthSplat integration address v1's limited evidence about alternative fusion strategies and applicability beyond its original configuration. Runtime breakdowns and more specific failure conditions also make the claims easier to assess. The DepthSplat test remains small and statistical uncertainty is still unreported, but the added validation provides a clear substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both complete PDFs describe the same SplatVoxel research, despite the changed title and emphasis. Their methods, experiments, equations, figures, and appendices can be reliably matched.

after.justification: V2 retains original reconstruction and streaming results and adds view-count generalization, training comparisons, temporal-fusion controls, runtime measurements, and DepthSplat integration results.

before.justification: V1 reports original static-scene reconstruction, dynamic streaming, and ablation results in Tables 2–5, with additional sequence-level results and qualitative examples in the appendix.

results.title: Learning Efficient Fuse-and-Refine for Feed-Forward 3D Gaussian Splatting

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same contributions: general synthetic-image and DeepFake detection with explanations, expert-comparable performance without an additional classifier, and a seven-category FakeClue dataset exceeding 100,000 images. Additional evidence does not materially redefine these claims.

C2.justification: V2 introduces substantive limitations absent from v1: inherited annotation-model biases, missed fine-grained artifacts, and reduced sensitivity to high-fidelity synthetic images (Appendix F). It adds interpretations concerning alignment with human artifact perception and category-dependent performance, plus discussion of deployment errors and computational-access limitations in Appendix G.

D1.justification: Appendix H supplies seven real/fake prompt pairs and aggregation instructions previously unavailable in v1. V2 also explicitly identifies Qwen2-VL as aggregator, specifies the GPT-4o snapshot, and marks FakeClue-trained expert baselines. The abstract changes a promised code/data release to reported availability of code, model weights, and data; external availability was not verified.

E1.justification: The named benchmarks and detection/explanation tasks are retained. Appendix C adds testing on compressed, resized, noisy, and otherwise transformed FakeClue images, extending input conditions. Appendix D disaggregates existing LOKI coverage rather than establishing a newly added domain.

E2.justification: Table 2 adds CNNSpot, FreqNet, Fatformer, UnivFD, AIDE, and NPR to the FakeClue/LOKI comparison; CNNSpot and UnivFD previously appeared only in the DMimage comparison. New Table 8 substantially broadens LOKI comparators, including MiniCPM-V-2.6, Claude-3.5-Sonnet, and Gemini-1.5-Pro.

E3.justification: Section 4.3 revises the stated learning rate from 2e-4 to 2e-5, retaining two epochs, eight A100 GPUs, and batch size 32 per GPU. Appendix C introduces specified distortion settings, including JPEG qualities, resizing scales, and Gaussian-noise variances. The learning-rate revision does not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Appendices C–D add systematic robustness testing across twelve perturbation conditions and category-level generalization analysis. Appendix B supplies benchmark-separated training-strategy results. The existing explanatory-text ablation is retained; the dedicated DD-VQA explanation examples in v1 Figure 6 are removed, while the real-image case figure gains another example.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or statistical significance tests for its experiments. The additional results retain point-estimate reporting.

E6.justification: V2 adds expert-baseline, perturbation, and category results in Tables 2 and 7–8, including 89.5% FakeClue accuracy under Blur3 versus 98.6% on original images. Table 3 changes Gram-Net's real-image Acc/F1 from 22.8/34.1 to 62.8/54.1. Existing main-table FakeVLM scores are retained; conversion from decimals to percentages is not a performance change.

M1.justification: The architecture, loss, full fine-tuning, and explanatory VQA procedure remain unchanged. However, Section 3.2 changes the stated annotation-prompt count from 12 to 14. Since v1 already covers seven categories and illustrates a face prompt but lacks the full templates, the PDFs do not establish whether this reflects a procedural change or corrected documentation.

P1.justification: The main section sequence and contribution narrative are retained. V2 condenses several dataset, training, and results paragraphs, clarifies aggregation terminology, renames the DeepFake category to face manipulation, updates affiliation text, and adds appendix cross-references and acknowledgments.

P2.justification: V2 changes the two-column layout to a single-column conference format, expands Table 2, and adds Tables 7–8. It relocates retained figures, removes the introductory and dedicated DD-VQA case figures, and adds a dataset gallery, benchmark-separated training chart, and radar summary. The real-image figure expands from two examples to three.

R1.justification: V2 adds citations including LEGION, GPT-ImgEval, newer LMM-efficiency and geospatial work, and newly compared detectors. FWA and CDFA citations now identify detection papers instead of unrelated works. These are localized reference and contextual updates; the central positioning against generic LMMs and tampering-focused systems remains unchanged.

T1.justification: The encoder, projector, and training-objective equations are unchanged. Equation 1 makes the candidate-caption set and aggregation prompt explicit but restates the existing aggregation operation. Neither version provides theoretical propositions or proofs.

improvement.justification: V2 addresses substantial reproducibility and validation gaps by supplying annotation prompts and robustness results only referenced in v1, adding expert comparisons on the primary benchmarks, and documenting annotation bias and high-fidelity failure cases. These gains outweigh the loss of dedicated DD-VQA explanation examples. Reporting remains imperfect: some LOKI baseline scores differ between Tables 2 and 8 without a clarified setting difference.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same FakeVLM/FakeClue work, with matching architecture, contributions, and experiments. Text, equations, tables, and figures are readable. V1 ends with references; v2 includes Appendices A–H, allowing reliable comparison of the supplied material.

after.justification: V2 retains the original experimental results and additionally reports distortion robustness and category-level performance in Appendices C–D.

before.justification: Sections 5.3–5.5 report original FakeVLM detection, artifact-explanation, and ablation results on FakeClue, LOKI, DMimage, DD-VQA, and FF++.

results.title: Spot the Fake: Large Multimodal Model-Based Synthetic Image Detection with Artifact Explanation

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction retain the same central findings and contribution: shorter contexts improve standard-task learning, and short-to-long scheduling improves performance and efficiency while preserving long-context capability.
