The headline claims of gains up to 3.7% and training-time savings up to 22% remain unchanged.

C2.justification: v2 adds an optimization-stability explanation connecting shorter contexts to smaller attention logits, smoother losses, and more controlled gradients. It newly attributes RULER differences to synthetic-benchmark variability and discusses compatibility with alternative attention architectures. Appendix A.1 explicitly identifies computational scaling limits and the absence of theoretical analysis; Section 4.3 also narrows improvement over IntraDoc from all benchmarks to many.

D1.justification: v2 adds substantial resource and data documentation: A.9 specifies A100/H100 hardware and training costs, including approximately 200 hours on eight A100s for a 1B, 8K-context run; A.10 supplies corpus and benchmark length statistics; A.11 supplies asset licenses. It also clarifies baseline use of Flash Attention 2. The code link, core configuration tables, and implementation pseudocode already existed in v1.

E1.justification: v2 Appendix A.7.3 substantially expands evaluation coverage with TOEFL and QuALITY reading comprehension, PopQA within retrieval-augmented QA, and many-shot classification on DBpedia, AGNews, Amazon, Yelp, and SST2. Existing training corpora and earlier evaluation tasks are retained.

E2.justification: Corresponding comparisons retain Random, IntraDoc, BM25, Dataset Decomposition with one or eight cycles, continual pretraining, and alternative schedules. New architecture and task experiments compare Random with SkyLadder rather than introducing another competing algorithm. The expanded discussion of Li and Jin does not establish additional evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: v2 adds Gemma3-like 120M/360M and Qwen2.5-0.5B experimental configurations, stability measurements over the first 30K training steps, and FLOPs evaluation. Its new McNemar tests use full benchmark test sets, explicitly distinguished from OLMES's sampled evaluations. These are additions to the experimental design; the original training hyperparameters remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's attention-sink and entropy analysis, v2 Section 4.6 investigates maximum attention logits, loss fluctuations, and gradient norms across context lengths. Appendix A.7.4 adds tests of applicability to hybrid attention and Qwen-style architectures, while A.10 analyzes corpus and benchmark length distributions. Existing scheduling ablations are retained.

E5.justification: v1 provides point estimates and a heuristic loss-difference threshold. v2 introduces paired McNemar significance tests for the main benchmark comparisons, with significance markers in Table 1 and procedures in A.7.3. Its checklist newly states that pretraining runs were not repeated because of cost; this is disclosure, not an increase in runs.

E6.justification: Most existing benchmark scores are retained, but Table 7 changes continual pretraining's long-context score from 2.7 to 10.0 under the same reported schedule. New results include Random versus SkyLadder RAG averages of 30.3 versus 35.5 and many-shot classification averages of 73.9 versus 76.5. v2 also adds architecture, stability, dataset-statistics, and FLOPs results, including reported compute reductions of 14.7% and 26.3%.

M1.justification: The blockwise causal mask, linear window-expansion rule, integration with intra-document masking, and Flash Attention pseudocode retain the same procedure. Hybrid-attention and Qwen-style models are additional experimental configurations; no new SkyLadder algorithmic component is specified.

P1.justification: The main five-section narrative remains recognizable. v2 tightens wording, moves coding experiments into the results subsection, and consolidates efficiency, attention analysis, and related-method comparison under Analysis and Discussion. It expands appendix organization and adds a conference checklist, but largely preserves the existing exposition rather than rewriting the paper wholesale.

P2.justification: v2 adds a training-stability plot and tables for stability, new tasks, architectures, and dataset statistics. It moves long-context columns from Table 1 into Table 2, adds significance markers and a FLOPs column, and revises captions. The NeurIPS formatting also substantially changes typography, equation placement, and figure/table positioning.

R1.justification: v2 adds citations for Gemma3, Kimi K2, and additional reading-comprehension benchmarks, and replaces the unrelated Zhang 2020 citation for SlimPajama with its actual dataset reference. Appendix A.8 expands comparisons with sequence-length warmup and GrowLength, while retaining the original positioning around simultaneous efficiency and performance gains.

T1.justification: v2 A.6 adds an explicit mathematical definition of per-token context size as the number of accessible, unmasked tokens and derives its uniform distribution under Random causal masking. v1 displayed this distribution without that formalization. The scheduling mathematics is unchanged, and neither version provides theoretical guarantees or proofs of effectiveness.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the evidence for preserving long-context capability: v1 relied mainly on MDQA/RULER, whereas v2 adds broader 3B reading-comprehension, retrieval-augmented QA, and many-shot evaluations. Architecture tests and stability diagnostics address generality and mechanism, while significance testing and resource disclosures improve assessability. These gains address important validation gaps rather than merely increasing reported performance. Statistical assurance remains incomplete because training runs are not repeated and the McNemar significance threshold is unspecified.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe SkyLadder and contain readable main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices. Corresponding methods and experiments can be matched despite reorganization, renumbering, and additional material in v2.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments and adds long-context evaluations, architecture comparisons, training-stability measurements, and dataset analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original language-model pretraining experiments, downstream evaluations, scheduling ablations, attention analyses, and training-time measurements.

results.title: SkyLadder: Better and Faster Pretraining via Context Window Scheduling

C1.justification: The central claims of activation-based task-specific selection and improved effectiveness and robustness remain. v2 sharpens the contribution around model-centric, monosemantic representations and withdraws v1's categorical first-use claim for SAE-based selection by acknowledging concurrent work. The rename and expanded abstract do not themselves constitute a new algorithmic contribution.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive explanations concerning activation overlap, length bias, poorer selection at 10%, and possible redundancy in synthesized data. Its limitations replace the claim of easy extension to other training stages with an untested-extension qualification and add the text-only boundary. However, it removes v1's warning that greedy selection ignores diversity while Appendix D.4 describes MONA's selected data as more diverse.

D1.justification: v2 newly documents GPU types, concrete input formats, BGE chunking and pooling for long inputs, the LLM2Vec checkpoint, polysemantic activation extraction, and algorithm pseudocode. These supplement already reported training hyperparameters and SAE access information; BGE processing details do not establish that existing experiments changed. Both versions still describe code release as future work.

E1.justification: OpenHermes-2.5, LESS, the six target benchmarks and the physics knowledge-recall task are retained. v2 adds GPT-4o-generated instruction data through the TyDiQA self-instruct comparison in Appendix D.4, providing a limited additional training-data source without adding a target benchmark or domain.

E2.justification: The established selection baselines remain. v2 adds LLM2Vec to the main comparisons in Tables 1–2 and GPT-4o Self-Instruct to a separate TyDiQA comparison in Table 6. These are bounded extensions of the existing comparison suite.

E3.justification: v2 adds LLaMA2-13B evaluation and controlled settings for sparsity, similarity metrics, aggregation and activation extraction. The reported MBPP protocol changes from one shot in v1 Table 2 to three shots in v2 Table 3, without establishing that retained results were rerun. Table 9's OpenHermes-2.5 caption conflicts with Figure 3's LESS setting, so it does not reliably establish another source-dataset change.

E4.justification: v2 adds polysemantic-versus-monosemantic activation comparisons, Math/Code activation visualizations, sparsity and similarity-metric ablations, similar-versus-dissimilar selection controls, and length-normalization analysis. These directly examine previously under-tested design choices. The earlier layer analysis, LLM-analyst case study and physics recall analysis are retained, sometimes relocated.

E5.justification: Both versions average the random-selection baseline over three seeds. Neither introduces confidence intervals, significance tests, uncertainty bars or a broader repeated-run reporting practice. Individual activation traces in v2 Figure 4 are sample visualizations, not uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial results for LLaMA2-13B, LLM2Vec, Self-Instruct and component analyses; Table 2 reports a MONA average of 46.65 for 5% OpenHermes-2.5 selection. Most matched Table 1 values remain unchanged. The OLMo-7B DLRDS-BGE GPQA entry changes from 23.97 to 23.88, and its average from 31.85 to 31.83. New appendix tables also disclose task-level results underlying retained plots.

M1.justification: NAS is renamed MONA, but the procedure retains SAE TopK activations, token averaging, an averaged target prototype and generalized Jaccard ranking. Maximizing similarity replaces minimizing one minus similarity, which selects equivalently. Length normalization was already present in v1 Equation 8; its new analysis does not establish a method modification.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, methodological explanations and related-work narrative are extensively rewritten. NAS becomes MONA, experiments are reorganized around explicit research questions, visualization and ablation sections are introduced, and retained supplementary material is redistributed into an expanded appendix structure.

P2.justification: The document changes from two-column to predominantly single-column layout. Figure 1 is substantially redesigned, the workflow is revised, selection-ratio lines become grouped bars, and activation visualizations and a combined ablation figure are added. Tables gain method groupings and ranking emphasis, with new result tables and relocated retained case-study and prompt displays.

R1.justification: v2 substantially revises positioning around data-centric versus model-centric representations and acknowledges Yang et al.'s concurrent diversity-driven SAE selection, replacing v1's first-use positioning with a semantic-relatedness distinction. It also adds relevant literature on LLM2Vec, domain shift, sparse coding, CATS and Self-Instruct. This changes the novelty argument beyond citation-format updates.

T1.justification: Appendix D.5 adds a localized approximate derivation of length bias under sum aggregation, using nonnegative activations and magnitude-scaling assumptions, followed by a normalization argument. Section 2.1 also corrects the optimization expression to depend on candidate subset D and distinguishes the target task from its representative examples. No general performance theorem is added.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens empirical support for the unchanged method by directly testing activation decomposition, similarity metrics, sparsity and normalization, addressing v1's limited validation of these central choices. Larger-model evaluation, LLM2Vec comparisons and revised novelty positioning further improve the paper. The unexplained MBPP shot change, conflicting Table 9 caption, under-documented Self-Instruct comparison and removed diversity caveat weaken particular claims, but the added component evidence provides a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work, despite the revised title and NAS-to-MONA rename. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables and appendices support comparison; localized reporting inconsistencies do not prevent matching the work.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds larger-model evaluations, additional comparators, activation visualizations and component ablations.

before.justification: v1 reports original instruction-tuning experiments, layer and selection-ratio analyses, LLM-assigned data-quality scores, and physics knowledge-recall results.

results.title: Task-Specific Data Selection for Instruction Tuning via Monosemantic Neuronal Activations

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the same central contributions: compact sparse-Gaussian representation, SVQ and local-distinctiveness pruning. The headline claims of approximately 49–50% storage reduction, approximately 4.1 MB on Mip-NeRF 360 and 600+ FPS are unchanged.

C2.justification: New Section 5 explicitly bounds OMG by its underlying densification method, explains failures on large Zip-NeRF scenes and discusses integration with MCMC. New appendix discussion interprets sparse-compressor failures, Morton-order scalability and deployment on weaker GPUs. These substantially expand applicability and mechanism discussion. However, Appendix B's claimed Morton speedup contradicts the timing assignments in Table 9.

D1.justification: v2 newly specifies lambda=2 and documents the Zip-NeRF/MCMC training budget, densification interval, feature-introduction schedule and larger SVQ codebooks. Appendix A also explains how the sparse comparator combinations were trained. Most original implementation details and the project URL are retained; the checklist additionally states that supplementary code is provided.

E1.justification: v2 adds evaluation on the larger, more complex scenes of the Zip-NeRF dataset (Table 7 and Section 5), extending coverage to a regime where the original baseline densification becomes inadequate. All three original datasets and their per-scene coverage are retained.

E2.justification: The comparison set expands substantially: Mini-Splatting joins Tables 1–3, LocoGS-L is added to the Tanks&Temples and Deep Blending comparison, and RVQ joins the quantization comparison. New experiments evaluate 3DGS-MCMC, Zip-NeRF and SMERF, plus Mini-Splatting combinations with Compact-3DGS and LocoGS. These are reported comparisons, not citation-only additions.

E3.justification: New protocols include MCMC evaluations at 500K/1M Gaussians, Zip-NeRF training with 3M Gaussians for 150K iterations, COLMAP-initialized LocoGS comparisons and GTX 1080 Ti timing. The VQ comparison changes appearance codebooks from 2^13 to 2^14 entries, expands to three OMG sizes and reports codebook-initialization time instead of total training time. The original OMG training schedule remains unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 adds LD scoring without attribute compression (Figure 5), removal of SVQ (Table 4), RVQ and expanded VQ comparisons (Table 5), and transfer to MCMC (Table 6). Appendices A–C additionally test competing compressors with sparse Gaussians, Morton-order approximation against KNN, and rendering on weaker hardware. These substantially extend the questions tested beyond v1's ablations.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. The new checklist explicitly acknowledges the absence of error bars but introduces no statistical estimation or uncertainty-reporting procedure.

E6.justification: Original OMG benchmark and per-scene values are retained, but substantial new results are added. Examples include MCMC+OMG achieving 26.69 PSNR at 29.0 MB on Zip-NeRF and OMG-XS rendering at 106 FPS versus LocoGS's 73 FPS on GTX 1080 Ti. Table 5 replaces the VQ-XS result of 26.97 PSNR/3.99 MB with 27.06/4.21 under revised codebooks, not a same-setting gain. Figure 4 also uses different views and results.

M1.justification: The architecture, SVQ procedure and training objective remain intact. Equation (8) changes the stated local-distinctiveness score normalization from 1/K, the neighbor count, to 1/D, the feature dimension. This is a limited scoring-formula revision, without evidence of different pruning decisions. The generalized feature notation still uses D=3 in the documented original setup.

P1.justification: Most introductory, methodological and concluding prose is retained. Local wording is refined, the ablation discussion is reordered and rewritten in places, and a limitations section, acknowledgements and NeurIPS checklist are added. The appendix is reorganized into lettered sections; this is not a wholesale rewrite of the scientific narrative.

P2.justification: The paper changes from a two-column layout to a single-column NeurIPS format. Figure 4 replaces its views and OMG-M/stump panels with a LocoGS comparison and enlarged crops; Figure 5 is new. Tables gain comparisons, Table 5 is substantially restructured, and the retained post-processing table is transposed. Existing appendix results are relocated and reformatted rather than removed.

R1.justification: v2 adds references to Zip-NeRF, SMERF and 3DGS-MCMC, connecting OMG to large-scene rendering and an alternative densification framework. The existing related-work taxonomy and positioning against Gaussian compression approaches remain largely unchanged.

T1.justification: Equation (8) revises the mathematical definition of the LD score by replacing normalization by K with normalization by D. The remaining rendering and quantization equations are retained. Neither version presents formal theorems or proofs, and none are added.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens support for the central design choices through direct RVQ comparisons, uncompressed LD controls and sparse-compressor experiments. MCMC and Zip-NeRF evaluations, paired with explicit baseline-dependent limitations, address important gaps in v1's evidence about applicability. The new Morton/KNN timing table remains internally inconsistent: it assigns 4100 ms to OMG and 28 ms to KNN while the text claims Morton is 146 times faster. This weakens that specific conclusion, but the broader validation and clearer applicability boundaries provide a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same OMG research, with matching architecture, core experiments and per-scene results. Their text, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable and support a reliable comparison despite substantial formatting changes.

after.justification: v2 retains the original empirical results and adds quantization comparisons, MCMC integration, Zip-NeRF evaluation, sparse-baseline experiments, neighbor-search comparisons and lower-end GPU measurements.

before.justification: v1 reports original OMG rendering, compression, timing and ablation results on Mip-NeRF 360, Tanks&Temples and Deep Blending, including per-scene and compression analyses in the appendix.

results.title: Optimized Minimal 3D Gaussian Splatting

C1.justification: Rebalancing existing datasets becomes a third explicit contribution in v2's abstract, introduction and conclusion. V2 also replaces the headline maximum diversity/performance improvements with an average-performance-gain claim and strengthens the scalability description to approximately linear or better growth.

C2.justification: V1 presents seed dependence as limiting Evol-Instruct's dataset expansion; v2 instead evaluates its expansion and interprets competing methods as exhibiting saturation or instability. New distributional analyses attribute rebalancing benefits to broader, more uniform coverage. Appendix A.8 newly acknowledges that generated-answer accuracy is not validated.

D1.justification: V2 adds a TreeSynth code-access link, explicit size-matching instructions, the embedding model, a sample-routing prompt and the balancing threshold. Appendix A.9 discloses eight 80-GB H100 GPUs, roughly 30,000 GPU-hours and software versions. The displayed SimpleToM conversion template is also corrected: v1 Figure 21 requests answer reasoning, whereas v2 Figure 25 specifies story conversion.

E1.justification: GSM8K, MATH, MBPP, HumanEval and SimpleToM remain the downstream benchmarks. V2 adds a limited application scenario on SimpleToM: rebalancing existing Temperature Sampling and Persona Hub corpora, extending TreeSynth's evaluated task from generating data from scratch to redistributing supplied datasets.

E2.justification: V2 adds Persona Hub as an evaluated attribute-driven synthesis comparator across mathematical, coding and SimpleToM experiments. The SimpleToM comparison also drops v1's zero-shot references. Temperature Sampling, Evol-Instruct and the human-curated datasets remain; Native Trainset is renamed Vanilla Data.

E3.justification: V2 adds LLaMA3.3-70B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct generation settings and evaluates Evol-Instruct across growing datasets up to 100k. The reported GSM8K learning rate changes from 1e-5 to 1e-4. SimpleToM switches from GPT-4o generation to LLaMA3.3-70B-Instruct, revises prompts and increases the reported corpus from 4k to 40k, with evaluation focused on LLaMA3.1-8B. These are reported setting changes, without establishing which retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: New t-SNE analyses examine distributional coverage across synthesis methods and before versus after rebalancing (Figures 4 and 7). Section 4.3 additionally tests whether balancing existing synthetic datasets improves diversity and downstream accuracy. The earlier attribute-adherence case studies are retained in Appendix A.7 rather than newly added.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental run counts, random-seed values, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. V1's unfilled statistical-significance checklist does not constitute uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: V2 adds extensive results for two additional generators, Persona Hub and rebalancing. Table 3 reports accuracy changes from 78.9 to 86.8 for balanced Temperature Sampling data and from 85.7 to 88.6 for balanced Persona Hub data. Retained entries also change: the GPT-4o/Qwen MATH Evol-Instruct score is 45.34 in v1 Table 1 versus 61.10 in v2 Table 2. Revised protocols and replaced SimpleToM experiments prevent treating all cross-version differences as comparable performance gains.

M1.justification: The original partition-and-synthesize procedure is retained. V2 adds a substantive dataset-rebalancing procedure: route existing samples through the tree, downsample overrepresented leaves and synthesize samples for underrepresented leaves to meet a threshold (Section 3.3 and Algorithm 1).

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, experimental narrative and conclusion are substantially rewritten. Related work, pseudocode, benchmark descriptions, implementation details and case-study discussion move into a structured appendix. Terminology is revised, and the unfinished NeurIPS checklist is removed.

P2.justification: The detailed tree illustration is redrawn and moved from v1 Figure 4 to v2 Figure 2. Results are reorganized into generator-specific tables with average columns and a separate SimpleToM table. V2 adds t-SNE displays and numerical scaling tables, redraws scaling plots with additional curves, and restyles appendix prompt boxes.

R1.justification: V2 adds Persona Hub and t-SNE citations and explicitly discusses persona-driven synthesis. References to Gaining Wisdom from Setbacks, SciLitLLM and statistical rejection sampling are removed. The broader positioning of hierarchical partitioning against fixed attributes and local generation remains substantially intact.

T1.justification: The mathematical partition definitions and disjointness/coverage conditions remain equivalent. Replacing complementarity terminology with exhaustiveness does not alter them. The rebalancing extension adds an algorithm, but no new theorem, proof or substantive theoretical derivation.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens validation beyond v1's single generator and fixed-size Evol-Instruct scaling reference through additional generators, Persona Hub comparisons and expanded scaling evaluations. The tested rebalancing extension and new implementation, compute and limitation disclosures also improve usefulness and reproducibility. Uncertainty reporting remains absent, and the claim of superiority at every scale has a counterexample in Table 6, but these weaknesses do not outweigh the substantial gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe TreeSynth, with readable main text, equations, tables, figures and appendices. The retained material can be matched across substantial reorganization, supporting a reliable comparison.

after.justification: V2 reports original synthesis, fine-tuning, scaling and dataset-rebalancing results in Tables 1–8 and Figures 4–8, including appendix experiments.

before.justification: V1 reports original data-synthesis and model-fine-tuning experiments, including diversity scores, downstream performance and dataset-scaling results in Table 1 and Figure 3.

results.title: TreeSynth: Synthesizing Diverse Data from Scratch via Tree-Guided Subspace Partitioning

C1.justification: The abstract and conclusion retain the same central claims: preference-guided diffusion generates diverse designs beyond the training data, outperforms inverse alternatives and remains competitive with forward methods. The introduction's new contribution bullets restate these claims; additional experiments supply supporting evidence.

C2.justification: v2 adds a Bradley-Terry/reward interpretation of preference guidance, advice against extreme guidance when diversity matters, and an interpretation of runtime scaling with dimensionality versus objective count. The stated limitation concerning fine-grained control over objective trade-offs remains unchanged.

D1.justification: v2 newly documents the 54k/6k training-validation split, linear noise schedule from 0.0001 to 0.02, task dimensions and hypervolume reference points, metric calculations, A100 hardware and approximately 56 GPU-hours. It also supplies a code link. These substantially expand reproducibility information without establishing that previously unspecified settings changed.

E1.justification: v2 adds 18 MO-NAS tasks: C10/MOP1-9 and IN1K/MOP1-9. These extend evaluation to discrete architecture selection with prediction-error and hardware objectives, beyond the retained synthetic and RE engineering tasks (Section 5; Tables 8, 24 and 25).

E2.justification: Benchmark tables retain ParetoFlow and the same nine MultiHead/MultipleModels variants. However, the unconditional-diffusion comparator in v1 Figure 2 is omitted from the corresponding v2 Figure 3. No-guidance is evaluated separately through w=0 in the new ablations.

E3.justification: v2 introduces systematic evaluations at guidance weights 0, 5, 10, 20 and 50, four diversity-criterion configurations at w=10, and training-runtime comparisons on ZDT1 and RE61. These substantially expand the controlled evaluation design. Existing benchmark metrics and the 256-design budget remain; the newly disclosed training split does not establish a change to earlier experiments.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's pruning comparison and qualitative guidance demonstrations, v2 directly tests guidance strength and Crowding, SubCrowding, Hypervolume and No Diversity choices (Section 5.3, Figure 4, Tables 10-21). It also adds runtime analysis and sample visualizations across eight additional tasks. The earlier unconditional denoising panels are removed.

E5.justification: Both versions report results averaged over five random seeds with ± values. v2 extends this reporting practice to new experiments and plots, without introducing a different run count, confidence-interval procedure or significance test.

E6.justification: The retained per-task benchmark table values are unchanged. v2 adds extensive NAS, ablation and runtime results; for example, Table 1 reports MO-NAS average ranks of 1.86 for PGD-MOO and 4.67 for ParetoFlow. These are newly evaluated outcomes, not performance improvements over v1 under retained settings. Dataset-best average-rank entries and unconditional denoising panels are omitted.

M1.justification: The DDPM, MLP architectures and Algorithm 1 remain. Equation 7 changes crowding normalization from whole-dataset extrema to current-front extrema, and v2 represents discrete NAS designs through continuous logits. These are limited changes to the stated procedure. New log-probability wording is not reconciled with Algorithm 1's unchanged gradient of p.

P1.justification: The introduction is condensed and reorganized around contribution bullets, and the related-work section is extensively rewritten. Method explanations are expanded, a dedicated ablation subsection is introduced, and the former results-only appendix becomes separate experimental-setting, dataset, computational-resource and results sections.

P2.justification: v2 adds a workflow schematic, ablation graphics, multi-task sample plots and numerous dataset, runtime and experimental tables. Existing average-rank columns are consolidated into Table 1, the ZDT2 denoising figure loses its unconditional row, and the document adopts a substantially different conference layout with resized and relocated displays.

R1.justification: v2 adds references connecting the method to Bradley-Terry preferences and DPO, discusses robust guided diffusion and an offline-optimization survey, and cites NAS benchmarks. Its principal positioning as a diversity-aware inverse approach alongside ParetoFlow and surrogate-based methods remains.

T1.justification: Equation 7 substantively revises the crowding-distance definition by normalizing within the current front instead of the entire dataset. Existing Pareto definitions and diffusion equations remain. Appendix A spells out existing evaluation metrics, and no new theorem or proof is provided.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation by adding discrete NAS evaluations and quantitative tests of guidance and diversity components that v1 assessed mainly through pruning and qualitative comparisons. The new split, noise-schedule, reference-point, resource and code-access disclosures also address important reproducibility gaps. SubCrowding remains undefined and classifier-score wording remains inconsistent with Algorithm 1, but these weaknesses do not outweigh the substantial gains in empirical scrutiny and documentation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same PGD-MOO research. Their main text, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable and support reliable matching despite substantial reformatting and additions.

after.justification: v2 retains these original results and adds neural architecture search evaluations, component ablations, runtime measurements and sample visualizations.

before.justification: v1 reports original PGD-MOO experiments on synthetic and RE engineering tasks, including hypervolume, diversity, pruning comparisons and generated-sample visualizations.

results.title: Preference-Guided Diffusion for Multi-Objective Offline Optimization

C1.justification: The abstract, contributions, and conclusion change from Gaussian optimality for SD-LTC alone to optimality for both SD-LTC and PD-LTC. The private-randomness contribution changes meaning: v1 claims a rate strictly better than the twice-distortion limit, whereas v2 claims attainment of that limit under perfect or near-perfect perception.

C2.justification: v2 withdraws the interpretation that Gaussian experiments support R(D/2,infinity) not being the private-randomness limit. It explains why sufficiently large private dithers must extend outside lattice cells and specifies the relevant flatness-factor requirements. It also adds a limitation concerning integration with image-compression hyperpriors that implicitly use deterministic dithering.

D1.justification: New Appendix B specifies factorized entropy densities for NTC, RealNVP densities for LTC, 100 training epochs, test-split averaging, and an NVIDIA RTX5000 GPU. These are newly documented settings, not demonstrated changes to existing experiments. Previously stated linear-transform and MLP details are relocated; the empirical choice of the new dither scale s remains unspecified.

E1.justification: v2 retains Gaussian, Physics, and Speech evaluation and adds compression of 28-by-28 MNIST images. This extends evaluation from low-dimensional synthetic and measurement/audio vectors to a substantially higher-dimensional image domain.

E2.justification: Matched experiments retain the same deterministic, private-dither, shared-dither, and quantized-shared-dither NTC/LTC comparisons, including nesting ratios 2 and 3. Gaussian comparisons still include RCC at dimensions 1 and 8. MNIST extends the existing comparator family; rearranged main-text plots do not remove comparisons retained in the appendices.

E3.justification: The added MNIST protocol uses latent dimension 8 and discriminator-based test Wasserstein evaluation (Appendix B). Section 5.2 also changes the stated lattice assignments from Speech/E8 and Physics/Lambda16 to Physics/E8 and Speech/Lambda16. Since v1's Speech ablation already uses Lambda16, this reported correction does not establish that experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: The Speech lattice-choice and STE-versus-noisy-proxy ablations are retained, moving from v1 Figures 12–13 to v2 Figures 11–12. The sliced-Wasserstein validation with 20 and 50 projections is also retained. MNIST adds benchmark evidence without a distinct new ablation or robustness analysis.

E5.justification: Tables 1–2 retain identical estimates and standard errors. Neither version reports training-run uncertainty, confidence intervals, or significance tests, and v2 adds no repeated-run or training-seed information.

E6.justification: v2 adds a full set of MNIST rate-distortion and rate-perception outcomes across the NTC/LTC and dithering variants (Figures 5–6 and 8). The existing Physics, Speech, RCC, ablation, and sliced-Wasserstein results are retained. The substantive empirical addition is image-compression evidence, rather than a demonstrated same-setting performance improvement.

M1.justification: Definitions 3.2 and 3.4 introduce a scale s for the private decoder dither: PD-LTC changes from gs(yhat+u) to gs(yhat+su), and QSD-LTC similarly scales its private fine-lattice dither. This is a limited procedural generalization; SD-LTC and the basic training objectives remain unchanged.

P1.justification: The introduction, related work, and method exposition are extensively condensed and rewritten. Numbered related-work subsections become thematic paragraphs, much RCC background moves to Appendix A, experimental details are consolidated in new Appendix B, and the private-randomness proof is reorganized around explicit lemmas. These changes extend beyond scientific additions and renumbering.

P2.justification: Figure 1 changes from a two-by-two arrangement to one row. The standalone Gaussian-limit plot is removed, a new latent-channel schematic is added, and the real-world comparisons are regrouped into multi-dataset grids incorporating MNIST. Appendix plots and ablation panels are resized and rearranged, with substantially denser figure layouts.

R1.justification: The private-randomness contribution is repositioned as attaining an established limit, with Yan et al. (2021) newly cited, rather than achieving a rate below the twice-distortion benchmark. Section 2 also credits Saldi et al. (2015) with the earlier perfect-perception coding theorem, revising v1's attribution to Theis and Wagner (2021). New polar-lattice and optimal-transport references support the revised proof.

T1.justification: v1 Theorem 4.6 claims achievability of Rp(D,0), below R(D/2,infinity). v2 Theorem 4.5 replaces this with optimality at R(D/2,infinity). Appendix D introduces explicit flatness-factor conditions, achievable-region bounds in Lemma D.5, revised Wasserstein arguments, a polar-lattice construction, and an extension to perfect perception. Proposition 3.3 is also generalized to scaled dithering.

improvement.justification: The decisive gain is the revised private-randomness argument: v1's below-limit claim and unqualified total-variation-to-Wasserstein step are replaced by explicit dither scaling, flatness-factor conditions, and moment-controlled Wasserstein bounds in Appendix D. This addresses important gaps in a central contribution. MNIST results and implementation disclosures add useful support. Denser figures and the unspecified empirical choice of s remain weaknesses, but do not outweigh the substantial improvement in theoretical justification.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same lattice-transform compression work. Their complete main texts, figures, equations, references, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison despite substantial revisions.

after.justification: Section 5 and Appendices C and E retain original compression experiments and statistical-distance estimates, and add MNIST results.

before.justification: Section 5 and Appendices B and D report original Gaussian, Physics, and Speech experiments, ablations, and empirical sliced-Wasserstein estimates.

results.title: Optimal Neural Compressors for the Rate-Distortion-Perception Tradeoff

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion move from competitive geolocalization performance to state-of-the-art claims across five datasets, explicitly including superiority over coordinate-space generative methods. This substantially broadens the performance claim while retaining SHDD, CS-UNet, latent diffusion, and spatial generalizability as the central contributions.

C2.justification: v2 explains the hybrid's poorer GWS15k performance through harmful gallery bias under spatial distribution mismatch, adding an applicability qualification. Section 5.3 also proposes a multiscale explanation for faster convergence. The earlier resolution, quadratic-dimensionality, and numerical-stability limitations remain in Appendix A.4 despite being shortened in the conclusion.

D1.justification: Appendix A.5 adds training and inference pseudocode, and v2 explicitly identifies image augmentation within the existing 16-sample ensemble. It adds operation timings and revises the training-degree summary from 15/23/31 to 23/47. Most optimizer settings, hardware information, and detailed operations were already documented.

E1.justification: Evaluation expands beyond Im2GPS3k to YFCC-26k, GWS15k, OSV-5M, and YFCC-4k. This adds street-view coverage and, particularly, the GWS15k scenario whose spatial distribution differs from MP16. MP16 remains the stated training dataset for the GeoCLIP-style evaluations.

E2.justification: v2 Table 2 adds evaluated comparisons with vMF, vMFMix, Diff R3, FM R3, and RFM S2, including a longer-trained RFM S2 variant. These introduce direct generative geolocalization comparators absent from v1. The original Im2GPS3k comparator set remains.

E3.justification: v2 introduces a separate generative-comparison setup and density/coverage metrics in Table 2. It also changes the reported DDPM sampling count from 100 to 200 and the main hybrid configuration from L=47 to L=23. These establish reported setting changes, without establishing which retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds a reverse-diffusion trajectory visualization in Appendix A.1, a brief augmentation/averaging check reporting GeoCLIP street accuracy falling from about 14% to below 10%, and component timing analysis. Existing degree, gallery, encoder/decoder, perturbation, loss, and network-width ablation results are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-training-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests, or run-to-run uncertainty. The 16 generated predictions are inference ensembles, not statistical replication of experiments.

E6.justification: v2 Tables 1–2 add extensive benchmark and distribution-quality results. The Im2GPS3k hybrid row also changes: street accuracy becomes 15.3 instead of 14.4, for example, but its degree changes from L=47 to L=23, preventing a same-setting gain interpretation. The standalone L=47 Im2GPS3k scores and existing generalization/ablation values remain unchanged.

M1.justification: The SHDD encoding, KL-divergence objective, mode-seeking decoder, frozen CLIP conditioning, and CS-UNet remain unchanged. LocDiff-H retains the earlier LocDiffusion+GeoCLIP procedure of restricting retrieval to 200 km neighborhoods. New pseudocode and augmentation descriptions do not establish a new underlying method.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related-work discussion, and experimental narrative undergo substantial rewriting. Preliminaries and parts of the encoding explanation are condensed, experiment subsections are reorganized, and appendix sections are inserted. The method name, author information, conference header, and citation style also change.

P2.justification: The main text changes from two columns to one, with extensive reflow and resizing. Table 1 becomes a three-dataset comparison, and v2 adds generative-comparison and operation-timing tables, a diffusion-step figure, and two algorithm displays. Existing figures and appendix results are retained and repositioned.

R1.justification: v2 makes Dufour et al.'s generative geolocalization work central to its positioning, contrasting latent multiscale diffusion with raw-coordinate diffusion and flow matching. Related work and the introduction are revised accordingly, with additional references including flow matching, SatCLIP, and GAIR. This substantially expands the relationship to relevant prior approaches.

T1.justification: The principal SHDD definitions, KL/Wasserstein argument, decoder equations, and spherical-harmonic formulas are retained. v2 Section 5.3 adds a limited asymptotic complexity argument claiming O(1) encoding time under parallel evaluation and O(d) space; it does not add a new correctness proof.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses an important evidence gap in v1: the latent-diffusion approach lacked direct comparisons with generative geolocalization alternatives and was evaluated on only one benchmark. Tables 1–2 substantially strengthen validation, including a spatially mismatched dataset that exposes the hybrid's limitations, while pseudocode improves inspectability. The gains outweigh the remaining weaknesses, although blanket superiority claims exceed the mixed results, notably the coverage comparisons in Table 2.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SHDD-based image geolocalization work, renamed from LocDiffusion to LocDiff. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison despite substantial reformatting.

after.justification: v2 retains original experimental results and adds evaluations on further datasets, comparisons with generative geolocalization methods, and additional computational measurements.

before.justification: v1 reports original geolocalization experiments, gallery-generalization tests, computational measurements, and appendix ablations on encodings, perturbations, losses, and network width.

results.title: LocDiff: Identifying Locations on Earth by Diffusing in the Hilbert Space

C1.justification: The central claims about collaboration, inverse-client sample complexity, and momentum mitigating heterogeneity remain. v2 adds an explicit third contribution claiming validation on real environmental monitoring data, with corresponding additions to the abstract and conclusion.

C2.justification: v2 substantially expands the explanation of conditional gradient bias, its relationship to step size and local computation, and differences from delayed-gradient approaches. It also interprets SCAFFOLD's behavior through client participation. New Appendix F discusses limitations of Markov modeling, unavailable tight Markovian lower bounds, and the difficulty of controlling mixing properties in real data.

D1.justification: Beyond retaining the synthetic-data recipe, v2 documents seasonality removal with statsmodels, feature removal, missing-value imputation, normalization, and virtual-client construction. It newly identifies Grid'5000 CPU models and states that reproduction instructions and MIT-licensed code accompany the supplemental material. The supplied PDFs establish these disclosures, but do not verify the external code package.

E1.justification: v2 adds PM2.5 prediction on the Beijing Multi-Site Air-Quality dataset, extending evaluation beyond synthetic two-state Markov regression. Synthetic coverage remains in Appendix E.3, but the independently restarted batch-stream scenario evaluated in v1 Appendix G is removed.

E2.justification: v1 experimentally compares only Minibatch SGD, Local SGD, and Local SGD-M. v2 adds SCAFFOLD to the pollution-data heterogeneity comparison in Figure 1 while retaining the original three algorithms. The additional methods in the theoretical comparison table are not experimentally evaluated.

E3.justification: The new pollution experiments introduce a 36-month training/12-month testing split, virtual clients with 6- or 12-month windows, nine input features, and new client-count, local-step, and learning-rate settings. Appendix E.2 additionally tests local step sizes 0.1/K and 0.01/K. These are new protocols, rather than evidence of same-setting improvements over v1.

E4.justification: v2 adds seasonality, autocorrelation, and feature-correlation diagnostics in Figures 3–6, plus a Local SGD step-size scaling analysis in Table 2. It removes v1's independent-versus-dependent batch analysis, the trajectory grids at mixing times 10 and 1000, and the 10-client portion of the mixing-time sweep. Selected synthetic sensitivity analyses remain.

E5.justification: v1 reports averages over 10 seeds and displays shaded bands without identifying their statistical meaning. v2 explicitly reports 95% confidence intervals in Appendix E.1–E.2 and provides mean-plus-interval entries in Table 2. The stated run count remains 10; an increase in runs is not established.

E6.justification: v2 adds pollution-data convergence results, including limited improvement from increasing K for Local SGD and SCAFFOLD under the reported settings. New Table 2 reports, for example, mean gradient norms of 0.00506 ± 0.00076 at K=10 and 0.00233 ± 0.00030 at K=100 with eta=0.1/K. Selected synthetic results are retained, while several v1 result grids and the batch-independence finding disappear.

M1.justification: The Minibatch SGD, Local SGD, and Local SGD-M update procedures remain unchanged. v2 clarifies stream indexing and corrects the minibatch summation in pseudocode; v1 already specifies that averaging operation in Appendix A's equations. Revised convergence assumptions do not introduce a new optimizer.

P1.justification: v2 substantially rewrites the Markov-process setup and discussion, reorganizes discussion around sampling, heterogeneity, and client count, and shifts the main experimental narrative to pollution data. The separate proof appendices are consolidated into Appendix D, with dedicated comparison, experimental, and limitations sections. Notation explanations, a contents list, and a conference checklist are added.

P2.justification: The main paper changes from two-column to single-column layout, and plots are rearranged into horizontal panels. Table 1 moves to Appendix C and gains method groups and an assumptions column; diagnostic figures and Table 2 are added. v1 Figures 1, 5, and 6(d–f) reappear as v2 Figures 7–9, while other synthetic displays are removed.

R1.justification: New Appendix C substantially expands positioning beyond v1's MAG and i.i.d. lower-bound comparison. It compares assumptions and rates across centralized methods, FedAvg-M, FedAvg-M-VR, FedLSA, SCAFFLSA, and FedHSA, and discusses their bias-control techniques. New references support the revised assumptions, heterogeneity discussion, and real-data experiments.

T1.justification: v1's main analysis assumes uniform ergodicity and uses mixing-time and transient total-variation terms. v2 introduces bounded transition-density Assumption 3.2, a conditional change-of-measure argument, and bounds involving C_infinity/nu_ps, substantially revising Theorems 4.5, 4.7, and 4.9 and their corollaries. Appendices B and D add supporting proofs and alternative bounds. Some restatements remain inconsistent: Theorem D.3 omits nu_ps, and Corollary D.7 retains the old tau expression.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the treatment of data dependence through an explicit history-conditioned error analysis under a newly stated density assumption. Pollution-data experiments with SCAFFOLD and a step-size control address v1's reliance on synthetic validation, while uncertainty reporting and substantive limitations improve transparency. Some synthetic robustness evidence is lost, and Theorem D.3 and Corollary D.7 contain inconsistent restatements, but these shortcomings do not outweigh the gains in justification and empirical relevance.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Streaming Federated Learning with Markovian Data by the same authors. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison despite substantial revisions.

after.justification: v2 Section 5 and Appendix E report original pollution-data experiments, step-size sensitivity results, data diagnostics, and retained synthetic experiments.

before.justification: v1 Section 5 and Appendix G report original synthetic Markovian regression experiments, including client-count, local-step, mixing-time, and batch-dependence comparisons.

results.title: Streaming Federated Learning with Markovian Data

C1.justification: V2 adds the explicit headline claim that heuristic generation solves more tasks overall than direct LLM planning, especially for non-reasoning models, and extends the Fast Downward superiority claim to V3. The central contribution of reusable domain-dependent heuristics outperforming traditional heuristics remains intact.

C2.justification: V2 adds interpretations concerning reasoning versus memorization, useful candidate diversity, and imperfect heuristic selection. Section 6 explicitly discusses dependence on PDDL, uncertain generalization, prompt dependence, and implementation constraints. Appendix B additionally explains heuristic behavior and failure mechanisms across six previously undescribed domains.

D1.justification: Appendices A, C, and D add extensive generation, end-to-end, and ablation prompt listings, including example heuristic code and planner structures; embedded PDDL files are abridged. V2 also documents domain parameter ranges, identifies V3 version 0324, specifies training-run memory limits, and supplies a code-and-experiment-data archive reference. These disclosures do not by themselves establish changes to existing experiments.

E1.justification: V2 retains the eight IPC domains and adds reusable-spanner dynamics, Blocksworld with randomly renamed symbols, and the new Rod-Rings domain. These extend evaluation to changed action semantics, obfuscated inputs, and a distinct planning domain.

E2.justification: Table 2 adds direct end-to-end planning with Gemini Flash, Flash Thinking, DeepSeek V3, and R1 as evaluated comparators. Table 3 additionally includes V3-generated heuristics in the Fast Downward comparison. The existing classical and learned heuristic baselines remain.

E3.justification: New protocols include one LLM call per test task with VAL validation, ablations evaluating all 25 candidates under five-minute limits, and additional o3 configurations. Appendix E measures expansions per second on jointly solved tasks, excluding preprocessing. The main selected-heuristic evaluation retains its 30-minute/8-GiB limits.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's candidate-count analysis, v2 adds eight prompt-component ablations, tests probing memorization through modified, obfuscated, and novel domains, and a cross-planner throughput analysis. These examine prompt dependence, generalization mechanisms, selection quality, and implementation efficiency.

E5.justification: Table 4 newly reports standard deviations of candidate performance and specifies exclusion of failed heuristics from average coverage. V1 reports averages without comparable dispersion reporting. This characterizes candidate variability; it does not establish repeated full-pipeline experiments or uncertainty estimates for the headline comparisons.

E6.justification: Table 2 replaces V3's total coverage of 283 with 343, changing its ranking; v2 specifies version 0324 while v1 leaves the version unspecified, so this is not an established same-configuration gain. R1's 373 and Pyperplan hFF's 243 remain unchanged. V2 adds direct-planning, ablation, robustness, o3, and throughput results, while removing the original per-model failure rates and detailed sampling curve.

M1.justification: Both versions generate candidate Python heuristics, evaluate them with GBFS, select by training coverage with an agile-score tie-breaker, and reuse the selected heuristic. The Blocksworld and Spanner code listings are unchanged. Expanded documentation and additional evaluated models do not establish a change to the proposed procedure.

P1.justification: The method exposition is substantially condensed, prompt and checklist material is reorganized into Appendix A, and existing heuristic explanations are consolidated in Appendix B. Experimental discussion is reordered, related work is tightened, and a dedicated limitations section and additional appendices substantially restructure the narrative.

P2.justification: V2 expands Tables 2 and 3, adds parameter-range, ablation, and throughput tables, and removes v1's cost/failure table and candidate-count figure. The plan-length/expansion plots are retained and renumbered. Appendix listings are reformatted and expanded, substantially changing the document's visual organization.

R1.justification: V2 adds discussion and citations for Tree of Thoughts, Algorithm of Thoughts/AoT+, planning formalization, and supporting theoretical background. It removes Ling et al.'s heuristic-discovery discussion and several broader planning references. The principal positioning relative to Tuisov, Katz, Silver, and FunSearch remains.

T1.justification: Appendix B adds limited theoretical assertions, including Miconic's 2-approximability, Sokoban's PSPACE-completeness, and the claim that the selected Sokoban heuristic cannot overestimate optimal plan length. The core planning assumptions and agile-score formula remain unchanged; no new proofs are supplied.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens v1's evidence with direct end-to-end baselines, component ablations, and altered/novel-domain tests. Expanded prompt documentation, code/data access information, and explicit limitations also improve reproducibility and critical assessment. These gains outweigh the removed failure-rate and sampling-curve detail, although the new tests provide suggestive rather than conclusive evidence for reasoning over memorization.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching relocated material.

after.justification: V2 retains original planning experiments and adds end-to-end LLM comparisons, prompt ablations, altered and novel domain tests, and runtime analysis.

before.justification: V1 reports original heuristic-generation experiments, candidate-count sensitivity analysis, and planning results on 720 test tasks across eight domains.

results.title: Classical Planning with LLM-Generated Heuristics: Challenging the State of the Art with Python Code

C1.justification: The central claim of faster asynchronous post-training with competitive or better performance remains. v2 narrows the abstract's categorical claim that on-policy algorithms are inherently incompatible with replay buffers to a lack of natural robustness to diversified replay data. It also foregrounds robustness as asynchrony increases and applicability through 7B models, without replacing the main contribution.

C2.justification: Beyond v1's exploration and replay-based explanations, v2 interprets the new ablations through KL regularization, reference resetting and task-dependent benefits of importance sampling. Appendix D discusses the stability/adherence tradeoff controlled by beta and reset frequency, explains differences from Kimi's reference policy, and identifies reward-hacking settings as an untested direction. These substantially expand the mechanism discussion and applicability qualifications.

D1.justification: v2 newly provides a code-repository link, PRIME-RL implementation information, TBA′ hyperparameters in Table 4, and detailed GRPO reproduction settings in Appendix E.1, including TRL 0.17.0, DeepSpeed ZeRO Stage 2 and 4×A100 80 GB hardware. The original TBA hyperparameter tables are largely retained and renumbered.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates GSM8K, TL;DR summarization and GPT-2/Llama red-teaming. v2 retains that coverage and adds MATH training with MATH-500 evaluation and generated Countdown problems for TBA′ (Section 6; Appendix C), substantially expanding reasoning-task coverage.

E2.justification: v2 adds an evaluated synchronous GRPO baseline on GSM8K, Dr. GRPO and IcePop comparisons on MATH/Countdown, and a Kimi-K2-style objective comparison on Countdown (Figures 1, 6, 10 and 11). These extend the actual comparator set beyond v1; CISPO's appearance in gradient comparisons alone is not counted as a separate evaluated baseline.

E3.justification: New TBA′ protocols use Qwen2.5-7B-Base and Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507, 2- and 10-step staleness, 400/500 training steps, and a 9,000/1,000 Countdown training/test split (Section 6; Appendix C; Table 4). v2 also expands PFT comparisons to asynchronous settings and tests K=20 versus 40 completions at fixed batch size on GSM8K. Original TBA settings are largely retained.

E4.justification: The original GSM8K and TL;DR ablations remain as Figures 12 and 14. v2 adds tests of disabling importance sampling or reference resetting, replacing clipping with masking, and robustness to increased staleness (Figures 6–10). Table 5 and Appendix E.1 additionally examine completion-count effects, GRPO training dynamics and unsuccessful asynchronous GRPO configurations.

E5.justification: Appendix B.3 newly specifies three runs per GPT-2 red-teaming configuration, where v1 only stated multiple runs. v2 also reports standard deviations for the completion-count ablation and displays separate Countdown replicates. Existing mean/standard-error reporting remains; the newly disclosed red-teaming count does not establish an increase in runs.

E6.justification: v2 newly reports GRPO's 49.05% GSM8K accuracy and the K=20/40 ablation accuracies of 54.61%/54.89%. Figures 6–11 add TBA′ results showing greater stability than Dr. GRPO/IcePop at 10-step staleness and similar Countdown performance to Kimi-K2-style training. Table 1 adds asynchronous baseline scores. The original 54.6% TBA headline result and relocated red-teaming table remain unchanged.

M1.justification: v2 retains buffer-based TBA and introduces TBA′ in PRIME-RL: fixed-staleness training without the original replay sampling, constant beta with periodic reference-policy resetting, and clipped importance sampling. Appendix D also evaluates an IcePop-masking variant. These additions change the update and data-use procedures, rather than merely documenting another implementation.

P1.justification: v2 revises the abstract and introduction, reorganizes the method overview around two implementations, combines metric/baseline paragraphs and subdivides the preliminaries. Appendix organization and discussion headings also change. Much of the retained experimental prose remains close to v1; the substantial scientific additions do not amount to a pervasive rewrite of existing text.

P2.justification: v2 adds Figures 6–11 and 13 and Tables 4–5, expands Table 1 into staleness blocks, and adds GRPO to Figure 1. The original red-teaming Table 2 moves to Appendix G as Table 6, while original ablation figures become Figures 12 and 14. NeurIPS formatting also changes typography, captions and page layout.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands positioning against recent asynchronous RL objectives and systems. Sections 2–3 and Appendix D distinguish near-on-policy approaches, connect GFlowNets with maximum-entropy RL/path consistency, and discuss ProRL-style resetting, Dr. GRPO, CISPO, IcePop and Kimi K1.5/K2. This adds substantive relationships and novelty qualifications beyond v1's related-work discussion.

T1.justification: v1 provides the TB/VarGrad objectives without the later gradient analysis. v2 adds Section 3.3, Appendix A's derivation, and Appendix D's formal gradient comparisons with Proximal RLOO, CISPO, Dr. GRPO and Kimi-K2-style objectives. It establishes the stated on-policy connection to mean-baseline REINFORCE with KL-regularized rewards and qualifies that connection off-policy.

improvement.justification: v1 demonstrates useful speedups but provides limited objective-level analysis and component isolation. v2 substantially strengthens that foundation through gradient derivations, controlled resetting/importance-sampling ablations, modern baseline comparisons and larger-model experiments, supported by additional implementation details. The Kimi comparison also usefully qualifies the method's positioning. Larger-model evidence concerns the new TBA′ variant, and uncertainty reporting remains uneven, but the gains in explanatory support and empirical scrutiny are substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same TBA research, and their text, equations, figures, tables and appendices support reliable comparison. Retained material can be matched across renumbering and relocation, including the original ablations and red-teaming table.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds original MATH/Countdown evaluations, GRPO benchmarking and component ablations in Section 6 and Appendices C–E.

before.justification: Section 5 and Appendices A–C report original TBA experiments on GSM8K, TL;DR summarization and automated red-teaming, including scaling and hyperparameter ablations.

results.title: Trajectory Balance with Asynchrony: Decoupling Exploration and Learning for Fast, Scalable LLM Post-Training

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the same central contributions: adapting frozen SAM2 through the token and three modules, improving VCOS with minimal prompts, transferring to CAD and preserving access to SAM2's original capabilities. Additional evidence and revised numerical gains do not redefine these main claims.

C2.justification: v3 newly explains why token interactions change SAM2 outputs despite frozen parameters and why disabling the additions restores original behavior (A.5 and A.9). It also discusses SAM2-Adapter comparison fairness, prototype behavior and explicit limitations involving shot changes and long occlusions (A.4, A.10-A.11), substantially extending v1's interpretation and applicability discussion.

D1.justification: Appendix A.1 newly documents eight-frame clips, 1024x1024 inputs, 256x256 targets, batch size four and mask resizing for memory encoding. v3 reports code availability rather than a future release. Conversely, v1's StepLR specification disappears; this is lost documentation, not evidence that the scheduler was removed.

E1.justification: Both versions use MoCA-Mask/MoCA-Mask-Pseudo, CAD and SUN-SEG-Easy/Hard for the same animal and polyp segmentation tasks. Additional experiments vary backbones, click budgets or evaluated frame subsets within this retained coverage.

E2.justification: v3 adds SAM2-FT, with its mask decoder fine-tuned, to all three prompt settings in Table 1. Appendix A.4/Table 10 additionally evaluates retrained SAM2-Adapter, previously only cited. These introduce important adaptation-specific controls; A.4 acknowledges that SAM2-Adapter uses different temporal and prompt settings.

E3.justification: Section 4.1 changes the reported training budget from 15 to 10 epochs, without establishing whether existing experiments were rerun. New protocols evaluate Hiera-B+/L, 2/3/5-click budgets, first-frame-only segmentation and runtime/FLOPs, including latency on a 106-frame video. Dataset splits and the seven segmentation metrics remain unchanged.

E4.justification: The original component, distance-metric and prototype-count ablations remain. v3 adds tests of logit averaging, first-frame performance, token count, sampling/clustering choices and click sensitivity, plus efficiency profiling, prototype-similarity maps and further qualitative cases (A.3, A.5-A.8 and A.11-A.12). These substantially expand investigation of design choices and behavior.

E5.justification: Appendix A.3 newly specifies random seed 42 for sampling click prompts; v1 gives no seed. Neither version reports repeated-run counts, error bars, confidence intervals or significance tests. v3 explicitly acknowledges the absence of statistical significance reporting in its checklist.

E6.justification: v3 adds substantial results for new comparisons, sensitivity tests, ablations and computational costs. Table 2 also revises existing Hiera-S entries: CamSAM2 box-prompt mDice/mIoU changes from 75.5/65.4 to 76.4/66.1. These are revised reported results, not established same-setting gains given the changed training-budget description. Original Hiera-T, CAD, SUN-SEG and Tables 5-7 values are retained.

M1.justification: The decamouflaged token, IOF, EOF, FPS plus one-iteration k-means in OPG, BCE/Dice objective and logit-averaging inference remain unchanged. Appendix explanations, including bypassing the added modules to recover SAM2, do not establish a revised VCOS algorithm.

P1.justification: The main narrative and much of the prose remain closely matched. v3 tightens explanatory and results paragraphs, moves training/inference from Section 3.6 into Section 4.1, updates author information and adds acknowledgments, appendix subsections and a checklist. Existing prose is locally revised rather than comprehensively rewritten.

P2.justification: v3 replaces the two-column layout with a single-column conference format, redraws Figure 1 and restructures Table 2 with backbones in adjacent columns. It also adds Tables 8-16 and Figures 5-9. These include new analyses and illustrations alongside redisplayed results, constituting substantial visual and layout changes.

R1.justification: v3 adds HQ-SAM as inspiration for the existing averaging strategy and explains its distinction from earlier SAM2 studies and SAM2-Adapter more explicitly (Section 2.3 and A.4-A.5). Most cited works and the broader positioning are retained; publication and bibliographic updates do not constitute new research coverage.

T1.justification: Equations (1)-(7), defining feature fusion, prototype generation and the training objective, are unchanged. Neither version provides theoretical results or proofs. The added mechanism discussions and empirical analyses introduce no substantive mathematical derivation.

improvement.justification: The fine-tuned SAM2 control addresses an important gap in v1's evidence for architectural benefits beyond task adaptation. New averaging, prototype and first-frame analyses, measured overhead, reproducibility details and explicit failure conditions substantially strengthen validation and transparency. The unexplained epoch revision, omitted scheduler detail and absent uncertainty estimates remain weaknesses, and the SAM2-Adapter comparison has unequal inputs. Nevertheless, the added controls and explanations provide a clear substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe CamSAM2, with matching architecture, equations and core experiments. Text, tables and figures support reliable comparison. v1 ends with references and has no appendix; v3 includes a readable appendix and conference checklist.

after.justification: v3 retains original empirical evaluations and adds baseline comparisons, sensitivity experiments, ablations, runtime measurements and qualitative analyses in its appendix.

before.justification: v1 reports original CamSAM2 evaluations on MoCA-Mask, CAD and SUN-SEG, qualitative comparisons and component ablations in Section 4.

results.title: CamSAM2: Segment Anything Accurately in Camouflaged Videos

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction revise headline speedups from 8.32×/3.51× to 7.98×/3.48× for GSM8K/MATH. The conclusion adds qualifications about a suitable pruning rate and sometimes preserving or improving accuracy. The central contributions remain completion pruning and dynamic allocation.

C2.justification: Section 5 newly explains that CPPO does not accelerate completion generation, limiting speedup when generation dominates, and identifies inference acceleration as complementary. It updates the model-scale limitation and future priorities. Appendix E also explains the smaller GSM8K accuracy improvement for the 7B model through its higher initial accuracy and limited remaining headroom.

D1.justification: Appendix B adds pseudocode specifying pruning-dependent batch and step counts and explains that implementation allocates questions before pruning to exploit parallel generation and prefix sharing. v2 also documents use of verl. These clarify reproducibility, while the principal hyperparameters, reward specifications, prompt templates and code-access link are retained.

E1.justification: Both versions train on GSM8K and MATH and evaluate on their test subsets plus AMC2023 and AIME2024. The added experiments vary models, frameworks and optimizers within this retained mathematical task coverage.

E2.justification: v1's principal comparison is against GRPO. v2 adds evaluated DAPO and DrGRPO comparisons, including their CPPO combinations, in Table 3, and REINFORCE++ and PPO without KL divergence in Table 11. This substantially broadens the competing optimization methods considered.

E3.justification: v2 adds experiments on verl, Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct on MATH, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct on GSM8K, and Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct on GSM8K. Table 11 also introduces a PPO comparison using group size 1 versus 16 for the other algorithms. These expand experimental configurations substantially; the existing decoding rules, metrics and principal hyperparameters remain.

E4.justification: The completion-count study, matched-question-batch comparison, pruning-metric ablation and component ablation retain their evidence. The reward curves and case studies are moved into Appendices H–J, with the same examples and findings. The added model and optimizer benchmark scores do not introduce a distinct diagnostic or stress test.

E5.justification: Tables 1–2 newly specify three independent training runs and report means and standard deviations for GSM8K/MATH accuracy, training time and CPPO speedup. v1 provides point estimates without run-count or uncertainty reporting. This materially strengthens statistical reporting, although the OOD columns and added comparison tables remain point estimates; v1's actual run count is unspecified.

E6.justification: Main-table point estimates are replaced by three-run summaries: for example, GSM8K CPPO accuracy at 87.5% pruning changes from 80.41% to 80.01±0.38%, and speedup at 93.75% changes from 8.32 to 7.98±0.23. Tables 3 and 8–11 add substantial results, including DAPO+CPPO retaining 78.01% accuracy with 1.78× speedup. These additions use distinct configurations and do not establish gains over v1 under identical conditions.

M1.justification: Section 4.3 and Table 3 add DAPO+CPPO and DrGRPO+CPPO training variants, extending the pruning approach to other policy optimizers. The original CPPO objective, absolute-advantage selection, reward functions and allocation strategy remain. Appendix B principally clarifies implementation rather than establishing a changed original algorithm.

P1.justification: The experimental narrative and appendix organization are substantially reworked: stability discussion, case studies and completion examples move from the main text into Appendices H–J; algorithm documentation receives Appendix B; and references move before the appendices. Experimental subsections are reorganized and limitations rewritten, although much introductory and methodological prose is retained.

P2.justification: v2 adds five experimental tables and an algorithm display, reformats Tables 1–2 for uncertainty reporting, and relocates several existing displays. v1's two-panel reward Figure 4 becomes enlarged separate Figures 5–6 in the appendix, while its completion examples and case tables are redistributed. These are substantial display and layout changes.

R1.justification: v2 adds references for DAPO, DrGRPO, REINFORCE++, HybridFlow/verl, speculative sampling and EAGLE. These support targeted positioning of CPPO as compatible with other optimizers and complementary to inference acceleration. The existing related-work narrative is largely unchanged.

T1.justification: The explanation following Eq. (7) corrects the positive-advantage clipping condition from probability ratio < 1+epsilon to > 1+epsilon. This repairs a mathematical condition; the objectives, gradient derivation and reward definitions otherwise remain substantively unchanged.

improvement.justification: v1 leaves variability in its central speed–accuracy comparisons unreported and evaluates a narrow optimizer/model selection. v2's three-run summaries in Tables 1–2 and broader comparisons in Tables 3 and 8–11 substantially improve the evidence for reliability and applicability. Appendix B clarifies implementation, and Section 5 identifies the generation-time bottleneck. Uncertainty reporting remains incomplete for supplementary comparisons, but the revision materially strengthens empirical support and qualification of the claims.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe CPPO. All 16 pages of v1 and 19 pages of v2, including equations, figures, tables and appendices, are readable and support matching content across the reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds three-run summaries, other RL algorithm comparisons, and evaluations with larger and different model backbones.

before.justification: v1 reports original CPPO-versus-GRPO accuracy and training-time measurements, pruning and component ablations, training curves and generated examples.

results.title: CPPO: Accelerating the Training of Group Relative Policy Optimization-Based Reasoning Models

C1.justification: The central joint-training and zero-shot-generalization claims remain. V2 extends the contribution to comparison-specific RL achieving superior comparison performance from 5,000 preference pairs; the abstract and conclusion now encompass this trained comparison capability.

C2.justification: V2 adds a proposed explanation linking weak distortion sensitivity to semantic pretraining, interprets the threshold sweep as reduced dependence on tuning, and explicitly identifies broader AI-generated-image and video applications as limitations. These supplement the retained interpretations of multitask benefits and generalization.

D1.justification: V2 specifies the Instruct checkpoint, KL weight of 0.001, and learning-rate endpoint of 10^-9; these are additional disclosures, not established changes to existing experiments. Appendix C documents the comparison-training recipe and approximately 20-hour runtime on 16 A100 GPUs. The explicit repository address is replaced by an unspecified promise to release code and models.

E1.justification: V2 adds DiffIQA preference pairs for comparison training and SRIQA-Bench, also called SRBench, for systematic evaluation of regression-based and generative super-resolution outputs against imperfect references. This substantially extends v1's qualitative comparison coverage. The seven scoring datasets and DQ-495K remain; TID2013 is mentioned as A-FINE training data, not Q-Insight training data.

E2.justification: The score-regression comparison removes HyperIQA and DBCNN from v1 Table 2 when it becomes v2 Table 1. New Table 5 compares Q-Insight with PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS, A-FINE, and DepictQA on reference-based comparison. AgenticIR remains the degradation comparator.

E3.justification: V2 introduces comparison training on 5,000 preference pairs for eight epochs with batch size 32. Its new evaluation uses 100 low-resolution references with ten SR outputs each, reporting regression-specific, generation-specific, and overall ranking accuracy plus correlations. Original scoring/degradation splits and metrics remain unchanged.

E4.justification: V2 supplements the retained multitask ablations with a focused reward-threshold sweep from 0.15 to 0.50 in Table B and four comparison case studies in Figures B–E. Figure A is the relocated v1 Figure 4, not a new multitask analysis.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated evaluation runs, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. V2's benchmark annotator counts describe dataset annotation rather than uncertainty estimation for the reported model results.

E6.justification: Retained scoring, degradation, and multitask-ablation values are unchanged, while HyperIQA/DBCNN entries disappear. New SRBench overall accuracies are 75.51% for zero-shot and 82.80% for trained Q-Insight, versus 62.96% for DepictQA and 82.40% for A-FINE. A-FINE still leads generation-specific accuracy. V2 also adds threshold results and corrects the stated correlation improvement from approximately 0.2 to 0.02.

M1.justification: V2 adds a comparison-specific RL adaptation with correctness and format rewards, defined in Appendix C, and an Image A/Image B/Similar output. V1 uses the model only zero-shot for comparison. This extends the procedure while retaining the core architecture and scoring/degradation components.

P1.justification: V2 rewrites and expands reward explanations, retitles Section 4.5, and organizes prompts and supplementary experiments into Appendices A–C. The introduction's argument, main section sequence, and much of the prose remain intact, making this a targeted restructuring rather than a wholesale rewrite.

P2.justification: Experimental displays expand substantially through the new comparison Table 5, threshold Table B, and Figures B–E. The prompt table moves from Table 1 to expanded Table A, the qualitative ablation moves from Figure 4 to Figure A, and existing result tables and figures are rearranged. The shortened scoring table also removes two method rows.
