T1.justification: V1's Theorem 3.3 on unbiased, consistent empirical-loss estimation and Corollary 3.4 for variable group sizes are removed, including their supporting argument. The uniqueness theorem and proof survive, with the proof relocated to Appendix B; v1's sampling-support Corollary 3.2 becomes v3's Theorem 3.2. Thus the estimator guarantees are genuinely lost, while the central optimality results remain.

improvement.justification: V1's practical stability and versatility claims lacked original experimental support. V3 adds multi-task comparisons, mechanism ablations, ten-seed variability, and implementation/resource details, substantially improving evidential support and reproducibility. These gains outweigh the loss of the estimator theorem and corollary, although the retained uniqueness result still does not establish every claimed optimization-convergence guarantee.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe GVPO and retain matching central objectives, derivations, and optimal-policy results. All pages, equations, figures, tables, and v3 appendices are readable. V1 has no appendices; its absence of experiments is established by inspection.

after.justification: V3 reports original mathematical-reasoning experiments, ablations, repeated-seed evaluations, and summarization experiments including human evaluations in Appendix C.

before.justification: V1 presents theoretical derivations and comparisons with prior methods, but no original experimental, simulation, or data-analysis results.

results.title: GVPO: Group Variance Policy Optimization for Large Language Model Post-Training

C1.justification: The central claim that one example can match training on thousands, with the same headline scores, remains. v3 narrows effectiveness from 'nearly all' examples to 'many', explicitly claims gains beyond format correction, and qualifies entropy-only improvements as weaker than the format-reward baseline. The conclusion also adds an anti-overfitting interpretation.

C2.justification: v3 substantially revises interpretation by attributing much improvement to format correction while identifying residual advantages over that control. It adds explanations involving prompt complexity and occasional errors sustaining policy signals. Appendix D.1 explicitly states that one-shot RLVR does not save computation and that the selected example need not transfer optimally across models.

D1.justification: Most learning rates, loss weights, hardware information, precision discussion, and resource links are retained or relocated. v3 adds concrete details such as the dataloader's drop_last requirement, the format-reward criterion, and the numerical perturbation procedure for corrupting integer and fractional labels.

E1.justification: The six mathematical benchmarks and ARC-Easy/Challenge remain unchanged. Training scenarios expand modestly: beyond v1's individual incorrect-label tests, v3 examines widespread random-label corruption and a calculation-only version of the multistep training problem (Appendices C.2.4–C.2.5). These extend conditions within the existing mathematical domain.

E2.justification: v3 adds format-reward RLVR to the principal Qwen comparisons, in-context learning with π1 and official Qwen exemplars (Table 16), and a DeepScaleR model trained on 40k examples (Table 12). These introduce substantial evaluated alternatives beyond v1's existing base-model, full-set RLVR, and loss-component comparisons.

E3.justification: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B evaluation changes from an 8k-token limit to reported 8k and 32k settings, with revised decoding settings in v3 Appendix B.5. v3 also evaluates two additional Qwen model configurations and introduces QwQ-32B correctness judging and pass@8 evaluation, distinct from the retained average-pass@1 metrics.

E4.justification: Beyond retained loss and label ablations, v3 adds extensive format-confounding checks, dataset-wide label-noise robustness, prompt-complexity ablation, test-response-length analysis, pass@8 trajectories, and policy-loss dynamics. These test substantial new explanatory questions. The earlier distilled-model training curves in v1 Figures 6 and 12 are removed.

E5.justification: For distilled-model evaluation, v3 Appendix B.5 specifies avg@16 for MATH500, Minerva Math, and OlympiadBench and avg@64 for AIME/AMC, replacing v1's one/eight-sample evaluation defaults. This changes evaluation replication, not documented training-seed replication. Neither version reports confidence intervals or variability across independent training runs.

E6.justification: Headline Qwen results, ARC scores, and existing loss-ablation values are retained, but substantial results are added. For example, v3 reports a format-reward baseline of 65.0% on MATH500 and 28.7% average (Table 8), plus new model, prompting, robustness, and pass@8 results. Distilled-model scores are replaced under revised evaluation conditions, not improved under an unchanged protocol.

M1.justification: The historical-variance selector, example duplication, outcome-reward training, and GRPO/PPO procedures remain unchanged. The loss definitions are retained from v1 Appendix A.1 in v3 Appendix B.1. Format-only rewards and in-context learning are added controls, not replacements for the proposed procedure.

P1.justification: v3 extensively condenses and rewrites the main experimental narrative, moves related work and extended discussion into appendices, separates detailed training/evaluation settings, and adds a contents section and a more structured analysis appendix. These are substantial organizational changes beyond adding experiments or renumbering sections.

P2.justification: v1's Figure 2 bar chart becomes v3 Table 8, the π13 example moves from Table 2 to appendix Table 21, and the entropy-results display is condensed with full results retained separately. v3 also adds format-baseline curves, numerous analysis tables and plots, and an evaluation-length comparison, while removing the distilled-model training curves.

R1.justification: The positioning against LIMR and concurrent four-example RLVR remains. v3 adds Absolute Zero to discussion of minimal-supervision RLVR and introduces references supporting LLM judging, in-context learning, label-noise robustness, and exploration. EMPO and TTRL were already cited in v1; their expanded positioning is not a newly added citation.

T1.justification: The historical-variance definitions and GRPO, advantage, KL, and entropy equations remain mathematically unchanged. v3 Appendix D.3 adds an informal explanation for persistent policy signals after near-saturation, but no new formal assumptions, derivations, theorems, or proofs.

improvement.justification: v1 did not adequately separate its large accuracy gains from output-format correction. v3's format-reward controls, in-context comparisons, and format-insensitive judging substantially address this central confound while demonstrating remaining advantages (Tables 14–16). Narrower generality claims and explicit computational limitations further improve calibration. Some distilled-model trajectory evidence is lost, and training-run uncertainty remains unreported, but the central empirical claim now has a substantially stronger evidential basis.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same one-shot RLVR study. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison despite substantial reorganization.

after.justification: v3 retains original experiments and adds format-reward comparisons, in-context learning evaluations, label-noise experiments, prompt ablations, and other original analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original RLVR experiments across mathematical benchmarks and ARC, including comparisons across models, training examples, algorithms, and loss ablations.

results.title: Reinforcement Learning for Reasoning in Large Language Models with One Training Example

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the dual-level reasoning contribution, joint optimization claim, and headline 13%/19% benchmark improvements. Revised contribution wording and additional supporting evaluations do not materially redefine these claims.

C2.justification: Appendix B.2 adds explanations for zero-shot planning failures: omitted objects and plans poorly matched to generation capabilities. Appendix C newly discusses obstacles to video extension, including reward design, suitable unified models, and GRPO computational costs. Existing interpretations of planning, diversity, and ensemble rewards are retained.

D1.justification: Appendices B.3–B.4 substantially expand reproducibility information: eight graduate raters, visual-appeal-only ranking instructions, eight H800 GPUs, approximately 16 hours of training, and Table 7's training steps, batch/group sizes, accumulation, guidance scale, gradient clipping, and resolution. These are newly documented details; the code address remains unchanged.

E1.justification: Appendix A and Tables 5–6 add GenAI-Bench and TIIF-Bench Testmini to the retained benchmarks. Coverage expands to professional designer prompts, counting, comparison, logical conditions, and fine-grained instruction following involving style and text rendering. Training-data coverage is unchanged.

E2.justification: Tables 5–6 introduce evaluated comparators absent from v1's comparisons, including Midjourney v6, LWM, Liquid, UniTok, Mogao-7B, LlamaGen, LightGen, and Infinity. Figures 9–12 also add Janus-Pro with zero-shot semantic-level CoT. Comparator membership in Tables 1–4 remains unchanged.

E3.justification: Added evaluations introduce TIIF-Bench Testmini with short/long-prompt reporting, GenAI-Bench basic/advanced aggregates, and a control applying T2I-R1's generation pipeline to unmodified Janus-Pro. Existing experimental settings are retained; newly disclosed training parameters and participant counts do not establish changes to those experiments.

E4.justification: Appendix B.2 and Figures 9–12 add a focused qualitative analysis of whether zero-shot semantic planning suffices without BiCoT-GRPO training. Figures 8 and 13–14 extend visual ablation and diversity examples. The quantitative reward and CoT ablations remain unchanged.

E5.justification: Neither version reports evaluation confidence intervals, error bars, significance tests, or uncertainty across training runs. The ten-images-per-prompt Vendi-score procedure already appears in v1 and is retained. Additional human-study participant information does not introduce uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: Tables 1–4 retain their numerical results. New Table 5 reports T2I-R1 GenAI-Bench basic/advanced overall scores of 0.88/0.73 versus Janus-Pro's 0.84/0.65. New Table 6 reports TIIF-Bench short/long overall scores of 68.59/67.19 versus 66.50/65.02. These are added evaluations, not improvements over v1 under retained settings.

M1.justification: The semantic-then-token generation pipeline, joint BiCoT-GRPO objective, Janus-Pro backbone, and reward ensemble are unchanged. The added zero-shot pipeline is an experimental comparator, not a revision to T2I-R1.

P1.justification: The experimental narrative is substantially reorganized: setup moves from Section 4.1 to Appendix A, and detailed ablation and human-study explanations move to Appendix B while the main discussion is condensed. Appendices organize results, implementation information, and limitations. Local terminology edits also distinguish detector D from ORM O.

P2.justification: Figure 5 is reformatted, v1 Figure 6 is split across v2 Figures 6–7, and existing chameleon examples move to Figure 8. New Tables 5–7 and additional qualitative displays, especially Figures 9–14, substantially expand the visual presentation. Tables 1–4 preserve their numerical content.

R1.justification: v2 adds references supporting the new benchmarks and comparators, including GenAI-Bench, TIIF-Bench, Mogao, UniTok, and LightGen. The related-work narrative and novelty positioning remain substantially unchanged. Citation renumbering and duplicate-reference adjustments do not constitute additional research-positioning changes.

T1.justification: The CoT definitions, GRPO objective, probability ratios, and reward equations retain their mathematical content. Equation numbering and placement change, but no substantive definitions, derivations, assumptions, or proofs are added.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses v1's sparse reproducibility documentation and limited evaluation coverage through Table 7, compute and human-study details, and two additional benchmarks. The same-pipeline zero-shot control also helps assess the contribution of training beyond prompt planning. That control remains qualitative, statistical uncertainty remains absent, and the GRPO equation reference becomes incorrect, but these limitations do not outweigh the substantial gains in documentation and empirical scrutiny.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe T2I-R1 and BiCoT-GRPO. Their text, equations, tables, and figures support reliable comparison. v1 ends with references; v2 includes readable Appendices A–C and additional visualizations.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds GenAI-Bench, TIIF-Bench Testmini, and qualitative zero-shot semantic-CoT comparisons.

before.justification: v1 reports original T2I-CompBench and WISE evaluations, reward and CoT ablations, a human study, and image-diversity results.

results.title: T2I-R1: Reinforcing Image Generation with Collaborative Semantic-level and Token-level CoT

C1.justification: The Poisson framework and exact likelihood identity remain central, but v4 expands the main claims to synthetic distribution recovery, robustness across distribution families, and competitive generation quality. v1 foregrounded up-to-80% NLL reductions and faster convergence on images/music. The novelty framing is also qualified: v4 Appendix H explicitly acknowledges that LTJ uses the same Poisson–Bregman loss form, emphasizing its different likelihood connection.

C2.justification: Beyond the proof-of-concept qualification already in v1, v4 explicitly discusses limited training, fixed logistic parameters, low-SNR image denoising instead of generation from pure noise, and untested conditional/OOD settings (Sections 5.4 and 6). It distinguishes the exact identity from the learned-denoiser bound and discusses continuous-NLL incompatibility and failures on skewed Beta distributions (Section 4 and Appendix C.4).

D1.justification: Appendices B–C add substantial reproducibility information: synthetic network/optimizer settings, density-estimation procedures, evaluation sample counts, and the MIDI-to-audio pipeline with spectrogram parameters. v4 also adds an implementation link. However, its first-page availability statement conflicts with the checklist's planned future release, so actual code availability is unresolved from the PDFs.

E1.justification: Beyond the retained CIFAR-10 and Lakh MIDI coverage, v4 evaluates six synthetic count distributions, eight non-negative continuous distributions, independent bivariate extensions, and two correlated count models (Section 5.1 and Appendix C). These substantially expand distributional coverage and evaluation of joint dependencies. Figure 3 also adds a NYC Taxi distribution example.

E2.justification: v1's quantitative comparisons center on Gaussian DDPM/IDDPM, ITDiff, and noise/loss cross-training variants. v4 adds evaluated LTJ and D3PM comparators in image/music quality Tables 3–4, and LTJ in synthetic Tables 1 and 7–9. Their discussion or citation in v1 did not constitute these experimental comparisons.

E3.justification: Reported real-data training changes from 50 to 600 epochs, and log-SNR sampling from 1,000 to 100 values (v1 Section 6.1/Appendix E; v4 Appendix B.1). New protocols include synthetic WD and empirical-PMF NLL, rest-excluded music evaluation, and image/audio quality metrics, with image quality assessed through low-SNR denoising. These reported settings do not establish that retained results were rerun. The 1,024-note music description already appeared in v1 Appendix E.1.

E4.justification: The original cross-training and denoising analyses remain. v4 adds the music likelihood comparison excluding rests, examples examining Monte Carlo approximation error, and piano-roll/pitch-distribution diagnostics discussing structure, outliers, and sparse regions (Table 2b, Section 4, Appendix B.5.1). Appendix C.5 additionally tests recovery of dependent count distributions.

E5.justification: v1 does not specify repeated-run evaluation or define uncertainty estimates. v4 reports five-run synthetic evaluations, standard-deviation reporting, and ten-resample bootstrap uncertainty for PMF/PDF estimates (Appendices C.2–C.5 and checklist item 7). These are newly documented statistical practices, not evidence of an increase over a known v1 run count.

E6.justification: The original CIFAR and full-data music likelihood entries are retained, but extensive new results appear. Rest-excluded music NLL is 1.41 for Gaussian+MSE versus 0.23 for ItDPDM (Table 2b). New PoissMix WD is 0.99 for ItDPDM versus 3.76 for DDPM and 1.21 for LTJ (Table 1). Rankings are mixed: Table 3 reports music FAD of 0.64 for ItDPDM versus 0.61 for D3PM. These are added comparisons, not same-setting improvements over v1 scores.

M1.justification: The defining Poisson corruption, PRL, observation normalization, and iterative sampling procedure are retained. v4 adds a concrete timestep-conditioned, three-layer ConditionalMLP denoiser for synthetic experiments (Section 5.1 and Appendix C.2), extending the architecture instantiations beyond v1's image and music networks without replacing the core framework.

P1.justification: The main narrative is extensively rewritten and reorganized. v1's separate formulation/framework sections are consolidated, numerical and experimental details move into reorganized appendices, and existing pseudocode moves into the main text. Dedicated limitations, broader-impact, and checklist sections are added. The changes substantially alter exposition and navigation independently of the new experiments.

P2.justification: The main text switches from two columns to one. v4 redraws the diffusion taxonomy, replaces the image-sample grid, combines the original likelihood tables into Table 2, and assembles the original loss/convergence plots into Figure 7. Readable typeset algorithms replace appendix screenshots, while new distribution plots, piano rolls, histograms, and comparison tables substantially expand the visual presentation.

R1.justification: The short diffusion overview expands into substantive positioning against Blackout Diffusion, Beta Diffusion, SEDD, continuous-time discrete score models, blurring diffusion, and edge-preserving diffusion (Section 7 and Appendix K). Appendix H/Table 10 adds an extensive LTJ comparison and acknowledges the shared loss form. This changes research positioning beyond citation-format or bibliographic updates.

T1.justification: v4 Appendix F substantially repairs v1 Appendix C's central KL-derivative proof by including differentiation of the probability weights and proving a Poisson–Stein identity. Equation 19 restores the e^alpha Jacobian missing from v1's log-SNR expression. v4 also adds the converse proof for the Gamma-prior characterization and an explicit vector-channel extension. Most existing tail-bound and continuous-time derivations are retained.

improvement.justification: v4 addresses important weaknesses in v1 through direct comparisons with discrete competitors, systematic distribution-level evaluation with uncertainty, explicit generation-quality limitations, and repair of the central pointwise KL derivation. These substantially strengthen the paper's support and assessability. Mathematical consistency remains incomplete: Equation 19's Jacobian is absent from Algorithm 1/Appendix A.2, and Table 10 reverses PRL's arguments relative to Equation 5. Those limitations qualify, but do not outweigh, the substantial gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ItDPDM research and contain readable main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices. Existing material can be matched across the substantial reorganization; no material reading gaps prevent comparison.

after.justification: v4 retains original empirical results and adds synthetic-distribution experiments, multivariate evaluations, image/music quality measurements, and qualitative music analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original CIFAR-10 and Lakh MIDI experiments, including likelihood measurements, cross-training comparisons, convergence curves, and denoising examples.

results.title: ItDPDM: Information-Theoretic Discrete Poisson Diffusion Model

C1.justification: The introduction's first contribution narrows its stated target from both verbosity and likelihood displacement to likelihood displacement. v2 explicitly says ComPO was not specifically designed to address verbosity, while retaining the empirical claim of benefits for both issues. The principal algorithmic and convergence contributions remain.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations of the perturbation and clipping tradeoffs, discusses difficulties in replacing the hard data threshold with confidence-based interpolation, and develops the applicability argument for refining existing aligned checkpoints. The limitations concerning offline learning, helpfulness-focused evaluation, and full-model perturbation are substantially retained.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code-access pointer alongside the existing model-release information. Appendix D newly reports approximately four hours of additional ComPO training and 12 minutes for pair division, plus hardware information for the memory comparison. Existing dataset links, checkpoint sources, and default settings remain.

E1.justification: Both versions use UltraFeedback for preference alignment and evaluate on AlpacaEval 2, Arena-Hard, and MT-Bench. The added studies remain within this coverage; no distinct data population, domain, or task is documented.

E2.justification: The benchmark comparators DPO, DPOclean, and SimPO remain. However, Section 4.3 and Appendix D newly include DPO and SimPO in the memory comparison, reporting 77 GB and 69 GB on H100 GPUs against approximately 23 GB for ComPO on A40 GPUs. v1's resource analysis reported ComPO measurements alone.

E3.justification: New experiments vary perturbations from 800 to 5400, one versus three perturbed layers, gradient thresholds, and 100 versus 300 noisy pairs. Table 10 compares ordinary-DPO and DPOclean initialization. The added Arena-Hard comparisons use GPT-4.1 judging rather than the original GPT-4 Turbo protocol. Existing benchmark settings are retained.

E4.justification: v2 adds controlled performance analyses of perturbation count, layer coverage, gradient clipping, and noisy-pair count in Tables 4–7, plus the initialization comparison in Table 10. These substantially expand validation of the practical heuristics beyond v1's sparsity plot, oracle-feedback robustness analysis, and qualitative examples, which are retained.

E5.justification: v1 already reports five-run means and standard deviations, best-of-five results, three likelihood trials, and eight-run oracle-feedback statistics. v2 retains these practices and applies the existing mean/standard-deviation reporting to added experiments. No new uncertainty-estimation procedure or increase in the original run counts is documented.

E6.justification: The original main and appendix table results are retained, while Tables 4–7 and 10 add substantial results. For example, Table 6 reports AlpacaEval LC of 23.42 ± 1.03 without clipping versus 25.91 ± 0.95 at lambda_g = 0.00022. Resource measurements are also added. New Arena-Hard scores use a different judge and are not same-setting revisions of earlier scores.

M1.justification: Section 4.2 adds a multi-layer adaptation that perturbs the MLPs in layers 30–31 alongside the output layer, extending v1's output-only practical implementation. The comparison oracle, gradient estimator, clipping and update rules, and Algorithms 1–2 remain unchanged.

P1.justification: v2 makes localized revisions to the abstract, introduction, and limitations, adds Section 4.2, and expands and renames the efficiency subsection. Author and publication-header text also change. Most of the existing exposition and overall organization are retained.

P2.justification: Four new main-text tables and Appendix Table 10 substantially expand the result displays. Existing tables are resized or repositioned, Table 3 moves upward, and Figure 2 is reduced and regrouped with appendix statistics. The two figures' plotted content and the three qualitative examples are retained.

R1.justification: Appendix B adds a focused discussion of learning from noisy preferences and compatibility with conditional DPO. Four references are added, covering preference variance, margin matching, Cal-DPO, and reward-augmented data. The established positioning relative to DPO and comparison-based optimization remains.

T1.justification: Section 2.1 drops the explicit beta > 0 condition from the background DPO loss description. This is a limited omission of a stated mathematical condition; the comparison-oracle definitions, Theorem 3.1, and Appendix C's propositions, lemmas, and proofs remain unchanged.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses an important validation gap in the practical method: Tables 4–7 directly test clipping, perturbation budgets, layer restriction, and training-data scaling, while Table 10 tests whether clean-only DPO initialization is necessary. These controls substantially strengthen the evidence behind the practical design choices. Code-access and runtime information also improve reproducibility. The gains remain bounded by predominantly Mistral-based additions and by changed judges or hardware in some comparisons.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe ComPO, with readable main text, equations, figures, tables, and Appendices A–E. The retained material can be matched reliably despite additions, renumbering, and layout changes.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds perturbation, clipping, layer, training-size, and DPO-initialization experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original LLM alignment experiments, benchmark scores, likelihood measurements, computational measurements, repeated-run results, and qualitative examples in Section 4 and Appendix E.

results.title: ComPO: Preference Alignment via Comparison Oracles

C1.justification: The stated contribution now explicitly includes adapting MR-MTL alongside Ditto, and the introduction specifies cross-silo pFL as the target setting. The central claim that adaptive latent-space constraints help particularly under feature heterogeneity is retained.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive explanations of why Synthetic data can disadvantage weight penalties, why feature and weight constraints may complement each other, and why constraining additional layers may hinder learning. Section 5.1 and Appendices D–H expand communication, privacy, computational, applicability, and theoretical limitations, including the MR-MTL failure on Fed-ISIC2019. Several mechanism explanations are explicitly conjectural.

D1.justification: Appendix D newly identifies the qpth solver and the deep-kernel network's four linear layers with hidden dimension 50. Appendix F and Table 5 document MR-MTL tuning and selected hyperparameters. The under-five-minute Synthetic runtime statement changes from data generation to training all methods. The code-access link and existing hardware disclosures remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same CIFAR-10 heterogeneity settings, two Synthetic settings, Fed-ISIC2019, and 50-class, three-channel RxRx1. The new MR-MTL experiments reuse this coverage without introducing another task, population, or input scenario.

E2.justification: Previously cited but unevaluated MR-MTL becomes a baseline for its MK-MMD20 and MMD-D extensions in Table 4. Existing comparators are retained. Table 1 also displays Ditto directly using scores already reported in v1 Table 2.

E3.justification: Appendix F adds MR-MTL-specific hyperparameter searches while retaining the existing models, training schedules, and checkpointing. Appendix B.4 changes the stated RxRx1 learning rate from 0.001 to 0.0001, matching Table 3 in both versions. This corrects the reported setting without establishing that experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: The penalty-weight sensitivity, constraint-depth ablation, and optimized-versus-fixed-kernel analyses retain identical plotted results in Figures 2–3. The MR-MTL appendix adds benchmark comparisons, without a new ablation, robustness test, or error analysis.

E5.justification: v1 reports three-run means without dispersion. v2 newly supplies standard deviations for the principal Ditto/MMD comparisons in Table 6 and the MR-MTL results in Table 4. The original three runs and seeds remain unchanged, with seed information moved to Appendix B; no significance tests are added.

E6.justification: Table 4 adds MR-MTL and extension results across all seven dataset settings. For example, RxRx1 accuracy is 64.065 for MR-MTL versus 66.673 with MMD-D, whereas Fed-ISIC2019 decreases from 70.628 to 70.366. These are newly reported comparisons, not improvements over v1 scores. Original accuracy means in Tables 1–2 and plotted results in Figures 2–3 are unchanged.

M1.justification: Appendix F introduces an implemented MR-MTL adaptation using the MMD penalties. Unlike Ditto, it constrains local models against their aggregate without separately training global models. The original Ditto algorithm, MMD objectives, and kernel-update procedures remain unchanged.

P1.justification: The introduction and related-work narrative are revised, explanations are clarified, and the existing constraint-interaction discussion receives its own subsection. The title expands FL to Federated Learning, and author information changes. The main section sequence and much existing prose remain intact; most added length documents new substantive content.

P2.justification: New Tables 4–6 present MR-MTL results, its hyperparameters, and a consolidated uncertainty display for the original results. Table 1 gains a Ditto column and revised ranking emphasis. Figures 1–3 retain their visual content, with placement, sizing, and caption adjustments.

R1.justification: Section 2 adds substantive comparisons with FedProto and earlier fixed-MMD FL methods, including FedMMD. New Appendix E positions the approach relative to split-model methods and other pFL families, including FedPer, FedRep, APFL, FedBN, HypCluster, and FedPop. This substantially expands novelty and applicability positioning.

T1.justification: Appendix D.1 adds asymptotic runtime derivations for Ditto and both MMD extensions, assuming one constrained layer and kernel optimization every local step. Existing mathematical definitions and objectives remain unchanged. Appendix H sketches a possible theoretical setting but supplies no new convergence or optimality proof.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens two weaknesses of v1: transfer beyond Ditto was untested, and principal comparisons lacked uncertainty reporting. MR-MTL experiments, including negative findings, and standard deviations make the evidence more informative, while implementation disclosures and closer prior-work comparisons improve reproducibility and positioning. The new complexity analysis is internally inconsistent about latent-space versus kernel-weight dimensions, but this localized flaw does not outweigh the empirical and reporting gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same adaptive MMD-based personalized federated learning work. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable matching across versions.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds original MR-MTL experiments in Appendix F, Table 4.

before.justification: v1 reports original experiments on CIFAR-10, Synthetic, Fed-ISIC2019, and RxRx1, including performance results in Tables 1–2 and ablations in Figures 2–3.

results.title: Adaptive Latent-Space Constraints in Personalized Federated Learning

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the central claims: fully unsupervised zero-shot tabular embeddings, no target-dataset fine-tuning, competitive clustering, and fast inference. The added experiments do not redefine these headline contributions.

C2.justification: V2 adds interpretations concerning complementary prior components, categorical-data sensitivity, robustness, and possible prior overfitting at larger token dimensions or with TabICL. It also explains the suitability of k-means and acknowledges that systematic investigation of genuine failure cases remains open. Section 2.2 adds a broader generalization assurance based on the new theorem.

D1.justification: Section 3.1 clarifies the absence of label embeddings, a query set, and an additional MLP decoder. Appendix E adds baseline repositories and specifies averaging TabPFN's per-column embeddings and following SCARF's example procedure; Appendix G provides new experiment recipes. Section 3.3 also drops v1's explicit 'without regularization' qualifier without documenting a calibration rerun.

E1.justification: The same 34 OpenML and two sets of 20 synthetic datasets are retained. Appendix G adds noisy and outlier-contaminated inputs plus four constructed scenarios: Cluster-Imbalance, Covariance-Scaled, Moons, and Connection. This extends test conditions within the existing clustering task.

E2.justification: Tables 1–2 and Appendix F.1 add IDC and k-means on TabPFN-Unsupervised and SCARF embeddings, substantially broadening comparison beyond the previous classical and autoencoder-based methods. Existing comparators remain; the calibration table and runtime figure retain their original comparator sets.

E3.justification: New experiments introduce controlled prior combinations, token dimensions of 32/128/512/768, and clustering-backend comparisons using the same checkpoint. Appendix G also specifies Gaussian noise with standard deviation 0.05 and 5% injected anomalies, evaluating the latter only on original points. These substantially expand evaluation design while retaining the main benchmark's preprocessing, metrics, and sample limits.

E4.justification: The original loss-component ablation is retained. Section 3.5 and Appendix F.4 add prior-component ablations, while Appendix G investigates noise/outlier robustness, token-size sensitivity, output clustering, backbone substitution, and challenging cluster geometries. These address several previously untested design choices and failure conditions.

E5.justification: Both versions report five-seed averaging for the main ARI and Brier comparisons. V2 adds no uncertainty intervals, dispersion estimates, formal significance tests, or explicit increases in repeated runs. Its noise standard deviation describes an experimental perturbation, not uncertainty in reported results.

E6.justification: V2 adds extensive baseline, prior-ablation, robustness, architecture, and special-case results. For example, Table 25 reports Moons ARI of 98.80 for ZEUS, 48.67 for k-means, and 49.23 for GMM. Original ZEUS aggregate ARIs remain 57.43/89.03/86.33, and the original Brier and regularization results are retained. Revised rank summaries reflect the expanded comparator pool rather than a same-setting performance decline.

M1.justification: Appendix G.4 adds a ZEUS+TabICL variant that substitutes the transformer backbone within the existing unsupervised pipeline. The default ZEUS architecture, synthetic prior, losses, and inference procedure remain unchanged; Section 3.1's additional architectural explanations are disclosures rather than demonstrated revisions.

P1.justification: V2 makes localized language corrections, updates author affiliations/contact information and publication status, and expands architectural and prior-generation explanations. It adds subsections for the new material and moves licensing from Appendix G to H, while largely preserving the existing narrative and section order.

P2.justification: The hard-clustering tables gain three comparator columns. New Table 5, Tables 18–20, and Tables 21–25 display prior ablations and supplementary experiments, substantially expanding the visual evidence. Appendix tables are redistributed and recaptioned, and Figure 3 is enlarged; the four original figures retain their substantive content.

R1.justification: V2 adds citations to SCARF, the OpenML platform review, TabICL, and Attention Is All You Need. These support added comparisons, implementation choices, and background; the overall positioning as PFN-inspired unsupervised tabular representation learning remains stable.

T1.justification: Appendix B.1 introduces Theorem 1 and a three-step proof claiming componentwise approximation of arbitrary mixture distributions through neural transformations of Gaussian mixtures. V1 contains the PFN/Bayesian connection but no corresponding theorem. Section 2.2 now invokes this result to support synthetic-to-real generalization.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens the empirical assessment by adding relevant representation-learning baselines and testing previously unsupported choices of prior, architecture, and clustering backend, alongside robustness and difficult cluster geometries. These experiments expose meaningful tradeoffs, including poorer real-data performance with larger tokens or TabICL. The gains outweigh a theoretical overreach: the new distribution-approximation argument does not establish Section 2.2's broad assurance of successful clustering on arbitrary real mixtures.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ZEUS research. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable matching across additions, relocation, and renumbering.

after.justification: V2 retains those original empirical results and adds baseline comparisons, prior ablations, robustness tests, architectural experiments, and special-case evaluations.

before.justification: V1 reports original clustering, calibration, runtime, and regularization experiments on OpenML and synthetic datasets, with detailed appendix results.

results.title: ZEUS: Zero-shot Embeddings for Unsupervised Separation of Tabular Data

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the same principal contributions: a dexterous garment environment, automated collection from one demonstration, and generalizable hierarchical manipulation. The additional experiments support these existing claims without materially redefining their scope.

C2.justification: v3 distinguishes collection-pipeline transfer from policy transfer and discusses sensor noise, simulation gaps and baseline failure mechanisms. It replaces the missing-teleoperation-comparison limitation with explicit failures involving occlusion, severe deformation and unusual garment geometry (Appendix I.3). Appendix C also expands arguments about dexterous hands versus parallel grippers.

D1.justification: v3 documents manual filtering and reuse of LeapMotion poses, teleoperation devices, 50 demonstrations per real-world task, and the additional hardware and camera setup. Existing GAM/SADP training hyperparameters and compute details remain unchanged. Removing the checklist also removes the explicit repository URL, while the project link and release statements remain.

E1.justification: The ClothesNet assets, 15-task environment, 14 evaluated simulation tasks and original four real-world tasks remain. Section 6.3.2 adds real-world Hang Trousers coverage and a policy-transfer scenario for Hang Trousers and Wear Hat using matched simulation and physical robot hardware.

E2.justification: Beyond retained DP and DP3 comparisons, Table 7 adds ACT, pi0 and RDT on four simulation tasks and real-world Fold Tops. Eureka adds numerical comparisons on Hang Coat and Wear Bowlhat; its remaining entries are unreported. This substantially broadens the evaluated comparator families.

E3.justification: v3 adds simulation-only versus simulation-plus-15-real-world-example training, automated versus teleoperated data controls, and pooled simulation/real-world data for VLA fine-tuning. It also identifies the retained real-world results as trained on real data, revising v1 Appendix F.3's blanket simulation-only training statement. This reporting revision does not establish that the unchanged original results were rerun.

E4.justification: The GAM/SADP ablations remain. New analyses test whether automated demonstrations match teleoperation data quality on three tasks (Table 6), whether real-world training examples mitigate transfer degradation on two tasks (Table 4), and how reliably and quickly the collection pipeline produces demonstrations (Table 5).

E5.justification: Both versions specify 50-episode simulation evaluations with three seeds and mean ± standard deviation, plus successful-trial counts for real-world evaluation. The added comparisons follow these reporting practices without introducing new uncertainty estimators, confidence intervals or significance tests.

E6.justification: Tables 2–3 retain their original values. New Table 4 reports simulation-only transfer success of 8/15 for Hang Trousers and 9/15 for Wear Hat, versus 13/15 each with added real-world data. Tables 5–7 add collection outcomes, teleoperation-trained results and new baseline scores. Section 6.1 also revises the reported collection-time range from 30–60 to 30–80 seconds.

M1.justification: Sections 4–5 retain GAM correspondence learning, demonstration retargeting and SADP's architecture and conditioning. The expanded LeapMotion discussion documents pose selection and reuse without establishing an algorithmic revision. Added transfer and training-data experiments use the existing policy.

P1.justification: v3 divides the real-world section into two transfer routes, expands the LeapMotion explanation, inserts appendix sections C, F and G, and removes the NeurIPS checklist. Most existing prose and the overall narrative structure are retained.

P2.justification: v3 substantially expands result presentation through a new transfer-experiment Figure 10 and Tables 4–7 covering transfer, collection efficiency, data sources and broader baselines. Existing environment and physics figures are reordered, and Table 3 is relocated; the original method diagrams and task illustrations are largely retained.

R1.justification: v3 adds Bathe's finite-element-method reference and Müller et al.'s position-based-dynamics reference. Appendix G extends comparisons and positioning to VLA and RL approaches, while Section 2's related-work discussion and principal novelty framing remain unchanged.

T1.justification: Appendix A retains the same adhesion and Coulomb-friction equations and associated definitions. No new formal assumptions, derivations, theorems or proofs are introduced.

improvement.justification: v3 addresses v1's explicit lack of a teleoperation-data comparison and separately tests policy-level sim-to-real transfer, while broadening baselines and stating concrete policy failure conditions. These changes substantially strengthen validation and clarify what the real-world evidence establishes. Limited experiment sizes and new reporting errors, such as Table 5's 96.2% paired with 50/51, temper confidence but do not outweigh these gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DexGarmentLab environment, automated data collection pipeline and HALO policy. Their main text, figures, tables, equations and appendices are readable and matchable despite renumbering and removal of v1's checklist.

after.justification: v3 retains these results and adds policy transfer experiments, collection measurements, training-data comparisons and additional baseline evaluations in Tables 4–7.

before.justification: v1 reports original evaluations on 14 simulation tasks and four real-world tasks, including component ablations and baseline comparisons in Tables 2–3.

results.title: DexGarmentLab: Dexterous Garment Manipulation Environment with Generalizable Policy

C1.justification: The central Bayesian survival-model, scalability, calibration, and discrimination claims remain. The conclusion adds an explicit novelty claim for integrating established Pólya–Gamma/Poisson augmentation with Bayesian-network linearization, refining how the methodological contribution is positioned.

C2.justification: Section 5.2 newly interprets overlapping but shifted posteriors as mild-to-moderate prior sensitivity and emphasizes balancing flexibility with regularization. It also acknowledges fifth-place KM-Calibration performance alongside D-Calibration success. Existing limitations concerning factorization, local linearization, and full-dataset computation are retained.

D1.justification: Appendices J–K add implementation sources for Sumo-Net and DQS, SurvivalEVAL metric APIs, and configuration-specific runtime information replacing rough timing summaries. Core architecture, optimization, normalization, hardware, and NeuralSurv's MIT-licensed code availability were already documented in v1.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same synthetic survival generator and eight benchmark datasets: COLON, METABRIC, GBSG, NWTCO, WHAS, SUPPORT, VLC, and SAC3. The added runtime and prior-sensitivity analyses reuse existing datasets.

E2.justification: Sumo-Net and DQS join the ten retained deep comparators throughout the synthetic, central benchmark, and sample-size ablation comparisons (v2 Tables A3, A5, and A7). The CoxPH, Weibull AFT, RSF, and SSVM comparisons already existed in v1.

E3.justification: v2 adds D-Calibration and KM-Calibration to the existing C-index and IPCW IBS evaluation. New protocols measure COLON runtime at N = 25, 125, and 250 across three network configurations, and compare Gamma(1,1), Gamma(2,2), and Gamma(0.5,0.5) priors. Existing benchmark splits and training budgets remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Appendix M.3 adds prior-variance sensitivity experiments on COLON, METABRIC, and GBSG. Appendix K adds runtime comparisons across sample sizes and network configurations. These investigate prior dependence and computational scaling; the N = 250 ablation itself was already present in v1.

E5.justification: v2 introduces systematic chi-squared D-Calibration testing, reported p-values, and rejection decisions at 0.05 across experiments. Table A11 also reports posterior medians and 95% intervals for phi. The existing five-fold evaluation and 90% survival-function bands remain; no increase in repeated runs is documented.

E6.justification: All matched original C-index and IPCW IBS entries are retained. Substantial new results cover Sumo-Net, DQS, both calibration metrics, runtime, and prior sensitivity. For example, Table A11 reports COLON C-index values of 0.671 under the default prior and 0.593 and 0.512 under alternative priors; these are different settings, not a deterioration between versions.

M1.justification: The sigmoidal hazard model, Gaussian weight and Gamma baseline priors, Pólya–Gamma/Poisson augmentation, MAP linearization, and EM/CAVI procedures remain unchanged. Alternative priors and network configurations appear as experimental variants, without revising the proposed method.

P1.justification: Section 2 expands the survival-analysis introduction, adds a hazard-function subsection, and reorganizes normalization explanations. Attribution and conclusion passages are revised, Appendix M gains descriptive subsections, and acknowledgments are added. Most methodological and appendix prose is retained.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is redrawn with Sumo-Net replacing DeepSurv. Existing deep-comparison tables gain comparator rows, while new calibration panels, a runtime grid, and a prior-sensitivity table substantially expand the visual presentation. Retained tables are redistributed and renumbered.

R1.justification: v2 adds references on sigmoidal point processes, calibration, SurvivalEVAL, Sumo-Net, and DQS. Sections 3 and 6 more explicitly attribute the augmentation and linearization components to prior work. The method-property summary also changes DeepSurv's Bayesian-uncertainty designation, while the broader literature-review structure remains.

T1.justification: Theorem 3.1, formal assumptions, EM/CAVI derivations, computational-complexity argument, and Appendix N proofs remain unchanged after matching equation numbering. Appendix J.3 supplies standard calibration-metric formulas and explanations without revising the theoretical framework.

improvement.justification: Direct calibration evaluations address v1's reliance largely on IBS to support its central calibration claim. Added competitors, prior-sensitivity experiments, and comparative runtimes substantially improve assessment of robustness and practical costs, including less favorable KM-Calibration findings. Localized reporting errors remain: Table A10 marks p = 0.759 as failing and p = 0.038 as passing despite its 0.05 threshold. These errors limit confidence in those annotations but do not outweigh the stronger empirical scrutiny and transparency.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same NeuralSurv work and provide readable methods, equations, figures, tables, and Appendices A–N. Retained content can be matched reliably across renumbering and reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds calibration evaluations, runtime measurements, and prior-sensitivity results.

before.justification: v1 reports original synthetic survival experiments, benchmark evaluations, and a sample-size ablation in Section 5 and Appendix M.

results.title: NeuralSurv: Deep Survival Analysis with Bayesian Uncertainty Quantification

C1.justification: V1 describes very few prior attempts at learning from diverse hand contacts. V2 strengthens this to no prior attempt and explicitly claims HACO is the first dense hand contact method trained on a large-scale dataset. The central BCS/VCB contributions and claims of contact-estimation and downstream benefits remain.

C2.justification: Beyond v1's self-contact limitation, v2 discusses missing temporal context, possible failure of mean-based BCS on multimodal distributions, weak hand-hand performance and the inability of positive-hand-only evaluation to assess hand-level false positives. Appendix A.6 also interprets the new controlled comparisons as evidence for task-specific design beyond training-data scale. These substantially expand the paper's qualifications and interpretation.

D1.justification: V2 reports publicly available code and provides a repository address, replacing v1's release promise. It adds smoothness-loss implementation details and explains baseline reproduction, replacement of body-model components with MANO, HaMeR mesh inputs, and use of reproduced versus released implementations. Test-memory measurements replace model-memory figures. These materially expand access and reproduction information, although some new loss parameters remain unspecified.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same 14 datasets and cover the same hand interaction types, dense contact estimation and two downstream tasks. The new comparisons and reduced-data ablation reuse existing datasets; HIC, RICH and Hi4D were already evaluated in v1.

E2.justification: V2 adds MANO-based, retrained hand variants of POSA, BSTRO and DECO in Table A3. Table A4 adds direct contact comparisons with DefConNet, CHOI Stage 1, DICE InteractionNet, LatentAct's Data Engine and EasyHOI; EasyHOI previously appeared only in the downstream reconstruction comparison. Table A1 also removes the ObMan-mean initialization comparator.

E3.justification: Section 5.1 revises the reported training total from 840K to 655K images without explaining the difference. New experiments train hand-adapted baselines on the same 14 datasets, reproduce contact modules under specified configurations, and compare training on 1, 3 and 14 datasets. The resource table also replaces model memory with test memory. These are reported protocol changes and additions, not proof that every retained experiment was rerun.

E4.justification: V2 adds a focused training-size ablation using MOW alone, three hand-object datasets and all 14 datasets (A.7, Table A5). It also removes the ObMan-mean condition from the initialization ablation. Existing sampling, loss, interaction-composition and backbone analyses remain, although their reported scores are revised.

E5.justification: V1 provides no seed or repeated-run information. V2's checklist newly states that results came from randomly seeded runs without cherry-picking and explicitly acknowledges absent error bars. It supplies no run counts, seed values, confidence intervals or significance tests, so increased repetition is not established.

E6.justification: Many results are revised: HACO's MOW F1 changes from 0.531 to 0.522, while Table 4 changes full-model RICH F1 from 0.528 to 0.781 and Hi4D F1 from 0.828 to 0.565. Backbone scores and rankings also change. V2 adds extensive baseline results in Tables A2–A4 and training-size results in A5. Given the revised training total and procedure description, these are not established same-setting gains or losses. Downstream Tables 6–7 remain unchanged.

M1.justification: Relative to v1's direct VCB supervision, Section 3.3 of v2 specifies a progressive CB-to-VCB weighting schedule and an additional false-positive regularizer. These extend the stated training procedure while retaining the architecture, balanced contact sampling and core VCB formulation. The PDFs do not establish when these additions entered the implementation.

P1.justification: The main narrative and section sequence remain largely intact, with localized rewriting and clearer distinctions between vertices and hand instances. V2 adds acknowledgements and a NeurIPS checklist, moves references before the appendix, and inserts two appendix subsections. Most existing exposition is retained rather than extensively rewritten.

P2.justification: V2 adds four substantive appendix tables, A2–A5, and a ground-truth column to Figure 3. The previous backbone and resource tables become A6 and A7; the initialization table loses one row and the resource table changes its memory column. Existing qualitative predictions and appendix figures are retained. The expansion of comparison displays is substantial beyond pagination changes.

R1.justification: Appendix A.6 substantially broadens positioning from full-body contact estimators to learned and heuristic hand-contact modules, explaining their earlier exclusion and distinguishing HACO's standalone role. Ten cited works are added, including DICE, LatentAct and SAM2. Previously cited CHOI remains and gains direct evaluation; its disappearance from the main related-work paragraph is not removal from the paper.

T1.justification: Appendix A.1 adds self-connections to the adjacency specification and maximum normalization of neighborhood contact and non-contact aggregates before the isolation score. This alters the described mathematical construction of the smoothness loss, although the displayed Equations (1)–(14) remain unchanged. Neither version supplies theoretical theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially addresses a central weakness of v1's evidence: Table A3 compares against hand-adapted baselines trained on the same 14 datasets, reducing confounding from training coverage and body representation, while Table A4 adds relevant hand-contact competitors. Explicit evaluation limitations and reported code access further improve transparency. Unexplained revisions to sample totals and scores, incomplete new loss specifications and absent uncertainty estimates remain weaknesses, but the stronger comparative evidence provides a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe HACO, with readable main text, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices. Corresponding material can be matched despite reference relocation, appendix expansion and renumbering.

after.justification: V2 reports original experiments, including revised existing results, additional baseline comparisons and a training-dataset-size ablation in Tables A2–A5.

before.justification: V1 reports original dense hand contact experiments, component and backbone ablations, and downstream grasp optimization and reconstruction results in Tables 2–7 and A1–A3.

results.title: Learning Dense Hand Contact Estimation from Imbalanced Data

C1.justification: The abstract, contributions and conclusion now claim experimentally demonstrated text-to-image potential, previously future work. v2 removes the explicit claim of being the first fully convolutional backbone to achieve SOTA diffusion performance and narrows broad superiority language to recent models and specified comparisons. Original ImageNet numerical claims remain in the paper.

C2.justification: Appendix F removes the limitation that text-to-image generation was unexplored while retaining the model-scale limitation. New discussion interprets MS-COCO results as supporting larger-scale text-to-image applicability. Appendix D's explicit caveat about not surpassing every generative model is removed; the original locality and channel-redundancy explanations remain.

D1.justification: Algorithm 1 adds tensor shapes, padding, reshaping and grouped-convolution implementation details; the text identifies CLIP's 77-token input and module placement. v2 also explicitly states that existing ablations omit CFG. Original configuration, hardware and training-time tables and the repository pointer remain unchanged, while pointers to uncompressed supplementary samples are removed.

E1.justification: v2 adds training and evaluation on MS-COCO for text-to-image generation and an ImageNet 1024×1024 generation scenario. v1 evaluates DiCo only on class-conditional ImageNet at 256×256 and 512×512; its existing PixArt/FLUX attention visualizations do not constitute DiCo text-to-image evaluation.

E2.justification: The original comparator sets are retained. New Table 3 introduces text-to-image comparisons including AttnGAN, DM-GAN, U-Net, U-ViT-S/2, MMDiT and MMDiT+REPA. Appendix Tables 12–13 add comparisons involving FlowDCN-S/2, SiT-S/2, REPA and LightningDiT.

E3.justification: New protocols include matched 33M models trained from scratch for 400K iterations at 1024×1024 without CFG, a 400K-iteration comparison retaining FlowDCN's isotropic architecture and training setup, and an 800-epoch modern-DiT comparison with a 679M proposed model. Original ImageNet training settings remain unchanged. Table 1 also relabels throughput from it/s to image/s without explaining a measurement change.

E4.justification: v2 compares cross-attention with text-conditioned depthwise convolution and tests replacing MultiScale DCN with the Conv Module while retaining FlowDCN's architecture and training setup. These add focused component analyses. Existing architecture, activation, kernel-size, CCA and attention ablations, together with scaling analyses, are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions report point estimates without experimental seed counts, repeated-run counts, confidence intervals or significance tests. v2 introduces no new uncertainty-reporting procedure.

E6.justification: Original numerical results are retained. New results include MS-COCO FIDs 4.87/4.93 for the two DiCo variants, versus 4.14 for MMDiT+REPA; 1024×1024 FID 102.60 versus DiT's 113.06; and FlowDCN-setting FID 52.1 versus 54.6. Table 13 reports FID 1.33 versus LightningDiT's 1.35 under a new 800-epoch setup, not a same-setting improvement over v1.

M1.justification: Section 3.3 adds two text-conditioning mechanisms after each Conv Module: cross-attention and dynamic 9×9 depthwise kernels derived from CLIP embeddings. Algorithm 1 implements the latter. These introduce new inputs and block computations beyond v1's class-conditioned model; the original backbone and CCA remain unchanged.

P1.justification: Changes comprise localized abstract, contribution and conclusion revisions, new method and experimental paragraphs, acknowledgements and publication-header updates. Most explanatory prose and the main section and Appendix A–G organization are retained.

P2.justification: v2 adds four compact comparison tables and Algorithm 1, introduces a Token Mixing Type column in Tables 1–2, and adjusts captions and placement. Existing diagrams, plots and sample-gallery images are retained; gallery running headers are removed. These are localized additions and layout changes.

R1.justification: v2 adds targeted citations and discussion for FlowDCN, LightningDiT and text-to-image methods, and withdraws the explicit first-fully-convolutional-SOTA priority claim. The existing related-work organization and central positioning of convolution as an efficient alternative to Transformers remain largely intact.

T1.justification: The diffusion formulation, losses, classifier-free guidance expression and CCA equation are unchanged. Neither version supplies theoretical propositions or proofs; the new conditioning algorithm is a procedural addition.

improvement.justification: The controlled FlowDCN substitution and modern-DiT comparisons substantially strengthen evidence that the convolutional components remain competitive beyond the original setup. The implemented text-conditioning extension and MS-COCO evaluation establish applicability that v1 left untested, while 1024×1024 experiments strengthen efficiency-scaling evidence. More restrained novelty claims improve calibration. New protocols remain tersely documented and the text-to-image speed claim lacks timing figures, but these limitations do not outweigh the substantial gains in validation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DiCo research. Their main text, equations, figures, tables and Appendices A–G are readable, and retained material can be matched across relocation and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains these original results and adds MS-COCO text-to-image experiments, ImageNet 1024×1024 evaluation, and FlowDCN and modern-DiT comparisons.

before.justification: v1 reports original ImageNet generation experiments, architecture and component ablations, scaling measurements and generated samples.

results.title: DiCo: Revitalizing ConvNets for Scalable and Efficient Diffusion Modeling

C1.justification: The central claims about mitigating suppressors through local generative explanations remain. v3 adds an abstract claim of physiologically plausible EEG explanations and extends the conclusion's claimed superiority from two image benchmarks to three datasets. This broadens the application claim without redefining the main contribution.

C2.justification: v3 adds substantive interpretations of MRI threshold-dependent rankings, superpixel limitations and high-signal rank deficiency. Appendix F explains why faithfulness metrics can reward suppressor attributions. The EEG discussion acknowledges missing attribution ground truth and interprets physiological plausibility. The original dedicated Limitations paragraph remains substantially unchanged.

D1.justification: Appendices C–D supply dataset-generation instructions, network architectures, optimizer and stopping settings, 200-trial tuning budgets, search ranges, software versions, hardware and timing information that v1 relegated to unavailable supplementary material. These substantially improve reproducibility documentation without establishing changes to the original training settings. The code-access URL is retained.

E1.justification: v3 adds a real EEG left-versus-right fist classification application, extending coverage beyond synthetic images and artificial-lesion MRI. Appendix G.1 also evaluates intermediate mixtures of white and correlated noise, extending the previously reported endpoint noise scenarios.

E2.justification: The named image-benchmark baselines and toy-example comparators remain; Section 4.3's change from eleven to nine methods corrects the count rather than documenting removals. The new EEG evaluation adds raw EEG instances as a physiological reference comparator alongside LIME and PatternLocal (Section 5 and Figure 12).

E3.justification: New protocols include EEG preprocessing, a ShallowFBCSPNet classifier and physiological evaluation using SSD, dipole fits and eLORETA. Appendix G crosses MLP/CNN models with EMD/MSE tuning on 8×8 datasets containing 10,000 samples. Tables 6–7 introduce numerical MRI evaluation using all attributions versus those above 0.9; v1 used that threshold only in displayed overlays.

E4.justification: Where v1 only references supplementary analyses, v3 supplies representation/regularization comparisons, a white-to-correlated-noise sweep and architecture-by-tuning-objective ablations (Figures 8–10 and 13–17). Table 5 adds a matrix-rank diagnosis of high-signal instability, and Tables 6–7 expose sensitivity to attribution thresholding.

E5.justification: Appendix D.1 newly discloses fixed random seeds through pl.seed_everything, while Appendix G.2 specifies that shaded bands represent standard deviations across test images. v1 already displayed standard-deviation bands. Neither version establishes repeated independent runs or an increase in run counts.

E6.justification: v3 supplies extensive numerical results absent from the supplied v1, including MRI tables, runtimes, EEG dipole fits and appendix curves. MRI Table 6 reports EMD 0.166 for PatternLocal versus 0.101 for Integrated Gradients; thresholded Table 7 reports 0.102 versus 0.166. These are newly reported, protocol-dependent rankings, not evidence of a same-setting improvement between versions.

M1.justification: The local surrogate-to-pattern transformation, reconstruction objective in Equation 6, ridge/LASSO options and input representations remain. The Equation 7 correction aligns its first expression with the covariance/variance form already stated in v1. Newly disclosed estimation details, including Appendix B.3's shrinkage discussion, do not establish a revision to the underlying explanation procedure.

P1.justification: The main six-section sequence remains. v3 tightens prose, condenses Section 3's explanatory paragraphs, changes latent-variable notation from s to m and replaces vague supplementary references with explicit appendix links. Appendices A–G organize the additional material and provide a notation glossary, while the main narrative remains recognizable.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is redrawn as an explicit four-step workflow, existing plots are restyled, and MRI panels are updated. v3 adds EEG temporal, spectral and source-localization displays, quantitative MRI and runtime tables, representation comparisons and extensive ablation plots. These substantially expand and revise the visual presentation.

R1.justification: v3 adds supporting references on PredDiff, covariance shrinkage, nonparametric covariance estimation and EEG acquisition, decoding, SSD and source localization. Appendix F extends the positioning against faithfulness-based evaluation. The central relationship to Pattern, PatternNet, PatternAttribution, LIME and SHAP remains.

T1.justification: Equation 7 replaces the erroneous feature-second-moment inverse with the surrogate-response second moment. Appendix B.1 derives the ridge solution and states the centering assumption needed for its covariance form. Appendix B.3 adds formal bias, variance, bandwidth and sample-complexity reasoning absent from v1; Appendix B.2 expands the toy derivation.

improvement.justification: v3 resolves substantial reporting deficiencies in the supplied v1 by making derivations, implementation settings, quantitative MRI results and robustness analyses available, while correcting Equation 7. These additions make the method considerably easier to reproduce and critically assess. The MRI tables reveal weaknesses that temper the retained broad superiority claim, and EEG evidence establishes physiological plausibility rather than attribution correctness. Those limitations remain, but the gains in transparency, technical completeness and assessable evidence are substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same PatternLocal research, and their text, equations, figures and tables support comparison. The supplied v1 ends after its references despite referring to supplementary material; v3 includes Appendices A–G. Appendix additions therefore establish newly available documentation and evidence, not necessarily newly conducted work.

after.justification: v3 retains original experimental results and reports additional EEG evaluations, MRI scores, runtime measurements and appendix analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original XOR simulations, quantitative XAI-TRIS experiments and qualitative artificial-lesion MRI results in Figures 2, 4 and 5.

results.title: Minimizing False-Positive Attributions in Explanations of Non-Linear Models

C1.justification: The abstract and four introductory contributions retain the same central claims: mutual-information reduction, an optimal rectified-flow imputer, connections to existing methods, and strong tabular/image performance. The new conclusion summarizes these retained contributions.

C2.justification: v3 substantially expands applicability and interpretation: it explicitly prioritizes distributional sampling over point prediction, explains the choice of rectified flow, acknowledges that the objective is not designed for MNAR, and interprets runtime scaling through vectorization. It retains the computational and population-level limitations and proposes a future time-series extension.

D1.justification: v3 adds an implementation URL, source information for additional baselines, and execution-time information. Hardware specifications remain unchanged, while v1's explicit recommendation of 100 Euler steps disappears. Detailed hyperparameters remain deferred outside the supplied PDFs.

E1.justification: The underlying datasets are retained, but UCI evaluation expands from MCAR to MAR and MNAR missingness scenarios. CIFAR-10 evaluation also gains a downstream ten-class classification task beyond reconstruction and distributional fidelity.

E2.justification: Compared with v1 Figure 4, v3 Figure 5 adds MIWAE, Sinkhorn, and TDM to the UCI comparisons while retaining the existing methods. The new runtime comparison also evaluates DiffPuter, previously only discussed, and includes the comparator labeled MOT in Table 6.

E3.justification: Existing dataset sizes and MCAR evaluations are retained. New protocols include MAR at reported 40%/80% missingness conditioned on a randomly selected half of the variables, MNAR at 20%/40%/60%, aggregate dataset rankings, classification accuracy, and timing 1000 samples across 50–5000 dimensions.

E4.justification: v3 adds robustness evaluations under MAR and MNAR and a dimensionality-dependent runtime analysis, including runtime failures and out-of-memory outcomes. These substantially extend v1's MCAR missing-rate analyses and retained image reconstruction examples.

E5.justification: The ten-run, mean±standard-deviation convention is retained. v3's checklist additionally identifies random masks/seeds as variability sources; this is a limited reporting clarification, without evidence of increased repetitions or a new uncertainty-estimation procedure.

E6.justification: The original toy-data and CIFAR fidelity tables retain their values, while v3 adds MAR/MNAR MMD results, aggregate rankings, classification accuracies, and runtimes. For example, Table 3 reports accuracy of 0.364 for MIRI versus 0.212 for HyperImpute at 60% missingness; Table 6 reports respective 5000-dimensional runtimes of 1.30 and 57.54 hours. v1's numerical UCI prose summaries are removed.

M1.justification: The MIRI updates, rectified-flow training loss, imputation ODE, initialization options, and Euler solver are retained. Appendix F extends the theoretical treatment to MAR and derives the same optimality condition, without introducing a different implemented procedure.

P1.justification: v3 extensively edits the abstract, introduction, background, and experimental narrative. It restructures the contribution list, folds Practical Implementation into Section 3.4, moves the sequential-imputation appendix forward, and adds a separate conclusion and checklist. These are substantial editorial and structural changes beyond the added scientific material.

P2.justification: v3 adds ranking, classification, and runtime tables plus MAR/MNAR plots, and expands the MCAR chart with additional comparison series. It relocates the unchanged sequential-imputation schematic and combines the three existing appendix image grids into Figure 8 panels. The main result figures retain their original image content.

R1.justification: v3 adds references for MIWAE, optimal-transport imputation, TDM, MMD, and McFlow, changes the introductory normalizing-flow attribution, and removes MisGAN. The central positioning relative to GAIN, round-robin methods, and conditional generative imputation remains intact.

T1.justification: New Appendix F formulates a conditional-mutual-information objective under MAR and derives the same conditional-distribution optimality condition as Proposition 2. Appendix E also corrects the KL factorization in v1 Appendix D and explicitly derives its imputer-independent term. The original principal propositions and theorem remain.

improvement.justification: v1's MCAR-only validation and qualitative computational-cost discussion gain MAR reasoning, MAR/MNAR comparisons, broader baselines, downstream classification, and measured scaling. Together these substantially strengthen evidence about applicability, practical utility, and computational cost. The explicit MNAR limitation also improves qualification of the results. Hyperparameter and classifier documentation remain incomplete in the PDFs, but these limitations do not outweigh the substantial gains in validation and transparency.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MIRI research. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and included appendices are readable and support reliable comparison despite substantial reorganization.

after.justification: v3 retains those original experiments and adds MAR/MNAR evaluations, downstream CIFAR-10 classification, and runtime measurements in Section 5 and Appendices H–I.

before.justification: v1 reports original Gaussian-mixture, UCI tabular, CIFAR-10, and CelebA experiments, including numerical results and imputed samples in Section 6 and Appendix F.

results.title: Missing Data Imputation by Reducing Mutual Information with Rectified Flows

C1.justification: The central contributions and claimed first application of RLVR to optimization modeling remain. V3 extends the empirical contribution to a 32B model, explicitly claiming superiority over DeepSeek-V3 and OpenAI-o3 on most benchmarks; its main table actually names DeepSeek-V3.1. V1 instead emphasized the 7B model's competitiveness with DeepSeek-V3.

C2.justification: V3 newly interprets LP-derived feedback as combining outcome and process-aware rewards. Appendix 12 develops an explanation for textual reasoning's limitations based on globally interacting constraints and computational demands, and interprets the error breakdowns. The conclusion also identifies persistent reward hacking and limited IndustryOR/OptMATH performance, substantially expanding the discussion of mechanisms and boundaries.

D1.justification: V3 supplies the previously absent prompts, reward specifications, seed-data description, training-data selection, Verl hyperparameters, and decoding settings. It reports 10,000 training examples selected from approximately 70,000 and 7B training on eight H100 GPUs for 384 GPU hours. It also adds code and corrected-data access information. These are documentation additions, not evidence that all underlying settings changed.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate NL4OPT, MAMO Easy/Complex, IndustryOR, and OptMATH. The new solver-free and SFT comparisons examine different procedures for these retained optimization tasks. Newly documented curation, sample counts, and model scales do not establish additional domains or problem families.

E2.justification: The main comparison replaces DeepSeek-V3 with DeepSeek-V3.1, adds DeepSeek-R1, OpenAI-o3, and OptMATH-Qwen2.5-32B, and removes GPT-3.5-turbo and Chain-of-Experts. Appendix 12 additionally reports solver-free Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct/Math4Opt-RL results and a base-model/SFT/RL comparison, substantially broadening the evaluated comparison methods.

E3.justification: V3 adds a trained 32B configuration, solver-free and SFT comparison setups, and a separate stochastic evaluation using temperature 0.5 and top-p 0.95. The main pass@1 criterion remains relative error below 1e-6. Dataset corrections and sample counts are newly documented, but v1 lacks enough detail to establish when those settings changed.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained KL and reward ablations, Appendices 12-13 add stochastic-generation robustness, solver-dependence and SFT comparisons, error-category breakdowns, and two IndustryOR case studies examining execution and logical-modeling failures. Table 13 also supplies KL-ablation results for NL4OPT and MAMO Easy that were absent from v1.

E5.justification: V1 reports point estimates without uncertainty summaries. V3 Table 8 introduces mean accuracy and standard deviation across multiple generation runs for all five benchmark columns. This is a limited new uncertainty analysis; the run count and seeds are unspecified, and no increase in training repetitions is established.

E6.justification: The reported 7B MAMO Complex accuracy changes from 62.1% to 51.7%, OptMATH from 29.0% to 30.5%, and macro average from 62.1% to 60.6%. Ablation values also change, and substantial new results include the 32B model's 68.3% macro average and appendix comparisons. These are revised reported results, not established same-setting performance changes. The self-consistency results are retained unchanged.

M1.justification: The instance-enhanced voting procedure, REINFORCE++ objective, Partial KL restriction, and two-stage reward structure remain unchanged. The appendix supplies previously missing reward and prompt specifications, while the 32B experiment applies the existing framework at another scale; neither establishes an algorithmic revision.

P1.justification: The abstract and substantial introduction passages are rewritten, main results move ahead of self-consistency, and ablations receive separate subsections. The new appendix adds extensive explanatory organization, including a tutorial on optimization-modeling components and a worked example, followed by dedicated prompt, reward, implementation, and analysis sections.

P2.justification: V3 retains the original two diagrams and adds the SIRL training diagram as Figure 3. It expands and relocates the main comparison table, adds Tables 5-13, and introduces numerous boxed prompts, code examples, and case-study responses. These substantially expand the visual presentation beyond numerical updates.
