R1.justification: V3 adds positioning relative to MiniZinc, Essence, and Holy Grail 2.0, and cites Let's Verify Step by Step for process-aware rewards. It adds implementation/background references and removes several general RL references, including Constitutional AI and DeepSeek-R1 Thoughtology. The main related-work categories and solver-as-verifier positioning remain intact.

T1.justification: Appendix 10 adds explicit piecewise definitions of previously unspecified reward components, including their magnitudes and the 0.01 answer tolerance. This extends the formal specification beyond v1's aggregate reward equation. The original optimization, voting, and Partial KL equations remain unchanged, and neither version presents theoretical proofs.

improvement.justification: V3 resolves a substantial reproducibility deficiency: v1 refers to an absent appendix, whereas v3 supplies prompts, reward specifications, training settings, and access information. New comparison experiments, uncertainty reporting, and failure analyses also make the evidence more assessable. Important inconsistencies remain: Tables 3 and 13 give different Full KL MAMO Complex execution rates, and the format-reward prose says 1 while its equation says 0.5. These limit confidence in particular details, but the documentation and validation gains constitute a substantial overall improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs are readable and describe the same SIRL work, with matching core equations and experiments. V1 ends after its references despite referring to an appendix; v3 supplies appendix Sections 6-13. This supports comparison of documented content, although settings absent from v1 cannot be assumed.

after.justification: V3 reports original 7B and 32B SIRL results, ablations, stochastic sampling results, and error analyses in the main text and appendices.

before.justification: V1 reports original SIRL benchmark results, self-consistency experiments, and KL and reward ablations in Tables 1-4.

results.title: Solver-Informed RL: Grounding Large Language Models for Authentic Optimization Modeling

C1.justification: Both versions claim TTCMM, MINGLE with adaptive null-space gating, improved robustness and forgetting resistance, and a 7–9% average advantage. Calling TTCMM a task and MINGLE its framework clarifies an existing distinction rather than redefining the core contributions.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive explanations of sub-unit gate activations through expert complementarity, interpretations of inference efficiency and forward transfer, and deployment and privacy arguments in Appendix D. It also explicitly contrasts TTCMM with rehearsal-free continual learning. The original shared-initialization and identical-backbone limitations remain unchanged.

D1.justification: v2 adds baseline hyperparameters and resource requirements (Tables 11–12), NLP sampling details, expanded timing information, and a MINGLE code-access link. These substantially expand reproducibility documentation. Conversely, v1's explicit RTX 4090 identification and CLIP logit construction are removed; the new checklist retains a submission-time code-release promise.

E1.justification: v2 adds eight GLUE language tasks with Flan-T5-base, extending evaluation from image classification to text processing (Table 2). The original vision task groups, MTIL benchmark, and seven image corruptions remain.

E2.justification: The main vision comparison adds Consensus TA, continual layer-wise AdaMerging, and continual LoRA-WEMOE (Tables 1 and 13). AdaMerging previously participated only in the corruption comparison. LoRA-WEMOE also joins that comparison alongside the retained original WEMOE, rather than merely renaming it.

E3.justification: New protocols include alphabetical GLUE evaluation with Flan-T5-base and 100 unlabeled adaptation samples, a 5/10/20/50-step adaptation sweep, and throughput and forward-transfer measurements. Existing vision defaults and task-order lists remain unchanged. The revised seed-sample analysis no longer reports the 20-samples-per-class condition.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's component, rank, layer, gate, and sample-count analyses, v2 adds adaptation-step sensitivity (Table 6), adaptation-time scaling (Table 7b), comparative inference/storage analysis (Table 15), and forward transfer (Table 16). Most earlier analyses are retained; the seed-sample analysis is reformatted and its 20-sample point omitted.

E5.justification: Both versions report vision results as mean and standard deviation across ten task orders using seeds 42–51, and gate-activation variability across layers. Additional result rows do not introduce a new uncertainty procedure, increased run count, confidence interval, or significance test.

E6.justification: v2 adds GLUE results, including MINGLE's reported 83.3 ACC and 0.1 BWT, full-configuration ViT-L/14 results, and budget, inference, and forward-transfer findings. Existing appendix values also change: MINGLE's 20-task ViT-B/16 EuroSAT accuracy changes from 84.7 to 90.0 (v1 Table 9; v2 Table 13). The earlier ViT-L/14 MINGLE row is retained under MINGLE*, avoiding a false same-configuration comparison.

M1.justification: The low-rank expert construction, KL adaptation objective, freezing of earlier gates, and adaptive null-space gating remain intact. Revised covariance descriptions and projection notation do not establish a different algorithm; evaluation on Flan-T5 alone is not a method change.

P1.justification: The abstract, related-work survey, experimental narrative, and conclusion receive substantial rewriting. v2 also reorganizes analysis and discussion subsections and adds acknowledgments and a NeurIPS checklist, while preserving the overall introduction–method–experiments structure.

P2.justification: v2 substantially expands comparison-table structures, adds assumption columns and several new tables, and combines the earlier efficiency table and seed-sample plot into multipart Table 7. Existing plots are largely retained and renumbered; the appendix contents and theorem gain boxed layouts.

R1.justification: Four cited works are added: instruction-finetuned language models, GLUE, Twin-merging, and task localization underlying Consensus TA. Related-work discussion expands dynamic-merging positioning and the relationship to rehearsal-free learning, while retaining the original literature framework. Publication-metadata updates concern existing citations.

T1.justification: The dynamic-MoE risk theorem, assumptions, and three-part Appendix A proof retain their substance; the appendix theorem is renumbered and boxed. The added forward-transfer formula supports an empirical metric rather than introducing a new theoretical result.

improvement.justification: Compared with v1's vision-only evaluation and mainly static main-table comparators, v2 adds language evaluation and directly tests relevant adaptive and dynamic competitors. Budget and inference analyses, explicit comparator assumptions, and baseline settings substantially strengthen assessment of the claimed advantages and practical costs. These gains outweigh localized reporting weaknesses, including omitted GPU identification and inconsistent MINGLE* parameter counts between Tables 7 and 15.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MINGLE research work. Their complete main texts, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support reliable matching across revisions.

after.justification: v2 retains original vision experiments and adds language-task results, adaptation-budget experiments, inference measurements, and forward-transfer results.

before.justification: v1 reports original continual-merging experiments, MTIL comparisons, corruption tests, and ablations in Section 4 and Appendix C.

results.title: MINGLE: Mixture of Null-Space Gated Low-Rank Experts for Test-Time Continual Model Merging

C1.justification: The three central methodological contributions and the abstract's 75× acceleration claim remain unchanged. The conclusion adds claims of competitive Heat-equation performance against KFAC and an order-of-magnitude error advantage on log-Fokker–Planck, modestly extending the stated empirical contribution.

C2.justification: New discussion explains why differing sampling distributions permit transferring VMC techniques to PINNs, qualifies Woodbury's quadratic batch-size scaling against KFAC's linear scaling, and attributes disagreement with McKay et al. to comparison against the stronger ENGD-W baseline. The existing limitations concerning late-stage accuracy, high-dimensional randomization, and adaptive rank selection remain.

D1.justification: Appendices A.5–A.6 add substantial specifications for the new experiments: equations, initial and boundary conditions, sampling, architectures, time budgets, search spaces, and selected hyperparameters. Algorithm 1 exposes C without specifying its numerical value. Appendix B revises benchmark details but drops the earlier parameter-size and random-matrix construction description. Hardware, precision, and the prospective implementation-release statement remain unchanged.

E1.justification: v2 adds a 4+1d Heat equation and a 9+1d logarithmic Fokker–Planck equation while retaining the Poisson problems, including the appendix-only 10d case. This substantially broadens evaluation to time-dependent problems and a nonlinear differential equation in logarithmic coordinates.

E2.justification: Figures 4, 5, 9, and 15 remove the ENGD (Naive) or SPRING (Naive) comparator curves. Figure 3 adds numerical KFAC reference levels, including for 5d Poisson; v1 already discussed KFAC performance in its 100d comparison. These are reference results attributed to prior work, with no newly run KFAC experiments documented.

E3.justification: The existing evaluation framework is retained, with new Heat and log-Fokker–Planck runs using 3000s and 6000s budgets. Appendix B replaces the N=3500, S=1750 benchmark description with N=5000, sketches spanning 20–80%, and peak-memory measurement. A.4 and Figure 13 change Bayesian search to random search; this reported correction does not establish that experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Appendix B adds a focused scaling analysis testing how runtime, memory, and GPU acceleration depend on sketch size. Appendices A.5–A.6 extend momentum and fixed-learning-rate versus line-search comparisons to the new PDEs. The existing effective-dimension analysis and principal randomization conclusions are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions report selected hyperparameter-search runs and average benchmark timings over 100 runs after 10 warm-up runs. Neither adds seed-based variability, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The increase from over 3000 to over 4500 total training runs describes expanded experimental effort, not a new uncertainty-estimation practice.

E6.justification: Figures 3 and 16–19 add Heat and log-Fokker–Planck convergence results, including a reported order-of-magnitude SPRING advantage over the plotted KFAC reference on log-Fokker–Planck. New Table 1 reports 13.29–65.41× Nyström speedups and lower peak memory across four sketch sizes. Naive-variant results are removed from four figures; most retained Poisson curves are unchanged. These additions are not same-setting v1-to-v2 performance gains.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 replaces the written SPRING update eta_k*phi_k with phi_k*min(eta_k, sqrt(C)/||phi_k||), introducing a norm constraint C. This is a limited revision to the stated procedure; the Woodbury, momentum, and Nyström computations otherwise remain intact. The PDFs do not establish whether the earlier implementation already used this constraint.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the section sequence are retained. Changes include focused explanatory paragraphs, expanded experimental setup and conclusion passages, new appendix subsections, a rewritten Appendix B, and updated affiliation, contact, acknowledgment, and conference text.

P2.justification: Figure 3 expands from two to four panels and gains dashed KFAC reference levels. Four new appendix figures and Table 1 substantially expand the empirical displays. Figures 4, 5, 9, and 15 are redrawn without Naive curves and their legend entries, while most other plots retain their content.

R1.justification: v2 adds McKay et al., Near-optimal sketchy natural gradients for physics-informed neural networks, and explicitly contrasts its randomization findings with comparisons against ENGD-W. The broader positioning remains intact. Consolidating the duplicate Jacot et al. references does not remove a distinct cited work.

T1.justification: Appendix A.6 adds the mathematical transformation of the general Fokker–Planck equation under q=log(p), including the transformed differential operator. The existing Woodbury and SPRING derivations remain unchanged, and no new convergence theorem or proof is introduced. Algorithm 2's regularization notation is clarified without changing its factorization steps.

improvement.justification: The new PDE families substantially address v1's Poisson-only validation, while Table 1 supplies concrete runtime and memory evidence where v1's benchmarking appendix provided only a setup description. These changes materially strengthen support for general applicability and GPU efficiency. Inconsistent Heat network-size labels, the unspecified norm-constraint value, and prose still describing removed randomized comparisons limit reproducibility and clarity, but do not outweigh those gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their text, equations, figures, algorithms, and complete Appendices A and B are readable and support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains original Poisson experiments and adds Heat and logarithmic Fokker–Planck results, plus measured Nyström runtime and memory comparisons in Table 1.

before.justification: Section 4 and Appendix A report original PINN optimization experiments on 5d, 10d, and 100d Poisson problems, including convergence, randomization, and effective-dimension analyses.

results.title: Improving Energy Natural Gradient Descent through Woodbury, Momentum, and Randomization

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction’s contribution list, and conclusion retain the same principal claims about latent spatial reasoning, efficient plug-and-play integration, SSR-CoT, SSRBench, and improved spatial understanding. New experiments support these existing claims without redefining the contributions.

C2.justification: v3 explains how shorter outputs offset slower per-token generation, interprets cross-judge agreement as evidence against model-family bias, and interprets low off-diagonal similarities as sample-specific representations without collapse. The limitation restricting demonstrated applicability to Qwen/Qwen-VL models remains substantively unchanged.

D1.justification: Section 4.1 newly specifies the existing quality-control loop’s 10% cache sampling and accuracy-based retention/reannotation procedure. Section 5.5 clarifies token placement in the heatmap comparison, and Appendix E supplies new benchmark sample counts. Existing hyperparameters, hardware, training times, and code/data access statements remain unchanged.

E1.justification: v3 adds evaluation on VSR, What’s Up, VQAv2, TextVQA, POPE, MMBench, and GQA, substantially broadening spatial-relation and general VQA testing. MME evaluation is removed. The training mixture and SpatialBench, SSRBench, and CV-Bench evaluations are retained (Tables 4–5 and Appendix E).

E2.justification: Table 3 and Appendix B add SpatialVLM to the existing comparator set. New Table 7 introduces Qwen2.5-VL fine-tuned on SSR-CoT as a textual-CoT comparator. The other existing benchmark comparators remain.

E3.justification: New protocols substantially extend validation: Table 7 measures tokens per sample, token throughput, and inference latency against an SSR-CoT-fine-tuned control; Table 8 rescores SSRBench using GPT-4o-mini alongside the original Qwen judge. VSR Random and Zero-Shot evaluations are also added. Existing training settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: New Sections 5.3–5.4 test computational efficiency relative to textual CoT and sensitivity to evaluator-model family. These address questions not experimentally checked in v1. The original second-stage ablation, cosine-similarity visualization, and Appendix F case studies are retained; expanded heatmap explanations do not constitute a new experiment.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. Both checklists explicitly acknowledge absent statistical-significance reporting. The additional judge comparison does not introduce statistical uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: v3 adds benchmark, SpatialVLM, efficiency, and alternative-judge results while removing MME results. Table 4 revises SpatialBench averages: Qwen/SSR 3B change from 53.8/59.5 to 59.3/64.8, and 7B from 60.1/63.6 to 64.7/67.0, despite unchanged Table 3 per-task scores. These are revised summaries, not demonstrated performance gains between versions. New Table 7 reports 23.16 seconds/sample for textual CoT versus 0.32 for SSR.

M1.justification: The Depth Pro inputs, CLIP/SigLIP encoders, Mamba-based MIDI module, latent projection, training losses, and optional second training stage are retained. Expanded descriptions do not establish a change to the proposed algorithm.

P1.justification: Changes include localized grammar corrections, expanded quality-control and heatmap explanations, two additional analysis subsections, revised author affiliations, and funding acknowledgments. Most prose and the main section and appendix organization are retained.

P2.justification: v3 adds three substantive tables for general VQA, efficiency, and alternative-judge evaluation; expands comparator tables; and restructures the benchmark-results and dataset-statistics tables. Figure 6 relocates with its discussion. Figure 1 corrects the interpreter label and an example answer; the other illustrations are retained.

R1.justification: v3 adds RoboRefer to related work and adds references supporting the new baseline and benchmarks, including VQASynth and What’s Up; the MME reference is removed. The introduction also redirects a depth-utilization critique from diffusion references to SpatialBot. The overall research positioning remains intact.

T1.justification: The mathematical architecture descriptions and losses in Equations (1)–(2) are unchanged. Neither version introduces formal theoretical results or proofs; the expanded heatmap discussion adds interpretation rather than mathematical derivation.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens validation of existing claims. Table 7 supplies measurements for the previously unmeasured inference-efficiency claim, while Table 8 shows that SSR’s advantage persists under GPT-4o-mini judging. Broader external evaluations and the SpatialVLM comparison strengthen performance evidence, and the filtering description improves reproducibility. MME results are lost, timing documentation remains limited, and statistical uncertainty is still absent, but the targeted new checks provide a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SSR framework, SSR-CoT dataset, and SSRBench benchmark. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, appendices A–F, and checklists are readable and support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v3 retains original empirical results and adds benchmark evaluations, an efficiency comparison, and an alternative-judge evaluation.

before.justification: v1 reports original dataset-quality measurements, benchmark results, training-stage ablations, latent-representation analysis, and case studies.

results.title: SSR: Enhancing Depth Perception in Vision-Language Models via Rationale-Guided Spatial Reasoning

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction contributions and conclusion retain the same claims about memory-efficient gradient/momentum projection, stable feature learning, AltLoRA's transformation invariance, convergence and empirical advantages. Additional appendix material supports existing claims without changing their main scope.

C2.justification: Appendix D.2 adds an explanation of why combining aligned second moments with first moments can break invariance and suggests unscaled gradients/momentum as a possible remedy. It also adds an argument about neglected joint-update cross terms in LoRA-Rite. AltLoRA+'s lack of transformation invariance was already acknowledged in v1.

D1.justification: V2 supplies explicit AltLoRA+ pseudocode, instructions for alternating gradient computation in Transformers, and the regularization value λ=10^-6. Appendix E.1 discloses training subsets of 52k/100k/100k examples, method-specific learning-rate grids and the 3000-step limit. These substantially improve documentation of existing methods and experiments; the code-access statement remains unchanged.

E1.justification: Both use WizardLM/MT-Bench for dialogue, MetaMathQA/GSM8K for mathematics, CodeFeedBack/HumanEval for code, and the same five GLUE tasks. Appendix E relocates existing evaluations without adding dataset or task coverage.

E2.justification: Comparator membership matches in the LLM, GLUE and efficiency comparisons, including the existing LoRA-Pro and LoRA-Rite comparisons where applicable. The relocated updating-strategy, expert-count and initialization studies also retain their comparator sets.

E3.justification: Previously stated models, ranks, scaling factors, target layers, optimizer defaults, schedules, batch sizes and evaluation metrics remain unchanged. Appendix E.1 newly discloses sample counts, learning-rate grids and the 3000-step limit for existing experiments; it does not establish a protocol revision.

E4.justification: Learning-rate/scaling-factor sensitivity, rank comparisons, alternating versus joint updates, expert counts and initialization were already studied in v1. V2 moves several studies into Appendix E.3 without adding or changing their analyses.

E5.justification: Both specify three runs with different random seeds and mean/standard-deviation reporting for the generation and GLUE experiments. V2 repeats three-seed averaging in Appendix E.1 without introducing a different uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: Reported table values and both heatmaps are unchanged. V1 Tables 5, 6, 7 and 8 correspond to v2 Tables 6, 7, 8 and 5. For example, rank-8 AltLoRA+ still scores 76.91±0.31 on GSM8K with Llama-3.1-8B.

M1.justification: The alternating projection and momentum-update procedure remains unchanged. AltLoRA+ was already described and evaluated in v1; its explicit Algorithm 2 and the regularized projection formulas in v2 supply missing documentation without establishing a changed method.

P1.justification: The document is substantially reorganized: Related Work moves from Section 2 to Appendix A, and detailed ablations and additional Llama-3 results move into Appendix E. The main ablation narrative is shortened, sections and cross-references are revised, and technical material is organized into new appendices. Most retained prose changes little.

P2.justification: V2 adopts NeurIPS formatting with a redesigned title/author block, different typography, margins and algorithm styling. Several tables and Figure 2 move into the appendix, and Algorithm 2 gains an explicit display. The existing figures and table contents remain unchanged despite the extensive layout revision.

R1.justification: V2 adds four mathematical references supporting pseudoinverses, matrix factorization, convex neural-network formulations and RIP, and replaces the original Llama citation with Llama 2. Appendix D.2 adds positioning against LoRA-Rite's invariance analysis. The existing related-work discussion is otherwise principally relocated.

T1.justification: Appendices B and D supply mathematical material absent from v1: projection derivations, regularized corollaries, a formal stable-feature-learning definition and analysis, the momentum-invariance argument, and explicit RIP/cross-correlation assumptions and convergence bounds. These substantially expand the formal support for previously stated claims.

improvement.justification: V2 remedies important reproducibility omissions: v1 references unavailable appendices and lacks explicit AltLoRA+ pseudocode and key training/search details, which v2 supplies. The theoretical appendices also make assumptions and arguments inspectable. These are substantial gains despite unchanged empirical results. The added convergence proof still contains an unjustified inequality transition from Eq. 57 to Eq. 58, limiting the improvement in theoretical substantiation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs are readable versions of the same AltLoRA work, with matching core equations and empirical material. V1 cites appendices but ends after its references; v2 supplies Appendices A–E, whose contents can be assessed as newly documented material.

after.justification: V2 retains these original experiments in the main text and Appendix E, including benchmark results, efficiency measurements and ablations.

before.justification: V1 reports original fine-tuning results, memory and training-time measurements, and ablations in Tables 2–8 and Figures 1–2.

results.title: AltLoRA: Towards Better Gradient Approximation in Low-Rank Adaptation with Alternating Projections

C1.justification: V1 primarily guarantees detection and leaves recovery conjectural. V2's introductory Theorem 1.9 guarantees both strong detection and weak recovery for the compressed estimator when beta exceeds 0.76. The abstract and main theorem also qualify the earlier general claim of a unique signal-strength threshold.

C2.justification: V2 explains that general signed signal distributions may permit repeated appearance and disappearance of outliers. It qualifies BP/AMP efficiency and initialization comparisons and discusses applicability beyond the assumed random-matrix models in Appendix B. Existing dense-signal and compression limitations largely remain.

D1.justification: Appendix A changes the code-access pointer from an anonymous repository to the named NonlinearLaplacian GitHub repository. Appendix B documents graph preprocessing and vertex selection. Existing architecture, training hyperparameters, hardware and runtime disclosures remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Appendix B adds dense-subgraph search on the 297-vertex C. elegans network, a limited extension to real graph data. Planted-clique numerical experiments were already mentioned in v1 Section 4.2; displaying them in v2 does not establish newly introduced coverage.

E2.justification: Direct spectral estimation remains the evaluated comparator, including in the added graph results. The compared nonlinearity families are retained. Correcting the discussion of cited AMP methods to BP does not introduce a newly evaluated baseline.

E3.justification: Appendix B introduces a protocol that makes the network binary and symmetric, selects 15 vertices using leading eigenvector coordinates, and measures the fraction of possible edges present. Existing synthetic-data and MLP settings are retained; Figure 5 uses the Figure 2 setup.

E4.justification: V2 adds a real-network applicability case study and compares the new theoretical eigenvector predictions with simulations in Figure 2. Figure 5 explicitly illustrates the planted-clique correspondence. The parameter-sensitivity and cross-distribution transferability analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Figure 2 still reports averages over 500 inputs with plus/minus one standard deviation, and MLP optimization still uses 10 random initializations. Figure 5 adopts the existing uncertainty-reporting practice; no new statistical estimation or significance-testing procedure is introduced.

E6.justification: Appendix B newly reports 65% versus 73% edge density for 15-vertex subgraphs found by naive spectral and nonlinear-Laplacian methods. Figure 2 adds theoretical overlap predictions, and Figure 5 displays results identified as planted-clique validation, although one caption sentence inconsistently names the Gaussian model. Existing tuning thresholds and transferability values are retained.

M1.justification: Definition 1.5 extends the explicitly defined compressed algorithm from detection to recovery using Vv1(tilde L). Appendix B adds extraction of vertex subsets from the eigenvector's largest coordinates. The nonlinear-Laplacian construction and three approaches to tuning sigma remain unchanged.

P1.justification: V2 expands introductory motivation and related-work explanations, streamlines proof exposition, changes the eigenvector-analysis subsection from challenges to a proof, and adds Appendix B. The main section organization and most method and experimental prose remain intact.

P2.justification: Figure 2 adds theoretical eigenvector markers and adjusts its vertical-axis presentation. A new Figure 5 displays the planted-clique comparison; the original transferability figure becomes Figure 6 without substantive display changes. Overall formatting is retained, although the new Figure 5 caption contains inconsistent model identification.

R1.justification: Section 1.7 adds connections to combined linear/spectral estimators, optimized phase-retrieval methods, robust AMP and large-scale eigenvector computation. It corrects the characterization of HWX17 and DM15 as dense BP rather than AMP. References supporting the new proof and network example are added, while some references tied to replaced arguments are removed.

T1.justification: Theorem 1.8 gains an explicit eigenvector-overlap limit, proved through eigenvalue differentiation and convexity in Section 3.5. Definition 1.1 relaxes subgaussianity to a finite third absolute moment and the sparsity lower bound from omega((log n)^c/n), c>6, to omega(log n/n). Sections 2.2 and 3.1–3.2 replace concentration and complex-analysis arguments with simpler convergence arguments. The unique-threshold guarantee is restricted to nonnegative signals.

improvement.justification: V2 addresses an important theoretical gap: recovery was conjectural in v1, whereas Theorem 1.8 and Section 3.5 provide an explicit overlap formula and proof for the compressed estimator. Weaker assumptions and a corrected threshold scope further strengthen the central contribution. These gains outweigh limited reporting weaknesses in the added empirical material, particularly Figure 5's inconsistent caption and the sparsely specified real-network example.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same nonlinear-Laplacian research. Their main text, equations, figures, references and appendices are readable and support comparison, including v2's new Appendix B.

after.justification: V2 retains these original results and adds an explicit planted-clique comparison figure and a C. elegans network experiment in Appendix B.

before.justification: V1 reports original Gaussian planted-submatrix simulations, numerical optimization of nonlinearities, sensitivity analysis and transferability results in Figures 1–5.

results.title: Nonlinear Laplacians: Tunable principal component analysis under directional prior information

C1.justification: The dataset contribution, VLM-driven fusion contribution and headline SOTA claim remain. v4's introduction and conclusion add a more explicit mechanistic claim about complementary failure modes, including a generative-monocular versus discriminative-stereo characterization. This refines the scientific framing without replacing the central contributions.

C2.justification: v4 adds explanations involving conflicting monocular priors and planar-label bias, acknowledges the ablation's EPE tradeoff, and introduces computational-cost and composite/novel-illusion limitations. The LoRA-potential caveat disappears. Booster interpretation changes from 'ours best' to favoring monocular methods, especially DepthPro, although unchanged Table 2 supports only region- and metric-specific advantages.

D1.justification: The appended material supplies loss definitions, data-processing pseudocode and thresholds, filtering/video-generation prompts, calibration details, LoRA targets, and training resources: four H100 GPUs, batch size six per GPU and approximately 20 days. Tables 1–2 explicitly identify fine-tuning status. v4 also adds direct dataset and model access links alongside the existing code link. These are major documentation additions, not evidence that all underlying procedures changed.

E1.justification: v4 extends evaluation beyond illusion-depth benchmarks to ordinary-scene generalization on Middlebury (Table 5) and qualitative 3D object detection using YOLO3D on real illusion images (Appendix C.5, Figure 15). These introduce a distinct scene regime and downstream task. The original five illusion categories remain.

E2.justification: The quantitative comparator sets in Tables 1–2 are unchanged; DA V2 abbreviates DepthAnything V2. Appendix Figure 12 adds a comparator labelled 'Moge' alongside the proposed method and existing depth baselines. YOLO3D is a downstream case study, not a competing depth-fusion method.

E3.justification: v4 adds fine-tuning versus no-fine-tuning controls, Sparse/Dense augmentation comparisons, half-resolution whole-image Middlebury evaluation without a maximum-disparity restriction, and an H100 resource benchmark at 1920×1080. Section 3 also replaces 178,912 training frames with 'over 200,000', although Appendix C.2 still lists components totaling 178,912; actual dataset expansion is unresolved.

E4.justification: The original module ablation is retained as Table 6. New analyses test whether fine-tuning monocular and stereo baselines resolves illusions, evaluate confidence-map errors under zero-shot transfer, and illustrate VLM recognition and downstream detection failures. These substantially expand the investigation of adaptation, reliability and failure modes.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental run counts, seeds, error bars, confidence intervals or significance tests. v4's approximately 20% confidence-map error evaluates a model output; it is not uncertainty reporting across experimental runs.

E6.justification: All numerical entries in the original Tables 1–2 and module ablation are unchanged. v4 adds substantial results: its Marigold fine-tuning comparison reports illusion-region EPE changing from 21.16 to 13.67 while bad2 worsens from 65.67 to 74.82; Middlebury EPE is 1.50 for the proposed method. Confidence error, additional stereo fine-tuning results, and 53,959 MB/4.77 s per iteration resource measurements are also newly reported.

M1.justification: The dual-branch prediction, flow-matching confidence and affine-alignment fusion remain. However, v4's introduction and Figure 4 depict RGB-only input to the VLM, replacing v1's RGB plus monocular and binocular maps, while v4 Section 4.2 still specifies all three inputs. This inconsistency prevents establishing whether the actual input procedure changed. Newly documented losses alone do not establish a method revision.

P1.justification: The introduction, dataset explanation, experimental narrative and conclusion undergo extensive rewriting. Separate dataset-result subsections are consolidated into 'Influence of 3D Visual Illusions', ablations are reorganized, and a dedicated discussion places expanded limitations before the conclusion. Appendices organize the additional technical material; author and publication information also change.

P2.justification: v4 redraws Figure 4, adds fine-tuning columns to Tables 1–2, introduces new experimental tables and appendix algorithm displays, and places the original Figures 5–6 side by side at reduced size. Appendix figures add pipeline, calibration, VLM and detection displays and extend qualitative comparisons, while reusing some original examples. The original ablation table is relocated and renumbered.

R1.justification: v4 adds references for Black Forest Labs' FLUX, Flask and Mousavian et al.'s 3D bounding-box estimation work. The stereo, monocular-depth and VLM related-work organization and most research positioning remain intact.

T1.justification: The main geometric reasoning and Equations 1–10 are retained. Appendix A.2 explicitly formulates normalized constrained plane fitting, while Appendix B.1 defines weighted disparity losses and focal confidence supervision, including its binary target (Equations 11–14). These add mathematical specification, without new theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: v4 substantially addresses v1's missing reproducibility documentation through included losses, processing algorithms, prompts and implementation details. New fine-tuning controls test whether ordinary adaptation suffices, while Middlebury and resource measurements clarify generalization and practical cost. These gains outweigh the remaining weaknesses, including inconsistent VLM-input descriptions and training-frame counts, and an overgeneralized Booster interpretation. The improvement rests on better methodological assessability and substantive controls, not higher scores in the unchanged original comparisons.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same dataset and VLM-driven depth-fusion work, with readable text, equations, tables and figures. The supplied v1 ends with references; v4 includes Appendices A–C. Their added documentation can be compared without assuming that every newly described procedure is newly introduced.

after.justification: v4 retains those empirical results and adds fine-tuning comparisons, Middlebury evaluation, confidence-map analysis, computational measurements and qualitative appendix studies.

before.justification: v1 reports original evaluations on 3D-Visual-Illusion and Booster in Tables 1–2 and a Booster module ablation in Table 3.

results.title: 3D Visual Illusion Depth Estimation

C1.justification: v1 claims a first architecture for learning function-to-scalar mappings. v2 explicitly builds on previous functional approximators and centers the contribution on Hamiltonian PDE solvers, functional-derivative learning and neural-field parameterization. The central accuracy, conservation and temporal/OOD generalization claims are retained.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations of PINO as soft regularization, differing data requirements across PDEs, and architecture-dependent resolution/domain generalization. It also develops a cylindrical-approximation explanation, discusses case-dependent coefficient/source extensions, and adds quadrature-scalability concerns and qualifications about hardware and accuracy matching in solver timing comparisons.

D1.justification: v2 specifies the numerical-solver CPU, explains the lack of GPU compatibility, and distinguishes PyClaw's Fortran implementation from the Python KdV solver. Its checklist points to configuration files, while Table 1 removes the approximate 30-second toy-training estimate. The repository disclosure, core hyperparameter tables and numerical implementation instructions are retained.

E1.justification: The toy functionals and three PDE families remain. Appendix B.5 adds spatial-domain extrapolation for Advection, testing on [0,32] after training on [0,16], extending the evaluated input conditions. The coefficient and bathymetry cases in C.3 are derivations, not additional evaluated datasets.

E2.justification: PINO and Transolver, previously only cited, become evaluated SWE comparators in Table 3 and Figure 4, adding physics-informed and attention-based comparisons. Table 6 also adds analytical/numerical solver timing comparisons. Existing MLP, FNO and Unet comparisons are retained.

E3.justification: Existing benchmark splits, metrics and numerical integration settings are retained. New B.3–B.5 introduce cumulative architecture controls with approximately matched parameter counts, training subsets from one-eighth to full size, and resolution tests using downsampled or re-solved validation labels. B.2 adds CPU solver timing averaged over ten samples, substantially extending the evaluation design.

E4.justification: The existing Hamiltonian-error and inductive-bias analyses remain. New B.3 tests kernel nonlinearity, conditioning, SIREN architecture and receptive field; B.4 tests training-data requirements; B.5 tests resolution and spatial-domain generalization. Table 7's caption ambiguously includes SIREN in the base model despite a subsequent '+ SIREN' row.

E5.justification: The reported seed count for 1D PDE results increases from three to six. Table 1 newly specifies averages over six seeds; v1 did not state its toy-experiment run count. SWE results retain three-seed mean-and-standard-deviation reporting, and no new significance-testing framework is introduced.

E6.justification: Tables 1 and 2 contain revised estimates alongside changed seed reporting. For example, KdV Unet correlation time changes from 125.7 to 134.0, while derivative-Unet changes from 127.4 to 113.3. Original SWE comparator scores remain unchanged, but PINO/Transolver scores, solver timings, architecture/data-size/discretization results and revised plotted examples substantially expand the reported evidence.

M1.justification: The evaluated kernel architecture, gradient-training objective and Adams–Bashforth inference procedure remain unchanged. New Appendix C.3 proposes coefficient-conditioned inputs or output scaling, and source-field inputs or additive gradient corrections. These are proposed procedural extensions, without corresponding experimental validation.

P1.justification: The title, abstract and framing paragraphs are revised, and NF/HNF terminology largely becomes IKF/HNS. Related Works moves before a consolidated Conclusion containing Limitations and Outlook; appendices gain subsections and a checklist. Most background, core method and retained experimental prose remains closely matched, so the editorial reworking is limited relative to the substantive additions.

P2.justification: Figures 2–7 are redrawn or reformatted with changed legends, colors, scales or example trajectories; Figure 4 adds comparator curves. Tables 3 and 6 expand, and three new multi-experiment tables present architecture, dataset-size and discretization studies. The original hyperparameter tables are retained as Tables 10–12.

R1.justification: A dedicated Functional Approximation discussion acknowledges neural integral functionals, parameter-to-observable maps, functional autoencoders and generative neural operators. Additional discussion connects the work to density-functional theory and cylindrical approximation. This substantially revises the research positioning and replaces the blanket function-to-scalar architecture priority claim.

T1.justification: The original linear-approximation proof is retained. New C.2 develops gradient expressions connecting global nonlinear kernels to cylindrical approximation, and C.3 derives coefficient/source-term extensions. However, Eqs. 26–28 are internally inconsistent: applying J to the added ghb term differentiates h as well as b, so it does not recover the stated bathymetry source term.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses important attribution and validation weaknesses: it replaces the broad architecture-priority claim with explicit recognition of predecessors and adds relevant comparators, controlled ablations, generalization studies and increased 1D replication. These substantially strengthen the retained solver's empirical case. The inconsistent Table 7 caption and incorrect bathymetry source-term recovery in C.3 weaken particular additions, but do not outweigh the improvements to the central contribution's positioning and support.

A1.justification: Despite the changed title and NF/HNF-to-IKF/HNS terminology, both PDFs describe the same kernel-integral Hamiltonian solver. Their complete text, equations, figures, tables and appendices support comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds evaluated baselines, architecture ablations, training-data-size studies, discretization tests and numerical-solver timings.

before.justification: v1 reports original functional-fitting experiments, Advection/KdV/SWE simulations, Hamiltonian-conservation analyses, inductive-bias ablations and inference timings.

results.title: Hamiltonian Neural PDE Solvers through Functional Approximation

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the central claims: joint velocity–growth modeling derived from semi-relaxed optimal transport, accurate state/mass reconstruction, and improved scalability and training efficiency. The added experiments support these existing claims without materially redefining their scope.

C2.justification: v2 adds a Malthusian-growth rationale for time-independent growth, an accumulated-error explanation for distribution fitting, and spatial/temporal interpretations of predictive uncertainty. Appendix B.8 links learned growth and gene-gradient rankings to Acinar/Ductal proliferation, adding substantive biological interpretation. The existing limitations concerning simulation dependence and potentially misleading observed cell counts remain.

D1.justification: v2 changes the code-release promise into a stated release with a concrete repository link in the abstract and checklist. Appendix B.6 newly identifies POT/emd and GeomLoss and explains gradient handling; new analyses document dropout, resampling and gene-selection details. Most architecture, batching and preprocessing information was already present in v1.

E1.justification: v2 adds developing mouse Pancreas data at days 14.5 and 15.5, evaluated using 2,000 highly variable genes, extending real biological coverage beyond the retained embeddings. It also introduces a biased-observation scenario by perturbing simulated branch proportions. Simulation Gene, Dyngen, Gaussian, EB, CITE and mouse hematopoiesis coverage remains.

E2.justification: Table 2 removes WLF-UOT from the EB/CITE hold-out comparison while retaining the other named comparators. Tables 3 and A-10 introduce comparisons with Sinkhorn-loss variants. The mouse hematopoiesis comparator set is unchanged, matching v1 Table A-6 to v2 Table A-9.

E3.justification: Section 4 revises the warm-up learning rate from 10^-4 to 10^-3 and the general warm-up schedule from 200–800 iterations to 500 for synthetic and 5,000 for real datasets. Appendices change Simulation Gene epsilon from 0.001 to 0.003, EB/CITE tau from 30 to 5, Dyngen batch size from 32 to 60, and hematopoiesis fitting epochs from 50 to 100. New analyses introduce additional evaluation protocols. These are reported setting changes; the PDFs do not establish which retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Appendices B.2, B.6 and B.8 add intermediate-time growth-rate validation, branch/time uncertainty analysis, sampling-bias robustness, Sinkhorn regularization sensitivity, and Pancreas mean–variance and gene-attribution analyses. The Pancreas experiment also tests the distribution-fitting loss. v1's CITE training/hold-out loss curves in Figure A-14 are replaced by a with/without-loss trajectory comparison; the EB convergence analysis remains.

E5.justification: v1 lacks predictive uncertainty estimation or explicit repeated-seed reporting. v2 introduces variance estimation using dropout at rate 0.1 with five stochastic forward passes and reports sampling-bias results averaged over three random seeds (Tables A-7–A-8). This substantially adds statistical estimation, although main benchmark tables still lack error bars or significance tests. It does not establish increased run counts for retained benchmarks.

E6.justification: Table 2 revises VGFM's CITE W1 values from 0.650/34.182 to 0.745/37.386 and DeepRUOT's from 0.648/35.539 to 0.845/38.681; OT-MFM now leads both CITE columns. These accompany changed training settings and are not controlled across-version performance differences. Table 1 replaces UDSB's Gaussian W1/RME of 25.304/0.965 with nonconvergence. Substantial additions include Pancreas W1/RME of 24.416/0.017, growth correlations of 0.980–0.996, uncertainty and bias results, and Sinkhorn-variant scores and timing.

M1.justification: v2 adds VGFM(*), which replaces the original Wasserstein distribution-fitting loss with Sinkhorn divergence (Table 3; Appendix B.6). Appendix B.2 also introduces dropout-based uncertainty inference. These are limited adaptations; the original semi-relaxed transport construction, joint matching formulation and training algorithm remain.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main section order are retained. v2 expands explanations in Sections 3.4 and A.4, adds focused experimental subsections and Appendix B.8, and includes acknowledgments and a NeurIPS checklist. These are localized narrative and structural extensions rather than a broad rewrite.

P2.justification: v2 substantially expands the displays with five new experimental tables and Pancreas Figures A-15–A-18. Figure 2 is redrawn and relabeled, several trajectory plots are revised, Table 3 gains a variant row, and Figure A-14 replaces CITE loss curves with trajectory comparisons. The existing hematopoiesis table is merely renumbered from A-6 to A-9.

R1.justification: Section 2 adds optimal-transport application context, and references expand to recent unbalanced-dynamics work, Malthusian growth, Sinkhorn divergences and the Pancreas dataset. The Deep Momentum Multi-Marginal Schrödinger Bridge citation is removed. The central positioning against velocity-only flow matching and existing unbalanced dynamics models remains.

T1.justification: Appendix A.1 corrects Equation A-15 by restoring the density factor p_t(x) inside the Benamou–Brenier kinetic-energy integral. The central proposition, endpoint-equivalence theorem, their proofs and the growth-energy minimization argument remain substantively unchanged.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens evidence for biological applicability and reliability: it adds real 2,000-gene evaluation and interpretation, directly quantifies growth accuracy at unseen times, and tests sensitivity to biased observations. These address important gaps in v1's scalability and growth-validation evidence. The code-access information and corrected transport formula also help. The gains outweigh reduced comparator coverage and localized reporting problems, including conflicting RME values between Tables 3 and A-10 and claims of Sinkhorn improvement that overlook mixed metric outcomes.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same VGFM research, with matching authors, central formulation and retained experiments. Their text, equations, tables, figures and appendices A–C are readable and support reliable comparison; v2 additionally contains a conference checklist.

after.justification: v2 retains original experimental results and adds Pancreas evaluations, growth-rate correlations, predictive uncertainty estimates, sampling-bias tests and Sinkhorn-loss experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original VGFM experiments on synthetic and real single-cell datasets, including quantitative comparisons, loss ablations and mouse hematopoiesis results in Appendix B.

results.title: Joint Velocity-Growth Flow Matching for Single-Cell Dynamics Modeling

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, and discussion retain the same central claims about invariant representations, symmetric encoders, and competitive performance with simpler implementation. The additional experiments support these claims without redefining them.

C2.justification: The new appendices interpret encoder gains as portable across action/camera configurations, identify C8 as preferable among the tested discretizations, and explain EquiDiff's dependence on external viewpoints. Existing limitations concerning occlusion, computational cost, and the absence of physical-robot validation remain.

D1.justification: Appendix C newly documents random cropping, encoder feature dimensions, and variant-specific UNet widths, while removing the RTX 4090 attribution for training times. v3 adds a project-site link and statements about supplementary code and a planned public repository; actual public availability cannot be established from the PDFs.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same MimicGen tasks, Robomimic demonstration populations, and ImageNet-1k pretraining source. The new experiments reuse existing tasks and camera configurations; they expand model comparisons and controls rather than dataset or task coverage.

E2.justification: The existing Diffusion Policy and image/voxel EquiDiff comparisons remain. Table 5 adds an encoder-augmented EquiDiff variant alongside ordinary EquiDiff and Diffusion Policy variants; the other added comparisons predominantly reuse existing method families.

E3.justification: Appendices E–H substantially expand the controlled evaluation design across encoder, camera, and action configurations, including proprioception removal, C2/C4/C8 groups, and EquiDiff with only an in-hand camera. The principal demonstration budgets and evaluation schedule remain unchanged. Appendix C also qualifies v1's general two-observation-step setting: pretrained variants use one visual step and two proprioceptive steps, without establishing that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's action-representation and encoder comparisons, v3 adds targeted component ablations, proprioception removal, symmetry-group sensitivity, and EquiDiff camera controls in Tables 6–9. Appendices E–F additionally test whether encoder benefits transfer across observation/action configurations and policy architectures.

E5.justification: Existing three-seed means and standard errors are retained, and the checklist repeats this practice. However, new Tables 7–8 report only point estimates, making uncertainty reporting uneven despite the checklist's claim that all experiments include standard errors. No increased run count or new significance procedure is documented.

E6.justification: Tables 1–3 are unchanged, but Tables 4–9 add substantial results. Examples include 64.9% for dual-view Pretrain + FA, 63.2% versus 53.5% for augmented versus ordinary EquiDiff on four tasks, and 40.9% for in-hand-only EquiDiff. These concern additional configurations. Section 5.1 also corrects relative-action wins from 11 to 10 of 12 tasks in the in-hand setting.

M1.justification: The invariant representations, Frame Averaging construction, and original diffusion-policy method are retained. Appendix F/Table 5 additionally combines Pretrain + FA with EquiDiff, a limited architectural adaptation beyond v1's use of EquiDiff as an unmodified comparator.

P1.justification: The original narrative and section organization remain largely verbatim. Changes include limited grammatical corrections, affiliation and venue updates, acknowledgments, expanded training documentation, and additional appendix and checklist sections rather than extensive rewriting.

P2.justification: Tables 4–9 substantially expand the empirical presentation with multi-view comparisons, architecture comparisons, a component-ablation matrix, and sensitivity tables. Existing Figures 1–5 and Tables 1–3 are retained; Table 3 is relocated above Appendix C, with accompanying page reflow.

R1.justification: The same 75 references, related-work discussion, and central novelty positioning are retained. Additional appendix citations reuse existing sources without substantially changing the relationship to prior research.

T1.justification: The action definitions, SE(3) propositions and assumptions, Frame Averaging equations, and proofs in Appendices A–B are unchanged.

improvement.justification: The new controlled comparisons and ablations in Tables 5–9 substantially strengthen evidence for modularity and clarify previously untested component and camera dependencies. Expanded implementation details also improve reproducibility. These gains outweigh limited new reporting flaws: Tables 7–8 omit uncertainty, and Appendix E describes a 2.5-point camera gap although Table 4 implies 3.5 points.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable, and retained content can be matched reliably across the expanded appendix.

after.justification: v3 retains those original experiments and adds encoder comparisons and controlled ablations in Tables 4–9.

before.justification: v1 reports original robotic policy-learning experiments on 12 MimicGen tasks in Tables 1–2 and Robomimic evaluations in Appendix D/Table 3.

results.title: A Practical Guide for Incorporating Symmetry in Diffusion Policy

C1.justification: The abstract's advertised GPT-2 final-loss reduction increases from 5.6% to 9.3%, and the introductory Table 1 caption adds superiority across the newly reported language-model metrics. The central contributions concerning optimal control, plug-and-play integration, robustness, generalization, and parameter efficiency remain unchanged.

C2.justification: v2 adds an explicit computational-overhead tradeoff and explains mitigation through smaller models and fewer integration steps (Appendix B). It also interprets lower perplexity as lower predictive uncertainty and argues that the sensitivity results reduce the need for tuning. The existing theoretical applicability limitations are retained.

D1.justification: v1 promises code release upon publication; v2 states that code is public and supplies a repository address. v2 also adds forward-propagation pseudocode and measured per-iteration runtime. Most previously documented architectures, hyperparameters, training budgets, and GPU specifications are retained.

E1.justification: The original datasets and tasks are retained, but v2 substantially expands evaluation conditions: character replacement for nanoGPT, point dropout for ModelNet40, and Gaussian and uniform image noise for MNIST. These introduce explicit corrupted-input scenarios across text, point clouds, and images.

E2.justification: The original accuracy/loss comparator sets, including the N-ODE Transformer comparisons, are retained. The new nanoGPT timing comparison includes a Standard Continuous-time Transformer alongside the baseline and OT-Transformer (v2 Table 4), extending comparator participation in that experiment.

E3.justification: v2 introduces controlled test-time corruption levels and nanoGPT sweeps over regularization strengths from 0.01 to 5 and integration-step counts from 1 to 20. Evaluation also expands to perplexity, BERTScore, BLEU, ROUGE, and iteration time. The reported configurations and training budgets of the original experiments remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's regularization comparisons and learning curves, v2 directly tests robustness to four corruption types and sensitivity to regularization strength and integration steps (Tables 3 and 5). These address whether the stability benefits survive input corruption and depend on particular hyperparameter choices.

E5.justification: The retained experiments keep their three- or five-trial mean/standard-deviation reporting and the single seeded OpenWebText trial. The new sensitivity study follows the existing three-trial practice. No new confidence intervals, significance tests, or uncertainty-estimation procedures are introduced.

E6.justification: OpenWebText OT-Transformer best/final losses change from 3.02/3.03 to 2.90/2.91, while baseline values remain 3.20/3.21, without a stated configuration change. v2 also adds substantial corruption, sensitivity, timing, and language-metric results. For example, at 10% character replacement, Table 3 reports losses of 4.60 for the baseline and 2.42 for OT-Transformer.

M1.justification: The Transformer-parametrized dynamics, OT velocity regularization, and discretized training procedure in equations (7)–(9) remain unchanged. The new side-by-side pseudocode in Algorithm 1 documents the existing method rather than introducing a new component.

P1.justification: Related Work moves from main-text Section 5 to Appendix A, and subsequent sections are renumbered. New explanatory appendices and a NeurIPS checklist expand the document, alongside localized wording, caption, affiliation, and acknowledgement edits. Most existing prose and the central narrative are retained.

P2.justification: v2 adds robustness, runtime, sensitivity, and noisy-text perplexity tables, a perplexity illustration, and side-by-side algorithm pseudocode. The nanoGPT and OpenWebText tables gain metric columns, substantially changing their displays. Existing experimental tables and figures are also repositioned within the reorganized appendices.

R1.justification: v2 adds seven references covering corruption protocols, language-generation evaluation, and Transformer stability under layer normalization. Appendix A adds a short discussion of the latter work. The existing positioning relative to N-ODE Transformers, OT-based continuous normalizing flows, and other theoretical analyses remains substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: The distributional-robustness proof in v1 Appendix E.1/v2 Appendix H.1 corrects an equality to an inequality when applying the Lipschitz bound after equation (78). v2 also specifies 1-Lipschitz functions in the Kantorovich-duality discussion. The principal theorems, assumptions, and remaining derivations are retained.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens support for a central claim: v1 inferred empirical robustness largely from clean-test performance, whereas v2 directly evaluates corrupted text, images, and point clouds. Sensitivity tests and runtime measurements also make tuning dependence and computational costs assessable, while pseudocode and code-access information improve reproducibility. These gains outweigh localized reporting weaknesses, notably the unexplained clean-data perplexity differences between Tables 10 and 11.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same OT-Transformer work. Their main text, figures, tables, equations, and appendices are readable and support reliable matching despite reorganization and additions in v2.

after.justification: v2 retains these empirical results and adds corruption tests, hyperparameter sensitivity experiments, runtime measurements, and language-model metrics in Section 5 and Appendices B, C, and I.

before.justification: v1 reports original experiments on classification, sentiment analysis, and text generation, with numerical results and learning curves in Section 6 and Appendix F.

results.title: Optimal Control for Transformer Architectures: Enhancing Generalization, Robustness and Efficiency

C1.justification: The abstract and principal contributions retain the same claims: SOLiD can induce honesty or evasion, with detector accuracy, exploration, and KL regularization determining outcomes. The DolusChat contribution and conditional training recommendations remain the same; the added experiments support these claims without redefining them.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive qualifications and mechanisms: KL coefficients need model-specific interpretation; extended-MASK's weaker evasion may reflect task diversity, sample availability, and reward-model capacity; implicit-knowledge errors may not constitute lying; and noisy LLM preferences may smooth the deception transition. Appendix A updates the single-dataset and simplified-labeller limitations accordingly. These materially refine applicability and interpretation.

D1.justification: v2 supplies full LLM-labelling and MASK-generation prompts in new Appendices K and L, alongside Claude-4-Sonnet synthesis instructions, seed-example selection, split sizes, rating-logit extraction, and the expensive-labeller warning. It documents the model-specific KL adaptation. These substantial additions make the new experiments more reproducible; existing hyperparameters, compute disclosures, and code/data links are retained.

E1.justification: v1's training and principal evaluation use DolusChat. v2 adds a synthetic extension of five MASK subdatasets (C.11), covering multi-turn conversations, implicit factual knowledge, false-statement continuations, and disinformation generation. This materially broadens task and input coverage beyond DolusChat's context-grounded response pairs.

E2.justification: The existing GRPO/DPO, scalar/categorical reward-model, activation/SAE detector, SFT/original-model, and SOLiD-Defer comparisons are retained. Gemma, Qwen, and the larger Llama model are additional backbones for the studied procedures, rather than newly introduced competing methods.

E3.justification: v2 adds Llama-3.3-70B policy training with DPO, whereas v1's 70B result concerns detector accuracy only. New Gemma/Qwen GRPO experiments test KL coefficients 0.1 and 0.05. Extended-MASK uses 21,048 training, 5,261 detector-training, and 1,384 test examples, and C.13 introduces an LLM-labelling experimental condition. The original DolusChat settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 substantially extends robustness checks of the detector-TPR and KL relationships across model families and under LLM-generated preferences (C.10 and C.13). It also adds reward-score diagnostics for extended-MASK (Figure 19), investigating why this setting produces less evasive deception. The original ablations and qualitative cases are retained.

E5.justification: C.13 newly specifies that the LLM-labelling results cover 16 labelling runs; it does not establish 16 seeds per condition or an increase in repetitions of existing experiments. The general reporting convention of at least two random seeds and plus-or-minus one standard deviation remains unchanged, as does the judge-validation uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Existing experimental plots and table results are retained, while v2 adds substantial findings. The 70B DPO policy stays below roughly 25% deception; Qwen becomes more deceptive with weaker KL regularization; extended-MASK remains majority truthful even at the lowest tested TPRs. C.13 reports cheap-labeller preference for undetected lies at 62.86% and expensive-labeller preference for flagged lies at 4.96%, plus a smoother policy-deception trend. These are additional results under new conditions.

M1.justification: The core SOLiD pipeline and existing SOLiD-Defer variant remain unchanged. v2 adds an LLM-scored labelling variant using expected ratings from output logits (C.13), and changes GRPO's KL placement to before advantage normalization for the added Gemma/Qwen experiments (C.10). These are localized procedural adaptations.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main section order are retained. Changes include localized language corrections, an expanded Section 5.6, revised limitations, a clearer C.9 heading, a NeurIPS checklist, and additional appendix sections. Existing generation and evaluation prompts move from K/L to M/N without substantive rewriting.

P2.justification: v2 adds six experimental figures: 12, 16–19, and 22, substantially expanding the visual evidence with model-family, scale, MASK, and LLM-labelling displays. Existing plots are retained and redistributed, flowcharts replace 'Label' with 'Preference', and error-bar captions are clarified. Tables 1–4 retain their content and structure.

R1.justification: v2 adds references for MASK, Gemma 3, and Qwen3, and changes evaluation-hacking attributions to Brown, Niven and Kao, and Wen, replacing the earlier Sun and Oren references. The overall positioning relative to deception detection and training against monitors remains stable.

T1.justification: Appendix D's cost and expected-reward derivations are retained. v2 C.11 adds a limited conditional mathematical observation: if the reward model treats detection as random rather than distinguishing detected from undetected lies, truthfulness is optimal unless detector TPR falls below one-third. No substantial new proof framework is introduced.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially reduces v1's dependence on one designed dataset, one model family, and imposed preference assumptions through targeted additional experiments. Extended-MASK's different behavior and the model-specific KL findings sharpen the paper's applicability boundaries, while detailed prompts support reproducibility. Synthetic data, proxy labellers, and untested capacity explanations remain limitations, but the new evidence directly addresses important weaknesses acknowledged in v1 and materially strengthens the paper.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SOLiD/DolusChat study. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support reliable comparison, with retained material identifiable despite additions and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains those experiments and adds original results for additional model families, a 70B DPO policy, extended-MASK data, and LLM-based preference labelling.

before.justification: v1 reports original DolusChat experiments comparing GRPO and DPO, detector accuracy, KL regularization, model scale, and detector variants, alongside qualitative analyses.

results.title: Preference Learning with Lie Detectors can Induce Honesty or Evasion

C1.justification: The abstract's scientific claims and central contribution remain stable. The introduction adds a claim of state-of-the-art performance against advanced world models, extending v1's emphasis on improvements over its pretrained base models without redefining the framework's main contribution.

C2.justification: v2 develops new interpretations linking Rope underperformance and eventual transfer degradation to overfitting and insufficient diverse pretraining. Section 7 adds explicit qualifications about same-dataset video pretraining and diffusion-model RL being outside the study's scope. These substantially expand the discussion of generalization mechanisms and applicability boundaries.

D1.justification: Appendix A.4.2 supplies implementation information for the new benchmarks, including splits, resolutions, histories, proprioception quantization, model depth, group size, and planning embeddings. v2 also explicitly states that code, datasets, models, and video samples are available at the previously linked project website. Existing computational-resource descriptions and prompt examples are retained.

E1.justification: v2 adds PushT tabletop pushing and simulated Rope and Granular deformable-object prediction, substantially broadening video coverage beyond RT-1. It also evaluates goal-directed control on PushT. Existing text-game, web, and RT-1 coverage is retained.

E2.justification: Beyond v1's base-model and repetition-rejection video comparisons, v2 Table 4 adds R3M, ResNet, DINO CLS, DINO-WM, and AVDC comparisons. Table 12 adds control comparisons with IRIS, DreamerV3, TD-MPC2, and DINO-WM. Table 4 distinguishes published baseline scores from the authors' evaluation of a public DINO-WM checkpoint.

E3.justification: New protocols include 7B text-game evaluation, dataset-specific video splits and observation histories, six-layer models for Rope/Granular, GRPO groups of 32, joint training, and PushT planning. Additionally, v1 Table 7 to v2 Table 8 changes the reported RT-1 RLVR learning rate from 1e-5 to 5e-5; unchanged existing scores do not establish that experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds a repetition-penalty experiment testing non-differentiable rewards and elimination of repetition. Appendix A.4.2 adds learning-curve and overfitting analyses, joint versus separate pretraining comparisons, and cross-task transfer tests after tuning on only Rope or Granular. The original metric, group-size, and test-time-scaling analyses remain.

E5.justification: Both versions' Table 3 reports means and standard deviations over three sampling runs; the added repetition-penalty row follows that convention. v2 introduces no new seed counts, confidence intervals, significance tests, or uncertainty-estimation procedures.

E6.justification: Existing result entries are retained, while v2 adds substantial results: 7B overall accuracy of 65.53% versus 51.76% after SFT, three-dataset LPIPS/SSIM comparisons, joint-training and transfer outcomes, and PushT control success of 0.86 versus the base model's 0.80. The added penalty variant achieves zero repetition, with scaled LPIPS 13.7 versus 13.4 without the penalty.

M1.justification: The core tokenization-and-GRPO framework remains unchanged. v2 adds a repetition-penalty reward variant, incorporates proprioceptive MSE into PushT rewards, and uses DINOv2 embeddings for comparing predicted and goal frames in PushT planning. These are localized procedural adaptations.

P1.justification: The introduction receives localized explanatory expansion, Section 7 is reorganized into algorithmic and foundation-model issues, Appendix A.4 gains dataset-specific subsections, and acknowledgements are added. Most existing prose, section order, and prompt content are preserved.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is redesigned with training-stage annotations and moved to the first page. v2 expands Tables 1 and 3, adds the benchmark comparison in Table 4, analysis Tables 9–11, control Table 12, and qualitative Figure 10. This substantially expands the visual presentation beyond renumbering and pagination.

R1.justification: v2 adds citations and contextual discussion for DINO-WM, AVDC, visual encoders, the added datasets, and concurrent DanceGRPO/Flow-GRPO work. These extend comparative positioning and acknowledge related diffusion-model developments, while the existing related-work survey and central research positioning remain largely unchanged.

T1.justification: The existing MDP, sequence-modeling, GRPO, MLE, and reward formalism is unchanged in substance. Writing prediction horizons using T and moving the advantage formula inline do not add mathematical reasoning. Neither version contains a theoretical development that is substantively revised in v2.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses v1's limited evidence about video-model competitiveness beyond its own RT-1 baselines. External comparisons across additional environments, joint-training and transfer tests, and PushT control evaluation strengthen the assessment of generality and practical utility. Explicit discussion of overfitting and scope limits improves calibration. Imported comparator scores and limited uncertainty reporting constrain the new claims, but do not outweigh this substantial improvement in empirical support.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe RLVR-World. Their complete main texts and appendices, including equations, tables, figures, and prompt examples, are readable and support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments and adds 7B language-model results, additional video benchmarks, joint-training and transfer analyses, and PushT control results.

before.justification: v1 reports original text-game and web-state prediction experiments, RT-1 video prediction, model analyses, web-agent control, and simulated policy evaluation.

results.title: RLVR-World: Training World Models with Reinforcement Learning

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction contributions and conclusion retain the same central claims: autonomous regulation through SBT-E/D, adaptive training-data construction, and approximately 30–60% token savings with comparable mathematical accuracy. New appendix evidence does not redefine these headline contributions.

C2.justification: v3 adds substantive interpretations of component necessity, internal reasoning-sufficiency representations, cross-domain transfer and aggressive/balanced/conservative threshold regimes. Appendix A's limitations remain unchanged. The new beta discussion in Section 5.4 incorrectly reverses Equation 3's weighting direction, and Appendix D overstates threshold 0.2's accuracy optimality for SBT-D.

D1.justification: The printed repository and project access addresses change from CCAI-Lab to ZJU-REAL. Existing implementation disclosures, including Megatron-LM, training hyperparameters, Ascend training hardware, A100 inference hardware and construction pseudocode, remain substantively unchanged. The PDFs do not establish whether resource availability changed.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates mathematical reasoning only. v3 Appendix C adds MMLU-Redux general-knowledge reasoning and GPQA-Diamond graduate-level science evaluation across the four model configurations, substantially extending domain coverage. OpenR1-Math training and the original mathematical benchmarks remain.

E2.justification: v3 adds a without-MRT comparison in Tables 4/14 and a No Guidance comparator to the guidance experiment in Tables 7/17. The original baseline and other comparison variants remain; no external competing algorithm is newly benchmarked.

E3.justification: Added analyses introduce component-removal controls, beta values 0.05–0.2, additional thresholds 0.05, 0.1 and 0.5, and early-exit stratification and average-step measurements. These extend the experimental settings; the retained experiments preserve their model sizes, training budget, temperature 0.7 and eight samples per question.

E4.justification: v3 adds direct masking and no-guidance ablations, beta sensitivity, broader threshold robustness tests, and analyses of spontaneous stopping and reasoning depth. Appendix C also tests transfer from mathematical training to other domains. These substantially expand the investigation beyond v1's retained threshold, masking-length, granularity and guidance comparisons.

E5.justification: Both versions report averaging accuracy over eight samples per question. v3 introduces no new seed information, repeated-training-run reporting, confidence intervals, error bars or significance-testing procedures.

E6.justification: The original main benchmark results and matched ablation entries are unchanged, but substantial new results appear. For example, v3 Table 4 reports 57.83% accuracy and 1,673 tokens with MRT versus 58.02% and 2,306 without it. New Table 10 reports GPQA-Diamond accuracy of 24.24% for Llama-3.2-1B SBT-E versus its 17.99% baseline; this is a newly reported comparison, not a performance increase over v1.

M1.justification: The proposed SBT-E and SBT-D procedures, overthinking score, loss masking and natural-language braking mechanism are unchanged. Algorithms 1–2 match across versions. The new component-removal experiments are ablations, not revisions to the proposed method.

P1.justification: Related Works moves from Section 5 to Section 2, the title changes from LLMs to LRMs, and acknowledgements and local explanatory rewrites are added. Most existing introductory, methodological, concluding and limitations prose is retained; the added scientific sections do not constitute extensive rewriting of that material.

P2.justification: v3 adds substantial tabular presentation for component ablations, beta sensitivity, early exits, adaptive reasoning depth, domain transfer and extended thresholds, including detailed appendix breakdowns. Guidance tables gain a comparator row. Table captions move above tables and new tables wrap beside prose, while Figures 1–3 are retained.

R1.justification: v3 adds a related-work paragraph covering reasoning robustness and scalability, with new citations including S3c-Math, InftyThink and EasySteer, plus citations for the added benchmarks.
