The existing research taxonomy and SBT's positioning remain substantially intact; publication-metadata updates are not new cited works.

T1.justification: The reasoning-efficiency, marker-ratio and composite-score definitions in Equations 1–3, the token-level alternative, and the algorithmic formulations are retained. Neither version provides formal theorems or proofs; the added sensitivity discussions do not introduce new formal theory.

improvement.justification: v1's evidence was confined to mathematics and lacked direct removal controls for masking and braking guidance. v3 addresses these important gaps through non-mathematical transfer tests and component ablations, supplemented by broader sensitivity and stopping-behavior analyses. The reversed beta explanation and overstated threshold-optimality language weaken parts of the interpretation, but the added controlled and cross-domain evidence substantially strengthens the paper's empirical support.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Self-Braking Tuning work. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable and support comparison after matching relocated and renumbered content.

after.justification: v3 retains those original experiments and adds component ablations, sensitivity studies, autonomous-stopping analyses and evaluations on non-mathematical benchmarks.

before.justification: v1 reports original fine-tuning experiments across four model configurations and mathematical benchmarks, along with trajectory analyses and ablation results.

results.title: Let LRMs Break Free from Overthinking via Self-Braking Tuning

C1.justification: The central claims about effective low-label SGPO and ensemble-guided exploration remain. The introduction and Discussion now single out DAPS as strongest overall, replacing the earlier emphasis on CG and DAPS jointly, and add an explicit performance claim against latent-space Bayesian optimization with APEXGo.

C2.justification: The Discussion adds explanations involving APEXGo's trust-region calibration and latent-space geometry, and suggests selecting guidance strength using sample uniqueness and novelty. It removes the limitation that only proteins with many homologs were studied, while retaining qualifications concerning oracle generalization, native functions, and limited fitness labels.

D1.justification: v2 documents GB1 augmentation and oracle training, and adds APEXGo implementation details, training epochs, and acquisition budgets in Appendix A.6. ARLM preparation and steering hyperparameters are updated. The existing code-access information, architecture tables, and hardware discussion remain substantially unchanged.

E1.justification: v2 adds GB1 binding optimization across all 56 residues alongside TrpB enzyme activity and CreiLOV fluorescence (Table 2). This introduces another protein family and fitness objective, with evaluations spanning prior generation, steering, and adaptive optimization.

E2.justification: Figure 6 newly evaluates APEXGo and adds Continuous+NOS to the adaptive comparison, whereas NOS previously appeared only in single-round steering comparisons. Appendix A.4.4 also substantively revises the ARLM+DPO baseline from ranked to weighted loss.

E3.justification: Appendix A.1 replaces variable-length, gap-removed ARLM training fragments with gap-filled sequences and introduces mutations near sequence starts. Table A3 changes the DPO learning rate from 1e-4 to 1e-6 and selected beta from 2 to 0.1, and expands NOS parameter sweeps. GB1 and APEXGo also introduce additional training and evaluation protocols.

E4.justification: The existing NOS sensitivity analysis expands to varying step size and iteration count as well as lambda. Appendix A.4.4 adds qualitative checks of DPO learning-rate failure and alternative loss performance. The ensemble-versus-single-model ablation remains unchanged in Table A4 and v1 Figure A6/v2 Figure A7.

E5.justification: Both versions report ten standardized steering datasets with standard-deviation error bars in Figure 5 and five random initializations for adaptive experiments and ensemble analyses. New results extend these practices without changing repeat counts or introducing new uncertainty-estimation or significance-testing procedures.

E6.justification: v2 adds extensive GB1 results, including oracle Pearson correlations of 0.89 for training, validation, and testing in Figure A1, plus new APEXGo and Continuous+NOS adaptive results. ARLM, DPO, and NOS results on retained tasks are also revised under changed settings, so they are not same-setting performance gains. Table A4's numerical entries remain unchanged.

M1.justification: The proposed discrete DAPS procedure, classifier guidance, and ensemble-based adaptive optimization in Algorithm 1 remain unchanged. The revised DPO loss concerns the comparison baseline; added benchmarks and preprocessing revisions do not introduce a new proposed method component.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and Discussion receive localized rewrites and clarifications. Affiliations, conference information, and acknowledgments expand, and a new APEXGo subsection precedes the appendix results. The main section sequence and most technical exposition are preserved.

P2.justification: Figure 5 and the novelty figure expand from six to nine panels, while Figure 6 changes from a two-by-two model/task grid to three dataset panels with revised legends. GB1 oracle and prior displays are added, Figure 3 gains a latent-optimization branch, and Tables 1–2 expand. The ensemble-diversity figure is retained and renumbered.

R1.justification: Sections 1–2 and Table 1 substantially expand positioning relative to zero-shot design, adaptive search, GFlowNets, and latent-space optimization, including Jain et al. (2022) and Torres et al. (2024). Brookes et al. (2019) is reclassified from Generative: Adaptive to SGPO, and the claimed gap in prior adaptive optimization is softened. These are substantive changes beyond publication-metadata updates.

T1.justification: Equation 21 changes the formal DPO objective by adding fitness weights to the previously unweighted ranked-loss expression. The diffusion and guidance equations, DAPS approximation and convergence discussion, and adaptive algorithm otherwise remain unchanged; no new proof is supplied.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the comparison by addressing v1's acknowledged NOS/DPO tuning concerns, adding the relevant APEXGo baseline, and testing GB1 binding with a much smaller natural MSA. These changes improve the fairness and breadth of evidence supporting the central conclusions. The new GB1 training count in Table 2 is not clearly reconciled with Appendix A.2's split description, and oracle-generalization limitations persist, but these qualifications do not outweigh the stronger comparative evidence.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SGPO study and contain readable main text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices. Shared content can be matched reliably despite additions, revisions, and figure renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains original computational experiments and adds GB1 evaluations and additional adaptive-optimization comparisons, including APEXGo.

before.justification: v1 reports original computational experiments on TrpB and CreiLOV, including oracle validation, guided generation, adaptive optimization, and ensemble analyses.

results.title: Steering Generative Models with Experimental Data for Protein Fitness Optimization

C1.justification: The central claims about learning positive-eigenvalue KEFs, resolving degeneracies, and designing perturbations remain. The abstract and contribution list broaden the claimed demonstration scope from task-trained RNNs up to 64D to a 668D RNN fitted to mouse neural recordings.

C2.justification: v2 adds qualifications about non-square-integrable KEFs, instantaneous perturbations, stochastic dynamics, and uncertainty in fitted flows. It also offers an explicitly speculative explanation of FTLE gradient limitations. The existing limitations concerning full access to the dynamics and absent approximation-error guarantees remain.

D1.justification: v2 adds a GitHub code-access link, optimization pseudocode, input-scaling information, and detailed per-system sampling distributions and covariance construction in Appendix G.1. However, it removes v1's explicit relaxed perturbation objective, and architecture and sampling descriptions conflict between the main text, Appendix F, and Table 1/G.1.

E1.justification: v2 adds a 668D RNN fitted to mouse neural recordings, extending evaluation beyond task-trained neural networks to a data-fitted neural application. Synthetic systems, ecological dynamics, limit cycles, and flip-flop tasks remain covered. The dimensionality sweep expands configurations of the existing flip-flop task.

E2.justification: The kinetic-energy contrasts and perturbation comparisons against the target-attractor direction and sampled separatrix points remain. FTLE/LCS methods are newly discussed and cited, but are not added as empirically evaluated comparators.

E3.justification: Appendix H adds a 32–512D scaling experiment using a fixed depth-20, width-550 KEF network; v1's 64D demonstration specifies width 400. The new neural-data experiment fixes external input at 0.9 and introduces separate hyperparameters. Its architecture is inconsistently documented: Table 1 specifies depth 7 and width 1200, whereas Appendix F still assigns depth 20 and width 400.

E4.justification: Appendix H/Table 2 adds a focused scalability analysis testing how training time and curve-validation accuracy vary with RNN dimensionality. The existing degeneracy examples and eigenvalue-sensitivity analysis are retained as v2 Figures 9–10.

E5.justification: Both versions retain independently initialized KEF examples and randomized validation curves. v2 introduces no new performance-related run counts, seed reporting, confidence intervals, significance tests, or uncertainty estimates. Discussion of uncertainty in fitted dynamics is conceptual.

E6.justification: v2 Figure 8 replaces the main 64D validation display with new 668D validation and perturbation results: R² is 0.941, versus 0.995 for the different system in v1 Figure 7, so this is not a matched performance decline. Table 2 adds scaling results, including 128D: 572 seconds and R² 0.867; 512D: 718 seconds and R² 0.996.

M1.justification: The core PDE ratio loss, balance regularization, and ensemble framework remain. Appendix G.1 adds a limited sampling adaptation for the data-fitted RNN: constructing an anisotropic covariance from forward-evolved states, extending v1's isotropic Gaussian sampling recipe. Algorithm 1 otherwise largely restates the existing optimization.

P1.justification: v2 rewrites the KEF motivation, ensemble explanation, and perturbation setup, and adds acknowledgements and appendix subsections. The main section order and much of the existing prose remain; the revision does not extensively reorganize the narrative.

P2.justification: v2 adds the conceptual mapping schematic in Figure 2, redraws low-dimensional and limit-cycle panels with labeled log-kinetic-energy and absolute-KEF colorbars, and replaces the main high-dimensional result display. It also expands Table 1 and adds Table 2 and Algorithm 1. These exceed simple renumbering or numerical updates.

R1.justification: Section 2 substantially expands positioning through FTLE/LCS approaches and prior results connecting KEFs to stable manifolds. The discussion and Appendix H also add stochastic-modeling, active-learning, and high-dimensional PDE literature. These are substantive additions beyond the bibliographic updates to retained references.

T1.justification: New Appendix J introduces formal definitions, a constant-sign-near-attractors assumption, and Proposition 1 with a proof that a sign-changing KEF zero lies on the separatrix under these conditions. v1 contains illustrative analytical derivations but no corresponding proposition. This is a conditional, one-way result, not an approximation-error guarantee.

improvement.justification: The 668D neural-data application and dimensionality-scaling study substantially strengthen evidence for the paper's intended high-dimensional neuroscience use, which v1 supported mainly through a 64D task-trained example. Appendix J adds conditional theoretical support, while detailed sampling instructions and code-access information address reproducibility gaps. Conflicting settings and removal of the explicit perturbation penalty weaken documentation, but do not outweigh these substantial gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work and provide readable main text, figures, tables, equations, and appendices. The retained material can be matched across renumbering, with appendices A–I in v1 and A–J in v2.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds separatrix and perturbation analyses of a 668D neural-data-fitted RNN, plus dimensionality-scaling results.

before.justification: v1 reports original KEF-training, separatrix-validation, and perturbation experiments on synthetic systems, an ecological model, and trained RNNs, including a 64D example.

results.title: Finding separatrices of dynamical flows with Deep Koopman Eigenfunctions

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction contributions and conclusion retain the same central claims: adaptive LLM-guided exploration, plug-in compatibility across discrete and continuous RL algorithms, and performance improvement up to 37.27%. The additional evidence does not redefine these claims.

C2.justification: V2 supplements the general hallucination limitation with specific skewed-output failure hypotheses and initial-state conditions under which state-agnostic guidance may fail. It adds interpretations of history, prompting and cost trade-offs, removes the speculation that GPT-4o is too sophisticated, and discusses capability limitations using the new Qwen-size results.

D1.justification: V2 adds per-task runtime and API-cost profiles, explicit prompts for automatic-description variants, and window/threshold settings for adaptive updates and safeguards. The original hardware and base hyperparameters remain. Documented code access changes from the anonymous repository to a named GitHub repository.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same 15 Atari and five MuJoCo tasks. The additional experiments reuse this coverage. The reversed-starting-position scenarios in Appendix J.3 are hypothetical, not newly evaluated environments.

E2.justification: The original comparator sets are retained, including NoisyNet and RND in Appendix C and the RL algorithms in Figure 3. The added time-budget comparison reuses NoisyNet; Qwen models and safeguards are configurations or variants of LLM-Explorer.

E3.justification: V2 adds a wall-clock-matched comparison using 500k LLM-Explorer steps and additional NoisyNet training steps, plus evaluations varying Qwen model size, trajectory history, adaptive-update thresholds and prompting/safeguard configurations. It also introduces KL-based diagnostic metrics. These supplement the retained original training settings.

E4.justification: V2 adds model-size sensitivity, history-length tests, adaptive-update comparisons, automatic-description and template/example ablations, and failure diagnostics with safeguard experiments on Qbert and Seaquest. These investigate substantial new questions beyond the retained workflow and M/K ablations.

E5.justification: Both versions average three random seeds and report standard-deviation bands in learning curves. Added experiments follow the same averaging practice, without new confidence intervals or significance tests. The new KL summaries diagnose output skew rather than uncertainty in performance estimates.

E6.justification: Original benchmark values, including the 37.27% mean Atari improvement, are retained. V2 adds extensive results under additional conditions: Table 8 reports Alien scores of 414.79 versus 377.64 for LLM-Explorer and time-matched NoisyNet; Table 13 reports Qbert scores of 316.92 with KL clip (old) versus 301.97 without safeguards. Cost, model-size, history and prompting results are also new.

M1.justification: The core two-LLM pipeline remains unchanged, but Appendices G–J substantially extend the evaluated procedures: multiple-episode inputs, reward-progress-triggered updates, automatic task descriptions, KL-based fallback safeguards and selection between two generated distributions. These are implemented experimental variants, rather than replacements for the default method.

P1.justification: Most existing prose is retained. Section 4 gains a computational-overhead subsection and revised trade-off organization; appendix headings and references are adjusted. V2 also adds acknowledgments and a NeurIPS checklist and updates author footnotes and conference identification.

P2.justification: V2 adds substantial tabular displays for computational cost, model sizes, trajectory history, update scheduling, automatic descriptions, KL diagnostics and safeguards in Tables 1, 5 and 8–14. Existing tables are renumbered and some relocated; Figures 1–9 retain their content.

R1.justification: V2 adds references to Self-Consistency and Self-Refine, connecting them to the safeguard experiment and possible future mitigation. The existing references, related-work discussion and central novelty positioning remain unchanged.

T1.justification: The MDP formulation and equations (1)–(3) are retained. Neither version provides theoretical proofs. V2 adds empirical KL diagnostics and procedural heuristics, without new formal propositions, assumptions or derivations.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens assessment of practicality and reliability. V1 reported token consumption and left hallucination mitigation to future work; v2 adds runtime/API costs, an equal-wall-clock NoisyNet comparison, failure diagnostics and tested safeguards. The additional sensitivity and prompting studies clarify design choices and applicability. These gains outweigh minor new reporting inconsistencies, including the duplicated template-only description in Appendix I and conflicting Alien baseline values in Tables 7 and 9–10.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same LLM-Explorer work. Their text, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable, and retained content can be matched despite additions and renumbering.

after.justification: V2 retains those empirical results and adds computational-cost measurements, controlled comparisons and experiments on method variants in Section 4 and Appendices F–J.

before.justification: V1 reports original Atari and MuJoCo training results, baseline comparisons, component ablations and sensitivity experiments in Section 4 and the appendices.

results.title: LLM-Explorer: A Plug-in Reinforcement Learning Policy Exploration Enhancement Driven by Large Language Models

C1.justification: The abstract's central claims—that individually fair classifiers can produce unfair ecosystems and fairness adjustment can worsen ecosystem fairness—remain unchanged. The introduction and discussion add explicit claims covering Equalized Odds and Demographic Parity, while the introduction removes the explicit first-paper assertion.

C2.justification: The discussion adds a regulatory tradeoff between ecosystem fairness and competition benefits, and specifies remaining utility-model limitations. Appendix C.2 newly characterizes the subset experiment's harm magnitude as small. Appendix B.2.1 also adds an incorrect explanation that increasingly accurate DP classifiers have correlations approaching zero; perfect nonconstant classifiers instead have correlation one.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code-repository pointer in Section 5 and documents the Adult prediction target, input features, and protected attribute in Appendix C.4. The existing Fairlearn reference and approximate home-computer runtime disclosure are retained.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates only Lending Club loan repayment prediction, using mortgage status as the protected attribute. v2 adds Adult Census Income prediction above $50,000, with gender as the protected attribute, substantially extending the evaluated population, prediction task, and domain.

E2.justification: Both versions compare ecosystems before and after the same fairness adjustment; no alternative mitigation baseline is introduced. The added random forests serve as ecosystem participants in three-classifier experiments, rather than comparison methods against a proposed algorithm.

E3.justification: The original experiments retain their stated settings. Appendix C adds independently sampled training sets, three-classifier configurations, and Adult experiments with White/non-White training partitions. It also introduces the after/before EOC ratio, conditional on worsening, as an additional evaluation measure.

E4.justification: v2 adds analyses of how large fairness deterioration is when it occurs, and tests its persistence under independent training samples and three-classifier competition (Appendix C.1, C.3, and C.5). These substantially extend the earlier prevalence analysis. The different-borrower-subsets experiment in C.2 already existed in v1.

E5.justification: Both versions state 500 repetitions per training size for Experiments 1–3 and report standard errors and 95% confidence intervals. The added tables extend the existing uncertainty-reporting practice to additional outcomes; no changed run count, seed disclosure, or new inference procedure is stated.

E6.justification: All four original likelihood-CI rows are preserved in v2 Tables 1 and 3. Tables 2 and 4–12 add conditional effect sizes and results for the additional experiments. Section 5 also changes the reported 100k harm frequencies for Experiments 1 and 2 from 30.0% and 15.6% to 30.1% and 15.8%, despite retaining their confidence intervals.

M1.justification: The classifier training and Fairlearn fairness-adjustment approach are retained; no new learning or postprocessing algorithm is proposed. Revised fairness definitions are theoretical changes, while random forests enter as components of additional evaluation configurations.

P1.justification: Proofs are consolidated into Appendix A, while the earlier appendix's utility and multiple-lender extensions move into Section 3. Experiment 4 moves to Appendix C. The model, related-work discussion, contribution roadmap, and concluding discussion are substantially reorganized or rewritten.

P2.justification: The document adopts a substantially denser conference layout with redesigned title and author blocks and different typography. v1's four-row Table 1 is split between v2 Tables 1 and 3, and ten additional tables present effect sizes and new experiments.

R1.justification: v2 adds Bower et al. (2017) and Dwork and Ilvento (2019), acknowledging their prior insight that individual classifier fairness need not compose. It replaces v1's broad priority positioning with distinctions based on decentralized competition, parallel decisions, correlations, and quantified unfairness. This substantively revises the relationship to the closest prior research.

T1.justification: Section 2 replaces unconditional WE/WEC welfare definitions with v-EO/v-EOC definitions conditioned on Y=1, a substantive mathematical revision. Appendix B adds EDC/DPC definitions and corresponding bounds and derivations. The utility and multiple-lender extensions now in Sections 3.1.1–3.1.2 already appeared in v1 Appendix A.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the evidence beyond v1's single-dataset harm frequencies through Adult results, conditional harm magnitudes, and independent-training and three-classifier checks. It also acknowledges important prior composition research. Conditioning welfare on Y=1 resolves the mismatch between v1's unconditional welfare definition and EO. The new claim that near-perfect classifiers' correlations vanish is incorrect, but this localized explanatory flaw does not outweigh the empirical, definitional, and positioning gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their complete text, equations, tables, and appendices are readable, and retained content can be matched across the reorganization.

after.justification: Section 5 and Appendix C retain those experiments and report additional Adult, independently sampled training, and three-classifier experiments, together with harm-magnitude results.

before.justification: Section 5 reports four original Lending Club experiments. Table 1 gives confidence intervals for the frequency of ecosystem fairness worsening after individual fairness adjustment.

results.title: Fairness under Competition

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction add conversion of pretrained RoPE transformers into PaTH through continued training as a headline contribution. This substantially extends the contribution beyond v1's attention mechanism and training-from-scratch experiments, while retaining the original expressivity and generalization claims.

C2.justification: New Section 6 identifies BF16 instability, the need to clip beta, larger-head computational costs, and limitations concerning rotational inductive biases. Section 4.3 adds tentative explanations for math/code gains and explicitly discusses conversion failures in extensively trained models. These introduce substantive applicability boundaries and failure qualifications absent from v1.

D1.justification: v2 adds conversion token budgets, the 1:1:1 continued-pretraining mixture, the SmolLM2 checkpoint stage and access link, and a BF16 beta-clipping requirement. Existing kernel links and Appendix B's optimizer, hardware, and training-time details remain. The clipping disclosure does not establish that the earlier experiments changed.

E1.justification: v2 adds DCLM, Python-Edu, and MegaMathWeb training data and expands evaluation to mathematical reasoning, program generation, and knowledge benchmarks, including GSM8K, MATH, TheoremQA, HumanEval, MBPP/MBPP+, MMLU, and GPQA Diamond. The original synthetic, language-modeling, and long-context coverage is retained.

E2.justification: The original experiments retain their comparator sets, including RoPE, SBA, and FoX. New Table 4 additionally reports an uncontinued Base teacher control alongside the RoPE and FoX comparison rows, providing a limited expansion of the baseline comparisons.

E3.justification: The original 760M-model, 50B-token, 4096-context setup is unchanged. Section 4.3 adds conversion experiments with SmolLM2-1.7B before WSD decay and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, specifying 100M-token and 3B-token distillation stages and 21B-token continued pretraining for the SmolLM2 experiment. The Qwen experiment omits continued pretraining.

E4.justification: Table 5 adds a case study of converting an extensively trained Qwen model, revealing task-dependent losses as well as gains. This supplements the retained OOD and length-generalization analyses. Because model identity and continued-pretraining conditions differ between the conversion studies, it is not a controlled ablation of pretraining history.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed counts, repeated-run counts, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The added conversion tables retain the existing practice of reporting point scores without uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: Tables 4–5 add substantial conversion results. Table 4 reports PaTH scores of 20.1/25.6/51.3 on GSM8K/HumanEval/MBPP+, alongside RoPE's 19.9/23.1/47.1. Table 5 reports mixed Qwen conversion outcomes: HumanEval falls from teacher 82.32 to student 77.44, while TheoremQA rises from 18.12 to 21.88. These are new experiments; the original tables, plotted findings, and appendix benchmark scores remain unchanged.

M1.justification: The underlying PaTH and PaTH-FoX mechanisms remain, but Section 4.3 introduces a substantial conversion procedure for pretrained RoPE models: attention-output MSE distillation, output KL distillation, and subsequent continued pretraining. This adds training objectives and a training pathway absent from v1.

P1.justification: The narrative largely retains its structure, with a new conversion subsection and limitations section, a renamed Appendix B, condensed related work, and localized wording corrections. The preprint footer becomes a NeurIPS 2025 conference footer. These edits do not amount to extensive rewriting or reorganization.

P2.justification: v2 adds conversion Tables 4–5 and renumbers the existing appendix tables as 6–7. Existing figures retain their plotted content while moving with text reflow. Equation displays are rearranged and boxed, and highlight colors are softened; the overall visual format remains similar.

R1.justification: v2 adds RADLADS as the conversion precedent, references for new data and models, and connections to ENTP and Causal Attention with Lookahead Keys. It shortens the positional-encoding survey and removes several references, including Cable, ModuleFormer, and the automata-cascade citations. The central positioning relative to RoPE, algebraic positional encodings, and linear RNNs remains.

T1.justification: Section 3.1 corrects attention products from Q^T K to Q K^T and the UT expression from WDW^T to DWW^T, repairing dimensional inconsistencies. Section 3.3 corrects boundary-key block indices from j to i. The NC1 and FFLM theorem statements and Appendix A proofs are unchanged.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens practical applicability by demonstrating conversion of existing 1.7B and 7B models, addressing a question left open by v1's 760M training-from-scratch experiments. Reporting conversion failures alongside successes, correcting dimensionally inconsistent equations, and documenting concrete stability and efficiency limitations also improve reliability. Conversion details remain incomplete and the proposed explanation involving extensive prior training is not isolated experimentally, but the evaluated conversion pathway and clearer applicability boundaries provide a substantial net gain.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe PaTH Attention and contain complete, readable main texts and appendices. The methods, equations, figures, tables, and proofs can be matched reliably despite reflow and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds pretrained-model conversion experiments using SmolLM2-1.7B and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct in Section 4.3.

before.justification: v1 reports original synthetic-task experiments, kernel timing measurements, 760M-parameter language-model evaluations, and detailed long-context results in Appendix B.

results.title: PaTH Attention: Position Encoding via Accumulating Householder Transformations

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, and conclusion retain the same central claims: the first non-autoregressive RDB generator, joint graph-conditioned generation, and superior inter-table fidelity across six databases. The additional experiments support practical applications without redefining these headline contributions.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive explanations of dimension tables as fixed metadata, graph-generator adequacy and its limits on more strongly correlated structures, DCR evidence concerning memorization, and size invariance from local GNN processing. These extend interpretation and applicability boundaries beyond v1's receptive-field discussion and general future-work paragraph.

D1.justification: v2 supplies a code repository link and states that reproduction instructions are available there. It documents dimension-table selection and counts, revised model and training configurations, and a hardware change from RTX 2080 Ti to A100-PCIE-40GB. Appendix E adds experimental procedures and reports generation within two hours for the scaling experiments.

E1.justification: The six synthesis databases remain unchanged, but Appendix E.2 extends evaluated task coverage to conditional missing-value imputation on California. It tests missing parent or child tables and missing rows or cells; v1 mentioned imputation only as a potential application.

E2.justification: Table 1 retains SDV, SingleTable, Denorm, and ClavaDDPM with unchanged participation. Within Table 2, a real-graph comparison variant replaces the separate neighborhood-size comparison, while Sequential remains. The comparator change is therefore confined to internal variants; new privacy and structural comparisons reuse ClavaDDPM.

results.title: MODEM: A Morton-Order Degradation Estimation Mechanism for Adverse Weather Image Recovery

R1.justification: v2 adds references for scaling laws, SAC, DMC, and the two Yarats papers supporting the added experiments. Its positioning relative to MoE, sparse training, and concurrent pooling approaches remains substantially unchanged; the updated publication information for Trumpp et al. is not a new cited work.

T1.justification: Section 2.1 adds the expectation operator missing from v1's definition of the action-value function, making a limited formal correction. The GAP equation and parameter-count expressions remain unchanged, and neither version supplies theoretical propositions or proofs.

improvement.justification: The continuous-control and additional-agent evaluations substantially strengthen evidence for generality beyond v1's discrete-action experiments. The added encoder control and sparsity/depth sweeps also test the central bottleneck explanation across previously unchecked conditions. Together these materially strengthen the empirical case, although added-agent specifications remain brief and the existing disagreement between four added encoder blocks in Section 3.2 and two in the experimental appendix remains unresolved.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same GAP study, with matching authors, central method, and experiments. Their text, equations, figures, table, and complete appendices support reliable comparison, including matching relocated and renumbered material.

after.justification: v2 retains these empirical results and adds SAC experiments on DMC, DrQ variants on Atari100K, and additional architectural and sparsity analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original Rainbow and DER experiments on Atari, Atari100K, and Procgen, together with architectural comparisons, training diagnostics, and appendix results.

results.title: Mind the GAP! The Challenges of Scale in Pixel-based Deep Reinforcement Learning

C1.justification: The abstract and principal contributions retain meta-learned data valuation, compute savings up to 46.6%, and generalization across 50M–1B evaluation models. Explicitly describing value as relative to the meta-objective restates a dependence already established in v1's formulation and limitations; the central scientific claims remain the same.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations linking scores mainly to document count, length, and non-alphanumeric content, and suggests unexplained regression variance may reflect patterns beyond the tested heuristics. It also explains population resets as promoting generalization across training stages. These extend the existing interpretation, while Appendix C's substantive limitations remain unchanged.

D1.justification: v2 specifies MixFlow-MG rematerialisation and saved inner gradients, clarifies FLOP accounting including filtering and oversampling, and documents the new analysis through heuristic definitions in Table 1, DataTrove provenance, feature normalization, and regularization settings. The existing hardware and training budgets are retained; no new DataRater code or dataset release is announced.

E1.justification: The Pile, C4/noclean, and C4 remain the training corpora, with the same validation, Wikipedia, and five downstream evaluations. The new comparisons and diagnostics use existing coverage. Corrupted-data examples and conversational fine-tuning extensions already appear in v1.

E2.justification: v1 evaluates filtering primarily against unfiltered training. v2 adds three evaluated perplexity filters adapted from Ankner et al. (2025): PPLX (Top), PPLX (Mid), and PPLX (Bot) in Figure 10, followed by detailed comparisons with PPLX (Mid) in Figure 11. This substantially expands the competing filtering methods.

E3.justification: Appendix A adds a dedicated comparison using 150M inner, scorer, and evaluation models, distinct from the main results' 400M inner models. Selected discard fractions are 90% for PPLX (Mid) and 75%/50%/25% for DataRater across the three corpora. New diagnostics use 25,600 Pile sequences. Separately, the reported cosine weight-decay schedule becomes cosine learning-rate decay, without establishing that earlier experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained scale, discard-fraction, and checkpoint analyses, v2 adds filtering sensitivity comparisons with perplexity methods, per-model meta-update norm traces, checkpoint score correlations, and heuristic correlation/OLS/Lasso analyses. Figures 10 and 12–15 substantially expand evidence about filtering behavior, stability, and what the scores capture.

E5.justification: v2 adds 10-fold cross-validation repeated five times for the Lasso analysis. This is a new statistical estimation procedure, not evidence of five repeated language-model training runs. Figure 9's existing 95% confidence intervals are retained; the new filtering comparisons do not add uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: Original Figures 1–9 and the numerical contents of v1 Table 1, now v2 Table 2, are retained. New Figure 11 reports DataRater best in 16 of 21 cases, PPLX (Mid) in four, and unfiltered training in one. New analyses report OLS R2=0.766, Lasso R2=0.753, and late-checkpoint score correlations above 0.95. These are additional findings, not improvements to the original same-setting scores.

M1.justification: Section 2 corrects the stated filtering rules: the oversampled batch size changes from N*rho/(1-rho) to N/(1-rho), and pointwise acceptance gains a binomial coefficient. These are limited corrections to the specified curation procedure; the architecture, meta-objective, and Algorithm 1 remain unchanged. The PDFs do not establish an implementation change.

P1.justification: The abstract, section order, and most existing prose are retained. v2 makes targeted implementation and related-work rewrites, adds explanatory paragraphs and named topics within Appendix A, updates cross-references, and expands acknowledgements. This is a localized narrative expansion rather than extensive restructuring.

P2.justification: v2 adds six substantive displays: filtering comparisons, update-norm traces, two correlation heatmaps, and regression coefficients in Figures 10–15, plus a heuristic-definition table. Existing Figures 1–9 are retained; the original performance table is relocated and renumbered as Table 2. The appendix's visual evidence is substantially expanded.

R1.justification: v2 adds Ankner et al. for perplexity filtering, Guo et al. for semi-supervised bilevel weighting, Li and Gong for multilingual reweighting, and the DeepMind JAX ecosystem reference. These modestly broaden positioning and attribution. The MixFlow-MG publication update represents the same cited work.

T1.justification: Section 2 inserts the missing binomial factor C(B-1,s) into the pointwise acceptance probability and corrects the oversampling expression. These repair mathematical statements underlying filtering. The main bilevel formulation and Appendix B's noise-based reasoning remain unchanged.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses an important weakness in v1: the absence of an evaluated alternative filtering method. The controlled perplexity comparisons, stability diagnostics, and score analyses substantially strengthen the empirical assessment, while corrected filtering formulas and added implementation details improve correctness and reproducibility. The new comparisons still lack uncertainty estimates, and regression residuals do not establish that unexplained patterns are valuable, but these limitations do not outweigh the substantive gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe DataRater: Meta-Learned Dataset Curation. Their full text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support reliable matching, including the retained results table and expanded Appendix A.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds perplexity-filter comparisons, meta-training diagnostics, and statistical analyses of learned scores in Appendix A.

before.justification: v1 reports original language-model training experiments, compute savings, downstream evaluations, filtering sensitivity analyses, and qualitative examples in Figures 1–9 and Table 1.

results.title: DataRater: Meta-Learned Dataset Curation

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same central contributions: LLM refinement of tree rules, gradient-based prediction correction, avoidance of sample serialization and LLM fine-tuning, and strong tabular prediction performance. The additional experiments support these existing claims rather than redefining them.

C2.justification: Appendix A.12 adds a concrete interpretation of refinement through feature importance and rule structure. Appendix A.14 newly acknowledges that advantages over conventional methods narrow as dataset size increases, and proposes limitations of independently trained Random Forest rules as an explanation. These materially expand the mechanism discussion and qualify applicability beyond v1's broadly favorable interpretation.

D1.justification: v2 supplies the previously absent algorithm listing, prompt template and output format, dataset properties, TALENT preprocessing and implementation references, leaf-model choices, and leaf-count information in Appendices A.1–A.4. It also adds a source-code access link. These substantially improve technical disclosure, although the PDFs alone do not verify the linked resource's availability.

E1.justification: Tables 19–20 add evaluation on rl, GiveMeSomeCredit binary classification, and Year regression beyond the original twelve tasks. Year substantially extends scale and dimensionality to 515,345 samples and 90 numerical features. GiveMeSomeCredit classification is a distinct task from the retained Credit_reg regression evaluation, regardless of possible overlap in their underlying data.

E2.justification: Appendix A.8, Tables 12–13, adds evaluated ResNet and SAINT comparators to the conventional-method comparison shown in v1 Figure 4. The main LLM comparator set is retained; additional related-work citations do not establish further evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: v2 reports additional 16-shot and 512-shot evaluations, plus 128-shot classification results, within the retained tasks. It also specifies Qwen3-32B backbone experiments and a one-to-ten-query sensitivity sweep. These extend the reported settings; the original accuracy and NRMSE metrics remain unchanged, and newly disclosed implementation settings do not establish changes to existing experiments.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's limited component ablation and visual analyses, Appendices A.6 and A.10–A.12 provide backbone sensitivity, expanded component combinations across all twelve original tasks, query-count sensitivity, and a Credit rule-refinement case study with SHAP analysis. These examine additional questions about component interactions and refinement mechanisms. Figure 8 merely redisplays the existing prediction visualization.

E5.justification: Tables 8–9 newly report standard deviations averaged across datasets for the LLM comparisons. However, v2 removes v1 Section 5's statement that performance is averaged over five independent runs. This changes uncertainty reporting without establishing that the number of runs increased or decreased.

E6.justification: The matched main-text tables and figures retain their results, while the appendices add extensive numerical entries for additional settings, baselines, ablations, and datasets. For example, Table 20 newly reports Year NRMSE of 0.8015 for DeLTa versus 0.8090 for FT-Transformer. These are additional results, not evidence of improved performance over v1 under identical settings.

M1.justification: Section 4 retains the same Random Forest rule extraction, LLM refinement, leaf-specific gradient prediction, and additive error correction in Equations 1–6. Appendix A.3 newly specifies CART for classification and TabPFN for regression within Gradient Net; v1 leaves that implementation open, so this establishes additional disclosure rather than a method change.

P1.justification: The main paper largely preserves its wording and section sequence, with small grammatical corrections, updated affiliations and conference information, and added acknowledgments. v2 appends a checklist and organized supplementary sections, but does not extensively rewrite or reorganize the existing narrative.

P2.justification: v2 adds substantial supplementary presentation: detailed dataset and result tables, expanded ablation tables, a sensitivity plot, and prompt and rule examples. Some displays repeat existing material, notably Table 14 reproducing Table 3 and Figure 8 reproducing Figure 5. The main figures remain substantively intact with layout and sizing adjustments.

R1.justification: v2 adds citations including PTaRL, DRL, TabNet, TabTransformer, TabR, TALENT, and SHAP, broadening supporting literature and documenting supplementary analyses. The main related-work narrative and the claimed distinction from serialization-based prediction and prior feature-generation work remain essentially unchanged.

T1.justification: Appendix A.5 adds a first-order Taylor-expansion argument for the existing loss-decrease proposition, explicitly invoking convex loss and an approximate negative-gradient correction. Its Proposition 2 restates the main proposition rather than introducing a separate theorem. The main definitions and Equations 1–6 are retained.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially closes reporting gaps left by v1's absent cited appendices. Concrete prompts and implementation choices, fuller comparisons and ablations, broader evaluation, and explicit scalability limitations make the method and its supporting evidence much easier to assess. The removal of the five-run statement weakens statistical transparency, and the added loss-decrease argument remains heuristic, but these limitations do not outweigh the substantial gains in completeness and empirical support.

A1.justification: Both PDFs are readable versions of the same DeLTa work, with matching methods and main experiments. The supplied v1 ends after its references despite citing appendices; v2 includes Appendix A.1–A.16. Newly supplied appendix content can be compared as documentation, without assuming the underlying work was newly performed.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and reports additional benchmark evaluations, backbone comparisons, sensitivity analyses, and a SHAP case study in its appendices.

before.justification: v1 reports original classification and regression experiments, runtime measurements, component ablations, and prediction visualizations in Section 5 and Figures 2–5.

results.title: LLM Meeting Decision Trees on Tabular Data

C1.justification: The central contribution remains sequential, Bayes-assisted PPI. V2 explicitly qualifies the abstract and introductory coverage claim as asymptotic and acknowledges the existing multivariate extension in its discussion, refining the scope and precision of the headline claims.

C2.justification: V2 substantially expands practical qualifications: it explains how preprocessing and monitoring start times affect coverage, attributes unsuccessful Bayes assistance on Genes to prediction bias, and discusses conservative multivariate regions. Section S6.3 also distinguishes predictive accuracy from task-dependent rectifier quality, while the discussion adds computational and delayed-start considerations.

D1.justification: V2 adds a Python implementation repository link, detailed preprocessing and grid-initialization instructions, and the previously unspecified Student-t prior degrees of freedom of 2. It reports Apple M4 Pro hardware with 24GB memory instead of the Intel i7-11850H and explicitly states the already-used parameter-free alternative's formula.

E1.justification: V2 retains the three original mean-estimation datasets and adds Census linear regression, Healthcare logistic regression, and Genes median estimation. It also evaluates five-dimensional mean estimation, substantially expanding coverage beyond v1's scalar-mean experiments.

E2.justification: Corresponding experiments retain the classical, PPI/PPI++, and Gaussian, Laplace and Student-t prior comparisons. The improper-prior alternative already appeared in v1 Section S9. Added tasks reuse existing comparison methods or subsets of them.

E3.justification: The biased-prediction simulation changes noise scale from 10 to 1, bias range from [-5, 5] to [-1.2, 1.2], and default t-star from 100 to 500. New experiments introduce filtering, logarithmic preprocessing, pilot-centered parameter grids, task-specific monitoring starts, and multivariate radius evaluation.

E4.justification: V2 adds multivariate prior-bias sensitivity analysis in Figure S9 and a substantive preprocessing check in Figure S12. The latter exposes a nominal-coverage violation without Census preprocessing. Existing scalar bias, prior-scale and improper-prior analyses are retained, with revised biased-simulation evidence.

E5.justification: V1 Figures S6–S7 report 100 repetitions; corresponding v2 Figures S7–S8 report 1000. This establishes changed repetition-count reporting, but v2 Figure 2 still states 100 for results also displayed in Figure S7, leaving the actual count for shared panels inconsistent.

E6.justification: V2 adds predictor scores, multivariate radii, and regression/median results. Figure S11 shows Bayes-assisted PPI++ producing wider intervals on Genes; Figure S12 shows non-assisted PPI++ exceeding 0.1 cumulative miscoverage without Census preprocessing. Figure 2's results also change under revised simulation settings, so they do not establish a same-setting performance improvement.

M1.justification: The core PPI/PPI++ estimators and Bayes-assisted construction remain. However, the multivariate confidence-region formula changes from t/(2pi) in v1 Sections S5.2–S5.3 to t^d/(2pi)^d in v2 Sections S4.2–S4.3, correcting the reported radius for d greater than one.

P1.justification: V2 consolidates v1's separate stronger-rate development into the main theory and reorganized proofs, restructures the background and experimental appendices, and rewrites the discussion and alternative-CS exposition. It also adds a confidence-interval versus confidence-sequence explanation and an appendix contents list.

P2.justification: V2 adopts NeurIPS typography and page layout, changes figure placement, and redraws the biased-prediction plots with revised axes. It adds the CI/CS illustration, multivariate and additional-task plots, the preprocessing comparison, and predictor-performance Table S1. These are substantial display changes beyond renumbering.

R1.justification: V2 adds references supporting sequential error control, prediction applications, Genes data and the proposed Berry–Esseen guidance, while dropping Strassen and Kallenberg references. It refines the description of Csillag et al.'s assumptions from bounded outcomes to bounded e-values. The overall positioning relative to PPI and confidence-sequence research remains similar.

T1.justification: V2 introduces a little-o approximation-rate definition and Theorem 5 with a proof of asymptotic time-uniform Type-I error control. It adds explicit variance-estimation rates and scalar prior-support conditions and corrects multivariate normalization. KMT coupling and multivariate extensions already existed in v1's appendices; their relocation alone is not new theory.

improvement.justification: Compared with v1, v2 strengthens the inferential justification through explicit regularity conditions, mathematical corrections and an error-control proof. Its broader experiments also reveal practical failures rather than only successful scalar-mean examples, and implementation information improves reproducibility. These substantial gains outweigh remaining duplicated reference numbers and inconsistent repetition-count captions.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Bayes-assisted, anytime-valid PPI framework. Their full main texts and appendices, including equations, proofs, figures and tables, support reliable comparison despite substantial reorganization.

after.justification: V2 retains original empirical evaluations and adds multivariate simulations, regression and median-estimation experiments, predictor-performance measurements, and a preprocessing study.

before.justification: V1 reports original noisy- and biased-prediction simulations and experiments on Flights, Forest and Galaxies, measuring interval volume and cumulative miscoverage.

results.title: Anytime-valid, Bayes-assisted, Prediction-Powered Inference

C1.justification: The central claims about target-aware representations, classification leadership, and benefits from pretraining scale remain. The conclusion newly claims GBDT-level inference efficiency relative to ICL models and explicitly extends the future vision to tabular data combining numerical, textual, and image features.

C2.justification: v2 distinguishes slower training from inexpensive inference and attributes much baseline inference cost to text embedding generation. It adds class-count-related memory limitations, interprets feature-width cost growth, and proposes distribution-aware numerical encoding for regression. Existing regression, few-shot, and numerical-only evaluation limitations remain.

D1.justification: Appendix E adds baseline implementation information and RealMLP/LightGBM hyperparameter search spaces. Appendix F adds hardware disclosures, feature-group profiling details, and per-dataset tuning-trial counts. Appendix B clarifies LoRA placement. These substantially expand experimental documentation, while the code-access disclosure remains unchanged.

E1.justification: Both retain the reported 350-dataset pretraining corpus, 50-dataset benchmark comprising 14 classification and 36 regression tasks, and 20-dataset ablation subset. The new feature-count cost study samples existing pretraining datasets without establishing additional domain or prediction-task coverage.

E2.justification: v2 adds evaluated LightGBM, RealMLP, TabM, TabICL, and TabDPT baselines, including tuned and unlimited variants where applicable. Appendix G newly compares existing ablation variants against external baselines. Cost comparisons also change membership, omitting previously timed TabPFN-v2 and CARTE and introducing a CPU-only CatBoost control.

E3.justification: v2 substantially expands computational evaluation to separate training and inference latency and peak CPU/GPU memory, adds a CPU-only control, and evaluates feature-count groups across 45 sampled datasets. Appendix F.4 reports A100/8-core hardware for most evaluations, replacing v1's heterogeneous compute setup. Main prediction splits, sample limits, and four-hour tuning budgets remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Appendix A.3 adds qualitative tests of column names, target-value verbalization, and dataset-description prefixes. Appendix F.5 adds feature-count sensitivity measurements for runtime and memory. These extend the analysis while retaining the original encoder-unfreezing, pretraining-scale, and numerical-verbalization ablation results.

E5.justification: Both versions report ten random train-test splits and 95% confidence intervals using the same normal approximation. Expanded result tables retain this practice. Newly reported hyperparameter-trial counts describe optimization effort, not additional statistical replication.

E6.justification: v2 adds extensive baseline and cost results and revises existing entries. For C09 at 10K, TabSTAR AUROC changes from 99.3±0.1 to 94.0±0.8 and CatBoost-Tuned from 99.8±0.1 to 82.6±1.4, reversing their ranking (v1 Table 17; v2 Table 19). These revisions are unexplained. Aggregate scores and win rates also change; normalized scores use different comparator pools and cannot establish same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: The five-stage architecture, target-aware tokens, numerical encoding, interaction transformer, objectives, and pretraining/LoRA procedure remain unchanged. Clarifications about independent feature fusion and which layers receive LoRA adapters document the existing method rather than establish a procedural change.

P1.justification: The title changes to emphasize tabular data with text fields. Local rewrites clarify architecture, benchmark construction, and finetuning terminology, while Appendix F gains more explicit subdivisions. Conference, acknowledgment, and funding text change, but the main section sequence and most narrative remain intact.

P2.justification: Figures 2–3 are redesigned to group default/tuned and 10K/unlimited variants. Figures 5–8 add scaling and ablation-comparison displays. New cost, hyperparameter, and trial-count tables accompany substantially widened result tables and transposed win-rate tables. The original pretraining-scale summary is retained as v2 Table 29 after relocation from the main text.

R1.justification: v2 adds references to SCARF, LightGBM, TabDPT, and a self-supervised tabular-learning survey. Related work explicitly limits its scope to supervised learning and expands discussion of TabICL and TabDPT. The broader positioning around semantic, target-aware tabular foundation models remains stable.

T1.justification: The formal architecture definitions, numerical transformations, sequence construction, and mathematical objectives are retained. No new theorem, proof, or substantive derivation appears; the added discussion of attention costs and class-token counts elaborates existing architecture properties.

improvement.justification: The expanded comparisons address v1's important omission of strong MLP and additional foundation-model baselines, materially strengthening evaluation of its classification claim. More consistent hardware reporting and separate inference, training, and memory measurements substantially improve assessment of practical costs. These gains outweigh remaining reporting weaknesses, including unexplained C09 revisions and the conflict between excluding TabDPT regression results and reporting a regression win rate in Table 23.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same TabSTAR research despite the changed title. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete Appendices A–G support a reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains original benchmark and ablation results and adds baseline evaluations, computational cost measurements, and supplementary analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original classification and regression benchmark results, architectural experiments, and ablations in Sections 5–6 and the appendices.

results.title: TabSTAR: A Tabular Foundation Model for Tabular Data with Text Fields

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction now highlight donor-level representation learning in place of methylation among the six featured applications, although methylation remains in the appendix. The principal claims about distributional autoencoding, predictive sufficiency, and approximate Wasserstein geometry remain.

C2.justification: v2 interprets GDEs as learned Rao–Blackwellizations and attributes their small-sample advantage to the meta-distributional prior. It more carefully distinguishes intrinsic manifold geometry from ambient Wasserstein geodesics and qualifies generator smoothness as a modeling assumption. The Discussion's existing limitations are retained.

D1.justification: Appendix B.3 adds donor preprocessing, feature selection, architecture dimensions, joint training, and logistic-regression evaluation details. Section 2.2 and Appendix A.4 clarify training implementation, including using the generator's training loss without differentiating through sampling. The checklist adds configuration and notebook directory instructions; the repository link is unchanged.

E1.justification: v2 adds donor-level prediction of six disease categories using a 4-million-cell subset of a human prefrontal-cortex atlas (Appendix B.3), and Poisson zero-event probability estimation (Section 5.1). These extend both population and task coverage. All earlier applications remain, including methylation, relocated to Appendix B.1.

E2.justification: v2 Table 4 adds scVI to the existing perturbation comparison. New comparisons include naive and Rao–Blackwellized Poisson estimators in Table 1 and a purely supervised donor encoder in Table 3. Existing synthetic and biological comparator sets are otherwise retained.

E3.justification: New protocols include donor learning with 10% labeled data and a reported 10% completely held-out evaluation, plus Poisson estimation across sample sizes 10–10,000 using one million generated samples. These accompany new experiments; the settings documented for retained experiments are unchanged.

E4.justification: Section 5.1 adds a sample-size analysis testing GDE estimation efficiency against naive and Rao–Blackwellized estimators. Existing architecture comparisons, prior-weighting sensitivity analyses, geometric interpolation studies, and biological case analyses are retained.

E5.justification: The five-trial mean ± s.e.m. synthetic results and ten-split viral evaluations retain their reporting practices. The new Poisson and donor tables provide point estimates without additional run counts, uncertainty intervals, or significance procedures.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantive Poisson and donor prediction results. Table 1 shows GDE has the lowest Poisson MSE at n=10–1,000, but not 10,000. Table 3 reports semi-supervised versus supervised accuracy of 0.8887 versus 0.8791, ROC AUC of 0.5131 versus 0.4872, and F1 of 0.1479 versus 0.1293. Table 4 adds scVI R2=0.421491 and MSE=1.551414. Previously reported benchmark and biological results remain unchanged.

M1.justification: Section 3 changes the reported set-sampling rule from density ratios against the empirical label distribution to normalized densities against a fixed reference measure. v2 also adds partially labeled donor training combining reconstruction and disease prediction. The core encoder-generator framework is retained; the GNN-to-deep-sets terminology changes do not establish architectural replacements.

P1.justification: The methods section is substantially rewritten around a motivating example and a separate training subsection. Section 5 reorganizes the sufficiency and geometry narrative, incorporating the former prior-weighting subsection. Background and theory appendices are extensively rewritten, methylation moves to Appendix B.1, and implementation guidance, an expanded title, acknowledgements, and a NeurIPS checklist are added.

P2.justification: v2 adds a training algorithm display, Poisson and donor result tables, and an architecture overview table, and extends the perturbation table with an scVI row. Figure 2's panel descriptions are corrected, Figure 7's caption is clarified, and some figures are resized or relocated. Existing figure images are unchanged; appendix typography and table placement are adjusted.

R1.justification: v2 adds references on predictive sufficiency, cellular measurement noise, and the donor atlas, while removing several references associated with the earlier theoretical exposition. The statistical framing shifts toward classical sufficiency and Rao–Blackwellization. Positioning relative to kernel embeddings, Neural Statistician, and Wasserstein Wormhole remains essentially unchanged.

T1.justification: Appendix D.1 replaces the asymptotic Blackwell-equivalence argument with finite-sample sufficiency, minimality, and maximal-invariance results. D.2 strengthens regularity assumptions and qualifies loss-bias and generator-recovery guarantees. D.3 replaces total-variation reconstruction with bounded-Lipschitz reconstruction, adds smooth reconstruction assumptions, and rewrites the proof. Appendix C revises the Wasserstein manifold formalism and removes the Gaussian-mixture sufficient-statistics example; D.2 also corrects log-sum-exp normalization.

improvement.justification: The decisive gain is the repair of central theoretical weaknesses: Appendix D corrects the reversed TV/BL inequality, replaces total-variation reconstruction with qualified bounded-Lipschitz reconstruction, and explicitly requires correct specification for generator recovery. Clearer training guidance and additional experiments improve assessability. New results still lack uncertainty estimates, and Appendix A.5 contains stale cross-references, but these shortcomings do not outweigh the substantial gains in theoretical rigor and clarity.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Generative Distribution Embeddings work. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support reliable comparison, including material moved between sections.

after.justification: v2 retains these original results and adds Poisson estimation experiments, donor-level disease prediction, and an scVI comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original synthetic reconstruction benchmarks, geometric analyses, and six biological applications, with numerical and qualitative results in the main text and Appendix B.

results.title: Generative Distribution Embeddings: Lifting autoencoders to the space of distributions for multiscale representation learning

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same central contributions: exact reformulation of pullback Riemannian CFM in Euclidean coordinates, efficient manifold-valid generation, and realistic brain-connectivity synthesis for both covariance and correlation matrices. Added evidence supports these existing claims.

C2.justification: Section 6 adds uncertainty about alternative connectivity estimators, including partial correlations and graphical-Lasso precision, and strengthens the dimensionality limitation to exponential sample-complexity growth. Section 3.2 also explains the embeddings' selection for simplicity and identifies alternatives. These refine applicability and interpretation without changing the central conclusions.

D1.justification: v2 adds project-code and implementation links, RIEMCFM configuration details, and the One-Class SVM explanation for the already-used EvaGeM evaluator. Most existing training and hardware details move into Section 4.3. Conversely, v1's explicit affine-invariant tangent-space preprocessing description for CAS is omitted; this does not establish that the preprocessing itself changed.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate ABIDE, ADNI, OASIS-3, BNCI2014-002, and BNCI2015-001, retaining the same disease-classification and motor-imagery tasks and simulated-SPD scalability study. The new architecture experiments use the existing ABIDE coverage.

E2.justification: v2 adds affine-invariant RIEMCFM to both EEG comparisons in Table 1, providing an important direct manifold-based comparator. v1 discussed Riemannian CFM but excluded it as inapplicable. Existing comparators, including the separate SPD-DDPM timing comparison, are retained.

E3.justification: The reported integration setting changes from fixed-step midpoint to dopri5. Added experiments specify RIEMCFM's six-layer network and learning rate, and ABIDE sweeps over widths 8–1024 and one to four hidden layers. Figure 3 additionally summarizes performance through an average of quality F1 and CAS F1. These are bounded extensions within the retained evaluation framework.

E4.justification: New Appendix K systematically tests sensitivity to network width and depth, reporting quality and computational costs in Tables 3–4. This adds substantive evidence for the chosen shallow, 512-unit architecture that v1 lacked. Existing projection, constraint-satisfaction, and neurophysiological analyses are largely retained.

E5.justification: v2 increases the reported fMRI repetitions from five to ten subject-grouped splits and newly explains EEG standard deviations as computed over five inner splits and averaged over sessions. Table 1 adds one-sided paired Wilcoxon tests at alpha = 0.05, replacing bolding of numerical winners with significance-aware comparisons. Mean and standard-deviation reporting already existed in v1.

E6.justification: Table 1 adds RIEMCFM outcomes and training/sampling times, while Tables 3–4 add architecture-sensitivity results. Existing scores also change: DIFFEOCFM's ADNI CAS F1 is 0.35 ± 0.09 in v1 and 0.47 ± 0.10 in v2. These are revised results under changed reported settings, not an established same-setting gain. The OASIS-3 connectome panel is also replaced.

M1.justification: The pullback-CFM formulation, embeddings, objectives, and Algorithms 1–2 remain unchanged. However, the reported numerical sampling procedure changes from midpoint integration with step size 10^-3 in v1 Appendix J to dopri5 in v2 Section 4.3, constituting a limited inference-procedure revision.

P1.justification: The main narrative and section sequence are largely retained. Changes include localized explanatory additions, moving implementation details into the main text, reorganizing appendices, revising the conclusion heading, and appending a NeurIPS checklist. These do not amount to a broad scientific rewrite.

P2.justification: Table 1 is substantially redesigned with runtime columns, RIEMCFM rows, highlighted DIFFEOCFM rows, and revised bolding. v2 adds the performance-versus-cost Figure 3 and two ablation tables, and adopts NeurIPS formatting throughout. Figure 9b replaces v1 Figure 8b's duplicated ABIDE imagery with a distinct OASIS-3 panel; most other figures are retained and renumbered.

R1.justification: Related work adds connections to Lie-group reparameterization, manifold diffusion processes, and metric flow matching, including acknowledgment of an earlier precursor. The baseline discussion corrects v1's characterization of Riemannian CFM as inapplicable, recognizing its usable but costlier SPD implementation. The overall novelty positioning remains intact.

T1.justification: Propositions 1–3 and their proofs remain substantively identical, as do the pullback identities, affine-invariant quotient geometry, and projection derivation. Discussion of alternative embeddings and dimensionality limitations does not introduce a new formal result.

improvement.justification: The direct RIEMCFM comparison resolves an important baseline gap in v1 and substantially strengthens evidence for the central efficiency claim at similar EEG generation quality. Architecture ablations, explicit statistical comparisons, and the corrected OASIS-3 figure further improve empirical credibility. Some claims remain poorly reconciled with the revised results: Section 5.1 still asserts universally highest CAS scores despite counterexamples in Table 1, and the CAS preprocessing description loses detail. These shortcomings do not outweigh the substantial improvement in comparative evidence.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe DIFFEOCFM and contain readable main text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices. Corresponding content can be matched despite reformatting and appendix reorganization.

after.justification: v2 reports original benchmark results, including additional RIEMCFM comparisons, runtime measurements, and architecture ablations.

before.justification: v1 reports original generation-quality and downstream-classification results on five neuroimaging datasets, alongside computational and neurophysiological analyses.

results.title: Riemannian Flow Matching for Brain Connectivity Matrices via Pullback Geometry

C1.justification: The central contribution remains ESL and domain-informed runtime verification. v3 adds an introduction and conclusion claim that RvLLM achieves a better TPR/TNR balance than existing runtime detection methods, extending v1's effectiveness claims to explicit comparative superiority.

C2.justification: v3 explicitly conditions soundness on faithful expert encoding and describes specification/perception errors and bias as limitations (Section 3 and Appendix G). Appendix E attributes comparative performance to separating language understanding from symbolic reasoning. It removes v1's conjecture that DeepSeek-V3 favors language understanding over logical reasoning and the conclusion's explicit single-reasoning-strategy limitation.

D1.justification: v3 supplies the prompt documentation absent from the supplied v1: original queries, perception prompts, Level-2 instantiation, and follow-up templates in Appendix C. Appendices B, D–F add generation constraints, dataset examples, a worked specification, baseline configurations, and temperature information. These substantially improve implementation transparency without proving changes to the original implementation.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same three task domains using 304 railway-law scenarios, 100 generated numerical comparisons, and 40 A-Level inequality problems. Appendix B supplies dataset descriptions, and Appendix D illustrates an existing task; neither establishes additional dataset or task coverage.

E2.justification: v3 adds evaluated SelfCheckGPT and domain-constraint prompt augmentation, termed LLM-as-a-judge, across all three tasks (Figure 3 and Tables 3, 9–11). v1 discusses SelfCheckGPT in related work but provides no corresponding experimental comparison. These additions substantially broaden the comparator set.

E3.justification: New comparisons introduce selected target-model subsets and a stated common DeepSeek-V3 verifier/judge configuration in Appendix E, although this is not reconciled with the main text's same-model setting. Inequality evaluation expands beyond erroneous answers to report TNR on correct answers and token costs. Legal class counts change from 280 unsafe/24 safe to 281/23; this does not establish that experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Appendix D adds a detailed error case tracing how RvLLM identifies an animal-transport violation missed by Qwen-plus. Appendix E adds a token-cost comparison for inequality verification. Existing inequality error-category and perception-agent analyses are retained, without new robustness or sensitivity sweeps.

E5.justification: Unlike v1, Appendix F reports preliminary runs until outputs stabilize and asserts negligible variance at temperature 0.5. This adds qualitative repeatability information, but supplies no run counts, seeds, measured dispersion, confidence intervals, or significance tests. It does not establish increased replication.

E6.justification: Figure 3 and Tables 3, 9–11 add cross-method detection results and inequality token costs. Existing results also change: Qwen 2.5 (7B) inequality errors increase from 23 to 25, with DeepSeek-based detection changing from 52.2% to 48% (v1 Table 3; v3 Table 4). Legal Qwen-turbo combined TPR changes from 75% to 74.7%. Numerical-comparison Table 2 is unchanged; the revisions do not demonstrate same-setting performance improvements.

M1.justification: The ESL-based procedure retains Level-1/Level-2 interpretation, rule normalization, forward chaining, and follow-up query generation. v1 Sections 3–4 correspond to v3 Sections 2–3. Added prompts and worked examples document the existing procedure without establishing an algorithmic change.

P1.justification: Related work moves from Section 2 to Section 5, and Appendices A–D substantially expand the exposition through forward-chaining, dataset, prompting, and application walkthroughs. Additional comparison, statistical, and broader-impact discussions reorganize the explanatory structure, although much of the original method prose remains intact.

P2.justification: v3 adds comparative bar charts, a four-panel forward-chaining illustration, nine prompt figures, and several case-study and comparison tables. Existing figures are resized/repositioned, and Table 2 moves beside the new comparison table. Appendix Tables 9–10 partly redisplay or extend main-text comparisons rather than representing wholly separate experiments.

R1.justification: v3 adds an 'Expert systems with NLP' discussion connecting RvLLM to earlier symbolic/NLP systems, including SHRDLU and MedLEE. It also adds references on unit propagation and propagation completeness. Existing LLM-testing and runtime-verification positioning remains largely intact, making this a focused extension.

T1.justification: The core definitions and transformation equations remain unchanged, but Appendix A adds a multi-step mathematical forward-chaining derivation on another rule set. This example is internally inconsistent: its final inference uses ¬M∧K⇒N, absent from the initially stated rules. No new general theorem or proof is supplied.

improvement.justification: v1 lacks evaluated runtime-method competitors and the prompt appendices it references. v3 substantially addresses both deficiencies through actual baseline comparisons, inequality false-positive and cost results, and detailed dataset/prompt documentation. These materially improve assessability and reproducibility. The gains outweigh remaining weaknesses: inconsistent verifier-model descriptions, unsupported negligible-variance assertions in Appendix F, and the flawed worked derivation in Appendix A.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same RvLLM framework and three case studies, with readable text, equations, figures, and tables. v1 ends after its references despite mentioning appendices; v3 includes Appendices A–G. The supplied documents support a reliable comparison of their reported content.

after.justification: v3 retains these original experiments and adds evaluations against other verification methods, including detection rates and token usage in Appendix E.

before.justification: v1 reports original experiments on railway-law violation detection, numerical comparison, and inequality solving, including detection rates, error counts, and execution times in Tables 1–3.

results.title: RvLLM: LLM Runtime Verification with Domain Knowledge

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and discussion retain the central claim that a small, appropriately weighted sidekick improves prediction and uncertainty with fractional additional computation. The new comparisons support this existing contribution rather than redefine it.

C2.justification: v2 attributes advantages over deep ensembles to architectural diversity and temperature aggregation, recommends choosing the strongest affordable base model, and discusses IVON compatibility and Laplace hardware constraints. Some new interpretations overreach: the claimed IVON advantage across all metrics contradicts Table 3, and Table 4 shows lower Laplace AUROC despite the prose claiming improvement.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code-availability statement and repository link, specifies NVIDIA L40S training hardware, documents ensemble checkpoint sources and construction, and describes the last-layer Kronecker-factored Laplace implementation.
