These extend the existing reproducibility documentation; repository contents were not inspected.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate ImageNet, ImageNet V2, Caltech 256, and in-distribution and out-of-distribution iWildCam classification. New comparisons use these existing datasets. Adding ConvNeXt results on iWildCam expands model configurations rather than dataset or task coverage.

E2.justification: v2 adds evaluated pool-then-calibrate ResNet-50 deep ensembles with 2, 5, and 8 members, IVON with deterministic and sampled inference, and last-layer Laplace approximation (Tables 1–4). These substantive comparator families were not evaluated against Duos in v1.

E3.justification: Appendix A.2 changes iWildCam linear probing from 5 to 8 epochs, fine-tuning from 10 to 12 epochs, and Caltech fine-tuning from 20 to 16 epochs. Adaptive batch sizing becomes fixed sizes of 128 and 16. Soup construction changes from 32 candidates with 5 selected to 16 candidates with 3 selected. v2 also introduces base-model-controlled and FLOPs-controlled comparisons. These are reported setting revisions; the PDFs do not establish their execution history.

E4.justification: v2 adds analyses of ensemble-size and computational-budget scaling, including allocating compute to stronger Duo base models, and examines IVON inference with 2–32 samples. The original unweighted and UQ-only ablations, entropy comparison, and temperature-weight analysis remain.

E5.justification: v2 adds tabular ± summaries and specifies 32 sampled ensemble subsets drawn from 10 independently trained ResNet-50 checkpoints (Appendix A.5). This does not mean 32 independent training runs. The new ± quantities are not explicitly defined; Figure 1's standard deviation across model choices already appeared in v1.

E6.justification: Tables 1–4 add substantial comparative results. For example, Table 1 reports accuracy of 81.87±0.19 for ResNet-50 plus EfficientNet-B2 versus 81.97±0.13 for five ResNet-50 ensemble members, at 27% versus 400% additional FLOPs. Numerous existing plots change, and Figure 14 gains ConvNeXt iWildCam results. Revised fine-tuning settings prevent treating affected scores as same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: The proposed procedure remains independently trained large and small models combined through two logit weights optimized for validation negative log likelihood. Revised training budgets and additional comparator implementations do not change the Duo algorithm.

P1.justification: v2 adds Section 5.6, Appendix A.5, comparison Appendices E–F, and a NeurIPS checklist, moving full results to Appendix G. Local wording, spelling, affiliation, and publication-header edits accompany these additions; the existing narrative is largely retained.

P2.justification: v2 introduces four multi-metric comparison tables and expands the ConvNeXt result grids from three to five dataset columns. Several plots have revised axes and legends. Figure 8 changes its plotted base-model label and correlation value while retaining an inconsistent caption and discussion.

R1.justification: v2 adds the Laplace Redux and IVON references and positions Duos against these scalable Bayesian approaches. It also clarifies the distinction from Gontijo-Lopes et al. through fine-tuning paired models on the same data. Existing related-work coverage is retained.

T1.justification: The prediction, uncertainty, weighted-logit, and FLOPs-balance definitions remain substantively unchanged. A corrected closing parenthesis is typographical; neither version introduces theoretical results or proofs.

improvement.justification: v1 presents Duos as a cheaper alternative to deep ensembles without directly benchmarking that alternative. v2 substantially closes this central evidential gap through calibrated comparisons controlling the base model and inference FLOPs (Tables 1–2), supplemented by Bayesian baselines and additional reproducibility information. Unsupported interpretations of Tables 3–4, undefined ± summaries, and stale Figure 8 text weaken reporting reliability, but do not outweigh the stronger evidence for the paper's central efficiency argument.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Asymmetric Duos research, with readable text, equations, figures, and complete appendices. v1's full-results Appendix E is retained as Appendix G in v2.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical evaluations and adds direct deep-ensemble and Bayesian-method comparisons in Section 5.6 and Appendices E–F.

before.justification: v1 reports original classification, uncertainty, selective-classification, ablation, model-soup, and throughput experiments in Section 5 and Appendices B–E.

results.title: Asymmetric Duos: Sidekicks Improve Uncertainty

C1.justification: The general self-distillation contribution remains, but the headline empirical claim changes. v1 emphasizes avoiding temporal and spatial derivatives for image synthesis, favoring PSD. v2 instead presents Lagrangian methods as more stable and better performing than Eulerian and Progressive methods, and explicitly claims that the framework encompasses all known consistency-model distillation and direct-training schemes.

C2.justification: v2 shifts the explanation toward spatial Jacobians, stopgradient placement, and LSD's avoidance of bootstrapping. It newly attributes PSD's theoretical difficulty to compounding errors and distribution shift (Section 2.3), discusses uncertain convergence of stopgradient updates, and expands limitations concerning untested parameterizations, stabilization choices, hybrid objectives, and guidance. These materially revise the interpretation and applicability discussion.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code link, method-specific pseudocode, a configuration table, explicit histogram-based KL computation, FID checkpoint-selection procedures, EMA values, clipping, and embedding details. These substantially expand reproducibility documentation without establishing that every newly disclosed procedure changed. Some information is lost or inconsistent: v1's CIFAR GPU disclosure disappears, and v2 Table 2 lists 10,000 AFHQ evaluation samples while Appendix G.4 specifies 50,000.

E1.justification: Coverage expands from checkerboard and CIFAR-10 to include unconditional face generation on CelebA-64 and animal generation on AFHQ-64 (v2 Table 1 and Appendix G). Both original tasks remain. Conditional generation and guidance are discussed but do not constitute additional evaluated coverage.

E2.justification: The corresponding comparisons retain LSD, ESD, PSD-M, and PSD-U on checkerboard, and LSD/PSD comparisons plus unsuccessful ESD training on CIFAR-10. The added image datasets use these same methods. Newly discussed methods such as MeanFlow and Align Your Flow are not evaluated as additional baselines.

E3.justification: Reported training protocols change substantially: v2 adopts 75% diagonal batches and removes warm-up/annealing. Checkerboard width increases from 256 to 512 and batch size from 64,000 to 100,000. CIFAR-10 changes from 180,000 staged training steps at learning rate 0.001 to 400,000 steps at 0.01, with revised residual blocks and attention. Adam becomes RAdam, and the new image datasets receive separate 800,000-step protocols.

E4.justification: The step-count sweeps and gradient-norm study remain. v2 adds qualitative pilot comparisons of EMA versus instantaneous teachers and embeddings of (s,t-s) versus (s,t), and reports ESD instability across attempted stopgradient configurations (Appendices F.4 and G.2). v1's reported pilot comparison favoring off-diagonal-only sampling disappears. These are limited ancillary checks, not a systematic component-ablation suite.

E5.justification: Neither version reports independent training-run counts, aggregated seed results, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Both use fixed-noise qualitative comparisons. The additional EMA and evaluation-sample details in v2 do not provide uncertainty estimates across runs.

E6.justification: CIFAR-10 rankings reverse: v1 Table 2 reports one-step FID 38.01 for LSD versus 14.13 for PSD-U; v2 Table 1 reports 8.10 versus 13.61, with LSD leading at every reported step count. Checkerboard changes from PSD-U leading for two or more steps to LSD leading through eight steps. CelebA-64 and AFHQ-64 results are added. These are revised/new results under changed settings, not controlled performance gains over v1.

M1.justification: The three self-distillation families remain, but v2 adds conditional and classifier-free-guided formulations with conditioning inputs, guidance-scale sampling, and dedicated objectives (Section 3, Appendix F.5). Algorithm 1 also changes the training prescription to separate diagonal and off-diagonal loss batches, with explicit stopgradient variants. The guidance extension is proposed but not evaluated.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and algorithm discussion are extensively rewritten. Related work moves from Section 1.1 to Section 4, a conclusion is added, and the appendices are reorganized into dedicated connections, proofs, algorithmic details, and experimental subsections. Existing material is substantially restructured alongside the scientific additions.

P2.justification: The two original results tables become an expanded combined Table 1, and a new configuration Table 2 is added. Figure 5 expands into a three-dataset sample grid; checkerboard plots are regenerated, with Figure 3 changing its displayed multistep row from 16 to eight steps. Three detailed algorithm displays are added, while the principal schematics are retained and relocated.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands research positioning through dedicated derivations relating the framework to consistency training/distillation, MeanFlow, Align Your Flow, and shortcut models (Appendices B-D). It adds corresponding citations and emphasizes the distinctness of Lagrangian formulations. The operator-learning connection and Zheng et al. reference present in v1 are removed; the changes extend beyond bibliographic updates.

T1.justification: v2 adds continuity to Proposition 2.2, supplies characterization proofs and a discontinuous counterexample explaining the assumption, and develops continuous-time derivations connecting consistency training, MeanFlow, and Align Your Flow (Appendices C-E). It also corrects the ESD time index in equation (14) and restores the missing (t-s)^2 factor in the PSD loss identity. The principal Wasserstein bounds are retained.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens theoretical completeness by stating the continuity needed for the flow-map characterization, explaining its necessity, and supplying fuller proofs and connections. Detailed algorithms and metric/checkpoint procedures address important reproducibility omissions in v1, while two additional image domains broaden validation. Changed training settings prevent isolating the cause of the reversed rankings, and the AFHQ sample-count conflict remains. These limitations temper the empirical conclusions but do not outweigh the substantial gains in theoretical support and reproducibility.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same flow-map self-distillation work. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable matching despite substantial revision and reorganization.

after.justification: v2 reports original experiments on checkerboard, CIFAR-10, CelebA-64, and AFHQ-64, with quantitative results and generated samples in Section 5 and Appendix G.

before.justification: v1 reports original checkerboard and CIFAR-10 experiments, including KL/FID scores, generated samples, and training-gradient measurements in Section 4 and Appendix E.

results.title: How to build a consistency model: Learning flow maps via self-distillation

C1.justification: The introduction and conclusion newly assert that the formulation and methodology generalize across disciplines with only the hierarchy requiring adaptation. The central combinatorial-search contribution, four research questions, and principal HHS and ensemble claims are retained.

C2.justification: Appendix E explains reference divergence through alternative plausible hypotheses and the tradeoff between informative initialization and answer leakage, and identifies difficulty prioritizing experimentally essential details. Section 3.3 adds a diminishing-returns interpretation of reasoning steps, while Section 3.2 replaces inference about proximity to a global optimum with comparison of local optima. These substantially extend v1's limitations and interpretation.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code/data repository pointer and documents initialization by abstracting details, component decomposition, intermediate recall-scoring anchors, and expert auditing of evaluation prompts. These materially expand access and reproducibility information. They are newly disclosed details, not evidence that the underlying preprocessing or scoring procedures changed.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same 51-paper TOMATO-Chem benchmark for fine-grained hypothesis generation. The added diagnostics examine existing benchmark hypotheses; references to material science and broader disciplinary applicability do not establish additional tested coverage.

E2.justification: Table 2 adds ChemCrow, Qi et al. (2024), SciMON, MOOSE, and MOOSE-Chem as evaluated recall comparators, substantially expanding beyond v1's greedy-search baselines. It also includes in-context RL variants. The committee comparators remain unchanged, and HHS-1 recall is carried over from v1 Table 5.

E3.justification: v2 adds reasoning-step count as an evaluation measure and introduces expert error-coding protocols, with Tables 5-6 assigning 30 samples or pairs to one expert and 21 to another. The existing benchmark, recall normalization, and six-comparison voting protocol are retained; newly documented initialization details do not establish a change to the earlier experiments.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained ablations and four case studies, v2 examines rejected-candidate context feedback and the relationship between recall and reasoning steps. Appendices E-F add substantial analyses of reference alignment, essential-detail coverage, HHS failure types, and reasons for its advantage over greedy search.

E5.justification: Both versions report six LLM judgments per pair with presentation order balanced. Neither introduces experiment-level seed reporting, confidence intervals, significance tests, or comparable uncertainty estimates; the added expert frequencies are descriptive results.

E6.justification: Table 2 adds baseline and variant scores plus reasoning-step measurements: HHS with in-context RL reports 33.63% soft recall and 21.29% hard recall over 531.08 steps. Appendix E newly reports 60% reference divergence and approximately 50% coverage of required important details, while Tables 5-6 add error frequencies. Tables 1, 3, and 4 retain identical percentages.

M1.justification: The default five-level HHS search, stopping rule, recombination, and search prompt remain unchanged. Section 3.3 introduces in-context RL variants that insert an unsuccessful candidate into the context before generating another candidate, a limited procedural adaptation.

P1.justification: v2 revises the contribution list and conclusion, condenses the Q4 discussion, clarifies terminology, and moves the recall explanation into an expanded appendix. These are selective edits within the retained main-section structure; the existing case studies, evaluation instructions, and search prompt are preserved.

P2.justification: The small wrapped recall table becomes an expanded, grouped comparison with a reasoning-step column and incorporates the former HHS-1/HHS-3 recall table. v2 also adds an input/output overview figure and two expert-analysis tables, substantially expanding the visual presentation of comparisons and diagnostics. Existing figures are resized and table captions repositioned.

R1.justification: v2 adds references including ChemCrow, MOOSE-Chem3, Romera-Paredes et al. (2024), LLM-SR, and AlphaEvolve. Section 4 extends the positioning to possible experiment-guided discovery through feedback in the background survey. The principal distinction from coarse-grained hypothesis generation remains intact.

T1.justification: Section 2.2 broadens the formal edit-space definition to include adding new concepts and deleting individual details, beyond v1's detail-addition and concept-deletion formulation. The hierarchical factorization is unchanged. Appendix C's new equations restate the existing recall metrics rather than introducing new mathematics.

improvement.justification: v1's quantitative comparisons centered on closely related search ablations, with practical diagnosis largely confined to selected examples. v2 addresses these important gaps through established-method comparisons, explicit reasoning costs, and systematic expert evidence about missing details and feasibility failures. Clearer evaluation documentation and a code/data pointer also improve reproducibility. Unequal reasoning costs and untested disciplinary generalization remain limitations, but the added evidence substantially improves the paper's assessability and characterization of practical limitations.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MOOSE-Chem2/HHS research, with matching methodology and benchmark. Their complete main texts, appendices, equations, figures, and tables support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains these empirical results and adds baseline comparisons, context-feedback experiments, reasoning-step measurements, and expert diagnostic analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original hypothesis-generation experiments, LLM and expert comparisons, recall measurements, and ensemble evaluations on its chemistry benchmark.

results.title: MOOSE-Chem2: Exploring LLM Limits in Fine-Grained Scientific Hypothesis Discovery via Hierarchical Search

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution bullets and conclusion retain the same substantive claims: personalized detection as fine-grained identity recognition, the three-stage multimodal VIPGuard framework, VIPBench, and superior detection and explainability. Added supporting experiments do not redefine these central contributions.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive applicability boundaries: sensitivity to head rotations exceeding roughly 50 degrees, age differences, and limited use of audio or temporal information. It also adds interpretations concerning stage synergy, possible token overfitting, transfer enabling annotation-free customization, and semantic cues explaining corruption robustness. These qualifications and mechanisms were not developed in the supplied v1.

D1.justification: Appendices D.1 and E supply previously unavailable optimizer, learning-rate, batch-size, epoch, resizing and prediction-scoring details, plus face filtering, sampling ratios and annotation prompts. TransFace is identified as the default similarity model. The release-on-acceptance promise is supplemented by a code URL and noncommercial, reviewed-request dataset access terms; external availability was not checked.

E1.justification: The underlying training sources, 22-identity VIPEval benchmark, forgery generators, CelebDF and DF40 coverage remain unchanged. v2 adds evaluation under Gaussian noise, blur and JPEG compression, plus automatic identity/token selection when multiple VIPs are protected. These extend input and deployment scenarios within the existing task.

E2.justification: Tables 1–4 retain the same conventional detectors, identity-aware methods and MLLM competitors. The added backbone, face-recognition component and training-stage comparisons vary VIPGuard itself rather than add competing detectors to those benchmark comparisons.

E3.justification: The added experiments introduce substantial controlled variation: textual supervision in Stage 3, training-stage combinations, available authentic-image counts, token lengths from 8 to 128, and 3B/7B/11B backbones. Appendix D.4 specifies three intensities for each corruption. These are additional experimental protocols; newly disclosed settings for the retained experiments are reproducibility information rather than evidence of rerunning them.

E4.justification: v1 mentions supplementary ablations but supplies none. v2 provides stage-removal, reference-image-count, token-size, backbone and face-recognition-component analyses, along with annotation-free and adaptive-selection comparisons and corruption robustness tests. Figures 8–11 also add genuine-pair and forgery explanation cases beyond the retained Figure 5 examples.

E5.justification: Neither PDF reports repeated-run counts, detector-training seed studies, confidence intervals, significance tests or error bars. The added results remain point estimates. Varying generation seeds to create synthetic images was already described in v1 and is not uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: All numerical entries in Tables 1–4 are unchanged. v2 adds extensive results in Tables 5–10 and Figures 6–11, including adaptive selection averaging 98.01% AUC versus 98.23% with supplied tokens, and strongest-noise performance of 94.12%. Table 5 reports image-only customization at 95.86%, but its annotated InSwap value of 99.43% conflicts with 96.40% in Table 1, limiting interpretation of that comparison.

M1.justification: The three-stage VIPGuard architecture remains intact. Appendix D.3 adds Adaptive VIPGuard, which uses face recognition to select the appropriate VIP token automatically. Section 5.1 also introduces a Stage 3 variant without textual annotations. These are limited procedural extensions; expanded attention formulas and implementation disclosures do not establish a redesigned core method.

P1.justification: Most original main-text prose, contribution bullets and the conclusion are retained. Changes include localized copyediting, separating problem formulation from method overview, revising reference/query terminology, adding an annotation-free subsection and appendix roadmap, and updating publication and funding text. The supplementary expansion primarily adds content rather than extensively rewriting the existing narrative.

P2.justification: v2 substantially expands the visual presentation with ablation curves, robustness and variant tables, full explanation conversations, facial-attribute examples, annotation prompts and dataset-construction diagrams. Tables 1–4 are relocated or reformatted while retaining their results; existing diagrams and captions receive smaller revisions. The new displays make previously unavailable analyses and procedures inspectable.

R1.justification: v2 adds citations including FakeShield, AvatarShield and VLforgery Face Triad, expands the discussion of the already cited X2-DFD, and explicitly contrasts its unseen-source setting with prior identity-aware assumptions in Section 4.1. The broader positioning around personalized semantic detection remains unchanged.

T1.justification: Section 4.1 explicitly formalizes the exclusion of source identities from the available reference set. The written autoregressive losses change conditioning from the preceding token to the full preceding sequence, and attention inputs are explicitly defined. No theorem or proof is added. Equation 7 nevertheless includes fquery although adjacent prose says that representation is replaced by the VIP token.

improvement.justification: v2 resolves important gaps in the supplied v1, which referred readers to unavailable supplementary support. Stage/component ablations, corruption tests, detailed training and data-construction procedures, and concrete failure conditions substantially strengthen evidential support and reproducibility despite unchanged headline scores. The conflicting InSwap value in Table 5 and inconsistent feature notation in Equation 7 are drawbacks, while uncertainty reporting remains absent. These limitations temper but do not outweigh the substantial improvement in assessability and transparency.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same VIPGuard/VIPBench study, and their supplied text, equations, tables and figures are readable. v1 ends after the references despite mentioning an appendix; v2 includes Appendices A–E. Newly supplied appendix material can be compared as added documentation, without assuming its experiments were newly conducted.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and additionally reports annotation-free customization, component ablations, adaptive token selection, corruption tests and further explanation examples.

before.justification: v1 reports original detection experiments on VIPEval, CelebDF and DF40, comparisons with other MLLMs, and model-generated explanations in Tables 1–4 and Figure 5.

results.title: Guard Me If You Know Me: Protecting Specific Face-Identity from Deepfakes

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same central contributions: dynamic centralized orchestration, reinforcement-driven adaptation, improved quality and efficiency, and emergent compact cyclic structures. The abstract's added code link does not alter these scientific claims.

C2.justification: Appendices A and C add explanations for uneven efficiency gains, possible limitations from optimization budget and hyperparameters, and difficulties comparing training costs across methods. Appendix D newly identifies coarse terminal rewards, a fixed agent/tool pool, miscoordination, and deceptive agreement as limitations. These substantially expand the qualifications surrounding the retained claims.

D1.justification: v2 supplies a code-repository link, agent/action inventories, and role and action prompt templates in Appendix B. It explicitly documents the 200-sample optimization limit and reports eight A800 GPUs, 28.8–78.4 GB peak memory per GPU, and 2–6 hours of training in Table 3. These substantially improve implementation and resource disclosure.

E1.justification: The four quantitative benchmarks are retained. Appendix A.4 adds ALFWorld embodied interaction, illustrated through one THOR task involving a remote control and floor lamp. This extends coverage to an interactive scenario, but no aggregate ALFWorld evaluation is reported.

E2.justification: Table 1 retains the same foundation-model comparators, Self-Refine, AFlow, MacNet, and EvoAgent in both model subspaces. The added embodied case study introduces no evaluated comparator; the new related-work citations are not additional baselines.

E3.justification: Appendix A.2 adds evaluation using performance divided by token cost. The new ALFWorld case uses a maximum chain length of 50, one exploration trajectory, and GPT-4o-mini for all agents. Existing benchmark settings are unchanged; the explicit 200-sample optimization limit is additional disclosure.

E4.justification: Appendix A substantially expands analysis of efficiency and collaboration: cost dynamics across the remaining model configurations, performance-per-token trajectories, concrete agent-interaction motifs, and an embodied execution case study. The original reward-weight and depth/width sensitivity analyses remain.

E5.justification: No new repeated-run counts, seed information, confidence intervals, or significance-testing procedures are supplied. LOWESS smoothing is retained for the additional curves; the computational-resource ranges are not reported as uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: Table 1 is numerically unchanged, including the evolved Titan Puppeteer average of 0.7731. However, Figures 8–9 add extensive cost, agent-count, and performance/cost trajectories, including settings without consistent improvement. Figures 10–11 add qualitative interaction and embodied-execution evidence, substantially expanding the reported results.

M1.justification: The centralized agent-selection procedure, REINFORCE optimization, aggregation, and quality–cost reward remain unchanged. Appendix B documents agent prompts; Appendix A.4 applies the framework to another environment without introducing a new algorithmic component.

P1.justification: The main section order and nearly all existing prose are retained. v2 clarifies the explanation accompanying Equation (6), updates contact and conference information, adds an acknowledgement, and organizes new material into appendices. There is little rewriting or restructuring of the existing narrative.

P2.justification: The appendix introduces extensive multi-panel plots, agent-topology diagrams, an environment-frame sequence, boxed prompt templates, and two tables. Figure 8 both redisplays the existing Titan curves and adds other configurations. Main-text figures are also repositioned or resized, notably Figures 2–3.

R1.justification: Seven cited works are added, with the previous references retained. Section 4 now acknowledges classical multi-agent reinforcement learning as inspiration for coordination and role specialization; additional appendix citations include ALFWorld, AlphaMath, and MindStar. The principal positioning against LLM-based orchestration methods remains unchanged.

T1.justification: Appendix A.2 introduces the performance/cost score, explicitly defined as task performance divided by token cost. This is a limited mathematical-definition addition. The graph and Markov formulations, optimization objective, and reward equations (1)–(6) remain unchanged, with no new theorem or proof.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially improves evidential completeness and reproducibility: it supplies cost evidence referenced but absent from v1, documents agent prompts and computational requirements, and explains settings where efficiency gains are inconsistent. Its concrete limitations also make the retained claims easier to assess. The ALFWorld evidence remains illustrative and repeated-run uncertainty is still unreported, but these limits do not negate the substantial gains in documentation and empirical scrutiny.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Puppeteer research and have readable text, equations, tables, and figures. v1 ends after its references despite mentioning an appendix; v2 includes Appendices A–D. Their absence from the supplied v1 is established, rather than an extraction gap.

after.justification: v2 retains these empirical results and adds cost and performance trajectories, agent-interaction examples, and an ALFWorld execution case study in Appendix A.

before.justification: Table 1 reports original evaluations on GSM-Hard, MMLU-Pro, SRDD, and CommonGen-Hard. Figures 2–7 report learning dynamics, topology analyses, and sensitivity experiments.

results.title: Multi-Agent Collaboration via Evolving Orchestration

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contribution list and conclusion retain the same scheduling contributions and headline 3.76x average/7.54x maximum speedup claims. Additional experiments support existing claims without redefining the central contribution.

C2.justification: V2 adds interpretations connecting oversized buckets and memory imbalance to OOM risk and rollback safeguards. Appendix A attributes small loss differences to floating-point accumulation order. These refine v1's existing computation/memory trade-off explanation and training-equivalence discussion.

D1.justification: V2 clarifies that global batch size equals DP degree times BatchSize, describes the sorted-batching implementation, adds round-robin pseudocode and clarifies rollback's state arguments. Existing hardware and profiling details remain. Detailed settings for the new LoRA runs are still sparse.

E1.justification: Documented dataset and task coverage remains Wikipedia, LMsysChat1M and ChatQA2-Long-SFT for long-context fine-tuning. The added analyses reuse existing coverage; larger-model LoRA experiments expand model/training configurations without identifying additional datasets or tasks.

E2.justification: Beyond v1's DeepSpeed baseline and component variants, v2 evaluates LongAlign's sorted-batching strategy across all six Figure 3 settings. Tables 3–4 additionally compare round-robin scheduling with Skrull, substantially expanding the evaluated scheduling alternatives.

E3.justification: V2 introduces 14B/32B LoRA configurations, a bucket-size sweep, rollback controls and per-iteration memory measurements. It explicitly specifies DP=1 and CP=8 for the sensitivity study, differing from v1's blanket DP=4 setup; this is a reported setting revision, not evidence that experiments were rerun. Figure 3's original configurations remain.

E4.justification: V2 retains the component and batch-size ablations, adding bucket-size sensitivity through OOM, scheduling comparisons with and without rollback, and a four-iteration memory case study. Appendix A also adds a training-loss comparison testing whether scheduling affects convergence.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals or significance tests. The new minimum/maximum tuples described as memory usage across GPUs do not constitute run-to-run uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Original Figure 3 values remain, while v2 adds sorted-batching scores, 1.40x versus 1.17x Skrull/RR speedups, rollback-related OOMs, bucket-size results, LoRA speedups of 2.37x/2.54x and similar training-loss curves. Its prose inconsistently attributes 3.76x to both DeepSpeed and sorted batching before separately reporting 3.45x against sorted batching; these should not be treated as equivalent comparisons.

M1.justification: The proposed DACP/GDS scheduling rules, objectives and Algorithms 1–2 remain unchanged. Algorithm 3 makes state arguments explicit and permits an absent load array, without establishing changed behavior for Skrull's normal scheduling path. The added round-robin algorithm is a comparator.

P1.justification: Most introductory, methodological and concluding prose is retained. Changes include localized evaluation and related-work revisions, author affiliations, acknowledgments, small wording corrections and appendix reorganization into precision validation, scheduling algorithms and performance modeling.

P2.justification: V2 redraws Figure 2, adds a comparator series to Figure 3, and replaces the small batch-size plot with a two-panel Figure 4 covering sensitivity and LoRA. It adds two case-study tables and a loss figure. The original FLOPs figure and communication table are retained and relocated. New Table 4's latency caption conflicts with its memory interpretation in the text.

R1.justification: V2 removes the assertion that LongAlign's sorted batching breaks training equivalence and drops the separate ChatQA 2 paper reference while retaining its dataset citation. Several other references receive publication metadata updates, without representing newly cited research.

T1.justification: The scheduling formulations and performance-modeling equations 1–16 are unchanged. V1's performance-modeling Appendix A becomes Appendix C in v2. The new loss comparison supplies empirical validation, not a new mathematical derivation or proof.

improvement.justification: V1 lacked an evaluated competing scheduling strategy, direct rollback validation and a convergence check. V2 addresses these important gaps through sorted-batching comparisons, controlled OOM/memory analyses and training-loss validation, substantially strengthening support for the scheduler's benefits and behavior in the tested settings. Sparse LoRA settings and numerical/caption inconsistencies limit reproducibility and clarity, but do not outweigh these gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Skrull and provide readable main text, equations, figures, tables and appendices. Retained content can be matched reliably across the appendix reorganization and expanded evaluation.

after.justification: The original experiments remain, supplemented by sorted-batching comparisons, bucket-size and rollback studies, larger-model LoRA results and training-loss validation.

before.justification: Section 5 reports original training-speed measurements on three datasets, DACP/GDS component ablations and batch-size sensitivity experiments.

results.title: Skrull: Towards Efficient Long Context Fine-tuning through Dynamic Data Scheduling

C1.justification: Both versions claim precise token-level manipulation through imperceptible visual perturbations, greater visual than textual susceptibility, applicability across eight tasks and a watermarking application. The added evidence does not redefine these central contributions.

C2.justification: v2 interprets the new component and sensitivity results, explains limited transfer through the precision required for output control, and adds momentum's per-iteration runtime tradeoff. The existing limitations concerning cross-model transfer and longer target sequences remain.

D1.justification: v1 only points to supplementary code; v2 additionally supplies a repository pointer. New disclosures include a default momentum coefficient of 0.9, manipulation-pool sources and construction, GPT-4o-generated targets, sample prompts and outputs, and explicit prompts for the sponge and watermarking examples. These disclosures do not establish changes to previously used settings.

E1.justification: Appendices F-G add manipulation under defense conditions and cross-model transfer scenarios. The eight task families and named benchmark corpora remain; the larger manipulation sample primarily changes sampling rather than task coverage.

E2.justification: Table 11 newly compares full VMA against three component-reduced controls: neither transformation nor momentum, transformation alone, and momentum alone. These controlled comparisons were absent from v1. Newly cited prior attacks are not newly benchmarked.

E3.justification: v2 adds evaluation on 1,000 randomly sampled image-prompt-target triplets while retaining the five-prompt, ten-image, ten-target analysis. It also introduces Phi3 hyperparameter sweeps, component controls, defense testing and source-to-target model evaluation. Section 2.3 clarifies evaluation reasoning without establishing a change to the retained GPT-based judging procedure.

E4.justification: New Section 6 tests learning-rate sensitivity, momentum sensitivity and the separate contributions of transformation and momentum to success and convergence. Appendices F-G add defense robustness and cross-model transfer analyses, substantially extending v1's diagnostic evidence.

E5.justification: Neither version supplies repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals or significance tests for the empirical results. The added checklist answers yes to statistical-significance reporting, but provides no corresponding uncertainty estimates or procedures.

E6.justification: Original Tables 1-8 retain their values. New results include manipulation ASRs of 92.41%, 89.35%, 89.99% and 89.71% in Appendix E; defense ASRs of 84.32%, 90.40% and 72.6%; and cross-model transfer ASRs of 8.58%-20.16%. Table 11 adds component results ranging from 71% success and 104 iterations to 96% and 26 iterations. These are additional evaluations, not same-setting improvements over v1.

M1.justification: The target-sequence objective, sigmoid-based differentiable transformation, momentum optimization and Algorithm 1 are unchanged. The new component studies evaluate existing ingredients rather than introduce a revised attack.

P1.justification: v2 corrects 'You' to 'Your' in the title, updates the publication footer and adds localized explanations. It inserts ablation and social-impact sections, Appendices E-G and a conference checklist, while preserving most existing prose and the main narrative.

P2.justification: v2 adds ablation Tables 9-11, prompt and target-output Tables 21-22, and transfer matrix Table 23. The sponge and watermarking tables gain prompt columns, and the sponge table gains original outputs. Existing figures and other experimental displays are largely retained, with relocation and renumbering.

R1.justification: Six references are added. Appendix A.2 expands discussion of Adam-based transferable attacks and backdoor-trigger approaches, including BadVision and Shadowcast, while retaining the original positioning around precise output manipulation.

T1.justification: The mathematical definitions, two theorems, certified-radius corollary and Appendix D's lemma and proof are retained without substantive changes.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens empirical justification: Table 11 directly tests the proposed optimization components, Appendix E expands manipulation evaluation beyond five prompts, and Appendices F-G test defenses and quantify the previously asserted transfer limitation. These address important validation gaps in v1. Defense settings remain underspecified and statistical uncertainty is still missing, but the added controlled and boundary-testing evidence provides a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same VMA research. Their text, equations, figures, tables and appendices support comparison, including matching retained material across relocation and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains these original results and adds component ablations, hyperparameter studies, expanded manipulation evaluation, defense tests and cross-model transfer results.

before.justification: v1 reports original experiments across four VLMs, including output manipulation, seven application tasks, modality sensitivity and qualitative examples.

results.title: Attention! Your Vision Language Model Could Be Maliciously Manipulated

C1.justification: The abstract and conclusions broaden the work from one-hop dependency parsing to multilingual parsing, non-linguistic graph inference, and k-hop GAT parsing. Investigating GNN-based refinement changes from future work in v1 to a claimed confirmed extension in v2. The central normalization benefit and up-to-85% parameter-reduction claims are retained.

C2.justification: V2 interprets its new evidence as supporting language-independent and non-linguistic applicability, and discusses why multi-hop refinement offers less benefit for semantic than syntactic parsing. The depth discussion changes from sharp failures under short training to dataset-dependent instability after longer training. Appendix B interprets shrinking or reversing normalization advantages as further support for depth compensation.

D1.justification: V2 adds treebank split counts and source links, identifies the mBERT checkpoint, and documents graph-feature construction, coordinate concatenation, adjacency inputs, and approximate model sizes. The abstract's code pointer changes from an anonymous repository to the author's GitHub repository. Existing hardware, optimizer, and main-experiment compute disclosures are retained.

E1.justification: V2 retains the original six datasets and adds syntactic parsing in Arabic, Chinese, Italian, Japanese, Spanish, and Wolof. It also evaluates unlabeled graph inference on PCQM-Contact, CIFAR10 Superpixel, and QM9, substantially extending language, domain, and task coverage.

E2.justification: The Bhatt et al. baseline in Table 3 is retained. V2 additionally evaluates unnormalized biaffine–GAT parsers against their normalized counterparts on the original six datasets (Table 7), adding an architectural comparison family without expanding the named external baseline set.

E3.justification: The deep-BiLSTM experiment changes from 2,000 training steps in v1 Appendix B.2 to 20,000 in v2 Appendix D.2. Added experiments introduce mBERT for multilingual parsing and controlled GAT-depth evaluations with zero parser BiLSTM layers; non-linguistic evaluation uses unlabeled F1. These are substantive experimental-design changes, not merely additional disclosure.

E4.justification: V2 adds analyses testing normalization across GAT refinement depths on linguistic and non-linguistic graphs. It also revises the deep-BiLSTM analysis with longer training and adds enEWT and SciDTB to that analysis. The original tagger, MLP-size, initialization, LayerNorm, and full-fine-tuning ablations remain.

E5.justification: The five-seed mean/standard-deviation and Wilcoxon reporting framework is retained, but v2 Appendix B specifies three seeds for the new non-linguistic experiments. The replacement depth plot also omits the p-values displayed in v1 Figure 5. The general five-seed statement and checklist are not reconciled with the three-seed exception.

E6.justification: Table 3 and the original supplementary tables retain their numerical results after relocation. V2 adds Tables 5–7, changes Figure 1's rank trajectories, and replaces the depth results under a longer training budget. New Table 6 reports CIFAR10 Superpixel F1 of 0.407 raw versus 0.531 normalized with one GAT layer, but 0.751 versus 0.703 with three, showing that the added findings include reversals.

M1.justification: V2 extends the original one-hop parser with repeated biaffine–GAT blocks before the final scorer (Appendix C, Figure 5). Appendix B also introduces a non-linguistic adaptation using graph features, GAT processing, and sigmoid edge predictions without MST decoding. These change architecture and inference, while retaining the original normalization rule.

P1.justification: The main section sequence and much of the prose remain intact. V2 makes localized language edits, standardizes BiLSTM-depth notation to N, adds acknowledgements, and reorganizes the appendices: the original full-results discussion moves from Appendix A to E, following the new studies and retained ablations.

P2.justification: V2 adds four tables and a GAT architecture diagram, and replaces the four-panel depth plot with a six-panel plot. Figures 1 and 2 are redrawn, Table 1 is reformatted, and retained figures and tables are relocated, including the full-results table moving from Table 4 to Table 13. These substantially expand and revise the visual presentation.

R1.justification: V2 retains the original 44 references and adds ten covering latent graph inference, GATs, graph benchmarks, multilingual Universal Dependencies, and ACE corpora. Section 2 adds a brief broader graph-inference framing, while the principal positioning relative to biaffine dependency parsers remains.

T1.justification: Section 3 replaces Claim 1's Frobenius-norm covariance inequality with monotonicity of total variance measured by covariance trace. V2 explicitly defines nested truncated-SVD approximations and supplies a new trace/Loewner-order proof, avoiding v1's unjustified assertion that increasing rank adds a positive-semidefinite covariance increment.

improvement.justification: V2 replaces an unsupported step in the central mathematical argument with a valid trace/SVD proof and substantially strengthens applicability testing through multilingual, GAT, and non-linguistic experiments. The longer-training depth analysis also addresses an important weakness of the original experiment. Broad generalizations still need qualification given Table 6's reversals, and seed and limitations-checklist statements remain inconsistent. Nevertheless, the improved formal support and broader empirical scrutiny provide a substantial net quality gain.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same normalization-based dependency-parsing study. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables, appendices, and checklists are readable and support reliable matching across revisions.

after.justification: V2 retains these empirical results and adds multilingual parsing, non-linguistic graph inference, GAT experiments, and revised depth experiments.

before.justification: V1 reports original experiments on six dependency-parsing datasets, including architecture ablations, fine-tuning results, and convergence analyses.

results.title: Dependency Parsing is More Parameter-Efficient with Normalization

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same central contributions: adaptive selection among four formats, Ada-GRPO addressing format collapse, approximately 30% average token savings, approximately twofold training speedup, and three reasoning modes. The new appendix evidence supports these claims without redefining their main scope.

C2.justification: New discussion identifies training-data bias as a cause of format collapse, explains smaller LLaMA savings through repetitive outputs, and discusses execution latency and resource costs. Appendix L adds specific limitations concerning predefined formats and missing hard-task training data. Appendix K expands the budget-estimation argument, although its claim of consistent L1 superiority with similar token usage overstates Table 12.

D1.justification: The original hardware, training frameworks, SFT/RL hyperparameters, and data-processing instructions remain unchanged. v2 supplies implementation information for interpreter execution and fallback, specifies the historical AIME training range and inference-time format exclusions, and identifies the L1-Qwen-7B-Exact checkpoint and budget-setting procedure.

E1.justification: v2 adds ARM evaluation on GPQA-Main, GPQA-Diamond, and StrategyQA, plus an AIME 1983–2024-only training condition. Table 11 additionally includes AMC and olympiad_bench in the L1 budget analysis. These expand task and training-data coverage while retaining the original training datasets and seven main evaluation benchmarks.

E2.justification: L1, previously compared with ARM only on CSQA in Figure 4, is additionally compared on the retained OBQA, GSM8K, MATH, SVAMP, BBH, and AIME’25 tasks in Table 12. The main Table 1 comparator roster and the existing THINKPRUNE comparison remain unchanged.

E3.justification: New evaluation designs include inference-time exclusion of selected reasoning formats, a LLaMA-3.2-3B configuration, and L1 budget sweeps at 512, 1024, 2048, and 3600 tokens. Appendix K.3 adds a separate comparison using aligned 7B DS-R1-Distill backbones and dataset-specific L1 budgets based on ARM’s token usage. The original main evaluation settings and Appendix D hyperparameters are retained.

E4.justification: v2 adds tests of whether biased training data cause format collapse (Tables 4–5), whether interpreter execution helps (Table 8), and what happens when Direct Answer, Short CoT, or Long CoT is unavailable (Table 9). Table 11 adds token-budget sensitivity analysis. The existing decay, reflective-word, and overthinking analyses are retained rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: The reflection analysis remains averaged over eight runs, moving from Appendix E to G. Existing pass@1 and majority@8 reporting is retained, and additional rows use that practice. Neither version reports confidence intervals, significance tests, or additional seed information that changes the uncertainty-reporting approach.

E6.justification: The original main tables and reflection results are unchanged, but substantial new results cover training bias, additional benchmarks, format ablations, LLaMA, and L1 budgets. For example, Table 6 reports StrategyQA accuracy/tokens of 73.8%/229 for ARM versus 72.9%/646 for GRPO. Table 9 reports AIME’25 accuracy falling from 16.7% to 8.3% when Long CoT is removed. These are added experimental comparisons, not improvements over v1 under unchanged conditions.

M1.justification: Equations 6 and 7 change the stated objective from averaging per-response token means to averaging all tokens within the response group. Appendix H also adds an optional inference procedure that executes generated Code and falls back to simulated output upon failure. The core SFT, diversity reward, decay, and four-format framework remain. The PDFs do not establish whether the objective revision reflects changed implementation or corrected documentation.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main section order are retained, with limited copyediting, updated affiliations and venue information, and new appendix cross-references. New appendix sections accompany the added studies; the existing reflection, overthinking, and length-penalty sections are renumbered or expanded. There is no extensive rewriting of the main narrative.

P2.justification: v2 adds eight substantive result tables, numbered 4–6 and 8–12, displaying training bias, additional benchmarks, format ablations, LLaMA results, and L1 comparisons. Existing figures and original table content are retained; the reflection table becomes Table 7, and Figure 5 moves from page 8 to page 9. The principal visual change is the substantial expansion of tabular evidence.

R1.justification: Six references are added: HybridMind, Chain of Code, OctoThinker, and sources for StrategyQA, GPQA, and LLaMA 3. They support the added experiments and implementation discussion. The main related-work organization and positioning around autonomous efficient reasoning remain substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: The objective normalization in Equations 6 and 7 changes from equal weighting of response-level averages to a token-level average across the group. These expressions are not equivalent for unequal response lengths. This is a localized mathematical revision; the reward, decay, advantage definitions, and absence of formal proofs remain unchanged.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation of the central design: training-bias and format-removal controls address questions left untested in v1, while GPQA/StrategyQA and LLaMA experiments broaden evidence for generalization. The new limitations also clarify applicability. These gains outweigh localized weaknesses: the loss-normalization revision is unexplained, and Appendix K.3 overstates Table 12, where ARM has lower OBQA accuracy and substantially higher AIME token usage than L1.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe ARM and Ada-GRPO. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support reliable comparison, including matching analyses that were relocated or renumbered.

after.justification: v2 retains these empirical results and adds training-data and reasoning-format ablations, GPQA/StrategyQA evaluations, LLaMA experiments, and further L1 comparisons.

before.justification: v1 reports original model-training and evaluation results, including Tables 1–2, training dynamics, a decay ablation, and appendix analyses of reflection and overthinking.

results.title: ARM: Adaptive Reasoning Model

C1.justification: The abstracts, contribution lists, and conclusions retain the same central claims: combining self-instruction and majority-voting rewards enables RL from limited data, outperforms iterative counterparts, and approaches training with extensive labeled data. The additional experiments support these claims without redefining them.

C2.justification: v2 explicitly discusses limitations for open-ended writing and process-sensitive tasks such as proofs, and interprets difficulty filtering as curriculum learning that reduces reward-estimation bias. It revises explanations of Reinforce++ robustness toward batch normalization and RLOO's amplification of reward errors, and further qualifies iterative improvement as capacity-limited. The main interpretation of SeRL's benefits remains intact.

D1.justification: Appendix C newly documents the ROUGE-L threshold of 0.7, 3-150-word limits, fuller keyword and initial-character exclusion rules, the one-quarter seed/three-quarter generated few-shot mixture, and the CoT sampling prompt. It also clarifies SR-DPO's reward-model identity, while Section 4.1 specifies the evaluation token limit. These address substantial implementation gaps. The abstract's public code link remains, while the additional anonymous link is removed.

E1.justification: v2 adds an actual medical-domain training and evaluation setting: MedQA supplies seed instructions, and evaluation covers MedQA, PubMedQA, and NephSAP (Appendix D.3). This substantially extends the mathematical training and math/general-reasoning evaluations retained from v1.

E2.justification: v2 adds SFT baselines using majority responses, correct responses, and responses distilled from Qwen2.5-Math-7B-Instruct (Table 8). Its reward-alignment comparison additionally evaluates entropy-based and CAI rewards (Table 11). These extend the actual comparator sets; the original I-RPO, SR-DPO, and RL-GT comparisons remain.

E3.justification: New evaluation designs include equal-step filtering ablations, training through six iterations, and medical training with 500 seed instructions against a full-10.2k-data baseline. Reward alignment gains MAE and MSE metrics. Section 4.1 also replaces the approximate 100-steps-per-7,500-instructions budget description with matched gradient steps; this reported revision does not establish that existing experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds individual filtering-component ablations (Table 3), filtered training curves alongside the existing unfiltered curves (Figure 2), analysis of convergence through iterations 4-6 (Table 9), and broader reward-reliability comparisons (Table 11). The original reward-hacking case study, RL-MV ablation, RL-algorithm comparison, and generated-data analyses are retained rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests for benchmark performance. The instruction-length and quality summaries with plus/minus values are unchanged between v1 Table 7 and v2 Table 12. The new reward-error metrics do not constitute uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Table 2 replaces v1's duplicated Qwen MMLU-Pro values: its initial average changes from 34.0 to 57.3, and iteration-3 average from 35.1 to 57.4. New Tables 3 and 8-11 add filtering, SFT, extended-iteration, medical, and reward-alignment results. Original Table 1 math scores remain unchanged; the revised Qwen entries should not be interpreted as a cross-version training gain.

M1.justification: SeRL retains online instruction generation, the same four filtering components, majority-voting rewards, shortest-response tie-breaking, and iterative RL updates. The expanded implementation description and revised Reinforce++ equations do not establish a change to the implemented SeRL procedure.

P1.justification: Most of the introduction, method narrative, and conclusion remain closely matched. v2 standardizes terminology, edits selected explanations, labels the ablation subsections, moves Reinforce++ exposition into Appendix C.1, and adds an appendix contents page and expanded subsection structure. Affiliations and acknowledgements also change.

P2.justification: v2 adds substantial tabular displays for filtering components, SFT strategies, extended iterations, medical benchmarks, and reward alignment (Tables 3 and 8-11). Figure 2 becomes a direct filtered/unfiltered training comparison. Existing benchmark highlighting is simplified, prompt displays are relabeled as boxes, and appendix figures are redistributed while retaining their underlying analyses.

R1.justification: Section 5 adds substantive positioning against WizardLM, TeaMs-RL, and RLSC, and the bibliography gains supporting RL and medical references. The central positioning relative to self-instruction, self-rewarding, and TTRL remains. Citation renumbering and publication-metadata updates are not substantive research-positioning changes.

T1.justification: Equation 1 changes the sampling distribution in the objective from the current policy to the old policy. Appendix C.1 replaces v1's return expression with accumulated reward/KL expressions and a terminal-reward derivation, alongside explicit advantage-normalization formulas. These are limited mathematical revisions to the existing RL exposition, with no new theorem or proof.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens support for the paper's central design and applicability: controlled filter ablations test previously unisolated components, and medical experiments extend validation beyond mathematical training. It also repairs the duplicated Qwen results, supplies important reproduction details, and better states applicability and iteration limits. Run-level uncertainty remains absent, and Table 11 does not explain how its majority-reward MAE/MSE values relate to the stated binary rewards. These reporting weaknesses temper individual findings but do not outweigh the substantial gains in validation and reproducibility.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SeRL research. Their complete main texts, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching relocated and renumbered material.

after.justification: v2 retains original experimental results and adds filtering ablations, SFT comparisons, longer training experiments, medical-domain evaluations, and additional reward comparisons.

before.justification: v1 reports original LLaMA and Qwen experiments on mathematical benchmarks and MMLU-Pro, together with reward-hacking, reward-alignment, and generated-data analyses.

results.title: SeRL: Self-Play Reinforcement Learning for Large Language Models with Limited Data

C1.justification: The central contribution remains localized adaptation with greater effective rank and comparable computational cost. The abstract and conclusion extend the claimed empirical applicability from code generation and commonsense reasoning to mathematical reasoning, language understanding, and image generation.

C2.justification: New results sections interpret mathematical performance as evidence of usable higher-rank capacity and GLUE/SDXL performance as evidence of applicability beyond decoder language models. The original gradient-entanglement explanation and limitations concerning uniform partitioning and low-rank blocks remain unchanged.

D1.justification: Appendix E substantially expands technical documentation through Tables 9–10, including optimizers, task-specific learning rates, classification-head learning rates, ranks, batches, and epochs; Section 4.1 adds hardware information. Conversely, v2 removes the explicit repository URL and original final-epoch checkpoint-selection statements. Its checklist asserts supplementary code availability without supplying a replacement repository address.

E1.justification: v2 adds MetaMathQA training with MATH evaluation, six GLUE tasks, and personalized image generation using Naruto-Blip-Captions. These substantially extend task and modality coverage beyond the retained code-generation and eight commonsense tasks. MNLI and QQP were not evaluated in v1, so their exclusion is not a removal.

E2.justification: Table 6 adds commonsense comparisons with Full-FT, LoRA-XS, LoRA-SB, MELoRA, rsLoRA, PiSSA, DoRA, BOFT, and LoRA-Pro; several scores are explicitly borrowed from Ponkshe et al. Table 7 additionally compares against VeRA and FourierFT on GLUE. The original LoRA, MoRA, and RaSA comparisons remain.

E3.justification: New protocols include rank-32 LLaMA3.2–3B commonsense evaluation, rank-8 RoBERTa GLUE experiments without MNLI-based transfer, and rank-128 SDXL training with a 90/10 split and CLIP/DINOv2 similarity metrics. Tables 9–10 specify additional training budgets and settings. Original benchmark settings are retained. Mathematical-model identity is inconsistent: Section 4.1 names LLaMA3.2–3B, while Tables 4 and 9 name Qwen2.5–1.5B.

E4.justification: The k sweep, hybrid-allocation sweep, gradient/outlier analyses, rank analysis, and resource comparisons are retained. Figure 8 corrects the presentation of the existing sweep rather than documenting a new analysis. The added appendix benchmark tables do not introduce a separate robustness or sensitivity study.

E5.justification: Neither version reports training-seed counts, repeated-run uncertainty, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The new checklist explains that error bars were omitted because of computational expense, but does not change the statistical reporting practice.

E6.justification: Original benchmark entries remain unchanged, while substantial new results appear. LLaMA3.2–3B commonsense averages are 84.6% for GraLoRA versus 81.3% for LoRA. Table 4 reports rank-128 MATH accuracy of 28.9% versus 24.7%. Tables 7–8 add GLUE and image-similarity results. The GLUE 86.0% 'Best GraLoRA' row combines taskwise maxima; individual GraLoRA and Hybrid averages are 85.8% and 85.6%.

M1.justification: The blockwise GraLoRA construction, local adapter ranks, and Hybrid GraLoRA combination remain unchanged. Applying these methods to additional architectures does not establish a new algorithmic component.

P1.justification: The experimental setup is reorganized, three results subsections and an additional-results appendix are inserted, and the former Appendix D becomes Appendix E. Acknowledgments and a conference checklist are added. Most existing introduction, method, analysis, and ablation prose remains substantially unchanged.

P2.justification: v2 substantially expands tabular presentation with mathematical, extended-baseline, GLUE, image-generation, and task-specific hyperparameter tables, while enlarging existing comparison tables. Figure 8 corrects the rank-group assignment and replaces three identical k=8 legend labels with k=2, 4, and 8. The other nine figures retain their content.

R1.justification: v2 adds citations supporting the new datasets and architectures, including MetaMath/MATH, GLUE/RoBERTa, and SDXL/Naruto, plus FourierFT and Ponkshe et al. The central positioning relative to LoRA and prior outlier research is largely unchanged; there is no substantial new related-work synthesis.

T1.justification: v1 identifies both the true weight gradient and the reconstructed adapter update as dL/dR. Equations 2 and 4 in v2 distinguish these quantities, correcting their mathematical identification. The update algebra, rank argument, assumptions, and appendix FLOPs derivation remain unchanged.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the empirical basis for GraLoRA's generality: v1's evidence centered on two decoder-language-model domains, whereas v2 tests encoder and diffusion architectures and adds much broader PEFT and Full-FT comparisons. The gradient-definition and Figure 8 corrections also improve accuracy. These gains outweigh the new mathematical-model naming inconsistency and weaker code-access documentation, although the continued absence of uncertainty estimates limits confidence in small reported differences.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe GraLoRA, and their main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support comparison. The original method and experiments can be matched despite expanded evaluation and renumbering in v2.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds mathematical reasoning, GLUE, image generation, and additional commonsense experiments. Some newly included baseline scores are explicitly attributed to prior work.

before.justification: v1 reports original code-generation and commonsense-reasoning experiments, alongside gradient, rank, memory, and training-time measurements.

results.title: GraLoRA: Granular Low-Rank Adaptation for Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning

C1.justification: The abstracts, contribution lists, and conclusions retain the same central claims: a pathologist-like agent, unified multiscale training, an expert-validated huge-region benchmark, and strong performance across three image scales. Rewriting and additional supporting experiments do not redefine these contributions.

C2.justification: v2 qualifies the above-expert PathMMU results through discussion of textual shortcuts and the expert lead on PathMMU-Pro. It adds interpretations of component contributions and OOD performance. Appendix D introduces substantive limitations concerning synthetic rather than observed clinical trajectories, restricted task scope, and training-data scale.

D1.justification: v2 explicitly documents patient-level splitting, clarifies that the complete cropped-view sequence enters reasoning together, and describes matched-split CPath-Omni retraining. Appendix C.2 adds benchmark construction details. Hardware, stage runtimes, optimization hyperparameters, and detailed prompts remain unchanged, with no new code or data access instructions.

E1.justification: Beyond the retained PathMMU and TCGA evaluations, v2 adds CPTAC-Lung WSI classification and BRACS benign/atypical/malignant region classification, extending evaluation to external cohorts. PathMMU-Pro adds questions designed to require visual discrimination while reducing textual shortcuts (Section 4.4 and Appendix B.3).

E2.justification: v2 adds CPath-Omni to the PathMMU-HR² comparison and a retrained CPath-Omni* to TCGA WSI classification. PRISM and TITAN become evaluated comparators in Figure 4. Quilt-LLaVA and PathGen-LLaVA WSI comparisons already existed in v1's Table 4 and are relocated into Table 3.

E3.justification: New controls replace learned screening with random selection of 70% of regions and replace navigation/reasoning with single-view descriptions. The added CPath-Omni* comparison uses matched-split retraining. PathMMU-HR²'s reported total changes from 1,688 to 1,668, matching the unchanged tissue counts; this supports a reporting correction, not an inference that the benchmark was resampled.

E4.justification: v2 adds component ablations, external-distribution testing, and a shortcut-focused PathMMU-Pro analysis, addressing component contributions, generalization, and benchmark bias. The 40-region pathologist study and Gemini agent failure analysis are retained and relocated, rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: Both versions report MIL results averaged over five random seeds and pass@k from eight generations across 40 regions. Relocating and explaining the pathologist study adds no new repetition or uncertainty-reporting practice. No confidence intervals or significance tests are introduced.

E6.justification: New results include 88.1% CPTAC-Lung and 64.3% BRACS balanced accuracy, 65.3% PathMMU-Pro full-set accuracy, and 80.3%/75.0% WSI balanced accuracy for the two component ablations. New comparisons place TITAN ahead on CPTAC-Lung and experts ahead on PathMMU-Pro Tiny. Existing CPathAgent headline scores in Tables 1–3 are retained; these additions do not establish same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: The Qwen3-14B/CPath-CLIP architecture, three-stage training, and screening–navigation–reasoning pipeline are retained. The expanded workflow description documents operations already represented in v1's examples and prompts; the corresponding training and inference prompts remain unchanged.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, and methods receive extensive rewriting. Workflow explanations expand while the training description is condensed. The pathologist evaluation moves into Appendix B.2, WSI comparisons are consolidated, and the appendices are reorganized around a new limitations section.

P2.justification: v1's architecture/training Figure 4 is removed, a new OOD Figure 4 is added, and the pass@k plot moves and is redrawn as Figure A9. WSI tables are consolidated and reorganized, while Tables A4–A5 introduce benchmark and ablation displays. The remaining appendix examples and prompts are largely retained and renumbered.

R1.justification: v2 adds references supporting CPTAC-Lung, BRACS, and PathMMU-Pro, and extends positioning against PRISM and TITAN through generalization and data-efficiency comparisons. The established distinction from static pathology models and PathFinder remains substantially intact.

T1.justification: Section 3.1 adds set and tuple notation for region grouping, prioritization, and navigation paths already documented through v1's examples and prompts. This is a formal restatement of the workflow, without new mathematical properties, substantive assumptions, derivations, or proofs.

improvement.justification: External-cohort tests and direct component ablations address important gaps in v1's evidence for generalization and component effectiveness. PathMMU-Pro evaluation and explicit limitations also improve the calibration of claims about expert-level reasoning and clinical applicability. These are substantial gains in validation, although the new data-efficiency comparison needs qualification: its 5,254-WSI count excludes the larger screening-overview pool documented in Appendix A.1.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same CPathAgent work. Their text, tables, figures, and complete appendices support comparison, including matching material moved between the main text and appendices.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds external-cohort evaluations, PathMMU-Pro results, and component ablations.

before.justification: v1 reports original patch-level VQA, huge-region analysis, WSI classification, description-generation comparisons, and pathologist evaluations.

results.title: CPathAgent: An Agent-based Foundation Model for Interpretable High-Resolution Pathology Image Analysis Mimicking Pathologists' Diagnostic Logic

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction contributions and conclusion retain the same claims: a first fully spiking unified frame-event tracker, RPM for padding-induced positional bias, STR for feature consistency, and favorable accuracy-efficiency tradeoffs. Additional documentation and experiments support these existing contributions without redefining them.

C2.justification: v2 expands the interpretation of VisEvent underperformance around scenario difficulty and dataset size, attributes gains primarily to RPM using the new input-count controls, and explains failure regimes for excessive or insufficient loss weights. Appendix I retains the pretraining limitation already discussed in v1 and identifies neuromorphic deployment as future work. The new 17.4-point VisEvent comparison uses different test subsets, limiting that interpretation.

D1.justification: v1 directs readers to an absent appendix for important details. v2 supplies SFA, event representation, response-loss and attention specifications; architecture and training hyperparameters in Tables 5-6; energy-estimation formulas and assumptions; and explicit VisEvent preprocessing and 320-versus-172 test-set distinctions. It also clarifies inference templates and provides a code/model repository link in place of a future-release promise. These substantially improve documented reproducibility without establishing corresponding implementation changes.

E1.justification: Section 4.1 newly reports ImageNet-1K pretraining for SpikeFET-Tiny and SpikeET, whereas v1 describes pretraining through frame-tracking datasets. FE108, VisEvent and COESOT remain the evaluation datasets, and the previously named tracking-pretraining datasets remain represented for Base. No new tracking task or evaluation domain is introduced.

E2.justification: Table 2 removes DiMP50 from the reported event-only FE108 comparison: its 57.1 AUC and 85.1 PR entries become dashes, although it remains a VisEvent comparator. Other comparator memberships are retained. Table 1's new early-fusion and pretraining markers disclose comparator settings rather than introduce new methods.

E3.justification: v2 adds four-input controls alongside six-input configurations, alpha/beta sweeps, and an RTX 4090 FPS/MAC/AC evaluation. Section 4.1 also narrows the previously general tracking-dataset pretraining description to Base. Most newly stated splits, optimization settings and budgets document existing experiments; the PDFs do not establish that retained results were rerun.

E4.justification: Table 3 adds controls testing whether RPM's benefits persist with one template per modality. Appendix F adds sensitivity analyses for response-loss and STR weights, Appendix A adds COESOT tracking examples, and Table 11 supplies layer firing profiles relevant to efficiency. Together these substantially extend the original component and fusion ablations.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or statistical significance tests for the experimental results. The added experiments retain point-estimate reporting.

E6.justification: Headline SpikeFET/SpikeET tracking scores are retained, but v2 adds input-count and loss-weight results, baseline energy entries, runtime/operation counts and firing-rate measurements. Tables 9-10 report 106, 49.26 and 185.87 FPS for Tiny, Base and SpikeET respectively. DiMP50's event-only FE108 scores are removed. Table 10 also reports SDTrack FE108 AUC as 66.56, contradicting 59.9 in both versions' Table 2; this is an unresolved reporting discrepancy, not a verified performance or ranking change.

M1.justification: The dual-single-dual architecture, RPM, STR, response loss and inference fusion remain unchanged. The appendix explains previously referenced SFA and CSWin-SSA components, while Section 3.4 clarifies first-frame template duplication; these disclosures do not establish a changed algorithm.

P1.justification: Edits concentrate on implementation and results explanations, a new Datasets subsection, explicit appendix cross-references, and author/publication information. The abstract's scientific content, introduction, related work, core method narrative and conclusion are largely retained. The supplement organizes substantial additional content without a wholesale rewrite of the existing narrative.

P2.justification: v2 adds qualitative Figures 7-8 and Tables 5-11, including a multi-page firing-rate table. Table 3 gains an Inputs column and two configurations, Table 2 is enlarged, Table 1 gains explanatory markers, and Figure 1 labels its horizontal axis as theoretical power. Existing method figures are retained, with some relocated through the revised layout.

R1.justification: All 55 original references are retained, and nine works are added, including ImageNet and sources supporting spiking activations, event representations and energy estimation. The appendix adds some positioning against alternative representations, but Section 2 and the central novelty positioning remain essentially unchanged.

T1.justification: Appendix B.1 adds an explicit firing-rate assumption and an integer-activation-to-spike-sequence derivation, while Appendix E supplies stripe/head definitions and a no-directional-bias assumption. These are limited formal additions for existing components. The original method equations remain unchanged, and no new theorem or proof is introduced.

improvement.justification: v1 relies on an absent appendix for essential implementation and energy-estimation details. v2 supplies these, documents model-specific pretraining and evaluation subsets, and adds controls and runtime evidence, substantially improving reproducibility and scrutiny of the efficiency claims. The contradictory SDTrack AUC values in Tables 2 and 10 and the new comparison across different VisEvent subsets weaken parts of the reporting. These require correction, but the substantial gains in accessible methods and supporting evidence establish a net overall improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SpikeFET work, and their text, equations, figures and tables are readable. v1 ends after the references despite mentioning an appendix; v2 supplies Appendices A-I. The supplied documents support comparison of the retained content and newly documented material.
