after.justification: v2 retains the original tracking results and reports additional input-count and loss-weight ablations, GPU runtimes, qualitative examples and layer firing rates.

before.justification: Tables 1-4 report original SpikeFET and SpikeET tracking results and component ablations.

results.title: Fully Spiking Neural Networks for Unified Frame-Event Object Tracking

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the same contributions: instant stylization from sparse unposed images, separation of structure and appearance, preservation of reconstruction capability, and generalization across scenes and styles. New evaluations support these existing claims.

C2.justification: New Section 5 explicitly weighs single-pass speed and accessibility against optimization-based geometry quality and scalability, acknowledging training-data demands, lower reconstruction fidelity and memory constraints. Appendix C adds explicit view-count and resolution limitations and proposed remedies. This substantially expands the earlier limitations discussion, which chiefly identified static-scene support.

D1.justification: Model architecture, initialization, training resolution, hardware/time, optimizer and learning rates remain unchanged, as do Appendix A's xFormers, DPT and baseline-training details. Project and baseline-checkpoint access information is retained.

E1.justification: The scene/style datasets and reconstruction/stylization tasks remain unchanged. The new metrics and voting study evaluate the already covered RE10K and Tanks and Temples domains without introducing new documented input conditions or task requirements.

E2.justification: StyTr2 newly appears in reported Tanks and Temples comparisons in Tables 3-4; v1's corresponding Figure 4 compared Styl3R with ARF, StyleRF and StyleGaussian. The existing RE10K and novel-view-synthesis comparator sets remain intact.

E3.justification: v2 adds ArtFID and RGB-uv histogram evaluation plus an online study asking voters to select the most harmonious integration of style and scene. It reports 1,274 RE10K votes, 294 Tanks and Temples votes and 392 ablation votes. These substantially expand evaluation beyond the retained consistency and reconstruction protocols.

E4.justification: New Table 5 quantitatively supports the existing relu3_1 versus relu3_1+relu4_1 content-loss ablation using ArtFID, histogram scores and human preferences. The question tested and Figure 7 are retained; identity-loss and input-view-count ablations are unchanged.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run or seed information, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. The new voting totals and percentages describe sample sizes and outcomes, without adding uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: Tables 3-5 add substantial perceptual and preference results: Styl3R receives 53.29% of RE10K votes and 38.78% of Tanks and Temples votes, with ArtFID scores of 35.12 and 38.05. The two-layer content-loss variant receives 64.80% preference. Earlier consistency/runtime scores and NVS scores remain unchanged; v1's NVS Table 3 becomes v2's Table 6.

M1.justification: Section 3 retains the same structure and appearance branches, attention mechanisms, two-stage training, identity loss and progressive multi-view training. Appendix C mentions VGGT only as a possible future replacement, not an implemented component.

P1.justification: v2 inserts a user-study paragraph, a Discussion section and Appendix C, renumbers the conclusion, and adds acknowledgements and the NeurIPS 2025 conference footer. These are localized structural additions; the abstract, introduction and method prose are essentially retained.

P2.justification: Three compact tables are added for preferences, perceptual metrics and ablation results, requiring local text reflow. The original NVS table is renumbered from 3 to 6. All fourteen figures, including the appendix galleries, retain their visual content.

R1.justification: v2 adds HistoGAN and ArtFID as evaluation references and VGGT as a possible future backbone. Section 5 expands positioning against reconstruction-then-stylization pipelines, while the related-work survey and central novelty positioning remain largely unchanged.

T1.justification: The mathematical model definitions, attention equation and training-loss equation are unchanged. The added evaluation metrics are cited without introducing new mathematical definitions, derivations, theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: v1's quantitative evaluation primarily measured consistency and reconstruction, leaving stylistic quality supported mainly by visual examples. v2's perceptual metrics, human preferences and quantitative ablation directly strengthen evidence for this central claim. The new discussion also makes important practical tradeoffs explicit. Together these substantially improve validation and qualification, although missing participant, sampling and uncertainty details still limit the user study.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Styl3R and provide readable main text, equations, tables, figures and appendices. Retained material can be matched reliably despite added sections and table renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains these empirical results and adds human preferences, perceptual metrics and quantitative ablation results in Tables 3-5.

before.justification: v1 reports original stylization, consistency, runtime and novel-view-synthesis results, along with ablations and additional qualitative outputs in the appendix.

results.title: Styl3R: Instant 3D Stylized Reconstruction for Arbitrary Scenes and Styles

C1.justification: v2 adds an explicit abstract-level contribution that trained models and source code are open-sourced; v1 already provided code access. The central contributions remain the four-stage task, targeted capability training, algorithm independence, and accuracy/efficiency benefits. Updated numerical evidence does not redefine these scientific claims.

C2.justification: The efficiency interpretation changes substantially: v1 attributes generally longer responses to repeated verification, whereas v2 distinguishes Q1.5B overhead from R1.5B savings and attributes decreasing length to better Fast Thinking bypassing Slow Thinking. v2 also qualifies the summarization interpretation with possible stochastic variation and drops the 7B nonconvergence qualification. The standalone limitations section disappears, although heuristic parameter selection and failure cases remain documented.

D1.justification: v2 updates the resource pointer and states that trained models are available alongside code. It newly discloses selection of the best validation checkpoint from checkpoints saved every 50 steps, without establishing that selection changed. Footnotes clarify the retained ablations' 6,000-token setting. Prompt templates, hardware, and stated training time remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same 129K training dataset and eight evaluation benchmarks: MATH500, AIME2024, AIME2025, GPQA Diamond, Olympiadbench, AMC23, Minerva Math, and CollegeMath. The new token-efficiency comparison reuses existing benchmarks without introducing a distinct task or test scenario.

E2.justification: New Table 2 substantially broadens comparison to efficiency-focused methods: ThinkPrune, Concise Reasoning, SR-FLOW, and AdaptThink. Their reported accuracies and available response lengths are compared with Thinker using figures extracted from their papers. The existing pretrained, QA baseline, ORZ, and SimpleRL comparisons are retained.

E3.justification: The main experiments reduce Verification from 6,000 to 2,000 tokens, while the retained ablations and 7B experiments still use 6,000. The 7B training curve extends from approximately 750 Thinker steps to 1,000 steps. New Table 2 adds benchmark-level accuracy/response-length comparisons; the existing Pass@1 evaluation averaged over 16 samples is retained.

E4.justification: v2 expands response-length diagnostics with explicit baseline, Fast Thinking, and cumulative-length comparisons for both 1.5B models in Figure 4, and revises the R1.5B reflection/length analysis. The summarization-removal ablation, earlier-checkpoint Fast Thinking ablation, and Appendix C case studies already existed in v1 and are retained.

E5.justification: v1 already reports standard errors. v2 newly reports three independent Q1.5B seeds, standard-deviation bands, per-seed scores and errors, question counts, and a cited standard-error calculation in Appendix B. This substantially expands uncertainty documentation without establishing v1's training-run count. Uncertainty entries for pretrained and SkipSum models are removed.

E6.justification: Table 1's Q1.5B baseline/Thinker/Fast averages change from 24.88/27.85/26.75 to 25.62/27.33/25.18. R1.5B Thinker changes from 49.80 to 50.98, and Appendix D's 7B Thinker from 58.91 to 59.09. v2 also adds accuracy/length results, revises response-length trends, and reverses the SkipSum/SkipSum-Fast row assignments in the retained ablation table. Changed budgets, aggregation, and training extent preclude interpreting these collectively as same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: Section 3.1 and Figure 2 change Verification from a long-budget stage, exemplified by 6,000 tokens, to a short-budget stage of 2,000 tokens. The four-stage sequence, rewards, stage-specific credit assignment, and training/inference transition rules remain unchanged.

P1.justification: v2 selectively rewrites the experimental discussion and conclusion, removes the standalone limitations and acknowledgement sections, updates affiliations and publication information, and adds Appendix E on societal impacts. The overall narrative structure and most method and case-study prose remain intact.

P2.justification: The results presentation is substantially revised: v2 adds the response-length Figure 4 and comparison Table 2, redraws multiple plots with revised legends and uncertainty bands, and replaces compact error tables with separate benchmark- and seed-level displays. The ablation table redisplays existing full-model controls, and Figure 2 recolors Verification to indicate its shorter budget.

R1.justification: Section 4 adds ThinkPrune, Concise Reasoning, SR-FLOW, and AdaptThink, positioning Thinker's structured task against approaches modifying rewards or algorithms for efficiency. A fifth new reference supports uncertainty calculation. These are focused additions within the existing research positioning.

T1.justification: The mathematical task definitions, objectives, and reward equations (1)-(4) are unchanged, as are the mathematical reasoning examples in Appendix C. No new theorem, proof, formal assumption, or substantive derivation is introduced.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens assessment of the central empirical claims by addressing v1's lack of reported training-seed variation and limited comparisons with efficiency-focused methods. Three-seed results, expanded uncertainty reporting, clearer checkpoint and budget documentation, and corrected ablation labels improve credibility and interpretability. Literature-reported comparator settings remain a limitation, and some uncertainty entries are lost, but these drawbacks are outweighed by the stronger empirical documentation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Thinker: Learning to Think Fast and Slow. All 21 pages of v1 and 23 pages of v2, including figures, equations, tables, and appendices, support comparison. Retained material can be matched despite renumbering and relocation.

after.justification: v2 retains original training and evaluation results, reports three-seed Qwen2.5-1.5B results, and updates the 1.5B and 7B evaluations. Its empirical evidence extends beyond the literature-reported comparators.

before.justification: v1 reports original PPO fine-tuning experiments, benchmark evaluations, ablations, and case studies for two 1.5B models, plus original 7B experiments in Appendix D.

results.title: Thinker: Learning to Think Fast and Slow

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and discussion retain the central claim: a differentiable graph-and-diffusion surrogate learns individual stochastic behavior and reproduces emergent dynamics beyond training. The additional experiments support this existing contribution rather than redefine it.

C2.justification: V2 adds explanations connecting larger agent populations to greater statistical coverage and fewer required ramifications, and attributes AR(1) failures to missing micro-level information. It also qualifies direct empirical application as requiring sufficient comparable agent-context observations. The original known-graph and complex-ABM limitations remain.

D1.justification: V2 documents the new GNN-only architecture and training settings and the AR(1) fitting procedure. Appendix A.5 revises training time from 7–12 hours to about one hour and 25-step generation from 10–12 seconds to about 7.5 seconds, without explaining the difference. Hardware, original GDN settings, and code access remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same three Schelling tolerance regimes and four Predator–Prey transition regimes. The added scalability studies vary grid size, agent count, and training samples within the retained Predator–Prey task, without introducing another domain or task.

E2.justification: V1 evaluates one ablation, renamed diffusion-only in v2. V2 adds a deterministic GNN-only comparator to the main quantitative and trajectory comparisons, plus an AR(1) macro-forecasting baseline in Appendix C.5 and Figure 20.

E3.justification: The original evaluation settings remain, but Appendix A.5 adds controlled sweeps over 50–500 ramifications and 2048–8192 agents, including a roughly constant-training-time tradeoff. New comparator protocols include MSE training with batch size 16 for GNN-only and separate least-squares AR(1) fits for macro variables.

E4.justification: V1 explicitly declines to evaluate diffusion removal; v2 performs that ablation and examines its spatial and temporal failures. Appendix A.5 additionally tests sensitivity to ramification count, scaling with agent count, and whether larger systems permit fewer ramifications at similar training cost.

E5.justification: V2 specifies ten runs for the ramification sweep and five for the agent-count and tradeoff studies, reporting means and standard-deviation error bars. The original eight-seed evaluations and 100 simulation rollouts remain unchanged; their replication count was not increased.

E6.justification: V2 adds GNN-only errors and failure patterns, AR(1) forecast trajectories, and scalability measurements. For example, its Table 2 reports EMD 0.0161 at 50 ramifications and 0.0088 at 500. The original plotted GDN/diffusion-only results and state-wise heatmap are retained; the additions do not establish improved same-setting GDN performance.

M1.justification: The proposed GDN architecture, ramification sampling, denoising objective, and generation procedure remain unchanged in Section 3 and Appendix A. The GNN-only model is an added comparator, not a modification of the proposed method.

P1.justification: Most prose and the main section sequence are retained, with targeted language, terminology, contact/header, and ablation-discussion edits. Appendix A.5 is reorganized, C.5 is added, and supplementary references are separated, without a wholesale narrative rewrite.

P2.justification: Main and appendix comparisons gain GNN-only panels or series, with revised axes, legends, and captions. V2 adds three scalability tables, three scalability figures, and the AR(1) comparison figure, and redraws Figure 1. Other appendix figures are matched retained displays despite renumbering.

R1.justification: V2 adds benchmark-justification references, including Jamali and Ten Broeke, and removes the Vaswani citation. Section 2 expands the distinction from Casert’s approach through its continuous-time and explicit-transition requirements. Core novelty positioning remains; relocated references and publication metadata updates are not new cited works.

T1.justification: Appendix C.5 adds the formal AR(1) recurrence and its Gaussian-noise assumption. The existing GDN equations, ABM definitions, and metric formulas remain unchanged, with no new theorem or proof.

improvement.justification: V2 addresses an important experimental gap by evaluating the diffusion-removal control that v1 dismissed. Together with controlled scalability studies, this substantially strengthens architectural validation and evidence about practical data and computational requirements. These gains remain substantial despite reporting problems: Figure 4 plots some new GNN-only sMAPE values above Equation 6’s upper bound of 2, and the large runtime revision is unexplained.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Graph Diffusion Network research and provide readable main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices A–C. Retained content can be matched despite additions and renumbering.

after.justification: V2 retains those original results and adds GNN-only evaluations, scalability experiments, and an AR(1) forecasting comparison.

before.justification: V1 reports original Schelling and Predator–Prey simulations, trained surrogate and ablation results, EMD and sMAPE evaluations, and spatial analyses in Section 4 and Appendix C.

results.title: Learning Individual Behavior in Agent-Based Models with Graph Diffusion Networks

C1.justification: The abstract, introductory contribution list, and conclusion retain the central claims about divergence-based labeling, immediate token routing, and improved performance-efficiency trade-offs. Headline claims, including 5.6B average parameters and approximately 2.8-fold generation-speed improvement, remain unchanged.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive interpretations of verifier reliability, transfer between model pairs, memory-traffic savings, and complementary trade-offs with MoE. It identifies sentence-reordering false positives and repetitive reasoning that exhausts the token budget as limitations. The conclusion replaces the greedy-only limitation with a qualification that alternative sampling has received limited validation.

D1.justification: v2 documents the sampling implementation, including k=1, divergence threshold 0.5, and deterministic continuations after sampled predictions. It reconciles the main-text layer count with the existing architecture appendix. Conversely, it drops v1's explicit speculative draft-tree depth and expansion-node settings. Most Appendix A implementation details, training hyperparameters, and code-access information remain unchanged.

E1.justification: v2 adds actual evaluation on Arena-Hard dialogue and MMLU-Redux-Philosophy, substantially extending coverage beyond the retained mathematics, coding, and science-QA benchmarks. Appendix B.1 also adds a human-annotated evaluation of semantic-divergence judgments.

E2.justification: The original main-table comparators remain, but v2 substantially expands evaluated comparisons with Qwen3 dense models and the Qwen3-30BA3B MoE baseline. Its new verifier comparison includes a human annotator and Qwen2.5-7B/3B alongside Qwen2.5-72B. RSD is added only to related work, not evaluated as a baseline.

E3.justification: New protocols include majority/unanimous human-label ground truths, cross-LLM router transfer, an easy/hard AIME partition, and stochastic generation/evaluation at temperature 0.6 and top-p 0.95 with a separate 16.1M-token labeling dataset. Section 5.4 now explicitly adjusts ablation thresholds, replacing v1's statement that other settings were fixed. The batch-size 2/4 speculative-decoding evaluation is removed.

E4.justification: v2 adds direct verifier validation and verifier-quality sensitivity, continuation-length sensitivity, cross-LLM transfer, SLM-size ablations, recall-versus-routing-rate curves, runtime and activation-interval analyses, and systematic failure analysis. These test assumptions largely unexamined in v1. Conversely, v1 Appendix B.1's speculative-decoding batch-scaling analysis is removed.

E5.justification: Appendix C.1.3 newly reports stochastic AIME pass@1 over 16 independent samples per problem. This documents repetition for an added experiment, without establishing additional runs of the original experiments. The existing across-question standard deviations and routing-percentile bands remain.

E6.justification: Tables 2–3 retain their values, but Table 4's Different variant changes from 19.7K tokens, 14.4% LLM usage, and 333 seconds to 21.0K, 13.1%, and 228 seconds alongside the revised threshold protocol. v2 adds extensive verifier, generalization, efficiency, failure, and sampling results, including 58% sampled AIME pass@1 at 8.6B parameters. It removes the multi-batch results and corrects Section 3.2's 3% usage attribution from the SLM to the LLM.

M1.justification: The core router and greedy routing procedure remain unchanged. Appendix C.1 adds a stochastic variant that samples initial predictions while retaining deterministic continuations for practical labeling; B.4.2 adds query-level selection between two R2R systems. These are bounded procedural extensions. The five-to-six-layer correction in Section 4.3 does not establish an architecture change: v1 Appendix A.1 already specifies six layers.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main narrative are retained. Changes include copyediting, updated conference and funding text, a shorter conclusion, and renaming Section 5.3 to Efficiency. Appendix results are regrouped; the former routing-algorithm appendix moves into C.2, and related work moves from C to D. Much of the expansion consists of new scientific content.

P2.justification: v2 adds numerous tables and three new analysis figures covering verifier checks, generalization, efficiency, compatibility, failures, and sampling. Table 4 gains a recall column and reordered fields; the old batch-scaling table disappears. Existing displays are also relocated: v1 Figure 7 becomes v2 Figure 11, and Table 6 becomes Table 9 without substantive content changes.

R1.justification: v2 adds nine references, including high-entropy-token research, RSD, new benchmark sources, and efficiency-analysis sources. It extends discussion of reward-guided routing, task-specific verification, and compatibility with MoE and query-level routing. The central positioning around immediate semantic-divergence correction and most existing related-work discussion remain intact.

T1.justification: Appendix C.1.1 introduces a probabilistic divergence-threshold formulation and asserts expected-quality preservation when calibrated to LLM self-divergence. This is new mathematical content, although no corresponding proof is supplied. The original deterministic definitions, equations, and Appendix E quality-guarantee proof remain unchanged.

improvement.justification: v1 lacked direct human validation of its semantic labels and systematic failure analysis. v2 addresses both and tests verifier quality, continuation length, and transfer across tasks and models, substantially strengthening evidence for the central routing assumptions and clarifying practical limits. These gains outweigh the removal of multi-batch baseline evidence and associated implementation details. The stochastic extension is useful, although its expected-quality guarantee remains asserted without a new proof.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same R2R work. Their main text, figures, tables, equations, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching material moved or renumbered in v2.

after.justification: v2 retains original R2R experiments and adds human-verifier comparisons, generalization experiments, efficiency and failure analyses, and stochastic-decoding results.

before.justification: v1 reports original R2R benchmark results, latency measurements, router ablations, and routing analyses, including Tables 2–6 and Figures 4–8.

results.title: R2R: Efficiently Navigating Divergent Reasoning Paths with Small-Large Model Token Routing

C1.justification: The first contribution removes the FSS-specific qualifier from its claim to first investigate SAM2's semantic structure. Headline performance margins are revised, including the LVIS advantage from 9.3 to 8.3 points. The central claims about latent semantics, unified segmentation, flexible prompting and efficiency remain.

C2.justification: V2 explains spatial continuity as a bias learned during pretraining rather than an architectural constraint, and expands the interpretation of adapter capacity and nonlinearity. It explicitly qualifies semantic-negative prompting as exploratory because standardized protocols and baselines are lacking. The existing limitations in Appendix A.1 remain essentially unchanged.

D1.justification: Compared with v1's brief implementation description, Appendix H discloses adapted layers, channel-dependent hidden widths, loss weights, gradient clipping, batch size 32 and eight A100 GPUs. V2 also specifies training sequence length, independent-target inference and prompt generation. Disclosure improves substantially, but Table 13 conflicts with the prose on Adam versus AdamW and approximately 20M versus 25M generalist trainable parameters.

E1.justification: The existing object and part segmentation benchmarks remain. V2 adds Pascal-5i and COCO-to-Pascal transfer, DAVIS video and flipped-frame conditions, and independent TSS image pairs. Negative-prompt experiments also introduce target-image corrections and additional contrastive references, substantially broadening evaluated scenarios.

E2.justification: Table 1 removes HSNet and VAT from the original benchmark comparison and adds HMNet; HSNet and VAT appear in the new Pascal comparison. V2 also evaluates AENet, PMNet and MONA, and introduces SAM2-based versions of PerSAM, Matcher, VRP-SAM and GF-SAM in Table 7.

E3.justification: Generalist model size is revised from 234M to 250M parameters, with larger adapters reported. New experiments introduce class-disjoint cross-dataset evaluation, spatial-coherence measurements under controlled flips, and varying negative-click counts. Training prose changes Adam to AdamW, although Table 13 still says Adam; this establishes a documentation revision, not that experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: V2 retains the existing PCA, linear-probing, fine-tuning and tracker-transfer analyses while adding substantial controls: SAM-to-SAM2 substitutions, training from scratch, full-model fine-tuning, MONA, adapter placement and encoder scale. The training-objective ablation expands into sequence-length sensitivity. New analyses examine part correspondences, cross-dataset robustness, negative prompts and spatial continuity.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests or uncertainty bars. Additional averages and result rows in v2 do not introduce a new uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: Table 1 replaces SANSA's LVIS 1-/5-shot scores of 49.8/55.9 with 48.8/53.9, and COCO scores of 60.1/67.3 with 60.2/64.3. COCO 5-shot consequently falls below GF-SAM's unchanged 66.8. Table 2 also revises results while reporting a larger generalist model. Numerous new entries cover comparator upgrades, ablations, transfer, negative prompts and spatial coherence; these are not evidence of uniform same-setting improvement.

M1.justification: The core frozen-SAM2 adapter pipeline, sequential training objective and segmentation losses remain. Appendix F adds exploratory semantic-negative extensions: inserting a negative reference with an empty mask into memory, or mapping negative-object features through an MLP into a learned negative token.

P1.justification: V2 reorganizes the method exposition to define the task first, separates domain/style generalization from ablations, and replaces the short ablation discussion with three explanatory questions. The appendices are reorganized and gain a roadmap and extensive explanations of evaluation conventions. Terminology is revised throughout, particularly from zero-shot to frozen or training-free.

P2.justification: Figure 3 is substantially redrawn, Figure 4 gains a correspondence panel, and Table 3 consolidates and restructures ablations. Domain-shift and part-segmentation galleries expand, a prompt gallery is added, and new tables display the additional experiments and hyperparameters. Existing PCA, probing and qualitative comparisons are retained or relocated rather than newly introduced.

R1.justification: Related work adds an explicit contrast between diffusion's spatial precision and DINOv2's semantic strengths, positioning SAM2 as combining both. New citations cover SAMwise, MONA, additional comparators, datasets and protocols; Appendix H adds in-context learning background. The central research positioning remains intact.

T1.justification: The pseudo-video, memory-attention, adapter and training-sequence equations retain their mathematical substance despite reordered presentation and revised indices. Neither version supplies formal theorems or proofs. The added spatial-coherence evaluation uses an existing metric rather than introducing new theory.

improvement.justification: V2 addresses important gaps with SAM2 comparator controls, targeted adaptation ablations, and controlled spatial-continuity and cross-dataset tests, strengthening evidence for SANSA's mechanism and generalization. The implementation and prompt-generation details substantially improve transparency. These benefits outweigh localized reporting flaws, including optimizer and parameter-count conflicts, unreconciled LVIS scores in Tables 1 and 9, and inconsistent fold means in Table 10.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe SANSA, with matching authors, core methodology and experiments. Text, equations, tables, figures and appendices are readable, allowing retained content to be matched across restructuring and renumbering.

after.justification: V2 retains original SANSA experiments and reports additional comparator controls, robustness tests, ablations and negative-prompt results.

before.justification: V1 reports original SANSA benchmark results, ablations, feature analyses, linear probing and annotation-efficiency experiments.

results.title: SANSA: Unleashing the Hidden Semantics in SAM2 for Few-Shot Segmentation

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, and conclusion expand the benchmark contribution to nine datasets and 87 scenarios, explicitly including real and rendered shifts. The central novelty, plug-and-play applicability, and multi-level/multi-prompt adaptation claims retain their previous meaning.

C2.justification: Appendix J adds an important applicability limitation: online adaptation underperforms episodic adaptation. It proposes error accumulation and model drift as explanations and discusses possible remedies. v2 also interprets longer-prompt behavior and qualifies ACDC reference comparisons because scene contents can differ. The original shared-projection-head limitation remains.

D1.justification: v2 documents ACDC processing with 224-by-224 patches and 112-pixel overlap, and describes ChatGPT-generated extended prompts with examples. Core implementation details remain unchanged. The repository target is identical, although v2 explicitly states that both code and data are available.

E1.justification: v2 adds ACDC driving scenes under real fog, night, rain, and snow, including reference images, and GTA-V rendered urban scenes. These extend the retained datasets and synthetic corruptions to explicitly adverse real conditions and rendered imagery; the reported benchmark expands from seven datasets and 82 scenarios to nine and 87.

E2.justification: Corresponding comparisons retain the same methods, including TENT, TPT, WATT, and CLIPArTT in v1 Table 4 and v2 Table 5. New experiments use existing non-adapted and TENT controls. Long-CLIP serves as an experimental backbone, rather than a newly competing adaptation method.

E3.justification: v2 adds one-step adaptation, online updates carrying parameters between batches, and Long-CLIP experiments with three textual-input variants. ACDC reference and adverse views are adapted independently. These introduce substantive experimental protocols; the original ten-step, batch-size-two episodic settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: New Appendices H-J and Tables 14-16 examine prompt verbosity, dependence on adaptation iterations, and episodic versus online adaptation. They test previously unexamined sensitivity and error-accumulation questions. Existing component, layer, template-count, backbone, and qualitative failure analyses are retained.

E5.justification: The Figure 1 caption newly specifies that its variance is computed across all samples and corruptions, clarifying uncertainty reporting. Both versions otherwise specify three repetitions with means and standard deviations; no increase in runs or new significance-testing procedure is reported.

E6.justification: Retained tables have unchanged numerical results. New Table 6 reports ACDC adverse-condition averages of 30.28 for MLMP, 26.29 for TENT, and 23.35 without adaptation; GTA-V scores are 28.84, 26.62, and 25.09 respectively. Tables 14-16 add prompt and protocol findings, including online V20-C performance of 71.77 versus 77.58 episodically. These are additional conditions, not revised same-setting scores.

M1.justification: Section 3 retains the same LayerNorm adaptation, intermediate-layer fusion, entropy-based inference weights, global CLS loss, and multi-prompt objective. The added experiments vary backbones and adaptation protocols without revising the proposed MLMP components.

P1.justification: There are localized language and cross-reference edits, shorter titles for Sections 3 and 4, and added correspondence information. Three appendix sections are inserted, moving former Appendices H-J to K-M. Most existing prose and the overall narrative structure remain intact.

P2.justification: Six new tables substantially expand the presentation: the paradigm comparison, ACDC/GTA-V results, three prompt/protocol analyses, and detailed ACDC reference/adverse results. Existing figures and tables are retained and reflowed, with Figure 1 receiving caption clarification. The substantial change is the new comparative displays, not pagination alone.

R1.justification: Section 2 and new Table 1 add a localized comparison with domain generalization, few-shot segmentation, and test-time training. Additional references cover these paradigms, the new datasets, Long-CLIP, TULIP, and adaptation pitfalls. The original positioning as the first fully test-time adaptation framework for OVSS is retained.

T1.justification: Equations 1-11, Proposition 1, and its Appendix A proof retain the same mathematics. The variance bound and the independence assumption used in the proof are unchanged; no new theorem or substantive derivation is introduced.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the central robustness claim through direct adverse-weather and rendered-domain evaluations beyond v1's synthetic corruptions and standard datasets. The new budget and online studies also expose practical behavior, especially dependence on resets, addressing important validation and applicability gaps. Table 14's optimistic interpretation of longer text deserves qualification because extended class descriptions lower absolute accuracy, but this limited weakness does not outweigh the stronger evidence and clearer limitations.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MLMP research work. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices support reliable comparison, including matching retained content across renumbering and relocation.

after.justification: The original empirical results are retained, alongside new ACDC and GTA-V evaluations and experiments on prompt length, adaptation iterations, and online adaptation.

before.justification: Section 5 and the appendices report original segmentation experiments, component ablations, computational measurements, and qualitative results.

results.title: Test-Time Adaptation of Vision-Language Models for Open-Vocabulary Semantic Segmentation

C1.justification: The benchmark, training-free method, and headline overall improvements remain the same. A limited quantitative claim changes: the introduction replaces the single 8.93% numerical-reasoning gain with 6.88% and 8.13% for GPT-4o and Gemini. The latter does not match the 7.80-percentage-point difference implied by Table 2.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations concerning generalization beyond dataset-specific visual properties, ground-truth stability under temporal offsets, and refinement improving graph correctness and usefulness. It documents specific failure mechanisms and qualifies API latency measurements. Section 5.1 also corrects the filtered subset's description from passing screening to being removed. Most original general limitations remain.

D1.justification: v2 newly provides a repository link and states that the dataset and source code are available. Appendix A.3 identifies annotators as authors and documents additional screening criteria; Table 10 supplies token usage and inference times. Hardware, default generation settings, model architecture information, and substantive prompt templates were already documented.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates data derived from Ego-Exo4D; LEMMA appears only in related work. v2 constructs and evaluates an additional 500-question LEMMA extension covering home activities and rectangular, rectified egocentric images (Appendix C.1, Table 7). It also examines temporally misaligned image pairs, extending coverage beyond synchronized inputs.

E2.justification: The principal DDCoT, CoCoT, and CCoT comparator set remains unchanged. However, v2 Table 9 newly compares these methods across Any/Ego/Exo/Both subsets, supplementing the earlier subset comparison of the default model, M3CoT, and its individual perspectives.

E3.justification: New experimental designs include 500 LEMMA questions, 80 examples assessed under 1–3-second synchronization offsets, and 120 examples evaluated for scene-graph FDR and answer accuracy. v2 also introduces text-only model evaluation and token/latency measurements. These additions substantially expand the evaluation protocol while retaining the original model settings and refinement-iteration setting.

E4.justification: v2 adds analyses of linguistic shortcuts, temporal-misalignment sensitivity, scene-graph quality before and after refinement, and computational cost. Figures 14–15 add conflict-resolution and failure cases, including erroneous information spreading during refinement. The original filtering, perspective, iteration, and qualitative analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions state that evaluations use three independent runs and report means and standard deviations. Retained result tables preserve their uncertainty reporting. The added analyses introduce no new seed information, confidence intervals, significance tests, or statistical estimation procedures.

E6.justification: Tables 1–3 and the open-source results in v1 Table 6/v2 Table 8 retain their values. v2 adds substantial results, including LEMMA M3CoT accuracies of 60.19% and 56.03%, temporal-offset label retention of 99%/97%/94%, refinement FDR decreasing from 9.37% to 6.21%, and text-only, subset, and cost results. New Table 10 reverses Gemini DDCoT/CoCoT accuracies relative to Table 2.

M1.justification: The three scene-graph perspectives, iterative information exchange, majority voting, and fallback response are unchanged. Corresponding appendix prompts retain their procedures, with only grammatical edits. Expanded annotation and filtering descriptions do not establish a changed construction algorithm.

P1.justification: The narrative is extensively reorganized: related work and the CoT overview move into main-text Section 6, single/multi-view analysis becomes Section 5.2, and appendix material is regrouped into benchmark details, evaluation settings, quantitative analyses, and qualitative examples. Widespread prose editing clarifies descriptions and cross-references.

P2.justification: v2 adds tables for text-only performance, LEMMA evaluation, comparative view-subset results, and computational cost, plus conflict-resolution and failure-case figures. Existing qualitative figures are reordered, and appendix figures, tables, and prompt boxes are reflowed. Most main-text graphics and existing table structures are retained.

R1.justification: v2 adds citations on multimodal modeling and scene-graph evaluation, including Panoptic Scene Graph Generation and Multiview Scene Graph, and replaces some introductory/model references. The central ego-exo and VQA positioning remains stable. Much of Section 6, including the CoT overview, relocates material already present in v1's appendices.

T1.justification: The method notation and procedural reasoning are retained, with no added or revised formal assumptions, theorems, proofs, or derivations. The new FDR and answer-accuracy descriptions provide operational criteria for empirical evaluation.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens evidence that was missing in v1: evaluation beyond Ego-Exo4D, direct measurements of scene-graph refinement, and quantified computational costs. Text-only controls, temporal checks, and failure cases also make applicability and weaknesses easier to assess. These gains outweigh localized reporting errors, notably the unsupported 8.13% Gemini numerical gain and the DDCoT/CoCoT accuracy swap in Table 10; the retained principal results remain unchanged.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same E3VQA benchmark and M3CoT method. Their main text, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable matching across relocation and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments and adds LEMMA evaluations, text-only controls, temporal-misalignment analysis, scene-graph quality measurements, and computational-cost results.

before.justification: v1 reports original evaluations of LVLMs and prompting methods on E3VQA, including category accuracies, perspective ablations, filtering analyses, and iteration experiments.

results.title: Towards Comprehensive Scene Understanding: Integrating First and Third-Person Views for LVLMs

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's three contributions and conclusion retain the same claims about guided active learning, targeted masking, biologically constrained SMC, and robust fitness–novelty optimization. The additional experiments support these existing claims rather than redefine the central contribution.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations linking fewer starting sequences to deeper exploration and more starting sequences to greater diversity, and motivates processing constrained charge classes first. It also interprets the new OOD results as evidence of robustness to distribution shifts and data scarcity. The existing limitations and future-work discussion are retained in Appendix B.

D1.justification: v2 adds a PROSPERO code-availability link, dataset and baseline license information, initial-dataset novelty values, and construction details for the new OOD dataset. Existing surrogate-training hyperparameters, EvoDiff size, hardware and runtime disclosures remain unchanged.

E1.justification: The eight original fitness tasks remain. Section 5.3 adds UBE2I structural-confidence optimization using pTM, with starting sequences 35 or 75 mutations from the wild-type while surrogate training uses nearby sequences. This introduces a different optimization objective and explicit distribution-shift scenarios beyond the original fitness and artificial-noise evaluations.

E2.justification: The ten external baselines and their membership in retained comparisons are unchanged. The new OOD and four-round tables reuse PEX, AdaLead, GFN-AL-δCS, LatProtRL and MLDE. CloneBO and other newly discussed methods are not added as evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: The original ten-round protocol is retained. The new OOD study uses ESMFold pTM as the oracle, four optimization iterations, 2,624 training sequences within five mutations of wild-type, and a 200-example low-data variant. Appendix A.2 also specifies short-sequence configurations for these experiments, establishing a substantial additional evaluation design.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained noise study and ablations, v2 adds explicit covariate-shift and low-data robustness tests. Appendix F tests the number of starting sequences on LGK, removes charge constraints while retaining the other components, and compares ascending, descending and random charge-class orders. Appendix D.2 extends early-round analysis beyond the existing maximum-fitness curves.

E5.justification: Both versions report means and standard deviations over five runs, with corresponding uncertainty bands in retained figures. The added tables follow this existing practice; no changed run count, new significance testing or new uncertainty-estimation procedure is reported.

E6.justification: All eight original tables retain their numerical entries, including v1 Table 4 relocated as v2 Table 9. Substantial OOD, early-round and ablation results are added. For example, the new severe-shift comparison reports maximum pTM of 0.672 ± 0.031 for PROSPERO and 0.652 ± 0.059 for MLDE (Table 4); these are new-condition results, not improvements over v1 scores.

M1.justification: The active learning loop, targeted alanine masking, charge-constrained EvoDiff sampling, SMC weighting and rollout selection remain unchanged. Explicitly listing the already-used coefficient k in Algorithms 2–3 clarifies their inputs; the additional variants are ablations rather than changes to the proposed method.

P1.justification: Most existing prose, including the abstract and conclusion, is retained. v2 clarifies the SMC explanation and notation, makes limited wording corrections, moves the Discussion to Appendix B, and adds an appendix contents page. These are localized explanatory and organizational edits rather than extensive rewriting.

P2.justification: v2 adds substantial tabular presentation for OOD comparisons, four-round summaries and three further ablation studies (Table 4 and Tables 10–19). The former main-text diversity table moves to Appendix D.1 as Table 9, and existing displays are rearranged. Figures 1–4 retain their underlying content.

R1.justification: New Appendix E substantially expands positioning against classifier and discrete diffusion guidance, SMC guidance and pseudo-marginal MCMC. It also develops a detailed comparison with the already-cited CloneBO, distinguishing the generative prior, weight computation and hard charge constraints. Additional citations in the main text broaden the discussion of model-based optimization and active learning.

T1.justification: Section 4.2 revises intermediate SMC targets from being 'not defined' to being 'defined only implicitly' and unavailable for direct weight computation. This is a limited correction to the mathematical rationale. Equations 1–12 remain unchanged, and no new theorem or proof is introduced.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation of the central robustness claim: v1's dedicated robustness study used injected surrogate noise, whereas v2 also tests explicit distribution shifts and data scarcity. Appendix F tests charge constraints with the other components intact and examines additional design sensitivities. Expanded research positioning and code-access information further improve assessability. The new OOD evidence remains limited to UBE2I and predicted pTM, but it addresses an important gap in the earlier evaluation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same PROSPERO research framework. Their main text, equations, figures, tables and complete appendices support reliable comparison, including matching relocated and renumbered material.

after.justification: v2 retains these empirical results and adds distribution-shift experiments, early-round summaries and further ablation results.

before.justification: v1 reports original computational experiments across eight protein fitness landscapes, biological plausibility evaluations, noisy-surrogate robustness tests and component ablations.

results.title: ProSpero: Active Learning for Robust Protein Design Beyond Wild-Type Neighborhoods

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same principal claims: simulation-efficient function-valued posterior inference, flexible discretizations, joint inference of vector-valued parameters, and scalability. The added experiments support these claims without redefining the central contribution.

C2.justification: V2 adds interpretations of mode and lengthscale sensitivity and explains iFNO's uncertainty failure as posterior collapse. Section 4.2 attributes the Gaussian performance gap to positional noise broadening the likelihood, but S7.1 finds little difference when jitter is removed, leaving that explanation unreconciled. The original high-frequency, sparse-observation, and domain-dimensionality limitations remain.

D1.justification: Tables S1–S3 replace coarse runtime bounds and a Gaussian-only size table with task-wide model sizes, total/per-epoch training times, and sampling times. S8.2 supplies iFNO architecture and training settings. Reported Gaussian FMPE sizes change from 34,212/149,032 to 86.3K/299K without an explained architecture revision. Hardware and the code-access pointer remain.

E1.justification: The four application areas remain. The new Gaussian stress test changes the prior lengthscale from 0.05 to 0.005, introducing higher-frequency functions as a distinct test condition (S5.1, S7.1). The 20-point SIRD and 500-parameter ice experiments already existed in v1.

E2.justification: Appendix S8.2 and Figure S9 newly compare Long et al.'s invertible Fourier Neural Operator with FNOPE and FNOPE (fix) on Darcy flow. The original NPE, FMPE, and Simformer comparator memberships remain in their corresponding experiments.

E3.justification: S2.2 revises the stated calibration aggregation from pooled ranks to averaging per-marginal EoDs. V2 adds 100-simulation settings for Gaussian and ice experiments, controlled hyperparameter sweeps, and an iFNO training protocol. Gaussian spectral padding changes from 200 to 20, while S4.1 now discards the zero imaginary Fourier coefficient. These are reported protocol changes; reruns of retained results are not established.

E4.justification: New analyses test Fourier-mode sufficiency and spectral recovery, masking density, base-distribution lengthscale, and positional jitter across Gaussian, SIRD, and Darcy tasks (S7.1–S7.3). Figure S9 adds error and posterior-variance diagnostics for iFNO. These substantially expand design validation beyond the retained sparse-observation and higher-dimensional ice studies.

E5.justification: Both versions specify three random seeds/runs and mean ± standard error for performance reporting. Posterior standard-deviation visualizations also predate v2. No increased run count, new confidence-interval practice, or significance-testing procedure is introduced.

E6.justification: Figures 3 and 6 add results at 100 training simulations. New ablations report frequency-recovery and hyperparameter-sensitivity findings. Figure S9 reports comparable predictive MSE for iFNO but calibration error around 0.25 and nearly vanishing posterior variance. Tables S1–S3 add extensive timing measurements; these are new results rather than demonstrated improvements over v1 under identical settings.

M1.justification: The FNO architecture, flow-matching objective, Gaussian-process base distribution, lengthscale heuristic, masking and positional augmentation, FFT variant, and vector-parameter head remain unchanged. The newly evaluated no-jitter variant is an ablation rather than a replacement of the proposed procedure.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main section sequence remain. Local explanations, notation, affiliations, and venue text are revised, and supplementary material is organized into ablations and additional results. The displayed joint loss disappears from Section 3.3 despite surviving surrounding references; the normalized loss remains in the appendix.

P2.justification: V2 adds substantial multipanel ablation displays and the iFNO comparison, and expands the resource table into three task-grouped tables. Figures 3 and 6 extend their simulation-budget axes, and predictive-MSE labels are clarified. Existing Darcy sample, mean, and variance displays are retained as Figures S6–S8 rather than newly added.

R1.justification: Related work expands to marginal inference and additional neural operators, including sensitivity-constrained FNOs, GNOT, latent neural operators, Transolver, and iFNO. It more explicitly distinguishes joint Bayesian inference from deterministic inversion and other conditional models. Four implementation/simulator references are removed, while the main positioning relative to FUSE and function-space diffusion remains.

T1.justification: S2.2 changes the mathematical definition of calibration aggregation, although its final averaging equation omits a summation symbol. S8.2 adds a derivation of EoD = 0.25 for collapsed point estimates under equally likely overprediction and underprediction. The original kernel-lengthscale derivation remains unchanged.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens design validation: the new ablations directly test frequency limitations and central hyperparameter choices, while the iFNO comparison distinguishes predictive accuracy from calibrated uncertainty. Detailed computational measurements also make practical efficiency assessable beyond v1's coarse bounds. These gains outweigh localized documentation defects, including the missing main-text loss, malformed calibration average, and unreconciled jitter explanation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe FNOPE and retain the same core method and four application areas. The main text, figures, tables, equations, and appendices are readable and support reliable matching across versions.

after.justification: The original empirical studies remain, supplemented by hyperparameter ablations, lower-budget experiments, computational measurements, and an iFNO comparison.

before.justification: Sections 4.2–4.5 and the appendices report original inference experiments on linear Gaussian, SIRD, Darcy flow, and Antarctic ice-shelf problems, including quantitative metrics and posterior visualizations.

results.title: FNOPE: Simulation-based inference on function spaces with Fourier Neural Operators

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution statements and conclusion retain the same central claims: minimum-complexity interpolation defines the target, loss-gradient updates fail under interpolation, the framework admits theoretical guarantees, and MinNorm-OG performs strongly empirically. The revised experiments support the same claimed contributions.

C2.justification: v2 explains why retraining succeeds on the simple color-only collapse target but struggles with image-content learning under restricted label-erasure budgets. It removes the earlier MNIST bimodality discussion and adds explanations for runtime differences. The conclusion's limitations concerning theoretical model classes and broader applications remain unchanged.

D1.justification: Appendix F adds implementation recipes for the new comparators, pretrained ResNet-50 initialization and staged training, and detailed preparation and optimization settings for CIFAR-10 collapse. Hyperparameter grids, hardware descriptions and asset information are revised. Conversely, v1's explicit first-five-trials tuning description and example search durations are removed, changing what can be reproduced from the documentation.

E1.justification: Multi-Class Label Erasure changes from MNIST and CIFAR-10 to CIFAR-10 and Tiny ImageNet. The reported Representation Collapse evaluation changes from binary MNIST digits with opposing colors to an explicitly defined ten-class CIFAR-10 task with randomly mismatched colors. These substantially revise the evaluated image populations and task complexity.

E2.justification: v2 adds Retrain and ℓ1-Sparse to the poisoning and image comparisons, and SalUn to both classification experiments, while retaining the existing baselines. The added Retrain comparator operates under the evaluation budgets and is distinct from the fully trained ground-truth reference already present in v1.

E3.justification: Poisoning changes its input interval from [-15,15] to [-5π,5π] and revises tuning grids. CIFAR-10 label-erasure training changes from 120 to 100 epochs and from learning rate 0.02 to 0.03. Representation Collapse replaces evaluation on relabeled training images with held-out test images and revises training, retain-access and epoch budgets. v2 also specifies pretrained ResNet-50 evaluation and a new runtime-measurement protocol.

E4.justification: The existing studies across epoch budgets and available retain data are revised. Label-erasure experiments now include multiple colored-forget sampling proportions, extending the previous fixed-proportion evaluation, and Section 5.2 adds a runtime analysis. These supplement the existing analyses without introducing a new component-ablation study.

E5.justification: For image experiments, v1 reports medians with central ranges or half-interquartile-range shading; v2 reports means with standard errors, still over five trials. Poisoning decreases from 20 to 10 trials and changes its trimmed-range reporting. Uncertainty remains available in Appendix F even where omitted from the main displays. This substantially revises statistical aggregation and uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Experimental results are extensively replaced or added. At 1,000 poisoning epochs, Table 1 changes MinNorm-OG's median from 0.84 to 0.63 and GD's from 1.58 to 2.61 under revised settings, so these are not comparable-setting gains or losses. v2 additionally shows Retrain outperforming MinNorm-OG on the revised collapse task and reports per-epoch runtimes. Two Ridge values conflict between v2 Tables 2 and 17.

M1.justification: The minimum-complexity objective, linearized orthogonality constraints and Algorithm 1 remain unchanged. The appendix retains the same MinNorm-OG projection update, regularization schedule and classification-gradient construction; revised benchmark architectures and tuning values do not change the proposed procedure.

P1.justification: The introduction and related work are tightened, general notation moves to Appendix A, experimental passages are rewritten, and a runtime subsection and Google Research affiliation are added. The overall section sequence and most method and theory exposition remain intact.

P2.justification: Poisoning visualizations expand from six to eight panels, result tables gain and reorder comparator columns, and main displays move uncertainty details into the appendix. Pareto plots are redrawn with revised legends and error bars; Appendix F introduces paired displays with and without error bars. A runtime table is added, substantially revising the empirical presentation.

R1.justification: v2 adds references for SalUn, sparsity-based unlearning and Tiny ImageNet, while removing the MNIST and AdamW reference entries. Its substantive positioning relative to influence functions, loss-gradient unlearning and orthogonal gradient methods remains unchanged.

T1.justification: The loss-gradient definition, Theorems 2.1 and 4.1–4.4, supporting lemmas and propositions, counterexample and projection derivation retain their mathematical substance. v1 Appendices A–D map to v2 Appendices B–E; the differences are renumbering, equivalent notation and prose edits.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses important evaluation gaps by adding budget-matched retraining and additional relevant comparators, testing Representation Collapse on held-out images, and measuring runtime rather than relying only on complexity arguments. These changes strengthen assessment of practical utility and reveal when retraining is preferable. The gains outweigh the reduced poisoning trial count and localized reporting defects, notably conflicting Ridge accuracies in Tables 2 and 17.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Machine Unlearning under Overparameterization, with matching authors, framework and theoretical results. Their main text, equations, figures, tables and complete appendices support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 reports original unlearning experiments on synthetic data, CIFAR-10 and Tiny ImageNet, plus runtime measurements in Tables 1–3 and Appendix F.

before.justification: v1 reports original Data Poisoning, Multi-Class Label Erasure and Representation Collapse experiments, including numerical results and Pareto curves in Section 5.1 and Appendix E.

results.title: Machine Unlearning under Overparameterization

C1.justification: The four principal contributions and sample-complexity conclusions remain. v2 explicitly adds a computational-separation claim in Section 1.2 and frames the abstract around sequential reasoning including CoT, modestly extending the stated contribution framing.

C2.justification: v1 presents trustable verification as guiding generation; v2 restricts this interpretation to stepwise soundness and small alphabets, explaining why it fails for overall soundness or large alphabets. New Remarks 2.1 and 4.2 clarify that acceptance need not establish proof completion and distinguish the guarantees from formal-logical soundness and completeness. These qualifications materially change the interpretation of central guarantees.

D1.justification: Both versions document abstract mathematical procedures. v2 adds no implementation package, hyperparameter or hardware specification, training-time measurement, data-processing recipe, or code/data-access information.

E1.justification: Neither version trains or evaluates on datasets or empirical tasks. The added planning and puzzle illustrations and USAT construction are conceptual or theoretical examples, not additional evaluated coverage.

E2.justification: Neither version evaluates comparison methods against the proposed learners. Additional citations to verification and generation methods in v2 do not constitute evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: Neither version reports experimental splits, metrics, budgets, model configurations, or testing procedures. Changes to mathematical learning guarantees are theoretical changes rather than evaluation-protocol revisions.

E4.justification: No experimental ablations, sensitivity tests, robustness evaluations, or error analyses are added or removed. Appendix B retains its mathematical examples; the added puzzle illustration is explanatory and the USAT separation is theoretical.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated runs, seeds, empirical uncertainty estimates, or significance tests. Confidence parameters and probability bounds occur within theoretical proofs, not experimental uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Neither version contains experimental scores or qualitative evaluation outcomes. New Table 1 summarizes existing theoretical sample-complexity rates; the new separation argument and revised proofs are assessed under T1.

M1.justification: Prefix-by-prefix verification, ERM-based learning, gold-trace negative-example construction, Algorithm 1, and the online learners in Example B.5 are retained. The revised soundness definitions and proofs do not introduce a different learning or inference procedure.

P1.justification: v2 revises the title, polishes language, adds explanatory remarks and acknowledgments, and introduces the existing SVPAC loss before Definition 3.1 instead of first inside a proof. The main section sequence and Appendix A–C organization remain intact.

P2.justification: v2 adds Table 1 comparing training data, algorithms, and theoretical sample complexities across verification goals. This consolidates material already present in v1. The single-column layout and Algorithm 1 display remain, with local pagination and spacing changes.

R1.justification: Section 1.2 substantially expands positioning through new discussions of interactive provers and exact learning, plus connections to planning, imitation learning, selective classification, robustly reliable learning, and strategic improvements. These additions explain relationships to several research directions beyond those covered in v1.

T1.justification: v2 Definition 4.1 explicitly defines acceptance through all prefixes and separates stepwise from overall soundness, with corresponding revisions to TVPAC definitions and guarantees. The proof of v1 Theorem 4.7, now Theorem 4.9, replaces an unjustified independence step with a union bound over verifier subsets. Remark 4.6 restricts generation–verification equivalence to small alphabets, and new Remark 4.7 establishes a USAT-based computational separation assuming RP differs from NP.

improvement.justification: Replacing the unjustified independence-based argument in v1 Theorem 4.7 with the subset union bound in v2 Theorem 4.9 repairs support for a central sample-complexity guarantee. The soundness distinctions and restricted generation–verification equivalence also reduce substantive ambiguity and overstatement. Together these changes substantially strengthen the mathematical reliability and precision of this theoretical paper.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same verifier-learning research. All 22 pages of v1 and 26 pages of v2, including Appendices A–C, are readable and support comparison despite the revised title and renumbered results.

after.justification: v2 remains theoretical. Its new summary table and computational-separation example report mathematical results, while empirical findings mentioned in related work are attributed to other papers.

before.justification: v1 reports theoretical bounds, proofs, and illustrative mathematical constructions, including in its appendices. It contains no original experimental, simulation, or data-analysis outcomes.

results.title: On Learning Verifiers and Implications to Chain-of-Thought Reasoning

C1.justification: The abstract, introductory contributions, and conclusion retain the claims of universal text/image-guided Gaussian stylization, joint appearance and geometry optimization, preserved model size, and strong quality and consistency. The additional experiments and Light configuration do not redefine these central contributions.

C2.justification: B.3.3 substantially expands the failure discussion beyond v1's reconstruction dependence and 2D quality limitations. It relates prompt generality, specificity, and length to CLIP representation problems, unwanted semantic features, and background artifacts, explicitly explaining how higher CLIP scores can accompany worse perceived quality. Section 4 also adds a patch-size explanation for repeated structures in 2D outputs.

D1.justification: Appendix A supplies Light settings: learning rate 0.002 and patch-loss weights 35 for 3D and 45 for video. v2 also specifies video resolutions and UVG downsampling, revises the reported 4D-scene hardware from RTX 4090 to DGX A100, and states that code is available rather than forthcoming after review. Most implementation documentation is retained.

E1.justification: Appendix B.5 adds four UVG sequences to the previously DAVIS-only video evaluation, extending coverage to longer videos under image and text conditioning. The four-modality task scope and other datasets, including the existing PanopticSports experiments, are retained.

E2.justification: v2 adds SGSST and ABC-GS to the 3D image-conditioned comparison (Table 1), and ViSt3D, AdaAttN, and ReReVST to the DAVIS image-conditioned video comparison (Table 18). These substantially broaden the evaluated comparator sets. The user study retains its original methods.

E3.justification: v2 introduces flow-warped LPIPS/RMSE evaluation at frame offsets 1 and 7, and Farneback flow comparisons at offsets 1, 2, 4, 8, and 16 (B.1.2). New protocols include Light configurations and 4D evaluation using 200 rendered views at 11 time points and 21 time points per test camera (B.3.4). The existing batch-size figure also relabels 3 as 4, without establishing a rerun.

E4.justification: The existing hyperparameter analyses are retained, while B.3.3 adds prompt-specificity and prompt-length experiments crossed with background-loss settings, examining semantic and background artifacts. v2 also adds standard-versus-Light comparisons and camera/time consistency analyses across batch sizes (B.3.4, Tables 16-17 and Figure 33).

E5.justification: The Friedman and Conover-Friedman tests, their p-value tables, and survey participant counts are retained. The added experiments do not introduce repeated-run or seed information, error bars, confidence intervals, or additional significance-testing procedures.

E6.justification: v2 adds baseline and Light results, UVG scores, non-CLIP consistency measurements, and prompt/time findings. In the corresponding DAVIS image-conditioned comparison, CCPL's CLIP-S changes from 18.89 to 68.89 and UniST's from 15.93 to 65.93, while CLIPGaussian remains at 74.31 (v1 Table 14; v2 Table 18). These are revised reported values, without a documented explanation for the increases.

M1.justification: The Gaussian representations, four-term loss, patch augmentation, and modality-specific optimization procedures remain unchanged. CLIPGaussian-Light adjusts existing learning rates and patch-loss weights; it introduces no new architecture, loss component, or algorithmic step.

P1.justification: Localized editing streamlines the introduction and expands selected explanations. v2 adds appendix subsections, a social-impact paragraph, acknowledgments, and a NeurIPS checklist, and updates affiliations and conference information. The main section order and most retained prose remain stable.

P2.justification: The two original 3D comparison tables are merged and expanded into v2 Table 1; the DAVIS tables are similarly combined into Table 18. Numerous new analysis and consistency tables and Figures 19 and 31-33 substantially extend the displays. Existing figures are relocated, the survey screenshot is enlarged, and Figure 7 gains resolution; retained qualitative galleries largely preserve their content.

R1.justification: Related work adds discussion of StyleDyRF, AdaAttN, ReReVST, ViSt3D, and StyleMaster, and elaborates the distinction from Instruct-GS2GS. Additional comparison and metric references include SGSST, ABC-GS, and StyleRF. This broadens the context while retaining the central novelty positioning; publication updates and consolidated duplicate references are bibliographic edits.

T1.justification: The representation and loss equations and existing CLIP metric definitions are unchanged. v2's added optical-flow formula documents an adopted evaluation metric; it introduces no new theoretical assumption, proof, derivation, or formal result.

improvement.justification: v1's quantitative consistency evaluation relied on CLIP-derived measures. v2 substantially strengthens scrutiny of this central claim through non-CLIP consistency metrics, broader comparators, longer-video testing, and concrete prompt-failure analyses. These additions expose meaningful tradeoffs and applicability limits. The unchanged superiority wording remains overbroad: v2 Table 20 favors Rerender over standard CLIPGaussian on DAVIS LPIPS/RMSE. Despite that unresolved overstatement, the broader validation and explicit failure evidence provide a substantial net quality improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same CLIPGaussian framework and provide readable methods, equations, figures, tables, and Appendices A-B. Retained material can be matched despite additions, renumbering, and layout changes.

after.justification: v2 retains these original results and adds baseline comparisons, UVG experiments, consistency measurements, and failure-case analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original stylization experiments across four modalities, quantitative comparisons, a 3D user study, and hyperparameter analyses.

results.title: CLIPGaussian: Universal and Multimodal Style Transfer Based on Gaussian Splatting

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction broaden the effectiveness claim to open- and closed-source candidate models. The abstract drops v1's specific improvement figures, while the introduction reports a broader 1.67%–9.33% improvement range. The central novelty, knowledge-shift modeling, and latency-trade-off claims remain.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations connecting transfer performance to learned relative RAG capabilities and residual failures to retrieval-induced degradation, task difficulty, and model-selection overconfidence. It interprets the new embedding ablation as supporting separate capability modeling. v1's discussion of future applications beyond RAG is removed, while the central knowledge-shift explanation is retained.

D1.justification: v2 supplies a code/data repository link, extends API-access disclosure to the added models, and explains the single-embedding ablation configuration and probabilistic supervision. Existing implementation settings remain unchanged. Inference-cost measurements move from v1 Appendix G to v2 Section 5.2; they are not newly reported.

E1.justification: v2 retains the five original QA datasets and adds HotpotQA multi-hop QA and WikiASP aspect-based summarization. Appendix F also introduces medical-to-Wikipedia QA and search-QA-to-medical transfer scenarios, substantially extending task requirements and domain-shift coverage.

E2.justification: v2 Table 3 adds GPT-4o, Qwen2.5-Max, and DeepSeek-R1 as individually evaluated model comparators. GPT-4o previously served inside the Prompt LLM routing baseline rather than as a candidate answerer. The routing comparators in the retained experiments are unchanged.

E3.justification: v2 introduces a six-model candidate pool for the NQ/WebQ comparison, two cross-domain training/testing protocols, and ROUGE-L evaluation for summarization. Its failure analysis excludes cases where all candidate LLMs fail and categorizes the remaining failures. Original QA sample counts, metrics, and training settings are retained.

E4.justification: v2 adds an ablation of the RAG Capability Embedding Layer, quantitative failure categories and analysis of cases where baselines succeed but RAGRouter fails, and cross-domain generalization tests. The original retrieval-noise analysis, sensitivity sweeps, and two successful routing examples remain; moving their displays does not constitute new analysis.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, standard deviations, or significance tests. Added results continue the existing point-estimate reporting practice; probabilistic training-label sampling is not uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: Retained results are unchanged, including Table 2's 64.46% average accuracy. New results include 59.38% versus GPT-4o's 57.71% in Table 3, 63.70% without RAG capability embeddings, a 12.95% failure rate in Table 12, cross-domain accuracies of 21.20% and 68.89%, and WikiASP ROUGE-L of 0.1981 versus KNN Router's 0.1881. These are additional results under distinct settings, not improvements over corresponding v1 scores.

M1.justification: v2 Appendix H introduces score-based probabilistic label sampling for WikiASP: a normalized continuous score s produces a positive training label with probability s and a negative label with probability 1-s. This extends v1's binary-correctness supervision. The original architecture, contrastive objectives, and routing procedure remain unchanged.

P1.justification: v2 changes the title, edits selected abstract, contribution, and architecture passages, and reorganizes experimental and appendix subsections. It adds appendix contents and funding acknowledgments and moves inference-cost discussion into the main text. Most original prose and the main narrative sequence are retained.

P2.justification: The experimental presentation expands with tables for stronger-model comparisons, failure categories, cross-domain transfer, and summarization. v1's combined ablation table becomes separate architecture and contrastive-learning tables. Existing sensitivity heatmaps move into the main text, and appendix figures and case tables are regrouped; these retained figures are not new analyses.

R1.justification: v2 adds the WikiASP and HotpotQA references and removes citations concerning distillation, parameter-efficient transfer learning, LoRA, and chain-of-thought prompting alongside the deleted future-work discussion. Related-work positioning against non-RAG-aware routers remains substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: Appendix H adds a limited mathematical extension to training-label construction: continuous scores define positive and negative label probabilities s and 1-s. The original routing formulation, loss equations, and response-reversal definitions in Equations 1–11 remain unchanged, with no new theorem or proof.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation by directly testing the distinctive RAG capability embedding, quantifying routing failures, and examining transfer beyond the original QA settings through stronger candidate models, cross-domain tests, and summarization. These additions address important gaps in mechanism attribution and applicability while preserving the original evidence. HotpotQA/WikiASP setup details remain incomplete and statistical uncertainty remains unreported, limiting the strength of the expanded generalization claims.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same RAGRouter work despite the changed title. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable, and retained material can be reliably matched.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds stronger-model comparisons, failure analysis, cross-domain evaluations, and summarization experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original routing-accuracy and latency experiments, component ablations, sensitivity analyses, and retrieval-noise evaluations.

results.title: RAGRouter: Learning to Route Queries to Multiple Retrieval-Augmented Language Models

C1.justification: The introduction adds a central contribution establishing an upper bound on strategic complexity for bounded piecewise-linear classes, including fixed-size ReLU networks. This substantially extends v1's polytope-specific upper-bound claim, while retaining the claims about complexity collapse, non-universality, and approximation gaps.

C2.justification: New Appendices A.2-A.3, C.1, and C.10 substantially expand applicability and interpretation: bounded input domains, obstacles to a general VC bound, extensions beyond Euclidean costs, and limitations under instance-dependent costs. They also develop implications for inversion, curvature regularization, interpolation thresholds, and model selection.
