D1.justification: v2 Section 6 adds a code-repository link for both experiments. Appendix D.1 further clarifies the existing grid approximation; the disclosed CPU allocation, sample counts, fitting procedure, and tolerance remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same bounded two-dimensional polynomial classifiers and synthetic class-conditional Gaussian classification problems. The additional discussion of other cost functions introduces no evaluated datasets or scenarios.

E2.justification: The approximation experiment retains the same comparators: unrestricted non-strategic classification and optimal linear classification, whose strategic and non-strategic classes coincide. No evaluated comparator is added or removed.

E3.justification: Appendix D retains the polynomial-degree and strategic-reach ranges, bounded input domain, 0.9 fitting tolerance, Gaussian-separation range, and 25 samples per class. The grid-based calculations and optimal-linear-classifier search are also unchanged.

E4.justification: The same experiments examine expressivity across polynomial degree and strategic reach, and accuracy across class separation and strategic reach. No empirical ablation, robustness test, or supplementary case study is added; the new appendix analyses concern theory and its implications.

E5.justification: Both versions report 100 instances for expressivity and 20 for approximation, with means and standard-error confidence intervals. No repeated-run, seed, or uncertainty-reporting procedure changes.

E6.justification: The experimental plots in v1 Figure 6 and v2 Figure 5 are identical, and their reported trends and comparator relationships are retained. The revised mathematical examples preserve their intended findings and are assessed under T1.

M1.justification: The underlying strategic-response model and experimental procedures are retained. Appendix C.10 discusses prospective inversion and curvature-regularization approaches without introducing an instantiated learning algorithm.

P1.justification: v2 combines 'Points' and 'Classifiers' under 'Underlying Mechanisms,' renames 'Model classes' to 'Class-level analysis,' and adds appendix subsections and acknowledgments. Copyediting and notation cleanup are widespread, but the original bottom-up sequence and most existing exposition remain.

P2.justification: Both versions retain eleven figures and no tables. v2 revises point-mapping arrows and explanatory captions, moves the curvature illustration from the main text to Appendix B.3, and relocates the unchanged experimental figure nearer the experiment descriptions.

R1.justification: v2 adds Huang (2020) and Petersen and Voigtlaender (2018) to connect piecewise-linear analysis with ReLU approximation. It also clarifies the borrowing from offset-curve theory and discusses restrictions of earlier optimization approaches, while retaining the existing related-work framework.

T1.justification: v2 adds Theorem 3 and Appendix B.10, bounding strategic VC dimension for piecewise-linear classes by O(dm log m + nu_p k log k); the original polytope bound remains as Theorem 4. It also revises the classifier construction in Appendix B.8 and replaces the flawed strategic-accuracy example in v1 C.8 with a corrected construction in v2 C.9. Equation (1) corrects the response objective from h(x) to h(x').

improvement.justification: The new piecewise-linear VC bound and accompanying proof substantially broaden the central learnability analysis beyond v1's polytope result to classes relevant to ReLU networks. Corrected mathematical constructions, explicit applicability boundaries, and code-access information further improve reliability and usefulness. The fully general learnability question remains open, and the empirical evidence is unchanged.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their complete main texts, figures, equations, and Appendices A-D are readable and support reliable matching across the restructuring and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments in Sections 6.1-6.2, Figure 5, and Appendix D.

before.justification: v1 Sections 7.1-7.2, Figure 6, and Appendix D report original experiments on polynomial expressivity and attainable classification accuracy using synthetic data.

results.title: Strategic Classification with Non-Linear Classifiers

C1.justification: The main claims now explicitly cover operation both with and without safety-prior prompting. The abstract highlights an 85.34% benchmark margin and 29.85% SFT mitigation improvement under the new setting, while the introduction retains the earlier prompted claims. The central contributions—evolutionary optimization, two datasets, and shortcut-learning insights—remain unchanged.

C2.justification: v3 qualifies fitness improvement as heuristic evidence for increasing true refusal likelihood, explains system-prompt effects through refusal bias, and interprets DarkIdol's results as reducing dependence on GPT-4o for generation. The shortcut-learning and early-layer interpretations, and Appendix C's white-box, computational-cost, and annotation-subjectivity limitations, remain unchanged.

D1.justification: v3 adds a code/data repository link and release statements, the GPT refusal-judging prompt in Appendix A.7, a DarkIdol checkpoint reference, explicit decoding settings, and the annotator count. The original safety-prior prompt moves to B.5. Core implementation templates and EVOREFUSE hyperparameters in A.3–A.6 are retained.

E1.justification: The datasets, domains, and underlying tasks remain unchanged, including the 582-example EVOREFUSE-TEST and 3,000-example EVOREFUSE-ALIGN. v3 adds evaluation without the safety-prior system prompt, extending coverage to an additional input-conditioning scenario.

E2.justification: The eight benchmark comparators, alignment baselines using OR-BENCH/PHTEST/PromptAgent, Few-Shot and DRO defenses, and Figure 2 comparison methods are retained. Table 10 varies EVOREFUSE's mutator model within the same pipeline.

E3.justification: v3 introduces an unprompted evaluation protocol with temperature 0.01 and GPT-based CRR judging; the prompted appendix uses temperature 1.0 and the original binary classifier. Section 4 changes the stated fine-tuning budget from three to five epochs. New experiments also introduce single-round mutation testing and a DarkIdol configuration. These are substantial protocol changes, without establishing that retained results were rerun.

E4.justification: v3 expands robustness analysis across prompted and unprompted evaluations, compares nine mutation strategies individually in Appendix B.4, and tests dependence on GPT-4o using DarkIdol in B.6. Table 10 reports five-iteration refusal rates of 0.46 for DarkIdol and 0.72 for GPT-4o. Existing component ablations remain, and Table 6 adds one attribution example.

E5.justification: Table 2 newly reports ranges across annotators, and Section 4 identifies three NLP practitioners. This adds uncertainty reporting for safety judgments. Figure 2 already contained standard-error shading in v1; v3 does not establish additional repeated model runs or newly specified random seeds.

E6.justification: v3 adds substantial benchmark and mitigation results under the new settings in Tables 1 and 3; v1's corresponding tables remain numerically unchanged as Tables 8 and 9. In the new benchmark setting, PH-GEN exceeds EVOREFUSE-TEST on DeepSeek-V3, with PRR 0.45 versus 0.38. Table 2 changes EVOREFUSE-TEST's reported unsafe fraction from 0.00 to 0.02 ± 0.02. Tables 7 and 10 add strategy and mutator findings.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1, the fitness function in Equation 5, mutation/recombination templates, safety filtering, and simulated annealing remain unchanged. The GPT-based CRR judge changes evaluation, not fitness computation. The DarkIdol experiment tests a different backend within the existing procedure.

P1.justification: v3 makes targeted rewrites to the results summary, experimental settings, and theoretical explanation, and adds appendix subsections B.4–B.6. It also updates author/affiliation information and adds author contributions, acknowledgments, and a NeurIPS checklist. The main section sequence and most existing prose remain intact.

P2.justification: The new main Table 1 uses a PRR-only layout; earlier Tables 1 and 3 move to appendix Tables 8 and 9. v3 adds compact Tables 7 and 10, annotator ranges in Table 2, and a row in Table 6. Table captions move above their displays. Figures 1–3 retain identical graphical content, with resizing and page reflow.

R1.justification: Reference 39, cited for TRIDENT-CORE, changes from Ji et al.'s PKU-SafeRLHF paper to Wu et al.'s TRIDENT paper. This changes the attributed source work. The related-work discussion and broader novelty positioning otherwise remain unchanged; other citation-number changes reflect reordering.

T1.justification: Section 3.2 and Appendix A.2 replace the earlier elitist ELBO/true-likelihood convergence argument and global-optimality discussion with convergence of record-best practical fitness only. Equation 6 restores the entropy term, refusal becomes response-dependent and stochastic, and assumptions are rewritten. v3 explicitly withdraws guarantees of monotonic improvement or convergence along the accepted-seed trajectory and of increasing true refusal likelihood.

improvement.justification: The decisive improvement is correcting an important mathematical overclaim: Appendix A.2 now limits convergence to record-best fitness and acknowledges that true refusal likelihood need not improve. Evaluations without forced safety-prior prompting and additional component tests substantially strengthen empirical support, while annotator ranges improve transparency. The prompt-effect interpretation remains confounded by different temperatures and CRR judges, but this does not outweigh the gains in validity and evidence.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same EVOREFUSE research. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices support comparison. The earlier main experimental tables can be matched exactly to tables retained in the later appendix.

after.justification: v3 retains original empirical results and adds evaluations without the safety-prior prompt, mutation-strategy comparisons, and an alternative-mutator experiment.

before.justification: v1 reports original benchmark evaluations, alignment experiments, attribution analyses, and optimization ablations in Tables 1–4, Figures 1–3, and the appendices.

results.title: EVOREFUSE: Evolutionary Prompt Optimization for Evaluation and Mitigation of LLM Over-Refusal to Pseudo-Malicious Instructions

C1.justification: The central contribution remains black-box semantic manipulation of agent preferences. However, the abstract and Discussion replace the blanket 100% success formulation with consistent preference redirection, and replace human-imperceptibility with visually subtle or natural edits. These meaningfully qualify the efficacy and stealth claims while retaining the main contribution.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations connecting proxy prompts to unknown queries, distinctive-feature anchoring to gradient allocation, and perceptual constraints to platform integrity checks. It interprets the new ablations as evidence about semantic-loss importance and component flexibility. Section 8 removes v1's open-source/synthetic-setting qualification, while the appendix acknowledges lower success in webpage settings. These substantially revise mechanism explanations and applicability discussion.

D1.justification: v2 adds a GitHub access pointer, more explicit algorithm bookkeeping, loss coefficients in the ablation tables, alternative model identifiers and a computational breakdown. Most architecture, optimizer and hardware details already appear in v1. Runtime documentation changes, but remains inconsistent: Section 5.2 calls 520/376/110 seconds per-iteration costs, while Table 11 labels them per-sample totals.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates COCO-based image selection. v2 retains this coverage and adds Flickr8k_sketch, ArtCap artistic images and an e-commerce webpage scenario (Appendix A.2.2 and A.2.6). These introduce different visual domains and page-level input conditions.

E2.justification: v2 adds SSA_CWA and SA_AET to the main attack comparison and the webpage comparison (Tables 1 and 10), alongside retained SPSA, Bandit and unoptimized diffusion. This substantially strengthens comparison against embedding-based attacks; these additions are evaluated methods, not merely citations.

E3.justification: v2 adds Mistral-small-3.2-24B, GPT-4o and CogVLM targets, Robust-LLaVA and additional defense configurations, plus controlled loss-weight, embedding and generator variations. The stated negative-prompt model changes from Llama-3-7B to Llama-3-8B. Table 11 specifies 10,000 steps over 50 iterations for Bandit, whereas v1 states a general 20-by-20 default. TRAP's 100-instance COCO evaluation and 20-by-20 budget remain.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's prompt, temperature, threshold and noise tests, v2 adds CIDER/MirrorCheck defenses, an adversarially trained target, loss-weight and component-removal ablations, embedding/generator substitutions and iterative refinement examples. The original threshold analysis remains represented in Figure 2 despite removal of its separate subsection and redundant plot.

E5.justification: Both versions retain R=100 randomized selections and provide no independent-seed counts or defined confidence intervals. v1 Figures 2–3 contain vertical bar-like marks absent from v2's redrawn Figure 2, but their statistical meaning is never explained. The PDFs do not reliably distinguish removal of uncertainty reporting from a marker-style change.

E6.justification: The original Table 1 cells are retained, while v2 adds substantial results: TRAP obtains 99%, 63% and 94% on Mistral-3.2, GPT-4o and CogVLM. The new webpage experiment reports 51%, 50%, 27% and 17% across its four targets. Additional dataset, defense and ablation outcomes are reported, and Figure 2 curves and runtime values change. The new target/scenario results are not same-setting performance declines.

M1.justification: The CLIP/Siamese/diffusion pipeline and three loss components remain. However, the reported masking operation changes from e_com multiplied by mean(A) to elementwise multiplication with A_final, explicitly combining the learned mask and segmentation mask. Revised Algorithm 1 also explicitly decodes and evaluates the final updated candidate. These are localized procedural revisions.

P1.justification: Sections 3–4 are extensively rewritten and reorganized, with expanded diffusion, CLIP, LPIPS and optimization explanations. Related work is condensed, Algorithm 1 moves to Appendix A, and threshold discussion is integrated into Section 6.2. The scale of explanatory rewriting and restructuring exceeds routine copyediting.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is redrawn with clearer Siamese-network and masking stages; Figure 2 expands to six models with a shared legend and revised styling. Table 1 expands, and defense, ablation, dataset and efficiency tables are added. v1's qualitative panel is retained as v2 Figure 3, while its redundant threshold plot is removed and a new iterative-refinement figure appears.

R1.justification: The three related-work themes and semantic-versus-pixel positioning remain. v2 condenses the classical attack catalogue, removing references such as GenAttack and NATTACK, and adds literature supporting SSA_CWA, SA_AET, defenses, additional datasets and alternative backbones. These are focused updates to the existing positioning.

T1.justification: v2 Section 4.1 replaces the generic selection mapping with an explicit cosine-score/argmax model, formalizes the selection event and adds a perceptual-budget constraint. Section 4.2 distinguishes an unknown user query from the attacker's guidance prompt. These refine formal assumptions and definitions; neither version provides a theorem or proof. Expanded textbook explanations of CLIP and LPIPS do not constitute new theory.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses v1's reliance on weak attack baselines and narrow evaluation through embedding-based comparators, additional model families, defenses, new domains and component ablations (Tables 1–10). These additions make effectiveness and failure conditions more assessable, while softened imperceptibility claims improve calibration. Sparse documentation of the webpage experiment and unresolved numerical/runtime inconsistencies limit reproducibility, but the stronger comparative and diagnostic evidence provides a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe TRAP by the same authors, with matching core components and overlapping COCO experiments. Text, equations, figures and tables support comparison. v1 ends with references; v2 additionally contains a readable Appendix A.

after.justification: The main text retains original COCO experiments and adds model and defense comparisons. Appendix A reports additional datasets, component ablations, a webpage scenario and computational measurements.

before.justification: Sections 5–6 report original experiments on 100 COCO image-caption pairs, including attack comparisons and prompt, temperature and threshold analyses.

results.title: TRAP: Targeted Redirecting of Agentic Preferences

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction retain the same unified fine-tuning contribution, three auxiliary tasks, and headline advantages over SSAN and Gemini2.5-flash. The revised conclusion emphasizes accuracy, scalability, and speed already claimed in v1. Wording such as 'super SOTA' does not substantively change those claims.

C2.justification: Section 5.2 shifts emphasis from domain-specific training necessity toward qualified held-out-domain generalization. New discussions interpret general-data mixing tradeoffs, representation compactness, token-error mechanisms, and CJK filtering. The limitations replace the absence of general VLM evaluation with unexplored task/domain mixture ratios. The unused synthetic-data limitation and CDM caveat are retained.

D1.justification: Appendix B.4 changes the reported training resources from four A800 GPUs and 78 hours to eight A800 GPUs and 20 hours; D.2 adds explicit normalization examples. Reporting remains inconsistent: the new checklist instead states four A800s and 96 hours, and describes a future code release despite the retained abstract's open-source claim. Actual resource availability cannot be resolved from these PDFs.

E1.justification: Section 5.3 adds LLaVA-OneVision training data and evaluates general multimodal understanding and mathematical reasoning on MMMU_val, Math-Vision, and MathVista_testmini. Appendix C.5 also evaluates CJK-containing HME100K samples previously excluded from recognition experiments. CROHME2023, MNE, MathWriting, and printed-expression coverage already existed in v1.

E2.justification: Table 1 adds evaluated ICAL and UniMERNet rows; the new CROHME2023 comparison includes TST and TST with external data. MathWriting gains Vanilla and dataset-specific Uni-MuMER comparisons. DenseWAP's CROHME2019 comparison is withdrawn. These extend or adjust an otherwise largely retained comparator suite.

E3.justification: v3 adds leave-one-dataset-out training, a 1:1 HMER/LLaVA mixture, a 7B configuration, CJK inclusion/exclusion controls, hallucination/omission metrics, and evaluation on the original unnormalized Im2LaTeXv2 test set. Existing reported settings also change: the main-text image count becomes 386K instead of 392K, and Appendix B.4 reports 3152 rather than 3125 optimization steps. These revisions do not establish which existing experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained component, complexity, repetition, and cumulative-data analyses, v3 tests dependence on individual training domains, model size, AST serialization, and counting formats. Appendix C.4 quantifies hallucinations and omissions by token type; C.5 tests filtering effects, and D.2 examines normalization sensitivity. These substantially broaden the investigation of design choices and failure conditions.

E5.justification: v1 provides point estimates without specifying run counts. v3's checklist explicitly states that each configuration was run once and that no error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests are reported. This newly discloses the statistical practice; it does not demonstrate a changed run budget.

E6.justification: v3 adds substantial results for the new evaluations and analyses, plus CROHME2023 and MathWriting entries. Uni-MuMER with external data changes from 71.93/73.67 to 72.66/74.30 for HME100K ExpRate/ExpRate@CDM, and from 84.32/88.99 to 88.19/93.29 in the principal printed-expression table. Figure 6 also changes. These are revised reported results, not established same-setting gains; v3 itself retains 88.99 for printed ExpRate@CDM in Table 17 while reporting 93.29 in Table 24.

M1.justification: The proposed procedure remains full VLM fine-tuning with Vanilla HMER, Tree-CoT, out-of-fold error detection/correction data, and Symbol Counting, followed by direct LaTeX inference. The larger-model, mixed-data, and alternative-format experiments do not replace the core method.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main section sequence are retained. Changes include localized copyediting, renamed headings, a rewritten conclusion, clearer appendix references, author/header edits, and added acknowledgements and a conference checklist. New analyses extend the existing structure without extensively reorganizing the original narrative.

P2.justification: v3 adds substantial tables for transfer, general benchmarks, representation choices, hallucinations, CJK effects, and CROHME2023. Existing tables gain rows or separate evaluation blocks, particularly the normalized/unnormalized printed comparison. Table 1 gains model-category headings, and Figure 6 has revised plotting and axis limits. The original framework and case-study figures are retained.

R1.justification: v3 adds references to TST and the Character Detection Matching paper and removes Elman's 'Finding Structure in Time.' Most other reference changes update metadata for the same works. Section 2 and the positioning against specialized architectures remain substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: Appendix C.4 introduces limited quantitative definitions: HTR is the percentage of predicted tokens absent from the ground truth, and MTR is the percentage of ground-truth tokens absent from the prediction, with token-type subdivisions. Neither version develops theoretical guarantees or proofs; the existing mathematical exposition and CDM counterexample remain.

improvement.justification: v3 addresses v1's explicitly acknowledged lack of general VLM evaluation and adds meaningful controls for domain transfer, representation choices, CJK filtering, and normalization. These experiments substantially strengthen the evidence behind the method and expose its boundaries. Single-run estimates and conflicting compute, release, and printed-score reporting limit confidence and reproducibility, but the expanded validation provides a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Uni-MuMER and contain readable main text, figures, tables, and complete appendices. Existing material can be matched across renumbering and relocation; v3 substantially expands the empirical evaluation.

after.justification: v3 retains original experimental results and adds general multimodal evaluations, leave-one-dataset-out experiments, representation ablations, and error and filtering analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original recognition experiments, component ablations, data-scaling experiments, efficiency measurements, and qualitative analyses in the main text and appendices.

results.title: Uni-MuMER: Unified Multi-Task Fine-Tuning of Vision-Language Model for Handwritten Mathematical Expression Recognition

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the same principal contributions: training-free feature-drift minimization, closed-form layer-wise merging, task-dependency analysis, and the reported 4.4-percentage-point ViT-B/32 advantage. The new appendix evidence does not redefine these main claims.

C2.justification: D.8 adds qualifications about narrower advantages on unseen tasks and task-dependent benefits from surrogate exemplars. D.11 interprets differing multimodal correlations through reasoning demands and modality interactions. The original limitations concerning strictly data-free use and more complex operations remain unchanged.

D1.justification: v2 adds an explicit source-code link and clarifies that exemplars are randomly drawn from training data and kept separate from evaluation data. It also identifies the Qwen checkpoints used in the new experiments. The split statement is newly disclosed information, not evidence of a changed split; existing hardware and implementation disclosures remain.

E1.justification: v2 adds eight GLUE language tasks and MTEB retrieval and clustering tasks, extending evaluation beyond vision and vision-language. It also adds unseen-task and corrupted-input scenarios and uses AOKVQA and IconQA as auxiliary exemplar sources alongside existing datasets.

E2.justification: Table 3 adds the Individual fine-tuned BLIP models as a reference comparator, absent from that comparison in v1. Comparator membership in the retained vision experiments is unchanged; the new appendix evaluations primarily reuse existing comparison methods.

E3.justification: New protocols include merging six experts and evaluating two held-out tasks, Gaussian-blurred or surrogate exemplars, seven corruptions applied to exemplars and test data, and restricted exemplar-class coverage. Language evaluations introduce RoBERTa and Qwen3-0.6B settings with classification, correlation, retrieval and clustering metrics. These are added designs, not demonstrated changes to the retained experiments.

E4.justification: Appendices D.8, D.9, D.11 and D.12 add substantial analyses of unseen-task transfer, calibration-data mismatch, corruption robustness, multimodal feature-drift correlations, and incomplete exemplar-class coverage. v1's existing parameter ablations, exemplar sensitivity, runtime and consistency analyses are retained.

E5.justification: D.11 and Table 17 add explicit Pearson correlation estimates between feature drift and loss changes across six BLIP tasks, extending the earlier visual association analysis. Three-random-exemplar averaging and the runs in Table 8 remain unchanged; no new confidence intervals or significance tests are reported.

E6.justification: Existing LOT results, including 82.7% for ViT-B/32 and 90.5% for ViT-L/14, are retained. v2 adds Individual BLIP scores and Tables 11–18, including a GLUE average of 63.13 and Qwen ArguAna performance of 47.36 versus Task Arithmetic's 30.86. These are additional results under new settings, not improvements over v1 under matched conditions.

M1.justification: The layer-wise objective, closed-form merging rules for linear weights, scaling factors and biases, and final lambda-weighted integration remain unchanged. Algorithm 1 corrects a comment without changing its operations; the additional backbones use the existing method.

P1.justification: The core exposition and section order are largely retained. Changes include updated author and affiliation text, expanded acknowledgments, corrected equation references and an algorithm comment, a NeurIPS checklist, and additional appendix subsections rather than extensive rewriting of the existing narrative.

P2.justification: Tables 11–18 substantially expand the displayed evidence with generalization, corruption, language-model, correlation and exemplar-coverage results. Table 3 gains a reference row, and the NeurIPS format reflows existing material and resizes Figure 2. Figures 1–3 retain their underlying analyses.

R1.justification: v2 adds references for RoBERTa, GLUE, MTEB and Qwen3 to support the language experiments. The related-work discussion and positioning against RegMean, Surgery and CAT Merging remain substantively unchanged; conversion to numbered citations is stylistic.

T1.justification: Appendix B corrects expert-side activations from f_k^(-1)(W_k) to f_k^(l-1)(W_k) in Equations 22–23 and subsequent steps, repairing the recursive proof's layer indexing. The feature-drift bound, assumptions, and closed-form derivations are otherwise retained.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens empirical support by testing language models and directly examining calibration representativeness, unseen-task transfer and corruption sensitivity, which v1 left untested. The Individual BLIP reference and clearer exemplar provenance also improve assessability. Localized reporting errors temper this gain: Table 11 reports 51.1 for an unseen-task average whose entries average 48.6, and D.8 claims surrogate-exemplar superiority despite OKVQA scoring 40.15 versus Task Arithmetic's 40.37. These errors warrant correction but do not outweigh the substantial expansion of relevant evidence.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe LOT Merging. Their complete main texts, figures, tables, equations, and appendices are readable and can be matched reliably despite formatting changes and additions in v2.

after.justification: v2 retains those experiments and adds original language-model evaluations, generalization tests, corruption studies, and feature-drift analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original vision and vision-language experiments, including performance comparisons, parameter ablations, exemplar sensitivity, and runtime measurements.

results.title: Towards Minimizing Feature Drift in Model Merging: Layer-wise Task Vector Fusion for Adaptive Knowledge Integration

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same central contributions: RDX explains representational differences, BSR evaluates difference explanations, and experiments recover known and discover unknown differences. The additional evaluations support these claims without materially redefining their scope.

C2.justification: v2 adds discussion of Euclidean versus manifold distances, OpenCLIP evaluator bias, and why isolating differences need not improve clarity or polysemanticity. It also expands the explanation of baseline failures on subtle CUB differences. Most earlier limitations are retained and moved into Section 5.

D1.justification: Appendix C.3 adds concrete TKSAE implementation and training details, including 50 concepts and 200 epochs, plus NLMCD embedding adaptation, cluster selection, and sampling instructions. Existing implementation and hardware disclosures remain. The abstract removes the direct code-repository link while retaining the project-page link; repository availability cannot be inferred.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same modified MNIST tasks, CUB concept removals, and ImageNet/iNaturalist class groups. The 'Clothes' entry becomes 'Mittens' with identical classes. The new consistency experiment changes sample counts within existing class distributions, rather than adding dataset or task coverage.

E2.justification: v2 evaluates top-k sparse autoencoders (TKSAE) and NLMCD, including a comparator explicitly designed for model comparison. Figure 3 replaces its SAE and PCA entries with TKSAE and NLMCD; SAE and PCA remain in appendix evaluations. These additions substantially broaden the comparison methods.

E3.justification: v2 adds OpenCLIP-based Clarity, Polysemanticity, and modified cross-model Redundancy metrics. Appendix A.5 introduces base/±20% sampling, conversion to hard clusters, and Hungarian matching on 1,200 shared images. These are substantial added evaluation protocols; the original training, dataset splits, and alignment settings are retained.

E4.justification: Appendix A.5 and Figure A11 add a systematic robustness experiment testing whether extracted concepts remain consistent when images are uniformly added or removed. It covers four retained ImageNet subsets and seven methods. Earlier distance-function, sampling, and alignment analyses remain present.

E5.justification: Tables A3–A6 add numerical mean ± summaries beyond v1's boxplots and point-valued tables. However, v2 does not clearly identify the statistic following ± or document additional repeated runs. The previously disclosed global seed remains unchanged.

E6.justification: v2 adds detailed BSR and SemanticLens results in Tables A3–A6 and consistency findings in Figure A11, where SAE is most consistent and RDX has relatively low disagreement. The reported early MNIST checkpoint accuracy changes from 94% to 95% in Figure 2 and the text, while Table A8 still states 94%; this is an inconsistent reporting revision, not an established performance gain.

M1.justification: The RDX pipeline retains ranked Euclidean distances, the locally biased difference function, spectral clustering, KNA sampling, and optional CKA alignment. The stated rank range changes from 0–n to 1–n, but this wording correction does not establish a different ranking procedure. The new metrics concern evaluation.

P1.justification: v2 makes localized prose and caption revisions, clarifies visual concepts, separates the monosemanticity discussion, and moves limitations and societal impact from Appendix A into the main discussion. Appendix material is reorganized, but the central narrative and method exposition remain largely intact.

P2.justification: The quantitative presentation expands substantially through four detailed comparison tables and a new consistency plot. Figure 3 is redrawn for the revised comparator set, appendix figures are relocated nearer their discussions, and the Yellow Back figure labels are corrected. Most existing qualitative grids and ablation plots are retained.

R1.justification: v2 adds eight references, including SemanticLens, NLMCD, k-sparse autoencoders, OpenCLIP, Hungarian matching, and Isomap. NLMCD is incorporated into the discussion of concept-based model comparison. The broader positioning against dictionary learning, representation similarity, and graph comparison remains stable.

T1.justification: Appendix B.2 adds a formal cross-model adaptation of redundancy: maximum cosine similarity to the other model's concepts, averaged over concepts and symmetrized across directions. Appendix A.5 also defines cluster disagreement after matching. The original RDX mathematical construction is retained, with no new theorem or proof.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation that previously relied mainly on BSR and generic explanation baselines. TKSAE and NLMCD address comparator relevance, additional explanation-quality metrics test complementary properties, and the consistency experiment examines reliability under resampling. These gains improve the evidence supporting RDX while acknowledging its lack of consistent superiority on every metric. Undefined ± summaries and the conflicting 94%/95% checkpoint reports weaken precision but do not outweigh the broader validation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same RDX research work. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable matching across relocation and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains these empirical results and adds comparator evaluations, SemanticLens metric results, and an experiment measuring concept consistency under dataset resampling.

before.justification: v1 reports original MNIST and CUB experiments, ImageNet/iNaturalist model comparisons, numerical BSR evaluations, qualitative explanations, and appendix ablations.

results.title: Representational Difference Explanations

C1.justification: The main contributions remain, but their scope is qualified. The abstract describes both attacks as tractable rather than computationally efficient approximations; the introduction says they tend to match or outperform alternatives, especially on larger datasets. It also removes the explicit contribution claim that BASE outperforms RMIA offline.

C2.justification: New computational discussion explains G-BASE's inability to batch target-node inference and its additional N×M cost, substantially qualifying practicality. Section 6 and Appendix F revise the online/offline interpretation: the theoretical reference distribution excludes the target, although practical approximations may benefit from in-models. Appendix H.2 also develops the explanation of noisy shadow-model signals limiting gains from better sampling.

D1.justification: v2 newly specifies target-training and audit-node fractions, balanced membership sampling, and the 20% audit subset exception for large-K Flickr/Github experiments. It documents one Gibbs sweep and a Metropolis-Hastings acceptance-rate target of 0.2–0.4. Conversely, it omits v1's explicit 1000-step burn-in, 500-step spacing, and 50% MLP edge-dropout specification. These omissions do not establish corresponding implementation changes.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate Cora, Citeseer, Pubmed, Flickr, Amazon-Photo, Github, CIFAR-10, and CIFAR-100 on the same graph-node and i.i.d. membership-inference tasks. The added diagnostics and changed model configurations do not introduce new dataset or task coverage.

E2.justification: Table 1 removes both MLP baseline variants, 0-hop and 0+2-hop, from the K=128 comparisons across all six graph datasets. They remain in the K=8 comparisons. LiRA and RMIA remain the principal statistical baselines.

E3.justification: Section 6 changes large-K G-BASE evaluations from 32 sampled graphs, or 16 for Flickr/Github, to 8. Offline BASE/RMIA hyperparameter selection changes from one simulated target to cross-validation over shadow models. Table 9 revises model configurations and online/offline comparisons; new protocols evaluate oracle masks, varying sample counts, and inference time. These are substantial reported evaluation changes.

E4.justification: The earlier three-sampler comparison is substantially expanded and revised in v2 Appendix H.2/Table 9, adding Gibbs sampling, ground-truth membership-mask diagnostics, and offline comparisons. New Table 10 tests sensitivity to 4–32 graph samples, and Table 11 examines computational cost. Threshold-calibration and mismatched-adversary analyses are retained rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: Tables 1–2 drop v1's explicit 'population' qualification for standard deviation, leaving its normalization unspecified. Both versions retain mean-plus-standard-deviation reporting over ten target models. This is a limited loss of statistical reporting specificity, not evidence of a changed estimator or increased run count.

E6.justification: Graph benchmark and robustness results change extensively in Tables 1, 2, and 8; for example, reported Cora/GCN K=8 BASE AUC changes from 81.48% to 82.45%. Gibbs, oracle-mask, sample-count, and timing results are added, while some earlier entries disappear. CIFAR results remain unchanged, moving from Table 10 to Table 12. Revised settings prevent treating all numerical differences as comparable performance gains.

M1.justification: Appendix B.2 adds Gibbs sampling as a fourth membership-mask sampling strategy for G-BASE, using sequential conditional membership updates. The practical BASE and G-BASE score formulas and existing sampling strategies remain, making this a limited procedural extension.

P1.justification: Explanations of approximations, experiments, and online/offline attacks receive localized rewrites. Appendix H is reorganized, moving ROC discussion from H.1 to H.5, and the preprint header becomes a NeurIPS 2025 header. The main section sequence and substantial portions of the prose remain intact.

P2.justification: v2 substantially restructures Tables 1 and 9, adds sample-count and runtime Tables 10–11, redraws ROC plots and legends, and adds the Github ROC Figure 7. Appendix ROC displays are relocated, and Figure 6 changes from Flickr/GraphSAGE to Flickr/GAT. The existing CIFAR table is retained as Table 12. Together these substantially revise the empirical displays.

R1.justification: v2 adds Watson et al.'s work on difficulty calibration, credits prior work for simulated-target threshold selection in Appendix C, and relates mean-confidence calibration to that literature in Appendix E.3. The broader related-work survey and research positioning remain largely unchanged.

T1.justification: Theorem 1 now retains a prior likelihood-ratio term Lambda and explicitly integrates over models conditioned on the target being absent. Appendix B.1 replaces the earlier approximate cancellation with a revised derivation; setting Lambda=1 becomes an explicit practical approximation in Section 4.3. Corollary 1 additionally states the membership-independence assumption on the prior. These substantially revise the central theoretical foundation.

improvement.justification: v1 presents its central theorem as exact despite an approximate prior cancellation in its proof. v2 retains that prior ratio and explicitly separates practical approximations, materially improving mathematical transparency. The oracle-mask, sample-count, and timing studies also address important gaps in validating approximation quality and computational claims, including G-BASE's substantial overhead. These gains outweigh the narrower losses of sampling details and high-K MLP comparisons.

A1.justification: Both PDFs are complete, readable versions of the same BASE/G-BASE study. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and Appendices A–H support reliable comparison, including matching relocated content.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical evaluations and reports revised graph results, additional sampling diagnostics, and inference-time measurements.

before.justification: v1 reports original membership-inference experiments on six graph datasets and CIFAR-10/100, including baseline comparisons, threshold calibration, robustness tests, and sampling analyses.

results.title: Practical Bayes-Optimal Membership Inference Attacks

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction retain the same contributions: identifying costly hyperparameter tuning, characterizing sensitivity, and proposing theoretically motivated selection without retraining. The added conclusion sentence about checkpoint sensitivity restates a finding already present in v1.

C2.justification: v2 adds a geometric explanation involving gradient directions, interprets the new constant estimates as support for assumptions in nonconvex settings, and suggests dataset redundancy explains limited effects from 10% removal. The original limitations concerning regularization-specific theory and reliance on LDS remain.

D1.justification: Appendix B.4 documents projected-FIM diagonalization and gradient-based estimation for the new assumption checks. Appendix D changes the listed repository location from the data-attribution-hp organization to TRAIS-Lab. Existing hardware, timing, and default-hyperparameter disclosures are retained.

E1.justification: Appendix C.5 adds an actual downstream data-selection/removal task on MNIST, CIFAR-2, and MAESTRO, extending evaluation beyond LDS. No new dataset is introduced: WikiText2/GPT2, including its language-modeling setting, already appeared in v1.

E2.justification: The new downstream comparisons include random removal and explicit default-regularization IFFIM/TRAK comparisons against their selected-regularization variants, alongside a full-data reference. The original sensitivity-study methods and spectral-quantile selection baselines are retained.

E3.justification: The downstream evaluation introduces removal rates of 10%, 30%, and 50%, using test accuracy for MNIST/CIFAR-2 and test loss for MAESTRO. New assumption checks use projection dimension 4096 and epsilon_g = 0.5. These are added protocols; the original LDS evaluation using 50 independently retrained models remains unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 Appendix B.4 adds empirical checks of Assumptions B.7 and B.9 on CIFAR-2 and MAESTRO, estimating their constants relative to the smallest eigenvalue. Figure 7 also extends regularization-sensitivity diagnostics to IFFIM and LoGra on WikiText2/GPT2. The existing subset-fraction robustness analysis is retained.

E5.justification: Appendix C.5 and Tables 2–4 introduce ten-seed experiments reported as means and standard errors. v1's LDS retrainings did not provide this uncertainty-reporting practice. This does not establish increased repetitions for retained experiments, and no formal significance test is specified.

E6.justification: v2 adds assumption-check measurements, Figure 7's LDS curves, and downstream results in Tables 2–4. For example, at 30% MNIST removal, TRAK Selected yields 83.84% accuracy versus 87.92% for TRAK Default; lower accuracy indicates stronger attribution. CIFAR-2 IFFIM Selected and Default have identical reported results. Original Figures 1–6 retain their results.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 still selects the candidate regularization value whose average surrogate indicator is closest to 0.5. The attribution procedures and projection formulations are retained; expanded notation and explanations do not change the algorithm.

P1.justification: Section 4 separates problem formulation from analysis, introduces notation before the theorem, and adds intuition and a proof sketch. Appendix subsections are expanded and renumbered, with local wording and conference-footer updates. Most existing prose and the overall narrative remain intact.

P2.justification: v2 adds the two-panel Figure 7 and three downstream-result tables. Existing Figures 1–6 retain their displays, with local relocation, including placing Figures 2 and 3 together. Table 1's caption moves above the table.

R1.justification: v2 adds Deng et al.'s 2025 data-attribution survey as reference 9 and cites it in the introduction. The remaining references largely match after renumbering, and the main novelty positioning is unchanged.

T1.justification: Appendix B.2 adds an assumption and derivation connecting the alpha weights to leave-one-out effects. Proposition B.8 restores a missing factor of n, propagated into the constants and inequalities in Lemma B.15's proof. The main sufficient-condition theorem and qualitative monotonicity result remain unchanged.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens practical validation beyond v1's LDS-only evaluation through ten-seed downstream experiments across three settings. It also repairs a proof-bound error and adds empirical scrutiny of theoretical assumptions. These address important evidential and mathematical weaknesses. The gains remain qualified: CIFAR-2 shows no IFFIM improvement, and the significance claims lack a specified formal test.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their main text, figures, tables, equations, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable matching across the revision.

after.justification: v2 retains those experiments and adds empirical assumption checks, WikiText2/GPT2 surrogate evaluations, and downstream data-removal results.

before.justification: v1 reports original hyperparameter-sensitivity experiments, surrogate-selection evaluations, and subset-fraction analyses in Sections 3–4 and Appendices A and C.

results.title: Taming Hyperparameter Sensitivity in Data Attribution: Practical Selection Without Costly Retraining

C1.justification: The original CLIP compositionality, retrieval and efficiency claims remain. v2 adds a third introductory contribution and a conclusion claim that CLIC vision features improve LLaVA compositional reasoning while preserving general VLM capabilities. This materially expands the claimed contribution beyond dual-encoder CLIP models.

C2.justification: v2 hypothesizes that reduced negative diversity explains the LLM-swapping variant's mixed results and interprets long-caption retrieval as evidence against concatenation shortcuts. Appendix A replaces v1's inability to test LLaVA with a limitation to the tested LLaVA setting. Figure 6 explicitly acknowledges persistent hallucinations in both LLaVA variants.

D1.justification: Section D.5 supplies model, dataset, resolution, batch size, training stages, baseline controls and codebase information for the new LLaVA pipeline. Appendix B.4 documents fine-grained POS processing, Gemini 2.5-Flash replacement candidates and preprocessing costs. Section D.1 also revises ambiguous GPU-hour wording to training durations on four A100 GPUs.

E1.justification: v2 extends evaluation beyond the retained CLIP benchmarks to GQA, TextVQA, ScienceQA-Images and MME perception through LLaVA. It also adds qualitative open-ended captioning and a long-caption retrieval scenario using multiple sentences describing one scene. These substantially broaden task and input-scenario coverage.

E2.justification: The original CLIP comparator sets are retained. New comparisons introduce an authors-trained standard LLaVA-1.5-7b control against its CLIC-equipped counterpart (Table 6), and an LLM SWAPS condition (Table 8). The earlier Non-random condition is retained as SAME NOUN, rather than newly introduced.

E3.justification: The new LLaVA experiment introduces 336×336 CLIP fine-tuning, an effective batch size of 40×8, staged projector/language-model training, matched baseline training and VQAScore evaluation. Long-caption retrieval introduces punctuation-based truncation within CLIP's 77-token context. These are added protocols; the original CLIP experiments retain their previously documented settings.

E4.justification: Appendix B.4 adds an LLM-swapping ablation and a manual quality audit of 75 negatives from each generation approach. Appendix E adds a long-caption test of concatenation shortcuts, success/failure cases across four SugarCrepe++ categories, and LLaVA captioning examples. The original component ablation is retained, moving from v1 Table 10 to v2 Table 4.

E5.justification: v1 provides point estimates without repeated-run uncertainty reporting. v2 Tables 10–11 introduce means and standard deviations over three independent runs for CLIC-LAION and CLIC-RedCaps across compositionality and downstream benchmarks. This establishes a substantial new reporting practice, although v1's unspecified run counts prevent claiming a particular increase in runs.

E6.justification: Matched original table values are unchanged, but substantial new results appear. v2 Table 6 reports WinoGround text scores of 36.7 versus 43.5 for CLIP-based versus CLIC-based LLaVA, while SQA-I scores are 69.2 versus 68.2. Additional results cover long-caption retrieval, repeated-run summaries, failure cases and negative quality: the manual audit reports 69% meaningful, grammatical negatives for LLM SWAPS versus 28% for standard CLIC.

M1.justification: v2 adds a LLaVA adaptation pipeline that fine-tunes both CLIP encoders, transfers the vision encoder, and trains the projector and language model (Sections 4.5 and D.5). Appendix B.4 adds an LLM-guided negative-generation variant. Equation (5) also changes the stated loss aggregation. The original concatenation and alternating-update scheme remains; implementation changes for retained experiments are not established.

P1.justification: v2 makes localized prose revisions, expands explanatory examples in Appendix D.4, consolidates the former SOTA subsection into Section 4.4 and introduces dedicated LLaVA sections. Repetitive appendix ablation discussion is shortened, and front matter is updated. Most existing narrative and the appendix organization remain intact.

P2.justification: v2 adds uncertainty tables, LLaVA and long-caption comparison tables, four illustrated success/failure tables with cosine scores, and a caption-response comparison figure. These substantially expand the visual evidence. The component ablation moves into the main text, while the original figures are retained and existing tables are redistributed.

R1.justification: Eight targeted references are added, including Gemini 2.5, VQAScore, Long-CLIP and works supporting the new VQA evaluations. The established positioning against NegCLIP, DAC, SVLC and TripletCLIP remains substantially unchanged; the additions mainly contextualize the new experiments.

T1.justification: Equation (5) moves the sum over four positive captions outside the logarithm: v1 takes the logarithm of summed positive-versus-negative probabilities, whereas v2 sums their logarithms. These expressions are not equivalent; v2 aligns with the stated per-positive penalty. This is a localized mathematical correction, with no new theorem or proof.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the evidence by adding repeated-run uncertainty, direct tests of negative quality and concatenation shortcuts, and explicit failure examples. Its matched LLaVA experiment addresses v1's stated transfer limitation, while Equation (5) corrects an important specification error. These resolve meaningful reliability, applicability and documentation gaps. The gains remain qualified: LLaVA results lack repeated-run uncertainty, SQA-I decreases from 69.2 to 68.2, and captioning hallucinations persist.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same CLIC study by the same authors. The complete main texts and appendices A–E, including equations, tables and figures, support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds authors-trained LLaVA comparisons, repeated-run measurements, long-caption retrieval and a manually assessed negative-generation experiment.

before.justification: v1 reports original CLIC fine-tuning experiments, compositionality and downstream evaluations, and component, training-duration and encoder-freezing ablations.

results.title: Advancing Compositional Awareness in CLIP with Efficient Fine-Tuning

C1.justification: The abstract and four stated contributions retain their substantive claims. A limited novelty qualification occurs when v3 removes the introduction's 'first' qualifier for OCB, alongside acknowledging related object-based concept-bank work. The principal performance, multilabel-classification and benchmark contributions remain intact.

C2.justification: v3 interprets the VOC ablation as evidence that global and object features are complementary, explicitly discusses linear-readout limitations on COCOLogic, and explains additional capacity, size and detection failures. These refine the existing account of applicability and noise sensitivity while retaining the original aggregation and pretrained-model limitations.

D1.justification: v3 adds an explicit code/data repository address in footnote 1 and states that COCOLogic scripts are provided there; v1 mentioned a repository without an address. The core Appendix C hyperparameters and hardware information remain unchanged. Repository contents or availability cannot be verified from the PDFs.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate PASCAL-VOC, COCO(h), COCO(l), SUN397 and COCOLogic with the same task coverage. COCOLogic's class rules and sample counts are unchanged. The added analyses vary configurations within these retained datasets.

E2.justification: v3 adds CLIP+MLP across all five benchmark settings in Table 1 and Coarse-to-Fine CBM (C2F-CBM) on SUN397 and COCOLogic in Table 2. These substantially broaden v1's comparisons with standard and equal-capacity SpLiCE-based CBMs.

E3.justification: Section 5 revises the stated COCOLogic metric from accuracy to balanced accuracy; retained numerical scores do not establish recomputation. Added protocols use a common LAION-based vocabulary and nonsparse OCB for the C2F-CBM comparison, and vary feature inputs, sparsity and minimum proposal size from 0.005 to 0.05.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained proposal-model, aggregation and object-count analyses, v3 adds image-only versus object-only controls (Table 4), capacity sweeps (Figure 8), minimum-size sensitivity (Table 10), and duplicate/irrelevant detection examples (Figure 9). These test additional explanations for gains and failure conditions.

E5.justification: Both versions specify means and standard deviations over five seeds. The new tables continue this practice, and the added checklist reiterates it. No increased run count, new uncertainty estimator or significance-testing procedure is reported.

E6.justification: Existing Table 1 rows and v1 Tables 3–7, retained as v3 Tables 5–9, keep their numerical values. Substantial new results include C2F-CBM versus nonsparse OCB on SUN397 at 70.12 versus 89.60, object-only VOC performance of 77.48, CLIP+MLP scores, and capacity/size sweeps. These are added comparisons and configurations, not improvements to the earlier reported scores.

M1.justification: The proposal filtering, image/object concept extraction, five aggregation options and linear predictor remain unchanged, including Algorithm 1. The shared-vocabulary and sparsity discussion clarifies the existing framework; nonsparse and object-only evaluations vary its configuration without introducing a new proposed component.

P1.justification: The main section sequence and much of the prose are retained. v3 locally rewrites the introduction, evaluation discussion and conclusion, renames Section 5.4, subdivides Appendix E, and appends a NeurIPS checklist. This is limited restructuring rather than a wholesale narrative rewrite.

P2.justification: v3 expands Table 1, adds comparison/ablation Tables 2, 4 and 10, and introduces the capacity plot and failure illustrations in Figures 8 and 9. It also revises Figures 4–5 captions and rearranges existing figures and appendix tables, substantially expanding the visual presentation of evidence.

R1.justification: v3 adds Prasse et al. (2025), DCBM, and distinguishes its image-level activation vector from OCB's combined image/object activations. The broader related-work coverage remains stable. Panousis et al.'s C2F-CBM was already cited in v1; its actual evaluation is new.

T1.justification: The mathematical definitions, filtering equations, aggregation formulas and COCOLogic rules are retained. Neither version supplies theoretical proofs. The added qualitative sparsity explanation and discussion of linear-classifier limitations introduce no formal assumption, derivation or theorem.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially addresses v1's limited comparator breadth and incomplete attribution of performance gains. The C2F-CBM and CLIP+MLP comparisons, broader capacity controls and global-feature ablation provide stronger tests of the central object-centric contribution, while failure examples clarify its limits. Reporting weaknesses remain: the metric revision leaves unchanged COCOLogic scores unexplained, and Table 10's COCOLogic trend is not consistently monotonic despite the accompanying prose. These weaknesses do not outweigh the substantially stronger comparative and diagnostic evidence.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same OCB framework and COCOLogic benchmark. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable and support reliable matching across the revision.

after.justification: v3 retains those original results and adds baseline comparisons, feature-removal and sensitivity experiments, and detection-failure examples.

before.justification: v1 reports original benchmark evaluations, aggregation and object-count ablations, and qualitative concept analyses in Section 5 and Appendix E.

results.title: Object Centric Concept Bottlenecks

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contribution list, and conclusion retain the same central claims: existing NCO models overfit particular constraint tightnesses, and varying-tightness training plus expert specialization mitigates this on CVRP and CVRPTW. The expanded appendix evidence does not materially redefine these headline contributions.

C2.justification: v3 explicitly qualifies the module as switching between specialists rather than learning one continuously adaptable policy. New discussions interpret vehicle overuse, justify practical capacity-range selection, assess solution-quality/runtime tradeoffs, and discuss applicability to complex routing problems and sensitivity to demand distributions. The original uniform-sampling limitation and future-work paragraph remain.

D1.justification: v1 promises a future code release; v3 reports released code and supplies a repository link. v3 also documents Top-K settings, auxiliary-loss weight 0.01, long-tailed demand generation, heuristic procedures, and runtime measurement conditions, including the CPU/GPU distinction. Conversely, the explicit POMO decoder-expert equations are removed and replaced by a less detailed encoder-placement description.

E1.justification: v3 adds VRPBTW100 and VRPBLTW100, KP200 evaluations, and CVRP tests with long-tailed customer demands. Appendix L also analyzes 192 CVRPLIB instances descriptively. These extend task requirements, domains, and input distributions beyond v1's CVRP/CVRPTW evaluations and retained TSP/OVRP similarity analyses.

E2.justification: The original nine NCO comparators and HGS remain in the corresponding CVRP comparisons. v3 adds a learnable Top-K MoE comparator against discrete switching in Table 10 and introduces OR-Tools as the reference in the complex-routing and knapsack comparisons in Tables 11 and 17.

E3.justification: The original training budgets and greedy-inference settings are retained, but v3 adds substantial evaluation protocols: a MEM-only control, matched-settings Top-K gating evaluation, runtime measurements for 10,000-instance datasets, vehicle-count metrics, and heuristic-based tightness measurements. Appendix O additionally evaluates fixed-capacity KP200 checkpoints across five capacities. The newly stated equal training-data budget clarifies existing settings rather than establishing a budget change.

E4.justification: v3 adds the missing MEM-only ablation in Table 4, tests discrete versus learned gating in Table 10, analyzes vehicle overuse in Table 13, measures MEM's computational tradeoff in Table 14, and tests demand-distribution robustness in Table 16. It also adds capacity-range justification and a knapsack case study. The earlier problem-similarity and batch-versus-instance training analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, error bars, confidence intervals, or statistical significance tests. Both answer 'No' to checklist item 7 with the same justification about deterministic inference and reporting mean objectives or gaps. The added results retain this reporting practice.

E6.justification: The original primary scores are retained, including Table 3's 1.86% average gap and Table 5's CVRPTW results. v3 adds substantial results: MEM alone averages 8.95% in Table 4; Top-K gating averages 2.17% versus switching's 1.86% in Table 10; augmented POMO averages 10.03% versus 20.91% on VRPBTW100 in Table 11. Runtime, vehicle-count, demand-shift, tightness, and knapsack outcomes are also new.

M1.justification: The varying-tightness training scheme and LEHD multi-expert architecture remain unchanged. However, v1 Appendix F replaces POMO's decoder with lightweight experts containing an added feed-forward layer; v3 Appendix G instead places the multi-expert module in POMO's encoder. This is an explicit architecture revision localized to the POMO adaptation.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main section sequence are retained. Changes include localized language corrections, a new introductory definition subsection, revised ablation and POMO descriptions, updated affiliations and funding text, and moving the checklist before the appendices. The standalone broader-impacts appendix is removed, with its general assessment retained in the checklist; the extensive new scientific content does not constitute a wholesale narrative rewrite.

P2.justification: v3 substantially expands the tabular presentation with runtime comparisons, gating results, multiple task panels, tightness calculations, vehicle counts, and demand-distribution tables. Table 4 gains a MEM-only row. Existing appendix tables are relocated and renumbered, while the three original figures are retained with sizing and layout adjustments.

R1.justification: The introduction updates its cited literature, adding works including CaDA, URS, ARS, and Rethinking Light Decoder-Based Solvers, while removing citations to the dual-aspect transformer, flexible neural k-opt, and DPN papers. Section 7's substantive positioning against fixed-tightness and varying-capacity training remains largely unchanged.

T1.justification: Appendix J introduces a general mathematical definition of tightness using normalized logarithmic changes in a reference heuristic's objective value between relaxed and extreme constraints. It specifies assumptions and instantiates the definition for CVRP, CVRPTW, and knapsack. This is distinct from v1's retained problem-similarity formula and time-window parameterization. No theorem or proof is added.

improvement.justification: v3 addresses important validation gaps in v1 through the MEM-only control, an alternative-gating comparison, broader task and distribution tests, and explicit computational-cost measurements. These strengthen both the overfitting diagnosis and the justification for the proposed design. The reported code release also improves reproducibility access. Statistical uncertainty remains absent, and the revised POMO implementation is less fully specified, but the additional controls and evidence provide a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work on constraint-tightness overfitting and varying-tightness training with a multi-expert module. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable. Retained material can be matched across appendix renumbering and relocation.

after.justification: v3 retains those empirical results and adds original gating comparisons, runtime measurements, complex-routing experiments, demand-distribution tests, and knapsack analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original CVRP and CVRPTW experiments, component ablations, and appendix analyses of problem similarity and training strategies.

results.title: Rethinking Neural Combinatorial Optimization for Vehicle Routing Problems with Different Constraint Tightness Degrees

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the claims of RL-enhanced embodied reasoning, the Robot-R1 benchmark, advantages over SFT and strong low-level reasoning relative to commercial models. The added evaluations supply evidence for these claims without materially redefining the main contributions.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations for weak planning-judge agreement, optimizer differences, limited low-level transfer to Bridge images, VLABench failures and the LIBERO object-category decline. These materially expand applicability boundaries and mechanism hypotheses. It also introduces strong seed-robustness interpretations, although Table 8 does not show improvement for every task and seed. The original xyz-only limitation remains.

D1.justification: v2 documents the high-quality SFT data-generation procedure and adds the GR00T-N1.5 implementation reference, diffusion-head training budgets, batch size, robot platform, demonstration counts and rollout counts. Appendix B.1 changes the stated 12-hour training account from one to five epochs while retaining the same hardware. These substantially expand implementation information without establishing a new code release.

E1.justification: Beyond the retained benchmarks, v2 evaluates real demonstration images from BridgeV2, VLABench reasoning categories, LIBERO manipulation tasks and four physical pick-and-place tasks using a Franka Research 3 arm. These substantially extend the represented environments and task requirements, including actual physical execution.

E2.justification: v2 adds evaluated RLOO and REINFORCE++ alternatives to GRPO in Table 7 and a high-quality CoT-SFT comparator in Table 13. The latter uses GPT-4.1-mini-generated reasoning rather than the original scripted supervision. These extend comparison to alternative RL optimizers and a different supervised-training regime; the original comparator sets remain.

E3.justification: Section 4.1 revises the reported training budget from one to five epochs; the training-curve caption changes Open-End/MCQA budgets from two/one to ten/five epochs. This establishes changed reporting, not that retained experiments were rerun. New protocols include blind scoring of 80 responses by eight experts, one-epoch Appendix C experiments, 50 rollouts per LIBERO task and 24 trials per physical task. Appendix C's one-epoch statement conflicts with Figure 11's blanket five-epoch description.

E4.justification: v2 adds studies of automatic-judge agreement with experts, dependence on the RL optimizer, sensitivity to sampling seeds, and RL following high-quality SFT initialization. These address evaluation validity and training robustness beyond v1's retained auxiliary-task and question-format ablations. The original qualitative examples are retained.

E5.justification: v2 explicitly reports two additional sampling-seed runs and presents individual results, means and standard deviations across three seeds in Table 8. Table 6 also introduces Pearson correlations against median ratings from eight experts. v1 contains neither practice; v2 does not provide confidence intervals or a formal significance test supporting its significance language.

E6.justification: The original benchmark and QA-ablation values remain unchanged, while Tables 6–8 and 11–15 add substantial results. These include planning judge correlation of 0.3315 versus approximately 0.89 for other categories, mixed VLABench transfer, and new baseline-versus-Robot-R1 control averages of 69.0% versus 71.8% on LIBERO and 16.67% versus 23.96% on the physical robot. These are newly reported comparisons, not performance gains between versions.

M1.justification: The core MCQA construction, auxiliary tasks, rewards and GRPO procedure remain unchanged. v2 adds limited adaptations: supervised initialization before Robot-R1 in Appendix C and a diffusion-policy head attached to the LVLM for downstream control in Appendix F. Renaming primitive movement and subtask reasoning does not change their underlying procedures.

P1.justification: v2 standardizes terminology, corrects some wording and updates affiliations, the conference header and acknowledgements. It introduces additional appendix sections and moves the original qualitative material from Appendix C to E. The existing main narrative is largely retained rather than extensively rewritten.

P2.justification: v2 substantially expands quantitative presentation with tables for judge agreement, optimizers, seeds, transfer, cold start and VLA control. Existing tables are renumbered and restyled. v1 Figure 4 is removed, but its MCQA curves remain in the combined appendix plot, matched from v1 Figure 12 to v2 Figure 11.

R1.justification: References 64–70 add work supporting RLOO, REINFORCE++, BridgeData V2, VLABench, GPT-4.1, GR00T-N1.5 and LIBERO. These contextualize the new experiments, while the original related-work discussion and principal novelty positioning remain substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: The state and waypoint definitions, GRPO objective, reward construction and open-ended reward formula retain their mathematical substance. Notation cleanup introduces no new assumptions, derivations, theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses two important gaps in v1: unvalidated automatic grading and the absence of physical robot-control evaluation. Human agreement measurements, optimizer and seed studies, and downstream control experiments strengthen the empirical basis, while mixed transfer outcomes expose limitations. Inconsistent epoch reporting and overstated robustness language remain weaknesses, but the added validation and practical testing provide a clear net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Robot-R1 and retain matching methods, experiments and supporting material. Their text, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds human assessment, optimizer and seed comparisons, transfer evaluations, and simulated and physical robot-control experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original Robot-R1 and SFT experiments on Robot-R1 Bench, EmbodiedBench Manipulation and SpatialRGPT-Bench, together with ablations and qualitative results.

results.title: Robot-R1: Reinforcement Learning for Enhanced Embodied Reasoning in Robotics

C1.justification: The central claims remain adaptation without parameter updates, STES and PG-ES example selection, and synthetic training enabling cross-domain prediction. Merging the synthetic-data contribution into the first contribution and removing some uses of 'rapid' do not substantively redefine these claims.

C2.justification: v2 distinguishes reduced adaptation cost from increased inference cost and documents failure with a small NBA example pool. It adds explanations linking PG-ES benefits to ambiguous initial predictions, pool relevance, and synthetic-to-real transfer. Appendix A.3 also explicitly qualifies comparisons across different architectures and training datasets.

D1.justification: v2 newly specifies eight context examples, dataset sampling rates and corresponding time horizons, precomputed context features, profiling hardware, batch-one memory measurement, and the upstream detector/tracker models. These disclosures do not establish changes to the original experiments. The project-page link is effectively unchanged, and the PDFs do not establish changed code availability.

E1.justification: v2 adds NBA SportVU rebounding and scoring subsets, extending evaluation into basketball motion. It also introduces detector/tracker-generated JRDB inputs and short-observation scenarios. ETH-UCY was already evaluated in v1's appendix and is retained, not newly added.

E2.justification: Tables 8 and 11–12 add ForecastMAE comparisons, reported RAN/MetaTra comparisons, and prompt-selection comparisons including feature similarity. RAN/MetaTra use differing architectures and training settings, so their scores do not establish matched-setting superiority. The original fine-tuning comparator set remains; identifying VPT Shallow with the Latent Corridors approach clarifies an existing comparator.

E3.justification: Added evaluation designs vary model dimensions (32/64/128), predictor depth (1/2/3), PG-ES iterations (1–4), and observation length (9/6/3 timesteps). v2 also introduces computational profiling and feature-distribution FID evaluation. The original chronological 80/20 split, K=20 prediction metrics, and 100-plus-400-epoch training schedule remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 substantially expands analysis with architecture/backbone studies, alternative selectors, perception-error and short-history robustness, iterative refinement, initial-error analysis, pool-quality analysis, and synthetic-to-real feature comparisons. Existing VTP, RCPE/SRPE, and pool-size studies remain. Figure 6 replaces v1's WildTrack pool-size comparison with an example-count comparison.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. The new scatterplots show variation across samples rather than uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: Tables 1–5 and the ETH-UCY results remain numerically unchanged. v2 adds architecture, basketball, robustness, cost, and diagnostic results; for example, Table 15 reports noisy-input JRDB minFDE20 of 4.33 for Social-Transmotion versus 2.79 for TrajICL. Figures 3 and 6 also contain revised curves without a corresponding explanation of changed experimental settings.

M1.justification: v2 adds experimental architectural and inference variants: ForecastMAE with its lane encoder disabled and repeated application of PG-ES (Tables 8 and 17). The standard STES/PG-ES procedure, RCPE/SRPE components, loss, and two-stage training remain unchanged. Renaming PredictionHead to MultiModalDecoder is cosmetic.

P1.justification: The main narrative receives local wording corrections, expanded adaptation explanations, a merged contribution list, and terminology changes. The appendix is reorganized from one broad experimental subsection into A.1–A.6. Most existing prose and the main section sequence remain intact.

P2.justification: v2 adds architecture, sports, robustness, and cost tables plus initial-error and pool-similarity scatterplots, and substantially rearranges appendix displays. Several example-count plots are redrawn. The old qualitative Figure 9 becomes Figure 11. Figure 6 replaces mismatched panels, but Figure 7 introduces duplicated JTA plots under the MOTSynth label.

R1.justification: Section 2's positioning is largely retained. New appendix discussion addresses architecture-coupled adaptation methods and comparison fairness, while additional citations support prompt-selection strategies, basketball evaluation, perception models, and efficiency discussion. Reference deduplication and bibliographic corrections do not remove substantive prior work.

T1.justification: The retrieval equations, training objective, and substantive mathematical formulation are retained. Section 3.1 explicitly describes K possible futures, restating the multimodal output already present in v1's Equation 5. Neither version provides theoretical propositions or proofs.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses important gaps in v1's practical validation: Tables 13–14 quantify adaptation savings and inference overhead, while Tables 15–16 test perception errors and limited observations. Backbone evaluation and the explicitly reported small-pool failure further clarify applicability. Figure 7's mislabeled duplication and the continued absence of uncertainty reporting limit confidence in parts of the evidence, but the added tests and qualifications materially strengthen support for the paper's central deployment claims.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same TrajICL research. All 16 pages of v1 and 19 pages of v2, including equations, figures, tables, references, and appendices, support comparison. Reporting inconsistencies do not prevent identifying the changes.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds sports-domain evaluation, robustness experiments, architecture studies, and computational measurements.

before.justification: v1 reports original trajectory-prediction experiments, baseline comparisons, ablations, and qualitative results, including ETH-UCY evaluation in its appendix.

results.title: Towards Predicting Any Human Trajectory In Context

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the same central contributions: reward-free trajectory augmentation using temporal embeddings, exploratory stitching and diffusion refinement to improve diffusion planning and offline GCRL. The added experiments broaden supporting evidence without changing these core claims.
