C2.justification: Section 3.1 newly argues that local retrieval does not require globally accurate temporal distances. Appendix C explains novelty-driven detours around embedding distortions, interprets parameter sensitivities, and clarifies that reward-free describes stitching rather than downstream reward use. The existing computational-cost and asymmetric-MDP limitations remain unchanged.

D1.justification: New experiment details specify reward-model training on original offline data and navigation preprocessing from 512-ray LiDAR to 64×64 occupancy grids and eight-dimensional beta-VAE representations, with trajectories collected over 5m ranges. Existing architecture specifications, hyperparameter table, hardware, runtimes and code-access information are retained.

E1.justification: v3 retains the eight OGBench settings and adds Hopper and Walker2d medium/medium-replay datasets for dense-reward offline RL. It also evaluates noisy, partially observable LiDAR navigation in building and corridor environments, substantially extending task and input coverage.

E2.justification: Diffuser, previously discussed as prior work, becomes an evaluated comparator against Diffuser trained with SCoTS augmentation in Table 11. Comparator membership in the retained main experiments is unchanged; the navigation experiment reuses HIQL.

E3.justification: The original OGBench settings and Table 5 are unchanged. New protocols include component-removal controls and beta, segment-length and retrieval-count sweeps; D4RL normalized-return evaluation with horizon 32, segment length 4 and 2M samples; and navigation evaluation over 100 episodes using short-range collected trajectories and processed LiDAR observations.

E4.justification: v1 includes controller-horizon and replanning ablations, qualitative novelty comparisons and refinement Dynamic MSE analysis. v3 retains these and adds direct temporal-embedding ablation, downstream HD/HIQL refinement ablations, and quantitative sensitivity analyses for novelty weight, segment length and retrieved-candidate count (Tables 6–10).

E5.justification: Existing OGBench reporting remains five seeds, 50 episodes per task and standard deviations. The new D4RL results explicitly average over 50 planning seeds, adding a distinct seed-reporting protocol. Navigation results specify 100 episodes but do not clearly define their run count or reported uncertainty.

E6.justification: Tables 1–3 retain their scores, while Tables 6–12 add substantial results. New comparisons include AntMaze-Giant-Stitch success of 7±2 without temporal embeddings versus 87±2 with them, D4RL average returns of 79.5 for Diffuser versus 87.2 with SCoTS, and building-navigation success of 27±7 for HIQL versus 53±4 with augmentation. These are newly reported comparisons, not revisions of earlier scores.

M1.justification: The core stitching algorithm, objectives and refinement procedure remain unchanged. Appendix C adds limited task-specific adaptations: a learned reward predictor labels augmented dense-reward trajectories, and a pretrained beta-VAE encodes LiDAR occupancy images for navigation.

P1.justification: Most prose and section organization are retained. v3 adds a methodological remark, notation clarification, Appendix C subsections, an impact statement and acknowledgements, alongside small language corrections and conference metadata. The code link moves to the abstract.

P2.justification: Appendix C gains a substantial suite of seven tables presenting component controls, parameter sweeps and additional benchmarks. Existing figures are retained; the novelty and long-horizon illustrations exchange order, Table 5 moves to a standalone page, and surrounding layouts reflow.

R1.justification: v3 adds references supporting the new experiments and planning context, including beta-VAE, HRL navigation and Fast Monte Carlo Tree Diffusion. The central positioning against reward-guided augmentation and test-time trajectory composition is unchanged. Publication updates to existing references do not introduce different works.

T1.justification: The diffusion equations, temporal-distance formulation, expectile objective and stitching scores remain unchanged. No theorem, proof or substantive mathematical derivation is added; the new embedding discussion provides qualitative reasoning.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens evidence for the method's design and applicability. Tables 6–10 supply direct component and sensitivity tests where v1 relied partly on qualitative illustrations or indirect Dynamic MSE evidence. Dense-reward and LiDAR-navigation experiments test previously unexamined settings. These additions materially improve empirical support, although implementation and uncertainty reporting for the new navigation experiment remain limited.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SCoTS research. Their complete main texts, equations, tables, figures and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison despite relocated material and added experiments.

after.justification: v3 retains those original experiments and adds component ablations, sensitivity analyses, D4RL locomotion results and mobile robot navigation results in Appendix C.

before.justification: v1 reports original SCoTS planning and data-augmentation experiments, including OGBench results and controller, refinement and replanning analyses. Appendix D separately identifies externally sourced baseline scores.

results.title: State-Covering Trajectory Stitching for Diffusion Planners

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the central claims of double robustness, semiparametric efficiency and favorable optimization-gap bounds. The additional experiments support the existing contribution rather than redefine it.

C2.justification: v2 newly interprets HH results through pairwise preference noise and discusses DRPO's performance relative to noise-aware DPO variants, including a conjectured benefit from adopting a noise-aware preference model. It also adds discussion of bound tightness. The original importance-sampling variance and model-scale limitations are relocated to Appendix E.

D1.justification: Appendix C adds the 7B model's training information, TRL/BF16 defaults for DPO variants, the custom Dr. DPO loss adaptation and the AlpacaEval reference-response setup. Existing hardware disclosures, DRPO hyperparameters and code-access information are retained.

E1.justification: v2 adds general-purpose instructions from AlpacaEval 2.0 as an explicit out-of-distribution evaluation for HH-trained models, substantially extending evaluation beyond the original training domains. IMDb, TL;DR and HH remain; the added 7B IMDb experiment changes model configuration rather than task coverage.

E2.justification: Empirical comparisons expand beyond PPO and DPO to Dr. DPO, rDPO, cDPO, CPO, ORPO, IPO and RSO in v2 Tables 2–3. IPO and RSO were previously discussed but not evaluated as comparators. The new out-of-distribution comparison also uses SFT-generated responses as its reference.

E3.justification: The added AlpacaEval protocol uses a GPT-4-Turbo-based judge, ordinary and length-controlled win rates, and SFT responses instead of the benchmark's default GPT-4-Turbo references. Appendix C.1 adds Qwen2.5-7B preference evaluation at sample sizes 500–3000. These are additional settings; Appendix C.2 retains GPT-4o-mini for the original PPO/DPO comparisons.

E4.justification: v2 adds an explicit distribution-shift test from HH training to general-purpose instructions and extends the controlled four-way preference/reference-model misspecification analysis to a 7B model. This broadens robustness validation beyond the original settings. The temperature studies and eight qualitative examples are retained unchanged.

E5.justification: Both versions report 500 simulations and 95% confidence bands for the original IMDb experiment. The added tables introduce no stated new seed or repeated-run protocol, confidence intervals or significance tests.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial numerical evidence. Table 2 reports DRPO-BT win rates of 57.5% against ORPO and 98.5% against IPO. Table 3 reports length-controlled win rates against SFT of 86.38% for DRPO-GPM and 92.16% for Dr. DPO. Table 4 adds 7B MSEs, including 0.000390 with both models correct at 3000 samples. Existing Figures 3–6 and qualitative results are unchanged.

M1.justification: The DR estimator, optimization objective and practical procedure remain unchanged, including importance-ratio clipping, Monte Carlo sampling, stop-gradient construction and KL regularization in Appendix B and Algorithm 1. Testing a larger model does not introduce a new method component.

P1.justification: Section 6 is reorganized and partly rewritten, the discussion is shortened, and limitations and broader impacts move to Appendix E. v2 also changes regret terminology to performance gap, corrects reversed DM/IS labels, and updates citation and author formatting. Most methodological and theoretical prose retains its original structure.

P2.justification: The document is extensively retypeset in NeurIPS format, changing typography, page geometry, author layout and float placement. Two main-text comparison tables and a 7B MSE table are added. Existing diagrams and plots are reused, while appendix tables are reflowed and renumbered.

R1.justification: v2 adds literature on noisy-preference optimization, multiple reference models, DR/OPE and the new evaluation benchmark. Section 5 explicitly positions its DPO analysis against bounds requiring linearity assumptions, while Appendix A.7 replaces an unresolved citation with rank-correlation references. The existing RLHF/DR positioning remains intact.

T1.justification: Appendix A.2 adds an explicit derivation of the reference-policy tangent space. Appendix A.5 inserts a missing coverage factor in an intermediate empirical-process bound. The principal assumptions, theorem statements and convergence rates otherwise remain unchanged apart from equivalent notation and renumbering.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses v1's narrow empirical comparison against PPO and DPO by adding relevant robust alternatives, explicit out-of-distribution testing and larger-model estimator validation. Table 3 also exposes limits to DRPO's comparative advantage, making the evidence more informative. The added win-rate tables lack uncertainty estimates and the main theory is largely unchanged, but the stronger comparative assessment constitutes a substantial overall improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DRPO research work. Their text, equations, figures, tables and appendices support reliable comparison despite substantial reformatting and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains these experiments and adds DPO-variant comparisons, out-of-distribution evaluation and 7B preference-estimation results in Tables 2–4.

before.justification: v1 reports original IMDb preference-estimation simulations and TL;DR/HH fine-tuning results, with temperature checks and qualitative examples in Appendix D.

results.title: Doubly Robust Alignment for Large Language Models

C1.justification: The abstract, introductory contributions, and conclusion retain the same central claims: distribution-aware embedding stability, an exact graph-filter characterization, a multilayer bound, structural interpretation, and task-agnostic attacks. The additional experiments support these claims without materially redefining them.

C2.justification: v4 explicitly explains that maximizing embedding disruption need not maximize misclassification, using Squirrel as evidence. It also cautiously suggests extending the analysis to MPNNs and discusses the efficiency-versus-optimality tradeoff of restricted greedy search. Earlier structural and depth-related interpretations remain.

D1.justification: Appendix C.2 newly specifies losses, Adam optimization, weight decay, training epochs, the 250-iteration PGD limit, and approximately ten-minute Cora attack times. v4 also clarifies the simplified GIN implementation and supplies technical details for the added experiments. The code URL and stated V100 hardware were already present in v1.

E1.justification: v4 retains the earlier datasets and adds Chameleon and Squirrel for heterophilic node classification, plus ogbn-arxiv, ogbn-mag, ogbn-products, and pokec for large-graph embedding attacks. This extends coverage to new graph populations, heterogeneous structure, and million-node environments.

E2.justification: Random and Wst-PGD remain the comparators in the existing experiments. Figure 5 adds a majority-class classifier reference, while Appendix C.8 evaluates a stochastic greedy version of the worst-case attack, Wst, alongside the new Prob approximation.

E3.justification: Appendix C.2 changes the reported node-classification learning rate from 0.001 to 0.01 and graph-classification hidden dimensions from 64 to {32,64}. Added experiments introduce deeper GIN configurations, H2GCN with specified heterophilic-data splits, and a 200-edge deletion protocol for large graphs. These are substantive reported setting changes and new evaluation protocols.

E4.justification: Appendix C.6 adds experiments varying the internal MLP depth of GIN to test applicability beyond the simplified convolutional architecture. Appendix C.8 adds computational scalability analysis with runtime and peak memory measurements. The earlier structural case study and five-layer depth/activation analyses are retained.

E5.justification: v1 reports downstream averages over five attack repetitions without dispersion in Table 1. v4 reports averages over ten pretrained models with plus-minus values and explicitly reports means and standard deviations for the H2GCN experiments. The existing 200 random-weight trials remain; this is not simply a five-to-ten increase in the same repetition count.

E6.justification: Table 1 is extensively revised: for example, MUTAG GCN accuracy after Prob-PGD changes from 0.29 to 42.89 ± 4.86%. Revised settings and aggregation prevent treating this as a same-setting performance improvement. Figures 2 and 5 also change, and Tables 5-7 add substantial results, including Squirrel's larger embedding disruption without the greatest accuracy degradation.

M1.justification: The original Prob-PGD objective and Algorithm 1 remain, but Appendix C.8 introduces a distinct scalable approximation, Prob. It samples candidate existing edges and greedily deletes the objective-maximizing edge at each iteration, substantially changing the search procedure and restricting attacks to deletions.

P1.justification: The main narrative and section structure remain largely intact. v4 locally rewrites experimental descriptions, expands implementation explanations, moves second-moment estimation from Appendix C.5 to C.3, and adds acknowledgments and revised author information. The new scientific sections do not constitute a wholesale language rewrite.

P2.justification: v4 adds the filter-reference Table 3 and experimental Tables 5-7; the earlier architecture table is retained as Table 4. Table 1 is redesigned for percentages and uncertainty, Figure 2 corrects the adjacency/Laplacian axis labels, and Figure 5 is redrawn with a majority-class reference. Existing appendix plots are consolidated and relocated.

R1.justification: v4 adds two Parada-Mayorga stability papers to related work and references supporting OGB datasets, H2GCN, and standard graph filters. The central positioning against worst-case stability analysis remains unchanged.

T1.justification: Remark 2 changes the permutation-alignment criterion from the unscripted spectral norm to the Frobenius norm. The principal stability theorems, assumptions, structural proposition, and proof arguments remain substantively unchanged; added standard filter and architecture formulas mainly expand exposition.

improvement.justification: v4 substantially strengthens empirical assessment and reproducibility: central downstream results gain model-level variability reporting, training details become more explicit, and new experiments examine deeper architectures, heterophily, and computational feasibility beyond small graphs. The Squirrel discussion also qualifies the connection between embedding disruption and classification failure. These address important reporting and validation gaps in v1. The scalability evidence concerns the greedy approximation, however, and does not establish scalability of the original full PGD procedure.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work and provide readable text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices. Retained material can be matched across section moves and renumbering.

after.justification: Original empirical results remain and are updated, with additional experiments on deeper GINs, heterophilic datasets, and large graphs in Appendices C.6-C.8.

before.justification: Section 5 and Appendix C report original simulations and adversarial-attack experiments, including embedding perturbations and downstream classification results.

results.title: On the Stability of Graph Convolutional Neural Networks: A Probabilistic Perspective

C1.justification: The main framework, efficiency, and modality-generality claims remain. V2 adds an explicit superiority claim for repository-level code completion and revises the headline RULER/BABILong gains from over 50%/27% to over 52%/34%. The underlying RULER/BABILong tables are unchanged, so these numerical revisions do not demonstrate improved method performance.

C2.justification: V2 adds substantive explanations linking pooling to contextual preservation, faster decoding to the smaller recomputed cache, and complementary heads to structural versus semantic retrieval. Section 5 newly discusses gathering reliability and redundant attention-score computation with Flash Attention. Appendices D.2 and E expand the interpretation of efficiency and head specialization beyond v1's narrower discussion.

D1.justification: V2 lists exact head/layer choices for both Qwen2.5-Coder models, discloses redundant attention-score matrix multiplication, estimates offline head-selection cost, and adds dataset/model license information. The previously specified Mistral, Qwen-7B, and Pixtral head choices and cache budgets remain unchanged.

E1.justification: V2 expands ∞-Bench from four English text tasks to ten, adding passkey, number and key-value retrieval, Chinese QA, code debugging, and mathematical finding. RepoEval adds repository-level API and line completion. These substantially broaden language, domain, and task coverage beyond the retained benchmarks.

E2.justification: V1 Figure 3 compares REFORM with H2O, InfiniPot, and InfLLM on NIAH; v2 retains only REFORM's heatmap and removes those comparisons. The principal benchmark and RAG comparator sets otherwise remain unchanged, and the added experiments use existing comparator methods.

E3.justification: New protocols include RepoEval with Qwen2.5-Coder 1.5B/7B, repository context excluding the target file, and edit-similarity scoring; Qwen2.5-32B evaluation; and separate prefill/decoding measurements on H200 with 200 generated tokens at 256k, 512k, and 1M contexts. The original H100, 10-token efficiency experiment remains, so these are additional settings rather than replacements.

E4.justification: V2 Table 6a adds sensitivity tests reducing the default 129-token pooling window to 5 and 17 tokens, testing the importance of preserving neighboring context. Appendix D.2 adds prefill/decoding and compress-plus-gather/recomputation latency breakdowns across context lengths. These materially extend the existing component and efficiency analyses; the original compression and head-selection ablations are retained.

E5.justification: V2 Table 8 specifies averaging over 20 runs for the new H200 latency measurements. The retained H100 experiment still reports averaging over 10 samples; this does not establish an increase in runs for that experiment. Neither version supplies confidence intervals, dispersion estimates, or significance tests.

E6.justification: V2 adds substantial benchmark, pooling, latency, and 32B-model results. For example, RepoEval 1.5B API completion scores 65.3 for REFORM versus 61.8 for InfLLM. The Mistral ∞-Bench average changes from 31.2 to 50.2 because coverage expands from four to ten tasks; all four shared task columns are unchanged. Matched RULER, BABILong, MM-NIAH, RAG, and H100 efficiency scores remain unchanged. NIAH baseline heatmaps and BABILong across-length averages are removed.

M1.justification: The compression, early exit, normalized head-embedding combination, similarity search, pooling, gathering, and KV recomputation procedure remains unchanged. The expanded head-selection explanation documents the existing procedure, and the code-model experiments apply it without introducing a new component.

P1.justification: V2 substantially reorganizes the narrative: Algorithm 1 moves to Appendix A, appendix ablations move into Section 4.5, and realistic-text, code, and multimodal evaluations are consolidated in Section 4.3. Introduction and method explanations are revised, and the supplementary material gains separate discussion, impacts, and licensing sections.

P2.justification: The main text changes from two-column to single-column presentation. RULER and BABILong tables are merged, RepoEval is combined with MM-NIAH, and ablation/efficiency tables become paired panels. Figure 3 shrinks from four comparator heatmaps to one, while new latency and larger-model tables extend the appendix displays.

R1.justification: V2 adds RepoCoder and literature connecting head selection to mechanistic interpretability, intermediate representations, and hybrid retrieval. The earlier text-embedding and Landmark Attention references disappear with edited passages. These extend the supporting rationale while retaining the central positioning against recurrent compression and random-access methods.

T1.justification: Appendix E.1 adds asymptotic reasoning under bounded chunk/query assumptions, assigning REFORM linear time and memory and contrasting recurrent and random-access baselines. The existing MNR definition and embedding-concatenation equation remain unchanged. Appendix E.2 supplies conceptual motivation for head selection, without a new theorem or proof.

improvement.justification: The broader realistic-task and larger-model evaluations substantially strengthen v1's evidence for general applicability. Pooling sensitivity and stage-specific latency measurements address previously untested aspects of gathering and computational cost, while new limitations and implementation disclosures improve transparency. These gains outweigh the loss of the NIAH baseline panels. The improvement rests on stronger validation and explanation, not the higher ∞-Bench average produced by changing task coverage.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same REFORM study. Their main text, appendices, equations, figures, tables, and algorithm descriptions are readable and support reliable comparison.

after.justification: V2 retains original empirical results and adds broader benchmark evaluation, code completion, pooling ablations, latency breakdowns, and larger-model experiments.

before.justification: V1 reports original retrieval, long-context benchmark, multimodal, ablation, embedding-head, and computational-efficiency experiments.

results.title: Compress, Gather, and Recompute: REFORMing Long-Context Processing in Transformers

C1.justification: Both versions claim that distilling anonymization and critique enables local self-refinement, competitive privacy–utility trade-offs against proprietary models, and continued gains beyond the training horizon. The dataset-release contribution remains in the introduction despite its removal from the abstract.

C2.justification: v2 interprets the new human and alternative-judge evaluations as supporting evaluator reliability. It qualifies latency comparisons because local and API infrastructure differ and explains the overhead of adversarial inference. Section 6 also proposes transfer to summarization and code generation without reporting experiments on those tasks.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code and implementation link, clarifies pseudocode initialization, and documents the latency setup. Conversely, Appendix D.5 removes the structured-output schema and its accompanying usage note. Existing training hyperparameters and most prompt and preprocessing details are retained.

E1.justification: Both versions use SynthPAI and the same main and hard evaluation sets covering eight personal attributes, including 500 synthesized hard examples. The added human ratings, judges, and model backbones evaluate retained task coverage.

E2.justification: The anonymization comparators remain Azure, Dipper, and adversarial anonymization using GPT-4o, GPT-4o mini, and Gemini 2.5 Flash. The added Mistral, Ministral, and Phi-3 models are SEAL backbones; Claude and Gemini are additional judges, not new competing anonymization methods.

E3.justification: v2 adds human evaluation with three raters and 100 samples, alternative-judge protocols, additional backbone configurations, and latency evaluation on 100 random samples comparing API GPT-4o with single-A6000 local inference. Sections 5.1/B.2 now specify GPT-4.1, whereas v1 specifies GPT-4 in the main text and GPT-4.1-mini in B.2. This changes the reported evaluator setting without establishing that retained results were rerun.

E4.justification: Section 5.3 adds human validation of utility judgments and robustness checks using Claude Sonnet 4 and Gemini 2.5 Flash. Appendix B.4 tests generality across additional architectures, and the latency analysis examines practical efficiency. The original training ablations and qualitative case studies remain.

E5.justification: v2 explicitly reports means and standard errors for the new latency measurements in Table 5. It adds no training-seed counts, repeated-training-run information, or significance tests for the central anonymization results.

E6.justification: Tables 1–3 and Figures 3–5 retain their results. v2 adds alternative-judge scores, human correlations of 0.717 and 0.814 and hallucination accuracy of 0.775, latency measurements, and additional-backbone results. Table 8 reports final overall scores of 0.374, 0.351, and 0.399 for Mistral, Ministral, and Phi-3 respectively. The new latency passage contains a discrepancy: GPT-4o with inference is 8.53 seconds in Table 5 but 8.57 seconds in the prose.

M1.justification: SEAL retains the same adversarial trajectory generation, three-task supervised training, DPO preference learning, and iterative self-refinement. Algorithm 1 makes initialization explicit and reorganizes equivalent trajectory-generation steps without establishing a different method.

P1.justification: Prose is extensively rewritten across the abstract, introduction, method exposition, results discussion, and explanatory appendices. Section 2 changes from Preliminaries to Related Work, terminology is standardized, and the document adds acknowledgments and conference information while retaining its broad section sequence.

P2.justification: v2 adds tables for alternative judges, latency, and additional backbones; enlarges Figure 1; and reformats Algorithm 1. The existing qualitative table moves to a dedicated page, and the boxed generation schema disappears. Most existing figures, table structures, and the overall visual format remain stable.

R1.justification: v2 adds Incognitext and explicitly contrasts it with SEAL's single-model generation-and-critique approach. It also adds Mistral and Phi-3 references and removes the GPT-4.1 announcement reference. Other bibliographic updates largely concern metadata rather than research positioning.

T1.justification: The privacy and utility definitions, training-pair conditions, SFT objective, DPO loss, and refinement formulation remain mathematically equivalent. The added explanation of DPO's beta parameter introduces no new derivation, assumption, theorem, or proof.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the credibility of the central evaluation through human validation of utility judgments and checks with two alternative LLM judges, addressing important gaps in v1's evidence. Additional backbone tests and measured latency better support generality and practical-efficiency arguments. The removed generation schema, unexplained evaluator-name change, and latency discrepancy limit reproducibility and precision, but the substantive validation gains outweigh these drawbacks.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SEAL study. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and Appendices A–D are readable and support a reliable comparison, including matching relocated and renumbered material.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds human evaluation, alternative-judge assessments, latency measurements, and experiments with additional model backbones.

before.justification: v1 reports original SynthPAI experiments, training ablations, model-scaling results, dataset-difficulty analyses, and anonymization examples.

results.title: Self-Refining Language Model Anonymizers via Adversarial Distillation

C1.justification: The principal shared-manifold, pullback-representation and efficient-approximation claims remain. The abstract and contribution list now claim validation across modalities, while the introduction drops v1's 'for the first time' novelty assertion concerning meaningful discriminative-model pullback metrics.

C2.justification: New Appendix A.2.2 qualifies the identical-manifold premise through bounded distortion, unrealistic identifiability assumptions, qualitatively different learned solutions and possible unions of manifolds. Added discussions address implementation-dependent runtime and limitations of multimodal augmentation. Conversely, v1's explicit warning about Diet's stronger constant-scaling and spherical assumptions is not retained.

D1.justification: v2 adds a project-code availability statement and repository link, explicitly specifies Adam for foundation-model heads, describes combining and subsampling anchors selected across models, and supplies detailed runtime information. Most architectural specifications, learning rates, batch sizes, training epochs and hardware disclosures were already present in v1.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates image-based retrieval and stitching. v2 adds Flickr30k vision–text retrieval using CLIP text encoders paired with different vision encoders (Section 4.2.3 and Appendix A.4.9), extending evaluation to a distinct modality and correspondence task. Earlier datasets remain covered.

E2.justification: Figure 3 and Section 4.1.1 add fitted linear and orthogonal mappings to the autoencoder retrieval comparison, which previously used only the relative-cosine baseline. Existing stitching comparisons and the principal vision comparator set are retained after matching the Pullback/L2 rename.

E3.justification: v2 introduces fixed-text-encoder multimodal comparisons without augmentation, farthest-point and k-means anchor-selection controls, and timed training and representation-generation experiments. Appendix A.3.7 also specifies an ImageNet train/validation/test subdivision of the original validation set, superseding v1's generic split description. This is a reported protocol revision; the PDFs do not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: New analyses test sensitivity to anchor-selection strategy (Figures 20–21), runtime–accuracy tradeoffs (Appendix A.4.10), and the effects of Fisher–Rao geometry on classification versus retrieval (A.4.11). Earlier analyses of anchor counts, Diet points, discretization steps and augmentation strengths are retained rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: The new checklist explicitly identifies table summaries as means and standard deviations, and A.4.10 explains cross-model uncertainty aggregation for decoder timings. The previously reported five anchor draws, five autoencoder training seeds and three stitching heads remain unchanged; no increase in repeated runs or new significance-testing procedure is established.

E6.justification: Matched aggregate results in Tables 1–2 and the earlier appendix tables are unchanged. v2 adds baseline curves, further pairwise MRR entries, anchor-selection results, timings and Fisher results. New Flickr30k comparisons report RelGeo(Diet) symmetric cosine MRR of 0.08–0.11 versus 0.01–0.03 for Rel(Cosine) in Figure 6. These are additional results, not improvements to the retained experiments.

M1.justification: The core straight-line algorithm, Diet objective and decoder architectures remain intact; RelGeo(Pullback) is renamed RelGeo(L2). Appendix A.4.11 additionally instantiates the previously discussed Fisher approach as RelGeo(Fisher), pulling the Fisher–Rao metric back from output probabilities. This is a limited metric variant within the existing framework.

P1.justification: v2 substantially rewrites the metric-choice explanation, moves and expands Diet background into the appendix, and combines the former separate experiment sections under a unified task-oriented structure. The appendix is reorganized into proofs, explanations, implementation details and results, followed by a new checklist. Terminology and citation formatting are also standardized.

P2.justification: v2 adds multimodal, anchor-selection and Fisher displays plus runtime tables, and expands dataset heatmaps from two to five metric rows. Figure 3 gains baseline curves, and energy plots gain clearer labels. Figure 5 replaces its mismatched MRR display with cosine-MRR values already shown in v1's Figure 13; this is a corrected display, not new performance evidence.

R1.justification: The new explanations substantially expand positioning around linear and approximate identifiability, citing Roeder, Nielsen and Syrota, and alternative accounts of learned representations through Brown and Pascanu. Nonlinear ICA and multimodal references are also added. Earlier alignment and geometry literature is retained; merged duplicate references are bibliographic cleanup rather than substantive removals.

T1.justification: Proposition 3.1 expands from curve-length invariance to also address manifold-coordinate invariance of length and energy. Appendix A.1 adds proof sections for the proposition and the distance–length–energy bound, which v1 stated without proofs. A.2.1 also makes the Diet generative assumptions more explicit, substantially expanding the formal treatment.

improvement.justification: The strongest gains are in validation and transparency: direct-alignment baselines strengthen the retrieval comparison, runtime measurements make efficiency tradeoffs assessable, and Fisher and anchor-selection experiments test consequential design choices. Flickr30k establishes additional applicability, while code-access information aids reproducibility. The new A.1.2 derivation contains length-versus-squared-length errors, and the explicit Diet scaling caveat is lost, but these shortcomings do not outweigh the substantial improvement in empirical support and practical assessability.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same relative geodesic representation framework. Their text, equations, figures, tables and complete appendices are readable and support reliable matching despite substantial expansion and reorganization in v2.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds multimodal retrieval, additional baseline comparisons, anchor-selection experiments, runtime measurements and Fisher-metric evaluations.

before.justification: v1 reports original geodesic-approximation, autoencoder retrieval and stitching experiments, vision-foundation-model comparisons, and appendix sensitivity studies.

results.title: Connecting Neural Models Latent Geometries with Relative Geodesic Representations

C1.justification: The PPAD-completeness headline is retained, but the computational problem referenced by the main contribution now requires stability only against exactly safe deviations, rather than all ν-safe deviations. This substantively redefines the central guarantee. Section 1.1 also adds an explicit impossibility claim for general efficient no-regret convergence and its application to black-box autobidding.

C2.justification: The added discussion in Section 1.1 explains why equilibrium convergence matters for advertising platforms and argues that convergence guarantees must exploit application-specific structure. The existing interpretation of correlation versus coupled constraints and the open question about constant approximations remain.

D1.justification: Neither version supplies software implementation settings, hardware information, experimental processing instructions, or code/data access information. The added construction and normalization details concern mathematical proofs.

E1.justification: Neither version evaluates datasets or experimental tasks. The expanded discussion of Internet advertising introduces application context, not an evaluated domain.

E2.justification: Neither version empirically evaluates comparison methods. References to equilibrium algorithms and additional cited work are theoretical context, not evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: Neither version contains an experimental evaluation protocol. Changes to approximation parameters concern mathematical reductions, not evaluation settings.

E4.justification: Neither version reports ablations, robustness tests, sensitivity experiments, or empirical case studies. Figure 1 and Appendix A retain their illustrative theoretical examples.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated experimental runs, seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests, or statistical uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: There are no empirical result entries, performance rankings, or measured numerical outcomes in either version. Revised theoretical guarantees and bounds are assessed under T1.

M1.justification: The reduction strategies remain the same, but the membership construction changes: Section 4 removes the identity blocks and corresponding zero entries from A and b, and Claim 4.5 revises the internal approximation parameters. These are localized changes to the computational reduction.

P1.justification: v2 adds a focused introductory discussion, reorganizes Claim 4.5's proof into three named steps, adds a normalization footnote and acknowledgment, and makes small wording and cross-reference edits. The overall section and appendix organization is retained.

P2.justification: Figure 1 and its caption are unchanged, but its placement relative to the surrounding argument shifts. The Appendix C.1 matrix display becomes shorter after block removal, and the expanded proof changes equation placement and page layout. There are no new figures or tables.

R1.justification: v2 adds Hart and Mas-Colell (2000), Agarwal et al. (2014), Balseiro et al. (2021), and Paes Leme et al. (2024) to support the learning and autobidding discussion. It also adds Ni et al. (2025) to the discussion of equilibrium existence without strict feasibility. The central positioning against earlier complexity results remains.

T1.justification: Sections 2.2–3 change admissible deviations from cost at most ν to cost at most zero, while allowing the equilibrium distribution itself cost at most ν. Lemma 3.3 and Equation (2) consequently require deviating marginals to match exactly. Section 4 and Appendix C revise the constraint correspondence, and Claim 4.5 receives new tolerance choices and a substantially rewritten proof of safety, deviation simulation, and equilibrium conditions. These changes alter the formal problem and its membership argument.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the central membership argument. It removes v1's identity-block constraints, which imposed nonpositive coordinates alongside a unit-sum requirement, and replaces the unsupported deviation-simulation step with an explicit derivation and revised error bounds in Appendix C.2. The material tradeoff is that this argument establishes the revised, weaker incentive condition against exactly safe deviations, rather than v1's claimed guarantee against all ν-safe deviations.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work, The Complexity of Correlated Equilibria in Generalized Games. All pages, including Appendices A–C, are readable; the equations and illustrative figure support a reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 remains entirely theoretical, including its appendices. The added autobidding discussion reports no original empirical results.

before.justification: v1 presents complexity reductions, mathematical proofs, and illustrative constructions, but no original experimental, simulation, or data-analysis results.

results.title: The Complexity of Correlated Equilibria in Generalized Games

C1.justification: The central SD-truthfulness, partition-rounding, and binary-EA contributions remain. Practical applicability is narrowed: tournaments used as a motivating application in v1 are replaced by threshold rewards, and v2's conclusion explicitly leaves tournament incentive guarantees unresolved.

C2.justification: V2 explicitly explains that correlated scores can let a dominated reporting strategy improve tournament rank, correcting v1's interpretation that SD-truthfulness supports tournament payments. It also adds a variance-control explanation for EA. Conversely, it removes v1's warning that optimal enforcement may overfit the simplified effort model.

D1.justification: V2 adds an experimental-code repository link, specifies the sensitivity simulation count, and documents threshold calibration and evaluation. However, v1 Appendix C.1's prior-sweep joint-distribution matrix and 0.01 step size disappear. The dataset information-structure parameters remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Both versions use binary compound-synthesis judgments and four-class tweet sentiment, with the same crowdsourcing-derived information structures. Prior sweeps, task-count sweeps, and multi-agent effort elicitation remain; reward functions and target effort values change within this coverage.

E2.justification: OA, PTS, CA, MA, and their existing partitioned or rounded variants remain in the comparisons. Original implementations move into Appendix E.2. The budgetary-efficiency plots retain the same six mechanism variants and optimal-linear-payment reference.

E3.justification: Section 7.3 replaces winner-take-all and Borda-count tournaments with fixed-threshold bonuses. Target efforts change from 0.7 and 0.9 to 0.6, 0.7, 0.8, and 0.9. V2 splits 10,000 simulations equally between estimating a 75th-percentile threshold and evaluating payments, substantially revising the payment-evaluation protocol.

E4.justification: The practical robustness check linking sensitivity to budgetary efficiency is substantially revised: tournament-based validation is replaced by threshold-payment validation across four effort levels. Enforcement-choice, prior-sensitivity, and task-count analyses remain. Appendix E.2 reorganizes the existing original-versus-rounded comparison rather than introducing a new ablation.

E5.justification: Section 7.1 newly specifies 20,000 independent Monte Carlo score samples, where v1 specified only T repetitions. This discloses a count without establishing an increase in runs. Neither version reports confidence intervals, significance tests, or seed-based variability.

E6.justification: V1 Figure 3's tournament-payment outcomes are replaced by v2 Figure 2's threshold-payment outcomes at four effort levels. EA-prior remains the lowest-payment mechanism among those plotted. These are substantially replaced results under different reward conditions, not evidence of a same-setting performance gain.

M1.justification: Direct rounding, partition rounding, and EA's enforced distributions, report flipping, and agreement scoring are retained. The general-signal integer-programming enforcement and optimal-enforcement rule move to Appendix C. Changed payment schemes concern the effort-elicitation evaluation.

P1.justification: The abstract and substantial portions of the introduction, model exposition, and mechanism discussion are rewritten and condensed. Sensitivity derivations, non-binary EA, optimal enforcement, and proofs are reorganized into Appendices A–F. Broader Impact and Acknowledgment sections are added.

P2.justification: V2 adopts a conference template with substantially different typography and title layout. Sensitivity plots are merged into a three-panel main figure and separated into four appendix panels; tournament plots are replaced by threshold-payment panels. Table 1 and plot legends are reformatted.

R1.justification: Appendix A adds focused comparisons with mutual-information mechanisms that v1 placed beyond detailed discussion. The Lu et al. (2024) citation is removed. The main research positioning and attribution of binary rounding to Miller et al. (2005) remain.

T1.justification: New Appendix A supplies explicit failure arguments for f-mutual-information, determinant-mutual-information, and pairing mechanisms, extending v1's largely intuitive discussion. The central rounding, binary and three-signal EA, optimal-enforcement, and MA results and proofs are retained after relocation.

improvement.justification: V2 resolves an important validity problem in v1's practical argument: SD-truthfulness was treated as sufficient for tournament incentives. Section 8 explains the correlated-score limitation, and Section 7.3 replaces tournaments with fixed-threshold rewards calibrated and evaluated on separate samples. This substantially improves alignment between the theoretical guarantee and experimental application, outweighing the loss of prior-sweep documentation and the optimal-enforcement caveat.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SD-truthfulness, rounding, and enforced-agreement study. Their main text, equations, figures, table, and appendices are readable and support comparison, including matching extensively relocated material.

after.justification: Section 7 and Appendix E retain original sensitivity evaluations and report budgetary-efficiency simulations with threshold payments.

before.justification: Section 7 reports original sensitivity and budgetary-efficiency simulations using information structures estimated from crowdsourcing datasets.

results.title: Stochastically Dominant Peer Prediction

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the same central contributions: joint generative shape-and-material estimation, multimodal interpretations of ambiguous static inputs, and disambiguation through differential motion. Revised wording and additional experiments support these existing claims.

C2.justification: V1 emphasizes restricted rotation axes and isolated objects. V2 explains generalization through local attention and training-shape diversity, recognizes multiple objects sharing rigid motion, and specifies failures involving deformation, distinct motions, transparency and translucency. It also explicitly identifies foreground segmentation as a requirement. These materially revise the stated applicability boundaries and mechanism explanations.

D1.justification: V2 newly documents foreground segmentation and background masking, describes multi-object and self-occluding training assets, and supplies FP32 model-size and GPU-memory information. It also provides a concrete project-page URL where v1 only mentions a website. The detailed architecture hyperparameters and training recipe remain unchanged.

E1.justification: V2 adds Stanford-ORB evaluation with moving-camera observations and systematic tests of random-axis rotations and random translations. These substantially broaden the tested motion and observation conditions. The synthetic training coverage, DiLiGent and MIT-Intrinsic benchmarks remain.

E2.justification: Table 1 adds Marigold–Albedo to the MIT-Intrinsic comparison. Figure 8 adds DiffusionRenderer to the real-video comparison, which previously compared against RGB-X alone. Adding a directly relevant video-based inverse-rendering comparator substantially strengthens comparison on the central motion task.

E3.justification: Existing training and Tables 1–2 protocols remain. New protocols include a controlled 174-object comparison across three motion conditions, six-scene Stanford-ORB evaluation using three nearby views, IID mean-prediction versus best-three evaluation with LPIPS, and FP32 resource profiling on one A100. These substantially expand evaluation design without establishing changes to the retained experiments.

E4.justification: New analyses test generalization to unfamiliar rotations and translations (A.7), sensitivity to IID prediction aggregation (A.5), and computational resource requirements (A.10). The original architectural and motion ablations, normal-estimation probing, and temporal-consistency discussion are retained, including relocated material.

E5.justification: Both versions retain ten stochastic predictions for the principal benchmark evaluations and 100-sample ambiguity visualizations. Neither adds training-seed replication, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. The new IID aggregation comparison concerns evaluation accuracy rather than uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: All retained entries in Tables 1–2 are unchanged. V2 adds Marigold–Albedo results of 0.72 SSIM, 0.11 RMSE and 19.86 PSNR, plus Tables 3–7. For example, Table 6 reports mean angular errors of 12.267, 15.062 and 16.652 for vertical-axis rotation, random rotation and random translation. Figure 8 expands qualitative comparisons, and Figure 4 replaces several predicted normal maps. These are additional or revised results, without evidence of improved scores on the retained evaluations.

M1.justification: The joint U-ViT3D-Mixer architecture, local spatial and temporal attention, channel mixers, attribute loss weights and DDIM inference remain unchanged. Appendix A.4's temporal-consistency guidance already appears in v1; its rewritten explanation does not establish a new procedure.

P1.justification: The introduction is substantially rewritten and reordered to present ambiguity before motion. Explanatory passages and the conclusion are revised, limitations move into Section 4.3, and the appendix is reorganized, including moving the probing experiment from A.6 to A.2 and separating appendix references. This is substantial editorial restructuring beyond the added experiments.

P2.justification: V1's combined Figure 7 becomes a retained ambiguity figure and an expanded real-video comparison in v2's Figure 8. V2 adds five tables, enlarges the main tables, refreshes some Figure 4 samples, and relocates the probing figure. The original appendix ablation figure survives as Figure 10. These substantially expand and reorganize the visual presentation.

R1.justification: V2 adds references to DiffusionRenderer, Stable Video Diffusion, the newer Marigold work and Stanford-ORB. It contrasts joint inference with DiffusionRenderer's attribute-conditioned outputs and removes Section 4.2's assertion that no joint video baselines exist. The broader positioning remains stable; most appendix references are relocated rather than newly added.

T1.justification: The formal imaging assumptions, diffusion equations and appendix reflectance formulation remain substantively unchanged, including Equations 1–14. Explicitly including the frame dimension in material-map notation clarifies the existing time-varying representation. No new theorem, proof or derivation is introduced.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens validation of the central motion-based perception claim through a relevant video comparator, quantitative captured camera-motion evaluation, and controlled unfamiliar-motion tests. These address v1's explicitly unresolved motion-generalization limitations. The IID protocol check and more precise applicability boundaries further improve transparency. The new evidence is mixed—Stanford-ORB shape error beats Marigold-e2e-ft on only two of six objects—and statistical uncertainty remains unreported, but the expanded validation provides a substantial overall quality gain.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same U-ViT3D-Mixer research work. Their complete main texts and appendices, including equations, figures and tables, are readable and support matching across revisions and relocations.

after.justification: V2 retains these original experiments and adds baseline comparisons, Stanford-ORB evaluation, motion-generalization tests, an IID evaluation-protocol comparison, and inference-resource measurements.

before.justification: V1 reports original shape and albedo benchmark results, architectural and motion ablations, ambiguity experiments, and an appendix probing experiment.

results.title: Generative Perception of Shape and Material from Differential Motion

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, and conclusion replace the claim that trajectory adjustment recovers rare or atypical modes with guidance toward posterior-likely, observation-consistent images. This qualifies one advertised contribution while retaining the framework's novelty, hard-consistency, calibration, reconstruction-quality, and diversity claims.

C2.justification: V2 interprets ensemble PSNR gains as evidence that samples surround the posterior mean and discusses broader pixel-space applicability and speed-quality tradeoffs. Existing limitations and failure explanations remain. The new ensemble interpretation overstates Table 7: FLAIR's LPIPS increases with averaging despite prose saying it decreases, and its PSNR gain is not consistently the largest.

D1.justification: V2 adds a stated source-code access link in the abstract, tuned likelihood weights and a regularizer scale for pixel-space experiments, runtime/memory measurements, and explicit pFID patch counts. The existing detailed SD3 implementation, hardware, preprocessing, and default optimization disclosures are largely retained. The linked resource itself was not inspected.

E1.justification: V2 adds CelebA-HQ through a pretrained pixel-space flow model and evaluation on 1,000 images for inpainting and ×8 super-resolution (Section 5.2, Appendix A.9). This extends dataset coverage within the existing face-restoration domain; the FFHQ/DIV2K tasks and editing examples remain.

E2.justification: The original ReSample, FlowDPS, RSD, and FlowChef comparisons remain. V2 adds an evaluated pixel-space comparison suite containing DDNM, DPS, Moment Matching, and ΠGDM (main Table 2, Appendix Table 5). Their earlier citation or use as implementation references did not constitute these comparisons.

E3.justification: V2 adds evaluation with a 256×256 pixel-space backbone, runtime comparisons using different VAEs/data-step budgets, eight-prediction ensembles, and smaller-subset statistical experiments. Appendix A.5 changes FlowChef inpainting from 50 to 200 NFE despite the retained equal-budget statement. Main Table 1 changes the noise label from 0.01 to 0.5%, while appendix tables retain 0.01; these reporting revisions do not establish that existing experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: New Appendix A.10 tests the speed, memory, and reconstruction-quality effects of a tiny VAE and at most five data-term steps. A.11 compares individual predictions with eight-sample averages to investigate posterior-mean estimation and perceptual tradeoffs. Existing component, weighting, captioning, posterior-variance, and failure-case analyses are retained.

E5.justification: V1 already reports sample-wise standard deviations and 32-sample posterior variability. V2 additionally reports three reconstructions per input on 100 FFHQ and 80 DIV2K images, standard deviations of aggregate metrics including FID, matched random seeds, and paired LPIPS t-tests against FlowDPS (Appendix A.12, Tables 8–16). This adds distinct uncertainty and significance assessments.

E6.justification: V2 adds pixel-space, runtime, ensemble, and repeated-reconstruction results. It also revises baseline FID entries: for DIV2K ×8 super-resolution, FlowDPS changes from 54.2 to 44.4 and FlowChef from 48.6 to 36.5. FLAIR's main Table 1 values and original component-ablation values remain unchanged. The new experiments have separate settings and do not establish improvements over v1's FLAIR scores.

M1.justification: Section 4 and Algorithm 1 retain the flow-matching objective, deterministic trajectory adjustment, calibrated weighting, and alternating regularization/data-consistency updates. Initialization notation is generalized. The pixel-space, smaller-VAE, step-budget, and ensemble experiments extend configurations and analyses without establishing a new core solver component.

P1.justification: V2 locally rewrites the abstract and contribution statements, clarifies initialization and terminology, corrects some notation and language, adds acknowledgments, and inserts new appendix subsections. The main section order and most existing explanatory prose remain intact; this is not an extensive narrative reorganization.

P2.justification: V2 adds a pixel-space comparison table and figure, displayed in both the main text and appendix, plus runtime, ensemble, repeated-reconstruction, and significance tables. Existing main-text displays are repositioned and some labels reformatted; appendix numbering restarts. The original qualitative and failure galleries are retained. These additions substantially expand the visual presentation.

R1.justification: Seven cited works are added, covering mixture guidance, divide-and-conquer sampling, midpoint guidance, decoupled noise annealing, the Moment Matching reference, and multimodal image fusion. These extend citations and support the new comparison, while Section 2's central positioning relative to variational posterior sampling remains largely unchanged.

T1.justification: The propositions and Appendix A.1–A.3 derivations are substantially retained. V2 makes time averaging explicit in gradient expressions and adds weighted-gradient Equation 10. As printed, that equation weights only the learned velocity, whereas Algorithm 1 weights the entire velocity difference, introducing a localized mathematical inconsistency.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially improves empirical assessability: the additional pixel-space prior and four comparators test applicability beyond the original latent implementation, repeated reconstructions address stochastic reliability, and runtime/memory analysis exposes previously unreported practical costs. These resolve important validation gaps in v1. The gains are tempered by conflicting noise/NFE descriptions, the new gradient-expression inconsistency, and ensemble claims that contradict Table 7, but the added evidence still provides a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Solving Inverse Problems with FLAIR. Their complete main texts, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support reliable matching across the revision.

after.justification: V2 retains those empirical results and adds pixel-space comparisons, runtime and memory measurements, ensemble experiments, and repeated-reconstruction statistical evaluations.

before.justification: V1 reports original reconstruction experiments on FFHQ and DIV2K, component ablations, posterior-variance measurements, image editing, and appendix analyses.

results.title: Solving Inverse Problems with FLAIR

C1.justification: The central claims about generating MIs from UDFs, extending local signs into global labels, and reconstructing non-manifold meshes are retained. The introduction nevertheless narrows the earlier open-surface statement to support for 'certain open non-manifold surfaces,' qualifying applicability without redefining the contribution.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive applicability limits: alpha-expansion is costly, erosion can eliminate small or thin regions, and non-orientable surfaces can lack a suitable MI. Appendix A explains how sampling and envelope choices cause holes, reconstruction failure, or incorrect merging. These materially qualify v1's robustness discussion.

D1.justification: The abstract adds a project source-code link. v2 also makes background-label handling explicit, supplies parameter-sweep values, and clarifies NU-NeRF input provenance as author-provided SDFs. The principal implementation details, including V100 hardware and 200 refinement iterations, were already reported in v1.

E1.justification: The original benchmarks and reconstruction tasks remain. Appendix B substantially broadens qualitative coverage to indoor scenes, medical data, and additional detailed objects in Figure 16, while Appendix C explicitly tests a non-orientable surface. Additional examples within the existing point-cloud, multi-view, and medial-axis settings also appear.

E2.justification: DCUDF and DMUDF remain the quantitative and point-cloud comparators. The multi-view comparisons retain NU-NeRF or NeUDF's extraction alongside DCUDF. Appendix comparisons use these same methods; deleting the conceptual representation table does not remove an evaluated baseline.

E3.justification: The original normalization, 256^3 grid, 100K-point Chamfer evaluation, and refinement budget are retained. Appendix A introduces sensitivity protocols varying downsampling voxel size from 0.002 to 0.01, r1 from 0.03 to 0.1, and r2 from 0.0025 to 0.02. These are additional experimental settings, not revisions to the original benchmark protocol.

E4.justification: v2 adds a before-and-after refinement comparison in Figure 4, three parameter sensitivity studies in Appendix A, an erosion-induced missing-facet analysis in Figure 10, and a non-orientable failure case in Appendix C. These substantially expand diagnostic evidence beyond v1's comparisons and retained Laplacian illustration.

E5.justification: v1 Table 2 reports single scores; v2 Table 1 adds medians and standard deviations alongside the unchanged means. This introduces dispersion reporting, but no repeated-run counts, seeds, or explanation of the population summarized by the standard deviations is supplied. Additional runs cannot be inferred.

E6.justification: All six original benchmark scores and their ranking are retained as means, including MIND's 2.917 on ShapeNet-Car and 1.770 on DeepFashion3D. v2 substantially extends the findings with median/std entries, refinement outputs, sensitivity outcomes such as failure at r1 = 0.03, explicit failure cases, and additional qualitative reconstructions. These are added findings, not improved scores under the original settings.

M1.justification: The local side field, erosion and alpha-expansion labeling, region merging, modified M3C extraction, and UDF/Laplacian refinement remain unchanged. v2 clarifies existing envelope and background handling; blockwise labeling and dilation are suggested alternatives, not implemented method changes.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main section order are retained. Local corrections and expanded explanations accompany a new limitations paragraph, Appendices A–C, funding acknowledgments, and publication/corresponding-author updates. This extends the document without extensive rewriting of its existing narrative.

P2.justification: v2 removes the conceptual representation table, restructures the numerical table into Mean/Median/Std columns, annotates introductory diagrams, and adds refinement, sensitivity, failure, and reconstruction figures. Original Figures 4–8 remain as Figures 5–9; some appendix views reuse existing cases with close-ups rather than supplying wholly new results.

R1.justification: v2 adds citations to Hu et al.'s local-shape UDF framework, Du et al.'s implicit surface networks, and Kong et al.'s Voronoi-assisted UDF diffusion. The related-work organization and central positioning remain largely intact. DCUDF2's publication update and reference renumbering do not constitute additional research comparisons.

T1.justification: Equations (1)–(4) and their mathematical formulation are unchanged. Appendix C/Figure 17 adds a geometric counterexample and topological argument: a surface allowing traversal between opposite sides without crossing a boundary cannot support the required distinct MI labeling. No general proof is added.

improvement.justification: v1 makes broad robustness claims without parameter studies or concrete failure analyses. v2 substantially improves their assessability through sensitivity tests, explanations of erosion failures, and an explicit non-orientability boundary, supported by clearer implementation guidance and code-access information. The gains concern validation and transparency, not higher benchmark means. Reporting remains imperfect: the expanded table drops the earlier 10^-3 scale label and leaves the standard deviations' basis unspecified, but these weaknesses do not outweigh the substantive improvements.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MIND research, with readable text, equations, tables, and figures. v1 ends with references; v2 additionally contains Appendices A–C, which are included in this comparison.

after.justification: Section 4 retains the original empirical results, while Appendices A–C add parameter studies, reconstruction examples, and failure cases.

before.justification: Section 4 reports original reconstruction experiments, including Chamfer distances in Table 2 and qualitative comparisons for point clouds, multi-view images, and medial axes.

results.title: MIND: Material Interface Generation from UDFs for Non-Manifold Surface Reconstruction

C1.justification: The introduction removes explicit claims of improved V1 predictivity and maintained similar clean accuracy, and highlights back-end generalization. The abstract updates the reported robustness margins from 8.5% to 9.3% and from 7.3% to 6.2% with PRIME. The central contributions of biologically constrained front-ends, improved alignment and robustness, and complementary augmentation gains remain.

C2.justification: The expanded ablations substantially revise component interpretations: M cells and contrast normalization support neural alignment despite limited robustness effects, while removing VOneBlock largely preserves aggregate robustness. v2 adds explanations involving filtering, local competition, and ensemble suppression of useful stochasticity. It removes the earlier interpretation of reduced mean adversarial robustness and newly discusses light-adaptation instability without contrast normalization and possible task-driven front-end fine-tuning.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code-and-model-weights link, optimized parameters and kernel sizes in Table E2, per-variant calibration details, and explicit skip-connection and contrast-normalization-ablation implementations. Appendix A also documents additional back-end integration details. These substantially extend v1's search bounds and training information, although Table E2 reports a P-cell optimum of −0.12 outside its stated search interval.

E1.justification: Both versions use ImageNet-1k, ImageNet-C, the same five domain-shift datasets, cue-conflict images, BrainScore benchmarks, and grating-based response evaluations. Additional architectures, ablations, and inference procedures reuse this coverage. The added empirical V1 curves illustrate published responses rather than introduce a new evaluation dataset.

E2.justification: v2 adds VOneResNet50+PRIME to the main robustness comparison in Table 5 and CORnet-Z as a base-model comparator in Appendix D.2. The existing ResNet50, VOneResNet50, EfficientNet-B0, PRIME-trained ResNet50, and adversarial-training comparisons are retained.

E3.justification: PGD changes from 16 to 64 iterations, step size from budget/8 to budget/32, and gradient samples from 32 to 10. New variant and back-end adversarial evaluations use six attacks. Appendix E also changes the reported EfficientNet optimizer from SGD to RMSProp and maximum learning rate from 0.1 to 0.256. Exact stronger L2 budgets remain unresolved: v2 Table 4 lists 2.4 and 9.6, while its prose retains 1.2 and 2.4.

E4.justification: The four original component ablations expand to include P-cell and VOneBlock removal and an LGN–V2 connection variant, with new neural-alignment and adversarial analyses (Table 6 and Appendix D.1). v2 adds PGD-iteration convergence controls, revises gradient-sampling sensitivity tests, extends back-end generalization, and tests ensemble size and aggregation location.

E5.justification: Main adversarial and aggregate tables change their reported seed counts from two to three. Table 5 newly supplies mean±SD for ResNet50+PRIME, previously shown without uncertainty. Mean±SD remains the established reporting practice; no confidence intervals or significance-testing framework is added.

E6.justification: Results change throughout the paper. Table 1 reports EVResNet50 V1 predictivity changing from 0.379 to 0.364, response-property alignment from 0.808 to 0.826, and shape bias from 46.3% to 48.9%; Table 2 clean accuracy changes from 71.7% to 70.4%. Under the respective attack protocols, EVNet/VOneNet adversarial means change from 25.9/26.6% to 28.3/26.1%, reversing their ranking. Numerous variant, back-end, and ensemble results are added. These are revised-method or revised-protocol results, not controlled cross-version performance gains.

M1.justification: Section 2.1 replaces the parameterized Naka–Rushton light-adaptation function with (x − xbar)/xbar, substantively changing a central front-end computation. v2 also introduces an LGN–V2 skip-connection variant and multiple-pass activation-aggregation procedures in Appendices D.3 and E.3. The overall SubcorticalBlock–VOneBlock architecture remains.

P1.justification: There are targeted edits to the abstract, contributions, results, and discussion; Section 3.4 is refocused on EVNet variants, and Appendices B and E gain more explicit subsections. Affiliations, contact information, and the conference header change. The overall organization and substantial portions of the explanatory prose remain.

P2.justification: v2 adds Table 6 and figures for empirical V1 curves, PGD convergence, and inference ensembling. The four-category corruption plot becomes a 15-corruption display including PRIME variants. Figure 1's light-adaptation schematic is redrawn, tuning plots are revised, and appendix tables expand to display additional variants, architectures, and optimized parameters.

R1.justification: Section 1.1 adds a focused discussion of subcortical ideas in edge detection, Retinex, multiscale representations, and modern CNNs. The discussion adds the Bitter Lesson and neural-scaling literature and sharpens positioning around separate P/M pathways. The principal VOneNet-centered research positioning remains.

T1.justification: Equation 2 substantively revises the mathematical definition of light adaptation and removes its exponent and centering-bias parameters. The DoG and contrast-normalization definitions, push-pull identity and assumptions, and Bayesian tuning objective remain. No new theorem or proof is introduced.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens evidence that was limited in v1: PGD convergence controls better support the adversarial evaluation, the VOneNet+PRIME comparator tests the incremental contribution more directly, and expanded ablations distinguish contributors to neural alignment and robustness. Parameter disclosures and the code/weights link improve reproducibility information, while narrowed claims acknowledge performance tradeoffs. These gains outweigh unresolved reporting problems, particularly the conflicting L2 budgets and the out-of-range optimum in Table E2.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same EVNet research work. Their complete main texts and Appendices A–E are readable, and visual inspection supports comparison of equations, figures, and tables. Some reporting inconsistencies limit individual numerical comparisons but do not prevent comparison of the revisions.

after.justification: v2 reports original results across the retained evaluations, with additional component studies, adversarial controls, CORnet-Z experiments, and inference-ensembling analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original neural-alignment, shape-bias, image-classification, robustness, ablation, and EfficientNet generalization results in the main text and appendices.

results.title: Explicitly Modeling Subcortical Vision with a Neuro-Inspired Front-End Improves CNN Robustness

C1.justification: The main abstract and introduction claims remain stable. The revised conclusion explicitly extends potential applicability beyond CLIP to any text encoder, citing BERT, and strengthens clean-performance wording to 'intact' despite reported clean-performance losses.

C2.justification: v1 explicitly leaves attacks on both modalities unstudied; v2 discusses its sequential bimodal evaluation and instead identifies joint training as a possible improvement. It also establishes a token-level robustness limitation, discusses weak typographic robustness, and adds a tokenization-based interpretation of FLUX's woman/woma failure.

D1.justification: Table 6 adds the FLUX.1-dev checkpoint source. Appendix D.3 documents its encoder-access restriction and generation resolution, while Table 13 clarifies that retained SD-1.5/SDXL COCO results use all 5,000 validation images. Existing LEAF hyperparameters, hardware descriptions and code/model access information remain.

E1.justification: v2 adds VTAB evaluation covering natural, specialized and structured tasks. It also introduces distinct testing scenarios involving combined image-and-text perturbations, token-level attacks and systematic typographic substitutions, substantially extending v1's evaluated coverage.

E2.justification: New retrieval Table 25 separately compares Original, vision-only robust FARE and LEAF; v1's retrieval tables compare original and bimodally robust models. New BERT Table 27 includes TextGrad alongside Original and Charmer reference results explicitly imported from earlier work. Existing main comparison sets are retained.

E3.justification: Added protocols include FLUX.1-dev evaluation on 100 COCO images with only its CLIP encoder attacked, and retrieval attacks applying 100-step APGD at 2/255 and 4/255 after k=1 text perturbations. v2 also introduces BERT-base training on SST-2 and transfer-attack source/target configurations. Retained experiments keep their stated settings.

E4.justification: v2 adds transferability analysis, typographic stress testing, bimodal retrieval attacks, TextFooler evaluations and the FLUX woman/woma case study. These substantially broaden robustness and failure analysis. The existing hyperparameter, embedding-collapse and adversarial-loss ablations are retained rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: Figure 7 specifies ten generation seeds for the new FLUX case study, and Table 27 adds a five-training-run averaging statement. The earlier three-seed experiment and existing plus/minus reporting remain. These additions do not establish increased run counts for retained experiments.

E6.justification: Main Tables 1–4 retain their values, but substantial new results appear. Table 25 reports LEAF recall@1 of 43.4/42.8 versus FARE's 36.6/35.8 under the two bimodal attack radii. Table 28 reports only 1.70% AG-News TextFooler accuracy for both original and robust ViT-L/14. VTAB, FLUX, transfer, typographic and BERT results are also newly reported.

M1.justification: The TextFARE objective, batched LEAF attack and semantic-constraint procedure remain unchanged in Section 3 and Algorithms 1–2. The BERT and FLUX experiments extend application of the approach without introducing a revised LEAF component or optimization rule.

P1.justification: v2 makes local language and caption corrections, expands the conclusion and appendix roadmap, and adds subsections for the new analyses. Most original prose and the main section sequence remain intact; the publication footer is also updated.

P2.justification: Substantial new displays include the multi-seed FLUX Figure 7 and tables for VTAB, FLUX examples, transfer and typographic attacks, bimodal retrieval, BERT and token-level attacks. The COCO generation table gains a FLUX block. Older displays are largely preserved but repositioned and renumbered.

R1.justification: v2 adds references supporting FLUX, FLAN-T5, BERT, VTAB, the accuracy–robustness tradeoff and the CoAttack-style evaluation. Appendix C and the central positioning relative to FARE remain substantially unchanged; bibliographic corrections do not constitute new research positioning.

T1.justification: The formal objectives, expansion/contraction and replacement definitions, and mathematical reasoning remain unchanged. No substantive theorem, proof or derivation is added.

improvement.justification: v2 materially strengthens validation of the paper's central robustness claim: Table 25 addresses v1's explicit lack of bimodal-attack testing, while the token-level and typographic experiments reveal important failure boundaries. VTAB and FLUX further test applicability. The bimodal evidence concerns sequential attacks, and the conclusion overstates clean-performance preservation, but these qualifications do not outweigh the substantial gains in empirical support and understanding of limitations.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same LEAF research work. Their full text, equations, tables, figures and appendices are readable, and retained material can be matched across renumbering and relocation.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds VTAB, FLUX, bimodal-attack, transfer, typographic and token-level evaluations, plus BERT training results. Table 27 separately identifies imported baseline results.

before.justification: v1 reports original training-efficiency, classification, retrieval, image-generation and embedding-inversion experiments, with additional results and ablations in Appendix D.

results.title: Robustness in Both Domains: CLIP Needs a Robust Text Encoder

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, and concluding summary retain the same claims: DCL approximates NSCL, NSCL minimizers exhibit collapse/simplex geometry, and directional variability explains few-shot recovery. Additional experiments and the revised bound do not redefine these headline contributions.

C2.justification: v2 explains the increasing training-time loss gap through greater same-class similarity and reduced cross-class similarity. It interprets the new cosine results as augmentation invariance without global collapse and RSA/CKA results as representation alignment. Section 5 retains the original limitations concerning minimizers, bound constants, and class-count dependence.

D1.justification: Appendix A adds ViT-B/16 architecture and resizing details, new dataset splits, and augmentation settings. Section 4.2 identifies the external pretrained-model source, and the checklist adds implementation and licensing disclosures. The original code and project links remain unchanged.

E1.justification: v2 adds Tiny-ImageNet and ImageNet-1K evaluation to the four retained datasets.
