Figure 9 covers Tiny-ImageNet, while Figure 5 evaluates an ImageNet-1K-pretrained model on mini-ImageNet and ImageNet-1K. This substantially broadens object-class coverage; v1 only cited ImageNet as mini-ImageNet's source.

E2.justification: The retained objective comparisons still evaluate DCL against NSCL. MoCo v2 already appeared in v1; ViT and external pretrained-model evaluations add settings rather than new competing objectives or baselines.

E3.justification: v2 adds ViT experiments, 300-epoch RSA/CKA comparisons with matched initialization and minibatch order, and cosine-similarity evaluation using five augmentations per pair after 2,000 epochs. Appendix A also changes the stated SVHN pipeline from 224-pixel to 32-pixel crops with reduced color jitter. This reported setting change does not establish that retained SVHN experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: New Tables 2-3 test augmentation invariance versus global collapse and DCL-NSCL representation alignment. New ViT and pretrained ImageNet analyses test the bounds and representation geometry beyond the original configurations. Conversely, v1 Figure 8's MoCo two-way bound-validation panels are removed; v2 Figure 11 retains only its all-class classification panels.

E5.justification: Checklist item 7 newly discloses that computationally expensive experiments were not repeated. Five-selection averaging, Table 1 standard deviations, and correlation/p-value reporting already existed. No increase in training repetitions or new uncertainty-estimation procedure is established.

E6.justification: Table 1 accuracies are unchanged, but bound curves are revised: Section 4.2 changes its m=500 example from below 0.45 to below 0.89, now explicitly for CIFAR10. New Table 2 reports same/different-sample similarities of 0.92/0.13 on CIFAR10; Table 3 reports RSA/CKA values spanning 0.81-0.91. ViT/ImageNet results are added and MoCo two-way results removed. The changed bounds are theoretical estimates, not accuracy gains.

M1.justification: DCL and negatives-only supervised contrastive learning retain the same objectives and procedures. ViT and pretrained SimCLR models extend experimental configurations without introducing a new proposed learning method.

P1.justification: The main section structure and most existing prose remain intact. v2 adds targeted experimental explanations and a NeurIPS checklist, expands Appendix A's subsection heading to include ViT, and moves the main-text UMAP explanation into Appendix A. There is no broad narrative rewrite.

P2.justification: v2 adds the CDNV schematic, pretrained-model and ViT plots, and two diagnostic tables. Appendix displays are reorganized: MoCo bound panels disappear, ViT bound panels are introduced separately, and Figure 13 combines retained MoCo variance plots with new ViT plots. These substantially expand and restructure the visual presentation beyond renumbering.

R1.justification: Six references are added for Tiny-ImageNet, ViT, CKA, RSA, PyTorch, and a CIFAR ViT implementation. The related-work discussion and positioning against earlier contrastive-learning and neural-collapse theory are unchanged; ImageNet's reference is retained and renumbered.

T1.justification: Proposition 1 replaces the 14-times-directional-CDNV plus 28.5-times-CDNV/m bound with a bound containing additional 1/sqrt(m) terms. Appendix C replaces its proof with a covariance-based derivation and revises Corollary 1's optimization, including a constrained optimizer and zero-B case. Variance definitions are also revised, although CDNV notation remains inconsistent between Section 3.2 and Appendix C. The other theorems remain unchanged.

improvement.justification: Appendix C replaces v1's erroneous 1/m-squared sample-mean variance step with covariance-based reasoning, while Table 3 directly tests representation similarity that v1 left as future work. Augmentation and ViT/ImageNet checks substantially strengthen support for central claims. Inconsistent CDNV notation, stale references to the old 14/28.5 constants, and removal of MoCo two-way plots remain drawbacks, but the targeted theoretical and empirical gains outweigh them.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work, with matching authors, objectives, losses, and core experiments. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and Appendices A-D are readable and support reliable comparison.

after.justification: Original empirical results remain, supplemented by ViT and pretrained ImageNet evaluations, augmentation-similarity measurements, and controlled RSA/CKA comparisons.

before.justification: Section 4 and Appendix A report original DCL/NSCL training experiments, few-shot classification results, loss trajectories, representation analyses, and MoCo experiments.

results.title: Self-Supervised Contrastive Learning is Approximately Supervised Contrastive Learning

C1.justification: The central contribution remains inference-time cryo-EM guidance that improves conformational coverage without retraining. However, v2 narrows the consistency claim: v1 says guidance ensures consistency with observations 'by construction,' whereas v2's Discussion says it biases sampling toward consistent models. The expanded experiments support the retained contribution rather than redefine it.

C2.justification: V2 newly identifies principled validation of models derived from low-resolution maps as unresolved. Section 4.1 also makes applicability restrictions explicit through selection of systems with at most two unique chains and fewer than 2,200 residues. The ablation interpretation becomes qualified to 'most' experimental maps. Existing optimization-instability and initialization limitations remain.

D1.justification: V2 adds a code-availability statement and repository address absent from v1. Appendix A documents preprocessing for the added systems, including density thresholds, ten-voxel padding, and YbbAP component removal at size threshold 100, alongside dataset-dependent guidance schedules. Existing software, alignment, and A100 hardware disclosures are retained.

E1.justification: Coverage expands from three biomolecular systems to six. Alongside the retained synthetic datasets and four P-glycoprotein states, v2 evaluates active/inhibited Pma1, open/closed CYP102A1, and bound/unbound YbbAP. This substantially broadens experimental validation to additional protein systems and map conditions, including a 6.5 Å map.

E2.justification: V2 adds Boltz-1 with random MSA subsampling as an evaluated comparator in Table 1 and new Table B1; v1 only discussed MSA-based alternatives. This introduces direct comparison with an important strategy for generating conformational diversity across the evaluated systems. Unguided Boltz-1, AlphaFold3, and ModelAngelo remain.

E3.justification: The reported real-map schedule changes from 125/25/25/25 warm-up/global/local/relaxation steps to 100/50/25/25, retaining 200 total steps; synthetic settings remain unchanged. Added experiments specify five samples at each MSA depth of 64–1024 and dataset-specific map preprocessing. ModelAngelo additionally receives TM-score evaluation. The existing best-of-25 selection framework is retained.

E4.justification: V1 ablates global and local guidance only on synthetic maps. V2 adds these ablations for all ten experimental maps in Table B1, testing whether their combination remains beneficial under real measurement conditions and revealing exceptions. Appendix sample-quality distributions also expand to the six newly evaluated experimental states.

E5.justification: Both versions use three replicates with 25 samples per replicate and report means with 95% confidence intervals for samples selected by map fit. V1 Table B1 becomes v2 Table B2 with the same uncertainty-reporting practice. Additional rows and changed interval values do not establish a new statistical procedure or increased replication.

E6.justification: V2 adds substantial results for the new systems, MSA baseline, and experimental-map ablations. For example, Table 2 reports Pma1 inhibited-state all-atom RMSD of 1.999 Å for CryoBoltz versus 6.140 Å for Boltz-1. Retained results also change: STP10 inward CryoBoltz Cα RMSD changes from 0.379 to 0.371 Å, and P-glycoprotein scores are revised. The latter accompany a changed guidance schedule, so they are not same-setting performance gains. Aggregate mean rows are removed.

M1.justification: The proposed method retains pretrained Boltz-1, DPS-based guidance, weighted-k-means point clouds, Sinkhorn global guidance, density-based local guidance, and unguided warm-up and relaxation. V2 adjusts experimental scheduling and map preprocessing without introducing a different model, guidance objective, or core method component.

P1.justification: The title changes from guidance of 'AlphaFold3' to 'protein structure prediction.' V2 polishes prose, groups results into synthetic and experimental dataset subsections, and adds a short conclusion. The introduction, background, method exposition, and appendix organization remain substantially recognizable; added experiments do not constitute wholesale narrative rewriting.

P2.justification: The empirical presentation is substantially expanded and reorganized: Tables 1 and 2 gain comparator or system columns and rows, Figure 6 and experimental-ablation Table B1 are added, and the original Table B1 becomes an expanded Table B2. The original RMSD histogram figure is split into synthetic and experimental figures with additional panels. Figure 2 replaces numerical stage boundaries with symbolic phase lengths.

R1.justification: V2 adds citations for deposited structures and the YbbAP study while retaining the methodological literature. Section 3.4 replaces the criticism of ROCKET's architectural restriction with a contrast emphasizing CryoBoltz's atomic-space optimization, and removes the description of ADP-3D as the 'first and only' demonstration. These are limited positioning refinements.

T1.justification: Equations 1–5, the forward-model assumptions, and Appendix A.4's optimal-transport and Sinkhorn definitions retain their mathematical substance. Using a variable phase length in the cosine schedule expresses the experimental scheduling adjustment rather than a new theoretical result. Neither version adds proofs or theorems.

improvement.justification: V1's real-data evidence depended on one protein system and lacked a tested MSA-diversification comparator. V2 substantially strengthens that evidence through three additional experimental systems, direct MSA-subsampling comparisons, and real-map guidance ablations that expose both benefits and exceptions. Clearer applicability limits, a more measured consistency claim, and added reproducibility information further improve the paper. Selection still favors systems with usable initial predictions, but the broader validation meaningfully strengthens the conclusions within that scope.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe CryoBoltz, with the same authors, guidance framework, and retained experiments despite the revised title. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices support reliable comparison.

after.justification: V2 retains original experiments and adds evaluations on Pma1, CYP102A1, and YbbAP, together with MSA-subsampling comparisons and experimental-map ablations.

before.justification: V1 reports original structure-prediction experiments on synthetic STP10 and CH67 maps and experimental P-glycoprotein maps, including baseline comparisons, ablations, and appendix analyses.

results.title: Multiscale guidance of protein structure prediction with heterogeneous cryo-EM data

C1.justification: Introduction contribution (v) newly identifies integrating surrogate reference functions with round-wise approximation as a technical-novelty contribution, elaborated in Appendix C. The abstract, conclusion, and headline claims about regret, burn-in, and switching/communication costs remain unchanged.

C2.justification: v2 clarifies that supported heterogeneity concerns exploration speed rather than different environments. Appendix C adds a substantive explanation of how surrogate references resolve simultaneous non-adaptiveness and avoid the additional logarithmic factor from the earlier empirical-process approach. Experimental interpretations remain unchanged.

D1.justification: The documented confidence-parameter prescription uses a tighter total-step bound: T1 changes from 2T0 + MHSA in v1 Section 5 to (1 + 1/[H(H+1)])T0 + MHSA in v2 Lemma F.1. Experimental hyperparameters, hardware, runtimes, and code-access statements are otherwise retained.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same synthetic tabular MDPs with (H,S,A) = (5,3,2) and (7,10,5), for single-agent and federated learning. The new discussion of heterogeneous exploration speeds introduces no additional evaluated scenario.

E2.justification: The six single-agent comparators remain the Hoeffding and Bernstein variants of UCB and UCB2, UCB-Advantage, and Q-EarlySettled-Advantage. Federated comparisons retain FedQ-Hoeffding, FedQ-Bernstein, and FedQ-Advantage. Newly discussed Fed-UCBVI is not experimentally evaluated.

E3.justification: Both retain M = 1 or 10, episode budgets of 300,000 or 2,000,000, uniform initial states, the same reward and transition generation, and the same logarithmically normalized metrics. The optional waiting variant is not evaluated.

before.justification: Section 6 reports original synthetic tabular-MDP experiments measuring regret and switching or communication costs, with results in Figures 4–7.

These expand the evaluated comparison methods; the newly discussed FoldX and Rosetta methods are not evaluated.

E3.justification: Added evaluations vary the inverse-folding model and ensemble generator on Protein G, and Figure 2 specifies 20 BioEmu samples for the new scaling experiment. Original filtering, correlation metrics and MD/MC settings remain. The NVT/NPT distinction in Appendix B.2 was already documented in v1, rather than introduced by this revision.

E4.justification: V2 adds substantial tests of dependence on the inverse-folding model, replacement of MD by BioEmu, richer sequence corrections, and sequence-only versus structure-based scoring (Section 4.4, Tables 2–3 and Figure 6). The original per-protein breakdown and Pearson/Spearman comparison are retained or redisplayed, not new analyses.

E5.justification: Both versions specify 100 bootstrap samples for Figure 1 and report standard errors. V2 continues standard-error reporting in its added tables without stating a changed resampling procedure, repeated-run count, seed policy or significance-testing practice. Differences in individual reported standard errors concern results rather than statistical methodology.

E6.justification: Table 1 is numerically unchanged, but Tables 2–3 and Figure 2 add substantial results. On Protein G, ProteinMPNN scores 0.40 for single-structure scoring and 0.58 with MD plus IDP correction; ESM-IF scores 0.69 with BioEmu versus 0.70 with MD, reaching 0.72 with either ensemble plus IDP correction. Some repeated uncertainties conflict: the Protein G folded-only MD standard error is 0.03 in Table 1 but 0.02 in Tables 2–3.

M1.justification: V2 implements BioEmu-generated folded ensembles as an alternative to MD, whereas v1 only anticipated using generative ensemble models in its discussion. This adds a practical sampling route within the retained free-energy scoring framework; the principal scoring expressions and original unfolded-state estimators remain.

P1.justification: V2 polishes prose and terminology across the introduction, methods and discussion, consolidates author footnotes, and adds an Ablations and scaling subsection before Results. The overall section sequence and appendix organization remain recognizable; much of the expansion documents scientific additions rather than a wholesale narrative rewrite.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is substantially redesigned with a structured formula matrix and Pearson-only plot; the original Pearson/Spearman comparison is redisplayed in Figure 5. The old per-protein Figure 2 becomes Figure 4. New Figures 2, 3 and 6 visualize scaling, theoretical regimes and ESM2 comparisons, while Tables 2–3 add structured comparisons and Table 1 is relocated.

R1.justification: Section 5 expands from nearby inverse-folding studies to the history of statistical potentials and comparisons with FoldX and Rosetta, including their sensitivity to backbone templates. V2 also discusses Deng et al.'s subsequent fine-tuning work and adds references supporting the new models and benchmark. The Lewis reference is a publication update to an already cited work.

T1.justification: Sections 2.3–3.1 replace the common-temperature assumption with potentially different latent temperatures and introduce explicit assumptions allowing temperature-conditioned likelihood ratios to be approximated by available models. Section 3.3.1 replaces the unfolded-structural-invariance justification with folding-probability regimes governing which pseudo-free-energy term dominates, illustrated in new Figure 3. The appendix monotonicity derivation is retained.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens the central argument by revising the temperature assumptions and replacing the broad unfolded-state-invariance justification with explicit applicability conditions. ProteinMPNN and BioEmu ablations, sequence-model controls and the additional multi-protein evaluation address important gaps in generality and practical feasibility left by v1. These gains outweigh localized weaknesses: overbroad ESM2 interpretation, inconsistent repeated standard errors, and loss of the exact ESM-IF checkpoint detail.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable and support comparison, including matching relocated material.

after.justification: The original analyses remain, supplemented by ProteinMPNN, ESM2 and BioEmu evaluations and results on a subset of the mega-scale stability dataset.

before.justification: Section 4 and Appendix B report original prediction correlations and molecular-simulation analyses on Protein G, Guerois and VAMP-seq.

results.title: Zero-shot protein stability prediction by inverse folding models: a free energy interpretation

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contribution list and conclusion retain the same central claims: GLS and its matching bound, competitive drafter-invariant multi-draft decoding, and improved multi-decoder compression. Additional evidence does not redefine these contributions.

C2.justification: v3 substantially expands applicability discussion through draft-count computation/memory tradeoffs, vocabulary and alignment limitations, and shared-randomness and floating-point requirements for distributed compression. Appendix D.2 also distinguishes output consistency from output quality and emphasizes that conditional invariance does not guarantee identical outputs.

D1.justification: v3 supplies an explicit code-repository URL, identifies Huggingface Transformers, and documents settings accompanying the Llama and CIFAR-10 additions, including patch dimensions and selected N and beta. Most existing implementation, hardware and training details are unchanged.

E1.justification: Appendix D.4 adds CIFAR-10 compression, extending image coverage from handwritten digits to color natural images. Gaussian sources and all five language datasets are retained. The Llama additions change model configurations rather than language-task coverage.

E2.justification: Comparator membership is unchanged in the retained experiments. The Llama evaluations reuse the corresponding SpecInfer, SpecTr and Daliri comparisons, while CIFAR-10 reuses the compression baseline. The new consistency analysis also uses the existing SpecInfer comparator.

E3.justification: v3 adds Llama 2-68M/7B and Llama 3-1B/8B configurations, plus a paired consistency protocol using ROUGE, fixed randomness and drafter temperatures 1.0 versus 0.5. CIFAR-10 introduces 16-by-16 side-information patches. These substantially expand evaluation design. Section 4.4's full-vocabulary statement is not reconciled with Appendix D.1's retained top-50 setting, so a change to the original sampling protocol cannot be established.

E4.justification: New Tables 7-8 examine empirical matching probabilities and LML-bound tightness on actual LLM distributions across draft counts. Appendix D.2 adds quantitative output-consistency tests and a GSM8K case study under temperature changes. These directly investigate practical consequences of the theoretical properties beyond v1's existing efficiency analyses.

E5.justification: The new consistency study specifies paired runs sharing a seed and averaging over four seeds, with uncertainty values in Table 9. Existing five-seed LLM, ten-repeat Gaussian and five-repeat MNIST reporting is retained; no increase in repetitions of those experiments is documented.

E6.justification: Original numerical results remain unchanged, while v3 adds Llama performance, matching probabilities and bounds, ROUGE consistency, CIFAR-10 distortion, and absolute baseline throughput. For example, new Table 9 reports GSM8K ROUGE-L of 0.745 versus SpecInfer's 0.647; Tables 15-16 report CIFAR-10 MSE of 0.0788 versus 0.0956 at K=4 and Lmax=4. These are additional results under newly reported evaluations.

M1.justification: Algorithms 1-2, the strongly drafter-invariant variant, compression sampling procedures, and documented neural architectures and losses remain unchanged. The additional evaluations do not document a new method component.

P1.justification: The overall narrative and most existing prose are retained. Local expansions add practical guidance, two limitations subsections, Appendix A.7, Appendix D.2 and acknowledgements, alongside wording corrections and updated conference text.

P2.justification: Seven new tables substantially expand the displayed evidence: Llama comparisons, empirical matching/bound comparisons, ROUGE consistency and CIFAR-10 results. Existing compression tables are retained and renumbered. Figures remain largely unchanged, with Figure 4 gaining a Rate (bits) axis label and several displays repositioned.

R1.justification: New references support the added discussions and experiments, including recursive speculative decoding, Gumbel-top-k sampling, CIFAR-10, ROUGE, Transformers and a speculative-decoding survey. Core positioning relative to Daliri and the matching-lemma literature remains unchanged. DROP was already cited in a v1 footnote.

T1.justification: Remark 1 and Appendix A.7 add proofs that the LML bound is exact for point-mass proposals, a single proposal, and identical target/proposal distributions. This supplements the bound's characterization; the main theorems, drafter-invariance definitions and existing derivations are retained.

improvement.justification: v3 addresses important validation gaps: v1 did not directly measure practical output consistency or compare its bound with empirical matching on real LLM distributions. The new analyses, additional model and image evaluations, exactness proofs and deployment limitations substantially strengthen support for the retained contributions. Reporting flaws temper this gain: Appendix D.2 names NaturalReasoning where Table 9 labels MBPP, and the vocabulary-setting descriptions remain unreconciled. These limit reproducibility of parts of the evidence without outweighing the broader improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same GLS research, with matching algorithms, theoretical results and original experiments. All 31 pages of v1 and 37 pages of v3, including appendices A-D, support comparison.

after.justification: v3 retains those empirical results and adds Llama evaluations, empirical matching-probability measurements, decoding-consistency experiments and CIFAR-10 compression results.

before.justification: v1 reports original toy-distribution simulations, speculative-decoding experiments, and Gaussian-source and MNIST compression results in the main text and Appendix D.

results.title: List-Level Distribution Coupling with Applications to Speculative Decoding and Lossy Compression

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction contributions and conclusion retain the same claims about pocket-localization failures, alignment and aggregation, and near-holo screening under structural uncertainty. The headline EF1% comparison of 11.75 versus 37.19 is unchanged; additional experiments support the existing claims.

C2.justification: V2 substantially expands qualifications and interpretation: structure-ID filtering may leave target redundancy, ECFP4 performance may exploit DUD-E topology bias, and larger pockets trade coverage against downsampling and irrelevant regions. Appendix D.3 explicitly acknowledges difficulties with flexible or disordered proteins and distinguishes pocket localization from full flexible-binding modeling.

D1.justification: V2 announces public implementation access and supplies an AANet code link absent from v1. New Appendix B.2 specifies ChEMBL molecule and activity filters, target mapping and masking of known positive pairs using UniProt IDs and InChI keys. Appendix D.1 also specifies uniform downsampling to at most 256 atoms, materially improving documentation of the existing pipeline.

E1.justification: V2 adds screening evaluation on 77 DEKOIS targets under holo, predicted-apo annotated and predicted-apo blind conditions (Appendix C.4, Table S10). This substantially extends the evaluated protein–compound data beyond the retained benchmarks; v1 mentioned DEKOIS only in baseline training exclusions.

E2.justification: V2 adds ECFP4 to the ligand-based comparison with AANet (Table S12), and GOLD appears as an additional docking comparator in Table S10. USR and PhaseShape were already evaluated in v1 Table S1. The main screening and pocket-identification comparator sets remain unchanged.

E3.justification: Appendix C.5 introduces a separate control excluding training proteins containing chains with at least 90% sequence identity to DUD-E targets, using MMseqs2 on PDBbind and ChEMBL. DEKOIS evaluation additionally reports EF0.5%, while the runtime comparison distinguishes 2.8M, 10M and 100M scoring workloads. These extend the evaluation design without establishing changes to the original main-table protocols.

E4.justification: V2 adds a substantial generalization check through homology removal (Table S11), runtime comparisons across workloads (Table S7), and quantitative coverage and atom-count analysis supporting the 10 Å radius (Appendix D.1). The original component ablations, detector-transfer tests, t-SNE analysis and failure cases are retained.

E5.justification: Appendix D.1 newly reports pocket atom counts using mean-plus/minus summaries, including 612.68 ± 240.75 and 199.32 ± 55.04, although the dispersion measure is unspecified. Both versions retain random seed 1 in Table S4; v2 does not add repeated-run uncertainty for screening performance.

E6.justification: V2 adds substantial results for DEKOIS, homology filtering, ligand-based screening, runtime and pocket coverage. DEKOIS predicted-apo blind EF0.5% is 13.33 for AANet versus 0.92 for DrugCLIP. Under the same stated settings, Table 1 also revises Glide's DUD-E holo EF1% from 18.07 to 17.25 and TankBind's LIT-PCBA experimental-apo blind EF1% from 1.97 to 3.42; corresponding AUROC entries change too. AANet's original headline scores remain unchanged.

M1.justification: The tri-modal alignment, cavity negatives, enlarged pockets and cross-attention aggregation remain unchanged in Sections 3.3–3.4 and Algorithms 1–3. Newly documented activity-pair masking and atom downsampling provide implementation details without establishing a revision to the original procedure.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main section order remain intact. V2 inserts ChEMBL-processing documentation, expands Appendix C, adds an Appendix D discussion, improves specific appendix references, and updates affiliations, acknowledgements and the conference footer. These are localized structural and editorial changes rather than a broad rewrite.

P2.justification: V2 substantially expands the appendix's tabular presentation with dedicated runtime, DEKOIS, homology-filtering and ligand-based comparison tables. Figure 3 is redrawn with revised phase labels and clearer training-data flow. Existing AUROC and full-holo tables are retained as Tables S8 and S9; Table S12 partly redisplays earlier USR and PhaseShape results alongside the new comparison.

R1.justification: V2 adds references to FlowDock, MMseqs2 and extended-connectivity fingerprints, and discusses PoseBusters when motivating physical plausibility. The ligand-based comparison broadens contextual positioning, but the main related-work narrative and novelty claims remain largely unchanged.

T1.justification: The pocket and IoU definitions, alignment and aggregation equations, and appendix metric formulas are retained. No theorem, proof or substantive mathematical derivation is added or revised; the new appendix discussion motivates existing design choices.

improvement.justification: V2 materially strengthens validation by addressing the target-redundancy concern left open by v1's structure-ID filtering: AANet retains its advantage under the added 90% sequence-identity exclusion control. DEKOIS evaluation and the ECFP4 comparison broaden scrutiny of generalization and benchmark bias. Detailed ChEMBL processing, implementation-access information and explicit flexible-protein limitations also improve reproducibility and scope. Screening uncertainty across training runs remains unreported, but the combined gains substantially improve the paper's evidential foundation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same AANet study. Their complete main texts, appendices, equations, tables and figures are readable and can be matched reliably, including material renumbered or relocated in v2.

after.justification: V2 retains those empirical results and adds DEKOIS evaluation, homology-filtered training comparisons, ligand-based comparisons and quantitative pocket-coverage analysis.

before.justification: V1 reports original screening experiments on DUD-E and LIT-PCBA, pocket identification on COACH420, component ablations and additional empirical analyses in the appendices.

results.title: AANet: Virtual Screening under Structural Uncertainty via Alignment and Aggregation

C1.justification: The abstract and central theoretical contributions remain essentially unchanged. The conclusion expands the demonstrated practical benefit of fixed thresholds from faster, more stable training to better classification accuracy, reflecting the new image experiments.

C2.justification: Section 6 replaces the speculative minority-class benefit with an interpretation of UTKFace results and narrows its learnable-threshold discussion to ONC1–2. It newly acknowledges that the existing ONC3 metric requires uniformly spaced fixed thresholds. Appendix D.5 explicitly limits the theory's agreement with real networks to qualitative behavior in important respects.

D1.justification: Appendix C adds image preprocessing, pretrained-backbone adaptations, architecture-specific hyperparameters, distributed training details and runtime information; Table 3 adds clog-log settings. The new checklist also reports supplementary code and run instructions, specifically identifying tabular logit/probit code. Actual supplementary-code availability cannot be verified from the PDFs.

E1.justification: v2 adds face-image age estimation on UTKFace, grouped into 20 ordinal classes, extending evaluation beyond the five retained tabular ordinal datasets. This introduces a substantially different input domain and prediction task.

E2.justification: Fixed and learnable thresholds remain the comparison pair in corresponding experiments. No external ordinal-regression baseline is added or removed; additional backbones and link functions are experimental configurations within the existing framework.

E3.justification: v2 adds accuracy, QWK, within-1 accuracy and minimum sensitivity, plus an adjusted ONC3 metric for fixed-threshold clog-log experiments. New UTKFace protocols specify an 80/20 stratified split, image preprocessing, three pretrained backbones and 300-epoch training. Appendix D.5 adds a 35-value regularization sweep. Existing tabular training settings are largely retained.

E4.justification: Appendix D.3 newly tests whether ONC extends to an asymmetric link function. Appendix D.4 examines consistency across image backbones, and D.5 directly tests EOS predictions against trained networks across regularization strengths. The last analysis reveals quantitative discrepancies that v1's numerical EOS illustration did not examine.

E5.justification: v1 already uses 30-holdout averaging and shaded uncertainty bands. v2 adds three-seed repetitions for UTKFace, documents their averaged error bands, and reports error bars for the EOS–network comparison. The precise statistical definition of the bands remains unspecified.

E6.justification: v2 adds results for UTKFace, clog-log configurations and additional metrics on retained datasets. Figures 3, 35 and 36 report zero minimum sensitivity for learnable thresholds across all three image backbones, versus positive values for fixed thresholds. Figure 39 newly shows network weight-norm saturation and transition points differing from EOS predictions. These are new findings under added or modified settings.

M1.justification: The central CLM/UFM formulation and threshold parameterization remain unchanged. However, Appendix D.5 explicitly adds feature-norm regularization to the DNN training objective for the new theory-validation experiment; this is a limited procedural adaptation.

P1.justification: The title, abstract and main section sequence are retained, with much introductory and formulation prose unchanged. Editing concentrates on experimental descriptions, discussion, conclusion and the revised mathematical appendix. v2 also condenses affiliations and adds acknowledgments and a conference checklist.

P2.justification: Existing six-panel metric figures become ten-panel displays, with reordered panels and logarithmic MAE axes. v2 adds UTKFace, clog-log and theory-comparison figures, expands the hyperparameter table and adds two UTKFace tables. The old strict-log-concavity diagram is removed with its replaced proof.

R1.justification: v2 adds Leindler, Brøndsted and UTKFace/ResNet/DenseNet references, while removing the Barbato and Brascamp–Lieb proof sources. Section 2 revises its description of linguistic collapse, but the overall positioning within neural-collapse research remains stable.

T1.justification: Appendix A.2 replaces v1's CDF-difference strict-log-concavity argument with a multidimensional translated-integral theorem, a geometric assumption and six supporting lemmas. Appendix D.3 also derives the asymmetric-link offset and defines an adjusted ONC3 metric. The main ONC and EOS theorem statements are largely retained.

improvement.justification: v1 explicitly could not evaluate the hypothesized minority-class benefit because its datasets yielded near-zero validation error. v2 addresses this limitation with a harder image task across three backbones and adds a direct theory–network comparison that exposes quantitative failures. These targeted checks substantially strengthen the empirical grounding and clarify applicability. The learnable-threshold ONC3 metric remains unresolved, and label-shift robustness is still not directly tested, but the expanded validation and more candid limitations provide a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ONC study, with matching CLM/UFM formulations and core theorems. Their main text, figures, tables, equations and appendices support a reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds UTKFace experiments, clog-log experiments and a direct comparison between theoretical predictions and trained networks.

before.justification: v1 reports original numerical solutions of the equations of state and neural-network experiments on five ordinal datasets, including training curves and feature visualizations.

results.title: Neural Collapse in Cumulative Link Models for Ordinal Regression: An Analysis with Unconstrained Feature Model

C1.justification: The core claims about diffusion refinement, hierarchical message passing, accuracy, and accelerated inference remain. v2's introduction additionally claims efficient transfer to much larger meshes while maintaining near-FEM accuracy, extending the claimed applicability beyond the original evaluations.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive interpretation of truncation-induced mesh degradation and the IMPACTPLATE tradeoff between lower displacement error and higher gradient error, hypothesizing low-frequency stabilization versus high-frequency refinement. This qualifies the accuracy–speed interpretation beyond v1's global-error analysis. The SO(3) limitation also changes from restricted applicability to tensor fields and anisotropic materials to potential accuracy benefits for orientation-sensitive predictions.

D1.justification: v2 replaces the future code/data-release promise with reported availability and a project link. It adds BSMS implementation access and detailed training settings, mesh-size statistics, expanded compute accounting, and clearer AMG implementation instructions. Table 1 removes the simulator-name column. These are documentation and access-information changes; external availability was not verified.

E1.justification: The three original physical tasks remain. v2 adds BENDINGBEAMLARGE and a small-to-large mesh transfer scenario, with 8,897 average nodes versus 744 for BENDINGBEAM (Appendix B, Table 1). This extends coverage to substantially larger input meshes within the existing beam-bending task.

E2.justification: The principal comparison expands from MGN and HCMT to include BSMS on all three benchmarks, including qualitative rollout comparisons. BSMS was only cited in v1. v2 also evaluates an HCMT-backbone control retaining DDPMs and ROBI, materially strengthening comparisons with alternative hierarchical architectures.

E3.justification: v2 adds a truncation sweep on one trained model, displacement-gradient evaluation, and fine-tuning versus training from scratch on large meshes. Appendix C changes RMSE normalization from 1/N_i to 1/(N_i N_j) inside the square root. Appendix D swaps reported HCMT training budgets from 2M/3M to 3M/2M iterations for IMPACTPLATE/DEFORMINGPLATE. These are reported protocol revisions; they do not establish whether existing experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: New analyses test whether AMPNs outperform an HCMT backbone under the same diffusion framework, how truncation affects displacement gradients and accumulated mesh damage, and whether pretraining aids larger-mesh learning. These appear in Figures 6–8 and 14–15. The K=5 and K=10 experiments already existed in v1 and are reorganized as ablations.

E5.justification: Both versions specify five seeds and mean/standard-deviation reporting in Appendix C; v1 already displays error bars and individual runs. v2 restates and extends this practice to added results, without introducing additional repetitions, confidence intervals, or significance tests.

E6.justification: v2 adds BSMS, HCMT-backbone, truncation, gradient-error, and transfer results. Table 3 reports large-mesh RMSE of 77.59 versus 215.50, in units of 10^-3, for fine-tuned versus from-scratch models. The reported BENDINGBEAM default-versus-one-step timing overhead changes from approximately 71% to 58%. Revised protocols limit direct cross-version performance comparisons, and some Table 3 entries disagree with plots, notably BENDINGBEAM MGN values and uncertainty in Figure 4.

M1.justification: Section 3.1 introduces configurable intermediate denoising truncation. v1 already described a first-step shortcut and separately trained shorter-diffusion models; v2 generalizes early stopping within one trained model. The AMPN architecture, diffusion objective, and underlying rolling inference remain essentially unchanged.

P1.justification: The main section sequence and Appendices A–E remain. v2 clarifies the rolling prediction/state-update explanation, streamlines coarsening prose, corrects terminology, and reorganizes variants and results into clearer subsections. A NeurIPS checklist is added, but most existing narrative is retained.

P2.justification: v2 adds gradient-error, truncation, and large-mesh figures plus a comprehensive numerical Table 3. Existing benchmark and rollout displays gain BSMS, the ablation display expands, and inference plots change their displayed variants and legends. The coarsening illustration moves from main-text Figure 3 to appendix Figure 10; Table 1 changes columns and adds the large-mesh row.

R1.justification: The bibliography retains the same 66 works. Related work adds an explicit explanation of physics-informed MeshGraphNets as a complementary FEM-based training approach, while BSMS becomes an evaluated comparator. The overall positioning relative to hierarchical GNNs and diffusion simulators remains stable.

T1.justification: Appendix C revises the explicit mathematical definition of RMSE by adding normalization over feature count. The principal DDPM and message-passing equations remain essentially unchanged, and neither version provides new theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: The HCMT-backbone control and gradient/truncation diagnostics address important gaps in v1: attributing gains to the architecture and detecting local failures hidden by displacement RMSE. Larger-mesh transfer evidence further strengthens applicability. Unexplained protocol revisions and discrepancies between some plots and Table 3 limit numerical reliability, but the added controls and failure analysis provide a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ROBIN research, with matching authors, methods, and original benchmarks. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support comparison despite substantial additions in v2.

after.justification: v2 retains original simulation evaluations and adds BSMS comparisons, truncation diagnostics, an architecture ablation, and large-mesh transfer results.

before.justification: v1 reports original model evaluations, timing experiments, and ablations on BENDINGBEAM, IMPACTPLATE, and DEFORMINGPLATE, including rollout visualizations in Appendix E.

results.title: Diffusion-Based Hierarchical Graph Neural Networks for Simulating Nonlinear Solid Mechanics

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same central contributions: deriving state-dependent guidance from an additive error model, outperforming CFG, remaining competitive with LIG, and adapting guidance to prompts and trajectories. The added evaluations support these claims without redefining them.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations for the new baselines' behavior and argues that simple MS-COCO captions under-test adaptive guidance. Appendix F.5 acknowledges failures to satisfy all prompt details. Section 5 replaces the lack of quantitative T2I evaluation with limitations concerning broader prompt coverage and larger architectures.

D1.justification: Appendices F.1-F.2 and Table 4 add baseline tuning details and optimal T2I hyperparameters; F.5 specifies additional qualitative settings. The T2I resource account changes from approximately 2,000 images in six hours on a GTX 1080 Ti to 3,000 in two hours on a V100. These describe different workloads, not a demonstrated speedup. Public code and prompt-data access remain.

E1.justification: v2 adds evaluation on MS-COCO captions, extending coverage beyond ImageNet and the existing handcrafted prompt dataset to a standard natural-image caption benchmark. The additional illustrative prompts use the retained difficulty categories. DiT and LAION-5B are proposed future directions, not evaluated additions.

E2.justification: Table 1 adds the linear guidance weight scheduler, called LinCFG elsewhere, and CFG++ to the ImageNet comparison previously containing CFG and LIG. LinCFG is evaluated with both samplers; CFG++ is reported only for PFODE. These are actual additional comparators, not merely new citations.

E3.justification: v2 introduces a quantitative protocol using 3,000 MS-COCO prompts, FID, FDDinoV2, Aesthetic Score, and metric-specific hyperparameter searches. It also specifies searches for the added baselines. For retained ImageNet experiments, Appendix F.1 changes the reported CFG sweep spacing from 0.125 to 0.1; unchanged scores do not establish that these experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Appendix F.5 extends existing prompt-dependent case studies by comparing unguided sampling, CFG, FBGpure, and FBGCFG for saturation and detail-following behavior. Table 4 additionally examines when adding base CFG helps T2I performance. The existing timing-parameter and mixture-coefficient sensitivity analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Removing v1's checklist also removes its explicit statement that only one FID/FDDinoV2 value is reported and its discussion of matching seeds across comparisons. v2 supplies no replacement benchmark uncertainty explanation. The same-seed caption for Figure 11 and existing Figure 4 error bars remain.

E6.justification: Existing Table 1 scores remain unchanged, but new baseline rows and the complete MS-COCO results are added. In v2 Table 2, FBGpure reports FID 18.63 versus CFG's 19.64, while FBGCFG reports FDDinoV2 52.14 versus CFG's 54.56. These are newly reported comparisons, not improvements over corresponding v1 scores. Additional qualitative results appear in Figures 12-19.

M1.justification: The additive-mixture guidance formula, posterior tracking, clamping, hyperparameter reparameterization, and CFG/LIG combinations are retained. Algorithm 1 is relocated and its conditional/unconditional input notation corrected; these edits do not introduce a different procedure.

P1.justification: The main section sequence and argument remain, while several method and results paragraphs are condensed or rewritten and citations switch to author-year style. Algorithm 1 moves to a dedicated appendix, experimental material gains subsections, the checklist is removed, and the writing-assistance disclosure is expanded.

P2.justification: v2 substantially expands the visual presentation with MS-COCO result and hyperparameter tables and Figures 12-19 showing comparative samples and guidance trajectories. Existing comparison tables gain baseline rows or columns. Earlier figures and sample images are retained, with resizing, caption edits, and relocation, including Figure 5 and Algorithm 1.

R1.justification: v2 adds references for CFG++, MS-COCO, DINOv2, DiT, and LAION-5B, and discusses the positioning of CFG++ and the previously cited weight scheduler. The broader relationship to CFG, LIG, autoguidance, and prior state-dependent guidance remains unchanged.

T1.justification: Equation 4 corrects the unconditional-distribution exponent from (1-lambda)/lambda, or gamma-1, to (lambda-1)/lambda, or 1-gamma. New Appendix A supplies the intermediate chain-rule derivation of the existing FBG score formula. The other substantive mathematical assumptions and derivations are retained.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses v1's explicit lack of quantitative T2I quality evaluation through the MS-COCO comparison and strengthens the ImageNet comparison with two additional baselines. The corrected CFG exponent and explicit FBG derivation also improve technical clarity. The new benchmark remains limited to 3,000 prompts without uncertainty estimates, and removing the statistical-reporting explanation reduces transparency. Nevertheless, the added evidence resolves a substantial validation gap and provides a clear overall quality improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Feedback Guidance of Diffusion Models. Their complete main texts and appendices are readable, and equations, experiments, figures, and tables can be matched despite additions and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds evaluated baselines, quantitative MS-COCO text-to-image results, and additional qualitative comparisons.

before.justification: v1 reports original ImageNet experiments with EDM2-XS, guidance-parameter analyses, and Stable Diffusion 2 experiments examining prompt and trajectory dependence.

results.title: Feedback Guidance of Diffusion Models

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, and conclusion retain the same claims: template-conditioned flow matching with differentiable refinement, the AlignDockBench contribution, and advantages over docking/alignment baselines, including difficult similarity and flexibility regimes. Additional appendix evidence supports these existing claims.

C2.justification: V2 substantially expands explanations of hydrogen-bond geometry, FMA initialization quality, PO's usefulness with other generators, and Vina scoring's benefit mainly after refinement. Its runtime discussion identifies CPU refinement as a bottleneck and explicitly limits applicability to ultra-large screening without acceleration.

D1.justification: V2 specifies donor-hydrogen pharmacophore placement, gives precise pointers to borrowed architecture algorithms, and elaborates weight-selection criteria for the existing ten-complex tuning set. It also documents separate CPU/GPU stage timings and cloud-cost assumptions. Existing training hyperparameters and data-access information remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Both retain the same training corpus and 369-pair AlignDockBench, including cross-docking and redocking. The added molecular case study stays within existing pose-refinement coverage; large-scale screening costs are projections, not evaluations on new datasets.

E2.justification: V2 evaluates HarmonicFlow and HarmonicFlow with PO, previously only discussed as related work. Tables S9 and S11 substantially expand comparisons through RDKit-centroid initialization, FitDock LB, and PO-refined Vina, LS-align, and FitDock LB configurations. Original Table 1 comparators remain.

E3.justification: Existing training settings, primary scoring protocol, and 263-molecule PoseBusters subset are retained. Added evaluation designs compare alternative initializers under identical PO hyperparameters, distinguish refinement of all ten candidates from refinement of the selected pose, and introduce strain-energy and clash-count measurements. HarmonicFlow receives an explicit best-of-ten RMSD comparison.

E4.justification: V1 primarily ablates PO, pocket inclusion, and sampling count. V2 adds alternative-initializer controls, individual optimization-loss ablations, Vina-score removal, refinement of other methods, RMSD distributions, strain/clash diagnostics, runtime scaling analyses, and a hydrogen-bond convergence case study.

E5.justification: Table S6 adds descriptive Pearson correlation estimates between runtime and ligand complexity. Existing mean-plus-spread reporting continues; no repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or formal significance tests are added.

Existing values also change: FMA-PO without pocket has mean RMSD 1.456 Å in v1 Table S5 versus 1.88 Å in v2 Table S10. Accurate-and-PoseBusters-valid rates change from 35% to 38% for FMA and 39% to 51% for FMA-PO in v1 Figure S6 versus v2 Figure S11, without documented setting changes.

M1.justification: The flow-matching architecture, harmonic prior, training objective, pose-selection variants, and two-phase coordinate optimization remain unchanged. Appendix B.2 provides additional hydrogen-bond modeling details without establishing a changed procedure.

P1.justification: The main narrative remains largely verbatim. Local changes include expanded pharmacophore explanations, reorganized Appendix D subsections, updated cross-references, small wording corrections, an acknowledgment, and the conference footer.

P2.justification: V2 adds a detailed model schematic, hydrogen-bond trajectory panels, RMSD distribution and strain-energy plots, and numerous comparison, runtime, and ablation tables. It expands the loss-ablation table, adds the previously reported FMA scores to Table 1, redraws the PoseBusters display, and relocates retained figures.

R1.justification: V2 adds references supporting GenBench3D strain analysis, group-ligand docking, and the GAR Tfase case study. It also develops an empirical comparison with the already-cited HarmonicFlow. Section 2 and the broader research positioning remain largely unchanged.

T1.justification: The flow-matching derivation, harmonic-prior definition, Gaussian-overlap formulas, and internal-energy equations are retained. The added hydrogen-bond discussion supplies mechanistic explanation rather than a new formal result or proof.

improvement.justification: V1 only partly isolated the sources of the reported gains. V2's common-refinement initialization controls and loss/scoring ablations substantially strengthen evidence for the distinct contributions of FMA and PO. Physical-quality diagnostics and runtime analysis also clarify practical limitations. Although some revised appendix values remain unexplained, these targeted additions materially improve experimental support and interpretability while retaining the original headline results.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same FMA-PO method and AlignDockBench study. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices A–D are readable and support reliable comparison across relocations and renumbering.

after.justification: V2 retains these original results and adds comparator experiments, component analyses, physical-quality measurements, and a hydrogen-bond optimization case study.

before.justification: V1 reports original docking and alignment results, runtimes, PoseBusters evaluations, redocking experiments, and component ablations in Table 1 and Appendix D.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same novelty, temporal watermarking, inversion-bound, and quality/detectability claims. The headline 61.96% context-FID and 8.44% correlation improvements remain unchanged. Replacing 'sampling-time' with 'generation-time' does not substantively redefine the contribution.

C2.justification: v3 interprets the new approximation measurements as supporting epsilon-exact inversion and extends its utility discussion to imputation and signal preservation. Appendix E.12 argues that measured latency is acceptable for streaming and identifies variable-length hashing without padding as future work. The original limitation concerning native streaming and per-timestep watermarking remains.

D1.justification: v3 discloses valid-bit handling for L > 2, specifies the retained forecasting experiment's 24-step horizon, and identifies the NVIDIA L40S hardware used for the new detection-timing experiment. Original training hardware, PyTorch version, data split, sampling information, and stated code link are retained.

E1.justification: v3 retains the five original datasets and adds ILI/Illness and Weather evaluations (Appendix E.7). It also adds downstream imputation and detection in mixtures of real, unwatermarked synthetic, and watermarked synthetic data, substantially extending task and test-scenario coverage.

E2.justification: Matched comparisons retain TR, GS, HTW, TabWak, and TabWak-transpose, with unchanged comparator membership in the BDIA controls and ablations. New benchmark evaluations reuse these methods; mixed-data detection uses GS and TabWak-transpose, already compared in the original TPR evaluations. TimesNet and TSG-Bench supply datasets or metrics, not new competing methods.

Retained experiments preserve their stated settings; the newly specified forecasting horizon is additional documentation.

E4.justification: v3 adds direct measurement of the x1 versus x0 approximation gap over 10,000 samples (Table 3), mixed-provenance detection analysis (Table 16), marginal/autocorrelation/skewness/kurtosis preservation analysis (Table 17), and detection-cost profiling (Table 24). Existing component ablations, attack tests, and interval/bit-length sensitivity studies are retained.

E5.justification: Appendix E.9 specifies 100 trials for the new mixed-data evaluation, adding experiment-specific repetition information. The original 100-trial attack evaluation, 50-round simulation, and uncertainty reporting remain unchanged; no increase in repetitions for retained experiments or new confidence-interval procedure is established.

E6.justification: Existing tabulated and plotted results are unchanged, while six new tables add substantial results. Examples include ILI and Weather Z-scores of 151.03 and 205.53, mixed-data TPR of 0.99–1.00 with 20 samples, imputation errors, approximation gaps, signal-characteristic measurements, and detection times of 1.50–7.47 seconds. These are additional evaluations, not same-setting improvements over v1.

M1.justification: Temporal chained hashing, seed shuffling, Gaussian mapping, BDIA-DDIM inversion, and detection remain unchanged. The added statement about using TabWak's valid-bit mechanism for L > 2 accompanies unchanged bit-sweep results and does not establish a procedural revision.

P1.justification: v3 lightly copyedits the prose, standardizes terminology, and expands the pipeline overview. It fills the previously empty nomenclature section, adjusts appendix headings, and updates affiliations and acknowledgments. The main narrative and most retained explanatory passages remain substantially intact.

P2.justification: v3 adds six result tables and a nomenclature display, places existing appendix tables alongside their associated discussions, and collects the synthetic-sample figures in Appendix F. The twelve existing figures are retained, with limited caption corrections rather than new plotted content. This substantially reorganizes the appendix presentation.

R1.justification: v3 adds TSG-Bench for the signal-characteristic metrics and TimesNet for the additional datasets. The positioning against earlier watermarking methods remains substantially unchanged. Updated publication metadata and consolidation of duplicate BDIA references do not constitute additional research-positioning changes.

T1.justification: Theorem 3.1, its Lipschitz assumption, and the Appendix C derivation retain the same mathematical content. The nomenclature list consolidates existing notation, and the new approximation-gap table supplies empirical evidence rather than a new theorem, assumption, or proof correction.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens empirical support for central aspects left less directly tested in v1: the initialization approximation, preservation of temporal statistics, and detection when real data are present (Tables 3, 16, and 17). Added imputation, dataset, and runtime evaluations improve evidence for practical usefulness, while implementation disclosures improve reproducibility. These gains retain the original results; the empirical checks do not resolve the unchanged formal proof or establish native streaming support.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe TimeWak, with matching methods, main experiments, and theoretical analysis. Their complete text, tables, figures, and appendices support reliable comparison, including matching relocated material.

after.justification: v3 retains those original results and adds dataset evaluations, imputation, mixed-data detection, signal-preservation measurements, approximation-error measurements, and runtime results.

before.justification: v1 reports original experiments on five datasets, including generation quality, watermark detection, attacks, forecasting, ablations, and simulations.

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution bullets, and conclusion retain the same claims of a training-free, transferable attack across eight detectors with limited text-quality degradation. The headline 87.88% average detection-rate reduction is unchanged; the new experiments support existing claims.

C2.justification: v2 adds explicit qualifications about occasional failures and backfires, explains MAGE's higher latency through its LongFormer architecture, and motivates the default masking parameters through effectiveness, quality, and speed tradeoffs. It also interprets the reduced SBERT similarity as acceptable. These extend practical interpretation without replacing the original transferability explanation.

D1.justification: v2 adds batching disclosures, detector architecture and parameter-size information, and the explanation that k=50 follows the HuggingFace default. The exact larger batch size used for the main experiments remains unspecified. The project link, generation and judging prompts, and two-A6000 hardware disclosure are retained.

E1.justification: Both versions use MAGE human and AI texts, KGW and Unigram watermarked derivatives, and the LLaMA2-generated KGW dataset for the watermark-stealing comparison. The added evaluations remain within this existing data and task coverage.

E2.justification: The corresponding comparisons retain simple paraphrasing, two- and three-round recursive paraphrasing, and watermark stealing with Mistral-7B and LLaMA2-7B. The eight deployed detectors also remain unchanged. SBERT is added as an evaluation measure, not an attack baseline.

E3.justification: v2 adds runtime evaluation on 100 texts at batch size 1, separate 500-text masking and guidance-frequency sweeps, and SBERT cosine similarity for quality evaluation. Appendix E adds a fixed 0.5 detection-threshold analysis over 24,000 neural-detector transfer cases. These substantially extend the evaluation design while retaining the original main-experiment settings.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's guidance-detector comparisons and quality analyses, v2 tests sensitivity to top-p and top-k in Section 4.4 and guidance frequency in Appendix D. It also adds output-length checks for timing comparisons, SBERT semantic-preservation analysis, and a sample-level failure/backfire audit in Appendix E.

E5.justification: v1 already reports means and standard deviations for quality measures. v2 additionally specifies five trials per configuration for the new runtime experiment and reports variability across those trials. This does not establish additional runs of the retained detection experiments; no new formal significance tests are reported.

E6.justification: The main Table 2 and watermark-stealing results are unchanged, but substantial new results appear in Tables 3, 4, 6, 8, and 10. For example, runtime is 7.18 ± 0.13 seconds for simple paraphrasing versus 10.20 ± 0.18 with RoBERTa-Large guidance; corresponding SBERT similarities are 0.8601 ± 0.0880 and 0.8082 ± 0.1006. Appendix E reports 995 threshold-crossing backfires among 24,000 transfer cases. These are newly reported evaluations, not improvements over v1 under the same settings.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1, the paraphraser prompt, and the default decoding procedure remain unchanged. Appendix D adds an evaluated inference variant that performs N−1 ordinary sampling steps followed by one detector-guided step. This limited procedural adaptation is used for ablation; it does not replace the main method.

P1.justification: Localized rewrites clarify that human-likeness refers to detector scores. v2 adds experimental subsections and appendices, expands the quality-evaluation overview, and updates conference and acknowledgment text. Most existing prose and the main narrative sequence are retained.

P2.justification: v2 substantially expands the tabular presentation with runtime, masking-sensitivity, SBERT, output-length, and guidance-frequency tables. Figure 5 is reformatted with clearer legend labels and spacing. The detailed quality-rating table moves from v1 Table 13 to v2 Table 11 beside its discussion; its values and the existing example tables are retained.

R1.justification: v2 adds the Sentence-BERT reference by Reimers and Gurevych for its semantic-similarity evaluation. The related-work discussion and positioning relative to paraphrasing attacks, watermark stealing, controlled generation, and BEAST otherwise remain substantively unchanged.

T1.justification: The mathematical definitions of the paraphraser and detector and the token-selection formulation remain unchanged. Neither version supplies formal transferability theorems or proofs. The added SBERT measure and ablations do not introduce a new theoretical argument.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens empirical validation by addressing v1's unmeasured runtime, untested decoding-parameter choices, and lack of quantified backfire analysis. Sections 4.3–4.4 and Appendices B, D, and E make practical costs and failure behavior assessable, while SBERT adds evidence about semantic preservation. These additions expose tradeoffs without removing the original evidence. Quality assessment remains automated, and the retained claims of statistical nonsignificance still lack a reported formal test.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Adversarial Paraphrasing work. Their text, algorithms, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support comparison, including matching relocated and renumbered content.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds runtime measurements, sensitivity experiments, semantic-similarity measurements, and failure analysis.

before.justification: v1 reports original detector-evasion experiments, automated text-quality evaluations, and a watermark-stealing comparison in Appendix A.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction’s contribution list, and conclusion retain the same central claims: reward-robustness duality, kernel lower bounds, limitations for kernel robustness and risk aversion, and rollout-sensitive robustness to structured perturbations. Added evidence supports these existing claims.

C2.justification: v3 explicitly qualifies the new baseline comparison: success against spatially correlated perturbations does not imply consistent superiority over robust RL methods. It also states applicability to continuous spaces under mild regularity assumptions and delineates the finite-state scope of A.7. Existing risk-aversion, sampling, and training-stability limitations remain.

D1.justification: Appendices B.3–B.4 document the added baseline tuning, checkpoint selection, goal sampling, and Ant reward, termination, entropy-feature, and obstacle settings. The code-access address changes from an anonymized repository to an identified GitHub repository; code availability was already stated in v1. Core implementation and hardware/runtime disclosures remain.

E1.justification: v3 adds Ant locomotion with an unobservable barrier requiring hurdling, extending coverage beyond MiniGrid navigation and Pusher manipulation. It also adds continuous reward-location perturbations in Pusher; v1 tested reward relocation only in MiniGrid.

E2.justification: The Pusher obstacle comparison in Figure 5(a) adds PRMDP and NRMDP to the retained unregularized, policy-entropy, and state-entropy methods. Both new comparators appear in the plotted results and have implementation settings in Appendix B.3, introducing explicit action-robust RL comparisons.

E3.justification: New protocols include 200 sampled Pusher goals at each displacement radius 0.1 and 0.15, modified Ant rewards and termination conditions, and obstacle-crossing success evaluation. Added robust baselines use 256-unit networks, hyperparameter sweeps, and checkpoint selection described in B.3. These are additions; retained experiment protocols are largely unchanged.

E4.justification: Robustness analysis gains tests of continuous goal-displacement magnitude in Pusher and barrier crossing in Ant. These extend the existing robustness questions. The rollout-budget, temperature, warm-start, and state/policy-entropy distillation analyses are retained without substantive redesign.

E5.justification: Both versions report 96% confidence bounds across 25 seeds and 200 evaluation episodes for the main experiments. The added Ant figure follows this practice, and the appendix distillation plots retain mean-plus-standard-deviation reporting. No changed empirical uncertainty-estimation procedure or repeated-run count is disclosed.

E6.justification: Figures 5–6 add substantial results for Pusher reward shifts, Ant obstacles, and action-robust comparators. Figure 5(a) reports approximately 0.02/0.03 obstacle success for PRMDP/NRMDP versus 0.37 for state entropy. State entropy also leads the added reward-shift and Ant comparisons. Retained experiments preserve their qualitative conclusions.

M1.justification: Appendix B.1 retains the same k-nearest-neighbor entropy bonus, intrinsic-reward discounting, and cosine temperature schedule. Joint state/policy-entropy training is also retained. The additional environments apply the existing procedure.

P1.justification: Edits are localized: clarified uncertainty-set wording and spatial-perturbation terminology, expanded experimental descriptions, relocation of the CVaR definition to Appendix A.6, and added acknowledgments and a NeurIPS checklist. The main narrative and most existing prose remain intact.

P2.justification: Figure 5 expands from three to four panels and adds baseline series; a new three-panel Figure 6 presents Ant results. Existing appendix figures are retained and renumbered. Table 1, the counterexample diagram, and surrounding text are repositioned, with additional title-page formatting changes.

R1.justification: v3 adds references on f-policy gradients, multi-agent exploration, empirical-distribution concentration, and entropy continuity, plus focused positioning against action-robust RL. Most related-work discussion is retained. The new PRMDP/NRMDP discussion cites reference [6], but that entry is a recommender-system paper, leaving an attribution mismatch.

T1.justification: New Appendix A.7 adds Corollaries A.1–A.2 and proofs extending reward and kernel robustness bounds to empirical entropy estimates. These introduce explicit finite-state estimation-error penalties and high-probability guarantees under an occupancy-estimation assumption. v1 discusses sample sensitivity but lacks these formal extensions.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens support for its retained claims. Appendix A.7 addresses the exact-versus-estimated-entropy gap in finite-state settings, while Ant, continuous reward shifts, and explicit robust-RL comparators address important gaps in empirical coverage. The mismatched baseline citation and stale ablation-panel references introduce documentation defects, but these do not outweigh the theoretical and evidential gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same study and contain readable main text, equations, figures, references, and Appendices A–B. Retained material can be matched across relocation and renumbering.

after.justification: v3 retains these experiments and adds Ant evaluations, Pusher reward-shift results, and comparisons with action-robust baselines.

before.justification: v1 reports original MiniGrid and Pusher experiments, including perturbation evaluations, rollout and temperature ablations, and entropy-distillation experiments.

C1.justification: The introduction adds a principal finding that noisy retrieval and open-ended questions reduce knowledge-update effectiveness, and qualifies existing domain/model comparisons as multiple-choice results. The abstract, contribution list, and conclusion otherwise retain the taxonomy, KScope, feature-analysis, and augmentation claims.

C2.justification: V2 adds explanations involving refusals and misleading context, including Gemma's increased absent knowledge without answer options. It explicitly confines the feature and augmentation analyses to gold-context multiple choice and revises the limitations after testing noisy retrieval and open-ended questions. Existing feature-based interpretations remain largely unchanged.

D1.justification: V2 specifies the top-ten-paragraph input and gemma-2-9b-it clustering model for its added experiments. Existing hardware, sampling settings, regression details, appendix prompts, and code-access information are retained; the code link is relocated. Retrieval and clustering implementation details remain brief.

E1.justification: The four datasets remain unchanged, but v2 substantially extends HotpotQA coverage to noisy retrieved context and open-ended answering without predefined options. V1 evaluated three-option questions, using gold supporting evidence for contextual knowledge. These additions change both input conditions and task requirements.

E2.justification: The context-augmentation comparisons retain original context, credibility enhancement, naive summarization, constrained summarization, and their combined strategy. Appendix C retains the majority-class dummy comparator for logistic regression. The additional HotpotQA evaluations reuse the existing nine target LLMs without introducing a competing characterization method.

E3.justification: Sections 5.2–5.3 introduce substantial additional evaluation protocols: supplying the top ten retrieved Wikipedia paragraphs and evaluating free-form responses through semantic clustering with gemma-2-9b-it. Existing experiments retain their settings, including temperature 1, 100 responses, 20 question paraphrases, and the original regression evaluation procedure.

E4.justification: V2 adds systematic tests of sensitivity to retrieval quality and answer format across nine LLMs. Figure 5 compares these conditions, while Appendix B Figures 18–19 examine transitions from each initial knowledge status. These analyses test robustness beyond v1's gold-context multiple-choice setting; existing sensitivity and augmentation analyses remain.

E5.justification: Neither version introduces a different repeated-run, seed, confidence-interval, or uncertainty-reporting practice. The KScope significance threshold, Bonferroni procedures, correlation significance annotations, and response-sampling counts are retained. The additional experiments do not introduce a new statistical reporting procedure.

E6.justification: Matched original results are unchanged, but v2 adds extensive status distributions and transition results. For Llama-8B on HotpotQA, Figure 5 newly reports 66.6% consistent-correct knowledge with noisy multiple-choice context and 88.6% with open-ended gold context, alongside the retained 95.2% for multiple-choice gold context. These are different experimental conditions, not same-setting performance changes.

M1.justification: The four-stage KScope procedure, response sampling, and context-augmentation methods are unchanged. Semantic clustering for open-ended responses was already specified in v1 Section 3.2; v2 evaluates that existing capability and identifies its clustering model rather than introducing a new method component.

P1.justification: V2 consolidates the original distribution and transition discussion into Section 5.1 and organizes new Sections 5.2–5.3 around evaluation settings. It adds scope qualifications, revises limitations, and updates the publication footer. Most prose and the overall narrative structure remain intact.

P2.justification: V2 adds Figure 5, combining two retained HotpotQA distributions with three new distributions, and adds appendix transition plots in Figures 18–19. Existing plots receive explicit setting labels and revised captions, with subsequent renumbering and reflow. The established visual designs are largely retained.

R1.justification: The reference list is identical, and the central novelty positioning is retained. Section 2 makes a limited substantive positioning change: the work now examines knowledge updates under both gold and noisy retrieval, whereas v1 described a gold-retrieval setting.

T1.justification: Sections 3.1–3.3 and Figure 2 retain the same knowledge-mode definition, five status conditions, empirical distribution estimator, statistical hypotheses, and hierarchical testing logic. No new mathematical assumptions, derivations, theorems, or proofs accompany the added evaluations.

improvement.justification: V1 explicitly left open-ended evaluation and noisy retrieval untested despite claiming broader applicability. V2 addresses both gaps across nine LLMs in Sections 5.2–5.3 and Appendix B, providing evidence of applicability and revealing important failure conditions beyond idealized evaluation. This substantially strengthens the paper's empirical support. The gains remain bounded by the HotpotQA-only extensions, brief retrieval/clustering documentation, and unchanged gold-context scope of the feature and augmentation analyses.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same KScope research work. Their main text, equations, figures, references, and appendices A–D are readable and support reliable matching across the revisions.

after.justification: V2 retains those original empirical results and adds noisy-context and open-ended HotpotQA evaluations, including detailed knowledge-status transitions in Appendix B.

before.justification: V1 reports original experiments characterizing nine LLMs across four datasets, feature-importance analyses, context-augmentation experiments, and supplementary results in the appendices.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the central claims of training-free, API-compatible DP image synthesis through textual intermediaries and image-space voting. The new evaluations support these existing contributions rather than redefine them. Changing headline FID inequalities to equalities does not alter the central scientific claim.

C2.justification: Appendix D newly attributes poor Cat/bird performance to low diversity rather than small sample size alone, adding a substantive applicability boundary. Section 4.3 links downstream gains to synthetic-data diversity. Section 7 explicitly acknowledges higher computational demands than PE and argues that diversity and generalization benefits justify the cost.

D1.justification: v3 newly supplies a code-release link and substantially expands resource disclosures. Section 7 replaces the brief 80 GB hardware statement with approximately 70 GB peak memory, 19 hours on an A800 or 15.5 hours on two A100s, PE resource comparisons, and token budgets. It also documents the new classifier and bird-subset construction; most existing hyperparameter tables are retained.

E2.justification: Table 1 adds DP-finetune comparisons on LSUN Bedroom, Cat, European Art, Wave-ui-25k, and Sprite Fright; v1 compares only SPTI and PE there, although DP-finetune already appears on MM-CelebA-HQ. The new classification evaluation also includes a classifier trained on real data as a reference alongside PE-generated data.
