Appendix D introduces a controlled design crossing two versus twenty bird classes with 200 versus 2,000 images. For retained Cat experiments, the reported lookahead degree changes from 8 to 4 for both SPTI and PE; this does not itself establish rerunning.

E4.justification: New Appendix D investigates whether the Cat failure reflects limited diversity or small dataset size through controlled bird experiments. Appendix B.3 adds training/test learning curves and comparative generated-face examples. The retained API-choice ablation also gains an Infinity backend in Table 4.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or formal significance tests for the empirical results. Added training curves and experimental conditions do not introduce uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: Numerous FID values and trajectories are revised. At epsilon=1, Table 1 changes LSUN Bedroom from 26.71 to 26.39 and European Art from 50.78 to 57.64. Table 2 reverses the SPTI backbone ranking: LDM versus SDXL changes from 37.96 versus 33.27 to 33.41 versus 34.17. New baseline, classification, bird, and Infinity results substantially expand the evidence. Cat changes cannot be treated as same-setting gains because its reported lookahead changes.

M1.justification: The central SPTI pipeline is retained. Algorithm 2 makes limited computational corrections: lookahead variations take the current caption population instead of N, embeddings are averaged without the extra Phi operation, and population expansion uses L-1 instead of K-1. These establish corrections to the specified algorithm, without establishing an implementation change.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main narrative structure are retained. v3 inserts a downstream-task subsection and new appendix analyses, expands the computational-overhead discussion, and makes local wording, citation, affiliation, and venue edits. Existing configuration and dataset appendices move from D/E to E/F.

P2.justification: Figure 1 redraws the SPTI flow to show private images as references for evolving random captions. Appendix FID plots are redrawn and reorganized into paired layouts. v3 adds classification and learning-curve figures, comparative face panels, and the bird-results table, while expanding Table 1 with baseline rows and Table 4 with an Infinity column.

R1.justification: v3 adds Kong and Syed's concurrent caption-based private photo-album synthesis and explicitly distinguishes its hierarchical fine-tuning from SPTI's API-based image voting. It also adds a Struct-Bench citation. The broader related-work organization and positioning remain largely unchanged.

T1.justification: The formal DP definition, Wasserstein formulation, histogram-sensitivity argument, Gaussian calibration and composition equation, and postprocessing guarantee are retained. No new theorem, proof, or substantive revision to the privacy reasoning appears.

improvement.justification: v1 primarily validated utility through FID and left the Cat failure unexplained. v3 adds direct downstream-utility evidence, a controlled diversity-versus-size investigation, broader DP-finetuning comparisons, and explicit computational costs, substantially improving empirical support and applicability assessment. Reporting consistency weakens because the abstract retains the earlier 26.71/33.27 headline values despite revised Tables 1–2. That defect limits numerical clarity but does not outweigh the substantive gains in validation and limitations analysis.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SPTI research work. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable, and retained material can be matched across renumbering and relocation.

after.justification: v3 retains original synthesis experiments and adds CelebA classification results, bird-dataset experiments, and further model-backend results.

before.justification: v1 reports original image-synthesis experiments, including FID comparisons across six datasets and image-voting and model-backend ablations.

The abstract adds an explicit low-data comparison claiming that π0 fails completely. This strengthens the comparative claim, although Table 4 reports 3.8% success for π0 trained with ten demonstrations.

C2.justification: v2 substantially expands mechanism and failure interpretation. Section 4.3 attributes heatmap benefits to denser supervision, spatial priors, and alignment, and interprets positional-feature degradation through feature-distribution shift. Appendix C.2 proposes explanations involving π0 overfitting and ACT's spatial generalization. Earlier limitations involving occlusion, long-horizon tasks, and unseen object categories remain.

D1.justification: Appendix A adds RTX 4090 inference hardware and timing information. Section 4.3 documents 309M versus 303M decoder sizes, the regression loss, positional-feature construction, and tuning details for the new controls. Existing BridgeVLA hyperparameters, freezing rules, training resources, and project access information remain unchanged.

Table 1 also adds direct-regression and positional-feature controls. The earlier pre-training comparator remains in Figure 3.

The original simulation protocols and BridgeVLA training budgets remain unchanged.

E4.justification: New Section 4.3 tests two central architectural choices: heatmaps versus direct position regression, and excluding versus injecting per-pixel 3D position features. Appendix C.2 adds qualitative baseline failure analyses. The pre-training ablation and existing robustness and object-grounding analyses are retained, rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: Appendix A newly specifies that inference latency is averaged over 100 trials. Existing simulation repetition and seed counts, and their uncertainty-reporting practices, remain unchanged. Additional ablation rows reuse the existing reporting style; no confidence intervals or significance tests are added.

E6.justification: New RLBench ablations report 31.4% and 56.2% versus retained BridgeVLA performance of 88.2%. Table 4 adds SpatialVLA results of 3.1%/28.5%, π0 at 3.8%, and ACT at 22.3%, versus BridgeVLA at 96.9%. Revised Basic counts yield 95.4% with three demonstrations under ten-trial evaluation, replacing v1's five-trial results; this is not a demonstrated same-setting performance loss. Average ranks change with the expanded Table 1 comparison, and Appendix A adds 0.21-second inference latency.

M1.justification: The proposed BridgeVLA architecture, heatmap pre-training, multi-view projection, action losses, and coarse-to-fine inference remain unchanged. The direct-regression and positional-feature variants introduced in Section 4.3 are experimental controls, not revisions to the proposed method.

P1.justification: The abstract and real-robot discussion are rewritten, architectural ablations are grouped in new Section 4.3, and Appendix C gains a Basic Setting subsection. Appendix A is renamed to include inference details. These are localized narrative changes; most existing sections and explanations remain intact.

P2.justification: Table 1 gains two ablation rows and an expanded caption, and a new Table 4 displays real-robot baseline results. Existing tables and surrounding text reflow, including separation of the appendix COLOSSEUM tables across pages. All 14 figures retain their substantive visual content.

R1.justification: The related-work section is retained, while Sections 4.2–4.3 and Appendix C.2 expand positioning against SpatialVLA, π0, and ACT in low-data learning. The CLIP reference is removed. The replacement π0 entry at reference 52 duplicates the work already cited as reference 6, rather than introducing a new unique cited work.

T1.justification: The policy and action definitions, truncated Gaussian heatmaps, normalization, and loss equations remain unchanged. New architectural explanations and empirical ablations introduce no formal assumptions, propositions, proofs, or mathematical derivations.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses two important evidential gaps in v1: direct real-robot comparisons with VLA methods and tests of the central heatmap and input-alignment design choices. Table 4 and Section 4.3 substantially strengthen support for the paper's data-efficiency and architectural claims. Reporting weaknesses temper this gain: the introduction retains 96.8% despite revised results of 95.4%, the RLBench prose retains an outdated rank, and the abstract overstates π0's failure. These inconsistencies do not outweigh the stronger experimental support.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same BridgeVLA work. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and can be matched across relocation and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds architectural ablations, real-robot baseline comparisons, and an inference-time measurement.

before.justification: v1 reports original simulation evaluations, real-robot success rates, and a pre-training ablation in Section 4 and Appendices B–C.

results.title: BridgeVLA: Input-Output Alignment for Efficient 3D Manipulation Learning with Vision-Language Models

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the central claims about advance reasoning-strength planning, directional activation control, termination-token effects, and two potential applications. The added concluding sentence restates the existing contribution.

C2.justification: v2 extends the termination-logit explanation to reflection-token modulation and interprets termination-logit changes as consequences of planning in Appendix C.5. Appendix E adds generalization interpretations, explains the 1.5B model's code-execution behavior through instruction-following failures and truncation, and acknowledges code-generation scoring difficulties. Section 6 nevertheless retains its now-outdated statement that other backbones are unexplored.

D1.justification: The new appendices document the multiplicative logit intervention and its tested factors, plus the narrower Llama steering range. Existing hardware, compute-cost, generation, probing, prompt, and code-access disclosures remain unchanged; detailed benchmark-specific reproduction instructions are not added.

E1.justification: Appendix E.1 adds scientific question answering on GPQA Diamond and both code execution and code generation on LiveCodeBench. These substantially extend the retained mathematical, MMLU, and AlpacaEval coverage. Code-generation evaluation reports reasoning length without accuracy.

E2.justification: Appendix C.5 adds direct multiplication of the </think> logit as an evaluated alternative/control to activation steering, with results in Table 3. Existing comparisons remain; the newly cited steering methods are not added as evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: v2 expands evaluation to DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B, using a steering range of -0.02 to 0.02, and introduces direct-logit interventions with gamma values 0.8, 1, and 2. These are additional evaluation settings, not revisions to the retained experiments' 9:1 split, generation temperature, or token budget.

E4.justification: Appendix C.5 adds substantive mechanism tests: effects on reflection-related token logits and whether manipulating only the termination-token logit reproduces steering behavior. These go beyond v1's comparison with EOS and random-token logits. Existing sensitivity plots and case studies are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions specify eight rollouts per question and the same accuracy-averaging procedure in Appendix A. v2 introduces no new seed information, confidence intervals, significance tests, or uncertainty-reporting procedure.

E6.justification: Table 1 and the original plotted results are unchanged, but Tables 2–10 add substantial numerical evidence. Examples include Llama probing correlations of 0.8423–0.8481 and MATH500 accuracies of 0–0.15% under direct logit scaling with gamma 0.8. These are newly reported experiments, not improvements over corresponding v1 results.

M1.justification: Both versions use the same Lasso probes, difficulty-based difference-in-means vectors, and additive activation steering. The additional model evaluations and logit-only control do not revise the proposed method.

P1.justification: Most existing prose remains unchanged. v2 adds acknowledgments, short explanatory insertions, and a Discussion appendix. The existing case studies move from D.2.2 to E.2.1, and Broader Impacts moves from Appendix E to F.

P2.justification: New Tables 2–10 substantially expand the visual presentation of mechanism controls, domain evaluations, and Llama probing and steering. Existing Figures 1–24 and Table 1 are retained, with limited spacing, pagination, and case-study placement changes.

R1.justification: v2 adds ten references, including representation-learning and steering work in Section 2.3 and LiveCodeBench for the new evaluation. The central novelty distinction from directions extracted using generated reasoning traces remains unchanged.

T1.justification: The regression, direction-vector, steering, and prediction equations remain equivalent. No theorem, proof, formal assumption, or derivation is added. The new logit-scaling formula specifies an experimental control.

improvement.justification: The added Llama experiments directly address v1's explicit lack of evidence beyond Qwen backbones. GPQA and coding evaluations broaden the empirical basis, while Appendix C.5 tests whether steering effects reduce to termination-logit manipulation. Together these substantially strengthen validation of the central claims. Missing code-generation accuracy, limited new experimental documentation, and the outdated limitations paragraph temper but do not outweigh these gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support reliable matching despite pagination changes and added appendices.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds logit controls, GPQA and LiveCodeBench evaluations, and experiments on a Llama-based reasoning model.

before.justification: v1 reports original linear-probing, activation-steering, token-logit, overthinking-detection, and efficient-inference experiments.

results.title: On Reasoning Strength Planning in Large Reasoning Models

C1.justification: V1 centers its contribution on combining cross-modal embeddings with unimodal experts while preserving alignment. V2's abstract, introduction, and contribution list broaden this to a general framework for unifying complementary cluster structures and constructing joint kernels for paired multimodal data. Cross-modal/unimodal fusion becomes a key application of that broader claim.

C2.justification: V2 adds substantive qualifications about signed kernels, hyperparameter dependence, larger fused dimensions, and dimensional comparability, with PCA suggested when compactness is required. It explicitly confines learned unitary alignment to cross-modal clustering. New discussion also explains where concatenation remains competitive and conditions the parallel-inference argument on sufficient memory.

D1.justification: V2 adds a project-code access link, explicit projection dimensions in experimental descriptions and table captions, separate profiling hardware and batch-size details, and unimodal-fusion pseudocode. These are incremental reproducibility disclosures; the original encoder choices, C-search range, and general two-RTX-4090 setup remain. Newly specified dimensions do not establish changes to earlier runs.

E1.justification: V2 adds multimodal classification on MVSA-Single and MVSA-Multiple, class-conditional ImageNet generation using DiT-XL/2, and a six-group profession/gender image-text clustering example using SD-XL Turbo outputs. These extend the represented data and task requirements beyond v1's retained classification, clustering, retrieval, and few-shot coverage.

E2.justification: V2 adds plain concatenation comparisons across classification and clustering in C.8, MobileCLIP and OpenVision comparison rows in Table 9, and CLIP-based c-VSG as the diffusion comparator in Table 12. COMM is not new: its results in v1's appendix Table 3 are incorporated into v2's main Table 1.

E3.justification: New evaluation protocols include diffusion assessment using precision, recall, density, and coverage, plus runtime and peak-memory benchmarking with batch size 128 on two RTX 3090 GPUs, including parallel RP-KrossFuse with projection dimension 5000. ImageNet testing also adds backbone configurations. These are additional protocols; the PDFs do not establish changes to the retained experiments' settings.

E4.justification: V2 expands backbone generalization analysis in C.6, adds inference and fusion efficiency profiling in C.7, and investigates when concatenation versus product fusion helps across supervised classification and unsupervised clustering in C.8. Figure 2 adds a complementary image-text clustering case study. The original expert, kernel, projection-dimension, and hyperparameter-C ablations remain.

E5.justification: The new checklist states that results average multiple runs and asserts small observed variance, while explicitly acknowledging absent error bars and significance tests. V1 already reports five-fold cross-validation for text experiments but lacks this general repeated-run disclosure. V2 supplies neither run counts nor seeds, and does not establish that more runs were performed.

E6.justification: Matched earlier benchmark tables retain their numerical values, but v2 adds substantial results in Tables 9–12 and C.8. Examples include MVSA-Single accuracy of 74.3% versus concatenation's 71.3%, and diffusion recall of 0.484 versus CLIP-based c-VSG's 0.413. Figure 1 also gains clustering scores. These are newly reported comparisons, not same-setting improvements over v1.

M1.justification: Appendix C.9 adds an inference adaptation that replaces CLIP embeddings inside contextualized Vendi Score Guidance with fused CLIP and DINOv2 representations. The core product-kernel, symmetrization, random-projection, and Fourier-feature constructions remain unchanged. The new unimodal pseudocode documents an existing case; the earlier cross-modal algorithm moves to Appendix A.5.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, contribution framing, and conclusion are extensively rewritten. V2 adds a limitations discussion, a related-work subsection, Appendix C.7–C.9, acknowledgments, and a conference checklist. It also moves cross-modal pseudocode to the appendix and foregrounds unimodal fusion, substantially changing the narrative structure.

P2.justification: V2 adds the generated image-text comparison in Figure 2, redraws the fusion schematic as Figure 3, and annotates Figure 1 with clustering scores. It brings existing appendix comparisons into the main text, expands Table 9, adds Tables 10–12, and adopts a different conference layout. Most earlier appendix visualizations are retained and reformatted.

R1.justification: V2 explicitly attributes the kernel-product/Kronecker identity to established kernel literature and adds a related-work subsection connecting the framework to generative-model evaluation and guidance, including KID and Vendi-based approaches. This substantially broadens research positioning beyond v1's emphasis on representation fusion and cross-modal alignment.

T1.justification: Theorem 1 changes its error bound from sqrt(B log(4n/delta)/l) to sqrt(2 B^2 log(2n^2/delta)/l). Appendix A.3 correspondingly revises the Hoeffding exponent and union-bound algebra. This is a localized mathematical revision; the propositions, feature-map constructions, and Theorem 2 remain substantively unchanged.

improvement.justification: V2 addresses two important gaps in v1: comparison against plain concatenation and measured computational evidence for scalability (C.7–C.8). These strengthen the justification for the fusion operation and clarify its practical value. Broader backbone checks and explicit applicability limitations further improve the paper. New application experiments remain sparsely documented and uncertainty is unquantified, but these limitations do not outweigh the substantial gains in comparative evidence and transparency.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same KrossFuse/RP-KrossFuse research despite the changed title and broader framing in v2. The methods, equations, results, figures, and appendices support reliable matching and comparison.

after.justification: V2 retains these empirical results and adds backbone comparisons, computational benchmarks, MVSA classification, and diffusion-guidance experiments.

before.justification: V1 reports original clustering, classification, image-text retrieval, few-shot learning, and ablation results in Section 6 and Appendix C.

results.title: When Kernels Multiply, Clusters Unify: Fusing Embeddings with the Kronecker Product

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contribution statements, and conclusion retain the same scientific claims: adaptive conditional computation, preference-driven training, plug-and-play integration, superior performance, and generalization. Additional appendix evidence does not redefine these headline contributions.

C2.justification: V3 adds substantive explanations linking PL to lower gradient variance, attributing the failure of neutralized pairs to lost supervision, and discussing expert capacity versus data volume. It also interprets the DPO and scalarization comparisons and explicitly acknowledges higher GPU memory consumption. The original limitations concerning complex constraints and large problems remain.

D1.justification: V3 replaces v1's future-release promise with a code/data repository link and an MIT release statement, documents the DPO reference-model procedure and training times, and reports GPU memory requirements. Table 17 revises three baseline licenses to 'No license' and adds PMOCO. However, the checklist still promises future release, leaving availability statements internally inconsistent.

E1.justification: V3 Appendix J extends evaluation to Bi-TSP and Bi-KP instances with 300, 500, and 1,000 nodes or items. This adds larger input-scale scenarios within retained task families; the original routing, knapsack, and KroAB coverage remains.

E2.justification: DPO, cited but not evaluated in v1, becomes an actual comparator in v3 Appendix K and Table 10 on Bi-TSP sizes 20–200. The comparator sets in the original benchmark tables remain unchanged.

E3.justification: V3 adds substantive experimental controls: DPO with a previous-epoch reference model, different expert counts including a variant trained on twice the data, WS-versus-Tchebycheff training, and initial-batch gradient and size-50 memory measurements. These expand the evaluation design; the original benchmark training budget, metrics, and augmentation settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: New analyses test whether zeroing preference signals for mutually non-dominated pairs harms learning, how expert count interacts with training-data volume, whether scalarization choice matters, and how PL affects gradient variance. GPU memory comparisons also expose resource costs. These substantially extend v1's retained component and hyperparameter ablations.

E5.justification: V3 adds gradient-variance estimates for the first five training batches in Appendix B and Table 3. This is new variability reporting, not evidence of additional independent training runs. The 1% Wilcoxon testing practice remains unchanged; neither version supplies seed counts or confidence intervals, and v3 explicitly acknowledges omitting error bars.

E6.justification: The original benchmark and matched appendix tables retain their numerical results, but v3 adds substantial new findings. For example, Table 9 reports Bi-KP1000 HV of 0.8408 for POCCO-W versus 0.2439 for WE-CA, while Bi-KP300 favors WE-CA, 0.6000 versus 0.5947. V3 also corrects the worst Bi-TSP200 ablation variant from POCCO-MED to POCCO-ME, matching Figure 4.

M1.justification: The CCO architecture, top-k routing, length-normalized Bradley–Terry preference loss, and Algorithm 1 remain unchanged. V3 clarifies the original four-FF-plus-one-ID expert configuration. DPO, neutralized preferences, and alternative scalarization are experimental comparisons or ablations, not replacements for the proposed method.

P1.justification: Most existing prose is retained. Related Works moves from Appendix A to Section 2, the gating explanation expands, terminology and grammatical errors are corrected, and acknowledgments and a NeurIPS checklist are added. The scientific appendix additions do not entail extensive rewriting of the existing narrative.

P2.justification: V3 substantially expands the tabulated presentation with new displays for gradient variance, neutralized pairs, larger instances, DPO, expert counts, scalarization, and memory use. Existing figures and benchmark tables are largely retained and repositioned. The asset table gains a PMOCO row and expanded license entries.

R1.justification: V3 removes the cited work 'Preference optimization for combinatorial optimization problems' by Guanquan Lin and colleagues. BOPO and ORPO remain the same cited works despite publication-detail updates. The new DPO comparison sharpens positioning within preference optimization, while the broader literature framing remains stable.

T1.justification: New Appendix B explicitly derives the gradient of the existing preference loss and contrasts it with REINFORCE. This adds mathematical reasoning, while the original definitions and method equations remain intact. The variance-reduction discussion supplies no formal variance bound or theorem.

improvement.justification: V3 fills important validation gaps in v1's argument for preference learning and computational efficiency: it directly compares DPO, tests preference-pair handling and expert capacity, and quantifies memory and training-time costs. These additions make the central design choices and tradeoffs substantially more assessable while preserving the original results. The gains are qualified by an unproved variance-reduction argument, absent error bars, and inconsistent release statements, but the added controlled evidence provides a clear overall improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same POCCO framework and contain readable main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices. Shared content can be matched reliably despite section moves and expanded supplementary material in v3.

after.justification: V3 retains those original experiments and adds results on gradient variance, larger instances, DPO, preference-pair handling, expert counts, scalarization, and GPU memory.

before.justification: V1 reports original benchmark evaluations, generalization experiments, component ablations, and hyperparameter studies for POCCO, including Tables 1–7 and Figures 3–6.

results.title: Preference-Driven Multi-Objective Combinatorial Optimization with Conditional Computation

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same contributions: isolation-based OOD scoring, decentralized comparison through parameter exchange, and class-conditioning. The claimed application scope and central performance claims remain unchanged.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive explanations of sensitivity to incorrect class predictions, limitations of frozen features, and robustness across aggregation weights. It expands the existing inference-cost caveat into discussion of asynchronous clinical workflows, parallel execution, and network latency. Some new robustness interpretations overgeneralize the mixed outcomes in Table 3b.

D1.justification: v2 replaces the promised-code placeholder with a concrete repository link, explains the fixed convergence parameters, and discloses execution of eight concurrent instances on a 24 GB RTX A5000. It removes v1's per-dataset total GPU-hour estimates. Existing architecture and training-hyperparameter tables remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same dermatology, chest X-ray, ultrasound, and histopathology coverage, including the same MIDOG domains and CCAgT/FNAC far-OOD tasks. The added class-prediction controls reuse these datasets and task requirements.

E2.justification: The benchmark comparators remain MSP, MDS, fDBD, ViM, iForest, CIDER, and PALM. The new runtime comparison reuses existing baselines, while the newly cited few-shot federated methods are discussed without being evaluated.

E3.justification: v2 adds controlled evaluations assigning incorrect classes to all targets, only ID targets, or only OOD targets, plus partial fine-tuning and runtime evaluations. Appendix G specifically lowers Dermatology's maximum rounds from 300 to 150 for additional runtime experiments. The original benchmark splits, metrics, and main training settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Table 3b and Appendix E add substantial analysis of dependence on predicted-class accuracy, including primary-model accuracies in Table 7. Appendix D reports worse performance with partial fine-tuning, and Appendices G–H expand runtime analysis. Existing augmentation, network-size, aggregation-weight, and PCA analyses are retained.

E5.justification: v1 reports benchmark point estimates without specifying repeated runs or seed variability. v2 reports three-seed means and standard deviations in Tables 1 and 13–14, explains variability of seed-wise macro averages, and adds runtime quantiles. This establishes new uncertainty reporting; v1's unspecified run count prevents inferring a particular increase in runs.

E6.justification: Many benchmark scores change under the newly specified three-seed aggregation. Table 1's CC-DIsoN average AUROC/FPR95 changes from 79.49/56.17 to 80.00/59.20. In Table 2, PALM's former far-OOD lead becomes a reported average AUROC tie at 98.3, with CC-DIsoN achieving lower FPR95, 4.4 versus 11.6. Class-error, classifier-accuracy, and detailed runtime results are also added.

M1.justification: Sections 3.1–3.3 and Algorithms 1–2 retain the same isolation objective, convergence score, decentralized updates, and class-conditional sampling. Clarified oversampling notation and newly discussed fine-tuning alternatives do not change the proposed procedure.

P1.justification: Localized edits polish the introduction and clarify labels, oversampling, and centralized versus decentralized operation. Author affiliations and contribution/venue footnotes change, and new appendix sections organize the additional analyses. Most existing prose and the main section structure are retained.

P2.justification: The tabular presentation expands substantially: Table 3 gains a misclassification panel, Tables 1–2 change metric ordering and statistical presentation, and Tables 7–14 add accuracy, runtime, and uncertainty displays. Figures 1–7 retain their visual content, with several relocated.

R1.justification: Section 2 newly distinguishes DIsoN from few-shot federated learning, citing FedAffect and Federated Few-Shot Learning. Additional references support discussion of imaging baselines, convergence thresholds, and clinical turnaround times. The original positioning relative to isolation forests and OOD detection remains intact.

T1.justification: Definition 3.1, Proposition 3.1, its assumptions, and the full Appendix B proof retain the same mathematical content. Distinguishing isolation labels from class labels and explicitly writing replicated target samples clarify existing notation.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens empirical credibility by supplying uncertainty across three seeds for the main benchmarks, testing dependence on class predictions, and quantifying runtime tradeoffs. These address important evidence gaps in v1. The code link also improves reproducibility information. Some new robustness prose overreaches—Table 3b reports ultrasound AUROC of 34.6 when ID classes are wrong—but this localized weakness does not outweigh the substantial gains in empirical scrutiny.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DIsoN research and contain readable text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices. The retained method and matched experiments support a reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains the original empirical evaluation and reports revised benchmark results, class-prediction robustness experiments, classifier accuracies, and runtime measurements.

before.justification: v1 reports original OOD detection experiments across four medical imaging benchmarks, together with ablations and qualitative isolation results.

results.title: DIsoN: Decentralized Isolation Networks for Out-of-Distribution Detection in Medical Imaging

C1.justification: The abstract, introductory contributions, and conclusion retain the same claims: FineHarm, native streaming monitoring, approximately 95%+ detection performance while observing 18% of tokens on average, and SCM-assisted safety alignment. Additional evidence does not redefine these contributions.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations concerning OOD generalization, component contributions, saturation at larger beta values, and one-token monitoring delay when detection is sufficiently fast. The generalization statement has an exception in Table 9, where SCM-0.5B trails HateBERT. Original limitations are retained in Appendix A.

D1.justification: v2 adds a project-page link, identifies nine source LLMs in the existing WildGuard data, and documents learning rates for HateBERT/ToxDectRoBERTa and the text-moderation-latest evaluation endpoint. Existing hardware, SCM training recipes, alignment settings, and annotation prompts are retained.

E1.justification: v2 adds detection evaluation on two external distributions, ToxicChat and ToxiGen, using FineHarm-trained SCM (Appendix C.5). v1 evaluated detection on FineHarm only. FineHarm and the MT-Bench/PKU-SafeRLHF alignment tasks remain; the newly listed source LLMs document existing data provenance.

E2.justification: Table 2 adds HateBERT, ToxDectRoBERTa, Google Perspective, OpenAI Moderation, and LlamaGuard3-8B as full-detection comparators. Some services already participated in dataset annotation, but not this reported comparison. Table 5 also adds Direct labeling to the annotation-strategy comparison.

E3.justification: v2 introduces external-distribution testing after FineHarm training and a latency benchmark comparing generation and detection at three model scales, using sequence lengths from 50 to 100 without acceleration. These extend the evaluation design; the original split, accuracy metrics, threshold selection, and retained training recipes are unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 adds holistic-loss ablations, the Direct annotation control, an explicit beta-sensitivity study, and OOD generalization tests. The existing logic-loss ablations move unchanged from Table 2 to Table 6, and the alpha-sensitivity plot is retained. One illustrative annotation example is also replaced.

E5.justification: The new latency benchmark reports ten repetitions per test sequence and minimum, maximum, and average latency (Table 3). This introduces limited variability reporting; classification results still lack repeated-seed information or uncertainty intervals.

E6.justification: Original SCM macro-F1 scores of 95.64/97.91/97.45, logic-ablation scores, and alignment results are unchanged. v2 adds baseline, latency, holistic-ablation, beta-sensitivity, and OOD results, plus Direct labeling at 95.38 macro-F1. SCM-7B newly scores 70.08 on ToxicChat and 70.88 on ToxiGen; these are new evaluations, not gains on the original test.

M1.justification: The FineHarm annotation procedure, SCM architecture, token/holistic supervision, logical-consistency loss, Delay-k stopping, and TokenDPO objective remain unchanged. New ablations and computational discussion evaluate or explain the existing method.

P1.justification: The discussion and limitations move from main-text Section 6 to Appendix A, and experimental subsections and appendix organization expand. Header information and several headings change, but the abstract, core method exposition, related work, and conclusion are largely retained.

P2.justification: The empirical displays expand substantially: Table 2 is reorganized, ablations receive an expanded separate table, and latency/OOD tables and beta-sensitivity Figure 8 are added. Existing Figure 7 retains its alpha curves with a corrected caption. The example table also changes its selection and ordering.

R1.justification: New citations cover HateBERT, ToxDectRoBERTa, ToxiGen, and speculative decoding. Appendix A adds a substantive distinction from speculative decoding through objectives, model roles, and computational savings. The main related-work section and overall research positioning remain unchanged.

T1.justification: Section 5.5 adds a latency model and expected-time derivation assuming uniformly distributed stopping positions and parallel generation/detection, followed by comparison with full detection (Equations 7–8). The original method's mathematical definitions and derivations remain unchanged.

improvement.justification: The external-distribution tests and established-moderator comparisons address an important weakness of v1: detection validation relied on FineHarm and a narrow comparator set. The holistic-loss ablation and latency measurements further strengthen evidence for the design and practical motivation. Although the latency argument remains conditional and the broad generalization interpretation overlooks an exception, the expanded validation substantially improves the paper's empirical foundation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SCM/FineHarm research. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support reliable comparison, including matching relocated material.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds baseline comparisons, latency measurements, ablations, and out-of-distribution evaluations.

before.justification: v1 reports original detection experiments, annotation comparisons, sensitivity analyses, and SCM-assisted safety-alignment results on MT-Bench and PKU-SafeRLHF.

results.title: From Judgment to Interference: Early Stopping LLM Harmful Outputs via Streaming Content Monitoring

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the central contribution: learning to generate self-edit data and adaptation directives through RL. The introductory single-passage improvement and few-shot adaptation claims remain unchanged. Revised CPT rankings and appendix findings do not redefine these core contributions.

C2.justification: v1 interprets lower CPT accuracy through possible gradient interference; v2 attributes higher CPT accuracy to aggregating generations and acknowledges GPT-4.1's lead. New discussion addresses proxy-reward cost versus direct adaptation feedback, unsuccessful format discovery without prompting, competitive structured heuristics, and possible capacity-dependent benefits with explicit scaling caveats. These substantially refine the method's interpretation and boundaries.

D1.justification: v2 adds the Generative Adapter backbone, Entigraph generation counts, proxy-grading categories and score scale, training-time comparison, and new prompt templates. Existing hardware, software, access information, and most hyperparameter documentation remain. Reproducibility is limited by the unreconciled LoRA table despite the new full-finetuning CPT description.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate ARC few-shot reasoning and knowledge incorporation using SQuAD v1.1 without passages in context. Expanding SQuAD evaluation from 200 to 2,067 passages changes sample coverage within the retained dataset and task, rather than introducing a new domain or task.

E2.justification: v2 adds evaluated comparisons with Generative Adapter and Entigraph, including entity-pair and pair-plus-triplet variants, in Tables 7–8. Table 10 also extends GPT-4.1-generated-data comparisons across prompting formats; v1's corresponding prompting table contained no such comparator column. The original main-table comparator sets remain.

E3.justification: Section 4.2 and Table 2 now report full finetuning for continued pretraining, replacing the LoRA setting documented in v1, and add the full 2,067-passage validation set. New experiments introduce Qwen2.5-3B, a Mistral-7B-based Generative Adapter comparator, and additional prompting and reward protocols. However, v2's retained Table 4 still lists LoRA parameters, leaving the CPT settings incompletely reconciled.

E4.justification: v2 adds model-size sensitivity analysis and an ablation testing whether a cheap rubric reward can replace the costly inner loop. The prompting analysis, moved from Appendix C to B.11, gains no-prompt and chain-of-thought controls. These examine capacity dependence, reward necessity, and reliance on explicit prompting; the forgetting analysis is retained.

E5.justification: Section B.2 retains three-seed averaging when scoring self-edits during ReSTEM training. The catastrophic-forgetting SEM table is unchanged. The added experiments introduce no new uncertainty-reporting practice, significance test, or stated increase in repeated runs.

E6.justification: Table 2 replaces the 200-passage CPT results: SEAL/GPT-4.1 synthetic-data accuracy changes from 43.8/39.4 to 58.2/59.4 under the newly reported full-finetuning setting, reversing their ranking. The new 2,067-passage results are 46.4/49.2. Additional tables report comparator, model-size, and proxy-reward outcomes, including 45.6% for proxy reward versus 47.0% for full SEAL. The retained implications-long Round 2 entry changes from 51.8 to 54.4. These are not collectively same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: The main SEAL algorithm remains unchanged. Appendix B.10 introduces an alternative training procedure that replaces the adaptation-and-evaluation reward loop with summed GPT-4.1 rubric scores for length, diversity, quality, and correctness. This is a substantive but bounded reward variant.

P1.justification: The main section order and most prose remain intact. Changes include localized introduction, related-work, and results rewrites, updated conference text, and moving Prompting from Appendix C to B.11 alongside new appendix subsections. This is not an extensive narrative restructuring.

P2.justification: v2 adds four result tables, expands Table 2 with another CPT column and explicit adaptation labels, and transposes and expands v1's prompting Table 6 into Table 10. These substantially extend the tabular presentation. Figures 1–6 and the overall page design are largely retained.

R1.justification: Related work expands with references including Generative Adapter, DataRater, Nemotron-CC, and RL's Razor. Transformer-Squared receives a more explicit explanation, and the appendices discuss SEAL's relationship to hypernetwork adaptation and structured synthetic-data generation. Entigraph's underlying work was already cited in v1; the overall research positioning remains.

T1.justification: The formal task/state definitions, RL objective, binary reward formulation, and stop-gradient derivation in Section 3.1 and Equations 1–4 are retained. No new theorem, proof, or substantive mathematical revision is introduced.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens empirical scrutiny through direct alternative-method comparisons and tests of reward-loop necessity and dependence on prescribed prompting. Reporting cases where competitors outperform SEAL gives readers better-supported boundaries than v1 provided. The gains outweigh reporting weaknesses: Table 4 still documents LoRA despite full-finetuning CPT, and Tables 7 and 9 give a 32.0 base accuracy inconsistent with 32.7 elsewhere. These limit reproducibility but do not erase the value of the added critical evidence.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Self-Adapting Language Models (SEAL), with matching authors, framework, and core experiments. Text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support reliable comparison. The earlier prompting appendix can be matched to its expanded replacement in v2.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds larger-scale continued pretraining, additional comparators, model-size analysis, and reward and prompting experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original ARC few-shot learning and SQuAD knowledge-incorporation experiments, including prompting analyses and sequential-edit forgetting results.

results.title: Self-Adapting Language Models

C1.justification: The abstract and Section 5.4 strengthen the GPT-4.1 comparison from approaching o1-preview to surpassing it. The central contribution remains eliciting reasoning through modular cognitive tools without additional training.

C2.justification: Appendix B adds interpretations connecting harder tasks with planning/checking, suggests a recall-and-backtracking recovery workflow, and acknowledges an accuracy-cost tradeoff. These qualify the retained modularity account; the existing limitations concerning mathematical tasks, manual tools and model-specific prompts remain.

D1.justification: Appendix A newly discloses decoding settings, including Qwen temperature 0.7, top-p 0.8 and top-k 20, and Llama temperature 0.6 and top-p 0.9. Algorithm 1 adds orchestration pseudocode. These improve documentation without demonstrating implementation changes; the detailed tool prompts were already present.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same mathematical coverage: AIME2024, MATH500, AMC and the math subset of Smolbenchmark. The added experiments reuse these tasks.

E2.justification: Table 3 adds Chain-of-Thought and code-only comparators for all four open-weight models across three benchmarks. Table 4 adds GPT-4.1 with cognitive prompting on AIME2024, beyond its earlier inclusion only in the Smolbenchmark comparison.

E3.justification: New evaluations introduce motivational-phrase removal, an executed-code control with outputs returned to the model, and output-token cost measurement. The retained benchmark sizes, model sizes, pass@1 scoring, answer parsing and GPT-4.1 judging remain unchanged as documented; newly disclosed decoding settings do not establish changed settings.

E4.justification: New Appendix B tests dependence on motivational phrases, analyzes tool frequencies across datasets and model families, examines tool co-occurrence, and measures computational overhead. The earlier individual-tool ablation and worked execution trace are retained, with the trace moving to C.1.

E5.justification: Table 1 newly reports Welch's t-tests finding baseline-versus-best-tool differences significant at p < 0.05. Appendix B.2 adds Pearson correlations of tool use. The existing declarations of 16 repetitions, more than eight runs, and standard errors are retained; no increase in runs is established.

E6.justification: Table 4 replaces GPT-4.1 baseline/tool scores of 26.7/43.3 with 32.0/53.0, retains o1-preview at 44.6, and adds cognitive prompting at 42.0. The PDFs do not explain these revised estimates. New comparator, ablation, tool-use and token-cost results substantially expand the evidence, while retained open-model scores stay unchanged. Section 5.1 also corrects the +26.7-point gain's attribution from backtracking to understand question.

M1.justification: The four cognitive tools, code tool, orchestration procedure and tool prompts are retained. Algorithm 1 documents the existing pipeline; removing motivational phrases is an experimental ablation, not a replacement of the proposed method.

P1.justification: v2 copyedits grammar and clarifies method descriptions while preserving the main narrative and section order. It adds acknowledgments and appendix subsections, and moves the existing Evaluation appendix from B to C.

P2.justification: Table 3 gains comparator rows and colored highlighting, Table 4 gains a prompting row, and Tables 5-8 plus Algorithm 1 introduce substantial new displays. Figure 2 is relocated with its plotted content retained; Figure 1 and the prompt/trace presentation remain essentially unchanged.

R1.justification: The cited works and substantive positioning around cognitive architectures, cognitive prompting, modularity, agentic tools and reinforcement learning are retained. The added CoT experiments use an already cited method.

T1.justification: Neither version develops formal theoretical results or proofs. The added pseudocode explains the existing procedure, and the mathematical examples are retained.

improvement.justification: v1 lacked CoT and code-only controls on its main benchmarks, leaving an important ambiguity about the source of its gains. v2 substantially strengthens that evidence through Table 3, supported by the motivational-phrase ablation, explicit token-cost analysis and improved implementation documentation. Reporting weaknesses remain: the GPT-4.1 revisions are unexplained, and the new Qwen2.5-32B code-only average is 50.2 although its three scores average 52.6. These issues temper, but do not outweigh, the stronger empirical controls.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same cognitive-tools work. Their main text, figures, tables and complete appendices are readable, and retained content can be matched despite appendix reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains original evaluations and adds comparator results, a motivational-phrase ablation, tool-use analyses and computational-cost measurements.

before.justification: v1 reports original benchmark evaluations, individual-tool ablations, prompting comparisons and an example execution trace.

results.title: Eliciting Reasoning in Language Models with Cognitive Tools

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and concluding claims retain the same three principal contributions, compact-model efficiency claims, and approximately 31% zero-shot and 21% finetuned error reductions. The added experiments do not redefine these headline claims.

C2.justification: v2 explicitly qualifies low-order feature similarity as a working hypothesis (Section 2). New analyses develop interpretations concerning masking-value stability, matched normalization context, and the masking explanation for poorer greedy decoding. Appendix A.9 also identifies limited transfer to pose tracking and proposes early electrode mixing as a possible boundary, substantially extending the mechanism and applicability discussion.

D1.justification: v2 documents implementation details for the added variants, including inverse spectral-mask mapping, mean imputation, and feature masking after the first emg2pose convolution. Figure 5 specifies activation sampling every 100th timestep from one session per test user. The original optimizer, schedule, hardware, runtime, and repository disclosures are retained.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates only emg2qwerty typing; emg2pose is merely cited. v2 adds actual hand-pose tracking experiments under user, stage, and combined generalization regimes (Appendix A.9, Table 10), substantially extending the evaluated task coverage.

E2.justification: The original typing comparisons retain Sivakumar et al. and the same model variants. v2 additionally evaluates the Salter et al. emg2pose baseline against adaptations using RTN, ACM, and their combination (Table 10).

E3.justification: v2 adds an 18-user training-domain beam-search evaluation and a separate 78/18 training/validation experiment retaining the original eight test users (Section 4.6, Appendix A.8). Added protocols also vary masking order, mask width, and normalization windows, and evaluate pose tracking with angular-error and landmark-distance metrics. These are additional experimental designs, not replacements of the original typing protocol.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's component and decoding comparisons, v2 tests pre-aggregation masking, ACM widths, RSG removal, RTN window matching, and mean-imputation masking (Tables 5–8). It also adds UMAP representations and alternative-split analyses (Figure 5, Table 9), substantially expanding evidence about mechanisms and robustness.

E5.justification: Appendix A.5 introduces two-tailed paired tests for the new sensitivity analyses, while the main comparisons retain one-tailed tests. Tables 5 and 6 newly provide standard deviations for some previously reported greedy and other-domain results. Neither version discloses seed or repeated-run counts.

E6.justification: Original typing CERs remain unchanged, including SplashNet's 35.67% zero-shot and 5.51% finetuned results. However, Table 1 revises baseline/mini/full-model GFLOPs from 201.325/118.346/229.384 to 61.61/36.84/71.38 under the same stated 30-second measurement description. v2 also adds extensive validation, ablation, representation, and pose-tracking results; these are new results under specified conditions, not same-setting accuracy improvements.

M1.justification: The principal SplashNet architecture and preprocessing remain unchanged. Appendix A.9 adds an adaptation for emg2pose: RTN and ACM operate on first-convolution outputs, with ACM zeroing 50% or 75% of features in specified training samples. This changes the procedure for the added task.

P1.justification: v2 makes targeted wording corrections and explanatory additions, moves the beam-search description from Appendix A.5 into Section 4.5, and adds acknowledgments and a conference checklist. The main narrative and most existing prose remain intact; the scientific appendix additions do not constitute wholesale rewriting.

P2.justification: v2 substantially expands the empirical displays with Tables 5–10 and the four-panel UMAP Figure 5. Tables 1 and 3 gain training-domain columns and explanatory captions, with gray text distinguishing those results. Original Figures 1–4 are retained.

R1.justification: Section 3, the 22 cited works, and the Split-and-Share novelty positioning are unchanged. Salter et al. and emg2pose were already discussed in v1; their additional experimental use does not introduce a new literature positioning claim.

T1.justification: The mathematical definitions and equations for spectral aggregation, RTN, masking, and encoder operations are unchanged. Neither version supplies theoretical propositions or proofs, and the added analyses are empirical.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses substantive evidential gaps in v1 through the masking-order control, normalization and masking sensitivity tests, and the alternative participant split (Tables 5–9). These strengthen assessment of the proposed mechanisms and generalization. Explicitly qualifying the low-order hypothesis and reporting weak pose-transfer gains also clarify applicability. Although the substantial FLOPs revision remains insufficiently explained, the added controls and more careful interpretation provide a substantial net quality improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SplashNet study. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support reliable matching across relocations and additions.

after.justification: v2 retains these experiments and adds original masking and normalization ablations, representation analyses, alternative participant splits, and emg2pose evaluations (Tables 5–10 and Figure 5).

before.justification: v1 reports original emg2qwerty zero-shot and user-specific finetuning experiments, architectural ablations, and participant-level CER results (Tables 1–4 and Figure 4).

results.title: SplashNet: Split-and-Share Encoders for Accurate and Efficient Typing with Surface Electromyography

C1.justification: v1's abstract and contribution statement emphasize quantified classification gains over KD and DIST. v3 replaces this emphasis with claims spanning CIFAR-100, ImageNet-1K and MS-COCO, including comparisons against feature-based methods. This materially broadens the empirical contribution claim while retaining the original methodological claims.

C2.justification: v3 interprets the detection results as evidence of structured knowledge transfer to dense prediction without detector modification. It also qualifies the sorting-cost limitation with an empirical claim of negligible overhead for common architectures. The aligned-label requirement and weak-teacher-confidence limitation remain.

D1.justification: v3 documents the new CIFAR recipe, including optimizer parameters, learning rate, weight decay, augmentations and temperatures, and adds detector specifications and measured training times. Existing PLD code and ImageNet resource details are retained. COCO schedules are described as identical without numerical schedule details.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates ImageNet-1K classification. v3 retains that coverage and adds CIFAR-100 small-image classification and MS-COCO object detection, substantially extending both the represented data and task requirements.

E2.justification: v3 Table 1 adds evaluated comparisons with AT, FitNet, PKT, RKD, SP, VID and DKD alongside KD and DIST. Table 7 also compares PLD with DKD for detection. These extend v1's comparator coverage substantially; the original ImageNet comparison sets are retained.

E3.justification: New protocols include CIFAR-100 training for 250 epochs with AdamW, batch size 128 and temperature 4 for PLD and DIST. COCO evaluation introduces Faster R-CNN/FPN configurations and val2017 AP, AP50, AP75 and object-size metrics. The original ImageNet training and validation settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: New Appendix I and Table 13 examine whether PLD's sorting operation introduces practical training overhead. The existing temperature, optimizer, logit-standardization, divergence and distribution-matching analyses are retained. The loss-landscape analysis moves from Appendix I to J without substantive change.

E5.justification: v1 explicitly reports no error bars or multiple runs. v3 adds three independent CIFAR-100 runs, different-seed information and mean-plus/minus reporting, but does not extend uncertainty reporting to the retained ImageNet results or COCO. Section 5.1 calls the uncertainty standard deviation, whereas checklist item 7 calls it standard error.

E6.justification: The matched original numerical results remain unchanged. v3 adds CIFAR accuracies, COCO detection metrics and CIFAR training times. New comparisons include mixed outcomes: CIFAR heterogeneous accuracy is 68.16% for PLD versus 69.51% for DKD; COCO AP is 32.47 versus 32.11 for ResNet-101 to ResNet-18, but 28.91 versus 29.24 for ResNet-50 to MobileNetV2.

M1.justification: The teacher-optimal ordering, teacher-confidence weighting and PLD objective in Section 4 remain unchanged. Appendix C contains the same executable loss implementation. The detection experiments introduce no documented algorithmic modification.

P1.justification: Substantial sentence-level rewriting affects the abstract, introduction, related work, method discussion and experimental narrative. Experiments are reorganized into dataset-specific sections, with the original ImageNet studies nested together. v3 also adds acknowledgments and a runtime appendix, making this more than a local wording revision.

P2.justification: v3 adds CIFAR accuracy-and-uncertainty, multi-metric detection and runtime tables, and reorganizes the main experimental displays. The full baseline-ablation table is redesigned with grouped headers and highlighted configurations. Original figure content is retained, with the two loss-landscape figures reordered and renumbered.

R1.justification: Nine references are added for CIFAR-100, COCO, FPN and additional distillation comparators, including AT, FitNet, PKT, SP, VID and DKD. Section 2 retains essentially the same positioning relative to ListMLE, P-ListMLE and RankDistil; the additions mainly support expanded experimental comparisons.

T1.justification: The formal PL model and PLD definitions, convexity argument, gradient derivation and smoothness analysis remain unchanged. Appendix A adjusts equation layout without changing the derivation. The runtime discussion restates the previously identified O(C log C) sorting complexity.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens v1's ImageNet-centered evidence through CIFAR comparisons with additional distillation methods, COCO detection tests and measured runtime costs (Tables 1, 7 and 13). These address important gaps in comparator breadth, task generality and practical efficiency while preserving the original method and results. CIFAR repeated-run reporting also improves empirical assessment. The benefits are qualified by inconsistent standard-deviation/standard-error terminology, incomplete COCO settings and broader 'consistent gains' wording that needs qualification where DKD wins.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same PLD research work. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, implementation listing and appendices are readable, and retained content can be matched across reorganization and renumbering.

after.justification: v3 retains these original results and adds CIFAR-100 classification, MS-COCO detection and runtime measurements, including Tables 1, 7 and 13.

before.justification: v1 reports original ImageNet-1K distillation experiments, ablations, distribution-matching measurements and loss-landscape analyses in Section 5 and the appendices.

results.title: PLD: A Choice-Theoretic List-Wise Knowledge Distillation

C1.justification: The central framework and influence-function limit claims remain. v3's abstract newly highlights transformer pruning and diffusion attribution, while its contribution list and conclusion make improved pruning performance an explicit practical contribution.

C2.justification: v3 adds an explanation of why fixing random seeds may not rescue classical attribution: chaotic trajectories and changed batching can move retraining to different optima. It interprets the pruning comparison as evidence that influence functions better approximate distributional outcomes. Existing asymptotic and nullspace qualifications remain.

D1.justification: Appendices E.1 and E.3 add substantial architecture, optimization, pruning-selection and influence-computation details, alongside fuller documentation of existing figures. Diffusion settings partly refer to another paper. A new inconsistency remains: E.3 describes Figure 3's lower panel as a Pearson correlation, whereas its axis and caption describe a gradient norm fraction.

E1.justification: v3 adds CIFAR-10 classification with training-data pruning and ArtBench-10 diffusion-model attribution. These substantially extend the evaluated tasks and domains beyond the retained synthetic regression, Concrete and MNIST settings.

E2.justification: The new pruning and diffusion experiments explicitly compare distributional attribution with single-model, fixed-seed influence functions. Pruning also includes models trained on all data as controls. The existing LDS comparison set—exact Hessian, block-diagonal Hessian, EK-FAC variants and unrolled differentiation—is retained.

E3.justification: v3 introduces a pruning protocol comparing model-specific versus shared subsets of 5,000 removed CIFAR-10 examples, retraining with matched seeds and evaluating accuracy and loss. It also introduces DDPM-loss-based attribution rankings for diffusion models. The original LDS protocol of 20 subsets with 10% removed remains unchanged.

E4.justification: Figure 7 adds a qualitative ArtBench case study comparing examples selected by Wasserstein, mean and fixed-seed influence. Appendix E.3 also newly reports a comparison involving Hessian-span-projected unrolled responses. Existing leave-one-out, learning-rate, MNIST variance and Hessian-normalization analyses remain.

E5.justification: v3 newly specifies 50 models for Figure 2 and reports 10 seeds for pruning and five for diffusion attribution. Pruning figures display individual seeded outcomes and averages. The retained LDS experiments still use 50 seeds and the same uncertainty-reporting format; increased repetitions of existing experiments are not established.

E6.justification: New Figures 6 and 12 report better average pruning accuracy and validation loss for distributional attribution than fixed-seed attribution; Figure 7 adds diffusion influence rankings. Retained Concrete/Tiny-MLP mean LDS scores also change: exact Hessian rises from 81.4% to 87.1%, and block-diagonal Hessian from 82.5% to 84.7%, reversing their ordering. Table 1 is unchanged.

M1.justification: The distributional influence definitions, unrolled-differentiation procedure, influence-function approximation and Hessian normalization remain substantively unchanged. Algorithm 1 packages steps already present in v1; the new applications do not introduce a new proposed estimator.

P1.justification: The narrative is substantially reorganized around what influence functions sample. v3 rewrites the abstract and introduction, moves practical discussion from Section 3.2 into a dedicated Section 5 after the theory, adds the fixed-seed discussion and reorganizes experimental documentation.

P2.justification: v3 adds pruning and diffusion displays, redisplays leave-one-out evidence in the main text and relocates the MNIST figure to the appendix. It also boxes the existing algorithm and revises the convergence plot's legend and training-time axis, changing its label from iterations divided by learning rate to their product.

R1.justification: v3 adds the Swin Transformer citation supporting the new application. The related-work discussion and positioning against previous influence-function, unrolled-differentiation and curvature-approximation research remain substantially unchanged; several other reference edits merely correct bibliographic metadata.

T1.justification: The distributional influence definition, convergence and Boltzmann-transport theorems, assumptions, and proofs in Appendices A and B are substantively retained. Explicit gradient arguments and identity-matrix notation are clarified without changing the mathematical reasoning.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens the connection between the framework and downstream usefulness. Unlike v1's mainly illustrative experiments, its ten-seed CIFAR-10 comparison directly tests whether distributional attribution improves pruning over fixed-seed attribution, reporting better average accuracy and validation loss. The diffusion case study and fuller experimental documentation broaden practical support while retaining the theory. Diffusion evidence remains qualitative, and the Figure 3/Appendix E.3 inconsistency limits clarity locally, but these do not outweigh the stronger empirical grounding.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same distributional training data attribution work. Their main texts, figures, equations, tables and appendices support reliable comparison despite the expanded title and reorganized presentation.

after.justification: v3 retains original empirical results and adds CIFAR-10 pruning experiments with a Swin transformer and ArtBench attribution examples from latent diffusion models.

before.justification: v1 reports original synthetic regression, UCI Concrete and MNIST experiments, including leave-one-out, distributional LDS and influence-ranking results.

results.title: Distributional Training Data Attribution: What do Influence Functions Sample?

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion expand the central contribution from aligned occupancy-image generation to unified occupancy-image-video generation with temporal coherence. Dynamic generation moves from an explicitly deferred capability in v1 to a claimed supported capability in v2.

C2.justification: v1's static-only limitation is replaced by discussion of autoregressive error accumulation, temporal drift and limited long-horizon synthesis in v2 Section 5 and Appendix E.2. New interpretations connect robustness to geometric alignment and RAG to grounded scene generation. The dataset-diversity and fixed-category limitations are retained.

D1.justification: Appendix A adds the video training and inference recipe, including reference-frame sampling, 100 training epochs, batch size eight, eight A100 GPUs, optimizer settings and autoregressive initialization. Appendix C adds stage-wise sampling steps, latency and GPU memory measurements. Existing occupancy/image implementation details and resource links are retained.

E1.justification: The datasets remain nuScenes and Occ3D-nuScenes, but v2 adds dynamic multi-view video generation and end-to-end planning evaluation using trajectory error and collision rates. Appendix C also evaluates corrupted layouts, adding an input-degradation scenario absent from v1.

E2.justification: Comparator membership is unchanged in the corresponding original experiments. The new video comparison reuses MagicDrive and DreamForge, already evaluated in v1. The additional appendix comparisons concern internal ablations and controls, without introducing a new external comparison method.

E3.justification: v2 adds substantial protocols for its new experiments: video interpolation from 2 Hz to 12 Hz, seven-frame training, FVD and UniAD perception/planning evaluation, Gaussian layout perturbations with 25% probability, and a study involving ten participants and 100 scene pairs. The original 700/150 scene split and retained experiment settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: New Appendix C tests removal of spatial conditioning, semantic versus vector layouts, propagation of layout noise, stage-wise inference efficiency, and generation with versus without RAG. These directly investigate conditioning, robustness and component utility beyond v1's retained occupancy and image-component ablations.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals or significance tests. The new human study supplies participant/sample counts and preference percentages, but introduces no uncertainty estimates or statistical testing.

E6.justification: The original quantitative results are retained. New Table 4 reports video FVD of 179.7 for X-Scene, 217.9 for MagicDrive and 209.9 for DreamForge, alongside perception and planning results; training clip budgets differ. Tables 10–14 add substantial findings, including text-only FID of 20.74 versus 11.29 and overall RAG preference of 77% versus 23%.

M1.justification: Section 3.2 adds motion-aware video diffusion to the retained occupancy-image pipeline. The extension introduces temporal self-attention, reference-frame features, relative ego-pose conditioning, temporal-layer fine-tuning and autoregressive video inference. This substantially expands the generation procedure beyond v1's static scenes.

P1.justification: Beyond the added scientific content, v2 substantially rewrites or condenses the abstract, introduction, related work, methodology overview, outpainting explanations, downstream discussion and conclusion. Numbered related-work subsections become compact paragraphs, and a new quantitative appendix reorganizes the supplementary narrative. Many detailed technical and prompt passages remain intact.

P2.justification: v2 adds an overview diagram, a video example grid, a video-evaluation table and five supplementary quantitative tables. The pipeline graphic is updated, and downstream and ablation tables are relocated. The earlier qualitative appendix figures are retained and renumbered, rather than replaced by new results.

R1.justification: v2 adds references including NeuralFloors/++, Text2LiDAR, LiDARcrafter and a 3D/4D world-modeling survey, while retaining the main related-work taxonomy and comparison with manual-layout approaches. Positioning now includes temporal dynamics, and Section 3.2 removes the explicit statement that the generation hierarchy is inspired by UniScene.

T1.justification: Section 3.2 adds a formally specified video-denoising objective conditioned on reference features and relative ego poses, using the existing squared-error diffusion formulation. The original graph definitions, triplane-attention equation and outpainting mathematics remain unchanged; no new theorem or proof is added.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens evidence for the paper's simulation and controllability aims. It addresses v1's acknowledged static-only boundary with a documented temporal module and video/planning evaluation, while Tables 10–14 directly test previously unisolated spatial controls, layout robustness and RAG utility. These additions improve empirical substantiation and reproducibility. Long-horizon drift remains acknowledged, and absent uncertainty estimates and incomplete noise/user-study details still limit the strength of some conclusions.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe X-Scene, with matching authors, core architecture and retained experiments. Their complete main texts, equations, tables, figures and appendices support reliable comparison, including matching material across renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds video-generation and planning evaluations, supplementary ablations, robustness and efficiency measurements, and a human preference study.

before.justification: v1 reports original occupancy and image-generation results, downstream training experiments, component ablations and qualitative scene-generation examples.

results.title: X-Scene: Large-Scale Driving Scene Generation with High Fidelity and Flexible Controllability

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list and conclusion retain the same claims about adaptive retrieval, Omni-Knowledge Indexing, efficiency and accuracy, and the HiVU benchmark. The new experiments provide supporting evidence without changing those claims' scope.

C2.justification: v3 adds discussion attributing the measured L3 construction overhead to graph building and explaining savings through adaptive scheduling and parallel execution. It removes v1's specific speculation about improved results from 671B models while retaining the model-scale and three-routing-level limitations.

D1.justification: Section 4.3 newly documents H20 hardware, 96 GB memory, batch size 2, dual processes and eight-GPU execution. Existing sampling settings and prompts remain unchanged. v3 also removes the 'open-sourced soon' statement while retaining the same code link; the PDFs alone do not establish actual code availability.

E1.justification: Both versions use HiVU, Video-MME and MLVU with the same video domains and QA coverage. The added router checks and timing measurements examine existing components on retained data; the 100-video timing subset changes the protocol rather than coverage.

E2.justification: The external comparator sets in Tables 1–4 are unchanged. New Table 6 evaluates Qwen2.5-1.5B and VideoLLaMA3-7B as alternative classifiers against the retained Qwen2.5-7B classifier, adding limited component-level comparisons.

E3.justification: v3 introduces classifier precision against HiVU level labels and controls forcing every query through L1, L2 or L3. Section 4.3 adds a distinct timing protocol on 100 randomly selected MLVU videos, separating construction and inference and testing single-process, dual-process and eight-GPU configurations. Existing benchmark protocols remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v1 ablates graph, visual and text retrieval and varies frame density. v3 retains these analyses and adds classifier replacement, classifier removal with fixed routing, and construction/inference/scaling analyses. These substantially expand direct examination of the central adaptive-routing and efficiency mechanisms.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests for the experiments. The new timing averages and randomly sampled video subset do not introduce uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: Tables 1–5, Table A1 and the qualitative examples retain their results. v3 adds HiVU classifier precisions of 0.41, 0.81 and 0.48; fixed L1/L2/L3 Video-MME scores of 64.2, 67.5 and 67.1 versus adaptive routing's 68.5; and extensive timing results, including single-process response times of 8/26/27 seconds by route and 20 seconds for AdaVideoRAG.

M1.justification: The classifier, three retrieval paths, multimodal indexing, evidence filtering, generation equation and classification prompt are unchanged. The added classifier substitutions and parallel-execution experiments do not establish a revision to the proposed algorithm.

P1.justification: Related Work moves into the main text, and appendices B–D become A–C. There are limited rewrites to contributions and limitations, expanded affiliation text and new experimental subsections, but most existing prose remains unchanged.

P2.justification: v3 substantially redesigns the document with recurring laboratory branding, running headers, blue headings, a shaded abstract box, wider text blocks and revised caption/table styling. Existing figures and tables are resized and redistributed, and Table 6 is added. All five scientific figure images retain identical content.

R1.justification: The same 53 cited works and substantive research positioning are retained. Related Work moves from Appendix A to Section 2; reference renumbering and expanded author names do not change the literature coverage.

T1.justification: The intent-classification formulation and piecewise generation equation (1) are unchanged. Neither version provides theorems or proofs, and the additions introduce no new mathematical definitions or derivations.

improvement.justification: v1's central adaptive-efficiency claim lacked direct classifier-removal tests and substantive runtime measurements. v3 addresses both gaps: Table 6 and fixed-routing ablations test the router's contribution, while Section 4.3 measures construction, inference and scaling costs with hardware specified. These additions substantially strengthen evidence for the central contribution while preserving earlier results. Missing uncertainty estimates and limited timing-methodology detail still constrain the conclusions.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same AdaVideoRAG framework and HiVU benchmark. Text, equations, tables, figures and appendices are readable, including the image-based appendix examples and prompts. Relocated sections can be matched reliably.

after.justification: v3 retains these empirical results and adds classifier comparisons, fixed-routing ablations and construction, inference and parallelization timings.

before.justification: v1 reports original evaluations on MLVU, Video-MME and HiVU, component ablations, a sampling-density study and qualitative examples.

results.title: AdaVideoRAG: Omni-Contextual Adaptive Retrieval-Augmented Efficient Long Video Understanding

C1.justification: The abstract and five principal contribution statements retain their substantive claims. The Discussion adds token search as a possible explanation for slow attention learning and identifies theoretical validation of this explanation as future work, modestly extending the concluding claims.

C2.justification: Where v1 leaves slow attention learning unexplained, v2 proposes a search phase in which attention gradually identifies relevant input tokens, drawing analogies with earlier learning-dynamics studies.
