Sections 4 and 8 explicitly distinguish this interpretation from a theoretically validated mechanism.

D1.justification: v2 supplies explicit per-task APM indices, a formal intervention mask, probe architecture and implementation details, and numerical settings for the new optimization studies. It also clarifies integer token IDs, random ARC-Easy sampling, and the fixed embedding width in the head-count experiment. These materially expand reproducibility information; the code link and hardware disclosure already existed.

E1.justification: Appendix B.7 adds a composite task requiring sequential output blocks for copying, two-element sums, and three-element sums. LLM diagnostic coverage expands from ARC-Easy to mathematical GSM8K prompts and ARC-Challenge prompts (Appendix E), substantially broadening the tested input populations while retaining earlier tasks.

E2.justification: Optimizer comparisons expand beyond Adam and SGD to Muon combined with Adam or AdamW, and standalone AdamW experiments. Figure 32 explicitly compares Muon training dynamics with the Adam experiment in Figure 2a. The existing attention-intervention and frozen-component comparisons remain unchanged.

E3.justification: New protocols include probing every 10 training steps with 1,024 training and 1,024 held-out samples, quantitative LLM repetition measurements, and sweeps over optimizers, learning rates, schedules, initialization scales, batch sizes, weight decay, and L2 regularization. These substantially extend evaluation design; the original main training protocol is retained.

E4.justification: New analyses test sequential partial-solution learning in the composite task, whether attention outputs contain decodable answers before the model succeeds, and sensitivity to numerous optimization choices (Appendices B.7, C, and G). Earlier architecture, softmax-attention, and SGD checks are retained rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: Neither version specifies repeated-run counts or seeds, and v2 adds no defined confidence intervals, significance tests, or uncertainty-estimation procedure. The newly disclosed smoothing in Figure 36 is for presentation, not uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: New findings include staged learning of the composite task, probe accuracy improving before model accuracy, repetition/collapse on additional prompt datasets, and optimization-dependent plateau behavior, including an approximately 40-step plateau with Muon plus Adam. Figure 8 also adds repetition-frequency curves and revises the ARC-Easy cosine traces. Most earlier experimental curves and the reported OLMo values are retained.

M1.justification: The main Transformer architecture, training objective, decoding procedure, and attention-bias/freezing interventions are retained. The explicit multiplicative mask clarifies the existing intervention. Probing and optimizer variations are additional experiments rather than revisions to the central model.

P1.justification: Most main-text prose and the overall section sequence remain intact. Editing concentrates on Section 4, the rewritten related-work discussion, merged subsection headings, and reorganized appendices separating model configurations from optimization settings. Equation numbering, bibliography style, venue text, and acknowledgments also change.

P2.justification: New displays cover the composite task, probing, additional LLM datasets, and optimization sweeps. Figure 8 gains repetition curves, a second axis, and an expanded caption; Table 1 gains a task and Table 2 documents APM sets. Existing figures are extensively redistributed, including the unchanged random-sampling plot moving from Figure 30 to Figure 25.

R1.justification: Sections 4 and 7 substantially expand connections to prior hidden progress, partial solutions, early repetition, attention interventions, attention transfer, and search dynamics. Added works include Abbe et al., Chang et al., Li et al., Panigrahi et al., and Varre et al. The positioning is more explicit about precedents; retained statistical-physics and simplicity-bias discussion moves to Appendix I.

T1.justification: The existing Transformer and metric equations are retained. Table 2 makes the existing task-specific APM position sets explicit, and the mask notation restates the previously described intervention. No theorem, proof, substantive derivation, or revised theoretical assumption is introduced; the search explanation remains a hypothesis.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens support for the paper's central empirical claims. Held-out probing corroborates hidden progress, optimization tests extend v1's architecture/SGD checks, and quantitative LLM repetition curves replace reliance on qualitative examples while broadening prompt coverage. Explicit APM specifications and clearer acknowledgment of prior findings improve reproducibility and positioning. The search mechanism remains unproved and run-to-run uncertainty remains undocumented, but these limitations do not negate the substantial evidential gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same study, with readable main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices. Retained material can be matched across appendix reorganization and figure renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments and adds a composite algorithmic task, attention-output probing, additional LLM evaluations, and optimization sensitivity experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original Transformer training experiments, attention interventions, and analyses of Pythia and OLMo checkpoints, including extensive appendix results.

results.title: What Happens During the Loss Plateau? Understanding Abrupt Learning in Transformers

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same claims about modular inference-time steering, multiple positive and negative objectives, robustness, and underrepresented behaviors. The headline 70% articulated-task success and 5.4-fold goal-conditioning comparison are unchanged.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations of cross-environment knowledge transfer (A.4), attributes CFG failures to conflicting, equally weighted guidance signals (A.5), and discusses the tradeoff between predicting final states and fixed-horizon future states (B.3). The main limitations section is retained.

D1.justification: v2 replaces broad tuning ranges with task-specific guidance settings in Table 4, discloses 10-step DDIM inference, specifies a 48-step real-robot prediction horizon and trajectory-based guidance examples, and documents CFG goal masking. These improve implementation disclosure without establishing that retained experiments were rerun. Hardware, training budgets, and promised code-release status remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same CALVIN environments, BlockTouch scenarios, and real-robot CupPreference, HiddenCup, and NovelBehavior tasks. The added comparisons reuse existing data and task coverage; changes in which models receive particular training subsets are experimental controls.

E2.justification: v2 adds hindsight-replay goal conditioning for UnderspecifiedObjectives and classifier-free guidance for MultiObjectives. It also adds DynaGuide-Sampling to the real-robot GuideRed comparison, where v1 compared only guided and base policies. These substantially strengthen comparator coverage in the corresponding experiments.

E3.justification: Added controls train goal conditioning on all CALVIN environments and train the dynamics model on the target environment alone. Additional baselines sample intermediate future goals or mask goal conditions during training. These extend training and control protocols within existing experiments; the original evaluation metrics and rollout settings are retained.

E4.justification: Appendix A.4 adds a dynamics-training-data ablation comparing CALVIN-D-only training with all-environment training across eight articulated behaviors (Table 5). The existing hyperparameter sweeps, noise-pretraining ablation, and BlockTouch case studies remain unchanged.

E5.justification: Both versions describe simulation uncertainty using one-sigma standard errors from six policy/split evaluations, and 20 real-robot trials without uncertainty intervals (Appendices B.4–B.5). The added tables report further uncertainty values without introducing a new estimation procedure or stating an increase in repeated runs.

E6.justification: Original Figures 4–9 retain their results, while Tables 2, 3, 5, and 6 add substantial comparison and ablation results. Examples include 60% red-cup success for the added sampling baseline versus retained 75% for DynaGuide and 55% for the base policy; switch-on success of 0.54 with target-environment-only dynamics versus 0.74 with all-environment training; and 11–17% no-behavior rates for CFG under negative guidance.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 corrects the specified stochastic-sampling update. v1 repeatedly assigns a^(k-1) without updating a^k inside the inner loop; v2 updates a^k for intermediate repetitions and assigns a^(k-1) on the final repetition. This is a limited pseudocode correction; the architecture, objectives, and guidance metric are retained.

P1.justification: There are localized rewrites in related work, baseline descriptions, and implementation discussion. Appendix A gains dedicated baseline subsections, the old ablation subsection becomes A.4, and a NeurIPS checklist is inserted. Most existing prose and the main narrative structure are retained.

P2.justification: The appendix gains four quantitative comparison/ablation tables and a task-specific hyperparameter table, substantially expanding its evidence displays. Table 6 highlights desired outcomes and failures with color. Algorithm 1's display expands, and retained Figures 8–9 move within the appendix; the original figure graphics remain unchanged.

R1.justification: v2 adds three cited works: bidirectional decoding, latent-space reinforcement-learning steering, and VLM-in-the-loop steering. Related work incorporates their sampling, initial-noise steering, and VLM-feedback approaches, while retaining the existing positioning of DynaGuide.

T1.justification: Equations 1–3 and Appendix B.3's Gaussian-latent and log-sum-exp derivation are retained. The added discussion of prediction horizons explains practical design tradeoffs without changing formal assumptions, derivations, or mathematical results.

improvement.justification: v1's central robustness comparison gave goal conditioning less training-data coverage than DynaGuide's dynamics model. v2 directly tests a goal-conditioned policy with the same broader data, adds hindsight and CFG comparisons, and measures dependence on dynamics training data. These controls substantially strengthen the credibility of the central comparative claims. Corrected pseudocode and more precise implementation details also improve reproducibility, although the small real-robot evaluations still lack uncertainty intervals.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DynaGuide research. Their main text, figures, tables, equations, and Appendices A–D support reliable comparison, including matching retained content across the expanded appendix and inserted checklist.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds baseline comparisons and a dynamics-training-data ablation in Tables 2, 3, 5, and 6.

before.justification: v1 reports original CALVIN simulations, BlockTouch experiments, and real-robot cup and mouse manipulation results in Section 4 and Appendix A.

results.title: DynaGuide: Steering Diffusion Polices with Active Dynamic Guidance

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, and conclusion retain the same central claims: MP16-Reason supplies diverse reasoning supervision, three task-specific rewards support GRPO training, and GLOBE offers interpretable, data-efficient geo-localization with strong open-source LVLM performance. Terminology edits and additional supporting experiments do not materially redefine these contributions.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive interpretations of multi-teacher bias reduction, student performance beyond its teachers, and dependence on backbone capacity and pretraining. Appendix A.2 distinguishes incorrect reasoning from plausible reasoning attributed to location-frequency bias and discusses the accuracy/latency tradeoff. Existing fine-grained localization limitations and privacy concerns are retained.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code/data repository link, exact dataset and geographic statistics, Microsoft Azure Maps geocoding instructions, H20 GPU allocations, vLLM deployment information, training throughput, and reward weights of 0.2/0.5/1. These materially improve documentation of previously unspecified choices. The existing prompt, training example, and optimizer hyperparameter table are retained; repository availability was not independently verified.

E1.justification: v2 adds OSV-5M mini-3K as a dedicated street-view transfer evaluation beyond the retained MP16-Reason and IM2GPS3K benchmarks. This substantially extends the tested capture conditions and generalization scope. The newly documented geographic counts and indoor/nature/urban breakdowns describe existing MP16-Reason coverage rather than establishing a changed training dataset.

E2.justification: The main comparison changes from v1 Table 1 to v2 Table 2 by adding Hybrid, RFM-YFCC, InternVL3-8B, and Doubao1.5-VL, while removing G3 (LLaVA). These additions broaden the comparison across model families and capacities. GeoReasoner becoming GeoReasoner-7B is a matched naming clarification, not a new comparator.

E3.justification: v1 evaluates MP16-Reason using city/country label accuracy and IM2GPS3K at three distance thresholds. v2 uses five distance thresholds, from 1 to 2500 km, across benchmarks. New protocols include fixed-33K curation controls, an InternVL3-8B backbone comparison, and single-H20 efficiency tests varying streaming and concurrency. The original prompt and optimizer settings remain substantially unchanged.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained SFT and reward-component ablations, v2 adds a no-CoT control, backbone and data-curation ablations, and reward-weight sensitivity tests (Tables 3–5 and 11). It also adds scene-specific robustness, street-view transfer, two failure cases, efficiency analysis, and reward trajectories. The Boston qualitative comparison is retained and relocated, not newly added.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed counts, repeated-run uncertainty, confidence intervals, or statistical significance tests. v2's reward curves have no uncertainty bands. The standard deviation newly introduced in the GRPO advantage is an algorithmic normalization term, not experimental uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: v2 substantially expands results through new comparators, distance thresholds, ablations, OSV-5M evaluation, scene breakdowns, and efficiency measurements. MP16-Reason scores are replaced under different metrics and cannot establish before-and-after gains. GLOBE's shared IM2GPS3K scores remain 40.18, 56.19, and 71.45; Qwen2.5-VL-7B's 200/750 km entries change from 43.14/58.96 to 43.11/58.93.

M1.justification: Section 3.2 changes the localizability reward from an image-only classifier to an LLM-based model conditioned on both the image and generated reasoning. This makes a key reward candidate-dependent. Equation 5 also changes the advantage from mean-centered rewards to division by the group standard deviation. These revise the specified optimization procedure, although the PDFs do not establish implementation history.

P1.justification: Section 4.2 is substantially rewritten from dataset-benefit and model-strategy narratives into category-based baseline comparisons and organized reward, backbone, and curation ablations. A dedicated experimental-results appendix now organizes supplementary material. The revision also standardizes localizability and visual-cue terminology and updates affiliations, publication text, and acknowledgements.

P2.justification: v2 redesigns the main comparison and reward-ablation tables with five distance thresholds and clearer category groupings. It adds dataset-statistics, backbone, curation, scene, street-view, failure, efficiency, and weight-selection tables, plus training curves in Figure 6. The existing qualitative Figure 5 moves to Appendix A.2.5; it is not a new result display.

R1.justification: v2 adds targeted references covering visual place recognition, GeoRanker, generative geolocation, OSV-5M, multi-teacher distillation, and newer LVLMs. The introduction newly acknowledges retrieval's advantage at fine spatial precision. These broaden context without substantially changing the paper's positioning around reasoning-driven, data-efficient geo-localization.

T1.justification: Equation 1 revises the formal localizability definition to condition on generated reasoning. Equation 5 replaces reward centering with standardization and explicitly defines the group mean and standard deviation. These are substantive but localized mathematical revisions; neither version contains a theorem or proof development.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses important validation gaps through fixed-size curation controls, a second backbone, and dedicated street-view transfer testing (Tables 4–5 and 8). The revised reward formulation removes v1's candidate-invariant localizability term, while additional implementation details, failure analysis, and efficiency measurements make the work more assessable and reproducible. Changed MP16-Reason metrics prevent direct accuracy comparisons, and repeated-run uncertainty remains absent. Nevertheless, the stronger validation and clearer specification constitute a substantial overall improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same GLOBE and MP16-Reason research. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support a reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 reports original benchmark and ablation results, supplemented by scene-specific evaluation, street-view testing, failure cases, efficiency measurements, and training reward trajectories.

before.justification: v1 reports original GLOBE benchmark results, training-strategy and reward ablations, and qualitative model outputs in Tables 1–2 and Figure 5.

results.title: Recognition through Reasoning: Reinforcing Image Geo-localization with Large Vision-Language Models

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, and conclusion retain the same principal claims: arbitrary-order HBF approximation, directional-smoothness regularization, and characterization of diagonal-network implicit bias. Additional validation does not redefine those contributions.

C2.justification: Appendix A.1 newly discusses breakdown at large step-size/momentum combinations, conjectures a validity criterion involving η/(1−μ)^2, and distinguishes fixed-momentum asymptotics from joint parameter limits. Section 5 adds stochastic generalization as a future direction. Existing interpretations of implicit bias and generalization remain.

D1.justification: The added MNIST experiment specifies the 784–128–128–10 layer sizes, SiLU activation, batch normalization, loss, batch size, and optimization hyperparameters. Existing hardware and experimental details are retained; no new code-release or access instructions are supplied.

E1.justification: Appendix C.3 adds MNIST classification training to the approximation-error evaluation. The CIFAR-10 experiment and synthetic two-parameter and diagonal-network regression tasks remain, making this a limited coverage extension.

E2.justification: The corresponding original experiments retain their GD, HB, RGF, and HBF comparisons. The added experiments reuse existing comparison methods; newly cited optimizer research is not introduced as evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: v2 adds Euler integration resolutions η/100 and η/1000 alongside η/10. The new MNIST experiment uses cross-entropy, batch size 60,000, learning rate 0.01, and momentum values 0.7 and 0.8. These are added experimental settings; the original settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Appendix C.2 and new Figure 3 test whether the two-parameter trajectory conclusions persist across three Euler integration resolutions. v1 reports only the η/10 resolution, without this solver-sensitivity check.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. v2's checklist explicitly states that no error bars are reported, without introducing an uncertainty-estimation procedure.

E6.justification: New Figures 3–4 report integration-resolution trajectories and MNIST error curves. The former preserve the trajectory ordering; the latter show lower settled errors for HBF than RGF at matched momentum. Original results are retained, including v1 Figures 3–4 becoming v2 Figures 5–6.

M1.justification: The HBF construction, correction-term recurrence, and truncation procedure are retained. Corrected third-order displays agree with formulas already present in v1's Table 1 and appendix. The newly evaluated nonlinear network does not constitute a new proposed method.

P1.justification: v2 adds an intuition paragraph in Section 2, reorganizes the Appendix A proof exposition, corrects theorem cross-references, and adds acknowledgments and a checklist. Most main-text prose and the overall section sequence remain recognizable.

P2.justification: Document-wide NeurIPS retypesetting changes fonts, margins, text density, title layout, and display sizes. v2 also adds a proof-flow diagram and two experimental figures, while resizing and relocating retained figures and tables. This is a substantial visual-layout revision.

R1.justification: Section 1.1 expands optimizer implicit-bias positioning through Wang et al. (2021, 2022) and Zhang et al. (2024). Other additions cite stochastic continuous-time analysis and learning-rate/momentum relationships. Li et al. (2021) and Nacson et al. (2019) are removed, while the principal HBF novelty positioning remains.

T1.justification: New Appendix A.1 states smoothness, bounded-derivative, and step-size/momentum validity conditions. Appendix A.2.2 replaces v1's schematic induction with explicit norm bounds tracking both accumulated error and error increments. Section 2.2.2 also corrects the third-order coefficient and restores the missing gradient-Hessian factor. These substantially revise the mathematical support for the central approximation guarantee.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens support for the paper's central guarantee: it replaces the terse error induction with explicit bounds, states previously implicit validity restrictions, and repairs inconsistent third-order equations. The Euler-resolution check and nonlinear MNIST experiment also address important gaps in validation. Although the proposed composite-parameter validity criterion remains conjectural, the combined improvements materially strengthen theoretical accountability and empirical support without changing the core method.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same HBF and implicit-bias research. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and Appendices A–C are readable and matchable. v2 additionally includes a NeurIPS checklist.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds numerical-integration sensitivity results and MNIST approximation-error experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original CIFAR-10 directional-smoothness measurements, two-parameter optimization simulations, and diagonal-network approximation-error and generalization experiments.

results.title: Heavy-Ball Momentum Method in Continuous Time and Discretization Error Analysis

C1.justification: The main contribution expands from cost reduction on two workloads to cost and latency reduction across five workload groups and two agent architectures. The abstract and conclusion replace 46.62% cost reduction with 50.31%, add a 27.28% latency-reduction claim, and revise reported accuracy retention from 96.67% to 96.61%.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive interpretations concerning GAIA's limited initial keyword reuse but useful replanning reuse, cache saturation near the number of unique task keywords, fuzzy matching's relevance/efficiency tradeoff, and cold-start overhead with possible offline prewarming. The earlier limitations and societal-impact discussion are retained in Appendix E rather than removed.

D1.justification: v2 specifies Python dictionary lookup, the all-MiniLM-L6-v2 fuzzy matcher and semantic-caching thresholds of 80%, 85% and 90%. Main-text Llama-3.2-8B references become Llama-3.1-8B, matching v1's appendices rather than establishing a model change. Hardware, API versions/prices, prompts and the promised future code release remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Beyond the retained FinanceBench and TabMWP coverage, v2 evaluates QASPER scientific-document questions, AIME 2024/2025 mathematics and GAIA tasks involving multi-step reasoning and tool use. This substantially broadens the evaluated domains and task requirements.

E2.justification: The four original named baselines and their participation in the retained benchmark comparisons are unchanged. Tables 5–6 add a fuzzy keyword-retrieval alternative evaluated against default exact matching. The added benchmark and latency comparisons otherwise use the existing accuracy-optimal and cost-optimal controls.

E3.justification: v2 adds a wall-clock benchmark using 100 randomly sampled FinanceBench queries, LRU cache-capacity sweeps, lookup timing up to one million entries, fuzzy-threshold experiments and cold-start tracking. GAIA uses Open Deep Research with GPT-4o/GPT-4o-mini. The original 200-question FinanceBench and TabMWP evaluation settings remain documented unchanged.

E4.justification: New Sections 4.3–4.5 analyze latency by component, cache-capacity saturation, exact versus fuzzy lookup scalability, fuzzy-matching accuracy tradeoffs and cache warm-up. These substantially extend the operational sensitivity analysis. Existing cache-hit/miss comparisons and Appendix C model-sensitivity studies are retained.

E5.justification: v2 explicitly reports averaging cache-lookup measurements over 100 trials in Section 4.4 and Table 5; v1 provides no corresponding repeated-trial reporting. Neither version supplies defined error bars, confidence intervals or significance tests for the main cost/accuracy results, despite v2's affirmative checklist statement.

E6.justification: The original benchmark plots, cost breakdown and Appendix C numerical results are unchanged. v2 adds substantial results: Table 1 reports GAIA APC cost/accuracy of $16.27/36.97%, versus $69.02/37.58% for the accuracy-optimal baseline; Table 3 reports FinanceBench latency of 1424.82 versus 1959.24 seconds. Tables 4–7 add cache-management findings. Revised headline aggregates cover expanded experiments rather than demonstrating a same-setting improvement over v1.

M1.justification: The core workflow, Algorithms 1–3 and appendix prompts remain unchanged. However, v2 implements optional fuzzy keyword retrieval and LRU eviction, previously left for future work, and reports automatic caching disablement when hit rates remain low.

P1.justification: The title and terminology adopt APC and test-time memory, and the abstract and concluding summary are updated. The Discussion becomes a Conclusion, with most discussion text moved verbatim to Appendix E; acknowledgments and a NeurIPS checklist are added. Most existing explanatory prose and appendix content remain intact.

P2.justification: v2 adds six experimental tables, retains but rescales and relocates Figures 1–5, and reformats the document in NeurIPS style. The appendix algorithms and model-sensitivity tables are consolidated into denser layouts. These are substantial display and layout changes beyond table renumbering.

R1.justification: Section 2.3 adds a focused comparison with classic case-based planning, distinguishing automatic LLM template extraction from symbolic planning. v2 also adds benchmark, agent-memory, context-caching and social-simulation references and removes Mind2Web. The existing positioning around serving efficiency rather than enhanced agent capability largely remains.

T1.justification: Neither version contains substantive theoretical results, proofs or formal derivations. The appendix algorithms and worked-example mathematics are unchanged; v2's standard dictionary lookup complexity statement does not introduce a new theoretical contribution.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses v1's narrow validation and untested deployment behavior through additional domains, a second agent architecture, measured latency, and cache-capacity, retrieval and cold-start analyses. These strengthen evidence for practical applicability and expose operating tradeoffs. Important limitations remain: the headline latency wording exceeds the single FinanceBench microbenchmark's scope, and Appendix B lacks dataset-specific setup for the added benchmarks. These weaknesses qualify, but do not outweigh, the substantial evidential gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same agentic plan-caching framework. Their complete main texts, figures, tables, algorithms and appendices support comparison despite changes in title, authorship and formatting.

after.justification: v2 retains those experiments and adds benchmark results, latency measurements, cache-management analyses and cold-start measurements.

before.justification: v1 reports original FinanceBench and TabMWP experiments, including cost, accuracy, cache-search analyses and model-sensitivity results.

results.title: Agentic Plan Caching: Test-Time Memory for Fast and Cost-Efficient LLM Agents

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contribution statements, and conclusion retain the same claims about native unified modeling, scalable visual representations, two-stage learning, language preservation, and competitive multimodal performance. The added experiments support existing claims without redefining their core scope.

C2.justification: v3 adds interpretations linking the language comparison to the importance of two-stage training and attributing AnyRes gains to finer visual detail. It newly attributes weaker fixed-token ChartQA performance to limited chart data during semantic distillation and proposes more OCR/document data. The existing text-rendering, resolution, and misuse limitations remain unchanged.

D1.justification: v3 adds the video fine-tuning data mixture and source, frame limits, evaluation-tool information, and AnyRes token counts. Most optimizer, hardware, training-duration, and access information is retained. However, Section 4.1 replaces the specific ShareGPT4-V recaptioner attribution with generic 'LMMs', reducing reproducibility detail without establishing an actual preprocessing change.

E1.justification: v3 adds video-question-answering coverage across six benchmarks, text-only knowledge/reasoning/code evaluation, and chart, document, infographic, and text VQA. It also adds OneIG-Bench, video-understanding fine-tuning data, and RefinedWeb for a training control. Conversely, v1's WISE world-knowledge generation evaluation is removed, rather than relocated.

E2.justification: Table 3 adds LLaVA-OV and BAGEL. The GenEval comparison adds BAGEL and MetaQuery-XL while removing SD3 (d=24); text-to-video VBench adds HaploOmni. New comparisons include proprietary and open video-understanding models, additional image generators, and original Qwen2.5 versus one-stage training controls. These substantially expand the evaluated comparator set.

E3.justification: New protocols include fine-tuning with 1.6M video and 1.1M image samples, zero-shot video evaluation with specified training/inference frame limits and subtitle conditions, and language evaluation using lm-evaluation-harness with a RefinedWeb co-training control. Table 14 compares 729 versus 5×729 image tokens using AnyRes. These are added experimental designs, not demonstrated reruns of the retained benchmarks.

E4.justification: The existing fusion, guidance/inference-step, and training-stage ablations are retained. New Table 13 directly tests language preservation against original Qwen2.5 and one-stage co-training at both model sizes. New Table 14 tests whether increased inference-time image tokens improve chart, document, infographic, and text understanding, substantially extending the diagnostic evidence.

E5.justification: v1 reports point estimates without uncertainty measures. v3 introduces ± values throughout the language-performance comparison in Table 13. Their statistical meaning and calculation are unspecified, and neither repeated-run counts nor seeds are supplied, so this establishes new uncertainty reporting rather than additional independent runs.

E6.justification: Substantial results are added for video understanding, OneIG, language retention, and token-count sensitivity. Examples include 79.0 NExT-QA accuracy for the video-tuned 7B model and MMLU 70.73 versus 28.43 for two-stage versus one-stage training. Retained GenEval scores of 0.73/0.76 and DPG-Bench scores of 85.02/86.14 are unchanged. The WISE overall scores of 0.35/0.39 are removed.

M1.justification: The VAE, dual-path fusion, language and flow heads, and core two-stage recipe remain intact. Equation (2) adds a 1/n normalization to the stated distillation loss, and Section 4.5 introduces an evaluated AnyRes inference variant. These are limited refinements; the PDFs do not establish that the normalization edit changed earlier training runs.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the overall section sequence remain unchanged. v3 expands the experimental discussion, renames Section 4.2 to explicitly include images and videos, removes Appendix A.3, makes small wording corrections, and expands acknowledgments. These are localized additions and edits rather than extensive rewriting.

P2.justification: v3 adds four substantive tables for video understanding, OneIG, language retention, and token-count analysis, removes the WISE table, and expands several comparison tables. It also adds explanatory gray styling in Table 3 and moves VBench captions above their tables. Figures 1–3 retain their visual content.

R1.justification: The comparative taxonomy expands substantially from v1 Table 11 to v3 Table 15, adding models such as UniDisc, Muddit, MMaDA, HaploOmni, Fudoki, and OpenUni. VARGPT is reclassified from unified to decoupled visual representations. New evaluation literature is incorporated and WISE is removed, while the overarching native-versus-assembled distinction remains.

T1.justification: Equation (2) changes the formal distillation-loss definition from a sum to its 1/n-normalized mean. The remaining mathematical formulation is retained, and neither version supplies theoretical propositions or proofs. This is a limited mathematical correction rather than a new theoretical contribution.

improvement.justification: v1's central language-preservation claim lacked direct language-task evaluation, and its video-understanding capability lacked quantitative validation. v3 substantially closes these gaps through the controlled comparison in Table 13 and explicitly fine-tuned video evaluations in Table 4; Table 14 also clarifies a visual-understanding limitation. Removing WISE and making the recaptioner less specific lose useful evidence and detail, and the new uncertainty terms remain undefined. Nevertheless, the targeted validation substantially strengthens the paper's central evidential support.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Show-o2 with the same authors, core architecture, and research objectives. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support reliable matching despite expanded evaluations and renumbering.

after.justification: v3 retains original empirical results and adds video-understanding, OneIG-Bench, language-retention, and image-token-count evaluations.

before.justification: v1 reports original Show-o2 understanding and generation results, controlled ablations, qualitative examples, and WISE evaluation results in Appendix A.3.

results.title: Show-o2: Improved Native Unified Multimodal Models

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the same claims about optimal resource allocation, solution-level redundancy bias, DORA's optimality and improved efficiency. The conclusion still reports the same 3.5-fold FLOPs reduction and fourfold latency reduction. Additional experiments support these retained contributions without redefining them.

C2.justification: Section 4.3 adds an interpretation of semantic grouping as improving intermediate search guidance. Appendix D adds explanations for hard-clustering weaknesses, degraded reward guidance at high temperature, embedding-capacity effects and robustness across model and PRM families. These substantially expand the mechanism and applicability discussion; the original limitations concerning PRM availability and low-confidence assumptions remain.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code-and-data release announcement with a repository pointer, plus technical information for the added experiments, including embedding-model sizes and tested parameter ranges. The original decoding settings, hardware description and prompt are retained in Implementation Details, moved from Appendix D to Appendix E.

E1.justification: v2 retains MATH500, AIME2024 and AIME2025 and adds actual evaluations on HMMT24, HMMT25, AMC23 and AMC24 in Table 1. These broaden the represented competition problems, question formats and difficulty distributions substantially within mathematical reasoning.

E2.justification: Temperature Sampling, Beam Search, DVTS and REBASE remain the search baselines. Table 4 newly evaluates KMeans and hierarchical-clustering alternatives against DORA's soft clustering, providing a limited extension of the evaluated comparison methods.

E3.justification: New configurations include LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct with Qwen2.5-Math-PRM-72B, Skywork-PRM-7B, alternative embeddings and parameter sweeps. Table 3 introduces a diagnostic that stops search after K steps and completes trajectories through temperature sampling. These substantially extend the evaluation design; the original main rollout budgets and decoding defaults remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 adds intermediate search-guidance analysis, hard-versus-soft clustering ablations, model-scale and PRM-family robustness tests, and temperature and embedding sensitivity studies in Tables 3–8. The existing difficulty analysis is retained in Appendix D.1 and Figure 5, rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: The efficiency comparison changes from point estimates in v1 Table 1 to explicit mean-and-standard-deviation reporting over three runs in v2 Table 2. Existing plot bands and the general five-run MATH500 and ten-run AIME statements remain. The three-run caption is not reconciled with those general statements; an increase in runs is not established.

E6.justification: The original performance plots, difficulty curves and MATH500 efficiency means are retained, but substantial results are added. For example, Table 5 reports 80.6 accuracy for DORA versus 79.2 for REBASE with the larger policy–PRM pair. Table 4 reports 68.7 for soft clustering versus 68.0 for the best KMeans setting. Added AIME24 efficiency results show equal 14.7 accuracy for DORA at 64 rollouts and REBASE at 256 rollouts.

M1.justification: DORA's embedding similarities, softmax-diagonal uniqueness weights, reward reweighting and rollout allocation remain unchanged in Equations 10–13, as does Algorithm 1. The new hard-clustering ablations evaluate alternatives without replacing the proposed soft-clustering procedure.

P1.justification: Most existing prose, including the abstract, introduction, theory and conclusion, is retained. Changes include localized experimental explanations, moving the difficulty discussion into a new More Experiments appendix, renumbering Implementation Details, and adding acknowledgements and a NeurIPS checklist. These do not amount to extensive rewriting of the existing narrative.

P2.justification: v2 adds dedicated benchmark, intermediate-step and ablation tables, substantially expanding the results presentation. The original efficiency table becomes a dataset-grouped table with standard deviations. The difficulty plot moves from the main text to the appendix as Figure 5, while the Beta-prior plot becomes Figure 4; their plotted content is retained.

R1.justification: Section 5 adds brief positioning against branch-and-prune and dynamic-decomposition approaches, citing TreeBoN, DISC, early-stopping self-consistency and difficulty-adaptive self-consistency. Appendix D also introduces the MTEB citation. The central novelty claim and existing related-work organization remain unchanged.

T1.justification: The Bayesian formulation, Assumption 1, Propositions 1–2, Theorem 1 and their Appendix B proofs are unchanged. Appendix C retains the same Beta-distribution explanation. The new empirical diagnostics introduce no revised formal theory or proof.

improvement.justification: v1 lacked direct tests of its clustering choice and dependence on temperatures, embeddings and PRM configurations. Tables 3–8 substantially address those empirical gaps through mechanism diagnostics and controlled robustness comparisons, strengthening support for DORA's central design. Broader benchmark coverage and explicit efficiency-result standard deviations further improve assessment. The unresolved three-run versus five/ten-run reporting discrepancy is a limitation, but the added validation provides a substantial net quality gain.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DORA research, with readable text, equations, figures, tables and appendices. Retained experiments and relocated material can be reliably matched despite the additional experiments in v2.

after.justification: v2 retains the original experiments and adds benchmark results, intermediate-success measurements, clustering ablations and robustness experiments in Section 4 and Appendix D.

before.justification: Section 4 reports original accuracy, pass-rate, computational-cost and latency results on mathematical reasoning benchmarks, including a difficulty-stratified analysis.

results.title: Every Rollout Counts: Optimal Resource Allocation for Efficient Test-Time Scaling

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same claims about synthetic-data-only heterogeneous fusion, automatic domain exploration, adaptive allocation, efficiency, and reduced capability imbalance. The new experiments support existing claims rather than redefining the contributions.

These extend the mechanism interpretations. Appendix E's limitations concerning fixed prompts and possible data-quality refinement remain unchanged.

D1.justification: v3 documents subsampling for the new controlled experiment, including 594 examples from each of three domains for applicable baselines, and supplies five generated question-answer examples. Existing training and generation settings, hardware disclosures, prompt templates, and code-access information remain unchanged.

Appendix G explicitly presents generated samples from the existing main experiments rather than introducing additional training or evaluation coverage.

Tables 2–3 also change the reported BBH setting from 0-shot CoT to 3-shot CoT while retaining scores; the PDFs do not establish reruns.

E4.justification: Appendix D adds a targeted leader-selection ablation: Table 5 tests whether fixing each source model as leader changes performance relative to random selection. Existing component, SWBLRT-parameter, sampling-ratio, and source-count analyses remain. Appendix G adds illustrative generated examples without a systematic quality analysis.

E5.justification: v1 provides point estimates without repeated-run uncertainty reporting. v3's Table 6 explicitly reports three independent runs and mean ± standard deviation for benchmark scores, overall scores, and Bohdi's generated-data count. This introduces systematic variability reporting for the controlled comparison, although it does not extend to all original experiments.

E6.justification: Table 5 adds fixed-leader averages of 49.14, 48.48, and 49.17 versus 50.79 for random selection. Under the new aligned-budget protocol, Table 6 reports Bohdi at 50.53 ± 0.36 versus the highest baseline average, SFT's 47.17 ± 0.57. These are added results under new conditions; original accuracy entries are retained, with relative-gain annotations converted to absolute differences.

M1.justification: Section 2 and Appendix B retain the same Sprout and Harvest operations, hierarchical Thompson sampling, SWBLRT-based IR mechanism, and Meditation–Enlightenment procedure. Fixed-leader configurations are experimental ablations, not revisions to the proposed method.

P1.justification: v3 updates affiliations and the conference footer, adds acknowledgements, expands Appendix D, and appends a synthetic-example section. Most existing prose and section organization remain intact; the additions do not constitute extensive rewriting.

P2.justification: v3 adds Tables 5–6 and boxed examples in Appendix G, compresses Tables 1–3, and expands captions to explain absolute gain annotations. Figure 2 corrects the reversed H1/H2 labels. Existing plots and the overall visual organization are largely retained.

R1.justification: The same 40 references and Appendix A discussion are retained. Positioning relative to explicit and implicit fusion, seed-based and seedless synthesis, and Condor is substantively unchanged.

T1.justification: The optimization objectives, hierarchical-bandit formulation, reward definitions, Bayesian updates, and SWBLRT likelihood-ratio derivation remain unchanged in Section 2 and Appendix B. Mathematical content inside the new generated examples is not new theoretical analysis of Bohdi.

improvement.justification: Table 6 substantially strengthens the central efficiency and stability evidence by adding approximately matched data budgets and three-run uncertainty estimates; Table 5 also directly tests leader selection. These address important weaknesses in v1's empirical support. The new controlled study covers only one target model, and v3 introduces a reporting error: Appendix D calls the TheoremQA gain 3.76 percentage points, whereas Table 3 gives 35.00 minus 31.75, or 3.25. These limitations do not outweigh the improved experimental controls and reliability reporting.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Bohdi and provide readable text, figures, tables, equations, and appendices. v1's Appendices A–F can be matched in v3, which expands Appendix D and adds Appendix G.

after.justification: v3 retains those empirical results and adds fixed-leader comparisons and a repeated-run comparison under approximately aligned data budgets in Appendix D.

before.justification: v1 reports original benchmark evaluations, component and parameter ablations, weak-to-strong fusion experiments, and runtime measurements in the main text and Appendix D.

results.title: Bohdi: Heterogeneous LLM Fusion with Automatic Data Exploration

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the same central contribution and performance claims: size-adaptive discrete graph diffusion with competitive property targeting and optimization. Additional evidence does not materially redefine these claims.

C2.justification: V2 adds substantive interpretations of near-zero-dipole failures, sampling speed through smaller intermediate tensors, and sensitivity of disconnected molecules to insertion timing. It also discusses adjacency-power features as a possible mitigation and acknowledges node–edge dependence in Appendix B.4. The original simultaneous-edit and disconnected-molecule limitations are retained.

D1.justification: V2 supplies a repository URL, explains caching per-molecule label distributions, and documents settings for the new studies. Existing architecture, pseudocode, splits and hardware disclosures largely remain. V1's explicit instruction to disable insertions/deletions during the initial optimization corruption is omitted; this omission does not establish a procedural change.

E3.justification: Appendix D.1 adds a separate optimization protocol with 100 candidates per round, top-ten selection and four rounds, alongside a 1000-timestep molecular-weight experiment. Other additions include diversity metrics, a 250-epoch padding comparison, and timing 128 samples under different latent initializations. The original benchmark protocols and dataset splits are retained.

E4.justification: V2 tests whether padding can substitute for explicit insertion/deletion, studies sensitivity to four scheduler/node-count parameters, and analyzes sampling speed across latent initializations. Appendices A.2 and D.4 additionally report qualitative label-distribution comparisons and failures near zero dipole moment. The original disabled-edit ablation and out-of-distribution analysis remain.

E5.justification: Both versions use the existing plus/minus reporting convention without newly specifying seeds, repeated-run counts, confidence intervals or significance tests. Additional candidate-generation rounds are evaluation-budget changes, not independent repetitions for uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: Tables 1–2 and the shared GRIDDD optimization scores remain unchanged, but v2 adds diversity, padding, timing and sensitivity results. Under the new multi-round protocol, Table 6 reports QED success of 64.1% versus EDM-SyCO's 46.4%, but DRD2 success of 19.7% versus 27.3%. These are additional results under different conditions, not improvements over v1's original protocol. CG-VAE's 2.3% DRD2 entry becomes unreported.

M1.justification: The architecture, DEL/DEL* mechanism, activation-time prediction, auxiliary network, loss and Algorithms 1–2 are retained. Corrections to the sampling formulas align them with v1's stated probability and absolute-distance descriptions; the PDFs do not establish a changed underlying algorithm.

P1.justification: The supplementary material is systematically reorganized into methodology, experimental details, computational considerations and additional results, with the checklist moved before the appendices. V2 also adds a computational subsection and rewrites the deletion-state explanation. This substantially changes document organization despite retaining most of the main narrative.

P2.justification: V2 adds four tables, expands Table 3 with diversity columns, and redraws Figure 3 as a wider plot with an explicit legend. V1's numerical out-of-distribution table is removed while its results remain plotted. Scheduler, architecture and molecule illustrations are retained but relocated and renumbered.

R1.justification: V2 adds Campbell et al.'s trans-dimensional jump diffusion and distinguishes its capabilities from GRIDDD. It also cites Liu et al. for the already-evaluated CG-VAE baseline and expands positioning against the previously cited Ketata et al. method. The broader related-work framework remains stable.

T1.justification: Equations 1–2 correct the probability expressions by introducing absolute values, including |n−n0| in the node-count distribution. Appendix B.4 adds mathematical reasoning about node-dependent edge transitions and the independence assumption. The main posterior derivation is retained, with no new theorem or proof framework.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens validation of the central contribution by testing a simpler padding alternative and directly comparing with EDM-SyCO under explicitly described protocols. Sensitivity, failure and timing analyses clarify practical strengths and weaknesses, while formula corrections improve mathematical accuracy. Removing the numerical out-of-distribution table and the corruption-setting instruction loses some detail, but these limited losses are outweighed by the stronger evaluation and explanation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe GRIDDD, with readable main text, equations, tables, figures, algorithms and appendices. Reorganized and renumbered material can be matched reliably.

after.justification: V2 retains those empirical results and adds padding comparisons, sampling-time measurements, EDM-SyCO comparisons, sensitivity tests and failure analysis.

before.justification: V1 reports original molecular property-targeting, optimization, out-of-distribution and ablation results on QM9 and ZINC-250k.

results.title: Graph Diffusion that can Insert and Delete

C1.justification: Both versions retain the central claims of training-free, query-agnostic compression with a fixed cache budget and strong streaming accuracy and efficiency. The conclusion is unchanged; the expanded experimental evidence supports the existing contribution rather than redefining it.

C2.justification: v2 adds task-specific interpretations of backward recall and real-time perception, and discusses compute-related energy savings and practical edge deployment. The positional-encoding caveat in Appendix B.4 and limitations concerning modalities and fixed budget allocation in Appendix H remain unchanged.

D1.justification: v2 supplies hardware, model, sampling-rate, duration, and memory-budget information for the added evaluations. Figure 1 also clarifies that its measurements use a single A100 80GB GPU. These substantially extend evaluation settings without revising the retained protocols.

Existing component ablations, hyperparameter sweeps, multi-turn examples, and query-dependence analyses remain unchanged.

E6.justification: New Table 4 reports OVO-Avg scores of 53.6 versus 51.7 and StreamingBench scores of 76.4 versus 75.2 for InfiniPot-V versus Uniform Select. Table 6 adds Jetson results: at 500 seconds, memory is 10.7 versus 39.0 GB and throughput 9.1 versus 1.2 tokens/s; at 600 seconds, Full KV runs out of memory. These are newly reported settings. Retained results are unchanged apart from equivalent rounding in Table 2.

M1.justification: Section 3 and Algorithms 1-2 retain the same continual compression procedure, TaR similarity scoring, VaN scoring with adaptive pooling, and combined token selection. The added evaluations do not introduce a method component.

P1.justification: v2 adds Section 4.4 and localized benchmark descriptions and discussion, lightly rewrites the RVS comparison, standardizes ablation terminology, and updates the publication footer. The overall narrative, method exposition, and appendix structure remain stable.

P2.justification: v2 adds Tables 4 and 6, relocates and renumbers the original ablation table as Table 5, and makes small Figure 2 styling and table/caption formatting adjustments. Existing plots and appendix displays are retained without substantive visual restructuring.

R1.justification: v2 adds citations and brief descriptions for OVO-Bench and StreamingBench, increasing the reference list from 52 to 54 works. Appendix F and the positioning relative to prior compression methods are otherwise unchanged.

T1.justification: The mathematical definitions and reasoning for TaR, VaN, adaptive pooling, and attention-based cache selection are unchanged in Section 3 and Appendices A and D. No theorem, proof, or formal assumption is added or revised.

improvement.justification: v1 motivates deployment on constrained edge devices but supports efficiency primarily with A100 measurements. v2 directly tests Jetson deployment, including successful 600-second inference where Full KV exhausts memory, addressing an important validation gap in the central application claim. The additional streaming tasks further strengthen empirical support. New comparisons and measurement documentation remain limited, especially for uncertainty and energy accounting, but the gain in practical validation is substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same InfiniPot-V work. Text, equations, figures, tables, and Appendices A-H are readable and can be matched across pagination and numbering changes.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds evaluations on OVO-Bench and StreamingBench and deployment measurements on NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin.

before.justification: v1 reports original video-understanding evaluations, TaR/VaN ablations, qualitative case studies, and memory/latency measurements in the main text and appendices.

results.title: InfiniPot-V: Memory-Constrained KV Cache Compression for Streaming Video Understanding

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, and conclusion retain the same claims: fine-grained multi-condition tokenization improves sign-video generation, with state-of-the-art quality, temporal coherence, and semantic fidelity. C2.justification: V2 adds targeted qualifications about pose-extraction errors, dependence on back-translator quality, nonexpert human evaluation, and temporal misalignment in token scoring. P1.justification: V2 adds acknowledgments, a NeurIPS checklist, and appendix sections, updates author and affiliation information, and expands selected evaluation explanations. Most existing prose and the main section sequence remain intact, with localized language corrections.

P2.justification: Tables 1–2 gain columns and comparator rows; Tables 6 and 9–11 and perturbation Figure 5 are new. Figure 4 is redrawn with revised axes and a replaced reconstruction panel, and Figure 2's caption expands. Existing appendix tables and qualitative case figures are retained under new numbering.

after.justification: V2 retains these empirical results and adds human evaluation, comparator results, initialization ablation, evaluation-model perturbation tests, and token-translation measurements.

P1.justification: There are localized language corrections, updated author/contact and conference information, a moved Boltzmann-generator paragraph, and new appendix sections. Most existing prose and the overall argument remain intact.

It also identifies severe-compression threshold failure and discusses calibration recovery. The existing limitations concerning temporal artifacts and future synthesis paradigms remain.

results.title: Seeing What Matters: Generalizable AI-generated Video Detection with Forensic-Oriented Augmentation

C1.justification: The abstract, four introductory contributions, and concluding summary retain the central claims about natural-gradient inference, temporal parallelization, continuous-time ELBO approximation, and improved drift estimation. Additional experiments and theoretical arguments support these retained contributions without redefining them.

C2.justification: V2 replaces the explicitly untested high-dimensional-scaling limitation with empirical support for Monte Carlo. Appendix L.2 newly qualifies drift-learning effectiveness through initialization sensitivity and SDE Matching's generally better drift recovery, while proposing full-grid updates as an explanation for SING's latent-state sample efficiency. The discussion also adds learnable inducing-point locations as future work.

D1.justification: Appendices L.1.3 and L.2 add reproducibility details for the new studies: simulation grids, noise parameters, learning-rate schedules, network activation, expectation approximations, and use of the authors' SDE Matching implementation without further tuning. Existing experimental recipes and code/data access information are retained.

E1.justification: V2 adds Lorenz-attractor data for known-drift state inference and joint inference/drift learning. This includes Lorenz dynamics embedded in larger latent spaces with 100-dimensional observations. The linear, place-cell, Duffing, and mouse datasets are retained.

E3.justification: The new Lorenz studies introduce single-sample Monte Carlo versus six-node-per-dimension quadrature, dimensions 3–50, and specified optimization schedules. The SDE Matching comparison varies training trials from 10 to 1,024 and evaluates normalized drift error on 1,024 independent trajectories. These are added protocols; retained experiments' settings are unchanged.

E4.justification: Figure 4 adds an expectation-estimator ablation testing Monte Carlo against quadrature across latent dimensions, including memory feasibility. Figure 7 adds a training-sample sensitivity comparison with SDE Matching. These extend the existing discretization, runtime-scaling, and neural-data analyses.

E5.justification: V2 specifies five Monte Carlo seeds for Figure 4, with standard errors described as negligible and omitted. Figure 7 reports ±2SE over ten random initializations and algorithm seeds. Existing uncertainty reporting is retained; these disclosures do not establish increased repetitions of earlier experiments.

E6.justification: New Figure 4 reports Monte Carlo/quadrature latent RMSE of 0.1419/0.1417 at D=3 and Monte Carlo RMSE of 0.6778 at D=50. Figure 7 reports, at 100 training trials, latent RMSE 0.50/0.67 and normalized dynamics RMSE 0.29/0.19 for SING/SDE Matching. At 1,024 trials, latent RMSE is 0.58/0.57. Original experimental results are retained.

M1.justification: The natural-gradient updates, Gaussian variational family, associative scans, and SING-GP are retained. Monte Carlo was already an expectation-computation option in v1 and is newly evaluated. Although v2 Eq. (9) loses the prior's tilde, the derivations retain the same discretized-prior objective.

P1.justification: V2 makes localized prose edits, clarifies trial-specific variational posteriors and uniform convergence, reorganizes parts of Appendix B, and inserts Lorenz subsections. Author/header text and bibliography formatting also change. Most prose and the overall section sequence are retained.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is substantially redesigned around the generative model, natural-gradient geometry, and natural parameters. New Figures 4 and 7 display the Lorenz results. The conference layout resizes and relocates figures and introduces wrapped displays. Original experimental graphics are reused; Figure 3E's caption corrects MSE to RMSE.

R1.justification: V2 adds works by Hasan et al., Wang et al., Zeng et al., and Royden/Fitzpatrick, and expands discussion of the previously cited SDE Matching. Positioning relative to Verma et al., GP regression, and parallel inference remains substantially unchanged. SDE Matching's publication update is not a new cited work.

T1.justification: Appendix E adds a conditional maximizer-consistency argument using compactness and uniform convergence, removes the extra differentiability assumption on A(t), and revises the proof using absolute continuity and explicit diffusion-matrix dependence. Appendix B revises the mean-parameter-space definition and relative-interior treatment. The original square-root discretization-error rate remains.

improvement.justification: V1 explicitly leaves high-dimensional inference untested and lacks an evaluated neural-SDE variational-posterior baseline. V2 addresses both gaps with the Lorenz studies, reports important drift-learning weaknesses, and makes the conditions connecting ELBO convergence to maximizer consistency explicit. These additions substantially strengthen empirical support and clarify applicability. The missing tilde in Eq. (9) is a limited notation defect that does not outweigh these gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe SING by the same authors. The main text, appendices A–L, equations, and experimental displays support reliable comparison despite reformatting and added studies.

after.justification: The original empirical studies are retained, with additional Lorenz-attractor experiments in Section 5.1 and Appendices L.1.3 and L.2.

before.justification: Section 5 and Appendix L report original synthetic inference and drift-estimation experiments, runtime measurements, and analysis of mouse calcium-imaging data.

results.title: SING: SDE Inference via Natural Gradients

C1.justification: The core claim of an unbiased SOC sampler using annealed reference dynamics is retained. The abstract and introduction now present NAAS more broadly as a framework supporting different SOC solvers, with adjoint matching as one instantiation. Independence from importance sampling is qualified through solver choice and training, refining the contribution's scope.

C2.justification: v3 adds substantive explanations of coarse prior learning versus residual transport correction, reduced optimization interference, guidance thresholds, and prior-driven mode reweighting. It also discusses computational disadvantages relative to AS, Hessian and two-network costs, unresolved optimization tradeoffs, and limitations of the LRDS comparison. These substantially expand the interpretation and applicability discussion.

D1.justification: v3 discloses a single NVIDIA A6000 for timing, reports runtimes, states that both controls use the same lightweight architecture, and describes retaining LRDS defaults while training longer for separation tests. It also explicitly attributes Table 2 comparison values to SCLD. Appendix D's original hyperparameters and evaluation implementation remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Appendix C extends synthetic coverage to GMM40 at dimensions 4, 16, and 100, and adds unequal-weight bimodal Gaussian targets at dimensions 16 and 32 with varying mode separation. These are meaningful extensions within synthetic sampling; all previous target families and the molecular application remain.

E2.justification: Table 3 adds PIS to the molecular comparison previously containing only DDS. New appendix comparisons evaluate LV-PIS for importance-weight variance, LRDS for mode recovery and MW54/Funnel sampling, a single-control joint-training variant, and two-stage AS without annealing. The original Table 2 comparator set remains unchanged.

E3.justification: New evaluations introduce joint versus alternating training controls, a matched two-stage non-annealed control, guidance-strength and mode-separation sweeps, absolute mode-weight error, importance-weight variance, and wall-clock measurement. These substantially expand evaluation design. Existing benchmark metrics, the stated 2000-sample evaluation, and the original hyperparameter table remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's prior-correction and MoS guidance-strength analyses, v3 tests joint versus alternating optimization, removal of annealing, dimensional scalability, importance-weight dispersion, GMM40 sensitivity to sigma_max, and recovery of unequal weights under increasing mode separation. Figure 8 also examines how guidance changes the learned prior and intermediate samples.

E5.justification: Table 2 retains identical plus/minus reporting, and the multiple-run plots are unchanged. Neither version specifies additional seeds, repeated-run counts, confidence intervals, or significance procedures. The new importance-weight variances in Table 6 are performance diagnostics, rather than uncertainty estimates for the reported benchmark results.

E6.justification: Table 2 and the existing DDS/NAAS molecular scores are unchanged, but v3 adds the PIS molecular row and extensive results in Tables 4–11. For example, joint versus alternating training gives MoS Sinkhorn distances of 597.99 versus 394.55. Table 5 adds dimensional-scaling results and reports 50-dimensional runtimes of 120 minutes for NAAS, 30–40 for SCLD, and 30 for AS.

M1.justification: The two-control SOC formulation, adjoint and reciprocal-adjoint objectives, replay buffers, and Algorithm 1 are retained. The alternative IWS-NAAS algorithm already appeared in v1. Newly evaluated joint-training and non-annealed variants are comparison controls, not replacements for the proposed method.

P1.justification: The abstract and substantial introductory passages are rewritten around informative reference dynamics and solver flexibility. Section 3.3 gains an extended explanation of the two stages, while a reorganized 'Further Discussion on NAAS' appendix incorporates previously separate material. The unfinished related-work placeholder is removed and acknowledgments are added.

P2.justification: v3 adds eight experimental tables and the multi-panel Figure 8, expands Table 3 with PIS, and revises Table 1's IWS labeling. Figure 1 moves earlier, and other displays are repositioned. The original seven figures retain their visual content; the hyperparameter table is retained as Table 12.

R1.justification: Appendix B.2 adds a focused substantive distinction from NETS: matching annealed intermediate densities versus NAAS's value-function-modified marginals. v3 also adds references to harmonic path integral diffusion, LRDS, and free-energy computations, removes FEAT, and replaces CMCD with CRAFT in the conceptual Table 1. The existing PDDS relationship is retained after relocation.

T1.justification: The principal theorems, corollary, lemma, and proofs are retained. The PDDS proposition moves from Appendix A.6 to B.3, and the importance-sampling derivation moves from Appendix B to B.4. The NETS discussion interprets the existing marginal-distribution result; it does not introduce a new theorem or proof.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens the evidence for important design choices through joint-training and non-annealed controls, and tests previously unexamined unequal mode weights and separation robustness. The NETS comparison and explicit cost discussion also address gaps in v1's explanation and positioning. These gains extend beyond additional benchmark scores. Limitations remain: new experiments lack repeated-run uncertainty and detailed budgets, and describing runtime overhead as minor understates Table 5's 120 minutes versus 30–40 minutes. Nevertheless, the added diagnostic evidence materially improves the paper overall.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same NAAS research work. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching relocated material.

after.justification: v3 retains these original results and adds experiments on optimization, dimensional scaling, importance weights, annealing, and mode-weight recovery.

before.justification: v1 reports original synthetic sampling and alanine-dipeptide results in Section 5, plus prior-correction and annealing-strength experiments in Appendix C.

results.title: Non-equilibrium Annealed Adjoint Sampler

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the same contributions: universal grounding through timestamp interleaving and adaptive scaling, hierarchical inference, efficient training, benchmark performance and downstream VideoQA benefits. Additional experiments support these retained claims without redefining the main contribution.

C2.justification: V2 adds interpretations concerning balanced short/long-video performance against closed models, consistency relative to VTune, and accuracy-versus-computation tradeoffs for processing strategies and thresholds. The existing limitations concerning task specialization, reasoning capabilities and fixed segment lengths remain unchanged.

D1.justification: Appendix E adds training-cost information: Table 11 reports 21, 12 and 24.5 hours for processing alternatives, and the text reports five additional days for short-video token compression in UniTime-Full. It also explains threshold routing and the hardware-imposed token ceiling. Existing optimization details, prompts and project link are retained.

E1.justification: The training datasets, five main grounding benchmarks and four VideoQA benchmarks remain unchanged. Appendix D adds Charades-CON and ActivityNet-CON evaluations involving paraphrased queries and shifted moments, extending test conditions within existing video domains.

E2.justification: Table 3 adds Qwen2-VL-7B and Qwen2.5-VL-7B baselines. New Table 5 compares Gemini-2.5-Flash/Pro, GPT-4.1-mini, GPT-4o and Seed1.5-VL. Tables 6 and 10 further add InternVL2.5 baselines and consistency comparisons involving Gemini 1.5 Flash, Video-LLaMA and TimeChat with and without VTune.

E3.justification: V2 introduces random-subset closed-model evaluation that excludes outputs without timestamps, consistency evaluation across three paraphrases and shifted moments, and controlled processing, threshold and token-budget sweeps. These substantially extend the evaluation design; the original training defaults and benchmark protocols remain unchanged.

E4.justification: V2 adds consistency testing, resizing-versus-compression controls, timestamp-versus-position-encoding ablations, and sensitivity analyses for both frame thresholds and token budget. Backbone analysis expands to InternVL2.5. The earlier Qwen size/type studies are partly incorporated into Section 3.4, rather than being entirely new experiments.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run uncertainty, random seeds, confidence intervals or significance tests. Table 10's bracketed values are relative consistency scores; averaging across three paraphrases defines an evaluation metric rather than uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Shared main benchmark, module-ablation, robustness and VideoQA scores remain unchanged. Tables 5–6 and 10–15 add substantial results, including Charades-STA mIoU of 63.15 versus 44.85 for timestamp insertion versus dense position encodings. V1 Table 9's Qwen2.5-VL UniTime results on ANet-Captions, QVHighlights and TaCoS are omitted. New subset results do not establish improvements over earlier full-benchmark scores.

M1.justification: Sections 2.1–2.3 retain adaptive frame scaling, timestamp interleaving, hierarchical inference, the autoregressive objective and video-centric training. Additional backbone experiments and explanations do not document a change to the proposed procedure.

P1.justification: V2 inserts closed-model and flexibility subsections, moves and reworks model ablations, reorganizes the later appendices, and adds cross-references, acknowledgements and the conference designation. Most existing introduction, method, related-work and conclusion prose is retained.

P2.justification: The table presentation expands substantially with closed-model, consistency, processing, encoding and hyperparameter displays. The separate model-size/type tables are recast into Table 6's baseline-versus-UniTime layout, Table 3 gains rows, and several displays move. The eight existing figures retain their substantive content.

R1.justification: Eight references are added, covering newly evaluated models and grounding-consistency research. Section 3.6 and Appendix D explicitly position UniTime against VTune's consistency-oriented training. The broader related-work taxonomy and earlier citations remain substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: Appendix D adds a mathematical specification of rephrased grounding consistency using IoU between predictions for original and paraphrased queries, averaged over three variants. The original task formulation, scaling equations, sequence construction and training loss remain unchanged; no theorem or proof is added.

improvement.justification: V1 lacked direct controls isolating timestamp encoding and resizing versus token compression. V2 supplies these controls and sensitivity/cost evidence in Tables 11–15, while Table 6 extends validation beyond Qwen and Appendix D adds consistency testing. This substantially strengthens support for central design and generality claims. Benefits are tempered by omitted cross-dataset backbone results and weaknesses in the new closed-model comparison: unspecified subset sizes, exclusion of untimestamped outputs, and a Seed1.5-VL prose score of 72.2 conflicting with Table 5's 73.69. These issues limit that comparison but do not outweigh the stronger component-level validation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same UniTime research work. Their complete main texts and appendices, including equations, tables and figures, are readable and support a reliable comparison.

after.justification: V2 retains original experimental results and adds closed-model comparisons, broader backbone evaluations, grounding-consistency tests and additional ablations.

before.justification: V1 reports original temporal-grounding and VideoQA experiments, module and robustness analyses, and additional model-size and architecture experiments in Appendix D.

results.title: Universal Video Temporal Grounding with Generative Multi-modal Large Language Models

C1.justification: The abstract and principal contributions retain near-minimax contraction and adaptation over anisotropic and composite Besov spaces. v2 makes the composite-Besov novelty more explicit, but v1's Table 1 footnote already distinguished earlier composite Hölder results. No new principal contribution is introduced.

C2.justification: Section 4 adds practical guidance favoring sparse architectures and sparsity-inducing priors, and explicitly extends the interpretation toward neural-network performance more broadly. Appendix A.2 explains why the scaled sigmoid accompanies unit-bounded functions. The existing computational and horseshoe-prior limitations remain.

D1.justification: The explicit prior hyperparameter recipe and approximating-network specifications are revised. v2 additionally details layerwise rescaling coefficients in C.5 and the exact network parameter count in C.8. These concern the theoretical construction; no implementation, hardware, runtime or code/data release is introduced.

E1.justification: Neither version trains or evaluates on datasets or test scenarios. Added discussion of images motivates the theory and does not establish additional evaluated coverage.

E2.justification: Neither version evaluates comparison methods experimentally. Table 1 compares theoretical literature; its revision does not add or remove evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: Neither version specifies an empirical evaluation protocol. Changes to theoretical network constructions, classification risk and norm inequalities belong to the model and theory assessments.

E4.justification: Neither version reports ablations, sensitivity experiments, robustness tests or empirical case studies. The additive, multiplicative, rotated and piecewise mathematical examples are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental repetitions, seeds, confidence intervals or significance tests. Revised probability bounds are theoretical derivations, not changes in empirical uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: No empirical result entries are added, removed or updated. The illustrative functions and principal contraction-rate orders remain the same; corrections to mathematical bounds and definitions are assessed under T1.

M1.justification: The network and prior families remain, but their specifications receive meaningful refinements. Example 3.5 changes the continuous prior's slab weight from 1/T to exp[-2 C_A(log n)^2] and revises its spike scale. Appendix A.2 replaces the ordinary sigmoid with a scaled sigmoid. These change the specified models without introducing a new inference framework.

P1.justification: The main organization remains. v2 polishes prose, expands motivation and discussion, adds acknowledgments and proof pointers, and consolidates selected appendix statements.
