The heavy-tail proof moves from v1 C.16 to v2 C.9, and classification inequalities are integrated into surrounding text or proofs.

P2.justification: Table 1 is reorganized into single-function and composite-function columns, and a new Table 2 summarizes assumptions and theorems. Figure 1 adds panel labels and color scales; Figure 2 gains color styling. These revise existing displays and add a summary without changing the overall layout substantially.

R1.justification: v2 adds Donoho–Johnstone (1995), Pope et al. (2021), and four references on CNN and transformer theory. Section 1.1 clarifies that Egels and Castillo's composite results concern Hölder classes, resolving misleading v1 prose while retaining its earlier table-footnote distinction. Publication updates concern already cited works.

T1.justification: Assumption (C3) now requires exponentially smaller tail mass in (log n)^2 and uses a smaller threshold. v2 C.12 replaces v1 C.10's binomial-tail argument, while C.13 adds missing weight-tail control and an explicit adaptive-shrinkage argument. Lemma B.4 revises approximation tolerance, depth and sparsity, supported by an expanded rescaling construction. Appendix A also corrects excess classification risk by subtracting Bayes risk and changes the empirical-norm upper-bound coefficient from 1/2 to 3/2. These substantially revise the mathematical support.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the paper's mathematical support by correcting the shrinkage tail-bound argument, supplying missing adaptive sieve control, expanding the bounded-weight approximation construction, and repairing the classification-risk definition. These address central deficiencies in a theoretical paper. The stronger shrinkage assumption narrows applicability, and new Table 2 incorrectly associates Theorem 3.14(i)/(ii) with prior families rather than assumptions (A4)/(A5). Those limitations do not outweigh the substantial proof corrections.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same study of posterior contraction for sparse Bayesian neural networks. Their complete main texts, figures, tables, equations and Appendices A–C are readable and support comparison.

after.justification: v2 remains a theoretical paper. Neither its main text nor appendices report original empirical outcomes; the figures illustrate specified functions and compositional structures.

before.justification: v1 reports mathematical results and proofs, without original experiments, simulations or data analyses. Its function plots are mathematical illustrations; Appendix A's empirical-norm results are theoretical.

results.title: Posterior Contraction for Sparse Neural Networks in Besov Spaces with Intrinsic Dimensionality

C1.justification: The central communication-reduction and acceleration claims remain. V2 qualifies the abstract's accuracy claim with 'across nearly all evaluated benchmarks' and describes accuracy as 'largely on par' in the contributions, while elevating possible validation-loss improvements into the abstract.

C2.justification: V2 adds the ensemble interpretation at zero synchronization, explains the computation-graph distinction, and discusses optional scaling and hardware-buffer alignment as accuracy/speed considerations. It removes v1's explicit caution about generalizing small-model trends and treating validation loss as a proxy. The training-speed projection limitation remains.

D1.justification: V2 adds a source-code link, NVIDIA device and NVLink specifications, the gpt-fast implementation reference, and GPT-XL configuration details. It also specifies training-speed micro-batches of 4 for TP4 and 8 for TP8/16; these disclosures alone do not establish changes to the corresponding earlier settings.

E1.justification: Both versions use RedPajama and the same seven evaluation benchmarks, alongside validation loss, training throughput and inference latency. Added experiments vary model architectures, synchronization, precision and hardware within these retained tasks; they introduce no new datasets or task requirements.

E2.justification: Fully synchronized models remain the accuracy and speed comparators, and Top-K and random masking remain the compression comparators. The added NVIDIA experiments use a different implementation framework but retain the full-all-reduce reference method.

E3.justification: Llama2-7B training increases from 90B to 160B tokens. V2 introduces a TinyLlama synchronization sweep, GPT3-XL training over 50B tokens, NVIDIA inference experiments using gpt-fast, and controlled precision/scaling experiments. These substantially expand experimental configurations and protocols.

E4.justification: V2 adds direct bfloat16-versus-fp32 accumulation experiments showing instability after approximately 15K steps (Appendix E.1), private-channel scaling ablations (E.3), and synchronization sensitivity across TinyLlama configurations. GPT-XL and NVIDIA experiments additionally test architecture and hardware robustness beyond v1's evidence.

E5.justification: Accuracy uncertainty margins appear in both versions. V2 additionally reports Welch's t-test, identifying the 7B BoolQ difference as marginally significant with p-value 0.046 and describing other accuracy differences as nonsignificant. Neither version specifies additional repeated runs or seeds.

E6.justification: Table 1 replaces the 7B results after longer training: baseline/CAAT-Net BoolQ changes from 62.75/62.29 to 64.89/62.51. TinyLlama scores and 130M curves are revised; GPT-XL, expanded synchronization and NVIDIA results are added. Training throughput values also change, including TP16 at p=0.25 from 110190 to 112456 tokens/s. These are revised or newly reported results, not established same-setting gains. Existing 34B/70B inference measurements are retained.

M1.justification: Private-channel correction changes from scaling weights at initialization in v1 Section 3.2 to multiplying activations by the corrective factor in v2 Section 4. V2 also introduces sequential logical-device inference with local summation when using fewer physical devices. The central partial-reduction and backward-synchronization procedures remain.

P1.justification: V2 substantially reorganizes the exposition: attention equations move to Appendix A, channel scaling moves into implementation, large-scale and synchronization experiments are combined, and compression accounting moves to Appendix D. The abstract, architectural explanation, inference discussion and experimental narrative are also rewritten.

P2.justification: Figures 3 and 4 become expanded multipanel displays, the compression table becomes Figure 5, and new diagnostic Figures 6–7 and evaluation tables are introduced. Architecture diagrams and captions are revised. The earlier 34B/70B speedup plots disappear, while their numerical tables remain.

R1.justification: V2 adds citations for context parallelism, LayerNorm and RMSNorm. It expands discussion of the already-cited Ladder Residual method and explains how competing communication demands motivate complementarity with overlap methods. The overall research positioning remains.

T1.justification: V2 generalizes the stated backward-pass derivation from RMSNorm to arbitrary normalization functions, including LayerNorm, and removes v1's Top-K MMSE-optimality assertion. The MLP/attention definitions, residual-gradient reasoning and Appendix C speedup derivation are otherwise retained, despite relocation and renumbering.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens empirical support for important implementation requirements through direct precision and scaling ablations, and tests robustness across synchronization levels, architectures and hardware. The code link and explicit BoolQ significance qualification improve reproducibility information and claim calibration. Training-speed evidence remains a 16-bit projection, and the retained 14% speedup statement conflicts with the approximately 16.4% implied by the revised Table 6. These reporting limitations temper, but do not outweigh, the substantial gains in supporting evidence.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe CAAT-Net. Their main text, equations, figures, tables and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including material relocated between sections.

after.justification: Section 5 and Appendix E retain original experiments and add GPT-XL evaluations, numerical-precision and scaling ablations, TinyLlama synchronization sweeps, and NVIDIA timing measurements.

before.justification: Section 5 and Appendix D report original model-training results, zero-shot evaluations, synchronization and compression experiments, and training/inference timing measurements.

results.title: Tensor-Parallelism with Partially Synchronized Activations

C1.justification: The abstract and central claims about extracellular-only biophysical inference, robustness to misspecification, and applicability to reconstructed morphologies remain substantially unchanged. The introduction expands the claimed scalable-inference contribution from diagonal covariance approximation to both diagonal and block-diagonal approximations.

C2.justification: V1 mainly gives generic warnings about approximation bias. V2 identifies concrete validity conditions involving integration steps, gating sensitivities, firing frequency, and electrode–compartment geometry. It explains RGC diagonal-EKF failure through measurement coupling, motivates preserving voltage correlations, and discusses reducing gating variances as a mitigation. These substantially qualify the method's applicability.

D1.justification: V2 newly states the multi-branch axial resistivity, but omits previously specified current-injection amplitudes for misspecification, RGC, and CA1 experiments. Software versions, hardware, and code-access information remain. Reproducibility also suffers from an unresolved discrepancy: Table 1 retains leak conductance 0.003 S/cm² while the revised single-branch plots mark approximately 0.0003 as the true value.

E1.justification: The simulated extracellular-inference tasks and RGC/CA1 morphology coverage remain. V2 adds explicit high- versus low-frequency spiking scenarios in a 100-compartment cable analysis (Figure B.2), extending the tested dynamical regimes. Changes in compartment counts within existing validation tasks are principally experimental-setting changes.

E2.justification: The simple-model comparison expands from EKF versus MSE fitting to full EKF, diagonal EKF, block-diagonal EKF, and MSE (Figure 2C). V2 also adds diagonal-versus-full EKF comparisons for the multi-branch model and diagonal-versus-block-diagonal comparisons for RGC, substantially broadening the evaluated comparator sets.

E3.justification: Section 4.1 changes from one compartment, 10 µm electrode distance, and 3 µV baseline noise to ten compartments, 5 µm, and 1 µV. Multi-branch injected current changes from 0.5 to 2 nA. RGC uses 10 rather than 169 electrodes and replaces the 0.1/10 µV sweep with low-noise experiments. CA1 noise changes from 1 to 0.1 µV and fitting switches from full to block-diagonal EKF.

E4.justification: V2 adds substantial approximation-validity analyses: firing-regime Jacobian heatmaps, measurement-coupling heatmaps, and diagonal-EKF parameter, voltage, and localization diagnostics (Appendix B; Figures E.2 and E.6–E.9). RGC becomes an explicit approximation-failure comparison. V1's RGC noise-sensitivity sweep is removed; the channel-misspecification tests and runtime analysis remain, with the former using revised setups.

E5.justification: V2 no longer reports the RGC ten-dataset replication and associated mean/standard-deviation summaries shown in v1's Appendix D. It reports over 100 RGC initializations instead of 100. Forty-dataset uncertainty reporting for simpler models remains. Missing replication reporting does not establish that fewer runs were performed.

E6.justification: V2 adds results showing block-diagonal EKF matching full EKF/MSE while diagonal EKF exhibits bias (Figure 2C). RGC results change from successful diagonal-EKF recovery to diagonal failure and block-diagonal success (Figure 4). CA1 recovery traces are replaced, with remaining errors emphasized for leak conductances. These involve changed formulations or settings, so they do not establish same-setting performance gains; the approximately twofold diagonal-EKF runtime result is retained.

M1.justification: V2 revises the stated observation model: transmembrane current includes surface area and capacitive current, yielding a voltage-only linear observation mapping (Section 2). It also introduces a block-diagonal EKF with dense voltage covariance and diagonal gating covariance, substantially extending v1's full and diagonal EKF procedures.

P1.justification: The exposition is substantially reorganized: Section 3.2 separates diagonal approximation, validity, and block-diagonal approximation; experimental passages are rewritten around approximation comparisons; and appendices place validity theory and geometric identifiability before experimental details. The abstract and broad six-section main-text outline remain largely unchanged.

P2.justification: V2 adopts a different conference layout and substantially redesigns the visual presentation. Figure 2 introduces boxplots and rearranged panels; Figure 4 replaces noise/conductance panels with approximation comparisons and a heatmap. Multiple diagnostic figures are added, and RGC noise-sweep displays disappear. Existing localization and runtime figures are retained under new numbering.

R1.justification: V2 adds Gold, Henze, and Koch (2007), 'Using extracellular action potential recordings to constrain compartmental models,' when defining transmembrane current. The broader literature coverage and first-to-fit positioning remain largely unchanged. Conversion to numbered references is stylistic.

T1.justification: V2 revises the transmembrane-current definition and derives the linear observation mapping. New Appendices B and C analyze Jacobian sensitivities and electrode coupling, define the BD(K) covariance family, and prove its closure under stated assumptions, with block update and complexity derivations. The earlier geometric unidentifiability argument is retained in Appendix D.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens the scientific foundation by correcting the main-text current formulation and replacing broadly favorable diagonal-EKF evidence with explicit validity conditions, a demonstrated failure case, and an evaluated block-diagonal alternative. These address central modeling and approximation deficiencies. Reduced RGC noise/uncertainty reporting, omitted stimulus amplitudes, and the Table 1/figure discrepancy weaken validation and reproducibility, but the gains in model specification and evidence about approximation limits outweigh those losses.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and can be matched despite substantial revisions and renumbering.

after.justification: V2 reports original simulation results for these neuron models, including comparisons of covariance approximations, reconstruction results, and analyses of approximation failure.

before.justification: V1 reports original simulations measuring parameter, voltage, and spatial recovery for simplified neurons and reconstructed RGC and CA1 morphologies, plus runtime experiments.

results.title: Identifying multi-compartment Hodgkin-Huxley models with high-density extracellular voltage recordings

C1.justification: The abstract and first contribution broaden the Infinity-focused scope to bitwise image generators, explicitly including Instella. The conclusion additionally claims a significant radioactivity-induced distributional shift with only 5% watermarked training data, substantially extending the stated applicability conditions.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations linking Instella/BiGR robustness limitations to their smaller token counts, hypothesizes that Infinity-8B's lower bias reduces robustness, and interprets weak radioactivity through distribution-level significance. Existing rotation, image-quality, and large-scale false-positive limitations remain.

D1.justification: v2 adds a BitMark repository link, single-scale pseudocode, baseline message lengths, and generation settings for the added models. Existing hardware and fine-tuning details remain. Some specificity is lost from the interpolation and convolution descriptions, while BiGR's added preprocessing noise is not quantified.

E1.justification: MS-COCO and ImageNet coverage is retained. v2 adds LAION POP for false-positive evaluation (Table 19), horizontal and vertical flipping, and combined rotation-plus-center-crop inputs, modestly extending the existing image-watermarking scenarios.

E2.justification: v1 reports BitMark's robustness without direct numerical comparisons against other watermarking methods. v2 evaluates RivaGAN, StegaStamp, and TrustMark on Infinity-2B images alongside BitMark in Table 2, substantially expanding the comparative evidence.

E3.justification: v2 introduces Infinity-8B and Instella configurations with delta=1.5, and BiGR configurations at two resolutions with delta=3 and 5,000 prompts. New protocols vary watermarked fine-tuning fractions, apply rotation correction with optional 50% center cropping, and transfer an MS-COCO-calibrated threshold across datasets. The original fine-tuning hyperparameters are retained.

E4.justification: New analyses test radioactivity under clean/watermarked training mixtures (Table 6), rotation correction with and without cropping (Tables 13–14), and false-positive calibration across datasets (Table 19). Existing bit-sequence, scale, watermark-strength, and Bit-Flipper analyses are retained under reorganized appendices.

E5.justification: v2 adds a one-tailed Mann–Whitney U test and p-value reporting for the radioactivity dilution experiment (Section 4.3, Table 6). Existing mean/standard-deviation reporting continues; neither version specifies repeated-training run counts or seeds.

E6.justification: Substantial new results cover baselines, additional models, and supplementary analyses. Examples include 22.7% TPR at 1% FPR after fine-tuning with 10% watermarked data, and newly measured rotation-correction TPRs of 18.4% without correction versus 98.3% with correction. Table 5 also changes Infinity-2B radioactivity from 99.7% to 100.0%, although v2's prose still says 99.7%.

M1.justification: The core bit-pattern logit bias and z-score detector remain unchanged. v2 adds single-scale embedding and detection procedures without multiscale residual processing (Algorithms 3–4), and introduces noise before encoding for BiGR detection (Appendix G). These are limited procedural adaptations.

P1.justification: The appendices are extensively reorganized: limitations and related work move forward, natural-image evaluation becomes an experimental subsection, and attack material is consolidated. The title and framing are revised, and a NeurIPS checklist is appended, although much existing prose remains.

P2.justification: v2 introduces a main comparison table with baseline/model rows and flipping columns, adds several experimental tables, and relocates the original watermark-strength table to the appendix. Existing figures are resized or repositioned, and the timing table is transposed. The original qualitative image content is retained.

R1.justification: v2 adds references to Instella, BiGR, TrustMark, StegaStamp, and RivaGAN, with corresponding model background and comparison positioning. The underlying discussion of LLM watermarking, diffusion watermarking, and model collapse is largely retained.

T1.justification: The bit-bias equation, z-score definition and null model, and green/red-list combinatorial reasoning are retained. Neither version supplies theoretical propositions or proofs; the new significance test is an empirical statistical procedure.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses important gaps in v1 through direct watermark-baseline comparisons and mixed-data radioactivity controls. Measured rotation correction and explicit model-specific weaknesses further strengthen evidence about practical applicability. These gains outweigh the new Table 5 table/prose inconsistency and incomplete specification of BiGR's noise preprocessing.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same BitMark research. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable, and retained material can be matched across renaming and reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds watermark-baseline comparisons, mixed-data radioactivity, rotation correction, additional model evaluations, and cross-dataset false-positive measurements.

before.justification: v1 reports original image-quality, watermark-robustness, timing, radioactivity, and ablation results in Section 4 and the appendices.

results.title: BitMark: Watermarking Bitwise Autoregressive Image Generative Models

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same central claims about the gradient–weight relationship, dynamic small-weight updates, efficiency, generalization, and reduced forgetting. Added experiments support these claims; LoGo was an appendix extension rather than a main contribution claim.

C2.justification: Section 6 explicitly warns that weak task similarity may favor full-update optimizers and emphasizes dependence on overparameterization. Appendix M adds a mechanism hypothesis for the pruned-initialization result. These extend the transferability and plasticity interpretations already present in v1 without replacing the central explanation.

D1.justification: v2 newly explains per-matrix flattening and chunkwise bottom-k selection and supplies Llama 3.2/LoRA hyperparameters, checkpointing, and hardware information. LoGo's implementation and hyperparameter documentation is removed. Existing experimental recipes largely persist; the chunking discussion is additional disclosure rather than evidence of a changed procedure.

E1.justification: v2 adds eight commonsense tasks, including HellaSwag, PIQA, ARC, and BoolQ, plus nine-class PathMNIST medical-image classification (Appendices J and L). GLUE, CIFAR-10, Flowers102, and GSM-8k remain. The pruned-initialization experiment changes model conditions within retained CIFAR-10 coverage.

E2.justification: v2 adds static-mask NANOADAM to the broader GLUE accuracy and runtime comparisons, beyond v1's SST-2 ablation. The commonsense comparison introduces rank-32 LoRA trained with AdamW or NANOADAM. Conversely, GSM-8k loses the LoGo comparator while retaining AdamW8b and MicroAdam.

E3.justification: New protocols include Llama 3.2 3B full finetuning and rank-32 LoRA, with two epochs, batch size 16, sequence cutoff 256, and gradient checkpointing. Additional controlled protocols vary mask and density intervals, group weights by pretrained magnitude, and test 80% magnitude-pruned initialization. The stated settings of the retained GLUE, vision, and non-LoGo GSM-8k experiments remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 adds realized-update analysis across weight-magnitude groups (Appendix C), mask/density-interval sensitivity tests (F.4), broader static-mask ablations (H.2), medical-domain transfer (L), and sensitivity to pruned initialization (M). These test dependencies and robustness questions beyond v1's existing masking and learning-rate analyses.

E5.justification: The ten-seed toy statistics and four-seed GSM-8k means and standard deviations are retained. v2 introduces shaded bands in Figures 4, 8, and 9, but does not define their statistic or contributing runs, while the ablation text still specifies a fixed seed. Whether these represent new uncertainty estimation or a plotting transformation is unresolved.

E6.justification: New results include commonsense average accuracies of 82.05% for NANOADAM, 80.65% for MicroAdam, and 73.14% for AdamW (Table 25), plus sensitivity, static-mask, transfer, and pruning results. Existing ablation curves also change: the large-weight accuracy curve in Figures 4/8 ends around 0.57 in v1 versus 0.62 in v2. LoGo's GSM-8k result of 35.54 ± 0.93% disappears; NANOADAM's 34.95 ± 0.64% and main Tables 1–5 remain unchanged.

M1.justification: v2 removes the distinct LoGo optimizer from v1 Appendix H and Algorithm 2, including its intersection of small-weight and large-gradient selections and selective momentum inheritance. NANOADAM's main procedure remains unchanged; the new description of chunkwise selection does not establish an implementation change.

P1.justification: Most main-text prose is retained with limited editing. v2 adds limitations and acknowledgements sections, extends the appendix organization, and presents the retained GSM-8k experiment separately in Appendix K after removing LoGo. The first-page status changes from preprint to NeurIPS 2025.

P2.justification: v2 adds displays for layerwise shifts, interval sensitivity, static-mask accuracy, and commonsense accuracy/memory/runtime, and expands the GLUE runtime table. Tables are systematically restyled, ablation plots are redrawn with shaded bands, and LoGo's pseudocode and comparison rows disappear. Most original figure subjects remain, often relocated.

R1.justification: New Appendix A elaborates distinctions from the already-cited Liao et al. method, while Appendix J explicitly positions NANOADAM as complementary to LoRA. The bibliography adds JUWELS and Malach et al. and removes the Vardi et al. single-neuron reference. Most related-work discussion remains intact.

T1.justification: Definition 2.1 now explicitly defines preservation of the top-k neurons. Theorem 2.2 replaces the terse exact-learning claim with explicit pretraining and small opposite-sign neuron assumptions and an O(epsilon) approximation bound. Appendix E adds a substantial perturbation argument using linearization and a Gronwall bound.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens scrutiny of NANOADAM: the brief convergence assertion becomes an explicitly qualified approximation claim with a developed argument, and targeted tests address masking sensitivity, static-mask alternatives, domain transfer, and initialization dependence. Implementation disclosure and explicit limitations also improve assessability. Removing the higher-scoring LoGo comparison loses useful evidence, and the unexplained plot bands limit statistical interpretability, but these drawbacks do not outweigh the stronger qualification and validation of the central approach.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Pay Attention to Small Weights and NANOADAM. All pages, including appendices, were readable and visually inspected; the retained experiments, equations, and displays can be matched despite reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds commonsense evaluation, sensitivity analyses, medical-domain transfer, and pruned-initialization experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original teacher–student simulations, GLUE finetuning, vision continual-learning experiments, ablations, and GSM-8k results.

results.title: Pay Attention to Small Weights

C1.justification: v1 centers its contribution on LGES and its I-ORIENT extension. v2's conclusion presents a family of less-greedy algorithms and claims that the insertion strategies improve existing GES-style searches more broadly. The retained speed, accuracy, and robustness claims therefore acquire a substantially broader algorithmic scope.

C2.justification: New Section B.1 explains why analogous filtering of deletions could preserve false adjacencies, how LGES searches fewer separating sets than PC, and why DAG selection warrants further study. Section 5.3 distinguishes the guarantees of SAFEINSERT plus I-ORIENT from the empirical advantages of LGIES. Existing causal-sufficiency and faithfulness limitations largely remain.

D1.justification: v2 identifies and supplies pseudocode for the implemented CPDAG-to-DAG selection procedure (Algorithm 7). It also documents the common Python implementation used for GES-family comparisons and exclusion of optimized XGES operators. These improve implementation disclosure; hardware, principal baseline parameters, and the stated project-code location remain unchanged.

E1.justification: v2 adds the sparser ER1 observational setting and extends interventional evaluation to ER3 graphs (Section D.1.4 and Figure 5). Observational learning, misspecified prior knowledge, interventional learning, and continuous/discretized Sachs data remain the same core tasks and domains.

E2.justification: XGES-0 and XGES become evaluated comparators in Section 5.1 and Figure 4b; their source paper was cited but these methods were not evaluated in v1. Comparisons also expand to the new LGES+ and interventional variants, while retaining GES, PC, NoTears, and GIES in the relevant experiments.

E3.justification: Within the retained simulation framework, v2's reported small-sample evaluation drops n = 500, and its scalability evaluation stops at 250 rather than including 500 variables. Example 2 changes from 1,000 to 100 samples per dataset. These revise specific settings; the principal data-generation procedure, accuracy measures, and 50-dataset design remain.

E4.justification: Figure 4b adds a systematic comparison testing whether less-greedy insertion helps across GES, XGES-0, XGES, and GIES. Density sensitivity is extended to ER1. Conversely, v1's scoring-operation analyses and detailed ER3 error and classification breakdowns disappear; the prior-misspecification analysis remains, reorganized.

E5.justification: v1 explicitly defines plotted error bars as one standard deviation across 50 random seeds. v2 retains error bars and reports 50 simulated datasets but removes their statistical definition from the captions. Its remaining table still reports mean ± standard deviation. This is a reporting loss, not evidence that retained experiments used fewer runs.

E6.justification: v2 adds extensive results for XGES and the new less-greedy variants. Table D.1.1 retains v1's 175-variable conservative LGES SHD of 42.04 ± 11.51 as LGES-0 and adds 39.457 ± 10.44 for the modified LGES. Example 2 changes from 69%/31% to 96%/4% under a changed sample size. Results for 500-variable graphs and several detailed metric breakdowns are removed; Sachs outcomes remain unchanged.

M1.justification: Beyond carrying the original LGES design into LGES-0, v2 introduces deletion/turning priority in LGES and forced-deletion restarts in LGES+ (Algorithms 1, 8–9). GGES accommodates mixed operator schedules. v1's LGIES meant LGES followed by I-ORIENT; v2 retains that pipeline separately and introduces LGIES variants that incorporate less-greedy insertion directly into GIES.

P1.justification: Several method and experiment sections are substantially rewritten. Section 3.3 separates initialization from guided search, Section 4 adds a structured explanation of orientation, and Appendix B is divided into design, limitations, and examples. Algorithm naming, contribution framing, and the terminology of model repairing versus prior knowledge are revised throughout.

P2.justification: The empirical displays are extensively redesigned. Figure 4 adds grouped cross-family comparisons; Figure 5 becomes a multi-panel accuracy/runtime comparison across densities. Appendix figures reorganize comparator groups, the small-sample heatmaps and accompanying table are replaced by line plots, and the large-graph table changes rows and metric structure. Explanatory graph diagrams are retained.

R1.justification: XGES shifts from a supporting citation to an explicit methodological predecessor whose heuristics are incorporated and compared against (Section 3.4). Section A.2.2 expands the distinction between perfect and misspecified background knowledge, including Knowledge-Guided GES. Additional references support prior-based scoring, DAG conversion/sampling, and discussion of hidden-variable settings.

T1.justification: Appendix C extends Theorem 1's argument beyond the original forward/backward procedure to turning and mixed insertion/deletion schedules. It supplies correctness arguments for the newly defined LGES and LGES+ variants, while carrying the original LGES argument into Corollary C.1 for LGES-0. The SAFEINSERT and I-ORIENT results are largely retained.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses an important gap in v1: XGES was cited but not evaluated. Direct XGES/XGES-0 comparisons and paired insertion-strategy tests across algorithm families substantially strengthen validation of the central idea. Extended correctness arguments and implementation explanations make the broader contribution more assessable. Removed stress-test results, undefined plotted error bars, and stale FAQ references to omitted settings weaken reporting, but do not outweigh the central validation gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs contain the same work, Less Greedy Equivalence Search, with complete main text and Appendices A–E. Text, equations, pseudocode, tables, and figures support reliable comparison, including content moved or renamed between versions.

after.justification: v2 retains original simulation and Sachs results and reports additional comparisons involving XGES and expanded less-greedy algorithm variants.

before.justification: v1 reports original simulations measuring causal-graph recovery and runtime, experiments with misspecified prior assumptions and interventions, and analyses of the Sachs protein-signaling dataset.

results.title: Less Greedy Equivalence Search

C1.justification: The three central contributions remain stochastic scale-separated dynamics, the PoE likelihood, and simulator-free learning. v2 extends the abstract, introduction, and conclusion's comparative claims to reduced-order modeling, explicitly claiming superiority over DMD and POD-SINDy, particularly for slowly decaying Kolmogorov n-width.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations for DMD's competitiveness on periodic cylinder flow and ROM difficulties on shallow water, plus specific limitations concerning local structures in three-dimensional turbulence and long-term chaotic stability. v1's excluded unstable Burgers trajectory and proposed stability-preserving remedy are no longer discussed; v2 does not establish whether that failure was resolved.

D1.justification: New Appendix G documents baseline implementations, cubic interpolation, POD-SINDy tuning and selected hyperparameters, and DMD regularization. v2 also supplies added-task preprocessing, revised architecture/training specifications, and cumulative training-time formulas. This substantially expands reproducibility information; the underlying code-repository location remains unchanged.

E1.justification: v2 adds one-dimensional wave advection and two-dimensional shallow-water radial dam-break evaluation, substantially broadening the represented dynamics and initial-condition families. KdV and cylinder flow remain; Burgers is retained in Appendix H.3 rather than removed.

E2.justification: v1's predictive comparisons use the implicit-scale baseline. v2 adds coarse DNS, DMD, and POD-SINDy to the retained KdV, Burgers, and cylinder experiments, as verified in Tables 1 and 3. Full DNS also supplies a computational-cost reference in Figure 8.

E3.justification: v2 introduces baseline dimension matching and validation-based POD-SINDy tuning, alongside protocols for the added tasks. Existing training settings also change: batch size and quadrature count decrease from 128 to 64, KdV training from 200 to 100 epochs, and cylinder training from 2000 to 1000 epochs (v1 Appendix G.5; v2 Appendix H.7).

E4.justification: v2 adds a substantive accuracy-versus-inference-cost study across four systems using NFE times state dimension (Figure 8), addressing efficiency beyond v1's accuracy ablations. Microscale-dimension and spatial diagnostics extend to the added systems. Existing drift-sensitivity and kernel-spectrum analyses remain, while the two-dimensional implicit-scale error/uncertainty comparisons are removed.

E5.justification: Test-set mean-plus-standard-deviation reporting and predictive covariance estimation remain. However, v1's implicit-scale predictive-standard-deviation maps in Figures 11 and 17–18 disappear; v2 Figures 20–22 retain only the multiscale uncertainty maps. Neither version reports a repeated-training-run or seed-based significance protocol.

E6.justification: v2 adds extensive baseline, wave, shallow-water, and cost results. Retained-case values change in both directions: KdV mean error at n_eta=1 changes from 0.103 to 0.197, while cylinder error at n_eta=5 changes from 0.031 to 0.009 (Table 1). Revised architectures and training settings prevent interpreting these as controlled same-setting gains or losses.

M1.justification: The coupled SDEs, PoE likelihood, and hierarchical variational training remain. However, v2 changes ReLU to LeakyReLU, revises convolutional architectures, and replaces cylinder flow's learned space/time coupling network with identity coupling and spatial Fourier features (v1 Appendix G.4; v2 Appendix H.6). These are architectural adaptations within the retained framework.

P1.justification: v2 extensively rewrites the method exposition, related work, experimental narrative, and conclusion, and standardizes encoder/decoder terminology. It moves Burgers into Appendix H.3, adds a dedicated baseline appendix, and reorganizes architecture descriptions and supplementary plots into clearer subsections.

P2.justification: Tables are restructured for expanded benchmarks and comparators, baseline prediction panels are enlarged, and a cost figure and supplementary-figure index are added. Many rotated full-page appendix plots are regrouped into upright multipanel layouts. These are substantial display changes beyond updated numerical entries.

R1.justification: The related-work discussion substantially expands positioning against global ROM, neural SDE closures requiring solver-based training, and hierarchical graph weather models. New references include Parish and Duraisamy, Gupta and Lermusiaux, Lam et al., and Oskarsson et al. These substantive comparisons go beyond the retained ROM/Mori–Zwanzig overview and bibliographic updates.

T1.justification: v1 Section 3 states an unweighted reconstruction mean that conflicts with its precision-weighted PoE expression in Section 4.4 and Appendix F. v2 removes that inconsistent equality and explicitly displays the weighted mean in Equation 9. The PoE, ELBO, predictive-moment, and memory-kernel derivations otherwise remain substantively equivalent.

improvement.justification: v1's broad predictive claims relied mainly on an internal implicit-scale comparison. v2 substantially strengthens their evaluation through coarse-DNS, DMD, and tuned POD-SINDy comparisons, two additional physical systems, and detailed baseline protocols (Tables 1 and 3; Appendix G). The cost-proxy study also addresses efficiency directly. Reduced comparative uncertainty reporting and the unexplained disappearance of the Burgers failure disclosure weaken transparency, but do not outweigh the substantial improvement in empirical support and reproducibility.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same stochastic multiscale modeling work. Their complete main texts and appendices provide readable equations, tables, figures, and experimental details sufficient to match content across the revisions.

after.justification: v2 reports original results across five systems, including Burgers in Appendix H.3, with baseline comparisons, ablations, and computational-cost analysis.

before.justification: v1 reports original trained-model results for KdV, Burgers, and cylinder flow, including error statistics, microscale-dimension ablations, and appendix diagnostics.

results.title: Learning Stochastic Multiscale Models

C1.justification: Multi-model mode connectivity becomes an explicit abstract claim and a new listed contribution, whereas v1 identifies merging more than two Transformers as future work. The broader-symmetry and width-heterogeneous claims were already present. The soft-alignment contribution is also qualified from improving outcomes in practice to potentially improving them.

C2.justification: v2 introduces a tentative explanation linking residual BookCorpus barriers to distinct solutions or disconnected minima and interprets the three-model surface as a shared low-loss region. Its limitations newly acknowledge architecture-changing reparameterizations. New Appendix F substantially expands implications for pruning, federated and continual learning, and robustness, without reporting experiments for those applications.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code-access link and expands the configuration table and implementation documentation for Tiny ImageNet and Tiny Shakespeare, including augmentation, calibration, early stopping, and hardware. BookCorpus hardware changes from four V100s to four RTX 4090s. Conversely, the explicit short merging-budget disclosures are removed.

E1.justification: v2 adds Tiny ImageNet image classification and Tiny Shakespeare language modeling to the retained CIFAR-10/100 and BookCorpus evaluations. This extends vision evidence beyond CIFAR and language evidence beyond BookCorpus; the additions were absent from v1's appendices.

E2.justification: The five methods in the main pairwise comparisons are retained. However, the width-heterogeneous comparison narrows: v1 Figure 3b compares weight matching with learned matching on CIFAR-10 ViTs, whereas v2 Figure 3c reports only learned matching on Tiny Shakespeare models. Weight matching therefore disappears as a comparator within that analysis.

E3.justification: The reported base-model optimizer changes from Adam to AdamW. v1's explicit merging budgets of 5 ViT epochs and 0.25 GPT-2 epochs are replaced by using the individual-model training setup. New experiments introduce different architectures, Tiny ImageNet temperature calibration, a wider width-ratio sweep, and three-model simplex evaluation. These are reported protocol changes; the PDFs do not establish which retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: The width-mismatch analysis changes from comparing coefficient-sampling ranges at a 512-versus-256 ViT configuration to testing four width ratios on Tiny Shakespeare. The original coefficient-sampling, initialization, convergence, soft-permutation, and eigenvalue analyses otherwise remain, despite figure and appendix renumbering.

E5.justification: BookCorpus gains mean and standard-error reporting in v2 Table 2, replacing point estimates in v1 Table 3. The general four-seed statement for the main ViT experiments disappears, while the four-seed initialization and three-seed soft-permutation disclosures remain. An increase in run counts is not established.

E6.justification: v2 adds benchmark results, three-model loss surfaces, revised width-mismatch curves, and base-model metrics. Learned matching achieves reported barriers of 0.00 on Tiny ImageNet and 0.02 on Tiny Shakespeare. CIFAR-10/100 table values remain unchanged; BookCorpus values shift slightly, including learned matching from 0.41 to 0.42 and weight matching from 1.57 to 1.56. Revised reported settings prevent interpreting these shifts as same-setting performance changes.

M1.justification: New Section 4.3 extends pairwise alignment to multiple models through iterative alignment to a shared universe, averaging of aligned parameters, and learned refinement over Dirichlet-sampled mixtures. This introduces a substantive merging procedure and objective. The pairwise Algorithm 1 and soft-permutation procedure are retained.

P1.justification: Existing exposition is substantially condensed and reorganized, particularly the LMC definition, results, weight-versus-learned analysis, and related work. Results shift from architecture-specific subsections to pairwise and multi-way discussion. Limitations move from the final appendix to Appendix A, and a new discussion appendix changes the closing narrative.

P2.justification: v2 consolidates the separate vision and BookCorpus result tables into a colored five-dataset table, expands the training-configuration table, replaces Figure 3's CIFAR plots with three different panels, and adds three-model contour surfaces in Figure 4. The eigenvalue and appendix ablation figures are retained and renumbered.

R1.justification: v2 adds Bengio et al. (2013) for straight-through estimation, Juneja et al. (2023) for interpreting language-model barriers, and Stutz et al. (2021) for robustness discussion. The new universe-matching procedure explicitly builds on the already-cited Crisostomi et al. (2024). The principal positioning against permutation-based alignment remains.

T1.justification: Section 2 adds a formal multi-model barrier over the mixture simplex and corresponding connectivity criterion. Appendix E also substantively revises v1 Appendix D's RMSNorm width-expansion derivation: it incorporates epsilon scaling and changes the transformed offset by a sqrt(M/N) factor. These alter mathematical content rather than merely notation.

improvement.justification: The added benchmarks materially strengthen evidence beyond v1's limited empirical coverage, while the multi-model formalism, procedure, and three-model experiment address an explicitly deferred capability. The revised RMSNorm derivation also strengthens technical support for width expansion. Less explicit merging-budget documentation and overextended claims about untested applications remain weaknesses, but the gains in empirical support and mathematical completeness substantially improve the paper overall.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Transformer alignment framework. Their full text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching relocated material.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds Tiny ImageNet, Tiny Shakespeare, and three-model CIFAR-10 alignment results.

before.justification: v1 reports original ViT and GPT-2 alignment experiments on CIFAR-10/100 and BookCorpus, together with width-heterogeneous experiments and alignment ablations.

results.title: Generalized Linear Mode Connectivity for Transformers

C1.justification: The abstract, introductory contributions, and concluding contribution summary retain the same central claims about CSS, differences across models, long-range integration, BagNet controls, and prediction of other evaluations. The additions support and elaborate these claims rather than redefine the main contribution.

C2.justification: v3 discusses possible distribution effects from the black-paint texture and argues that successful individual-image classification points toward configural failure. It also elaborates local-to-global consistency objectives versus reconstruction-based learning and interprets cumulative ablations as identifying irrecoverable intermediate-layer contributions. These refine the existing mechanistic account.

D1.justification: Appendix A.11 substantially expands model documentation beyond v1's family-level descriptions, listing architectures, adversarial-training epsilon values, sparsity levels, register variants, pretraining notes, and input resolutions. The new checklist also states that code and data release is planned; it does not establish completed release.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same nine-category anagram task and auxiliary shape-dependent benchmarks. Appendix A.10 expands the anagram sample from 72 to 1,440 pairs without documenting new categories, domains, or task requirements; this changes sample size rather than coverage.

E2.justification: v3 Section 7 and Table 1 add five ViT-B/16 comparators: relative positional embeddings, RoPE, RoPE plus absolute embeddings, mixed RoPE, and mixed RoPE plus absolute embeddings. The original model comparisons remain; Appendix A.11 documents the existing cohort rather than establishing another newly evaluated comparator set.

E3.justification: v3 adds evaluation of all 86 models on 1,440 anagram pairs and cumulative masking of blocks before or after a selected layer across four DINOv2 sizes and the ViT-B/16 baseline. These substantially extend sample size and intervention design beyond the retained original evaluation and single-block ablations.

E4.justification: New analyses test positional-encoding effects, whether later layers recover information disrupted by cumulative attention masking, and whether CSS rankings depend on the original small stimulus sample. Section 7 and Appendices A.5 and A.10 substantially extend the existing mechanistic and robustness evidence.

E5.justification: The one-tailed Williams tests over 86 models, including their statistics and p-values, are unchanged between v1 Appendix A.6 and v3 Appendix A.7. No study-specific repeated-run counts, seed reporting, uncertainty definitions, or significance-testing procedures are added; the checklist's generic guidance does not establish such changes.

E6.justification: v3 Table 1 newly reports CSS values of 38.89%, 51.38%, 51.38%, 48.61%, and 52.77% for the five positional-encoding variants. Figures 7 and 11 add cumulative-ablation similarity profiles and expanded-set scores, with original-versus-expanded CSS correlation r=0.99. These are substantial additional results under new configurations or samples; the original reported results remain unchanged.

M1.justification: The anagram synthesis procedure, patch configuration, category mapping, and joint two-image CSS definition remain unchanged. The positional-encoding variants and cumulative ablations are diagnostic experiments, rather than revisions to the proposed benchmark procedure.

P1.justification: v3 inserts a positional-encoding section, three appendix subsections, additional discussion, and a conference checklist, while preserving nearly all existing prose and its narrative order. Contact information, conference identification, and cross-references receive limited updates rather than extensive rewriting.

P2.justification: v3 substantially extends the visual evidence with cumulative-ablation Figure 7, expanded-set validation Figure 11, positional-encoding Table 1, and the model inventory. Figure 11 also redisplays original scores. All nine original figure images are retained, while the auxiliary-evaluation schematic and statistical table are resized or reformatted.

R1.justification: The related-work section and all 70 references are retained. The positioning of CSS relative to shape-versus-texture bias and earlier configural-shape research remains unchanged.

T1.justification: The synthesis equations, CSS definition and chance level, representational-influence definitions, and accuracy-corrected shape-bias formula are retained. No new formal assumptions, theorems, proofs, or mathematical corrections accompany the added experiments.

improvement.justification: v1's central benchmark conclusions depended on 72 anagram pairs; v3 tests 1,440 pairs and reports r=0.99 agreement, substantially addressing sensitivity to the small stimulus sample. Additional diagnostic experiments and model documentation strengthen evidence and transparency. A qualification remains: Figure 7 measures representation similarity, while its prose also claims irrecoverable CSS loss. This overinterpretation does not outweigh the substantial robustness gain.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Object-Anagram and Configural Shape Score (CSS) study. Text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support reliable matching across the added sections and renumbering.

after.justification: v3 retains these original results and adds positional-encoding comparisons, cumulative attention ablations, and evaluation on an expanded anagram set.

before.justification: v1 reports original model benchmarking, human behavioral results, attention ablations, representational analyses, and correlations with other shape-dependent evaluations.

results.title: Visual Anagrams Reveal Hidden Differences in Holistic Shape Processing Across Vision Models

C1.justification: The abstract and conclusion retain the same claims about automated bimanual demonstration generation, relational constraints, MCTS-enhanced reasoning, HGen-Bench and diffusion-policy data scaling. The introduction's central contributions also remain stable; the new appendix evidence supports rather than redefines them.

C2.justification: V1's limitations emphasize predefined primitives, long-horizon efficiency and the visual simulation-to-reality gap. V2 replaces this discussion with detailed manual-annotation requirements, stated restrictions on deformable/fluid simulation and dynamic-goal manipulation, and proposed extensions; the explicit visual-domain-gap caution is removed. It also adds interpretations of annotation failures, simulation pretraining and pipeline-stage reuse.

D1.justification: V2 adds deployment details including the head-mounted D435i camera at 640×480 resolution, FoundationPose initialization, annotation-evaluation asset sources and rendering software, and pipeline timing/token information. The original solver libraries, policy hyperparameters, prompt templates, substantive example code and project-access information remain unchanged.

E1.justification: V2 adds physical-robot evaluation of two retained tasks and five additional simulation scenarios: knob rotation, toaster pressing, safe-door opening, coordinated pot lifting and block stacking with barriers. Appendix C.2 also introduces quantitative annotation-transfer evaluation across sampled assets. These substantially broaden the evaluated environments and task requirements.

E2.justification: Table 6 introduces manual annotation as a timed comparator to automatic annotation migration, absent from v1's evaluation. The RoboTwin comparison, MCTS/non-MCTS comparison and four LLM-planner configurations are retained. The added discussion of augmentation frameworks does not provide new measured baseline comparisons.

E3.justification: New protocols include real-world training with 5 or 25 real trajectories versus 100 simulated plus 5 real trajectories, evaluation over 20 trials, and physical-object pose randomization. Annotation evaluation samples 20 assets per category, while the five additional tasks have specified randomization ranges. The original benchmark training and MCTS settings are retained.

E4.justification: V2 adds annotation-transfer accuracy and timing analysis with discussion of geometric failure cases, stage-by-stage resource analysis, and an obstacle-heavy stacking robustness test. The real-world study also tests the contribution of simulation data under limited real demonstrations. Existing MCTS-budget, plan-diversity and LLM-planner analyses remain.

E5.justification: The retained policy evaluations still report means and standard deviations using seeds 0, 1 and 2, and existing uncertainty displays are unchanged. New tables provide success counts or point estimates without introducing repeated-training-run information, confidence intervals or significance tests; their evaluation sample sizes are protocol additions.

E6.justification: The original numerical results in Tables 1–3 and the retained comparison plots are unchanged. V2 adds real-world collection success of 85% and 90%, and DP success of 65% and 70% with 100 simulated plus 5 real trajectories (Table 5). Tables 6–8 add annotation success of 90–100%, five-task success of 73–95.24%, and time/token measurements. These are newly reported results under additional conditions.

M1.justification: Appendix C.1 adds a real-world adaptation: FoundationPose estimates object poses to initialize simulation, and generated trajectories are executed on the physical robot. The central atomic-operation, relational-constraint, collision-management and STCR/MCTS procedures remain unchanged. Automatic annotation migration was already described in v1.

P1.justification: V2 substantially reorganizes the appendices: MCTS joins the implementation section, experiments are regrouped and reordered into C.1–C.8, and a contents guide is added. The dataset/benchmark survey moves into the main related-work section. Relational-constraint exposition and limitations are rewritten, alongside smaller terminology, task-label and front-matter edits.

P2.justification: V2 adds real/sim scene panels, an annotation-migration grid and a challenging-task montage (Figures 9–11), plus four empirical/resource tables (Tables 5–8). Figure 3 gains explanatory action labels, and Figure 8's transformation arrows are revised. Existing displays are relocated, including the unchanged LLM comparison from Figure 9 to Figure 12.

R1.justification: V2 adds targeted positioning against augmentation methods, including DemoGen alongside DexMimicGen, and discusses learned annotation alternatives such as RoboBrain, CAP-Net and Dex1B. It also adds supporting technical references. The existing framework comparison and central novelty positioning remain; the dataset/benchmark survey is largely moved from the appendix into Section 4.

T1.justification: Scene-scaling Equation (4) changes from O alpha = O' alpha' for quantities expressed in the respective local frames to alpha' = T_{O→O'} alpha, with quantities now defined in the original and scaled scenes' world coordinates. This revises the formal coordinate specification. The constraint-solver and MCTS equations otherwise remain unchanged, with no new proofs.

improvement.justification: V1 lacked physical validation and quantitative tests of annotation efficiency. V2 addresses these gaps with real-robot transfer experiments, annotation accuracy/cost measurements, harder manipulation scenarios and resource accounting, while clarifying important applicability limits. These substantially strengthen practical validation. The physical study remains limited to two tasks, and C.3 claims baseline superiority without reporting comparator scores, but these weaknesses do not outweigh the evidence gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe HumanoidGen and HGen-Bench. Their complete main texts and appendices, including equations, figures, tables, prompts and code examples, are readable and matchable despite reorganization and added experiments.

after.justification: V2 retains those original results and adds physical-robot experiments, annotation-transfer measurements, challenging-task evaluations and resource measurements in Appendix C.

before.justification: V1 reports original simulation results for demonstration generation, MCTS reasoning, diffusion-policy learning and comparisons across LLM planners in Section 5 and the appendices.

results.title: HumanoidGen: Data Generation for Bimanual Dexterous Manipulation via LLM Reasoning

C1.justification: v3's abstract, contributions, and discussion add demonstrated transfer to unseen molecular systems and a claim of at least sixfold acceleration over MD. v1 treated transferability as a possibility requiring future validation. The original fast-likelihood and alanine-reweighting contributions remain, while v1's explicit claim to be the first method recovering Boltzmann distributions without exact likelihoods is removed.

C2.justification: v3 interprets InfoNCE as improving mode weighting through regularization, explains the transfer rationale for training on emulator-generated samples, and discusses the new transfer accuracy–cost tradeoff. Its limitations replace untested transferability with observed degradation under transfer and limited architecture/hyperparameter exploration. These substantially extend the mechanism explanations and applicability boundaries beyond v1's alanine-focused discussion.

D1.justification: v3 newly supplies a code-repository URL, parameter counts, generated training-set sizes, separate emulator/EBM training specifications, and transfer-specific technical details. Appendices C and E document molecular features, graph-validity checks, TICA implementation, and larger model configurations. These substantially expand reproducibility information; much of the original architecture and hardware documentation is retained or relocated.

E1.justification: v3 retains the Gaussian-mixture, checkerboard, and biased/unbiased alanine experiments, then adds training on 200 dipeptides and evaluation on seven unseen dipeptides: AC, ET, GN, IM, KS, NY, and NF. Section 4.3 and Appendix G therefore expand molecular coverage and introduce an actual cross-molecule transfer scenario.

E2.justification: v3 adds Hutchinson trace estimation with 1, 2, 4, and 8 calls as a direct likelihood comparator in Table 7, and independent MD runs as comparators in the transfer experiments. The original alanine comparator set remains. TBG-ECNF extends the existing ECNF comparison to transferable models rather than constituting an unrelated new baseline.

E3.justification: New evaluation protocols include toy-density KL divergence, proposal/reweighted alanine Wasserstein metrics, TICA projections with a 0.5 ns lag, and a 30,000-sample TBG comparison. Transfer experiments use larger models, separate training budgets, and different integration tolerances. For existing training, v3 reports EBM scheduler patience of 30 instead of 20 and replaces the fixed bias multiplier 150 with a state ratio; these specification changes do not establish that earlier experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: The existing qualitative objective-function ablation gains quantitative KL results in Table 1. Appendices F.3–F.4 add estimated-versus-exact likelihood diagnostics, sensitivity to Hutchinson call count, and an independent-versus-OT coupling ablation. These investigate likelihood fidelity and training choices previously untested. The emulator endpoint/vector-field analysis is retained and relocated, not newly introduced.

E5.justification: Five-run alanine reporting is retained, but v3 Tables 3 and 6 explicitly identify the reported spread as standard deviation, whereas v1's captions only described results or errors across five runs. Appendix D.5 additionally distinguishes repeated alanine runtime measurements from averaging individual runs across seven dipeptides. No increase in repeated-run counts or new significance testing is established.

E6.justification: The matched emulator tables change E-W2 from 5.84 to 6.22 for ECNF, 3.76 to 4.99 for GVP-VF, and 1.76 to 3.11 for GVP-EP, while retaining their ranking and NLL/T-W2 values. Alanine free-energy estimates remain unchanged. Numerous new results cover KL, reweighted distributions, coupling, likelihood correlation, and transfer; the new transfer benchmark reports 4.005 hours for BoltzNCE versus 24.04 for MD, with larger mean free-energy error, 0.43 versus 0.18.

M1.justification: The core InfoNCE-plus-score-matching framework remains, but v3 adds a substantial transfer procedure: amino-acid and positional inputs, EBM pretraining followed by target-specific fine-tuning, rejection of invalid molecular graphs, and removal of the largest 0.2% of importance weights. Appendix E.8 also reports independent EBM coupling instead of v1's mini-batch optimal transport coupling.

P1.justification: v3 extensively rewrites and reorganizes the narrative. Previously separate background, EBM-training, and methods sections become a unified Methodological Framework; related work follows it; experiments are reorganized; and the emulator comparison moves to Appendix F. The abstract, contribution statements, mathematical exposition, and time notation are substantially revised independently of the added experiments.

P2.justification: v3 expands the main alanine results table with error and proposal/reweighted metric columns and adds quantitative-ablation, method-overview, parameter-count, likelihood, coupling, and transfer tables. New figures show dipeptide results and likelihood scatter plots. Existing dataset/emulator figures move to the appendix, and retained plots receive revised colors, labels, and captions. The changes substantially alter the visual presentation.

R1.justification: v3 adds references supporting molecular dynamics, annealed NCE, diffusion/flow matching, transferable datasets, and implementation choices, including Chehab et al., Timewarp, and deeptime. The generator/emulator/EBM positioning remains largely intact, with the explicit first-method novelty assertion removed. This expands context without fundamentally redefining the relationship to prior work.

T1.justification: Section 2.2 adds a conditional time-likelihood derivation explicitly accounting for time-dependent log normalizers, absent from v1's derivation. Most other mathematics is retained with reversed time notation. However, v3 Appendix A, Eq. (20), omits the alpha derivative required by Eq. (19), making its endpoint coefficient inconsistent with the stated linear schedule; this is a printed mathematical inconsistency, not evidence of an implemented algorithm change.

improvement.justification: v3 replaces v1's untested transferability with held-out-molecule evaluation using fine-tuning, and adds quantitative objective checks, a relevant approximate-likelihood comparator, and a coupling ablation. Together with expanded reproducibility information, these substantially strengthen the empirical foundation. Transfer accuracy remains below MD/TBG-ECNF, sample budgets differ, and the revised endpoint derivation introduces an inconsistency. These qualifications limit the claims, but the broader validation and documentation provide a clear substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same BoltzNCE research. All 19 pages of v1 and 26 pages of v3, including appendices, are readable and support comparison of text, equations, tables, and figures. Renumbered and relocated content can be matched.

after.justification: v3 retains original experiments and adds quantitative density evaluations, unseen-dipeptide results, Hutchinson estimator comparisons, and coupling experiments, including Tables 1, 4, and 7–9.

before.justification: v1 reports original synthetic-density experiments and alanine dipeptide emulator and reweighting results in Figure 2, Tables 1–2, and the appendix. These extend beyond results attributed to earlier work.

results.title: BoltzNCE: Learning Likelihoods for Boltzmann Generation with Stochastic Interpolants and Noise Contrastive Estimation

C1.justification: The central coupling, recall, planning, and reconstruction claims remain. v2 adds an explicit claim of demonstration in visually realistic navigation and replaces the Discussion's prediction about MEC inhibition disrupting hippocampal preplay with a prediction of MEC 'look forward' sweeps.

C2.justification: v2 explicitly acknowledges HPC/SMC-based planning while emphasizing its context dependence, and elaborates successor-representation compatibility through learned state transitions. It interprets the new robustness results as supporting operation with noisy or distorted grids. The limitations concerning supervised grids, boundary avoidance, and planning scale remain.

D1.justification: v2 supplies substantial new implementation information for BtnkMAE, including initialization, 100-epoch pretraining, relative learning rates, image resizing, positional embeddings, and encoder/decoder freezing. It adds project, simulation-suite, and vision-code access links. Joint planner/HC-MEC training is also made explicit, without establishing that the original procedure changed.

E1.justification: Beyond the retained synthetic spatial simulations, v2 uses ImageNet-1k for visual compression training and reconstruction, and HSSD panoramas in Habitat-Sim for visual navigation and sensory reconstruction. Supplementary Section 8 additionally covers noisy initial grid states and distorted grid representations.

E2.justification: The GC-only and full HC-MEC variants remain, with no added external method evaluated as a competing baseline. MAE and DETR supply components for the new visual system; they are not reported as head-to-head comparators.

E3.justification: New protocols include ImageNet pretraining, scene-specific panorama fine-tuning, and robustness evaluations reporting 4,096 planning trials per model, a 10 cm success threshold, goal distance, success rate, and detour ratio. Training-time noise and initial-state planning noise are tested separately. The original experimental settings are retained.

E4.justification: Supplementary Section 8 adds systematic tests of dependence on idealized grid representations: post-activation Gaussian noise during training, noise in the initial planning GC state, and sheared grid lattices. Tables 3–5 provide quantitative robustness evidence absent from v1; the original masking-ratio analysis remains.

E5.justification: Tables 3–5 add per-condition ± summaries for planning errors, whereas v1's ± descriptions concern trajectory lengths and spatial sampling counts. The new ± statistic is not explicitly defined, and no seed-level replication, confidence intervals, or significance tests are added.

E6.justification: v2 adds reconstructed images and quantitative robustness outcomes while retaining the original figure results. At noise standard deviation 1.0, Table 3 reports 5.30 ± 6.98 cm goal distance and 0.91 success for training-time noise; Table 4 reports 7.72 ± 13.24 cm and 0.85 success for initial-state noise. These are new conditions, not same-setting improvements over v1.

M1.justification: v2 adds a substantial visual encoding and reconstruction component: BtnkMAE uses a ViT-Large encoder, a single 1024-dimensional CLS bottleneck, and cross-attention reconstruction with two training losses. The visual HC-MEC implementation also adds layer normalization. The original recurrent planning mechanism remains.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, methodological exposition, and discussion undergo extensive rewriting and consolidation. Section 2 reorganizes explanations around conceptual roles and supervision, and the title changes from 'Intrinsic' to 'Internally Driven' path planning. Much of the original supplementary exposition remains intact.

P2.justification: v2 adds Figure 4, supplementary Figures S3–S6, and robustness Tables 3–5, substantially expanding the visual presentation of methods and evidence. S3–S4 repeat portions of Figure 4. Original Figures 1–3 and S1–S2 retain their graphics, while Table 2 is relocated and some captions and layout change.

R1.justification: v2 expands discussion of successor representations with successor-feature transfer work, adds pattern-completion and theta-sweep references, and cites the new visual components and simulation resources. It removes the RRT-Connect analogy and several supporting citations, while retaining the central positioning around complementary hippocampal memory and grid-based planning.

T1.justification: Equation (1) corrects the illustrative standard RNN recurrence from f(z_{t-1}) to f(z_t). The grid-phase formalism, displacement-averaging condition, and supplementary proof are otherwise retained.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens support for the central reconstruction mechanism by recovering recognizable panoramic views from planned sensory states, extending v1's synthetic sensory evidence. The robustness experiments directly examine dependence on ideal grids and noiseless dynamics, while implementation details and access information improve reproducibility. Visual validation remains qualitative, and robustness reporting has undefined ± statistics and an eight-model/nine-angle inconsistency, but these limitations do not outweigh the substantial evidential gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same REMI research, with readable main texts, equations, figures, tables, and appendices. The original experiments and supplementary material can be matched reliably to their counterparts in v2.

after.justification: v2 retains those results and adds visual reconstruction experiments in Habitat-Sim and quantitative planning robustness experiments in supplementary Section 8.

before.justification: v1 reports original neural-network simulations demonstrating spatial representations, sensory-cue recall, planning, and reconstruction of sensory activity along planned paths.

results.title: REMI: Reconstructing Episodic Memory During Internally Driven Path Planning

C1.justification: The introduction adds a claim of 55% Lite performance with updated AIRA-dojo and announces full-suite results. The central contributions concerning search/operator interactions and generalization remain unchanged, as do the abstract and conclusion's original 47.7% headline.

C2.justification: Appendix D newly attributes the additional Lite performance to high reasoning effort and infrastructure improvements, including caching to avoid rate-limit errors. Their individual contributions are not isolated. Existing interpretations of overfitting and the limitations concerning resources, operators, and contamination remain unchanged.

D1.justification: Appendix E.6 supplies the previously omitted crossover prompt, including parent-code inputs, memory, constraints, and output format. Appendix D adds information about reasoning effort, infrastructure updates, and baseline-result provenance. Existing hardware specifications, other prompts, hyperparameters, and code-access information are retained.

E1.justification: Appendix D expands actual evaluation from 22 low-complexity Lite tasks to all 75 MLE-bench tasks, adding 38 medium- and 15 high-complexity competitions. Added coverage includes multilingual question answering, recommendations, and autonomous-vehicle object detection. MLE-bench-30 is also reported as a subset of this coverage.

E2.justification: New Table 2 adds OpenAI's proprietary o3 and GPT-5 Thinking agents, both without browsing, as reported comparators on MLE-bench-30, with scores of 6% and 8%. These are distinct from the existing AIDE/AIRA o3 configurations. The original controlled comparator sets remain unchanged.

E3.justification: Appendix D reports additional o3 runs using high reasoning effort and improved filesystem/model caching, explicitly linking these configuration changes to the new Lite result. The original main experiments, medal metrics, and stated 24-hour, single-GPU protocol are retained.

E4.justification: The memory and search-policy ablations, extended-compute studies, validation/test and top-k analyses, variance analyses, and search-tree examples are retained. Appendix D adds benchmark and difficulty-group scores without introducing a new ablation, sensitivity test, error analysis, or case study.

E5.justification: The added full-suite evaluation states 20 random seeds, whereas the retained o3 Lite results specify 10 seeds in Figures 13–14. Table 2 introduces mean ± standard-error reporting alongside the existing bootstrap confidence intervals. Appendix D inconsistently calls its uncertainty estimates confidence intervals in prose.

E6.justification: New Table 2 reports AIRA greedy o3 medal rates of 31.6% overall, 55.0% low, 22.0% medium, 21.7% high, and 25.8% on MLE-bench-30; Table 3 adds 75 task-level results. The 55.0% result uses updated settings relative to the original 47.7%. Section 5.3 also corrects the oracle-selection gain from 9–11.6 to 9–13 points, while Figure 6 remains unchanged.

M1.justification: The search policies, operator design, fitness evaluation, and selection procedures are retained. Appendix E.6 newly documents the crossover prompt, but crossover and fitness-based parent selection already appeared in v1; this does not establish an algorithm change.

P1.justification: Changes include a short introduction addition, localized wording and author/date edits, new Appendix D and subsection E.6, and updated appendix references. Most prose and the main section organization remain unchanged.

P2.justification: v2 adds an aggregate comparison table and a full per-task table with complexity groups, years, and MLE-bench-30 markers, plus crossover prompt boxes. Existing Figures 1–17 are preserved, with some appendix material relocated and repaginated.

R1.justification: v2 adds the GPT-5 system card as a cited source for MLE-bench-30 and proprietary-agent comparisons. The existing related-work discussion and novelty framing are largely unchanged; the added Inspect publication date is only a bibliographic update.

T1.justification: The graph-search definitions, selection equations, UCT formulation, and MCTS backup derivation are unchanged. The backup discussion moves from Appendix D.1 to E.1; no new theorem, assumption, proof, or substantive mathematical revision is introduced.

improvement.justification: Appendix D substantially strengthens empirical validation beyond v1's low-complexity Lite tasks: the 20-seed full-suite evaluation establishes performance on harder problem types and exposes task-level failures. The crossover prompt also improves reproducibility. Combined reasoning/infrastructure changes limit attribution of the 55% result, and the SE/CI terminology needs clarification, but these limitations do not outweigh the substantial gain in evidence about the agent's applicability.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same AIRA research work. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices support reliable comparison, including matching retained material across appendix renumbering and relocation.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments and adds the authors' full-suite AIRA evaluation in Appendix D, separately identifying reproduced baseline results.

before.justification: v1 reports original agent evaluations on MLE-bench Lite, controlled ablations, validation/test comparisons, and extended-runtime experiments, including results in the appendices.

results.title: AI Research Agents for Machine Learning: Search, Exploration, and Generalization in MLE-bench

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contribution list and conclusion retain the same universal-drafter, cross-vocabulary distillation and adaptive-drafting claims, including the 1.5–2x headline speedup. The added experiments support these existing claims rather than redefine the core contributions.

C2.justification: v3 adds explanations of the larger-drafter acceptance/latency tradeoff, recovery under same-family target switches, and LFU's retention of frequently used n-grams. Appendix B.6.2 also qualifies cross-family switching as preferably requiring a fresh cache. The original limitations section remains unchanged.

D1.justification: Table 4 newly identifies pympler.asizeof.asizeof() as the cache-memory measurement routine and gives exact training counts for that analysis. Appendix D.5 documents eviction rules and capacity fractions. The original hardware, software and training-hyperparameter disclosures in Appendix A are retained.

E1.justification: The four datasets and underlying task domains are retained. Appendix B.6 adds distinct nonstationary scenarios: switching from GSM8K to MBPP+HumanEval during training and switching target models within an ongoing training stream.

E2.justification: New Table 14 evaluates LRU and LFU cache policies alongside no-cache and full-cache variants; v1 contains no eviction-policy comparison. Existing decoding and distillation comparators remain, and the model-scaling experiment reuses the direct-mapping speculative-decoding baseline.
