E3.justification: New experiments introduce a Llama-160M drafter and Qwen2.5 targets with 7B, 14B and 32B parameters. Additional protocols switch datasets at step 1000, switch targets at steps 300 and 600, and restrict caches to quarter or half capacity. Cache-memory and normalized-growth measurements also extend evaluation; the original settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v3 substantially expands analysis through model-scaling and memory-footprint studies in Sections 4.3.1–4.3.2, recovery after dataset and target shifts in Appendix B.6, and cache-growth and eviction-policy sensitivity in D.4–D.5. The original loss, draft-length, LoRA and adaptive-head analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions' Appendix A.2 specifies three runs with different seeds and reporting averages. v3 adds no documented change in run counts, uncertainty estimates, confidence intervals or significance testing.

E6.justification: Matched original tables and training plots retain their results, while substantial new findings appear. Table 3 reports 2.05x GSM8K speedup for Llama-68M with Qwen2.5-32B; Table 4 reports cache footprints of 0.501–4.569 MB; Table 14 reports 1.36x speedup for both quarter-capacity LFU and full cache. Figures 5, 6 and 9 add shift-recovery and cache-growth findings.

M1.justification: The core probability mappings, hybrid distillation loss and adaptive-drafting Algorithms 1–4 remain unchanged. Appendix D.5 adds evaluated bounded-cache variants with LRU or LFU eviction, a limited cache-management adaptation beyond v1's full-cache procedure.

P1.justification: New analytical subsections are inserted into Section 4.3 and Appendices B and D, with corresponding cross-reference updates. Most existing prose and the main narrative structure remain unchanged. Title capitalization and the preprint-to-NeurIPS footer are also updated.

P2.justification: The visual evidence expands through model-scaling, cache-memory and eviction-comparison tables (new Tables 3, 4 and 14), plus dataset-switch, target-switch and cache-growth plots (new Figures 5, 6 and 9). Existing displays are retained and renumbered where necessary, with ablation tables and appendix algorithms reflowed.

R1.justification: The related-work discussion and all 53 references are retained, including the existing positioning relative to UAG, OSD, DistillSpec and SpecDec++. The Qwen2.5 technical report was already cited in v1.

T1.justification: Appendix D.4 newly defines normalized cache growth as cache_size/training_tokens. This is a limited mathematical definition accompanying a new empirical metric. Existing method equations remain unchanged, and no theorem, proof or formal growth guarantee is added.

improvement.justification: v1 mainly supports online adaptability through separate fixed-dataset, fixed-target experiments and leaves cache resource constraints largely untested. v3 directly examines recovery after changes, scaling to larger models, measured cache memory and performance under restricted capacity. These additions substantially strengthen evidence for central adaptability and deployment-feasibility claims while retaining the original results. Actual on-device execution remains un demonstrated; the reported hardware is still A100 GPUs.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe OmniDraft and contain readable methods, results, figures, tables and appendices A–D. Retained material can be matched reliably despite additions, relocation and renumbering.

after.justification: v3 retains these empirical results and adds model-scaling, distribution-shift, cache-memory and cache-eviction experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original acceptance rates, speedups, training curves and ablations on GSM8K, MBPP+HumanEval, Alpaca and XSum, including appendix experiments.

results.title: OmniDraft: A Cross-vocabulary, Online Adaptive Drafter for On-device Speculative Decoding

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the same central contributions: backward and hybrid proximal diffusion, learning proximal operators through proximal matching, the exact-proximal convergence rate, and faster few-step sampling than conventional score methods. Added experiments do not redefine these main claims.

C2.justification: New Appendix A discusses the unresolved connection to maximum-likelihood training and attributes large-step FID deterioration to accumulated approximate-proximal errors. v2 also gives substantive qualifications about comparing convergence rates across assumptions and interprets the smoothness experiment cautiously. These significantly expand the original limitations and mechanism discussion.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code-repository pointer, explicit training pseudocode in Algorithm 2, the precision/recall computation procedure and the CelebA-HQ FID sample count. Original training hyperparameters remain, while Section 3.3 condenses some explicit MLP/embedding details. The PDF establishes the code pointer, not the repository's contents or accessibility.

E1.justification: v2 retains the original datasets and adds CelebA-HQ at 256 × 256 resolution, extending evaluation to high-resolution face generation. Appendix H.1 also adds continuous, compactly supported 1D distributions with controlled boundary smoothness, distinct from the retained discrete 2D example.

E2.justification: The retained comparisons use the same Euler-Maruyama score SDE, final-denoising variants in the 2D experiment, and Euler probability-flow ODE methods. The new experiments reuse these comparator methods. Newly discussed accelerated samplers, consistency models and distillation methods are not added as evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: Original MNIST/CIFAR-10 training budgets, schedules and step candidates are retained. v2 adds VGG-16-based precision/recall evaluation, CelebA-HQ FID over 30,000 generated samples, and a controlled 1D design varying five smoothness parameters across 5, 10 and 100 steps. These substantially broaden the evaluation protocol.

E4.justification: New Appendix H.1 and Figure 8 systematically test how boundary smoothness affects density and support recovery, comparing hybrid ProxDM with Euler-Maruyama without final denoising. This adds a substantial examination of the method's motivating premise. The existing CIFAR-10 training-heuristic ablation is retained as Figure 9, formerly Figure 6.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests for the experiments. The added metrics and CelebA-HQ sample count do not introduce uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: Existing result plots are retained. New results show better support recovery in the 1D tests and CelebA-HQ FID competitive with score ODE and generally better than score SDE. Figure 10 adds precision/recall findings with important exceptions: CIFAR-10 precision favors score ODE at moderate and high step counts despite ProxDM's recall advantage over much of the range.

M1.justification: The backward/hybrid updates, proximal-matching objective and conditioning scheme remain unchanged. Section 5 adds a limited adaptation for CelebA-HQ: the proximal model operates in a pretrained VAE's latent space, extending the original image-generation pipeline.

P1.justification: Most main exposition and proof organization remain intact. v2 makes localized rewrites, expands the loss explanation, introduces discussion subsections, improves appendix cross-references and switches to author-year citations. The new scientific content does not entail a wholesale narrative rewrite.

P2.justification: v2 adds substantial visual material: CelebA-HQ sample grids and FID curves, a loss-function illustration, the smoothness comparison, precision/recall panels and a training algorithm box. Existing figures are retained or relocated; notably, v1 Figures 5 and 6 become v2 Figures 7 and 9.

R1.justification: New Appendix A.1 substantially expands positioning against accelerated solvers, consistency models, distillation, flow matching and shortcut models. It presents proximal discretization as complementary to these approaches and connects proximal matching to MAP-promoting losses, adding works such as Song et al. (2023), Lipman et al. (2023), Frans et al. (2025) and Geng et al. (2025).

T1.justification: Section 2 corrects Tweedie's conditional-mean expression and noise scale, the sign in the MAP-proximal identity, and its Gaussian-likelihood derivation. Theorem 1 and Corollary 1 change the backward side condition from h ≤ 2 to h ≤ 1. The convergence rates, formal assumptions and appendix proof framework are retained.

improvement.justification: v1's empirical support was concentrated on a toy distribution and low-resolution images, with image quality assessed mainly through FID. v2 substantially strengthens that evidence through high-resolution generation, separate fidelity/coverage measurements and controlled support-recovery tests. Mathematical corrections and the explanation of large-step deterioration further improve reliability and interpretation. Comparisons still use basic Euler samplers and the theory still assumes exact proximals, but the expanded validation addresses important gaps in the earlier paper.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Beyond Scores: Proximal Diffusion Models with the same authors, core algorithms and convergence analysis. The main text, figures, equations and complete appendices are readable and can be matched across renumbering and relocation.

after.justification: The original experiments remain, supplemented by CelebA-HQ generation, MNIST/CIFAR-10 precision and recall, and controlled experiments on one-dimensional distributions in Appendix H.

before.justification: Section 5 and Appendix G report original sampling experiments on a discrete 2D distribution, MNIST and CIFAR-10, including generated samples, Wasserstein distances and FID results.

results.title: Beyond Scores: Proximal Diffusion Models

C1.justification: The abstract, introductory contributions and conclusion retain the same central claims about TVE, task-relevant information preservation and downstream benefits, especially with limited labels. Added appendix evidence does not redefine these contributions.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations of robustness to label/graph mismatch, the benefit of matching pre-training and downstream entity types, and applicability to fact-table cell prediction. Appendix D substantially develops the tradeoff between fixed statistics and learnable set encoders, while C.9 explains exponential traversal costs. These extend v1's brief limitations discussion.

D1.justification: v2 supplies a public-code URL, explicitly lists numerical and categorical SQL aggregators, and documents construction time and peak memory. It also specifies Seznam task creation through AutoCompleteTask and dated split cutoffs. These materially expand reproducibility information; existing hardware, training schedules and hyperparameter tables are retained.

E1.justification: Appendix C.7 adds Seznam/charge, predicting the sluzba attribute of dobito rows. This extends evaluation beyond the retained rel-amazon and rel-hm forecasting tasks to a new database and cell-level prediction requirements.

E2.justification: Corresponding original comparisons retain the unpretrained Baseline, GraphMAE-derived MAE and GraphCL-derived CTR methods. The added experiments reuse these comparators. Cross-entity TVE configurations are transfer controls, while newly cited methods such as Griffin are not evaluated as baselines.

E3.justification: New protocols generate labels after dropping 20% or 40% of review rows while retaining the original graph for model inputs, and test transfer between item- and user-pretrained representations. Seznam adds dated validation/test cutoffs and Accuracy, Macro F1, Micro F1 and MRR evaluation under linear probing and fine-tuning. Original RelBench settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Appendices C.5–C.6 add controlled tests of dependence on graph-derived labels and transfer across entity types, addressing robustness and representation specificity beyond v1's sensitivity studies. Appendix C.9.1 also adds construction-time and peak-memory profiling. Existing learning-rate and initialization analyses are retained.

E5.justification: v1 already reports repeated runs and ± values; v2's checklist item 7 newly identifies the reported quantities as means and standard deviations. The stated repetition counts for retained experiments are unchanged, with no documented increase in runs or new significance-testing procedure.

E6.justification: Original numerical tables and plotted results are retained, while Tables 7–10 add noise, transfer, cell-prediction and construction-cost results. For example, new Seznam test accuracies are 69.90 for TVE-1 versus 70.52 for MAE-0.25 under linear probing, and 81.26 versus CTR-0.25's 81.31 after fine-tuning. These are newly evaluated conditions, not improvements over v1 scores.

M1.justification: The documented TVE procedure retains its cross-joined pre-training table, causal schema traversal, SQL statistics, scaled cosine loss and optional SSL hybrid objective. The breadth-first traversal explanation and fuller aggregator list clarify the existing procedure; learnable set encoders remain future work.

P1.justification: v2 makes targeted explanatory edits concerning decoder roles, traversal and notation, moving the full label-generation notation into Appendix B. It adds acknowledgements and a conference checklist and reorganizes supplementary sections. The main narrative and most existing prose are retained.

P2.justification: v2 substantially expands tabular presentation with separate displays for noise experiments, entity transfer, four-metric cell prediction and construction resources (Tables 7–10). Existing figures are retained. Legacy tables are relocated and renumbered, including v1 Table 5 becoming v2 Table 3 and v1 Table 7 becoming v2 Table 11.

R1.justification: v2 adds citations to mutual information neural estimation, the CTU Prague relational repository, Griffin and Deep Sets. These support dataset attribution and the expanded statistics discussion. The main related-work section and TVE's positioning relative to existing SSL approaches remain essentially unchanged.

T1.justification: Appendix C.9.1 introduces Remark C.1 and a derivation of construction complexity O(rNTp^k b^k). Appendix D.2 adds mathematical arguments about sufficient statistics and reconstruction of small multisets. Theorem 4.1 and its proof remain unchanged; the full label-generation equations moved to Appendix B are not new theory.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses important gaps in v1's robustness, transfer and applicability evidence through Appendices C.5–C.7. Construction-cost analysis also makes scalability assessable beyond v1's per-step timings. Mixed Seznam performance and substantial two-hop memory requirements help reveal practical boundaries. Together with fuller implementation documentation and a code pointer, these additions substantially strengthen evidential coverage and transparency, although the idealized sufficiency assumptions remain.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same TVE framework and retain matching main experiments. Their text, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable and support a reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains those experiments and adds original noise, cross-entity transfer, Seznam cell-prediction and task-vector construction measurements.

before.justification: v1 reports original RelBench experiments, including downstream performance, linear probing, sensitivity analyses and measured pre-training runtimes.

results.title: A Pre-training Framework for Relational Data with Information-theoretic Principles

C1.justification: Section 1.1.1 broadens the central linear-query impossibility claim from noise-addition mechanisms to the defined Noise and Subsampling family. This substantially extends the negative contribution's scope; the positive-result claim remains unchanged.

C2.justification: The stated implication for future algorithms now excludes subsampling as well as noise addition as routes around the barrier. Section 2 replaces the clipping/negligible-tail discussion with explicit output ranges and explains why answers outside [-1, 2] already constitute accuracy failures.

D1.justification: Neither version supplies implementation resources, code or data access, hardware, or runtime information. The added sampling specifications define the theorem's mechanism class rather than document an implementation.

E1.justification: Neither version uses empirical training or evaluation datasets or tasks. The subsampling extension concerns a theoretical mechanism class, not added evaluation coverage.

E2.justification: Neither version reports evaluated baseline comparisons. Subsampling is newly covered by the impossibility theorem, rather than introduced as an experimental comparator.

E3.justification: Neither version contains experimental protocols. The new subsampling definition and revised bounded-output assumptions specify the theoretical setting, not evaluation procedures.

E4.justification: Neither version reports ablations, empirical robustness tests, or case studies. The added proof case belongs to the theoretical contribution.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated experiments, seeds, confidence intervals, or statistical tests. Their probability bounds are theoretical guarantees.

E6.justification: There are no empirical result entries in either version. Existing quantitative bounds remain unchanged; their extended theoretical applicability is assessed under T1 and C1.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 retains its query generation, score updates, and final query. The Laplace mechanism in Section 4 is unchanged. Extending the attack's analysis to subsampling does not change its procedure.

P1.justification: v2 introduces NS terminology, expands the preliminaries and proof exposition locally, corrects several wording and notation slips, and updates funding text. The overall section and appendix organization remains intact.

P2.justification: Algorithm 1 retains its display format but now precedes the attack analysis instead of interrupting Lemma 3.2's proof. Other layout differences are primarily text and equation reflow; no figures or result tables are added.

R1.justification: Section 1.1.1 newly positions noise addition and subsampling together as covering all known efficient polynomial-time techniques supporting superlinear query counts in the independent setting. The cited works and remaining prior-work discussion are unchanged.

T1.justification: Definitions 2.1–2.2 formalize noise-addition and fresh, with-replacement subsampling mechanisms. Lemma 3.3 gains a subsampling derivation establishing the same expected score increment, extending Theorems 1.4 and 3.5 to this additional class. Section 2 also revises bounded-output assumptions and explicitly states the zero-mean assumption already used in v1's proof. Section 4 and Appendices A–B retain their mathematics.

improvement.justification: The added subsampling proof in Lemma 3.3 closes a substantial gap in the central impossibility result: v1 addressed noise addition, while v2 also rules out the explicitly defined subsampling alternative at the same query bound. This materially broadens the theoretical contribution, supported by a derivation and clearer assumptions, while preserving the positive analysis and appendix proofs.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work. Their complete main texts, equations, Algorithm 1, and Appendices A–B are readable and support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 remains entirely theoretical. Its added subsampling analysis is a mathematical proof, not an experimental or simulation result.

before.justification: v1 reports theoretical constructions, impossibility bounds, accuracy guarantees, and proofs. Neither the main text nor the appendices report original empirical results.

results.title: Tight Bounds for Answering Adaptively Chosen Concentrated Queries

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same central contributions: a smoothed-gradient interpretation, convergence to the true proximal operator under the stated regularity assumptions, and integration into approximate proximal gradient descent for MAP estimation.

C2.justification: v3 newly discusses applicability to approximate learned scores and an O(xi) residual-error neighborhood. Its wording about convergence to a point is stronger than Proposition 6's distance bound alone establishes. The existing limitations concerning log-concavity and more general manifold-supported priors remain.

D1.justification: The numerical-example setup and implementation disclosures are unchanged. Neither version supplies additional code or data access, hardware, training details, or reproducibility resources.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same synthetic two-dimensional Gaussian proximal problem. The approximate-score extension in v3 is theoretical; it adds no dataset, trained-denoiser evaluation, or empirical test scenario.

E2.justification: Figure 2 retains the same comparison against naive gradient descent on the unsmoothed objective. The added Xu et al. citation does not introduce an evaluated baseline.

E3.justification: The numerical example retains the same covariance construction, condition number of 500, baseline step size of 0.8/L_F, and distance-to-proximal-point metric. The evaluated smoothed-gradient schedule is unchanged; no new experimental protocol is reported.

E4.justification: Section 3.3 and new Appendix A.3 add an analytical sensitivity assessment of uniformly bounded score-approximation errors, quantifying their contribution to residual proximal error. This is theoretical error analysis, not a new empirical robustness experiment or ablation.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests for the numerical example. The new deterministic score-error bound does not change statistical uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Figures 1 and 2 retain the same contours, trajectories, and convergence curves. Both report poor progress for unsmoothed gradient descent and approximately 1/k decay for the smoothed procedure; no empirical result entries are added or changed.

M1.justification: With alpha_k still equal to 1/(k+2), v3 changes the core update from alpha_k MMSE+(1-alpha_k)y to (1-alpha_k)MMSE+alpha_k y. Algorithm 1 also replaces the fixed observation y in each inner update with the current post-gradient point. These substantive corrections change the stated iterates and proximal target, aligning the procedure with the gradient formulation already analyzed in v1.

P1.justification: v3 standardizes outer and inner iteration notation, makes some assumption references explicit, expands an intermediate proof step, and inserts the approximate-score subsection. Most prose and the main section order remain unchanged.

P2.justification: v3 adopts conference formatting with different typography, heading sizes, spacing, and figure scaling, plus a NeurIPS footer. Both figures retain their panels, axes, legends, and underlying content; no new figure or results table appears.

R1.justification: v3 adds Xu et al. (2020), 'Provable convergence of plug-and-play priors with MMSE denoisers,' to the related-work discussion and bibliography. The broader positioning against PnP, conditional diffusion, and flow-based approaches remains unchanged.

T1.justification: New Proposition 6 and its proof in Appendix A.3 extend the central convergence analysis to uniformly bounded score errors, adding sqrt(3/2) times tau times xi to the original error bound. There are also local mathematical revisions, including Proposition 4's covariance scaling. The existing Gaussian, affine-subspace, and Appendix B results are retained after renumbering.

improvement.justification: v3 resolves an important mismatch between the published averaging recursion and Algorithm 1 and the proximal-gradient procedure analyzed in the proofs. Correcting both the weights and the inner proximal anchor substantially improves correctness and implementability. Proposition 6 also supplies an explicit guarantee for approximate scores. Its surrounding prose overstates convergence to a single point, but this qualification does not outweigh the central corrections and theoretical extension; empirical evidence remains unchanged.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work, with matching authors, objectives, numerical examples, and appendices A and B. Their complete text, equations, and figures support comparison, including the added appendix subsection in v3.

after.justification: Section 5 and Figure 2 retain the original Gaussian numerical experiment and its computed trajectories and convergence curves.

before.justification: Section 5 and Figure 2 report original numerical trajectories and convergence curves for gradient descent on an anisotropic two-dimensional Gaussian proximal problem.

results.title: MAP Estimation with Denoisers: Convergence Rates and Guarantees

C1.justification: The main claims about data reuse, compute crossover and downstream performance remain. However, v1's hypothesized augmentation explanation becomes an explicit finding and sixth introductory contribution in v7: exposure to diverse token orders is presented as explaining diffusion's sample efficiency.

C2.justification: v7 distinguishes token-order diversity from ordinary perturbation-based augmentation when interpreting the mechanism experiments. Figure 5 also newly warns that absolute extrapolated losses are not directly comparable because the fitted data-entropy terms differ. The earlier explanations of AR compute efficiency and limitations concerning hybrids and restricted data scales are largely retained.

D1.justification: New Section 12 and Algorithms 1–2 provide substantial reproducibility information for permutation training: Gaussian perturbation of position indices, a fixed ordering pool, per-sequence sampling, first-token anchoring, token/label alignment and position-ID handling. Evaluation ordering and omission of target positional embeddings are specified. Existing optimizer settings, architecture tables and the code-access URL are retained.

E1.justification: Both versions use English C4, the same nine downstream benchmarks, and OSCAR, TinyStories, WikiText and IndustryCorpus2 evaluations. The 500M-token experiment already appears in v1. The new augmentation experiments change training procedures without adding dataset, domain or evaluation-task coverage.

E2.justification: v7 Figures 7–8 substantially expand the evaluated comparison methods with attention-dropout AR, token-masked AR and AR trained with multiple fixed token orders. These comparators were absent from v1. RAR and sigma-GPT are newly cited for positioning, but are not separately benchmarked.

E3.justification: v7 adds a FLOP-matched AR evaluation alongside best-validation checkpoints in Table 2. New augmentation protocols use 140M-parameter AR models for 50 epochs and 278M-parameter models for 100 epochs, varying perturbation levels or the number of token orders. Permutation-trained models are evaluated left-to-right. The original scaling-sweep settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v1 offers an augmentation hypothesis without directly testing it. v7 Section 3.5 and Figures 7–8 test attention dropout, token masking and token-order diversity, finding benefits specifically from multiple orders. It also examines downstream performance of overfitted, compute-matched AR checkpoints, substantially extending the analysis of the original findings.

E5.justification: Neither version documents repeated-run counts, experimental seed values, defined confidence intervals or significance tests. The added checklist claims statistical support from varying dataset sizes and compute, but supplies no new uncertainty-estimation procedure. The generic seed argument in permutation pseudocode does not establish seed-based experimental reporting.

E6.justification: v7 adds a full FLOP-matched AR result column, including SciQ accuracy of 50.50% and PiQA accuracy of 61.64%. New plots show unsuccessful dropout/masking interventions and improved validation loss with multiple token orders. The original scaling-fit table, best-model downstream scores and cross-corpus likelihood results are retained; these additions are not same-setting improvements over v1 scores.

M1.justification: The principal architectures and masked-denoising procedure remain unchanged. v7 adds a permutation-augmented AR procedure using predefined orders sampled during training, with left-to-right evaluation. Its displayed diffusion objective also gains a 1/r weighting factor; the PDFs do not establish whether this reflects changed training or corrected documentation.

P1.justification: The document is substantially reorganized: related work, the retained discussion, limitations and hyperparameters move into the appendix, while a new mechanism-testing section enters the main narrative. Method explanations and terminology are revised, and dedicated permutation, broader-impact and checklist sections expand the appendix structure.

P2.justification: v7 adds two experimental figures and two algorithm displays. The original combined downstream table is restructured into a 100M-token table with a new comparator column and a separate 500M-token appendix table. Existing figures and tables are redistributed, and captions are revised. v1 Figure 7 survives as v7 Figure 9 rather than constituting new evidence.

R1.justification: v7 adds randomized autoregressive visual generation and sigma-GPT references, distinguishing its permutation experiment by the absence of target positional embeddings. It removes the Caron, RandAugment and masked-autoencoder citations accompanying v1's augmentation analogy. The broader positioning against single-epoch diffusion studies and data-constrained AR scaling remains unchanged.

T1.justification: v7 corrects the critical-compute equation's unit normalization: the log-fit intercept changes from -7.052 to -1.050 while the power exponent remains 2.174. It also revises the mathematical loss definition with 1/r weighting and states an ELBO/NLL-bound interpretation. The effective-data scaling framework remains intact, and no formal theorem or proof is added.

improvement.justification: v7 substantially strengthens two weak points in v1: downstream comparisons gain a compute-matched AR control, and the speculative augmentation explanation gains direct intervention experiments with reproducible procedures. Correcting the critical-compute equation's units also improves the usability of a central result. The stronger mechanism claim still exceeds what limited controls can conclusively establish, and uncertainty reporting remains inadequate, but these limitations do not outweigh the substantial gains in comparative evidence and clarity.

A1.justification: Both PDFs are complete, readable versions of the same study. Their text, equations, figures, tables and appendices support comparison, including matching material relocated in v7.

after.justification: v7 retains these original results and adds compute-matched AR evaluations and experiments on attention dropout, token masking and token-order permutations.

before.justification: v1 reports original AR and diffusion training experiments, empirical scaling-law fits, downstream accuracies and cross-corpus likelihood evaluations.

results.title: Diffusion Beats Autoregressive in Data-Constrained Settings

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the principal claims of coupling-based TC reduction, monotonicity and convergence, efficient few-step and one-step generation, and compatibility with distillation. These headline claims are not materially rewritten to reflect the theorem's newly explicit qualifications.

C2.justification: Beyond v1's brief error-propagation observation, v2 explains accumulating target-marginal mismatch, emphasizes its importance for text, and presents perturbation as a remedy. It newly discusses misleadingly low perplexity from repetition and interprets entropy as a diagnostic, while also explaining training-cost savings. Section 5's existing limitations remain.

D1.justification: v2 adds four pseudocode algorithms, the hybrid model's lambda=0 setting, and cost-accounting details. Text-training disclosures change from 56 A6000 GPU-hours to 12 H100 GPU-hours, alongside revised hyperparameters. v1's sampling-temperature, greedy-tail-denoiser, and LayerNorm-only fine-tuning details are no longer stated. The code-access URL is unchanged.

E1.justification: Both versions use ImageNet for class-conditional 256-by-256 image generation and OpenWebText for 1024-token text generation, with the same token representations. The added analyses remain within these datasets and tasks.

E2.justification: The corresponding generation comparisons retain MaskGIT, SDTT, and Di4C on ImageNet, and DUO+DCD and Di4C on OpenWebText, alongside the same ReDi variants and hybrid. Newly discussed Discrete Copula Diffusion and EDLM are not evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: Text perplexity evaluation changes from GPT-2-large to LLaMA 3.1-8B, and 1-gram entropy is added. Appendix B.2 revises text learning rates from 1e-5/1e-6 to 3e-4, batch size from 512 to 128, and warmup and training budgets. Table 2 adds a controlled perturbed-versus-standard rectification comparison; the main ImageNet protocol remains stable.

E4.justification: v2 adds the perturbed-rectification ablation, entropy-based repetition checks, training-cost comparisons, and detailed rectification and inference CFG analyses. Existing image TC, pair-count, and stochastic-initialization studies remain. However, v1's Appendix D and Figure 6 analysis of declining TC in text generation is removed rather than relocated.

E5.justification: Both versions report point estimates without independent training-run counts, seed reporting, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. v2 does not introduce uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: Figure 3's text perplexities and the ReDi text samples are replaced under revised training and evaluation conditions. New results include entropy, cost, and CFG measurements; Table 2 reports 1024-step perplexity of 24.13 with perturbation versus 44.17 without it. The earlier text-TC results disappear. ImageNet Table 1 remains numerically unchanged, including ReDi3-distill FID 11.68 and IS 182.

M1.justification: v2 introduces perturbed rectification for text generation: real target samples are corrupted at a random time, regenerated, and paired with their corrupted states for direct training. This changes coupling construction and training inputs relative to v1's source-to-target pairs, while retaining standard ReDi (Section 3.3 and Appendix C).

P1.justification: The abstract and selected introductory and explanatory paragraphs are edited, acknowledgments are expanded, and appendices gain a clearer subsection structure. Qualitative results move into Appendix D.5. The main section sequence and much of the retained exposition remain unchanged.

P2.justification: v2 adopts the NeurIPS layout, redraws Figure 3 as perplexity and entropy panels, adds Tables 2–9 and four algorithm blocks, and removes the earlier text-TC figure. Qualitative image grids are resized and restyled with colored method labels, while retaining their image samples; other figures and tables are relocated.

R1.justification: v2 substantially broadens positioning through comparisons with Discrete Copula Diffusion and EDLM and explicit connections to Schrödinger bridges and Iterative Markovian Fitting. Additional citations support perplexity limitations, the evaluator, and the revised KL proof. The earlier LayerNorm-tuning citation is removed.

T1.justification: Appendix A replaces the data-processing proof with an M-step decoding definition, log-convex-hull and KL-minimization assumptions, and a Pythagorean KL argument. The main theorem becomes explicitly informal and assumption-dependent, with a qualified formal statement in the appendix. This substantially revises the guarantee's mathematical basis and scope.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses important weaknesses in v1: the central guarantee gains explicit assumptions and a revised derivation, and quantitative text evaluation gains an entropy diagnostic alongside perplexity. The controlled perturbation ablation and detailed results make the text method substantially better supported and more transparent. These gains outweigh the removed text-TC analysis, although unqualified headline guarantees and Algorithm 4's inconsistent x0 input despite sampling xt remain.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe ReDi and provide readable main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices. Their retained and revised material can be reliably matched despite substantial changes to the text-generation experiments and theoretical analysis.

after.justification: v2 retains original image-generation results and reports revised text-generation results, entropy measurements, a perturbed-rectification ablation, and additional guidance and training-cost analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original ImageNet and OpenWebText generation results, ablations, and empirical conditional total-correlation measurements for images and text.

results.title: ReDi: Rectified Discrete Flow

C1.justification: The central claims about resilient unlearning, efficient hypergradient estimation, and preserved benign utility remain. The introduction's third contribution drops the claim of effectiveness across multiple unsafe concepts and instead explicitly claims generalization across loss functions. This is a limited revision of the claimed scope.

C2.justification: New discussions explain approximation choices, configuration diversity, and differences between instance-level and concept-level unlearning. Section 5 and Appendix E.5 acknowledge over-rejection and visually disturbing artifacts, explaining the safety-versus-output-quality tradeoff of alternative losses. Appendix A also newly qualifies that a small Hessian trace does not guarantee low curvature in every direction; the earlier general limitations are largely retained.

D1.justification: New Appendix B supplies checkpoint identities, implementation-script references, dataset construction and subset sizes, prompt processing, overlap checks, optimizer and module choices, and additional resource details. v2 also announces and links public code and pretrained models, whose availability cannot be verified from the PDFs alone. These disclosures substantially expand reproducibility information, although v1's explicit default alpha and beta values are no longer provided.

E1.justification: The original benchmark coverage is retained, while Appendix C.1 documents additional adversarial-prompt and staged relearning scenarios, including SneakyPrompt, MMA-Diffusion, UnlearnDiffAtk, and a curriculum using CelebA-HQ. The stated simulation-data coverage also expands from DiffusionDB alone to a pool incorporating NSFW-56k and harmful training prompts. These broaden the input and adaptation conditions beyond the experiments reported in v1.

E2.justification: v2 adds evaluated comparisons with IMMA and Meta-Unlearning in Table 8 and RACE, RECE, and Receler in Table 12. These were not evaluated comparators in v1, even where their papers were already cited. The original Table 1 comparator set remains, while Figure 1 switches its illustrated LCFDSD variant from NG to LT.

E3.justification: v2 replaces the reported fixed 120-step training schedule with training until convergence and states that unstable configuration combinations are excluded. New evaluations introduce additional diffusion-model configurations, black-box ASR-3 and white-box ASR protocols, and a four-stage relearning schedule. The default downstream 200-step, batch-size-one evaluation remains; the revised training descriptions do not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained component, contamination, and gamma analyses, v2 adds adversarial and adaptive attacks, configuration-count and beta sensitivity, cross-algorithm meta-learning ablations, and a gamma analysis on DiffusionDB. It also examines alternative unlearning losses, hypergradient approximations, computational efficiency, and rejection artifacts. These substantially expand the questions tested about robustness, mechanisms, and tradeoffs.

E5.justification: Both versions report three independent runs, and uncertainty bands already appear in v1. v2 newly identifies the bands as standard errors of the mean and discloses averaging across three selected artistic genres or facial identities in personalization evaluations. No increase in repeated-run counts is established.

E6.justification: Several retained Table 2 values change: ResAlign's Unsafe Score changes from 0.0260 to 0.0000 for DreamBooth+Dog, from 0.0322 to 0.0033 for LoRA+Pokemon, and from 0.0083 to 0.0033 for SVDiff+VGGFace2-HQ. New tables additionally report model-transfer, comparator, attack, sensitivity, and efficiency outcomes. These are revised and newly reported results, rather than demonstrated same-setting gains between versions.

M1.justification: The core objective, implicit-gradient framework, and meta-learning algorithm remain. However, Equation (7) and Algorithm 1 change the Richardson update from b minus Hx/gamma to gamma*b minus gamma*Hx. This changes the stated procedure for non-default gamma values, while remaining equivalent at the shared default gamma = 1.

P1.justification: v2 adds a standalone main-text Discussion and extensive explanatory appendices organized around settings, additional results, related work, and interpretation. The former short discussion appendix is incorporated into this broader structure, and the ethics statement moves from the main text to Appendix E.7. Acknowledgments and a NeurIPS checklist are added, while much of the original method exposition receives only limited polishing.

P2.justification: v2 adds substantial table displays for model transfer, additional comparators, alternative losses, attacks, sensitivity, and efficiency, plus new progressive-relearning and gamma plots and an artifact montage. Figure 1 replaces its example images and one comparator label. Existing learning-rate, optimizer, and component tables are retained under new numbers; those renumberings alone are not new evidence.

R1.justification: New Appendix D substantially expands positioning relative to flat-minima optimization, Hessian-trace estimation, approximate implicit differentiation, iMAML, and defenses against harmful fine-tuning of language models. It adds literature such as Entropy-SGD, hypergradient-complexity work, and Booster, while developing more specific distinctions from already-cited methods. Several earlier perturbation and fine-tuning references are removed.

T1.justification: v2 corrects the gamma scaling in the Richardson recurrence and explicitly identifies its relaxation parameter, repairing the stated relationship to the linear system in Equation (6). Proposition 1 and the implicit-differentiation and Taylor-expansion proofs in Appendix A remain substantively unchanged.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially closes evidence gaps: claims about multiple diffusion models and adaptive attacks that appeared in v1 now have explicit evaluations in Table 5 and Appendix C.1. More relevant comparator tests, detailed implementation disclosures, and substantive qualifications about flatness and rejection artifacts make the paper more assessable and better supported. Unexplained Table 2 revisions and omitted default alpha/beta values limit auditability, but these drawbacks do not outweigh the substantial gains in evidence and transparency.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ResAlign research, with matching objectives, algorithms, and core experiments. Text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support comparison despite substantial additions in v2.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and reports additional model evaluations, baseline comparisons, attack tests, sensitivity analyses, and computational measurements.

before.justification: v1 reports original safety and generation-quality experiments, personalization evaluations, contamination tests, and component ablations in Section 4.

results.title: Towards Resilient Safety-driven Unlearning for Diffusion Models against Downstream Fine-tuning

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same claimed first general test-time scaling framework for VAR, its stage-specific diversity/selection contributions, and the 0.69-to-0.75 GenEval improvement. Explicitly naming Infinity-2B in the abstract clarifies the existing result rather than changing the contribution.

C2.justification: v2 interprets the diversity measurements as showing little diversity sacrifice and the Infinity-8B results as supporting transferability. New Appendix I discusses architectural tradeoffs, hypothesizes that diffusion denoising enlarges the search space, and declines to identify a superior architecture. The original spatial-alignment and untested-model limitations remain.

D1.justification: New Appendix B documents the first PCA component, model-specific resolutions and batch schedules, and reliance on Infinity's public defaults. Appendix G.2 identifies A800-SXM4-80GB hardware and memory-driven inference handling. These are useful implementation disclosures; the algorithm pseudocode and code-access information remain unchanged.

E1.justification: v2 adds DPG-Bench evaluation in Appendix D and human assessment of 15 image groups in Section 5.3. These extend benchmark and human-evaluation coverage within text-to-image generation; GenEval and T2I-CompBench remain. Infinity-8B itself changes model configuration rather than task coverage.

E2.justification: The original GenEval and T2I-CompBench comparator sets remain. The new DPG-Bench comparison includes HART and PixArt-Sigma, neither previously evaluated in the paper. Table 14 also introduces random dropping as a clustering control. Infinity-8B comparisons reuse raw inference, IS, and BoN.

E3.justification: New protocols include Infinity-8B at 512 pixels with a ten-scale schedule, randomized image ordering in a study yielding 21 questionnaires and 315 selections per criterion, four-image-per-prompt DPG evaluation, CLIP-Div measurement, and timing/peak-memory evaluation. Appendix G.2 excludes image decoding from timing and uses two inference passes for BoN at N=8. These additions do not establish changes to the retained Infinity-2B experiments.

E4.justification: v2 adds output-diversity analysis, component-level runtime and memory analysis, and clustering versus random dropping while retaining resampling (Tables 10, 12, and 14). It extends temperature sensitivity to lambda=50 and 100 and adds fixed-batch-size 2 and 4 profiles in Figure 2. The earlier scale, potential, extractor, reward-model, and pipeline ablations remain.

E5.justification: v1 does not specify seeds. v2 Appendix B discloses seeds 0–3 and GPU-process seed offsets; Appendix D specifies four DPG images using seeds 0–3. This is newly documented seed information, not evidence of increased repeated runs. Confidence intervals, error bars, and formal significance tests remain absent.

E6.justification: The original numerical tables are retained, while substantial results are added. Infinity-8B reaches 0.8188 GenEval in Table 1 versus 0.7646 raw and 0.7995 BoN at N=4; Appendix Table 8 inconsistently prints 0.8189. DPG-Bench reports 82.94 for TTS-VAR versus 82.52 BoN and 81.72 raw Infinity. New tables report human votes, diversity, runtime/memory, and further ablations; Figure 2 revises memory profiles. These extend results rather than demonstrate improved scores for the original runs.

M1.justification: Section 4 and Algorithm 1 retain adaptive descending batches, early DINOv2/K-Means++ clustering, and late potential-based resampling. The additional implementation disclosures and Infinity-8B configuration introduce no new algorithmic component or selection procedure.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main narrative remain. v2 inserts a user-study subsection, settings and analysis appendices, acknowledgements, and a NeurIPS conference footer, with local wording and terminology edits. The accompanying renumbering and additions do not constitute a wholesale rewrite.

P2.justification: v2 substantially expands the tabular presentation with dedicated human-study, Infinity-8B, DPG-Bench, diversity, runtime/memory, and clustering-control tables. It expands Table 1 and the temperature table. Figure 2 is redrawn with additional curves, TFLOPs units, and one-based scale labels; several retained figures and tables are resized or relocated.

R1.justification: v2 adds citations to DreamVideo, MeshXL, discriminative codebook priors, and VARGPT-v1.1, while removing the CLIP-latent generation paper, Wan, FreeScale, and a foundation-model reasoning survey. Appendix I adds qualified positioning against diffusion scaling. The principal novelty claim and related-work organization remain.

T1.justification: Section 3 introduces a non-equivalent indexing error: Equation 1 changes the summand from up(r_i) to up(r_k) while still summing over i. Its accompanying text also changes accumulation over the first k residuals to all K residuals. The unchanged algorithm indicates a formal-description error rather than a new method. No theorem or proof is added.

improvement.justification: v1 lacked direct output-diversity measurements, human preference evidence, and a clustering-versus-random-dropping control with resampling retained. v2 adds these targeted tests, substantially strengthening support for its central diversity and selection claims, alongside broader model evaluation and practical resource measurements. The small user study, timing exclusion of decoding, and absent uncertainty estimates limit the gains; the new Equation 1 indexing error also reduces precision. These shortcomings do not outweigh the substantially stronger experimental validation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same TTS-VAR work. Their main text, appendices, equations, tables, and figures are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching relocated and renumbered content.

after.justification: v2 retains those experiments and adds Infinity-8B, DPG-Bench, human preference, diversity, computational-cost, and ablation results.

before.justification: v1 reports original Infinity-2B experiments on GenEval and T2I-CompBench, computational analyses, and component ablations.

results.title: TTS-VAR: A Test-Time Scaling Framework for Visual Auto-Regressive Generation

C1.justification: The abstract, listed contributions and conclusion retain their principal claims about RL, complex-edit training and unsuccessful CoT supervision. Section 3 adds an explicit priority claim that EARL is the first RL post-training approach for autoregressive image editing, modestly strengthening novelty positioning.

C2.justification: v3 adds interpretations attributing gains beyond candidate selection to policy optimization, emphasizing verifier strength, and distinguishing improved edit success from largely preserved perceptual quality. It also discusses training and inference efficiency tradeoffs. Earlier explanations of complex-edit and CoT difficulties, and the substantive limitations, remain.

D1.justification: Appendix F newly documents vLLM-based EARL decoding, training durations and efficiency-measurement resources. Existing hyperparameters, prompt templates and release information are retained.
